It seems like a good idea, but it's not. It takes the aspects of top-down shooters and roguelikes and presents the worst aspects of both. Roguelikes are dependent on the ability to at least pause (or not make a move) and think about your actions. Top downs is all abou ttwitch. Top downs are all about using your toys pretty much all at once, roguelikes are about tactics. Cryptark just doesn't make it work. The game sets you behind the eight ball from the get go on the difficulty and it always gets harder. There are no real classees to play with at first. So you're stuck until you "get gud", but there's no promise you will because the game punishes you on nearly every choice.
You have a limited bank with which to outfit your suit and go a salvaging, but the game often doesn't give you enough money in jobs to cover what it presented as the tutorial loadout. Combine that with the fact that many of the additional money challenges means hampering yourself deliberately.
So you're faced with the idea that you can either bleed money the whole time, or try and build up a reserve (a very roguelike strategy), but if you do you'll probably hemorrage money in deaths, because the game is about as balanced as an elephant on a seesaw.
It is not common for there to be a good twenty enemies on screen even when you have no choice of weapons. So you can very easily be swarmed through the level one hulks until you dip into the red. However, you can take the easy ships and go into the red slower.
It's a game that doesn't quite bring together everything it wants to do. If it had been one long dungeon that would have been something, but it's not. It forces you to basically play the worst parts of roguelikes and top-down shooters: The beginning when you have nothing. That's basically every mission because even if you get all these nice toys, you can't pay to use them.

I'm on the fence for Early Access games. Usually, I try to be patient until the game actually releases to play it. You get to build your own airship piece by piece and then fly it around.  If that sounds good to you then you should get this game.
Other good things:
-The materials you make your ship out of determine its durability and maneuverability.
-There is a story and an endgame, but you can keep playing after you've finished it.
-The materials you make your equipment out of affect the stats of the items.
-The grappling hook is fun.
-The late-game gas makes for some tense exploration moments when you have to get out of your ship.
-Increasing your stats gives you very useful perks.
-You have one chest of infinite holding and can place access points to it anywhere which makes item storage very simple.  Some may view this as a negative.
-Ramming other ships is super fun.
Bad things:
-The controls take some getting used to.  Everything has some weird kind of intertia to it, plus every ship I made had a tendency to drift.
-The view makes building a pain.  Foreground blocks can obscure the view of background blocks that they are not actually covering which makes it difficult to tell if your ship is airtight.
-There is only one method of fast travel and it is not very useful.  You will spend a lot of time just flying from one location to another.
-Building a stationary base is pointless.  The lack of fast travel means you would spend even more time just travelling to and from the base.  The power system in the game doesn't really update properly in a stationary base so it is hard to get power to devices without using a lot of generators.  It's even harder to get a stationary base airtight partly due to the view but also because you can't tell if the generated background blocks are blocking gas or not.  The item chest makes it so you don't need an area to store items.  I understand the point of the game is to build flying bases but some people would probably like to have a stationary one as well.
-Monster spawning can drive you nuts.  When a kraken spawns right beside you while you're looting a ship and you don't notice it until it has rammed a hole right through your ship and then you kill the kraken and just finish repairing your ship when another spawns right beside you and does the same thing.
I played through the game twice to get all of the achievements and enjoyed both playthroughs.

I have never had a smile on my face for so long as I've played a game in SUCH a long time. The short version of this review is: if you have any love for Genesis, classic Sonic, tough-as-nails platformers, flashy platformers, or just going fast and looking cool, buy this game. Now. THIS is how you remake/revive a series. THIS should have been Sonic 4.
Sonic 3 and Knuckles for the PC was the first game I ever owned, so it holds a very special place in my heart. For literally decades I have been disappointed with the releases in this series. The only games that came close to warming my heart were Sonic Rush and Generations.
But while Generations dances with nostalgia, Mania embraces it, treats it to dinner, drinks with it til 2 in the morning, and then wakes up next to it and gives it a kiss and tells it it wants to be with it forever. This game is fanservice porn. It truly understand what made the classic games special, and then jumps several stories higher, running with those ideas in ways that are unexpected, charming, and beautiful. The tributes and in-jokes to the previous games don't feel like petty, corporate pandering. A lot of work and love went into digging into the prior Sonic games and it seems like at every turn, the development team was asking "Okay, but how can we make this better?"
And they succeeded... in spades. The game plays magnificently. It plays like my childhood memories of Sonic games play in my head, which is INCREDIBLY difficult to do. The new systems do not detract from the feel of the game, and the inclusion of the ability to switch between the new movement engine and the older games is just so brilliant. Special stages feel fun. I have never been so damn excited to collect blue balls. All the bonus stuff unlocks at a great pace and makes me want to come back to see what's next. The bosses may legitimately be the best bosses I have ever seen in a platformer for a variety of reasons that I don't want to say here so I don't spoil. But, let's just say there's one boss that had me ecstatic due to a ♥♥♥♥ing brilliant twist. If I had to describe Mania's gameplay in a phrase, it'd be: unexpected, joyous twists.
The graphics are just eye candy in the best possible meaning of that work. All of the main characters have been given a fresh coat of paint. The environments are colorful, bright, and juicy. The new zones fit perfectly in the style of the old zones. This honestly feels like it could have been another lock on pack for Sonic 3.
The sounds are perfect. All the classic music has been remade, but given a modern flair. And yet... the remixes feel perfectly at home. As though they were off some secret Sega soundtrack CD that was hiding in a box somewhere. The new music is fresh, funky, and hits the feel of the original games.
This might be my game of the year. It's certainly the best remake/revival of a series I've EVER seen. And it really just makes me happy to play it. I'll be honest: as I've grown up, I've had the fear that I've lost that childlike wonder of games. That games were just losing their charm and I couldn't enjoy them in the same way I was when I was a kid. Sonic Mania showed me that's definitely not the case. I've had the biggest, stupidest grin on my face the whole time I've been playing it, and it's the first game in a long time where I've wanted to come home from work every day and play it like I did coming home from school with S3&K. It lived up to and surpassed all my expectations.
Hats off to Sega, Sonic Team, and the brilliant new developers they've found and hired. You ♥♥♥♥ing rocked this game.

What can I say about this game?
Well... it's a fun board game that combines aspects from games like Mario Party, Fortune Steeet and Dokapon Kingdom, and mixes it with characters from the Orange_Juice games, plus some original characters created for this game.
In Single Player, when trying to unlock every character through the campaign (the ones that come with the game by default, not the DLC ones), you're going to be at the mercy of the RNG over and over and over that sometimes you'll curse yourself, but still... Sometimes you win and sometimes you lose. It's the way of the RNG after all. Believe me, trying to unlock a certain character is a living pain.
: Don't choose QP as your first character.
In Multiplayer, that's when the fun really starts. You will have lots of fun playing with others. You will laugh at the situations that occur during the game, you'll feel pain because the RNG didn't like you, you'll cry because maybe you have lost so many games, and who knows? Maybe it will cause some discussions between players regarding your decisions, but that's where the magic of the game really is: The interactions between the players and how everything folds during your games.
About the other regards, the graphics are simplistic, but it accomplishes what it's intended. The character's designs are really cute. Special mention to Marie Poppo, the cutest of them all IMHO. The music? It's good for what it is. Catchy music all around, but if you don't like it, you can always mute the music and put other songs on your music player. Really, the gameplay is where the game really shines.
And also, buy the DLCs, it adds more content to the game, more characters to the mix and more variety in your strategies with more cards.
Do I recommend it? Of course, but keep in mind that if you don't like the anime-ish designs and don't like the RNG nature of this game, maybe you should stay back from this, regardless, give the demo a check and if you like it, buy it.

A serious throwback to the 90s JRPGs of yesteryear.
My only gripe with the game so far is melee combat. This stems from the cell-based structure of the game's aesthetic, so aiming with melee can be somewhat tedius. If you're not directly in front of your enemy, you won't land a single blow. Combine this with the bizzarre knockback you get everytime you bump into an enemy, and melee rapidly loses its appeal.
The music and the design of the game, however, really shine. It's a heartfelt nod to all of your favorite 8/16/32bit JRPGs from the SNES/PSX and earlier gaming years. Fans of titles like Chrono Trigger will feel very comfortable here in the world of Azuria.
For 5$, you most certainly get your moneys worth. There's a lot offered to keep you preoccupied: crafting, creature farming, house building (you can even plant decorative and functional flora as well) and spell crafting. Spell crafting is a very nice addition, because you can essentially craft any ability from a profession and use it regardless of what masteries you decide to pursue. So, if you're a lvl 9 billion Wizard of Icy Death, you can still pull out a rusty dagger and backstab foes if you're playstyle you chose begins to bore you.
The game's charm is highly understated and it becomes evident the longer you play, slowly getting sucked in by its vintage-game copycatism. It takes modern elements of the sandbox genre and does a very good job at blending it with the old school.
For 5$, you should definitely add this title to your library if you're any sort of RPG fan.

Gotham City impostors is an overlooked gem of the FPS genre. With customization and improvisational strategy light years beyond TF2, it competes in the same space as Valve's champion WITHOUT a shred of developer support. That's right, this game is "Dead," in the sense kids who wonder what DSL was use the word about games. Every week, NO patch appears to incrementally increase the power of the loudest forum whiners. NO new cosmetic packages are released at $2.99 a pop. No season pass is up for sale, followed by DLC that is not included in it. In point of fact what Monolith did by "abandoning" GCI when it went F2P was give us the best of both worlds: A game that has neither a price tag nor active marketing/Pay to win tendencies. I wish more developers would abandon their games!
As to the actual gameplay, it's stellar in all the ways that are underrated today. The key thing is the custom loadouts: Any weapons, gadgets, support items, body types, and perks, can be combined. Any strategy can be supported. What pre-defined classes there are are totally optional and practically unused, as players are allowed to develop their own methods and build an improvisational, customized playstyle and support it fully with their gear. This would be like allowing the scout to carry the heavy's minigun in tf2, only it slows him down when it's equipped. Want to combine a sniper rifle with a shotgun and bear traps to defend your nest? No problem. Rather back your sniping up with a machine gun and some motion sensors? Equally good. Want to build your strategy around grappling above players' heads and then dropping your massive weight on them? Try it, let us know how it goes. Whatever you want to attempt is up to you.
The result has been a little bit of a vidication for me; people sometimes argue that balance in a pvp game can only be maintained by constant, active adjustment in the form of buffing and nerfing by patch. Well, GCI has had none of that, and yet the complaints about OP builds (such complaining is immortal and without limit) have largely migrated from one build to another another. No strategy is singularly overpowered; you can get in a GCI forum and listen to guys shout about how ten different things are completely broken and overpowered. CK2 is a great strategy game.Handling your dynasty and/or your kingdom/duchy over hundreds of years.
The game has a rather steep learning curve if you're not familiar with Paradox Games.
At times, info and the impact of your decisions are a bit difficult to anticipate. Notably, when you get into tricky succession (ie : usually, when you're about to lose a lot to someone out of your dynasty), it's difficult at first to determine how you can prevent it, even if you can prevent it... or who is going to inherit if your change your law.
Succession, being a big part of the game, could be better handled with better interface display. It's better to manage once you get a sense of the succession laws and you handle your dynasty carefully (you have less tricky situations).
War and battles is handled at a basic level. You move your armies, you watch it fighting. You move your army to a county, you watch your troop besieging each castle and town.
Your action on the battles themselves is limited to chosing the leaders at the center or the wings. Pick the good leaders, pay attention to their troops and the leader's traits.
The game has a snowball effects during wars when, facing a relatively equal enemy, the first battles are often decisive. Once you start winning, the opposition becomes weaker and weaker, so you win constantly and so on.
And then, with the practice, you'll be able to manage your kingdom better and better from the start. Leading often to mid-game where you can dominate all your neighbors easily, if not half Europe (or more, depends who you play).
The consequence is the end of the game is really easy.
Now, it's not an easy game from the first session you play. It becomes easier the better you are at it. Not a big surprise.
But for some players, the game may show its limits
CK2 is still a satisfying game. Replayability lies much more into the many starts you can have. You have all the european dynsaties, minor lords and all, to toy with. Play pagans, christians fighting to defend Iberia, irishmen, try to rebuild the roman empire, play a count and work up to king or emperor, play various counties, duchies, kingdoms, empires, play various cultures, religions. You can play match-making in your court and weave dynastic succession, or conquer everything by the sword and hopefully still hold it after the conqueror death.
The game replayability lies in its very sandboxy aspect.
Now the DLCs.. It's a difficult topic. Some of them are offering a real value, some others are cosmetic.
Pay attention to player feedback about "content DLCs". The more recent DLC have a debatable value in terms of content, relative to their price, or relative to what the game will become.
CK2 is a great game and deserve to become a classic of strategy games. It's going to keep you satisfyingly busy during many many hours.

I was expecting this game to be nothing more than a shody mobile port and a cash-grab attempt by Microsoft using their most successful game franchise to appeal to casual gamers and nickel & dime them with microtransactions. However, it appears that this is not the case; for the Steam version of the game anyway. The game is underpriced if anything - at £3.99 it's the cheapest version fo the game, yet also the best. A good achievement list, weekly challenges, level-specific challenges and a sizeable number of levels along with leaderboards and a score system provide lots of replay value. So what about the game itself? Well, it's surprisingly solid as a stand-alone PC game. The controls work perfectly, visuals aren't far different to the mobile version but still a decent looking game, framerate is smooth and never dips, nice soundtrack too. You could never tell that the game was a "port" from touchscreen devices. The gameplay is actually very much like other Halo games. Sure, it's top down but the core elements of level design, enemies, weapons etc. are all very similar. Even the sounds and animations are directly copy-pasted. The result is a highly robust top-down shooter which appeals to almost anyone (unless you have an intense hatred for the Halo universe). The scoring system is perfectly designed; rewarding fast, skillful play. Overall, Spartan Assault faithfully replicates the Halo universe in a top-down environment and is a shining example of how to make a game which works just as well on a smartphone as it does on a mouse and keyboard or controller.

Sonic Mania is a joy. While many like to forget Sonic Generations and Colors happened, Sonic Mania is a return to form we haven't seen since the Advance games.
HOWEVER.
Denuvo. Up front, this has to be noted. As of writing, the game CANNOT be played offline. (EDIT: THIS HAS BEEN PATCHED. Sega's post on it here:
)
I would ask that Sega find another anti-piracy method. Not all of us have stable, constant internet connections. Not all of us want Denuvo on our systems (I doubt anyone does, really). In some cases, Denuvo has even been reported to slow down videogames, which makes the PC port, which is usually the objectively best running and looking version is, now the objectively worst version to have. I don't want to spend too much time harping on this but DRM usually doesn't prevent piracy, it only delays the inevitable, whilst worsening the User Experience of paying customers.
Onto the game itself;
It's great. The drop dash is a revelation. Christian Whitehead, Simon Thomley along with the rest of Headcanon and Pagoda West should all receive a standing ovation. Sonic Mania is good, it's well priced, it is a game very much worth your time. I'd encourage fans new to the series to first try out Sonic 1 on Android and iOS. It's free thanks to Sega's new Sega Forever promotion, and is a perfect introduction to the series; After all, this game sells you on nostalgia. But it's not just that,
For starters, the levels are all about twice as large as the Genesis levels. Act 1 will usually comprise of a remake of both acts of the Genesis counterpart, and Act 2 will put a big gigantic spin on the entire level with new gimmicks. If you were worried about rehashes, the crisp frame rate, new moves, elemental shields and placement of Special Stage rings change things up *just enough* to make an old stage feel fresh again, before Act 2 basically turns everything on its head. Even assests are brand new, such as with Green Hill Zone Act 2 looking more like the underground section in it's Generations counterpart.
However, it's the new content that stands out. Bossfights are fresh. So, sooo fresh. Chemical Plant has a super special surprise for longtime fans. The new zones also show off what a capable dev team can do. I won't spoil anything, but these are a real joy to play through. That feeling you had as a kid picking up Sonic for the first time is back, and a whole new generation of players get to feel that.
I do have a few complaints. One is that Tails and Knuckles don't get any fresh new moves. The Drop Dash replaces the insta-shield for Sonic (SPINDASHING IN MID-AIR WHY ON GOD'S GREEN HILL ZONE HAVE WE NOT THOUGHT OF THIS EARLIER) but Tails and Knuckles are almost unchanged, apart from crisp, crisp animations and sprites. Which isn't bad, but does feel like a missed opportunity. Knuckles' punch and Tails' tail spin was just enough in Sonic Advance to change up the gameplay, and whilst seeing a near perfect recreation of their Genesis playstyles is thrilling, their movesets now feel limited and less diverse, since Sonic's Drop Dash is so versatile. I mean this thing can help you scale everything but vertical walls. Some persistent problems reccur, such as bottomless pits in unfair places which can sometimes be really tough to avoid if you don't have a perfect grasp of Sonic's physics; Flying Battery Zone ate 9 of my lives because I ended up at the bottom of the stage and the wind mechanic kept rocketing me towards a pit. It soured my experience a little, and I kind of hoped the combination of the superfans making Sonic Mania would know not to let any of DIMPS' level design sneak into this masterpiece. Getting crushed because Sonic shoved a pixel into a solid object also occurs. And Sonic is slower underwater than he has ever been... Well, he accellerates slower, you can still reach stupidly fast speeds if you know what you're doing. The long zones also work against Sonic Mania, since when you Game Over, being sent to the beginning of a Zone can be extra punishing. Halfway through I was also sick of Blue Sphere stages, and once or twice I took a hit that knocked me right into them. Jumping into a Special or Bonus stage should be a much more deliberate thing, and it wastes time going into and out of Blue Sphere. And trust me, you're going to get sick of Blue Sphere. There's a limit to the fun you can have making increasingly faster 90 degree turns.  Also, there's this little known quirk about Sonic's physics, but if he is running on the ceiling, you have to hold right to go left, and left to go right. I know this because of countless hours of Sonic Advance 2. A lot of people don't. It's never explained, and when I started playing I'd actually forgotten about it until Flying Battery Zone which has a segment THAT WILL KILL YOU IF YOU DON'T KNOW THIS. You might never encounter this segment but it is necessary. It doesn't take a rocket scientist to figure out but it's super counterintuitive. I don't think it should be changed but it should definitely be explained a little better, along with other beginner's traps. Also, while lives and game overs are a cute throwback, ALL THE WAY AT THE BEGINNING OF ACT 1 is just tedious. Oil Ocean Act 1 can eat fist nipples. So can Oil Ocean act 2. And the boss. A lot of these stages become less cute if I'm forced to replay them.
But most of these are just my personal nitpicks.
Tee Lopes murders this soundtrack then necromances it. The music in the game is incredible, my God, perfect OSTs do exist. People always say that the best part of Sonic games is the music, and I can't speak for everyone but I'm finding it really hard to find anything to dislike. Fresh, crisp, and just a joy to play.
I'd still recommend the game but Denuvo needs to go. It has hampered otherwise great experiences and will prevent a great game from selling as many copies as it can. At the time of writing preordered copies also cannot be refunded, and if you want to lose good will, Sega, this is how you do it.
I think however that it's a testament to just how good this game is that I still recommend it despite the issues I've already mentioned. It really is *that* good. Play this game. But harp on about Denuvo, since it is a damn shame to have to round off such a glowing review on such a negative note.

The level design has defenitely improved since the game's ancestors, giving the feeling that the game is ENCOURAGING you to be fast, very seldom were there moments where you had to wait to proceed in a level, whereas in the earlier games, there were too many moments of waiting, in a game that specifically centers around SPEED (I really hated Sandopolis).
One of the things I noticed right away was that the music was redone to give help the game thrive in the modern world, with classics such as Greenhill Zone, Hydrocity, Lava Reef, etc. getting revamped and making the level feel more alive, and the new levels made me ecstatic, seeing that the levels could've only gotten better as time went on. What made me happy the most about the levels, was that in most cases, applying mainly to the classics, they retained some of the original level structure, like the beginning of Greenhill Zone, Chemical Plant, and Hydrocity. But when you get into the 2nd zone of each stage (now applying to all) new mechanics were introduced, and the level you knew before had been completely remodified, adding in new objects that would make the level more "it". Example, in the second stage of Titanic Monarch, there was now teleportation and the old gravity orbs (taken from one of the special stages in S3&K). Stuff like that made me happy.
Real quick though, whoever remade/produced the music, give them a promotion or raise or something. Let them not go uncommended.
All in all, the game lived up to the expectations we held, those of us who are hardcore 2D platformers and remember the good ol' Sonic, or those of us who have never given Sonic a chance until now. I seriously think that 2017 will be Sonic's comeback, if motivation for game producing does not falter.
P.S. No seriously, give the music producer a raise. I'm not kidding.

I'm not going to talk about DRM in this review, simply because there are so many other reviews which touch on it already. In case you don't know already, you CAN play it offline now, it's been patched. Okay, now on to the actual review...
At first glance Sonic Mania seems like just a rehash with some light extras thrown in. This is mainly because the trailers show off zones from past games but there's a difference in remakes/reimaginings and rehashes. You revisit some classic zones but they're completely different. However, there are plenty of original zones as well. So it's a well balanced 50/50 split. I'm happy to say that there are plenty of surprises in the game which explains why the trailers didn't show much of anything new or exciting.
There are 3 playable characters: Sonic, Tails and Knuckles. Each one with different abilities to make them fun to play as. And the controls feel responsive and spectacular. Make sure your pc/laptop/tablet is able to handle the game or you will get input lag or the game will not run optimally.
What impresses me most are the levels and the way they work in Sonic Mania, without spoiling anything I'll just say that every act not only has their own boss but also interactivity which makes them stand apart from one another. This is great to see as it makes each act more fun and lively than possible in the 90's. For example, balloons now have 3D physics which make it so that you can bounce off the surface of the balloon in virtually any direction.
The graphics are true to the originals but the color pallette has slightly been expanded. Lighting an shadowing effects has been implemented to take these pixels to the next level. The sound is exactly what you'd expect, it's just as diverse as Sonic Generations music. There's everything from classic music to heavy metal guitar riffs. It's a celebration of 25 years in the sound department.
Game length? The game takes the average user five to six hours to beat. While that may seem short, keep in mind that this is a very VERY fast-paced platformer game. What does this mean? This simply means that some of the acts are huge... REALLY huge. I have spent close to eight minutes in a single act trying to go as fast as I can. Some of the levels are not only huge but have so many intricate pathways and secrets.
Lastly I will talk about the replay value. There is plenty. Not only do you get different experiences with playing as all 3 characters but there is the collection of the seven emeralds and the bonus stages which earn you silver coins to unlock special things on the main menu. I'm not sure what secrets things await fans because I only have 3 silver coins at the moment which is hardly enough to unlock anything.
I highly recommend this to the hardcore Sonic fan. If you don't get this on pc, then get it on console. It's fun, colorful, it will make you happy when you play it and again, they fixed the offline bug.
Thank you for reading!

Cryptark is a game in the roguelike/roguelike genre with an overarching campaign option (randomly generated). There are other gameplay modes as well ("rogue", co-op for sure), but I've stuck with this one because it's so amazing. The essence of the game is that you are a space privateer earning money for space megacorps by looting a series of derelict spacecraft: essentially, by deactivating the core processor (a giant brain) to render the other defense systems harmless for later "acquisition." The style and atmosphere are great — edgy through the atmosphere, which is not overly dark thanks to a colorful semi-cartoon style and necro-but-entirely-non-human enemies.
But CRYPTARK captures some of the best of tactical incursion gameplay that reminded me of the original Metal Gear...Depending on the ship, that core CPU will probably be defended by a shield system which will have to go first, and perhaps by an alarm system as well, a non-essential but attractive option unless you REALLY like bullet-hell gameplay. Other possible systems include modules that manufacture security drones, central controls for door locks, and nasty ones like repair systems and the one that switches modules every 60 seconds. Medi/ammo stations are located as well and might well be needed. To properly give this one a go, everything is important, from choosing an entry point to double-checking the ship layout before going in. It's really cool. The ships are filled with a variety of "AI" or security robots of varying playstyles and degrees of nastiness, alongside mines, alarm triggers, space wreckage, and mini-game challenges that work. The player pilots the first of several exosuit types (the rest are unlockable through a cool design choice) armed with a basic set of weapons/power-ups that is boosted by randomly available tech upgrades scattered through the derelicts, adding yet another interesting choice to each mission.
The "strategic" layer is streamlined, with players choosing armament (including ammo amounts, hull points, etc.) and selecting one of several available ships for each stage before moving up the ladder towards the CRYPTARK, the mother ship of the derelict fleet. This part of the game adds welcome structure/breathing space to the missions themselves, which then take on strategic importance in return. Resource management is key to success here, as is the ability to, well, make the lesser of excrutiatingly painful choices.
I don't normally wax eloquent for reviews here, and no free copies floated around for this review. But CRYPTARK justifies the nerdiness here. For one, I love the strategic layer/tacical layer dichotomy in games, as well as titles that can fill that 10-30 minute slot and still offer a full experience - CRYPTARK is a clear winner here. But the real strengths I can see are the near-perfect game desing along with how well everything works together - from the internally consistent series of choices and levels requring intense action and thoughtful planning to the visual style and the abounding evidence of love and attention to detail. Gameplay is smooth and fun, weapons are awesome, and each ship feels different.
CRYPTARK won't be everyone's game. For one, it's hard. Painfully so. But just so that you love to hate it at times. I'm not even sure I want to enter the CRYPTARK - even getting there will be a real achievement for the average gamer.  Controls are very good in general but spread over several keys...it works well but takes some time to get used to and doesn't strike as being particularly ingenious. Finally, the format of randomly generated non-linear campaigns in an action roguelike will struggle not to be niche as it is. If these things don't put you off, though, CRYPTARK should not be ignored. There's a lot to like.

While Devil Daggers lacks many of the features modern FPS games boast, such as the ability to aim down sights, the ability to move at more than one speed, a story, and, in fact, guns, that simply stops it from getting bogged down by unnecessary mechanics, offering possibly the purest FPS gameplay one can find.
The player's abilities are extremely limited, being able to run, jump, hold left click for a machine gun style firing pattern, and double click for a shotgun style blast, but this ensures the player always knows what they can do, they can do it quickly, and they can switch between shooting styles with a fluidity reminiscent of Devil May Cry's on the fly Gun and Devil Arm switching.
These simple mechanics mesh with some outstanding enemy design to create tense battles, as enemies surround the player from all sides. While each enemy is programmed to behave in a certain way, the sheer volume of Lovecraftian horrors that spawn in the arena makes keeping track of them difficult, ensuring that the player is always kept on their toes. Thanks to the incredible sound design, each enemy has its own distinctive sound, which is necessary with the first person perspective to keep track of the arena.
If that sounds difficult, it's because it is- the game tasks the player with surviving for as long as possible, then uploads players' best times to a global leaderboard. The world record currently stands at a little over 1000 seconds, which equates to around 17 minutes. Most players' average campaign time will be between 45 and 60 seconds, with the game's only achievement being offered to the 0.1% of players that manage to survive for 500 seconds or more. This is not a game for people who won't enjoy dying over and again, or those looking for an in-depth story, but for those willing to be overwhelmed in an extremely difficult game with the only incentive being to "git gud", Devil Daggers is a good place to start.

I grew up with turn-based tactics games like Tactics Ogre and Final Fantasy Tactics, and it was always my favourite genre, but one thing those games often lacked was a multiplayer mode where you can play against other players. Therefore, I was very excited to hear that Atlas Reactor was a 4v4 PvP game. Despite it being turn-based, it’s still fast and furious as you only have 20 seconds to decide what to target, and where to move. It’s a constant stream of double-blind decisions where you’re guessing and second-guessing how your opponents will act and react to your positioning and threats.
The comparison to XCOM and DOTA is pretty accurate, so if you think DOTA is too fast, or you’d like to team up and play XCOM against other people, then give this a shot. It’s a game that rewards you for quickly assessing situations and correctly making decisions, as opposed to clicking quickly around the screen.
I play the game on Free Mode, which means that instead of always being able to play exactly the characters I want, I have to pick from a weekly rotation of characters. This suits me fine as I enjoy trying out different characters and filling roles that the team lacks. If you prefer specialising into 1 particular character, then maybe try the game out on Free Mode first before deciding to buy it – it’s currently £23 to unlock all characters forever, so you can play any of them whenever you want. I’m enjoying Atlas Reactor, I hope you try it and enjoy it too! :)

I do think I could write rivers of ink about this game but, mostly, that would be missing the point of a good review, in particular a review that should be good for new player.
So let's start with basics and the game's feeling: you control a dinasty, you get to decide things about your realm, your subjects and your family members... and then your ruler dies horribly and then you get a new character and everything can change (usually for the worse, true GOT style).
There is little logic in Crusader Kings II mechanics, and most of time this happens because it actually reflects historical Feudalism. If you like logical strategy games you are mostly in the wrong place.
That does not mean that you cannot find your logic trail here and there bust most of the time you just need to KNOW what triggers what. It is mostly about knowledge and less about strategy.
That said the best part is the narrative side. The mix of events, character personalities and objectives can create funny stories.
It is, and it has been for a while, my "just 5 more minutes" game, replacing Civilization, and I am quite confident it will stay like that for a while.
If you like this mix but also more coherent and hardcore strategy experience move toward Europa Universalis IV. That is the game for you.
UPDATE - JADE DRAGON: a few patches have passed and now the game it is even more complete. I will be honest, I like it more and more and in particular its RPG side grew quite a lot in the past two or three patches, changing subtly but surely the feeling of this game.
But Jade Dragon changed things even for the better: not only there are a lot of little quality of life improvements (also in the UI) but the ability to buy a casus belli really changed the pace of the game (maybe making it a bit easier) and removed those fastidious setbacks and log waits while you are just making the time pass until the marriage you arranged finally gives you the claim you are waiting for or your Chancellor succeeds against all odds.
I think this might become the final or almost final patch. With the interference of China, I think the geographical and historical scope of the game is complete and I can hardly think of anything to add.
Will we see a Cruisader Kings 3 in 2018 or 2019? I finally found this hypothesis probable. If that will be true, make sure to buy CKII in its full version with all DLCs, it is a glorious game.

Crusader Kings II has a steep learning curve.  The in-game tutorials aren't very helpful, and the amount of information available to you in the interface is initially overwhelming.  It wasn't until I consulted Youtube and wikis that I was able to really dive in and play.  Once you get the hang of it though, this game is incredibly addicting.   It's up there with the Civilization series when it comes to the impulsive "one more turn" mentality.
The real strength of CKII is it's role playing aspect.  You play as an individual ruler, and when your character dies you move on to the next heir in your dynasty.  There's a considerable variety of traits and attributes that give the characters great personality.  It also leads to some bizarre and often hilarious interactions with the AI.  This is the only game I can think of that has you practicing eugenics (breed the attractive geniuses and murder the hunchback imbeciles!) to ensure that your next character has decent stats.  It's also a bit dicomfiting to find yourself disappointed when you keep having daughters and no male heir (time to go into Henry VIII mode!), and become ruthlessly pragmatic dealing with your siblings and secondary or undesirable heirs.
CKII sometimes feels like a combination of cRPGs with board games, except instead of tons of flavor text and exposition you get to play through the stories and create your own narratives.  The other big distinction - from both styles of game - is the sandbox feel.  There are no real objectives or win conditions.  You get to dictate what you want to do and how you want to accomplish it.
There is a strong modding community for this game.  Most notably, the A Game of Thrones full conversion mod.  This plays like an entirely different game and is absolutely fantastic.  Look it up online to see the boatload of features available.  Honestly it's worth buying CKII
for ability to play this mod if you are a fan of ASoIaF.
Great for history buffs, strategy fans, and even RPG fans not averse to strategy.  The main limiting factor will be the learning curve, to become familiar enough with the base mechancis to be able to explore everything CKII has to offer.
Notes on DLC:  Though it's not absolutely necessary, I found the DLC to really enhance the game.  Make sure to get it on sale; the value proposition just isn't worth it at full price for most of these.  Comments on the main DLC expansions below
- If you want to play as Muslims.  AI uses the mechanics either way, so you can play as Christian first and see if you enjoy it before getting this to experience a very different play style.
- You need this to have retinues, which you absolutely want to have.
- Let's you play as a Merchant Republic (Venice, Genoa, etc.).  Unless you really want to play as one this is lower priority DLC; can wait until you've played through the other DLC enabled player/government types.
- Play as Vikings!!  Basically, unlocks 867 start date (standard is 1066) and lets you play as pagans and Zoroastrians.  Also, human sacrifice!
- Can play as Jews, and introduces bunch of religion based mechanics.  I'm not advanced enough to use much of this effectively yet, aside from the reliable 'Borrow money from the Jews' ----> 'Expel the Jews' combo to get you out of debt.
- Play as Hindu, Buddhist or Jain rulers in the Indian subcontinent.  Nice change of pace from your standard Christian feudal lord.
- Far superior replacement for the old ambition system.  Only worth it at sale price, since it doesn't add all that much content, but it's impactful enough that I don't think I could go back to old system after playing this.  Just be sure to turn AI seduction off in options.  Otherwise there is stupidly high chance for AI character to bang your wife/nieces/daugthers and give them herpes and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ children.
- Introduces Silk Road and ability to play as Central Asian nomads.  I mainly got this to be able to play as Dothraki in the AGoT mod.  Haven't played in unmodded CKII yet, but heard good things.
- Allows 769 start date, and custom kingdoms/empires.  Tribal mechanics are fun starting out early, but late game tends to be more stale as you get giant blobs making it hard to expand.
- Bunch of features related to disease; many new ways for your characters to suffer and die!  Fun DLC; recommended.
- Really divisive among the fanbase.  Have played this on multiplayer, and it's definitely not for me.  Unless the mechanics sound really good to you, avoid.
- Played on multiplayer.  Societies were fun in small doses, but the mechanic isn't interesting enough to justify buying the DLC.
- The only thing I'm interested in is the new CBs.  Might pick up when discounted to death.
As for minor DLC, can take or leave most of it, but the Ruler Designer is fun to play around with and create interesting and unconventional starting characters.  Using it disables achievements, but those are only active in Ironman mode anyways (lets you use only one save file) which is a pain especially while learning the game so they are likely to be disabled anyways.

In a market over-saturated with instant-satisfaction run-and-gun shooters, there has been a lingering void of video games that focus heavily on tactical decision-making, deception and patience. Frozen Synapse not only fills this void but also offers gameplay that remains and will remain addictive and satisfying for years to come. What makes this turn-based, strategic game extremely gratifying is the ability to not only issue complex multi-layered orders to each of your own individual units but also the ability to issue the same extent of orders to the units of your opponent — providing the capability to explore and simulate how you might expect your opponent to carry out his or her next move. Regardless of whether or not your opponent reacts in the way you might have prognosticated, the anticipation to see the outcome of the next move can at times be overwhelmingly exhilarating. This coupled with an exceptional soundtrack and visuals is indicative of how excellent indie games can be.

The Halo franchise has a rather lengthy history with its numerous titles, which spans over a decade since Halo: Combat Evolved in 2001. After Halo 2, the subsequent games were released only on console exclusive for the X-Box consoles. It would not be unusual, I think, for people who are primarily PC gamers to not be familar with this franchise.
This game was orginally Microsoft Windows 8, Windows 8 phone, X-Box 360, and Xbox 1  platforms  in 2013. This game is a top down first person shooter, unlike the other installements of the franchise which are all First Person Shooters, with the exception of Halo Wars which is a Real Time Strategy game. To my knowledge, this would be the first Halo title released on the PC since Halo 2 since 2007. This makes it an oddity.
The game is very simple in design, as it was meant for mobile devices.  Many missions can be completed in a few minutes, with only a handful of exceptions that require a little more time. This game can be completed in a couple hours, with further time for earning Gold Star ratings for each mission.
The story follows the stories of two Spartans Commander Palmer ( A familar face for those who have played Halo 4 on X-box 360) and Spartan Davis while they are stationed on a planet. During this time, there is a ceasefire between the Humans and the  Covenant after the events of Halo 3.  A rogue group of Covenant who have ignored the ceasefire.  This puts the events of this game somewhere between the aftermath of Halo 3 and before Halo 4. While it doesn't really bridge the gap between the two, it does give a little insight into things that happened in the aftermath of the War.
The controls are fairly smooth, with a few hiccups here and there. For some reason, your character will slow down to a walk, seemingly for no reason. I noticed this after a Melee. Give it a few seconds or just fire your gun some and the character will pick back up to their normal speed.  The only three keys that cannot rebound are the Left Mouse (Fire), Right Mouse ( Throw Grenade), and ESC ( Pause). The assorted Vehicles move with the same controls.  For players familar with Halo the vehicles operate in the same fashion as they always have. The UNSC Grizzly & Scorpion tanks lack the smooth turning of the Covenant Ghost ahd Wraith vehicles, but make up for it in endurance.
The graphics of this game are mediocore, but that is alright. The highlight of this game is the cinematics before each mission which, for a mobile based game, are pretty good looking.  I'd suggest looking them up, it may surprise you.
Missions tend to run either as one of the following or a combination: exterminate all enemies or selected units,  protect a unit/location, or some sort of time limit challenge. There is not hidden tricks; this game is straight forward with what it wants you to do.
There is no Co-op feature to this version of the game on Steam, yet it does have Acheivements. Speaking of them, they are all simple with some of them relying on patience. There are a few guides out there online if you require assistance.
This game did have Microtransactions, but there are none in this version.
Each mission has a preset loudout that can be customized to a very limited degree. EXP in other installments denotes a player rank, but this game uses it as currency for one time usages for weapons, player abilites ( Armor Abilities), and boosters (  More damage, faster  shield recovery, or increased point modifier).  The easiest way I found to earn EXP was to perfom A-1 of the campaign  with the Hollow and Pacifist Skulls on.  For those not familar with Halo, skulls at as modifiers that change gameplay in someway, typically making things more challenging be it stronge enemies or only recover shield for success melee attacks.   This grants  a 5x  multiplier to the your gains from the mission. It may take some getting used to, but  you can earn 1000 exp in a little over a minute.
All and all, it is not too shabby. It is at a fair price in my opinion, but I'd suggest waiting for it to go on and save a few dollars.

I'm going to have to say that I love this game, but I can't recommend it in its current status.
My reasoning: Steam is already a DRM system, and they included DRM that forces an online connection.  I am seeing information that they are fixing this, but I have heard tell of a 'one week online check in', which is outrageous.  Anything but full removal of the DRM is unacceptable.
There is no reason for this.  People who bought it for a console don't need to be online to play the game, so this form of discrimination against PC users is uncalled for and makes what would be a great 'on the go' game into a game you can only play at home.
Now, the game is REALLY good.  Like, if this flaw wasn't here, I'd tell you to buy ten copies.
It runs smoothly, I love the 'feel' of this game, it's like the best of Sonic Advance and the Genesis versions.  I love the bosses.  This game really could be a masterpiece.
But until the DRM is removed in its entirety (no 'one week check in' or 'online only'), wait for the holiday sale, if at all.

If you liked the first game, you will probably enjoy this one as well. Even if you haven't played the first you can still play this and not be confused.
The game's combat system is quite enjoyable all actions (movement, spells, attacks, and equipping while in combat) are done using action points. Environment can be set on fire, poisoned, covered in ice, water, steam, blood and they can be mixed together to create fun reactions :).
I've never had a battle play out the same way twice. Damage done is seperated into 3 parts (Physical, Magic and Pure) you can have armor that blocks physical and magic but pure damage as you might suspect ignores all armor. Once your or the enemies armor is reduced to 0 their HP starts to go down and they are open to status effects matching that damage type.
Your character's appearance can be customized quite a bit, the true customization is in the class building. Want to be archer that can sling fireballs go ahead, or a spear wielding dwarf that can sprout wings and jump across the combat area. (yup you can do that). Honestly, using AC III + IV + icebergs to sum up Rogue is not patronising, at all. Alternatively, as many have already put it in various reviews, Black Flag 1.5 is also a good alternative name for this entry of the Assassin's Creed series. Or, the way I call it, it is Black Flag Winter Edition which should be considered an expansion - if you remember this fancy word from before the introduction of DLCs and Season Passes. An expansion pack always upped the ante of the original game by adding new stuff and a bit of a higher difficulty level but - ultimately - a shorter story to complete.
Now, the above means that if you really want to play something new - i.e. have the next generation Assassin's Creed experience - you have to skip this one and move to Unity where you have the next-gen graphics and the new characteristics such as new gameplay elements and a completely new storyline in a new setting. However, do bear in mind that if you do so, you'll leave two of the greatest assets of the AC series (so far) behind:
1) a memorable protagonist who - unlike his predecessors before - joins the templars and kills assassins
2) the naval combat that was first introduced in AC III but we saw its full potential only in Black Flag
Now, Shay Cormac's story is - for me - very interesting from start to finish. The reason why he leaves the assassins and joins the templars made sense and I found it intriguing. And no, he doesn't just make up his mind and by joining the templars does not start desperately searching for his old pals from the brotherhood to eliminate them once and for all. It is a little bit more complicated than that - all the more reason to believe the assassins' and templars' ongoing (never-ending) conflict cannot be described as the story of Good vs Evil, Yin and Yang, etc. Shay's story is worth seeing it through till the very end.
Gameplay-wise, at one point when you turn and join the templars strolling in various settlements becomes even more exciting - you are hunted by assassins! The hay cart, for instance, your favourite spot for hiding, can now be occupied by assassins who are constantly looking for hurting you. You will not get desynced immediately if you fail to notice them in time but their one stab can significantly reduce your health. Your Eagle Vision helps you notice them from afar and when the vision is turned on you have the same compass helping you locate them than the one you used in the competitive multiplayer mode (which is now completely missing from this instalment).
Too bad the game is ridiculously easy this time. With all the easy counter system and the sleeping / berserk darts it was already very easy, however, Shay now is in possession of a grenade launcher. While two of its firing modes basically mean the same sleeping / berserk dart solution (but with area effect), an exploding grenade as the last resort is also available for you. AC couldn't have gotten any more steampunk, right?
There's also an interesting activity / side mission type labelled assassin interception: you first find their target then within the allotted time you need to find all assassins. This search mainly goes for the bonus - if you are unsuccessful the would-be victim will start their walk towards their destination and while along the way you can still protect the person - you'll just have a more challenging time.
The rest is pretty much the same. In fact, the creators desperately tried to introduce new stuff such as the destructible icebergs during naval battles that can harm other (mainly smaller) ships. Or the new narwal whale whose tusk is a must to craft some pretty nifty outfits / upgrades to your inventory. Since the North Atlantic map is constantly giving you the winter season it's better to remember not to swim for long as Shay can freeze to death! Also, the penguin effect looks great!
About maps: comparing the game to AC III is obvious once Shay sets foot in New York. And while we - again - have two maps with lots of water only one of them focuses on the ocean. The so-called River Valley has - well - a valley with long canals and many small settlements and the area is full of hills and mountains.
So, is Rogue worth the purchase?
+++ Yes, 3 new maps accompanied by a new story and so far - arguably - with the most interesting protagonist this time.
+++ Once again the open world is quite big with dozens of collectible items and to have everything found and obtain almost all achievements it took me 60 hours. Not bad for an "expansion", right?
+++ It nicely connects some dots - references can be found to AC III, IV as well as for Unity.
So, no negatives then? A must-have in the franchise?
--- While Shay's story feels unique it is much shorter. We have half of the memory sequences now compared to previous entries in the series. Make no mistake the game has its applicable pace to tell the story (not rushed, at all) but since there are so many collectibles I would have expected the same amount of main missions, too, for accompaniment purposes.
--- There's nothing really new here beside the story. Some new side missions / activities and what the winter season can add to the gameplay. It is not necessarily bad but since everything is more of the same the annoying stuff remains, too: the occasionally annoying target selection during naval battles (when you board a ship) and the too easy gameplay - there's next to no challenge once Shay gets his hands on the grenade launcher.
Rogue is a must have for all AC fans! The rest of you can just decide based on above review or by reading some more - after all, while I consider this more of an expansion its price tag could be a bit lower due to the same.

With a game like this, a game that seems like it should be so good, it's difficult to tell from reviews alone whether or not it's worthwhile. I knew going in that the game had a lot of negative reviews, but it was impossible not to at least give it a try and I'll admit, I really,
wanted this game to be good. I mean, it just sounds like it should be awesome. It's basically like
, a game I currently have nearly 2,000 hours of playtime in, with the ship-building mechanic from
, and set in a richly detailed steampunk world of floating islands and flying sky whales. There's no way this isn't the greatest game ever made. Right?
Sadly, it's not the greatest game ever made. In fact, it's not a great game at all, or even a good game, or even a mediocre game.
is a game which is fundamentally, fatally flawed. By way of explaining how, and because lists are easy to write, allow me to present to you The Top 3 Things Wrong With
!
Here's the thing about the graphics: some of them actually look amazing. The flying whales and the krakens that live in the lower regions of the world, and the larger objects like the giant balloons and clocktowers, are all lovingly rendered. The watercolor background is pretty nice too. It's obvious that the developers really worked hard on the graphics. So what is up here?
It looks blocky and awful, like my house is built from stacked up lincoln logs. This is because there's no blending or tiling with the graphics, which is weird because even
and
have that. Also, there's an awful lot of these blocks. In
your character is three blocks tall, and in
it's four. Here? Freaking eight! These blocks are tiny is what I'm getting at, which makes construction and destruction a massive chore.
What else makes construction a chore? The painfully bad attempt at 2.5D graphics. Everything is in this weird 3/4ths view which I'm sure the developers thought was just so cool, but really it just gets in the way. It's hard to know what block you're digging at with your jackhammer when you're mining, and it's hard to see what you're doing when you're building on a ship or a home base.
Also, what's with my furniture? It looks like it's just painted onto the wall instead of actually sitting on the floor.
I'll admit, math was never my big thing. I mean, I'm not completely stupid with numbers, but it never came as easy to me as other things. That said, what the hell do these numbers mean?
My ship's mass is only 524, and I have 1,389 vertical thrust, so shouldn't I be able to move up and down fairly well? No, I can't. For that matter, why is my vertical thrust only 1,389? My three propellers provide a total thrust of 13,500 (4,500 x 3), so how is that counteracted so greatly by a mass of only 524? And shouldn't my bouyancy of 30,000 totally cancel out the mass issue anyway? Honestly, it wouldn't be that big of a deal if I just knew what these numbers meant. Is my mass 524 kilograms? 524 tons? Who knows? The fact that there are no units given for these numbers just makes them all feel arbitrary.
And no, I'm not so stupid that I can't figure out adding a few extra propellers will let me move again, but I shouldn't have to guess at it. And if you DO want me to have to guess at it, then why bother giving me the numbers at all? It's not like they matter.
This issue doesn't only affect airships either. It's also a problem with armor, weapons, pretty much everything. Earlier in the game my character picked up a set of bronze full plate armor. I was excited because it gave her 30 more defense than my old set of leather-bronze bandit armor, so I put it on and went out to fight some people, and noticed that the bandits who were previously dealing 46 points of damage a shot with their pistols were now doing... 46 points of damage a shot. Seriously, what the Hell do these numbers mean?!
So, if I was designing a game about floating islands and airships, and I had to name what I thought would be the single most important aspect of the gameplay, the one thing that I absolutely had to make sure I didn't screw up no matter what, I would have to say that would be a good jumping mechanic. I mean, we're dealing with a game world where one missed jump means, at best, you fall and break your everything on the next floating island down, or at worst you fall all the way into the planet's core and burn to death. That's not a pleasant way to go.
That said, this game has what might just be the worst jumping algorithm of any game I've ever played. You move too fast, and it's too hard to control where you end up. Even walking is dangerous, as stepping off a slope means the jumping algorithm takes over and sends you rocketing over the nearest ledge straight to your death. I found that latching my grappling hook on to the ground was a necessary step whenever I was near a ledge, so that when I fell I would at least be able to stop myself.
Oh yeah, and let's talk about the grappling hook. I'll admit it's fun to swing around on and feel like I'm a steampunk Spiderman. Even so, the grappling hook isn't much better than anything else. It's too fiddly and too slow, it never seems to connect when you need it to, or else it connects to the wrong thing. Even when it does connect right, it's too unpredictable; sometimes you just stop and hang there, and other times you spin around at high speed, usually straight into your airship's propellers.
That brings us to the last mode of movement: airships. Airship movement is... passable. It's a bit wonky sometimes itself, mostly due to inertia and the difficulty of making yourself come to a complete stop. (Seriously,
had the inertial dampener system for a reason,
developers.) Also, my ship felt like it had a weird desire to keep drifting upward which always made it very hard to dock properly. Of course, there's also the weirdness of the numbers which I mentioned before, where you always seem to have either not enough thrust so you can barely move, or else too much so you rocket across the map with a slightest touch of the buttons. It's a good thing repairs to your airship are free, because you will crash into things constantly.

The game world is very interesting and well thought out.
It's just a shame that the game they built around this concept is so poorly built. Microsoft lately has been on a quest to re-release every sucessful game they ever had, updated and modernized. I have mixed feelings about this. Although I love these games and the re-releases are good the prices have been an issue. I don't feel that $30/40 is fair for these games, and they are on the right path by decreasing the price of RoN to $15 pre-release and $20 on release, which would be a fair price for other re-releases such as Age of Mythology and AoE 2. Now to the game itself.
Rise of Nations is one of, if not my favorite RTS game of all time. It blends various game concepts from games such as Civilization and Age of Empires and makes a masterpiece. This game is HEAVILY micro-management centric, where the nation with the greatest economic output, and the player who can manage that economic output efficiently, is going to win. Resources on the map are infinite, however productivity is everything, managing exactly how many woodcutting camps you need to sustain your growth without sacrificing, say mining metal for example. The combat in this game is also well balanced, focusing on a good mix of units rather than unit spam. Unique units are brought to the table just like in Civilization that each Nation has that can give them a slight advantage, however every unit always has a counter or way to be defeated. There's no "stacks of death" or "zerg rush" in this game, and that is one reason I also like it. I've been the smaller nation holding off spams of cheap units from bigger nations sucessfully many times. I wish more modern RTS games existed like this....I could only imagine the cores of this game being molded into a modern RTS...it would be grand.

Mutant Mudds is a superbly polished throwback to the days of yore when platformers punched back. Think back on the NES platforming days when health margins were slim, not-always-death-defying leaps across yawning chasms and over blood-soaked spike hazards required pixel-perfect precision. When battling through the deluge of wave after wave of enemies required lithe mastery and ingenuity. Remember the punchy tag-along sound tracks? Crisply sharp chiptunes chock-full of meaty square and triangle wave melodies, peppy & pleading with you to dry off your sweat-soaked palms yet again and continue onward, past that hundredth death.
The game is simple and straightforward: collect water spirits and complete levels to unlock the tools that will get you through the tight spots. Traverse worlds of grass, ice, fire, wind, and space, then traverse their ghost worlds. Be on the lookout for secret doors to worlds patterned after the palettes of the Virtual Boy and Game Boy. And, if you're still spoiling for a challenge, unlock granny (or rescue one or more of the freedom fighters imprisoned in hidden bubbles), and throw yourself at the challenges presented by CGA land. The CGA palette is as harsh as the trap-laden terrain is punishing.

After you collect certain milestones worth of gems, you unlock optional power-ups. The three power-ups you unlock are an extended shot, extended hover, or rocket jump. You can only have one at a time. Collecting all the things in a level will make the circle above the door fill-in so you know you got everything. There are also secret challenge levels within each level. Beating these will fill-in the other circle above the door. Eventually you unlock a second set of levels ("ghost levels"), which are the same levels as the main game, but the level design is harder and you can't kill the enemies normally. You can kill them with a specific power-up, but it only shows up a few times. But what makes it not as hard is that you can play as Granny through all these levels (after you beat the game) and have all three power-ups of extended shot, hover, and rocket jump while you play them.
What's different about "Deluxe":
The Deluxe version has added the "ghost levels" and more extra characters (which all play exactly like Granny).
What I like:
+ The use of the dimensions and collecting impulse creates some sort-of platforming puzzles.
+ Good challenge that only felt cheap on small occasions.
? Not really something I like, but there is a timer to show you how long you are taking in each level, but the game doesn't save your time or anything.
What I don't like:
- Bland characters and story. You and your grandma are saving the world from these mud aliens. You two are the only people in this world. There is nothing to the ending other than your grandma congratulating you.
- The placement of some of the checkpoints bugs me as they don't feel like they are placed at the middle of the level, so the front or back half will feel much longer than the other when you die and need to redo your platforming.
- Horizontal movement is kinda so slow. You travel a lot faster jumping up than you do walking left and right (nitpick).
Conclusion:
It is a fine game and I did mildly enjoy playing it. The appeal of this game is the platforming challenges. It is not a fast game though. The story and characters are not very detailed. I got everything in about 5 hours. If it looks interesting to you, I would recommend you wait to get this game on sale.

Mutant Mudds Deluxe has "tribute game" or "passion project" written all over it, but that isn't necessarily a problem, as long as it excutes those things well, and fortunately, it does do those things very well, while adding just the right ammount of elements from other games and just a tad of subtle yet noticable pop culture jokes/references.
So let's break things down, and find out how MMD emphasizes the "Mudds" in the game title
Its part Mega Man, with jumping, shooting, postioning yourself and timing yourself to avoid getting hurt, along with spikes of doom that take away all your health
It's part Earthbound with it's character and monster design as well as it's basic synopsis for the plot without Earthbound's in-depth story (but for a game like this story isn't needed, it can be nice, but not necessary)
The design of the main character looks like Jeff and Ness had a baby, and the monsters remind me of some of the monsters from Earthbound
The game is part Classic Mario and Super Mario World, with it's mult-path levels (in most cases from what I've played) and it's for the most part, easy to learn and understand platforming with a reasonable pace speed wise that crrawls up difficulty wise as you go as well as collecting coins
The game is part Sonic, with SOME of it's level design (the first world reminds me STRONGLY of green hill zone
The game is part Donkey Kong Country Returns, allowing you to go into the background
And lastly, the game is part 2-D Metroid, as some of the hidden  or alternate paths will require you to buy upgrades or revist old levels to find areas or secrets you previously couldn't explore
Where are the game's cons? From my experience with the game (you can argue a review like this may havve too little hours to be fair, but it does not requrie many hours to get the feel of the game tbh) The games cons in my opinion are that you have to find out yourself what the power ups do when you buy them with the coins you find (don't get me wrong, trying things yourself is how the NES era games were, but simple text descriptions or visual depictions can if anything eliminate guessing)
Music isn't groundbreaking, but it's definately catchy and fun to listen to, therefroe its memorable enough, but not along the lines of shovel knight or nuclear throne , but its music is fun  overall. Plus, as a bonus, the OST is free on Bandicamp, so even if you don't like it, at least you didn't lose any money
And from what I played, the game may feel a tad on the easier side, so maybe it's not for everyone
But despite these shortcomings, don't let those things deter you from an otherwise fun game that you can tell that, although (to my knowledge) maybe not the most groundbreaking or well known title, its a mash up game done right and it should get more attention with the other mash up games like Mercenary Kings and Streets of Rouge imo.

I've never really been a fan of those incredibly fast paced shooters such as Doom or Quake. Something about them never seemed all that appealing. My friend is absolutely obsessed with those types of games and will always tell me how much of an idiot I am for not playing them and that I should really give them a shot. So, as a compromise,I bought this.
Devil Daggers is a great game but also a very challenging one. The idea is simple enough. You just need to survive for as long as you can on a hellish platform as wave after wave of enemies swarms you. Sounds kind of dull now that I've written it, but it is anything but. You really need to learn to master this games mechanics if you ever want to get a time higher than 200 seconds. You need to be know the weapon better than the back of your hand (ironic seeing as the weapon IS your hand) and how to best utilize it for each enemy. Rocket jumping, shotgun blasting, short burst, bullet damage, precise aiming and strafing is necessary if you want to prevail.
The enemys are introduced slowly, but you better get used to them pretty quick, because the game is going to throw tons of them at you. Each enemy poses its own challenges, such as the flying monsters requiring you to shoot off every gem from its body before it will die, or the egg spawners who can steal your upgrade gems and turn them into more demons. The design of the demons is incredible and can make some of them really unsettling. Turning around and seeing a floating dark skull inches away from your face can be surprisingly scary when your not expecting it. Each demon has its own AI aswell, which gives them another layer of challenge and interesting design.
I will also quickly note that I love the sound design on this game. Wearing headphones or having good speakers can help you hear where the enemys are going to spawn, which sounds overpowered but actually just gives you a fair chance at staying alive. It is a great feature and I am very impressed with how accurate it is.
If its not obvious, I love this game. I think it is a fantastic and well executed fast paced shooter that really rewards you for your time and effort. A must have.
8/10
(P.S. Even after playing this for as long as I have and loving how it handles, I'm still not interested in Doom or Quake. And weirdly, my mate, who I said loves those games at the start of this review, doesn't actually like this game very much. Go figure.)

Atlas Reactor is a turn-based pvp Moba-like that pits teams of 4 against eachother in a wonderfully paced brawl to achieve either 5 kills, or whichever team can achieve the most kills in 20 turns. Although it is a tactical game, its quickly paced, forcing you to choose your actions wisely within a certain time-limit. I'm just going to go ahead and start listing my pros and cons
Pros:
-The free trial marketing module
Allowing you to play the FULL game with a free rotation of freelancers each week is all fine and dandy, and now that its out of beta you can open all of your lootboxes instantly, giving almost no tactical advantage between people who have paid for the game, and people who play for free. Paying for the game simply unlocks all of the characters and future characters for play whever you please, and enables you to play ranked mode (which hasnt been released yet).
-Interesting character pool
Each freelancer legitimately feels unique, and like they bring something different to the table from their peers. All freelancers have very clear strengths and weaknesses, which can be exploited. They all have 5 abilities including their ultimate ability, and each ability has what is called a "Mod", which allows you to augment each ability to have an extra effect. Each mod costs a certain amount of space, of which you can only fill up to 10, so you cant pick every 3 point mod.  This allows the feel of there not being a specific "Superior" mod combination, and allows each player to build their mods to their specific playstyle, and not just what's the strongest because that's a very blurred line.
-Discord Integration
I've yet to use this feature, but it seems really ♥♥♥♥ing cool. When you join a group with 3 other people, you have the option to instantly join a discord chat room with them via a button in the actual game itself. Voice communication is crucial for this kind of game, and the fact that that's integrated so smoothly feels very nice.
Cons
-The buiseness model
How you unlock skins, voice lines, and all cosmetic changes to your account is via lootboxes much like how overwatch works. There's even a in game currency system that you are provided with if you get duplicates of an item, or you can just flat out get the currency. This is honestly just a personal iff, because I hate in overwatch as well, so dont let this deter you from at least trying out the game.
Overall, I give it a 9.5/10. It was an extremely pleasant suprise, and without a doubt stands out from the drown and copy/paste most multiplayer games come out with. Definitely worth a shot.

Awesomenauts is a very interesting animal: a 2D Platforming MOBA.  It incorporates all the charm of a cartoonish 2d platformer with the core elements of a PvP MOBA.  Combine the two and you get a peculiar mix that appeals strongly to fans of both gametypes.
The only real downside of this game is that it doesn't make it immediately apparent that it is purely PvP.  If anything, the tutorial mission seems to be leading to a singleplayer campaign, but at its conclusion you discover that this is very much not the case. The game is ONLY multiplayer, save for an offline practice mode with bots.
From a personal perspective, I found this incredibly disappointing.  I was rather enthusiastic following the tutorial mission, but once it ended and I discovered the multiplayer only aspect my reaction was a puzzled, disbelieving "wut?"  I will admit that I am not the biggest PvP fan, but my disappointment goes beyond that.  This game's style and mechanics virtually beg for a singleplayer campaign, and it is tragic that it is absent.
With that in mind, I can still recommend this game to MOBA fans with a fondness for 2D platformers.  It definitely sets itself apart from the slew of samey crap MOBAs out there without straying too far from what makes the format popular, all while adding some unique appeal of its own.  If you like team PvP, this game is pretty fun.  If you want a more solo experience, you'll need to look elsewhere.
