Shards of Azuria is a charming game with quirky characters and hours and hours of content. The controls are a little hard to get used to at first but at its price point, this game is a steal!
Being a 2D game, the hardware capabilities of your PC aren't going to be pushed to the limit no matter what graphics card you have. Intel Integrated HD graphics should be more than enough to play this game. I personally haven't encountered any performance issues caused by any bugs. This game seems very well polished compared to a lot on the Early Access marketplace.
This game isn't going to blow you away graphically. However, for people who are fans of pixel art, I wholeheartedly recommend this game. The enemies come in a different variety of horrible beasts that leave me curious to find more of them just to see what they look like. Back in the town, there is still some pixel wonders to behold such as the Shard itself.
Unlike some similar games, Shards is a live action game (not turn-based). This makes it all the more tense when battling hoards of monsters. The landscapes are half procedurally generated which makes replayability a factor of the game.
The game ships with a wide variety of abilities that allow you to go about defeating an enemy in many different ways, be it with Might, Cunning or Mysticism.
You are also able to craft your own house and make it your own with the paint blaster. The crafting system is fully fledged and you are able to craft over 90 items.
The controls will more than likely seem strange at first, they take a bit of getting used to. As this is an isometric game, it's tough to determine which way is UP, DOWN, LEFT or RIGHT. There is a keybindings menu available for people to change up the controls if needed!
The music is reminiscent of 90s-esque RPG/Exploration games. It is definitely a welcoming, nostalgic treat.

Oblivion is a game from 2006 that I replayed now with a very interesting plot although at the same time different from the others. I'd have it as the typical game from a series but more relaxed, maybe a little softer, but it is still very good, though. As I wrote with the Skyrim's critic, I consider it necessary to play previous games to understand the plot correctly, because there is lot of relations bewteen games, and it's worth of it because it's a very work story. :) - With an other very funny parts in the game.
After Morrowind, there have been a improvement in always of gameplay. It have became easier in which comes to quests, map, fast travelling, etc. The AI has improve a lot, too. The story itself it's very good but some people made find it familiar. The few important characters (and a few secondary) are well work with their story behind and some kind of charsmatic. In other words, Oblivion can easily have your mind inside the game itself. I won't describe the plot of the DLC's but after playing the DLC's of other Bethesda's game (I mean, especially in saga Elder Scrolls and I could say even Fallout, although they're good too) but I can tell that Oblivion's & Morrowind's DLC's are literally an entire new world to the base game. Shivering Isles was & still being my favourite.<3
The weak points of Oblivion in my opinion are the lazy translation in spanish subitles with great fails of grammar, vocabulary and sometimes missing words. I advice that in this case it's necessary to listen and to know very well english to know that they really say, because they even change words and it's so bothering. Apart from the translation, there is a very low variety of voices. We can find all the elves NPC's sharing the same voices, and this happens to with nords and orcs. They could add differences between all the races. Finally we can find unique characters with a unique voice (special mention to Sean Bean). Also I recommend to patch the game with both official and unofficial patches, because that will fix very annoying bugs (it's not my case, but it seems it's very recommended).
So! As I said before, it's a very good game, also funny, very recommended, with a very good main quest and also side quests, with lovely characters and very inmersive. :)
As always, Bethesda did miracles with their creations!

I do think I could write rivers of ink about this game but, mostly, that would be missing the point of a good review, in particular a review that should be good for new player.
So let's start with basics and the game's feeling: you control a dinasty, you get to decide things about your realm, your subjects and your family members... and then your ruler dies horribly and then you get a new character and everything can change (usually for the worse, true GOT style).
There is little logic in Crusader Kings II mechanics, and most of time this happens because it actually reflects historical Feudalism. If you like logical strategy games you are mostly in the wrong place.
That does not mean that you cannot find your logic trail here and there bust most of the time you just need to KNOW what triggers what. It is mostly about knowledge and less about strategy.
That said the best part is the narrative side. The mix of events, character personalities and objectives can create funny stories.
It is, and it has been for a while, my "just 5 more minutes" game, replacing Civilization, and I am quite confident it will stay like that for a while.
If you like this mix but also more coherent and hardcore strategy experience move toward Europa Universalis IV. That is the game for you.
UPDATE - JADE DRAGON: a few patches have passed and now the game it is even more complete. I will be honest, I like it more and more and in particular its RPG side grew quite a lot in the past two or three patches, changing subtly but surely the feeling of this game.
But Jade Dragon changed things even for the better: not only there are a lot of little quality of life improvements (also in the UI) but the ability to buy a casus belli really changed the pace of the game (maybe making it a bit easier) and removed those fastidious setbacks and log waits while you are just making the time pass until the marriage you arranged finally gives you the claim you are waiting for or your Chancellor succeeds against all odds.
I think this might become the final or almost final patch. With the interference of China, I think the geographical and historical scope of the game is complete and I can hardly think of anything to add.
Will we see a Cruisader Kings 3 in 2018 or 2019? I finally found this hypothesis probable. If that will be true, make sure to buy CKII in its full version with all DLCs, it is a glorious game.

Crusader Kings II has a steep learning curve.  The in-game tutorials aren't very helpful, and the amount of information available to you in the interface is initially overwhelming.  It wasn't until I consulted Youtube and wikis that I was able to really dive in and play.  Once you get the hang of it though, this game is incredibly addicting.   It's up there with the Civilization series when it comes to the impulsive "one more turn" mentality.
The real strength of CKII is it's role playing aspect.  You play as an individual ruler, and when your character dies you move on to the next heir in your dynasty.  There's a considerable variety of traits and attributes that give the characters great personality.  It also leads to some bizarre and often hilarious interactions with the AI.  This is the only game I can think of that has you practicing eugenics (breed the attractive geniuses and murder the hunchback imbeciles!) to ensure that your next character has decent stats.  It's also a bit dicomfiting to find yourself disappointed when you keep having daughters and no male heir (time to go into Henry VIII mode!), and become ruthlessly pragmatic dealing with your siblings and secondary or undesirable heirs.
CKII sometimes feels like a combination of cRPGs with board games, except instead of tons of flavor text and exposition you get to play through the stories and create your own narratives.  The other big distinction - from both styles of game - is the sandbox feel.  There are no real objectives or win conditions.  You get to dictate what you want to do and how you want to accomplish it.
There is a strong modding community for this game.  Most notably, the A Game of Thrones full conversion mod.  This plays like an entirely different game and is absolutely fantastic.  Look it up online to see the boatload of features available.  Honestly it's worth buying CKII
for ability to play this mod if you are a fan of ASoIaF.
Great for history buffs, strategy fans, and even RPG fans not averse to strategy.  The main limiting factor will be the learning curve, to become familiar enough with the base mechancis to be able to explore everything CKII has to offer.
Notes on DLC:  Though it's not absolutely necessary, I found the DLC to really enhance the game.  Make sure to get it on sale; the value proposition just isn't worth it at full price for most of these.  Comments on the main DLC expansions below
- If you want to play as Muslims.  AI uses the mechanics either way, so you can play as Christian first and see if you enjoy it before getting this to experience a very different play style.
- You need this to have retinues, which you absolutely want to have.
- Let's you play as a Merchant Republic (Venice, Genoa, etc.).  Unless you really want to play as one this is lower priority DLC; can wait until you've played through the other DLC enabled player/government types.
- Play as Vikings!!  Basically, unlocks 867 start date (standard is 1066) and lets you play as pagans and Zoroastrians.  Also, human sacrifice!
- Can play as Jews, and introduces bunch of religion based mechanics.  I'm not advanced enough to use much of this effectively yet, aside from the reliable 'Borrow money from the Jews' ----> 'Expel the Jews' combo to get you out of debt.
- Play as Hindu, Buddhist or Jain rulers in the Indian subcontinent.  Nice change of pace from your standard Christian feudal lord.
- Far superior replacement for the old ambition system.  Only worth it at sale price, since it doesn't add all that much content, but it's impactful enough that I don't think I could go back to old system after playing this.  Just be sure to turn AI seduction off in options.  Otherwise there is stupidly high chance for AI character to bang your wife/nieces/daugthers and give them herpes and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ children.
- Introduces Silk Road and ability to play as Central Asian nomads.  I mainly got this to be able to play as Dothraki in the AGoT mod.  Haven't played in unmodded CKII yet, but heard good things.
- Allows 769 start date, and custom kingdoms/empires.  Tribal mechanics are fun starting out early, but late game tends to be more stale as you get giant blobs making it hard to expand.
- Bunch of features related to disease; many new ways for your characters to suffer and die!  Fun DLC; recommended.
- Really divisive among the fanbase.  Have played this on multiplayer, and it's definitely not for me.  Unless the mechanics sound really good to you, avoid.
- Played on multiplayer.  Societies were fun in small doses, but the mechanic isn't interesting enough to justify buying the DLC.
- The only thing I'm interested in is the new CBs.  Might pick up when discounted to death.
As for minor DLC, can take or leave most of it, but the Ruler Designer is fun to play around with and create interesting and unconventional starting characters.  Using it disables achievements, but those are only active in Ironman mode anyways (lets you use only one save file) which is a pain especially while learning the game so they are likely to be disabled anyways.

I recommend this game for an hour or two.  After which, I don't recommend it.
Pros:
1)Neat concept
Cons:
1)After hours of playing, I'm frustrated by my apparent inability to learn how to not be killed quickly by enemy
swarms

4)Encountered Artifacts that could be obtained if you didn't destroy ship repair--that's just stressful.  Ship repair needs to be destroyed, or else everything comes back quickly.
5)Burst machine gun useless.  You need the feedback of missed bullets in order to re-direct your bullet stream, but a burst machine gun doesn't allow for that feedback.
6)Smart machine gun often targeted enemies other than the one that was right in front of me.
7)Annoyed by repetitious dialogue.
8)Wish there was more freedom of level selection.
9)Enemies could cause you to fly across the screen.  Ok, but it happens too much--causes lack of feeling that I am in control.
10)Wish there were varied mission types.

Fun, difficult rogue-lite twin-stick shooter with a pretty unique approach and a great art style. The level generation is solid and varied, with a lot of strategic functional nodes in the structures that may or may not be present and serve as modifiers to the level, such as systems that govern enemy repair, alarms, shields, locks, drone production, sensor jamming and a surprising amount more. These wildcards combined with an interesting and well-designed procedural level generator keep the game fresh.
The controls are responsive and fluid, and a few other classes of combat suit can be unlocked which provide drastically different abilities and initial loadouts (I found the Salamander suit to be the first one that enabled me to progress more deeply into the game so far).
The weapons that become available are likewise quite varied and fun to use. There are melee attacks, shotguns, machineguns, smartguns, grenades, missiles, nukes, acid bombs, clusterbombs, flamethrowers, EMPS and more in just about every imaginable combination, as well as add extra armor plating, repair items and other upgrades that you recover from the derelict hulks.
The cost however is, well... the cost. As a scrapper, you must make your runs profitable to afford the equipment you deploy. You do get a rebate on unused gear after a successful mission, but you want to maximize profits by completing optional objectives when possible for extra dosh, and occassional special Artifacts which allow you to unlock more suits.
You pretty much want to git gud/lucky enough to obtain a couple of these babies as soon as you get a feel for what's going on. The first suit is a good all-rounder, but each of the others offers a somewhat different playstyle that may be more "suited" to you: Demolitions, Heavy, Stealth, and whatever the other one is that I haven't unlocked yet :P.
Features save slots for continuing a long run which you can only save to in-between missions, before selecting your next salvage target. This could be made a bit more clear. There is also local co-op, which would be a plus, except the rapid ramp in difficulty by the 3rd level, plus the unfortunate fact that ammo and armor is *shared* between players, effectively halving the loadout and doubling the player damage hitboxes, means you will really need to train up your co-op partner to not sponge hits and even then co-op still presents more of a handicap than advantage overall.
The art style is interesting, detailed and consistent, lending a strong, gritty sci-fi comic book feel to the game. The difficulty does ramp up considerably, forcing you to master the use of your arsenal, including shield blocks, boosts, melee and heavy weapons in addition to pew-pewing everything.
Gameplay that rewards skillful control and strategic loadout choices gets high marks from me. My only critiques would be the imperfect co-op and a learning curve that teaches you some very harsh lessons very soon, you should come prepared to adapt. I do wish there were a few more unlockables, such as alternate initial loadout items, but the challenge as presented is very well-done and will offer fans of solid action rogue-lites such as Spelunky, Teleglitch, Rogue Legacy or Enter the Gungeon a good run for your money.

I had previously bought, returned, and left a "Not Recommended" review for this game while in early access and I am quite pleased to say that this game has significantly improved since then.
Just on the technical side I haven't encountered any crashes or slowdowns, which was the main reason for the return before. Though there is a weird string of text in the top right when I'm in the customization bay.
The gameplay is a much smoother experience than before, really just cleaned up and with "quality-of-life" improvements. Like, information on each level's secondary objectives and which enemies and facilities are in the derelict are displayed in the pre-launch customization menu to help you design your build for that level without needed to jump back-and-forth between menus.
Also, you can now collect artifacts to unlock new mechs. Add that to the wide variety of weapon, tool, and consumables and there is a huge range of gameplay styles to play.
I am changing my review to a "Recommended" as I believe the game has significantly improved, not only from early access, but into a quality product all on its own. If you enjoy the difficulty, replayability, and over-arching progress that comes with most modern rogue-likes, and have a taste for customization that lets you loose to try seemingly ineffective designs, or even the fun of pre-planning and putting together a plan of action as you would in many tactics-heavy games. It's just missing something and is not nearly as compelling as the first game.  I can't really describe it.  One thing that does stand out is a Michael Bay reliance on explosions.  Sigh....

It has quite a lot of problems; The UI is less than stellar, the on-ground combat can be sort of dodgy, the character customisation  extends only as far as gender and hair colour, and the ship building, which plays a HUGE part in the gameplay experience is very awkward and basically not explained at all.
The crafting system is cool and accessible, and for the most part makes a lot of sense, suffers a lot because even if you know what to do, your character CANNOT make something without knowing the recipe. This bugged me a lot because although it makes sense for complicated things like engines and guns and machine parts, I find it very difficult to imagine my guy doesn't know how to make "cooked meat".
But honestly, it is still a really fun game! Even with the problems I mentioned, I've still already sunk hours into it and plan to sink many more.
The world feels HUGE, even though it is very specifically mapped out and not open ended like minecraft, it is still epic and massive.
When you know how the ship building works exploration feels big and adventurous, and occasionally if you find a large ruin or a cave system or something, exploration and materials gathering always feels cool and rewarding.
The game features a heavily used grappling hook mechanic (which I thought was lazy at first, but it REALLY grew on me when I used it) and when you get used to using it, it is such a cool way to get around and safely explore.
So yeah, the game has a few problems, but when you get into it and find your rhythm, they will take a backseat to your steampunk airship adventuring.

"I make my own luck"
These are the words that define a hero. Shay Cormac was young and idealistic. But throughout his life, he remained loyal and compassionate.
As a hardy AC fan, I was reluctant to get this as this is the story of an Assassin going rogue, turning coats and crossing over to the dark side - especially since I heard great things about Rogue. But I had never been more wrong or more clear in my love for this game and the others
Previous AC games were quite 'traditional' in the sense where the bad guys were bad and were easy to hate. But as said in my review of AC3, it started to blur the lines. This is where the Kenway line comes in. Beginning from Connor and Haytham in AC3, the grey areas of the Assassin-Templar conflict shift and change. It is not just about right and wrong anymore, but the means and intentions of achieving peace and such.
This is the story of a man living in time when the Assassin Brotherhood struggled hard to maintain righteousness. This game truly sets the tone of the question - 'Are all Templars evil? Are all Assassins' good?' From here on out, its a devil's trap, and you cannot help but see the grey and its A LOT harder to pick sides
Gameplay is much the same as the AC3, AC4 world. The naval combat and ground combat is the same as before, but set in a new and crisp environment. The graphics are way more stable than Black Flag, with no point in gameplay where glitch nor bug appeared - for me at least. The famously annoying amount of collectibles has returned, and its up to you if you wish to catch them all.
Plot is the compelling masterpiece. Not only does this tie in AC3 and AC4, but also a branch into the French Revolution in AC Unity. By this point, it would be good to mention - for maximum emotional impact, to play this first prior to ACU. Shay's story is dark and riddled with emotional turmoil. Betraying his former ideals and betrayed by his own brothers - the Creed is suddenly dark and unforgiving, something not seen since the Altair days.
Set in the Seven Years war which was a significant historical event which arguably was the impetus of the fall of the British hold on America - starting the American Revolution, and also the fall of the monarchy - kicking of the French Revolution. During this time, you will understand why Achilles in AC3 was so bitter and sad, how he learned life the hard way, and why he tries so hard to make Connor see it too. In this time, you feel the echoes of Black Flag, with the confrontation of Adewale, and his former captain's son. This game shows you the effects of the novelisation of AC3, Forsaken - Haytham choosing Templars over his conscious self and turning aside emotions.
Shay has to cut and kill his way through friends and family, to protect the world from pride and war. The Assassins are no longer the good guys, and Shay - a new Templar, is seemingly the only one more concerned with the lives of innocents than the conflict itself.
Something most other Assassins cannot say they have done.
By the end of this, though short but bittersweet, the emotional wallop is compelling. Be ready.

I picked Rogue up during a Steam sale when it was 66% off, because I felt really let down by Unity. At first I didn't want to give the Assassin's Creed franchise another shot, but I'd heard good things about Rogue and seeing it was a year old already and quite a bargain I thought to myself, why the hell not. So I bought it and I don't regret it.
You play as a templar this time, which is pretty interesting, though it took me a while to get along with that - I always really liked the assassins and betraying them felt kinda... awful. But I started to grow fond of Shay Comac, he's a bit of an idiot, but likeable. The story, too, is quite interesting - at least while you're in the animus. I never really cared much for the stuff you do at Abstergo.
What I really enjoyed in Rogue was the map you got. They gave you all kinds of stuff to explore: you get New York City, the rich landscapes of the Riverlands and the icy cold North Atlantic with a lot of bad weather, fish to hunt and ships to board. I've loved Black Flag for its marine missions, and I wasn't let down by Rogue on that. I spent so much time on the water, because it just felt pretty damn good.
However, Rogue, like any other of the latest Assassin's Creed games (though I haven't played Syndicate), is just that: an Assassin's Creed game. It's not really all that different. The only thing that makes it stand out from the others is the afore mentioned fact that you're a templar now. Ergo you have assassin's following you like all the time (which got annoying pretty soon, they aren't hard to find or to kill, but there's just so many of them, it bored me).
Rogue isn't as special as it'd like to be, but still worth playing if you've liked previous AC games. They could have made the templar-thing more interesting, but it's still a nice game to spend your time on, especially if you're into sailing and discovering.
If you like board games, if you like RPGs, if you like anime, then buy this.

Played this with a bunch of friends for ~5 hours during an Indie-Game Saturday event.
While I ultimately cannot recommend Windforge, it is probably worth the $15 pricetag.
Pros:
1. Wonderful artwork
2. Great game mechanic (Terraria but with fully functional aircrafts)
3. Lots of crafting recipes (I heard like 1500)
4. Cool map with drastically different 'biome'-esk areas and different windstream patterns, etc.
5. Pretty cool physics and engineering depth when building the aircrafts
Cons:
1. Dungeons could almost be considered broken in the state that they are in (finished game) - they are either randomly generated or just poorly made. They are way too big, too hard to get in to, and completely boring.
2. The AI is as dumb as can be as far as the enemies go
3. Probably the biggest con is that everytime you go to a new scene (next section of the map), everything resets. This is hard to describe but those that have played the game will absolutely agree. Basically if you are mid-fight and jump to the next scene usually by accident, the game loses all memory of said fight and all that you have is much less ammo to show for it. This is made worse by each section of the map being ridiculously small.
Meh:
1. Music is ok. Not great. They should also have breaks in it - playing for 5 hours straight I started to really notice this.
Overall, great great potential but I could not recommend the game. I certainly could see getting $1 an hour for this (for those that base value on that aspect).

You have free phase, for buffs/debuffs, dash phase, a chance to move out of the way, a blast phase, where everyone does their attacks at once, and a move phase at the end where you move your character, and each phase plays out simultaneously for everyone, in 4v4 pvp combat. You can play with and/or against bots if you prefer and complete daily missions this way too.
The problem is, it runs off of an almost SMITE-like business model, but scummy. You can buy ALL character's for $30, which is great, but they do NOT allow you to buy ANY characters at all with in-game currency. in-game currency is only for skins and ability augmentations. If you planned to pay $30 anyway to unlock all characters like you may have done in SMITE, then you will have no issue with this game and I recommend it. If you planned to play totally free, or slowly buy one or two characters and skins later if you liked the game, I wouldn't. They have a F2P rotation of a few characters you can play as a F2P player, but with no option to buy characters with in-game money, I can't suggest this game to anyone.
Good game, bad business model. Trion always finds a way to make something wrong with an otherwise great game.

Once you get a grip of the game mechanics and teamplay dynamics this game is a blast to play. For me it's like chess mixed with XCOM, then combined with hero abilities like in Overwatch or League of Legends with a pinch of borderlands character design/humour. It rewards quick thinking, planing ahead and outsmarting your opponent. All Freelancers have the tools for great mindgames which are the spice of this game.
If you have some friends to play with, do so. There is a high learning curve for the team dynamics and if you have a team of 4 it's easier to get into when you can communicate over the voicechat. But it's also enjoyable in soloqueue, just know your hero and the capabilities and you are good.
€30 is a bit pricey in my eyes if i compare it to other games, but the developers seem to be very enthusiastic about their game, i can only hope that this enthusiasm will stay with them for a long. Atlas Reactor is a rich game with very high replayability, if you are into a supercharged turnbased game, then i think it's money well spent.
Good thing there is a Free Version available, which let's you experience the whole game, the only downside is a limited Freelancer selection, which is random. Buying the game just unlock everything.
-----------------------------
Bottom line for me: Atlas Reactor is a great game with highly rewarding gameplay. Try it out first for a few hours, if you are lucky you get some really good Freelancers and if you like the game, consider spending the €30 to just unlock all Freelancer for convenience.

Frozen Synapse will make your head hurt, possibly in a good way. It's Flotilla with foot soldiers. You have a squad of guys who follow your orders to the letter; so does your enemy. The trick is you give orders in phases, and both sides execute their orders in real time. Ordered your men to walk up behind an enemy and blast him? Too bad, your enemy ordered that guy to turn around moments before you arrive.
It's pure tactics with no chance or twitch gaming in the way. Each battle is mathmatically solvable (To the point that you can simulate fights before you commit to your moves), there's no element of random here. It's a hard concept to wrap your head around, and you'll probably lose even the first single player mission many times before you get it, but once you do, there's multiple game modes, multiplayer, and an engrossing campaign to keep you hooked.

Despite a lack of love from PC gamers, Halo remains an interesting franchise with a number of fun games. But the series has as many flops as it has hits and Spartan Assault definitely falls into the former category. A top-down shooter, Spartan Assault lacks in variety and excitement. There just aren't enough weapons, levels, monsters or objectives, and the game very quickly becomes boring and repetitious. Far too many missions depend on keeping fragile NPCs alive, despite their having an intelligence that compares poorly to a flame-loving moth. I suppose one excuse for the game's poor showing is that it is, after all, nothing more than a downloadable arcade game, but seeing as other downloadable titles manage to offer far more fulfilling experiences, this excuse holds little weight. Three minutes into the first mission and I had seen pretty much all the game has to offer; ten minutes in and I was wondering if I should just write off my $5 and find something else to play, and three hours later - when I finally completed the last aggravating mission - I wondered why I had wasted so much time on such an awful game.

I also felt there could have been more interesting storylines developed around the several factions that reside in the Zone. I also wish the RPG elements had been improved upon. Experience points and level ups would have given me more incentive to explore areas of the map I didn't need to go to for specific missions, but as it stands I would rather just avoid coming into contact with unnecessary enemies since all I'd do is loose ammo and gain nothing as a result. I also wish the characters had been more complex and interesting, I had no real vested interest in any of the characters (even my own character was kind of a boring personality). Despite these areas that could have used improvement, I found the game to be very fun. Not a game I'll play more than once, but a game that was very enjoyable one time through.

Awesomeness:
Possibly a modern Indie classic (i.e. Spelunky). If your'e willing to sweat, this is a great taxation of planning, reflexes, and decision making. An amazing blend of oversight and both taut, moment-to-moment action and tense, slow suspense; all steeped in a Metroid-like, oppressive, sci-fi atmosphere.
It's awesome to see a game that's really about gameplay experience—the deep, technical practice of it and the tranported-to-another-worldness of it—in an era when cutscenes and postprocessing seem to consume 90% of AAA devs' efforts. Kudos, Alientrap.
Not-so-awesomeness:
Framerate issues: The devs seem very communicative and helpful and the game has progressed well, but I've encountered crippling framerate issues on my Macbook Pro (laptops seem to be main problems) (1-2fps in the later levels) since I first started playing it many months ago. I stopped playing for several months, hoping they'd fix the problems (they are very aware of them and have done a lot of work to address them), but coming back now I encounter the same problems in later waves. A "low detail" mode that they added staves off the problems till maybe a little later in the game than before, but I still face an invevitable degradation of performance until it's quite unplayable during the latter parts of a run. I've followed their technical  advice to improve performance, and I can run other major games fine on this computer (Starcraft II, Borderlands II), but CRYPTARK is still only playable for me for the earlier parts of the game.
I've still gotten tons of hours of great gameplay out of it, and it has been well worth my money, a few times over, but I very much hope I get to experience this whole game as it was intended to be experienced at some point (even without "low detail mode").

This game basically has everything: strategy, tactics, white-knuckle action, meticulous commando raids, brutal frontal assaults, resource management, realistic physics, great art, great music, humor, a million distinctive different weapons and items to play with.
The basic plot is that you're part of a space salvage crew who've won a big contract to strip ancient alient technology out of a fleet of derelict starships. But even though the aliens are long dead and their ships drifting with nobody at the helm, there are plenty of internal security systems still in operation: turrets, semi-autonomous drones, and other nasty surprises. So before the main salvage crew can go in and start tearing stuff out, somebody has to get to and disable the main security control system--and this is where you come in.
The developers care about the little things and that takes this game from good to great. The first time I left my shuttlecraft through the airlock, the music and SFX volume both dropped and I thought I'd found a bug--then I realized it was because I was now in space where sound doesn't carry. Sure enough, once I entered the derelict (but still pressurized) hulk through its airlock, the sound picked right back up.
The premise of why you're blowing up all these drones--who weren't bothering you before you came onto their ship uninvited, remember-- is so simple as to be refreshing: you're doing it because you're getting paid to. On top of everything else great about this game, there's a distinct contrast between your employers (a group of reptillian humanoids in suits and ties with posh English accents), and the multispecies blue-collar salvage crew who actually get things done. There are times I found myself methodically cruising through a level, sniping at mobs here and blowing up security systems there, that I found myself thinking "Just another day on the job." I haven't beaten the game yet so maybe it ends with an interstellar proletariat seizing the means of production--your crew maybe keeps the xenotechnology for themselves instead of turning it over to the Contractors, and if the Contractors don't like it, they can come and try to take it.
In short, if you like science-fiction roguelikes, twin-stick shooters, or joy and happiness, you owe it to yourself to try this game.

WARNING: THIS IS A REVIEW COMPLETELY BASED ON IT'S CURRENT STATE, PROS AND CONS ARE SUBJECT TO CHANGE.
I would recommend this game to anyone with the taste of being able to commandeer said made machines and roam an open world map full of quests, sidequests and lots of hidden secrets...
PROS:
-Beautiful music, fits all the different scenarios, like an intense battle with other privateers or arriving at a mysterious temple shrouded with fog and mystery
-The crafting is impressive, and it takes EFFORT (not like the "effort" of recent video games with this sense of genre)
and dedication to complete tasks, as such making said item for a NPC and such, and not to leave out the immense size of the crafting variety. And lastly a neat little tab system where different types of items would fit into, making the list of craftables a lot less intimidating.
-The UI overall is great, if not a little under-res, the colours are fitting and it looks like a UI that had time put in it.
-The stat system is great, it's compiled of agility, vitality, strength and wisdom and another couple. but the reason it's so good is that it is just that. a little bar that has a couple of milestones that come with awesome perks.
-Lastly, the story system. I love it! it is very gripping and i enjoyed every encounter with a fellow NPC, and the idea of the game's origin and story is compelling and not seen elsewhere.
CONS:
-The MAJOR thing i wanted to point out is the performance coding. it is absolutely horrible; there i am, chugging along in my airship untill i hit a town, and during my visit my fps (averaging at 120fps) drops to about 15 and shoots back up as soon as i leave the VICINITY of any town. and this thing crashes at least 2 times on one of my average sessions.
-The low resolution of the UI is a definite thorn on the rose. Get that tuned up.
-The combat system lacks and feels very slow, whenever i'm in a gun fight the projectiles move so slowly i imagine i'm the guy from the matrix and i pretend to duck and jump over them... and the damage of both myself and the enemy (the humans that is) are just making it look like we were fighting with nerf guns
-The crafting can be a bit intimidating if one takes a glance, and can sometimes be a bit TOO much effort, because either it's just me or the game because my greatest challenge so far is finding sand to make a glass bottle.
-You should only be able to repair in a close proximity.
Thanks for reading my review and i hope you all enjoy the game if you buy it now, but if you wait keep this game in the watch list, because it has great potential and its gonna have multiplayer! :) Have fun!

Mutant Mudds is essentially the retro revivial platformer that most people are looking for, it feels distinctly retro with modern touches. If you're looking for a well made platformer this is the one.
The only downsides I can think of is that the ice physics can be weird (Sometimes they even affect your speed and control while jumping.) and since the PC version lacks the 3DS's 3D funtion the different planes can sometimes become a bit confusing (With this mostly being an issue on the ghost levels since the enemy colors are harder to see in general.)

The physics in the game are lots of fun. The game is reminescent of Terraria, with superior controls, but it lacks the depth and variety. The game has a great asthetic, but a few problems and glitches really rob the game of its potential. Key items (i.e. vulcan forge), manage to disappear from your inventory such that they can't be replaced. Occasionally, critical story elements are skipped and the story can't advance as a result. The penalty (or lack thereof) of dying seems to undermine the challenge of the game. Finally, the game could use a bit more variety: you'll run through nearly all of the random encounters possible on your first trip to a different city--well before you complete the game. Also, the weapons are quite redundant. Summary: the game has great potential, but its nearly too glitchy to finish, and lacks the substance needed to reach its potential. I recommend the game, but it could be so much better with a few minor adjustments.

So, Cryptark.
The latest patch end of march 2017 has been a long time coming.
Too long probably.
Performance problems have all been solved.
The main gripe most people have is the difficulty of the game.
After trying the latest patch, I would actually recommend the game. Especially when discounted as it is now, it is a no brainer.
What you get for that :
You are a mercenary in mech suit in side/topdown view, with beautiful graphics, exploring a fleet of spaceship wrecks until the final one, facing ennemies and ship systems to reach the brain of each wreck and disable it.
Each level gives you the choice amidst 4-5 wrecks with side objectives to fulfill for additional financial reward.
Fulfilling all side objectives gives you bonus.
Furthermore, some wrecks have an artifact you will get if fulfilling an additional condition, artifacts are used to unlock more Mech suits models with different abilities.
You begin the game with a budget.
You can "die" and restart a level as long as you have the budget to do so.
The latest patch balanced the game with less strict secondary objectives (but still some VERY bothersome ones like 3 hull max HP, or 40k budget).
You choose your mech (7 are available unlocked with artifacts), equip it with 4 weapons/shield, choose to fill 3 utility slots like health kits / passive kinetc buffer.
What you can equip is unlocked as you gather technologies in the wrecks you explore, from nuclear grenades, electric arc saws, heavy machine guns etc.
The shield is pretty much a mandatory equipment to protect yourself from lots of enemies and damage. The last level being quite hellish in terms of enemies present.
The wreck ship systems are such as :  drone factories spawning enemies regularly, shield protecting other systems, repair systems repairing over tim other systems, shuffling systems moving systems around every minute.
Dealing with them requires some planning and strategy, specially when wanting to fulfill secondary objectives to get big bucks.
The game can be quite brutal for newcomers until understanding some priorities and ways of playing.
Planning comes first : which system to go for first. when to fight, but also when not to fight and run away.
Acquiring the reflex to use your shield etc.
----
My advice is to focus the choice of the wreck you are gonna explore based on how realistic accomplishing secondary objectives can be done.
Fulfilling all the 3 secondary objectives will give you far more money in the end that a wreck with better reward money but non realistic objectives.
Take your time. Know how to rush to some bothersome systems.
Don't hesitate to invest in equipment really. Even a 200-300k setup will be profitable in the end if you manage to accomplish all objectives.
I recommend to systematically avoid budget restriction objectives.
They make the game boring when you can not rush the wreck's core.
For a long time I found the game too hard but accepting to sometimes blow up and fail and going for realistic objectives are keys to have fun.
Abuse the shield mechanic.
Know that nuke grenades are awesome, along with the nuclear reactor shooter ...
And spend your budget ; ♥♥♥♥ the budget restrictions really.

Dunno why the metacritic score for this game is so low. I've played Minecraft, Terraria, Starforge, and Edge of Space (and tons of other procedural games), so you could say I'm into these types of games, and Ive actually had my eyes on this one since the days when it first entered greenlight (i actually voted for it). Finally got my hands on it, and I gotta say, of all the games ive mentioned above, Windforge was the right-off-the-bat funnest game, and it also shows the most promise. Right now, its an early access experience like you might expect, but the ship mechanics are awesome, the dungeons are tons of fun, and the balance between grinding materials/buying from merchants/unlocking schematics is leagues ahead of the other procedural gen games familiar to this.
If you like the genre, you're bored, and can spare $15, this game is worth it, if not now then at least for what it will be with sufficient backing and dev support.
The current bad parts just really have to do with content and variety. All that is probably bound to change, but to name a few in case the devs are watching, more enemy ship types at all stages of the game, more towns (maybe scattered small villages? just for the merchants? or even friendly merchant ships?) and definitly more enemies.
the biggest bug that's bothered me is randomly some items, after being crafted or purchased, wont move into my inventory, it will simply dissapear. That means the materials/dollars are gone. lost as much as 30k in one shot once. thats a lot for where i am in the game.
Otherwise its a wonderful experience and i will definitly keep playing and having fun while the devs do their work.
EDIT
My hours have continued to rack up in this game. Got a lot of things on my mind but wanna keep it short. The biggest thing is content (theres too few of it). I mean, obviously its early access and the game isnt finished, but for those wondering whether it will be a "complete experience" if they purchase the game right now, well it really depends on their expectations.
The fundamentals are there though. The ship-to-ship combat remains incredibly satisfying, theres tons of freedoms for modifying your ship (construction choices will seriously influence the way you explore/fight/survive), and after a little while the 2.5D graphics grow on you. At least they did for me. World seems to have a lot more detail and a bit of much needed depth. Yea, I guess construction can be a bit clunky, but personally I have adapted wonderfully. Its not perfect by no means, essentially if you want to have some precision, you wont be building anything fast. But destroying stuff with your jackhammer feels pretty good (especially with high strength), the grapling gun is just about the most amazing mechanic in any builder so far other than probably the ship mechanics. You can swing around, rappel, pull things, fly about basically like spiderman (after practice), with just one mouse button and WASD.
But again, need more content. More dungeons, more towns, more enemy ships and more everything. The game world is huge, and there should be more content propelling you out there into the dangerous unknown. Do you know how cool it is engineering a combat/exploration-worthy vessel air-tight-ready for the Gas? Then only have to employ it a couple of times? Oh wait, that second bit aint cool at all. But its the reality right now.

I forgot to mention this, because my PC's pretty meaty, but even it dips significantly in framerate every once in a while in this game, but sometimes for persistant amounts of time. I've seen others complain they cant run this game on a laptop (which seems rediculous to me in this age of computing), so be forewarned.

A free game with no danger of running out of content, Warframe is a contantly evolving, constantly improving game that has bullet jumped its way quite a distance from its original brief.
As you may have guessed, Warframe at its core is a co-op third-person shooter with a focus on mobility, combined with an RPG. This, combined with its beautiful aesthetics (Digital Extremes have taken great pains to make sure the game scales back comfortably for lower powered machines), ever-deepening lore and the more recent focus on 'cinematic' story missions leave plenty for everyone.
If you were concerned about Pay to Win - don't be. The premium currency of the game, Platinum, is used to either accelerate processes or buy cosmetics. It can also be traded with other players, meaning you can sell mods or parts to get hold of it without spending anything. Should you choose to buy platinum to support DE, be aware that the daily login bonus can occasionally give you a discount of up to 75%.
If you have questions about the game, I suggest consulting the Wiki, which is very well maintained by the community. Otherwise, ask in regional chat.
Oh, and to save you asking in-game: the Plains of Eidolon content is available from Cetus, on Earth.

No but seriously this game is really good. I started playing moba's with dota 2, but it is fairly dificult to get into. I kept going and after a while I finally started to know the game and what to do. With awesomenauts, it is a really big difference. Because it looks and actually is as well a platformer, it looks a lot easier then dota 2. It is actually, when you play the tutorial the basics are explained and.... Well to be honest there isn't really more to it. Not in a bad way, you see i've only played this game for about 3,5 hours when i'm writing this review, but I know actually quite a bit.
Now, to go into gameplay, the mechanics are easy, you don't have to use your keyboard to do abilities. In fact you only have 4 or 5: A basic attack(Left mouse button), 2 abilities(Middle mouse button and right mouse button) and a jump(Which is just W, and how you move yourself upwards and a spell to go back to your spawn.
The cooldowns on abilities are very low, and you can't really dodge other players, because it is 2D. So there is a lot of action and a lot less of farming and you don't miss the 4 extra players(because this game is 3 vs 3, instead of 5 vs 5 what other moba's use).Once you level up and become stronger with your character depending on your solar(money). You don't have to choose which ability you level up like with other moba's, but you do that with your money. Because of this you can't buy many universal items, the most are dependent on their abilities. There isn't mana which stops you from using abilities, but there are just cooldowns, stuns and slows etc. There are still updates and patches coming out, as well as new heroes. There is one compaint I have with this game: It uses hosts instead of servers. I can understand it, because you're a small company and this spares a lot of money and it is only 3 vs 3, but people getting a advantage with that is just really stupid.
About the soundtrack: This is, in my opinion, one of the best features in the game: every hero/awesomenaut/character has an individual soundtrack. This really makes the music fun to listen to, because you don't have that the music gets boring, because you listen to the same tracks every game.
In other words: a really fun game which helps getting people into moba's really well. It is really easy to learn which is just a huge plus, not having to spend almost 100 hours to learn a few mechanics of a game. I bought this when it was in the sale, for just 2,49, but I think it is definetly worth the 9,99 as well.
I give this game a 9/10.

I played that game a hell lot when it came out in 2006. And it was great ! Really.
Though even if i remember enjoying the game for its graphics and all the freedom it was giving me, i always felt a bit disapointed by the lack of depth and restraints comparred to its predecessor. But hey, the game was so lively and had stunning HDR effects !
And so 10 years later i wanted to go back in it, immerse myself in Cyrodill and, sincerly, i shouldn't have tryed... Oblivion simply couldn't deliver what it was offering to me anymore, for nowadays it's too overshadowed by how great Morrowind was in term of lore and mecanics.
What made Oblivion so promising was what were considered as stunning graphics in 2006. The sight of a fine HDR making lively environment, character being voice acted and such. But these aged so bad.
Even the artistic direction always been poor at its time. Characters design are horrible mainly because most of them were proceduraly generated by the engine, gameplay is stiff and akward and concepts that are inherited from Morrowind feel weird the way they are set.
I do recognize the game was kind of fun though, i mean most of the quests are pretty interesting and were quite a change from the regular fetch missions. Though the game brings you to supposedly epic moments like when you have to stand and defend bruma with a whole army of... 4 people, against waves of 2 by 2 daedra, and it feels really akward.
And even so, it only makes a third of the game.
Retrospectivly, it looks messy and clunky, from the way npcs act and move, the way they interract, trying hard to make you feels as if the game had a life on its own but it just doesn't work anymore.
I admit that it was a required leap for Bethesda in order to progress toward what has to become Skyrim, and it's still worth a try if you never played it just to realise the actual progression of the Elder scrolls serie. But if you want some Old school fashionned RPG, i'd rather recommend playing Morrowind again instead of Oblivion.
It's a matter of "Would you rather kill a god or just speed run thousands of same looking gates" thing.

To start, the gameplay is awesome, music is pretty good, weapon variety is nice and there's not too much difficulty in terms of understanding how the game works. You generally have 2 choices of ways to deal with a level: you can either try to go in guns blazing, mortars firing, lasers buzzing and rockets exploding, or you can play it slow and tactically. the first level or two, go ahead and go guns blazing. After that, you better make friends with the tab and shift keys fast. There's 5 ships in the game currently and the best is most defiently the salamander. It comes with hazard coating which protects you from fire and slime, important since 2 of your starting weapons are a flamethrower and a slime mortar, but it also comes with the all important melee saw which can be used as an offensive tool to kill or a defensive tool to knock enemys or bullets away. In general, make sure one of your weapons always has infinite ammo, be it from melee or from energy weapons, because you can run out easily in ships 4+ if you don't take enough ammo. As a general rule, explosives are awesome for taking out either juggernauts or ship systems. My favorite tactic with the explosives is nuke missiles to take out the systems since the explosion can damage systems even though some of them are shielded like the shield system. you can also use them to take out juggernauts, which you MIGHT have to do since juggies can go through ship walls, though it's balanced since they are huge targets and are SLOW. When your shields are down to no hull points, you can keep going, though you die in 1 hit, and speaking of, death sucks in this game. When you die, you lose your entire suit and an extra 100k on top of that. If you spend 350k+ on a ship and get screwed because you got lynched by juggernauts, you are out 450k. Until you are confident in your skills, ignore the "3 max hull" objective, because you will probably die.
Onto bad things about it: on later levels, unless you have a decent computer, your FPS will drop somewhat and will likely get you hit or killed. I would like to see some kind of graphics selector since a lot of things going on like that is crazy and kills my computer. I've also experienced some bugs in game. Once my game crashed while starting a mission and i spawned in with no weapons when I loaded the save. Another time, it crashed and i had to go into task manager to close the process so I could restart it.
In general, if roguelikes are your thing, this is a great game to play, and if they aren't, try it anyways. You might like it and if you do, you might find an entire genre you like.

I am sitting in my apartment now, and my soul is numb and weary.  A moment ago I was staring at a screen that tells me 'DEFEATED BY CRYPTARK'.  I must have stared at this screen for more than twenty minutes, dazed and unable to move.  My reward is negative one hundred thousand monetary units.  I have seen this screen before.  I have seen it many times.  Usually this screen angers me.  No... it usually enrages me.  The chair I'm sitting in is missing the right armrest because I tore it off in a fit of rage at the sight of this screen.  But this time is different.  The last level.  The last Artifact.  It is my goal, my mission, my reward, my... Precious.  I wanted it so badly.  Though I've tried in vain over and over again to quit this game, it beckons me.  It calls me.  Like heroin, I know this game brings me great pleasure.  But eventually, that pleasure will end in pain and emptiness.  To receive the last Artifact one must complete the mission with a 'Loadout' of a hundred thousand monetary units or less.  It is a seemingly impossible task.  After many futile and laughable attempts I finally stumbled upon a Loadout combination that brought me increasing success.  Time and time again I attempted this method, refining my strategy until this night I progressed much further than I ever had before.  Much much further.  With nothing but a Saw Arm Blade and a handful of nuclear grenades I snuck through the corridors and shafts, painstakingly murdering one by one the ancient long dead cybernetically animated creatures of the Cryptark.  I bathed their ship systems in nuclear fire.  I murdered them... until only one system remained.  The final Brain.  As I approached it, a mine lay in wait.  I saw it.  I attempted to delicately strike at it to destroy it while keeping my distance so as not to activate it.  I had but one life unit left after all my murdering.  I had used all the repair pods.  The mine exploded.  I don't know if I misjudged the distance or perhaps there was more than one mine.  I miraculously survived the explosion, yet through some sort of vile and twisted mockery of computation, some sort of insipid error of computer science, I was launched not away from the Brain system, but towards it, and pinned in a corner where I was cleansed of life and soul by its purifying energy waves of death.  It happened so fast.  I was so close.  Now I am dead.  My spirit floats among the grinning skulls of prehistoric aliens, haunting the Cryptark forever.  I am not angry now.  I am glad it is over.  The fear.  The anxiety.  The dread.  It's all over now.  I am at peace.

Assassin's Creed: Rogue is essentially Black Flag Lite. Considering that Black Flag is considered one of the best in the series (My personal favorites include BF and Brotherhood), it would make sense that they would try to make that lightning strike twice. The product we have is a shorter, slim version of Black Flag.
This is not necessarily a bad thing. Black Flag was plagued with one issue: It was riddled with "Follow the people and eavesdrop" which was one of the most annoying things I had to endure. It balanced out with greatly refined Naval combat (First introduced in AC3 but did next to nothing for you) and colorful characters that you empathized with and care about. They're trying to do the same thing in Rogue but with a smaller cast and more streamlined combat.
For example, metal was a commodity in BF that you had to cause a ruckus at sea and get wanted levels to face against higher level enemies. In Rogue, -every- enemy ship carries metal and you'll find your ship upgrade a hell of a lot quicker than in BF.
The same idea translates to the main story which hauls♥♥♥♥♥ Every mission seems to throw 5% completion on my save file. In ten hours you may very well already be at 50% completion which seems a bit short considering it's original asking price (I pre-ordered the deluxe, which is a bit cheaper now).
In essence, they trimmed the pointless fat of Black Flag but failed to replace it with substance or content, but that's still not a dealbreaker if you left BF thinking "I wish there was more sea stuff". Even then, Rogue didn't add much to it, but instead gave you more reasons to do it. If that makes sense.
Storywise, it's actually one of the more interesting ones. I still care very little about the "modern day" aspect of the games (Though I'm happy Desmond is out of the picture) but we're put in the shoes of an Assassin that witnessed (And unwittingly caused) a great disaster because the Assassins are meddling in things they don't completely comprehend, and did not take Shay Cormac's words in account when he is distressed at the mess they caused. After being shot off a cliff, Shay then meets several Templars that seem to refrain from the usual "Kick the dog" moments of series past and still press their goals with all the manipulation involved. Shay is out to stop the assassins from making more of a mess and keep them from accidentally (Or purposefully) murdering thousands of people at a time.
The story is clearly painted with the "Templars aren't really that bad, okay?" brush, but still offers the opposite opinion that I had been waiting for. We get a little more of that in Unity with Elise, who also isn't a knee-breaking lunatic.
Ultimately it's a great game. It's Black Flag: Templar edition. It's not as expensive as it was, so nab it now or on sale. It's not a bad buy if you're a fan of the franchise.

I keep seeing people say that this feels like early-access, and I agree. The inventory system is a joke, crafting is clunky, enemies often randomly despawn if you so much as blink, temples are annoying as all hell...
But... good lord do I love this game!
It caught my eye early-ish in development and seemed like an interesting premise, but the not-so-great reviews when it came out made it seem like quite a let-down. Seeing it in a bundle, I went for it, as I was curious.
And despite its faults, this game would be worth full-price.
The whole "the ocean is the sky!" concept is great fun. The music is beautiful. The crafting, despite its clunky nature, is quite nice. But more than anything, what really makes this game stand out is its absolutely amazing atmosphere.
I can't remember the last time a game drew me into its world as efficiently as this one has. From the forested skylands of the mid-realm, to the airy plateaus and meteor showers of the upper realm and down to the downright alien poison gas-choked lower realms, I haven't had this much fun with exploration in a long time. Good job.
It's not without its faults; far from it. But as far as I'm concerned, the good very much outweighs the bad and the ugly.
Devs are still working on it, so some of the issues may yet get resolved. If they don't, I do hope they learn from their mistakes in the sequel (and I do hope they make a sequel).

It's a shame that this game doesn't depict the war between Assassins and Templars as one of an ideological nature. Instead, it is the Assassins who now go about irresponsibly with pieces of Eden whereas the Templars ought to stop this from continuing, which reduces the story to a shallow battle of good vs. evil. That being said, the gameplay heavily relies on Black Flag, but that's allright by me. It works fine, and I primarily play Assassin's Creed games because of the narrative anyway. Also, although not very credible, it is pretty badass to play as a Templar, which explains the many hours I have put into it. I always like to think of this game as a gathering of many good aspects of some strategy classics from back in the day, such as  Empire Earth, Age of Empires, Total Annihilation, and Civilization II. It is a gem of the strategy genre that many are yet to experience, and should soon.
Difficult to point out special virtues in RoN. Perhaps the 18 technologically and aesthetically delineated civilisations, or the fast-paced urban improvements and clever use of the Academy as the core of a settlement's upgrades. Perhaps the military attrition that has just the right rhythm, allowing both the player and their opponents to constantly and progressively advance in warfare capacity and strength, and in a match each invasion feels like a whole new emotion - much harder to bring down an adversary in one shot here.
It is also commendable the way BH Games found to display a balanced, yet challenging temporal advancement system that takes you from the classic age to contemporary conflicts and geopolitics. You improve your technologies and expand your settlement across the neighbouring territories (and yes, the territories are another exciting feature in RoN) as you are justly rewarded with the chance of gripping at the next moment in human progress. I've seen few strategy games in which age advance is so balanced and perceptible through the player's actions and upgrade management (a system very similar to Empire Earth II, by the way).
The Extended Edition looks fresh, especially visually. However, and this could be something particular to my system – I’m yet to find out –, the buildings and upgrades icons are missing, and I hope a future update shall remedy this little issue (edit: it is apparently a first-launch issue; for those having the same problem, just quit and restart the game, and all icons should be back on). Apart from that, looks like good old RoN to me thus far.
Rise of Nations can snatch many an hour out of your weeks, a strategy masterpiece with which I have a history, not in vain, since its replayability factor is always able to drag me back to it and renew that history bringing to it more pleasurable gaming experiences. Besides, I can finally say that Steam has come miles closer to bringing all my dream games to its repertoire.

The question on most of the minds of people who played this game:
Does it hold up?
Yes.
Unlike Age of Empires II which, in my opinion, sadly doesn't stand the test of time, Rise of Nations is every bit as fun and engaging as it was more than ten years ago. It's also still a bit of a mess in its late game moments, which I'll address a bit later.
First off, for any new players donning their commander cap for the first time, what is Rise of Nations? It's best described, I think, as a cross between Age of Empires and Civilization. It is a real-time strategy game, first and foremost - worker units are recruited and instructed to gather the expected resources in food, wood, gold, iron, and later oil. They'll also construct military barracks, universities for gaining knowledge (which you'll spend to research technologies and advance through the ages), castles and forts for locking down territory, and perhaps most importantly of all - cities.
You'll begin the match with one city. Structures like temples and forts will push your borders out a bit for you, but the only way to really expand your territory effectively is to build new cities. You can then recruit from your new city more villagers, which will proceed to build all the same farms, temples, lumber mills and schools you constructed at your first city - and eventually, you'll start the whole process over again. There's a great sense of satisfaction in watching each of your cities grow from a humble huddle of townhouses to its full sprawl of market, temple, barracks, school and more.
Cities, as I mentioned, expand your borders, which are important primarily due to unit attrition. You can move your workers and military units within your own territory unfettered... but set foot on enemy lands, and you'll notice a red glow pulsing at their feet and a health bar that will slowly begin to dwindle. Supply wagons can be built, and as long as your units are within its effective range, they can pass into enemy lands without fear of damage. Should your wagon(s) be destroyed by the enemy, your units will immediately begin taking damage over time. In this sytem of attrition and supply, Rise of Nations creates a very unique combat game that can force the retreat of a march larger force or encourage players to slug it out along borders where they can effectively fight without fear of attrition.
As stated above, you'll progress from the sticks and stones of the ancient world on through the crossbows and knights of the middle ages - the tanks and bombers of the World War II-era modern age, ending finally in the information age, where stealth bombers and ICBMs run amok. It's exciting and interesting to see what units will open up to you in each era, and every civilization has several unique units available to it throughout time that inject enough variety to encourance players to give them all a try.
As I also stated above, the end-game of Rise of Nations is definitely its greatest weakness. One would expect the introduction of fighter jets, bombers, nuclear warheads and rocket artillery to be pretty exciting, right? Well, it mostly ends up creating a huge mess of a battlefield where's it's almost impossible to keep track of what's going on, who's killing who, or what's best effective against what. As nuclear warheads begin to drop and level cities, and certain technologies completely remove the wait time for recruitment (meaning you can keep clicking the "Rocket Artillery" icon and it will keep building them click after click after click instantly), the game loses any sense of cohesion and almost feels like a test of who can control complete and utter chaos.
Luckily, the custom options in the game allow you to not only set a limit on how far the game can progress (IE: you can stop all further advancement at the Gunpower Age, so no one can build anything more advanced than a musket), but also how quickly you can advance. At the slowest settings, you'll likely be able to fight several battles with each age's loadout of units - though you'll also be waiting around quite a bit longer for your research to complete.
Overall, I'm happy to report that Rise of Nations is still a whole lot of fun. It lacks the depth of a game like Civilization V, and the combat will feel pretty basic compared to more tenacious RTS fare Starcraft II and Company of Heroes 2 - but there's really something to be said for a game that can marry the territorial expansion and slog through time of the Civilization with more bread and butter RTS mechanics. It you enjoy strategy games, it's a steal at $20.

So I initially played the "F2P version" of this game, and was primed and ready to give it a negative recommendation based on that. The way the "F2P" is handled in this game is absolutely mind-boggling, and I was extremely turned off by it (and this was compounded by the fact that Trion has/had a hand in it). There's no in-game currency, meaning you can NEVER earn new characters; you're stuck with whatever the free rotation decides to give you for the week. Not only does that completely suck balls as a consumer, it's is a death sentence in a game that thrives on team composition. And as an extra special "F*ck you", they hardcap the number of loot boxes you can open... cuz reasons? Needless to say, I was ready to drop my negative review for the absurd business model alone... but then I played the game some more.
After playing a few rounds, the gameplay itself is CRAZY fun. Like, I'm thinking about the game when I'm not at home "fun". I ended up buying the $30 pack (no reason to get the others IMO), got access to the characters I actually found interesting, and I'm having a blast now.
The marketing for this game suffers from a serious case of miscommunication; this game is by no means a F2P title at all and shouldn't be labeled as such. The "F2P version" is more akin to a trial version, and Atlas Reactor should essentially be seen as a $30+ game with a demo. Mutant Mudds is a platformer where you have to take it slow, and analyze how to best use the different mechanics at your disposal (jumping, shooting, floating for a brief moment, and later in the game, doing a rocket jump) to beat enemies and avoid hazards, so you can advance through each stage.
This game is definitely not for the impatient! It gets progressively challenging, and the ghost levels are specially difficult because you can't kill the enemies, but to me, the game never went to the point of being frustrating or unfair. Also, once you get the rocket jump upgrade, you can use it to complete many difficult platforming sections with ease.
I also wanted to mention that the chiptune music in the game is, IMO, amazing. I can't remember the last time I heard such lively, catchy and well-made tunes in an indie game.
With 80 levels in total, cool art, excellent music, and very fun but challenging gameplay, I wholeheartedly recommend you buy Mutant Mudds if you enjoy platforming games.
I recommend this game even at full price, and if you wait for a sale, it really is a steal!

-The Old Gods (Set start date back to 867; Play as Vikings and Pagans)

-The Republic (Become filthy rich as the Venetians)
-Charlegmane (Set the start date back another 100 years from Old Gods)
To conclude I can say no more than buy this product if:
-You love history
-You love other Paradox games
-You enjoy grand strategy

Probably my favorite game of all time - most of time in this game was on my old Xbox 360 verson, but I just recently bought it again on here.
I can't say enough good things about this game, I really can't.  In an age where resource gathering/survival games seem to be all the rage, even though they provide no real point to them (i.e. no story, no goal besides surviving which isn't even a challenge after a certain point), the Elder Scrolls series (and games like it such as the Fallout series) still shine supreme in my opinion.
Incredibly huge world to explore (made all the larger via the expansions and the mod community), countless quests/stories to complete (if you so choose), decent interaction with the NPC's in the game, and a decent variety of baddies to fight.  I played this game off and on for probably three years on my old Xbox and never touched the main campaign.  Granted, if you sit at your computer everyday for hours on end, you can knock it out fairly quick (if you just burn straight through the main quest arc ignoring everything else along the way), so don't get me wrong.  However, take your time exploring, talking to characters, completing quests, etc. and I think you'll find this game sucking away days of your life before you know it.
If you buy the game, buy the "Game of the Year" edition as it comes with all of the downloadable content.  If the game is on sale, that's great, but this game is worth every penny in its asking price.  As I write this, the "Game of the Year" edition is a steal at $24.95 (even better if it's on sale), but I would happily have paid $59.99 for the game again and paid for the downloadable content separately - that's how much I love this game.
Who do I think would *not* like this game?  Anyone looking for a fast paced "run 'n gun" type of FPS (like Call of Duty) is probably not going to like this game's slower more deliberate pace.  That is slowed down even more if you take the time to explore everything in the game.  If you want to run through the main quest only, I'd say you could probably knock it out in about 25 hours.  If you take the time to do all there is to do, you're probably looking at anywhere from 100 to 200 or more hours - that's how much stuff there is to do in this game.  Games to compare it to - the Far Cry and Fallout series are about the only two other games that I've played like this one.  If you liked those, you'll like this one.
If I have a grip, it's that after playing Skyrim, I miss some of the features that were implemented into Skyrim (better crafting system where you could make your own armor, weapons, enchantments, etc.) that this one is lacking.  However, that's an incredibly minor complaint and it's nothing that should preclude you from looking at this game.

This is a great game to play, though I'll admit, it would of been much better if it had at least a co-op only because of the hilarity that could occur from such.
I loved the combat system, the grappling hook, and the music, though it would of been nice to have a slightly more upbeat song playing during combat, especially in the temples... I'll touch base on each of these of course.
The combat system: I loved the fact that you could fly your ship around and man the guns directly or from your control panel, which allowed you to either directly shoot at them from the turret, or fly around shooting sparatically at your opponent(the ai) not to mention that you could leave your ship, use your grappling hook to grab onto an enemy airship and climb aboard for a good old fashioned pirate raid. :D  I'll admit I wasn't a fan of using melee weapons(I discovered that you could use them to dig faster than your starter mining tool...) but I did play around with them abit and found that if I had chosen a good starter or built up my strength and vitality, it would of been a very interesting way to play.

Let's start with probably the most important thing: This is for all intents and purposes an amalgamation of past AC games. It uses the sailing mechanics of Black Flag with some of the places, characters and climbing of AC3. That said, it is perhaps the best parts of each of them.
The only problem was that it was too short, only 6 sequences. It felt much more like a place-holder or an explanation of the intervening years, than a full entry. Before I knew it, I had already accidentally finished most of the side missions and made it through the story.
The main character is interesting though and it's clear why he does the things he does, but the problem isn't with Shay. You never have to ask why he turns against the Assassins, but you will wonder why the Brotherhood is doing what it is that makes him leave. And the Templars don't have any better motivation in their grand plan other than just combating the efforts of the Assassins.
The modern day storyline is similar to Black Flag in that you play as another nameless, faceless Abstergo Entertainment employee who gets to go around providing IT support for coworkers while they're away from their desks. Every now and then you're pulled back to modern day to run an errand and find some misplaced iPads and then you get to go back to Shay. Sadly, Abstergo has gotten better at covering up their dirty laundry and the only information you get from hacking computers is about the people you're working with and the upcoming projects that Abstergo/Ubisoft have in the works. Maybe some day they'll actually make good on their teasing for a full-fledged Assassin's Creed entry set in China or Japan or India.
