"When taking off the rose-tinted glasses of how much this game was a success was from the shadow of Unity (basically, this game actually worked whereas Unity didn't), what we're left with is a game that, though it plays decent, fails in the sense of story. It added many new weapons from its predecessor (Black Flag), though the only one which was actually really *new* was the grenades, and added an admittedly interesting gas mechanic to the game. It also was much more filled and felt significantly less grindy than Black Flag; these were all great improvements to the series from the previous title, but unfortunately, these are the only positive things I can say about this game. What this game made up for in being playable, it lost in a dissapointing lack of charm.
**The remainder of this review contains massive spoilers, referrencing the end of the game**
Either due to false marketing on the community's behalf or on Ubisoft, we're lead to believe that the main character, Shay, is the victim of a massive betrayal and seeks revenge against the brotherhood. This story sounded interesting, and for many of us, it was the first time we'd see the story from a Templar's point of view. Or at least, that's what I expected, but not what I recieved. Shay was never the victim of a betrayal, but rather the victim of a mistake in which no one was guilty. Rather than confront his Mentor about what he witnessed, which would be the logical thing to do, Shay gets unrealistically emotional about the situation and blames everything on his Mentor. He then consciously decides to betray his brotherhood, and is retaliated against accordingly.
What follows isn't a story of revenge against the backstabbing brotherhood, but rather a convoluted scheme to stop a man who ends up listening to his own conscience in the end anyways, rendering Shay's entire mission completely pointless. He decides, for no other reason than one of the British officers was nice to him while he was injured, to help his hated rivals, the Templars, and eventually join their Order and assist the British in winning the Seven Years War.
My biggest complain about this game is that under no point of this game do you ever see the positives in joining the Templar Order. The Templars were never painted as the good guys, rather the game regularly reminds you that they are the bad guys, and the reasons for Shay's complete dedication toward the Order seems to entirely ignore his high moral stance which directed him to betray the Assassins. There never seems to be a point, other than the rosey tone of a single man who dies before Shay even makes the decision to join the Templars, where I (the player) feel like I should actually want to be a Templar.
As if the feeling of "why on Earth am I killing the good guys?" wasn't enough to make the game feel horrible, the ending seals this game as completely unnecessary and makes no sense. I'm not referring to the mission in Versailles (though the mission itself feels like an unnecessary and shoe-horned-in shameless advertisement for Unity), but rather the Naval Missions. I was quite confused while trying to complete the Naval Missions (which must be completed if you are to unlock much of the best stuff in the game) in that they no longer let you complete them until you "progress further into the story." This was right before the last mission of the game.
In case that wasn't clear, let me restate this: The final 5 Naval Missions, which are required for completion and for unlocking some of the best gear in the game, doesn't get unlocked until you've COMPLETED the game. Why? Were the developers afriad that I'd be cheating with Altïar's Swords on a mission which doesn't even let you use anything other than your Hidden Blades? Why was this required? So that people would be forced to play hours more of the game after they already completed the story? Who thought this was a good idea??
Overall, I think the game is fine. I never felt like I was doing the right thing, but so what? Plenty of games let you play as the bad guy (though they usually leave out the high sense of morality that constantly reminds you that what you did was morally sketchy and highlights that you're actually the bad guy in this game). The Naval Missions is a cheap and pathetic move on the fault of the developers, but hey, **at least the game plays on PC, Montreal!!**. But would I recommend it, though? No. It doesn't add much from Black Flag, and unlike this game, Black Flag had characters I actually could **care** about. I couldn't have cared less if the characters died; the fact that two of them were Haythem Kenway and Achilles Davenport defeated the possibility of that happening anyways. Comparing that to Black Flag, or more accurately Black Beard, it was geniunely disastrous watching Edward Thatch die. We had actually come to care about him and his death was genuinely devastating. In AC: Rogue, however, none of the characters invoke that amount of compassion. None of the characters seemed to have any real life. When they died, it was difficult to really think anything of it.
This game is fine, but you'd be better off playing Black Flag. "

Devil Daggers is the closest thing I have ever seen to a perfect game. I have never played anything like it. You know, back when I used to play games for 30 - 40 hours every two weeks, it was divided between at least 3 - 5 games. In less than a single week, Devil Daggers has not only taken my playtime from the last two weeks from 4.9 hours to 20 hours+, but it has made up about half (as of writing this) of my normal two-week playtime TOTAL. As of writing this, with 16 hours logged (probably 4 of which were spent on the homescreen), my high score is 192 seconds. So what is it about this game that's so captivating? Well, I'm gonna explain it all.
The Visuals:
The low-poly 3D models mixed with an extremely low resolution and dark, gritty color palette make this game look very unique. Even when things are far away and they are being drawn using less of the massive pixels in the resolution, you can tell exactly what you're looking at.
The Game Mechanics:
I have NEVER played a game with game mechanics as tight and polished as this one. Not even the overrated games of today (CS:GO, Rocket League, Overwatch, and so on) can come close to this. It's not overcrowded with different game mechanics but what they have work together in a very meaningful and seamless way. From the Rocket Jumping, Momentum, and Two-Purpose Daggers with travel time, to the spawn times of the enemies, the swarm mechanics (which I've never seen done so well before), and the shape/size of the platform. Everything. Not ONCE have I died and considered myself to have been killed by anything other than my own incompetence, and for a competitive, score based game, that is very important.
The Sound Design:
You know, as an amateur musician and aspiring audio engineer and producer, great sound design gives me a boner. I have reached the point where I've trained my ear to notice every detail of every sound, so the more you treat my ear and the better your sound works with what's being shown on screen, the more I have to rave about it. And let me just say.. This is quite possibly the single best sound design I have ever had the pleasure of experiencing in gaming. The most recent Battlefield games come close, but the sound here is so excellent that with enough practice you could probably play the game blind. Also, despite having no obligation to do so, the developer has added support for 3D binaural sound, which means when played with the right headphones, the skulls are suddenly floating right past your ear and behind your head and it feels as real as a fly buzzing around in the room near you. Every action, every enemy, and every position has a clear place in the frequency spectrum and overall soundstage of the game. Every sound adds to how satisfying the gameplay is, and you can't play the game without it. Believe me, I've tried.
The Addiction/Replayability:
I genuinely fear that this game has already started to make whatever self control for gaming I thought I had vanish entirely. Every run feels completely unique, and even though I know I'm seeing the same enemies I fought last round, it still feels like an entirely new experience with new decisions to make, new problems, and new ways for me to get myself out of a pinch. Everything just feels so dynamic, and I've played games with way more content that got old way quicker (My interest is still growing and has yet to hit a plateau). This has led me to "one more round" myself past midnight and into the wee hours of the morning.
The Performance:
I own a normal laptop. Quad-core 2.2ghz AMD A8 processor with AMD Radeon R5 Graphics and 12 GB of RAM. Not at all suitable for gaming. Well, I still get a solid 60fps early on and it still remains playable to the very last seconds of my 192 second record. If you have ANY sort of GPU, you have nothing to worry about. This is likely due to the massive pixels, low-poly models, and the fact that all that exists in the game world is a platform and hundreds of demons on it. Who knows? Maybe it's also some good old fashioned optimization.. That seems to be rare today, especially with every developer these days hopping on Unity or Unreal Engine.
The Verdict:
It's 2 am, and I'm tired. Just buy the game. It costs about as much as a fast food meal and it'll be 50 times as enjoyable for many hours longer. However, if you do buy it, prepare for a real challenge, one created simply by crafting creative enemy types to be fought with solid game mechanics instead of the generic cookie cutter fps enemies of today.

Assassin's Creed: Rogue is a strange outing for the series, serving as a spinoff, an "interquel" (chronologically between AC4 and most of AC3), and something of a last hurrah for the series before it stepped into the next generation (and unfortunately tripped and fell with the release of Unity). It's a game I have very mixed feelings about, for while it is undeniably a good game, I can't help but feel some sense of disappointment, as I think it could have been so much better...
Performance: It works!!! After the absolute disaster that was Unity, I refused to buy another AC game for PC without waiting to see the community's response (Still can't get Unity to work for me over a year later). Obviously Ubisoft is making an effort to improve their treatment of PC releases, as this game runs, for the most part, beautifully on my machine with the graphics settings pretty much maxed out, and I run it on a laptop with a core i7, 2.5 Ghz processer, and an AMD HD8970 graphics card, so we're not talking about a particularly beastly computer here. The only real issue I encountered was a consistent crash to desktop as soon as the game started, unless I set the environment quality to normal, which seems to have been a somewhat widespread problem. However, this issue was easily resolved and hasn't affected my enjoyment of the game at all, so I'd say it's mostly negligible.
Graphics: The game looks beautiful, with some really breathtaking environments. Assassin's Creed is one of the only games that after years of play, I still find myself just stopping and looking around at the environment, in awe of the level of detail and love that went into crafting these historical recreations. Of particular note here are the stunningly reflective waters of the Riverlands, and the sprawling and lively cityscape of New York. With that in mind, however, it should be noted that many of the models and animations are ripped directly out of previous entries in the series. A lot of what you see comes from AC3 or AC4, and while this didn't bother me in most cases, one thing that greatly disappointed me was the animation set for Shay, the main protagonist. Almost all of his combat finishers and free-running movements are virtually identical to Edward Kenway's animations from AC4, who already borrowed animations from Connor in AC3. It really took away from Shay's characterization, and I found it especially disappointing considering Ubisoft went to the trouble of crafting new animations for Adewale in Freedom Cry, which was merely a DLC expansion for Black Flag. You'd think a full release with a new protagonist would get special treatment, but instead they just lazily recycled animations we've already seen before. Bad form, Ubisoft.
Sound and Music: I got chills when I started up this game and heard the opening theme. This brilliant piece weaves together themes from throughout the series' history, including the AC3 main theme, "Ezio's Family" from AC2, and a very Irish take on what sounds like the "British Empire" theme from Black Flag. It really brings on the nostalgia for the greatest moments of the series, and leads you to believe that you're about to witness a pivotal moment in the series' overarching plot (sadly, this doesn't quite come to fruition). Overall, the music is really great in this game, epic and grandiose, and I loved the Irish flavor they brought to the table to accompany the series' first Irish protagonist. As always, they really hit the nail on the head here. As for sound effects and voice acting, you'll hear a lot of familiar sounds from AC4, which didn't need improvement, and the voice acting is as good as ever.
Story: To me, this is where the game really failed to deliver. We were promised a plot that would turn the series on its head, showing us the world from the perspective of the Templars, blurring the lines and making us see the humanity in both sides. Unfortunately, I would argue that the opening sequences of AC3 already accomplished that much better than this game ever did. I wanted to like Shay Cormac, our rogue-ish hero, but I just never really cared all that much. Especially after the emotional rollercoaster of Edward Kenway's pirate adventures in AC4, everything here just felt cold and disconnected. Without spoiling too much, I'll say that Shay's motivations for defecting to the Templar's just didn't make sense, and the portrayal of the Templars seemed completely off-base compared to the rest of the series. The game just tries too hard to make you like them, and instead of feeling like we're getting a closer look at the humanity within the Templar cause, it just feels like the same old "honorable, compassionate good guys" vs "cold, inhumane bad guys" story we've experienced before, only with the names of the factions switched.
There's also a modern day story in between sequences, but it's largely uninteresting (though Osto Berg does seem like an intriguing character), and the little pieces of lore you find  by hacking computers seem more like Assassin's Creed wiki entries to flesh out popular characters than anything else. I miss the mystery of deciphering Subject 16's encoded messages in AC2, and even the hacked information in AC4 had some level of intrigue that's largely missing here.
Gameplay: It's Assassin's Creed 4: Black Flag through and through. Almost nothing has changed in terms of mechanics. You'll still free-run and counter kill your way across the land, and you'll still sail for miles and engage in furious naval battles across the North Atlantic. However, the series does add in some new features. Shay has a couple unique weapons, the air rifle and the grenade launcher. The air rifle is virtually identical to the blowgun from AC4, but it's still a cool weapon. The grenade launcher, however, is new. You can fire sleep grenades, berserk grenades, or shrapnel grenades, and it can be great fun to fire one into a group of enemies from a high tree branch and watch chaos ensue. Otherwise, however, Shay's weapons are pretty much the same as Edward's.
Another new feature is the new Stalker enemies. They will hide in places traditionally reserved for yourself as the Assassin. You can find them using a compass-like indicator only available using Eagle Vision. Then, you can either walk by and let them come at you, only to counter-kill them, or you can smoke them out and hunt them down. It makes traversing the city more interesting and more dangerous, as the Stalkers can pose a real threat if they get a hit in.
A lot of the game will be spent at sea, sailing and engaging in naval combat, and it's as fun as ever. Shay's ship, the Morrigan, is notably faster and more maneuverable than the Jackdaw from AC4, which really helps streamline the naval gameplay. The ship is also equipped with new weapons. The first is the Puckle Gun, an automatic side-gun that actually makes boarding ships too easy, as you'll probably take out all the enemy crew before your ship even gets close enough to jump over. The second new weapon is the burning oil, which allows you to leave trails of fire behind you, and is much more effective in losing a tail than the explosive kegs from previous games. Finally, you get an upgraded ram that allows you to actually control your charge. Another new naval feature worth mentioning is that you can now be boarded by enemy ships if they ram into you, which is a surprisingly exciting and chaotic experience.
Besides the main missions, there's a ton of side content. You can conquer the gangs of New York, raid forts, hunt animals to craft upgrades, and pick up a ton of various collectibles, including chests, animus fragments, the new prosperities which increase your income, viking swords, templar crosses, and more. The naval campaign also makes its return, and if you're really bored, you can just go play checkers at a bar.
My final score: 7/10 Great game in many ways, but I'd probably wait til it's on sale to pick it up.

Imagine you have a jack-in-the-box. It has two panels and only one of them will open when you crank the handle.
Panel one contains a delicious marshmallowey treat.
Panel two contains an unavoidable punch aimed right at your crotch.
You have no choice which of these two panels will open - only whether or not you choose to open the box.
100% Orange Juice is this jack-in-the-box. It is every rage game you've every played rolled into one cutesy little anime board game, and they've gone one extra step and removed all skill from the game so that you know there will never ever be an escape from the insanity.
Nothing you do matters. Nothing you try will succeed unless the Random Number Generator wills it so. You will witness a player on full HP  use their strongest cards against a player with no cards and 1 HP... and lose. You will be two spaces from winnng the game and the game board will reverse direction on you. You will be carrying 500 stars and just "happen" to roll the exact number that will dump you on the boss NPC's tile where he will proceed to play your♥♥♥♥♥like a banjo before taking all of them.
Well, not
of your stars. You only lose half of them when you're KO'ed. But that's ok. The moment you revive some other player will swoop in like Tarzan meets Chris Brown and beat another half of your stars from you, essentially relegating you to the position of spectator while all the other players race around levelling up from their ill-gotten gains.
Does this sound fun? If so, congratulations, you are a masochist! The truth is that in 9/10 matches you play, this game is
fun. It's frustrating beyond all words and the only saving grace is that the one match that you win will feel like heaven for the 5 seconds you have before you crank that handle again. In the end though, it's not worth it the misery it will inflict upon you.
Save yourself. Save your genitals. Don't open the box.

TL;DR: A short, slow-paced but pretty enjoyable retro-platformer, provided you buy it while it's on sale, are a big fan of the genre, have patience and good timing (granted, that's a lot of prerequisites, but I had fun! YMMV.) Also it's possible to play with a controller and I definitely recommend it!
Mutant Mudds is a "2.5D" (you can move between up to three planes in a level) platformer with correct (if not very varied) pixel graphics and a solid, classic gameplay that may remind you of Gargoyle's Quest in that you can hover during a jump. And also in how slow your character moves.
Get through 40 levels, 20 normal ones and 20 "dark-world" ones (arguably more challenging). Collect all tokens in each of them. Find the hidden warp zone in each of the 20 normal levels. Lather. Rinse. Repeat. With enough tokens, you can buy power-ups (high jump, longer hover or faster gun with longer range), but until you complete the main game, you can only use one of those at a time. Once you unlock everything you can, you get to use all power-ups together, which allows you to unlock further warp zones requiring good mastery of all your special moves.
Now you need to be way into old-school platformers and be quite patient because:
- Your character is SLOW. Forget about Super Meat Boy.
- While most levels aren't too difficult, you do need good timing to jump, hover and end up on blinking platforms.
- High jump requires you to press jump and ONLY up. This makes sections where you need to jump, move while hovering and then high-jump relatively frustrating. I still managed to unlock all achievements in about 8 hours of gameplay.
- Admittedly, there isn't a lot of variety in enemy sprites.
Conclusion: I bought it on sale, and got a nice few hours out of it. 6/10, no regrets.

The game has just been banned in my house for glorifying dogfighting, (I don't share the opinion, my mom is one of those moral guardians) so I figure that now is a good time to give my overall thoughts.
First, I'd like to address the issues. For one, this game is rather unpolished, most notably in the Retro stages where I encountered glitches with both myself and enemy dragons. In one instance I got stuck in a platform and needed to reset, another time my sprite duplicated. As for the enemies, they suddenly teleported to different areas and their flight patterns were in broken loops. But these issues seemed to be exclusive to Retro mode because thats the mode I played the most, and I didn't find any bad glitches in the other modes.
Visually, the game could use a touch up as well. I like the attempt at making it look like an older, pixelly game, but the scenery is rather bland, as well as the dragon models.
As for the gameplay, it was reassuringly responsive, and the enemy hitboxes are clear. It's got a good blend of difficulty, which, obviously, is a must in video games.
Overall, despite the setbacks, I enjoyed this game. Nothing spectactular but it did hold my attention as a time-passer. I'll give it a 3.5/5, and I hope it improves steadily in the future.

I remember seeing this on Gametrailers before it came out, with me naming it "Call of Duty: Batman Warfare". At the time, it did seem like it was cashing in on the CoD craze, but not that it looked bad by any means - just that every company was doing it. Still, I was big into the Arkham series, and I eventually bought the game prior to it becoming F2P, but idiotically never played it during that time. I finally got to it, and I'm finding so far is what to be a very entertaining and competent spin on the Batman world. I was surprised I did so well in my first match with a shotgun. The game has tons of variety due to different weapon types, loadout potential, and gadgets that change the way you traverse the map, including be able to move faster with rollerskates and jump ramps, jump on trapolines, fly with jetpacks or use grapple hooks - it makes the game more interesting than a prototypical "Shoot 'em in the back" maze shooter. From the little I played, the game seems to have decent amount of content in terms of maps, weapons and cosmetic unlockables. Unfortunately, there are only four game types, and at the time of writing, players only play Team Deathmatch. This means there is a lack of players (since I often ran in the the same groups of people) and may potentially mean that there are issues with the other game types. It's a shame really, because except for the fact that more experienced players have access to some better gear (like every other modern multiplayer shooter), I didn't see any gameplay balance issues. I think it's purely due to the multitude of multiplayer alternatives, and that the most popular shooters are the "modern realistic" theme. While finding a game isn't too difficult, the lack of overall players makes this a hard suggestion since it's a multiplayer only title with a pretty small player base.
It is free however, so it definitely won't hurt to check it out if you're interested in the premise, and a handful of players are high ranked, so you may find enjoyment in this for the long run if you don't mind that you will only be playing TDM or you're able to muster up some group of people to play. I can't suggest you spend money on this as it may "die off" sometime unless you fall in love with the game.
I see myself playing this more, but I can't say if that's one more launch or one more year.

Do you like tactical games? Frozen Synapse is a great real-time simultaneous turns squad-based game.
Confused? Don't be. Let me explain: You have two players, each with a team of soldiers. Each player picks his soldiers' moves secretly. When they're both ready, they submit their moves and they are played out simultaneously.
It's really nothing like anything I've ever played. It's great, refreshing, brain-twisting gameplay and that's the stuff that actually matters in games, trust me.
There are a few problems which should not go without mention though: First, there's no support for more than two players. So you can't play co-op against the computer and you can't team up with others. Second, the gameplay feels a little barren, sometimes, the gameplay elements are too few. You could use this same argument against chess of course, so I'm not sure how valid it is.
Overall, it's a unique game that plays well so it's all good in my book.

It's really good to see this game really come together since playing the stage demo last July. The music and art style is compelling and the game as it is right now is very replayable.
Basically the premise is you need to visit several derelict ships and blow up their cores without getting killed by the ship's defense systems (drones, turrets, nukes, alarm systems, other fun stuff). In each stage of 'campaign' mode you choose one ship out of several to heist, buy your loadout and devise a plan on attack. Each ship is procedurally generated and are like little dungeons. You can vary weapons and tactics depending on what you're up against, and how much challenge you like. You get income from completing the mission and bonuses for completing under certain conditions (depends on the ship).
'Rogue Mode' is new as of this week (end of January) and I'm enjoying it because it's much simpler. No economy, just weapon and item pickups, same high difficulty, global unlocks (suits, etc) as you progress through the game. Basically this mode makes it more like Nuclear Throne, which is probably GOTY 2015 for me.
It's easier playing with the keyboard / mouse combo, but I enjoy the game more kicking it with a controller, much like their previous game, Apotheon. Speaking of which, I'm pretty sure controller input has improved (as of Jan 2016) over the last couple of months.
We'll likely see a few changes here and there, already there has been some changes to how the difficulty ramps up, as well as the overall game economy curve. So far the changes have resulted in less raging from my end.
Cryptark is easily worth the asking price. You're not just supporting a Canadian indie dev, you're getting a great game.

Do you like Halo? Do you enjoy top-down shooters? Can you enjoy casual games?
Then this game is for you. This game is clearly a mobile app game, and is in no way an FPS. It does share the common core elements of the Halo series, in which (1) you play a Spartan, (2) you carry two guns (three if you count dual wielding), plus two types of grenades and can hit stuff hard, (3) you can drive vehicles (more on that later), and (4) you get to squish grunts as much as your little heart can handle.
Controls are a little awkward at first, although you quickly get used to them once you do the tutorial. I've found using the same controls for vehicles is a little awkward, but it's not too difficult to manage.
Unlike other Halo games, this one is splint into clear, distinct missions (with no checkpoints) where you control one of two Spartans in a battle re-enactment simulator thingamawhatsit. The storyline is nice, and it gives some background to each mission, but they're ultimately irrelevant as each mission is pretty straightforward (go keep those guys alive, go kill those, stay alive for this amount of time). You can gain experience, which you can use to buy equipment upgrades in each mission (and each mission alone), however I've found that it isn't totally needed. You can activate up to two skulls to multiply your experience gain in each mission, however I've used them simply to make each mission more challenging.
So to recap: you aren't getting Halo, you're getting a fun little shoot 'em up game that takes place in the Halo setting, and can probably be finished in a day if you cared to. If you think that kind of experience is worth the price, then go ahead and buy this little game. But just remember, while it says "Halo," you aren't going to get the Halo experience we've come to expect from the console versions.

One Way To Die is a text-based adventure game, where your goal is to make it to the Fun Park and back again without dying. The idea behind this game is pretty awesome, although the execution thereof is poor in my opinion.
Pros:
-Interesting idea, the fact that they tried something different with a text-based game breaks away from what we know with games nowadays
-A large amount of different deaths in the game
-It is free, and reasonably small in size
Cons:
-Idea is executed poorly, deaths are random and making it to the Fun Park and back takes forever
-No options with regards to resolution
-The game requires a lot of reading, if this is not your sort of thing, you will completely hate this game
Overall, the game has some novel ideas, which could have been executed better. Worth a look if you enjoy reading and have the time for it, otherwise avoid.

It's so sad to see the barrage of bad reviews and people complaining and getting refunds over the Denuvo DRM that was implemented, that they aren't seeing the game for what it really is. When there's nothing to complain about, people will always try to find something!
I will tell you though, that the integration of Denuvo DRM has not affected me or my outlook on this game. Not. One. Bit. I'm always online anyways, and Sega just issued a patch that only has it "check in" once a week, so I can still play the game if my internet goes offline for a bit. Even if I couldn't play, I could, y'know, go outside.
But on to the actual game:
I was very excited for the release of Sonic Mania. I've been a Sonic fan since I was a young boy, and this game just tickles all of my nostalgia senses. The level throwbacks, the new abilities (I *love* the Drop Dash), the bonus stages that are reminiscent of previous games past, the super fluid and very expressed animation, the fantastic level design... all of it is just wrapped up in one perfect package.
What really made me excited for this though, was when I heard that Christian Whitehead was the lead developer on it. I knew immediately the end result was going to be solid gold. I was not disappointed. I've only played for a couple hours, but I see myself playing for many more.
Hats off to Christian Whitehead, PagodaWest and Headcannon! I hope the success of this title allows you to bring us more Sonic Mania in the future!

Okay, so let's begin with the basics.
This game is now Free to Play!
This game is a cartoony 2D sidecroller platforming MOBA distilled to it's most essential components.
Here are the MOBA elements you'll find:
-3 on 3 combat. Forget huge and confusing team fights. Here, you'll have plenty of opportunities to work closely with your teammates.
-There are lanes (2 or 1 depending on the map) defended by turrets that you must destroy.
-There are minion like droids that you must use to push the lanes and destroy said towers.
-There is a base (aka Solar Drill) that you must destroy to win the game.
-There is a jungle element as there are neutral creep creatures that you can kill for some hp gain.
-There are super minion like droids that spawn when you destroy an enemy tower.
-There are a total of 32 unique characters. 4 of them are free to play weekly in a rotating fashion. You can also purchase new characters either with in game currency or with real money. It is also possible to unlock all characters plus the ones who will be released in the future for $30.
-Each character has their unique 3 abilities (2 cooldown based and one auto-attack ability with no cooldown) along with complete voice acting, an original theme song and purchasable (most of them with real money) skins.
-Upgrades that you can buy in the game shop when going back to base or after dying (3 per ability + 3 general passive upgrades)
-Skill shots, DoT based abilities, melee or ranged abilities, passive buffs or debuffs, etc.
-Nearly all the usual CC mechanics (slows, snares, stuns, hooks, switching abilities, knockbacks, freezes, silences, etc.)
-Brush like zones where your character is hidden from sight, perfect for sneaky ambushes.
Here are the platforming elements you'll find:
- Lateral 2D movement, Single, double, triple or even quadruple jumping, flying, gliding.
- Jump pads that enable higher jumps in certain directions, present in all maps.
- Falling down from ledges, perfect for dodging those pesky skillshots.
All this sounds fine on its own but is ultimately something you'll have seen in tons of games that have been released before, after awesomenauts or that have yet to be released, so what makes this game special and worthy of your time and possibly money? Well it simply is the way this all blends together.  The fully animated  80s cartoons like characters with their unique  (and top notch) voice-acting. The beautiful drawn maps and their many subtleties. The improved (while still not perfect) matchmaking system. The glorious soundtrack with over 15 songs that can play during battle.
This is one of the best MOBAs out there. Please give it a try for your sake. You won't regret it.

Imagine you have a jack-in-the-box. It has two panels and only one of them will open when you crank the handle.

100% Orange Juice is this jack-in-the-box. It is every rage game you've every played rolled into one cutesy little anime board game, and they've gone one extra step and removed all skill from the game so that you know there will never ever be an escape from the insanity.
Nothing you do matters. Nothing you try will succeed unless the Random Number Generator wills it so. You will be carrying 500 stars and just "happen" to roll the exact number that will dump you on the boss NPC's tile where he will proceed to play your♥♥♥♥♥like a banjo before taking all of them.
Well, not
of your stars. You only lose half of them when you're KO'ed. But that's ok. The moment you revive some other player will swoop in like Tarzan meets Chris Brown and beat another half of your stars from you, essentially relegating you to the position of spectator while all the other players race around levelling up from their ill-gotten gains.

fun. It's frustrating beyond all words and the only saving grace is that the one match that you win will feel like heaven for the 5 seconds you have before you crank that handle again. In the end though, it's not worth it the misery it will inflict upon you.

A very interesting system, to be sure. I've had a lot of fun with the "free to play" version, but more on that in a minute.
The characters are all endearing and pretty fun to play once you get a grasp of the core mechanics, which are a fresh take on... MOBAs? Not really. There are no ingame upgrades, and most building is done pre-game. There are some really interesting concepts going on here, and I'm really waiting to see what comes of it when the cast expands a bit.
Which brings me to my main gripes. The cast is very small for this sort of game, weighing in at 5 supports, 5 tanks, and 9 DPS as of the time of this writing. If you are the type that likes switching characters and roles frequently, your interest will wane much faster than with other team based games. The core mechanics may carry the game for you, however.
Lastly, this game isn't actually a FTP. The FTP model works more as a demo, really. This is fine as far as I'm concerned, but it should really be listed in the store as such.
Additional plus, I'm running this on a potato and aside from the occasional framerate chug, I'm running it pretty fine.

My first 15 minutes impression of Mutant Mudds was it was an Amiga game emulating a SNES style platformer. In the same way Zool was Gremlin's answer to Sonic the Hedgehog, I didn't expect much longevity as aesthetics over style doesn't work for me. You can have all the lovely sprites in the world,  but if the level design sucks, there's nothing to keep the player interested. I'm pleased that I persevered with Mudds though as it does have decent levels to battle through,  and more importantly,  it gives the player reasons to return to already completed worlds. There's hosts of secrets,  many of which you can't find on first visit as you lack the necessary power-ups. I'm happy to say that the worlds in which you visit do have more in common with Super Mario than they do with the aforementioned Zool, or Superfrog, to name but a few.  This game is a completionists pipe dream. It's tough,  unforgiving and the ice levels p**s me right off to the point of vowing a negative review, but it is also very rewarding.  I thoroughly enjoy games that open up extra levels when you accomplish goals.  I've never had a much fun like that since Yoshi's Island on the Snes. It'll never beat its peers in terms of level design but if I were to compare,  I'd give it a b+ for effort.

This is my first Hidden Object Game and I largely wanted to play it because the flaming skull guy in the logo (technically Jessie James) looked super rad and I thought the idea of being sent on missions by the Ghost of Abraham Lincoln was hilarious. Plus, at the time of this writing, it's October, so on top of everything else, ghosts and flaming skulls are seasonally appropriate.
In terms of gameplay, well, I did not hate my time spent with Witches of Abraham, I guess. When people say to me "Hidden Object Game" I figure that's all there is to something like this -- going screen to screen, completing object lists. There's actually not a lot of Hidden Object stuff in this game, all told. There are maybe five total Hidden Object screens (give or take; maybe it's closer to eight), with the rest of Witches of Abraham playing out more like a point-and-click adventure game.
Puzzles themselves are nice and devious -- but not too devious, as at any time in the game you can click a hint button that will explicitly tell you the next step (or even solve the entire puzzle for you when it turns in to a "Skip" button). To be honest, I played most of this game while streaming it to some friends, so it really helped keep the pace up that we never got stuck for too long. Honestly, I wouldn't mind playing more of these games, if they're all like this.
My main issue -- and the one that makes me hesitate in my decision to give it a thumbs up or a thumbs down score -- is in the story itself. The plot here doesn't feel like it's given much room to breathe at all; you're whisked away through time to all these different points in history by Lincoln's ghost but the context of which feels kind of flimsy. I understand the basic beats -- something about evil Witches cursing the Lincoln family -- but this is only ever visibly present at one point in the story. The rest is all "Okay, you've run out of puzzles to solve here, on to the next time period!" It doesn't help that most characters are flat and uninteresting; the only stand-out in that regard is Jessie James, who only appears in a very (VERY) small handful of scenes.
(Even in the Collector's Edition bonus chapter, which is dedicated exclusively to James, he only appears at the beginning and the very end)
There just needed to be... more, I guess. Witches of Abraham is almost afraid to go full adventure game, even though the concept could have very well supported it. There's a fun story in here somewhere, it just never really gets told. Which is... kind of the entire reason I wanted this game.
Which means... No, I guess I can't recommend it.

I bought this Game a while back in a Huge Mumbo Jumbo Bundle together with all the other Midnight Mysteries in the Series and I must say I am not dissapointed.
Now before you think about getting this Game I recommend you to play Number 1,2,3 & 4 first before getting into this one. Why? Because it will all make alot more sense then.
The Game comes with the Collectors Edition and 1 Bonus Level also Unlimited HO Mode and great wallpapers, character explanations and even 2 different Screen Savers.
The Resolution of the Game can once again not be changed but is alot higher then it was in Number 1, 2,3 & 4. It actually was widescreen and really nice to look at. Unlike in Number 2, 3 & 4 there was no Crafting System this time, which personally didnt bother me I just noticed it.
The Story itself was amazing and is about the Assassination off Americas 16th President Abraham Lincoln. The Atmosphere was great and the animation is alot better in this game then it was in the other 4 Titles. I was actually quite suprised. This Game has a few Jumpscares here and there but not as commonly as Number 2&3 did.
The Artstyle is very good and looks honestly very pretty and alot more rich in colour then previous Games of this Series. It was really pleasant to the Eye and I loved every bit of it.
Unlike Number 4 the Puzzles got alot easier and were alot more fun to do. I am glad to see that they have overthought the Puzzle Difficulty as it was just the right difficulty that it should off been!
This Game has an build in Guide which I personally do love, as the steam overlay did not work properly for me. It is also rather useful as these games are not as popular as Csgo and sometimes finding a solution can be difficult. Having a inbuild Guide is a huge plus for me!
Unlike the other Games in the Series this one has no Steam Achievements but it does have ingame Achievements. I am not entirly sure why they would take this Feature out, but regardless the game is alot of fun!
All in all this Game is amazing and really left me with a good impression off it. I cant wait to continue the Journey with the next upcoming game!
I do recommend this Game to any HO Fan and of course to anybody that loves a great Story. However I do recommend getting it on Sale as 14€ for 4 Hours seems a bit pricey.

Truly successful and interesting multiplayer Medieval action games.

So my last review was made when I was fishing for attention so Im actually gonna review this game.
I've played more than 14 hours on Steam, I've played about 300 hours on the 360 version alone and I've had a blast every single moment.
I've beat the game multiple times and got so much enjoyment out of it, and that's without mods and just playing vanilla.
So many books to read and steal, and so many tomes and stuff to learn.
Guild quests and Arena challenges in the imperial colosseum.
Some quests are actually time dependent, unlike Skyrim where you just meet them whenever and it doesn't matter.
The dark humor, which Skyrim doesn't have, will keep you entertained for weeks, the weird robo animations and weird voice acting just add to the charm of this game.
Which reminds me, if you liked Skyrim, play this game.
If you haven't played either yet, play this game first, then play Skyrim.
I'm kidding, but for real Skyrim is really just dumbed down Oblivion, nothing other than Morrowind really compares to this game.
The amount of equipment and quests that you initially find to undertake is minimal compared to most games, but exploring the land and just experiencing the game is really the greatest part of Oblivion.
Like accidentally contracting Vapirism and having to do this really hard quest to get rid of it, but in Skyrim you literally just talk to a guy and he cures you.
There are so many mods out there for this game, I don't think it beats Skyrim but it's up there. You will have fun with this game.
You do have to talk to civilians and get the lay of new towns and areas before you find hints where new quests might be, but they are all worth it.
Enjoy breaking the law, and getting those stolen goods.

I came back and complete this game, achievements and all, and I stand by my review. I realize others will feel differently, but from my view this game’s puzzles and challenge are rudimentary and it has very basic audio, visual, and level design.
I will say that the extra levels were a nicer affair, better designed, and showed more polish. The platform elements in these were better thought out and changed things up nicely.
I don’t hate this game, I don’t even dislike this game, I still can’t recommend it.
This is a very simplistic, slow paced action platforming game. The controls are actually very well executed, but the game itself suffers from a bit of an identity crisis. The music, art design, and play seem stuck in 8-bit era mediocrity. The game just feels slow and kind of dull, and looks pretty much on par. The colors are more akin to the 16-bit era, but the rest is just kind of functional. Not a bad game, but not a good game either. Very average.
As mentioned the controls work very well and are very uncomplicated. I played using a game pad with no issue at all.
The level design is pretty plain. This might have been to keep the game fairly easy, but it comes across as being as unremarkable as this game's other aspects. I realize this is an indie game, but for money it could do with being a bit less amateur.
Enemy variety is lacking, while timing puzzles only slow things to a crawl or seem to frustrate due again to the lackluster pacing. I have not completed the game, and though I might try its rather dull style and bland play make it a challenge to come back for more.

The plague had struck Constantinople, a year prior my imbecile doctor killed my husband with some idiotic experiment involving a leach, so of course I had him killed. Months drone on, massive food shortages, I hear a noise in the night, my dear old grand mother is pigging out! I decide to spare her life, despite that we where starving at that point.
I couldn't stand it any more, I opened the gate so my son didn't die of starvation, instantly plague for everyone, my first born genius son, the crown prince of Rome was skilled enough to take up the roll of doctor, he saved my life (his mothers), 3 of his sisters and his younger (imbecile) brother, then he falls ill and dies.
Now my imbecile son is heir to The Rome Empire AND my grandmother died of plague within a week, really should of eaten her.
10/10 would die of plague again.

Mutant Mudds is a self-described “12-bit” platformer with simple pixel graphics and traditional side-scrolling gameplay. At first, I found the gameplay frustrating and off putting due to the fact that there is a distinct lack of momemtum and your character’s jump is very short and entirely vertical. This meant that I was falling into tiny gaps that wouldn’t have been a problem in virtually any other platformer. Thankfully, your character (if he has a name, I’ve long since forgotten it) is also equipped with a jetpack that can allow you to hover for short bursts. Learning how to use this jetpack, when to cancel it, and timing it to give a boost to your vertical jump, is key to navigating the levels. Once I had these skills down, I actually began to really enjoy the game and the level of challenge it presented.
Of course, Mutant Mudds isn’t a game about just jumping. The game starts with a brief cutscene showing that the Earth (or whatever Earth-like planet this is) is being invaded by Muddies. Why this game is called Mutant Mudds if the enemies are an alien species called Muddies, and seemingly not mutants, is something I have yet to sort out. Regardless, mowing down Muddies with your water gun is how you will spend most of your time, and it’s pretty fun. There are enemies that walk, enemies that fly, enemies that shoot, big enemies, small enemies, etc. Jumping through levels taking out enemies along the way falls into a really nice rhythm. There’s also 100 golden diamonds (i.e. coins) to get in each level and secret levels throughout with an even greater level of challenge.
Unfortunately, with no bosses, puzzles, or much of anything outside of the core gameplay, it definitely gets repetitive. There are a few worlds with different themes that should be familiar to any fan of platformers, such as the ice world or dungeon filled with lava, but they all play very similarly and have the same enemies. There are also “ghost” versions of the levels you can play where all the enemies are replaced by unkillable ghosts. While it’s a more interesting change up, it’s still really just more of the same.
The art and sound design in Mutant Mudds also don’t do it any favors. The art is clearly meant to evoke classic retro platformers but, unlike a Mario, Mega Man, or Sonic, it’s entirely forgettable. The music and sound effects are fine but simple and repetitive. I ended up playing most of the game on mute and either listening to my own music or podcasts.
And I haven’t even mentioned the gimmick yet. Mutant Mudds is played across three planes of depth. That is, you can travel between the normal plane, foreground, and background. I suspect that this effect was more impressive on the 3DS where the game was first released but, on PC, it’s a cool effect but somewhat unremarkable. I can see how this changing perspective could have been used to come up with some ingenious levels and challenges, a la FEZ and Super Paper Mario, but the developers sadly squandered it here. You move between the planes at fixed points in the levels and it has essentially no effect on the gameplay. There are no puzzles that rely on this mechanic and very few branching paths. It’s basically just an artistic choice and the game would hardly be different without it.
So, with all that said, should you play Mutant Mudds Deluxe? The answer will vary a lot depending on the person. If you love classic platformers and don’t mind a lot of repetition and a lack of strong identity, Mutant Mudds isn’t a bad choice. It’s core gameplay loop is definitely strong enough to satisfy a certain group of gamers. However, if you are looking for a game with original ideas, its own personality, or anything outside of typical platforming, you can safely stay away from this one. Overall, I enjoyed the game for what it is so I am giving it a recommendation.

The fifth Midnight Mysteries game has most of the elements that made the previous instalments enjoyable, but somehow their combination results in a bland and mediocre hidden object game.
I do not know why, but Witches of Abraham just does not seem to work, even though it uses pretty much the exact same recipe as the previous, much better games. Still, the components are just not coming together as a whole.
Unlike in previous games, the protagonist is not helping the ghost of a famous author but the spectre of Abraham Lincoln, who asks him to uncover the truth behind the Knights of the Golden Circle (a mostly forgotten pro-slavery group from US history). Therefore, the plot had the chance to explore something other than literary references, yet it just randomly throws in whatever Civil War era trivia the developers could think of, resulting in a mostly incoherent, confusing treasure hunt/ghost story.
Gameplay feels similarly tacky. The hidden object scenes are uncomfortably overcrowded, and the minigames do not help either as they feel more like afterthoughts that had little attention during game design. The result is still passable, but that is about it.

I am one of the few people who have never played one of the Halo games before. Mainly because I refuse to buy an Xbox, so all I knew about this game was the name tag that gets tons of hype. Granted I knew that this isn't the normal genre that Halo is best known for.
In this game you control a single soldier, you can carry two weapons and have various special abilities. I only found out about these until the last 2 chapters however. While the game is fairly short, and there is hardly any story line to it, the gameplay is somewhat addictive. I found myself being able to finish the game in one sitting. The individual levels vary between 2 minutes and 10 minutes long. The game is very fast paced and it doesn't give you chance to get bored.
Towards the end of the game, I found my self being very overpowered due to the fact that I had hoarded experience points (because I didn't know how to spend them) and could use the homing explosive drone on each of the final levels, which kind of made the whole ordeal very easy and probably ruined the experience a tad.
The enemy units are all very samey, throughout the game, varying from the regular grunts who just keep pouring into you, to your beefed up melee combat commanders who will kill you in one shot.
The controls are fairly simple. Move around with WASD and aim with the mouse. The vehicle controls on the other hand left me driving into walls without knowing which way to turn around for a few seconds each time, left me very confused.
You can't ask much more of this sort of game in terms of graphics, it's a very regular decent graphics top down shooter. Nothing more, nothing less. Yes there are prettier games out there, but my gosh there are plenty worse.
All in all, I'd say pick this game up on the cheap, or if you are a fan of the Halo universe, you may get a kick out of it more than anyone.

I'll try keep this review as simple as I can.
S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Call of Pripyat, is a post apocalyptic, open world, FPS game with some RPG and survival elements.
It's kinda like Fallout but with a more serious presence and tone. The game is VERY immersive. And little things like having to eat food to survive and trying to avoid radiation and figuring out anomalies helps to pull you into this game.
Story -
After the Chernobyl inccident, a 30km exclusion zone was delcared. However some people went into the zone anyways in search for valuable artifacts worth lots of money. These people are called STALKERS. However, this is very illegal of course. After Five military helicopters crash inside of the Zone, you are sent in to investigate. A military agent dressed as a STALKER. From the second you step into this world, you choose where to go and what to do. You can do missions for Bandits, or STALKERS or go out and investigate those helicoters if you like. But doing missions for local groups will help you gain their respect, and this can have its advantages.
Gunplay -
This is a FPS and so the gunplay is important and I feel must be looked at, and it's very well done. Honestly, you actully feel like you are shooting guns in this game and not just pea shooters. They sound great, look great and work great. You can lean for better shots and guns have various attachments and can be upgraded too.
The Open World -
While I believe out of all the Stalker games, this on has the smallest open world, you should not worry. There are three sections to explore and each section is between medium and small in size. Put together, the area is big. But going between these sections, the game requires a load screen. Honestly, this is one of my only cons.
Atmosphere -
The game makes you feel ike you are doing stuff. It doesn't bore you. Finding artifacts is great, they can be used to boost your stats when equiped and the game makes you earn them too. Nothing is ever really handed to you. You need to work, and be clever. The game is also eerie, and what I mean by that is when you walk through some of the abandoned streets or warehouses in the zone, you really feel like you're there. It's quiet, it looks and feels like a ghost-town, but never forget. Mutants can lurk in the shadows and surprise you. And yes, there are many Enemy mutants in the game as well as bandits and stalkers.
A-LIfe System -
One of the coolest parts of the game, and of the previous two games as well. In STALKER, each NPC goes and does it's own thing. They can patrol roads, attack and kill other groups of people. Loot dead bodies etc. And the wildlife does something similar. Certain widlife travel in packs, and attack other wildlife. You can wittness it a lot. And you can walk right into a STALKER attack on bandits and vice versa and you can choose to join or stay out of the fights. You can even see some of the Bloodsucker mutants or other mutants, take out entire platoons of stalkers sometimes and it's so awesome to see and adds to the games immersivness.
Verdict 9/10 from me, this game is one of my faves and I haven't even been playing it long but already I can recommend it fully. Deffo try out this game!

One Way To Die: Steam Edition is an interactive fiction about dying. There are a bunch of text explaining the story and there will be always several options to choose with randomized results after that.
The story in this game is very simple: it's about a man (you) who wants to go to and back to the last day opening of an amusement park. Although the choices will result in deaths or a continuation for the story, it won't affect the story that much. Most of the story is the same with just a little difference in detail or with an additional text explaining how the man dies.
The game itself is pretty randomized; you can die without even doing anything. Any choice you choose will result in death or not based on your luck. Although you can choose which result do you want if you buy the deluxe edition (and some achievement will only unlock with the deluxe edition), that will beat the purpose of the game.
Sometimes, you'll be a saboteur, the one who'll set up traps to make more deaths on the choices. There is also a counter-measure team for that, who'll disarm the traps. Whether you'll be the saboteur, the non-saboteur, or the one who disarm the trap is randomized.
The music is annoying. I have to mute the game in order to play it because it's terrible.
I can't really say much about the graphics because the game is just about a bunch of a text in a screen. It won't really matter for me if it's just a black and white in cmd style. At least the menu isn't hard to learn and the text is readable.
Pros:
- Multiple choices
Cons:
- Randomized results
It's just an interactive fiction with a lot of reused text between the scenes. Although there are multiple choices, the choice will either be death or survive; making the choice not even useful at all.

So this is a fun game. It's basically Terraria, except you can put propellers on your house and fly it around. Also, there's a heavier focus on story and exploration. The world is made up of a large amount of areas, aligned like a square grid. If I had to guess(didn't count it), I'd say it's a 20x20-ish grid, so around 400 areas in total. Each area I'd say is about "medium" in size, not very big, but by no means small. So there's plenty of exploration to do if that's you're thing. Some areas, mostly towns, are in the same spot or at least the same general area in each game, but every other area is randomly generated, so every game is different. The only exception is that some areas mostly quests and always towns, are not randomly generated but pre made.
Just like in Terraria, you can harvest blocks, craft items, build whatever you like, etc. Except you don't have all the recipes for all the items at the beginning, you either have to find them or buy them, and some specific recipes are received through a quest.
One thing I like is the ship building mechanic. You build a ship pretty much like you'd build a base in Terraria. You build the frame with whatever block you want, and each type of block has different health and armor, so a Iron hull is more durable than a wooden hull. Then you put on propellers(which you can find, build, or buy) so there's at least one facing up or down for vertical movement, and one facing left or right for horizontal movement. Then you place an engine(buy/build/find), and ship control panel(used to pilot it), then bam, ready to fly. You don't need a balloon like many of the pictures show, but it helps greatly, since it gives the structure bouncy which counters a lot of the ships weight. If you go the no ballon way, then you'll need either strong propellers or a lot of them. So long as all parts(propellers/engine/control panel) are connected to the same structure, then it's considered a ship. The game also does a great job of explaining this for the most part, though it doesn't give many hints for building from scratch.
Just make sure that when you build your ship, that it's not still connected to the area you're building it on. One way to counter this worry is to craft a single "starter ship frane"(not exact name), which is a platform/pallet like block which doesn't attach to anything. Just drop that down on a cheap pole and start building your ship. Be sure to register it with the dockmaster in a town.
Don't worry about building a ship right off the bat, since the game gives you one which works very well. You can make modifications of course. If you want to remove anything, not just blocks but placeable items too, use the dismantle tool.
There's also a stat system with some skills too. There's Strength, Agility, Vitality, and Wisdom. Each stat starts out at 5 or 10(forgot), and can go up to 100. You're starting class determines what stat starts at 20 in the beginning, but you can go to skill trainers who will raise your stat by 1 for a sum of money. Every 20 points in a stat will unlock a skill or passive. For example, you can unlock a skill from Agility which will let you double jump, and there's another skill which let's you jump off walls.
As for weapons, there's a lot of guns to mess around with, though I don't know how much variety there is yet. There's also plenty of side quests to go along with the main quest, or you could just explore the large world, checking out abandoned buildings and mines, or maybe just attacking pirate ships and stealing their stuff. There's a lot to do, and other than the first two areas(temple and 'ship repair' area), you're not forced to do the quest. After repairing your ship, you're free do do whatever you like.
Anyway, for any fan of Terraria I'd definitely recommend this game with it's general and ship building mechanics, Action/RPG gameplay, etc. Not sure how it stacks up against Starbound though, since I can't really afford much outside of bundles, but this game is definitely worth playing.

As a person who is a huge fan of games like Terraria, Minecraft, DayZ, and Dark Souls, this game pushes all of my buttons in the right sort of way. I purchased this game in a bundle ($3.00 for a Humble Bundle of 4 games) and honestly can't believe that I never played this game sooner, or even really heard of it for that matter. As many of the reviews of this game state that there is crashing problems, and janky controls and such, as of today I have not encountered any of these issues. Not sure If I'd pay the $14.99 they are currently asking on steam (cause I'm cheap), but if you can manage to pick this up in a sale or bundle, do yourself favor. GET IT!
Things I like:
-Just the right amount of hardness (everything from enemies, to quests, to mining. It all has just the right amount of danger to make it challenging and fun.)
-The freedom to build your own air ship ANY way you would like is just awesome. Most games don't come anywhere close to this much sandbox fun. Not to mention the thousands of approaches you can take to completing missions or fighting bosses. Drill through walls, build barriers, hijack ships, or take them head on.
-Tons of items to craft, and weapons and items to collect.
-The balance of weapons/leveling/health and such is spot on (So far)
-Graphics are not the best, but they are decent, as is the audio.
-Physics A+
-The world and storyline are original and creative.
Things I dislike:
-Not much
-Hatches can be quite annoying, and difficult to get through in panicky situations.
-There is so much content that a more in depth tutorial is needed.
-I wish they had a hardcore mode that enabled permadeath. Would make this game so effing hard! (but fun)
-U.I. could be a bit more streamlined.

Controls feel.. loose. Does that make sense? Pretty similar to controlling your character in Starbound on a low-gravity planet. Walking past some colourful plants at the beginning was kind of hard on my eyes, but I later would find out that they were supposed to stand out because you’re able to destroy them to harvest their contents. I jumped the second animal I saw and it got bugged in the wall behind me in its haste. The enemies move pretty unconvincingly in any case. Like in Starbound! But somewhat worse.
At the end of the first level was a whole “omigod you got the relic now the place is falling apart” thing, and all of the walls began turning into dirt for some reason; blocking the path I’d taken to get there. But it was happening slowly, so I tried to walk back out, and then I died due to unreasonable amounts of falling dirt. The menu presented to me was then “Go to town”, or “Load”, and the former was greyed out. So I loaded the autosave it had made for me, apparently right after I got the relic, but somehow without triggering the whole collapsing sequence. Still played the dramatic music, though.
I then realised that I could use the jackhammer to carve my way out of the side of the old, unstable ruins, and spent some time picking up rocks and stuff from a mountain I was briefly considering digging to the top of to see if anything was hidden there. When I got back to the ship, my partner in crime was all “Whoa what was happening back there?” and you don’t reply, and then you fly away and there’s a huge collapsing explosion of destruction just off-screen to the right where the big ruins were supposed to be collapsing but weren’t.
As the ship sailed away, the camera didn’t centre on my character, but it did pause and jump to centre on her when I pressed tab to open up the inventory, and I had a lot more fun than I ought to have then, showing that game what for. Take control of my camera angle, would you? They'll think twice before they mess with me again.
I would then find out in the captioned images between levels that our ship had sustained heavy damage from the hypothetical explosion, and that’s why we were flying away so fast, downwards. Immediately upon landing the terminal velocity crash, both of the crew members were totally okay, apart from the NPC one developing a sudden case of laziness and electing to be the foreman and tell you what to do while you go around making all the repairs to the ship yourself. Upon using the repair tool for a second on the balloon, it instantly repairs itself fully in terms of aesthetics, but when you talk to Ms Lazikens again she insists you need to like hold the button down on the balloon for a while to repair it fully. God. (Actually, all she says is to repair the balloon, I figured out the holding down of the button part by myself.)
She then says that “it will take some time to repair the ship fully”, you know by harvesting supplies in the form of block from the land we just crashed on, and then she talks about forges and recipes and oh god I’m going to stop playing for now because I realise that this is actually going to be probably exactly like a Starbound that isn’t as good as Starbound, because it doesn’t have as good mechanics and doesn’t have aliens and claims to be a Steampunk game but the entire plotline is centred around the fact that your society runs on Whale oil. And I didn't have the patience for Starbound.
I also had intended to go for the ‘Vegetarian’ achievement for eating no meat throughout the entire campaign but unfortunately walked over the dead bodies of the animals I’d slaughtered and my character immediately devoured them like a voracious ♥♥♥♥♥, thus RUINING EVERYTHING.
I got it for 0.20$ in the Humble Bundle. I may come back to it at some point, but I’m not largely motivated to. It was worth that price I think, but I can’t help but wonder if a lollipop would have been an even better deal.
I could have dipped it very briefly in water and then sucked that. Have you ever tried that? It’s lovely. I used to do that all the time when I was younger. In my youngling logic, I decided that because it was so nice after putting it in for just a moment, it must be even nicer if I leave it in for longer! So, I left my lollipop in a bowl full of water and went away. When I came back a few hours later, I was devastated to find that the water had consumed it whole! Wow, what can I say. I haven't really been that far into this. Partly because my skill set puts me at odds with these fast paced, dash and shoot, types of games. But from what I can tell. A progressive, rogue-like, arena shooter. Like a bullet hell game. But with hell spawn as bullets. Each "level" doesn't so much as start as it blends with the previous. With scarier looking creatures coming out of the dark dark mists of the abyss with every few kills.
It IS addicting. In the same way that Paranautical Activity was in the first weeks of owning it. Just without a random dungeon to crawl.  The demons know where you are. They are coming to you. I imagine it has something to do with the power infused blade you take at the beginning of the game.
The sounds are great. I mentioned headphones right at the beginning. Just do it! The monsters are scary. Make it loud enough that you can hear the music and then go to town. I found my self wincing and cringing in those tense moments were there were baddies on all sides. I love scary sounds. And each of these creatures has a particular creep about them to give you just the right amount of chills.
Finding out just how far you can go, or what new and well crafted beasts you will come across, is allot of fun. Or maybe you fall prey to the feeling of "I very, nearly, almost, did not die right there!!"

Also, leader boards. As in, the only true way to tell how far you got, is by seeing how many points you racked up. Seeing your best score right in front of you gives incentive to go for one more round. But the friends, and global leader boards, also hold some allure. For you competitive types.

Once again the Sonic fandom has disappointed me. I should really expect this by now, but somehow I'm still surprised the majority of the community is like this. You guys are seriously giving this game a negative review just because of a glitch at launch? Incredible. I never once ran into that glitch. Game launches don't always go off perfectly, guys, so why don't you learn some patience while SEGA works on a patch? You do realize that every unnecessary negative review will hurt the game's overall rating, right? I swear, sometimes this fandom has higher toxicity levels than the deepest cesspools of Chernobyl.
Anyway, Sonic Mania is a game that I have been waiting for for a long time. I preordered the collector's edition back in September of last year, and after the PC version was delayed twice, I was as antsy as the next guy. But I chose to think of the old adage, “good things come to those who wait.”
And boy did good things come. As soon as I saw the title screen, I knew I was in for a treat. The game is beautifully and fluidly animated at 60 frames per second, and that was true even at the title screen. Then I let it idle and was treated to an intro cinematic with an art style greatly resembling the one in Sonic CD. I was emotional before even getting into the actual game itself.
My first playthrough was as Sonic and Tails, and the game started with a cute sprite cutscene before throwing me into familiar territory. The sights, the sounds, the nostalgia. There was only once place I could be. That's right, it was Green Hill Zone once again. No matter how many times I hear that music – or an arrangement of it – or see its checkered soil, I get such a satisfying nostalgia trip. Green Hill looks pretty much the same right down to the pixel graphics, but Act 1 is noticeably longer; what would normally take me about thirty seconds in the original game took me at least two or three minutes to get through. The levels in this game are quite long and I even ended up getting a Time Over in the last Zone.
Sonic has a new ability where, if you mash a jump button in the air, he will do a Spin Dash when he lands. It sounds like a good idea on paper, but I honestly never ended up using this. You are also able to get Tails to fly you with a single controller. Once you are able to get the hang of this, this can come in very handy.
I hit some Star Posts along the way and saw the familiar ring of stars around it. However, I was well under fifty rings at this point – somewhere around twenty-five. So I jump in expecting a pinball bonus stage, or maybe even a gumball or glowball bonus stage. Instead, I was taken to an exact replica of the very first Special Stage from 3 & Knuckles. It's a good thing I spent the three days prior to launch playing the classic trilogy to warm up and celebrate, because I ended up dominating a good amount of them on day 1. It turns out all fourteen Special Stages from 3&K are in this game as well as many original ones. Getting all the blue spheres earns a silver medal and getting a perfect as well as all the spheres gives me a gold medal. As of typing this, I don't yet know what these do (no spoilers please).
I only wished this is how you collect Chaos Emeralds in this game, because I would have gotten them no problem. Instead, you are supposed to seek out giant rings a la 3&K. The closest parallel I can draw to Mania's Special Stages is Sonic CD. You are racing around a racetrack chasing a UFO holding the Emerald. Along the way, you are supposed to collect rings, which act as a timer, and – surprise – blue spheres. This time, blue spheres increase your speed to different levels, starting at Mach 1 and ending, I believe, at Mach 3. Player be warned, these can actually be pretty tough; I only got two out of seven in my first playthrough.
Each Act – there are two in each Zone – ends with a boss, again, a la 3&K. These can either be completely original bosses or bosses from the older days with some new twists added. Recent fan games have spoiled me; I expected an occasional ring to trickle in during the fights, but you are not given any with the exception of one or two in between phases. Be warned that these bosses are not playing around and will require a good amount of focus.
After the Green Hill Zone boss is defeated, I am shown a transition into the next level. This is where I would like to end spoilers, but long story short, it's another retro level. The whole game sort of plays out like Generations; you will go through some classic Zones – all of which have new layouts and some new gimmicks – as well as some new ones. Without detailing too much, I will praise the game for being made with love. When SEGA make an earnest attempt to make a great game, they really nail it, and this is one of those times. Mania references pretty much everything Sonic-related during the early to mid-nineties. Even the 8-bit games are represented. I even recognized Tails' pose at the end of an Act as a reference to official artwork from the classic era.
There are only two minor gripes I have with the game, but they're not enough to take away from my enjoyment of the game. First, I wish they would have made some kind of reference to Sonic 3D Blast. Second, while I enjoyed the transitions between levels and how they logically flowed into the next one, the game eventually seemed to forget about those transitions, which slightly disappointed me.
Bottom line, if you have ever played a Sonic game – classic or modern – and liked it, buy Mania. If you have not played a Sonic game before but love 2D platforming at it's finest, buy Mania.

is a fast-paced arena shooter that will always keep you moving and thinking ahead. Nowhere is safe and there are no brakes on this nightmarish fight for survival. The goal and main premise of the game is two-fold:

Atlas Reactor is a fun little game that takes some elements from turn based squad games (like XCom) and mixes them with other elements from MOBAs. You've got twenty seconds to enter your move for the turn, and then the action goes off.
It leads to fun mind-games where you're trying to decide whether your opponent thinks you will dash to that location over there, so they might attack that location instead of where you actually are, so you decide that since your correct course of action is so obvious, that you'll instead stay put and... then you find out they called your bluff.
Never go in against a Sicilian when death is on the line!
The character bios are awesome as well, especially Oz, the recalled toy-bot (for displaying freewill and weapon-grade lasers) and Quark, the homicidal... thingie... that just wants to tickle your neurons.
I recommend this game for anyone old enough to have played games like Jagged Alliance and who doesn't want to wade into the toxic morass of other MOBA communities.
Edit: Regarding the "free to try" nature of the game - they let you try the game out for free. It's not intended to be played forever like an actual free to play title. If you like the game, buy the damn package. If you don't, then stop complaining that they give you a random selection of four characters (that rotate) to play around with in the meantime.
