Slow, tedious, uninspired, uninteresting, pointless. Those are 5 good words to describe this game.
The problems start with character movement. Your walk speed is sooooo. Sloooooow. I have played walking simulators where you move faster than this game has you moving. The hover mechanic is alright and the unlockable mechanics are serviceable most of the time (upward dash has issues registering, though). But it doesn't matter, because the slow move speed slows the game to a crawl.
The level design is also rock-bottom in quality. Some of the levels are okay but... ehh, let's list some things that happen numerous times:
1. Enemies placed in a way that taking a hit is preferrable than trying to figure out/failing to dodge hits.
2. Blind upward dashes where if you jump before you dash, you'll hit a spiked ceiling... sometimes. Other points in the level you'll need to do a jump first, but you can't see far enough up to know whether or not you need to jump first.
3. Lopsided checkpoints. Frequently. They are very often misplaced, either too early or too late in the level.
4. Wildly varying level length. Some of the levels are on the short side, others can take minutes to clear.
5. The ones that take longer tend to have copy/paste level design where you do the same segment multiple times, point-for-point, needlessly dragging boring levels on even longer.
6. There's not a lot of variety in general, there's only so many different obstacles possible with the limited amount of game objects and there are far too many levels for how little variety they provide.
7. Foreground objects can get in the way of background objects, obscuring visibility. Legit fake difficulty, yo. The farthest back layer is too zoomed out most of the time anyways, character is way too small on-screen.
The game never gets too hard, really, which is maybe for the better as the controls aren't polished enough for really precise platforming. The music is decent and the graphics are decent, but the retro feel they gave off permeated into the game design and as a result makes it feel like a game that should've stayed in the time period it's trying to emulate.

Twenty years ago, we never would have guessed that today’s generation of consoles would embrace 8-bit side-scrolling platformers. With the release of titles like Terraria, however, this trend does not show any signs of slowing. As these games continue to grow in popularity, developers such as Renegade Kid are fusing the power of new hardware with older gameplay styles, resulting in fresh experiences such as Mutant Mudds Deluxe.
For those out of the loop, this is throwback 2D title with a unique twist. Unlike traditional releases in the genre, it requires you to leap into the background or jump out of the screen in order to explore different parts of each level’s environments. In some areas, there are as many as three planes layered on top of each other, offering a chaotic screen filled with moving enemies, platforms, and dangerous spikes.
The title tells the tale of an asteroid carrying a hoard of barbaric, brown monsters. Max, a blond-haired boy with a water gun and a jet-pack sets off to rid the world of the vermin by gathering star sprites. With the help of his Granny, the hero travels through five lands in his quest to eradicate the problematic pests.
Trying to wipe away the Mudds with a water gun is no easy task. There are several different kinds of enemies to attack, each with a different ability and movement pattern. Your weapon aims horizontally, has a limited range, and only fires the next water blast once the last one has disappeared. These limitations result in the cleanup operation being more difficult. You must attack or avoid moving Mudds while ducking through scrolling platforms, tight quarters, spinning hazards, and leaping fireballs.
Travelling through each level requires patience, timing, aiming, and trial-and-error. Each enemy travels on a predetermined path, and careful shooting, jumping, floating, and ducking is needed to avoid enemies and their attacks. You begin each level with three hearts, and halfway through there is a checkpoint where progress through the stage is saved. To add to the challenge, a time limit of four minutes is placed on each outing. Fortunately, it’s not too difficult to pass these quotas, but you will need plenty of skill to cross the finish line without losing a heart.
As you progress through the game, new levels and upgrades open up – assuming that you’ve collected the required number of star sprites. There are also Ghost Levels, which force you to slip past phantom Mudds that cannot be killed. The levels offer a real challenge, and avoiding the mutants requires real agility.
Upgrades, meanwhile, augment Max with the ability to shoot longer distances, add a longer lifespan to his jetpack, or the option to leap high into the air. You can only apply one of these upgrades at a time, but the enhancements allow you to complete levels much easier. You’ll also need to employ these additions to locate the hidden rooms in each stage.
Regardless of which power-ups you employ, this can be a challenging game – and depending on how tough you want it to be, there are ways that you can increase the difficultly. You can, for example, disable the abovementioned mid-level checkpoints, allowing you to choose whether you want to be forced to beat the entire level in one run or not.
The music and visuals are enjoyable throughout the game, although the song selection for each of the shadow levels does get a little stale after a little while. When jumping in and out of planes, it can be very chaotic, as the foreground remains visible while you play. This increases the challenge on some levels, requiring a much greater focus if you want to make it through unscathed.
There’s plenty more to do once the vermin have been scrubbed, too. Gathering all of the star sprites, all of the golden diamonds, completing the secondary levels, and the other special levels offers plenty for you to accomplish beyond the core campaign. Granted, it’s possible to finish the adventure in less than eight hours using the hardest settings – however, since so much of the game revolves around replaying the same levels multiple times, you may not be compelled to come back once you’re done. Furthermore, the conclusion of the adventure is lacklustre, forcing you to focus on the satisfaction that you obtain from finishing the levels rather than exciting cutscenes or plot twists.
Mutant Mudds Deluxe takes the old-school platforming formula and freshens it up with a unique twist. The dimension hopping hook augments a tactical layer to the traditional side-scrolling action, and the occasionally devilish difficulty will test your dexterity. While there’s a lot of content to get through, however, the adventure does get repetitive at times. Nevertheless, there’s not a whole lot of grime in this game – just good, clean fun.

Regardless of the Unity glitches and game crashes I've experienced with RA3, I'm still having fun building bots and having bot war.
RA3 might run better on your rig in standalone mode. In other words, shutdown Steam and start RA3 manually. Keep in mind you won't have access to any of the Steam features.
Compared to RA2 I actually prefer RA3 because it doesn't have some of the component limitations that RA2 had. For example, in RA3 you can cram a battery, control unit and a CO2 tank into the SAME spot without any adverse effects. I couldn't do that with RA2.
Anybody who tries to enter an illegal Ultra-weight bot into a Career Tournament is going to get PUNKED by a bot lockout without any warning. Ha Ha. Don't care who you are, that's funny right there and serves you right. Here's a clue... Ultra bots are Exhibition bots only.
There are 4 weight classes:
1. (L)ight, less than 400 kg
2. (M)iddle, 400 - 799 kg
3. (H)eavy, 800 - 1,299 kg
4. (U)ltra, 1,300 and up
The bot lab baseplate creator will not allow you to create illegal baseplates, but you can still shape strategically placed chassis vertices into illegal configurations in the extruded layer mode of the editor as long as it's not too complex. Just remember to include ambiguous vertices in the baseplate which you're going to associate with an illegal configuration.
For advanced bot model creation you'll have to manually edit the 'bot.json' script found in the '..\Users\(profile name)\Documents\RobotArena3\Profile0\Bots\(botUUID)' location. It's not hard, but very tedious work for creating fancy curves, elaborate points and edges, and performing negative scale functions which is not available in the game editor. This is also the same file which sometimes becomes corrupted with hidden spare parts, or 'null' parts, which you have to delete from 'bot.json' and reload your bot.
You can always tell if you've created something you should not have by observing crazy instability behaviors of your bot which is sometimes followed by a game crash. If your bot suddenly springs upwards to the roof of the arena and disappears, then that means DON'T DO WHAT YOU DID, change your bot and try again.
If your bot randomly explodes on the workbench table, then that means the 'bot.json' file is corrupt. Investigate and repair manually.
You don't really need a visible bot chassis to build a bot, but it helps to have one if you want armor. But this also means you can design the mechanics first, then go back and design your chassis later. That's something else you couldn't do in RA2, but can in RA3. You still have to determine your bot's center using a very tiny baseplate and chassis though. You can make it only 0.01 x 0.01 x 0.02, if you want to, then change it later.
Your bot doesn't even have to look like a bot. It can look like a forklift, dune buggy, race car, motorcycle, truck, UFO, Star Wars droid walker, or whatever is in your imagination. If it makes contact with the ground, then you can build it in RA3.
A hovercraft simulation is also possible by exploiting a few game glitches, but you have to be very careful of what components you choose to make it out of. Obviously you can't design one to survive in battle, but it's still fun building something whacky.
It takes up space in your computer. Don't install it.

It's a game that I recommended while it was in early access due to its polish, and the full release doesn't disappoint in this element. A well designed roguelike with challenging elements in its top down shooting from a strategy perspective, you have a variety of ACTUALLY DIFFERENT FEELING WEAPONS that are at your disposal that are fun and relatively easy to use. The developers understood each of the systems they put in place here, and not only implemented them rather well: but did it in a way where they all work together in harmony. That's a sign of a well thought out and executed plan: when each element complements the next. The weapon choices are better against certain enemies, certain objectives are easier with certain layouts, and if you don't play to your situation: you're going to get your butt handed to you. Everything gameplay wise feels like it was gone over with a fine tooth comb balance wise, so that it'd give the challenge that would take a while to overcome, and just hitting that frustration factor without going over the top.
The visuals are reasonable for a 15 dollar indie game, with a lot being lost in detail due to the amount that happens on screen, but still having a lot of detail none the less. The performance never dips under 60 FPS for me, but keep in mind that if you are watching video and are having sickness problems, that there's really not a lot you can do graphics wise to try to allevate that. In addition, the music is sub par, not standing out whatsoever, but that does allow the sound design to shine with some good little touches to help the overall presentation.
The only thing that holds things game back in the end really is what happens after you beat the campaign. You are hoping for more difficulty, more of a challenge at the end game, and it doesn't come. That could have really brought the game up to a level of a Rogue Legacy (I know it's not a shooter, but the replayability factor) in the roguelike/roguelite genre, but you're not going to get 30+ hours of gameplay here. 15 on the other hand, yeah, and it's going to be a fun 15 hours. Definitely worth a pick up.

Spartan Assualt is truely a poor-man's Halo. An exceedingly bland story gives reason to the series of short missions avialable to you, each no more than ten or twenty minutes long. Shooting requires you hold down the fire button, an odd choice that ensures the player is always forced to forsee where the simply-minded enemies will go rather than shoot at where they already are. Mouse control is usually better than a controller because you recieve a reticle to help guide your shots. However, vehicles such as the scorpian tank and the ghost become incredibly difficult to control unless a controller is used, due to the translation from a fully 3D Halo environments to this isometric one, a potentially maddeding issue given that a least a few missions openly try to make you use these vehicles.
The average mission in Spartan Assualt is bland. The music is nice, but if you're a Halo fan you'll probably have heard it all before and, if you're like me, you might just find the music oddly out of place. Enemies are easily killed, so it really is a good idea to turn on a few skulls (alter the game to modify the difficulty). However, none of the skulls ever felt like a real solution, and even the skull that was directly related to increasing "enemy difficulty" just made all the enemies more bullet-spongy.
In similer games, such as All Zombies Must Die and Nation Red, there is a tendency to throw large waves of easily killed bad-guys at you. In Spartan Assualt, there are never that many enemies, and increasing the difficulty just makes the same brain-dead enemies slightly tougher (more health). Given that Nation Red and All Zombies Must Die already exist, and have working mouse controls, I can't recommed this game.
Most importantly: if you're hurting for more Halo on PC, like I was when I bought this, you'll just end up disapointed.

Cryptark is a new and fresh roguelike currently in Early Access but you should keep a good eye on that one since it’s going to blow your socks off!
Especially if you like roguelikes.
You slip into the role of a Mercenary Captain which will lend her unique skills to anyone with enough money. You’re contacted by a rather shadowy government agent who has commissioned you and your crew to board and pacify the Cryptark.
That’s what you’re getting into. The question is … are you ready?
Time is Money and you don’t have any time. Keep that in mind while playing. Time is essential since you only have a specific amount of time to finish a level. I mean hey the government agent wants those space hulks in a timely fashion. You don’t want to disappoint him do you?
Time isn’t the only thing that you should pay attention to. Before you set out on a mission you’ll have to choose which of the four available space hulks you’re going to conquer. Choose your victim, err, Space Hulk wisely. Each of the Space Hulks has another difficulty and requires more money. So it’s up to you to decide whether or not you want to risk and spend more money for a greater reward. Each of the space hulks has different bonus objectives as well.
However. Before you set out on a mission you have to choose your loadout and that costs quite a fair amount of money. You can choose what kind of weapons you want to use on a mission such as the machine- or shotgun, the amount of grenades you’ll want to use and you can even upgrade your shields. So you see you can pretty much change everything before a mission and sometimes you even have to if you want those bonus goals. Some require you to go out on a mission with a max loadout of 60k for example.
The good and the bad part about the game is that you will be forced to tackle those goals at one point of the game. Because money’s everything in
. Once you’ve spend all your money it’s game over.
Let’s talk about a space hulk for a bit.
The goal of each mission is to go and destroy the core. But before you can do that you have to take out the shield system. You see the shield system protects the core from taking damage.
That’s not the only system that will try to make your life is hard as possible. There are all kinds of systems like sentry guns, a repair system which will repair the last destroyed system, a fail system, which will take control of the last destroyed system and so on. So you see you can’t just rush into a space hulk and hope for the best. You should have a plan and use your map.
In order to move through a space hulk you’ll have to defeat all kinds of enemies and collect key cards. A lot of doors are locked and you need a key card in order to unlock a door. That means that every locked door requires one key card.
Overall you’ll be put under quite a bit of stress while playing and to be completely honest … I seriously love it. I loved every minute playing it and I can see it become one of my favorite roguelikes rather easily. Of course that depends how this game evolves over the course of early access.

As a former RA2 player and fan of combat robotics in general, I was excited to hear that a sequal to the preivous title was finally being released. (Their timing also probably took advantage of the return of Battlebots to TV, but that's aside the point.) So I hastily bought it, eager to see it for myself.
It's been a while, so I apologize if I don't recall some details correctly.
The bot builder section was okay. It was a little hard to grasp at first, but I eventually figured it out, and it definately was more powerful than RA2 in many key areas. The crashes and subsequent glitching up of the designs were harder to manage, but fortunately a patch managed to fix it. This isn't to say that it is perfect, of course. The weight would sometimes change abruptly when you exited the build screen, and some things were stille a little... finicky. Tolerable, though, because surely the developer would iron these quibbles out.
Bot in hand, I started expedition mode. I was a little disappointed by the UI used to select the arena and opponents. It lacked a lot of the trimming RA2 had... you know, like the opponent's weight class. Guess they wanted to leave that for us to figure out. Nonethless, I started my match in the warehouse. After bearing through the surprisingly un-exciting announcer - even compared to RA2 - speaking, the match began. Bots slammed into each other. Parts flew. I pummeled my opponent apart, and prepared to land the killing blow, expecting the game to release sparks or even an explosion to come with my victory.
Instead, a pop-up instantaneously appeared over my bot, informing me that I had won. That was it. I couldn't even admire my handiwork thanks to it. As I later found out, this also occurred with immobalization, as well as being hit by a subway or falling into lava. Kinda anticlimactic.
So, I finally started the tournaments part. I liked these in RA2. I selected my bot, picked a tournament, hit continue, and....
nothing. Nothing happened when I clicked. To top it off, since I was technically entered in the event, it also locked my bot on the build section.
I hoped that the designer would fix these issues. Instead, they disappeared into thin air later the year.
I hope this was an informative cautionary tale.

Welcome to my first game review EVER. I'm doing it because of how polarized every review I read about Windforge is.
This is Windforge. I like it but it is not the game I was expecting in great and disappointing ways.
Windforge looks a lot like MinecraftTerrariaStarbound and it IS like them in that you mine things and build things, but that is really where the similarities end. The worlds of MinecraftTerrariaStarbound have a certain pace and feel about them. Those worlds welcome you, let putz around and figure things out at your own pace, and explore. The threat of night looms, but you'll never get into too much trouble that you didn't, in some way, go looking for.
SnowedIn compares Windforge to Contra and I think that needs to be bold and underlined with little arrows pointed to it. Windforge's world, while pretty, doesn't like you. You run at its pace, sometimes sprinting. After building my first ship from scratch, I wanted to find somewhere slow to test it out. Windforge laughed at my puny efforts and I promptly ran into three ships full of pirates. Trouble will find you. Sometimes giant, terrible trouble that has a lot of tentacles. Sometimes five of those kinds of trouble at once.
The game is hard and doesn't want to hold your hand. Exploration and mining is less about relaxing and watching TV on the second monitor (Something I often do in MinecraftTerrariaStarbound), and more of a white-knuckled experience where you feel naked outside of your ship and dread the tentacled horror. But what comes from this is an absolutely awesome feeling when you find your feet and come out on top. If you have ever successfully played Dwarf Fortress or Dark Souls, you know what I am talking about.
The bugs are apleanty, though. If those make you rage out, you will probably blow a few arteries. I haven't run into the corrupted save bug people are talking about, but it would definitely be very sad to lose the iron monstrosity I've created. Also, the lack of handholding goes a little too far sometimes: it took my quite a few hours of play before I figured out how to register a new ship with a dockmaster. The ship needs to be left at a specific spot at the end of and slightly under the dock. Then you go talk to the dockmaster. I found out by accident.
The last issue I have is a tricky one to work my way through. A part of the game involves going to various ancient temples and fighting bosses in them. The boss fights are amazing and intense, and what happens after each one is always exciting, but exploring the temples before the boss part is dull. I have a feeling that they are meant more as obstacle courses to do quickly and efficiently and not something to dungeon crawl through, though. The habits you formed playing Skyrim will not serve you well here.
So there you go.
TLDNR: I think Windforge is more like the unforgiving panic-shooters of yore than MinecraftTerrariaStarbound. Some people will love that and some people will be stressed and frustrated. Also, tharr be bugs.

Seriously this game is fun, as the description states, 100% Orange Juice is a goal-oriented boardgame, and a good one at that.
First you start by picking your character, each one has various traits, the more noticable ones being their stats, HP, Attack, Defense and Evade. Then you have their hyper card which is exclusive to that character. More on cards in a moment.
Then make a deck out of the cards you have. Now an interesting thing about the card system is that you don't draw from your deck, no, instead you draw from a deck that consists of all the cards from all players' decks, meaning you can draw something someone else wanted to draw in hopes of assisting in whatever strategy they had in mind and vice versa. Or you can add a bunch of bad cards and make other people get bad cards while you may or may not draw their supposedly good cards.
Next is the goal of the game, the whole point is to go around the board fulfilling "Normas" which you need to achieve 5 of to win the game, you start of having to get 10 stars, but after that you can change it up by going with either 2 wins (Killing a monster gets you one win, while killing another player gives you two, and killing a boss gets you 3) or 30 stars, then 5 wins or 70 stars, etc until your last Norma will either be 14 wins, or 200 stars. Now the trick here is often stars are often easier to amass than wins are, unlike wins, you can lose stars in different ways such as getting killed, landing on a drop space, or from the effects of cards.

This game is not bad. Actually, it is interesting how they put together the isometric system with a MOBA style of gameplay. It is a free to play game, where you are only free to play with the weekly free characters and an AI versus or PVP normal versus. No ranked games, no in game currency to buy the characters, only a very weird lootbox system where you can only open 1 box every 12 hours.
This game has a lot of potential, but, right now, it is just another MOBA. Sure, it is different from our top MOBAs like DotA or Heroes of the Storm, but with so many MOBA-alike games being made every day, this one does not have a kind approach to try to win over the customer. Having a free to play game where you can only have a taste of the game and charging over $30 to be able to actually enjoy it, is at least fair to the developers, but it is not wise to do it when you can play any of the other millions of MOBA at their full for no charge.
The game by itself is good enough to you actually give it a try, but not enough to stand out. The business model is risky and can make this game become other Evolve or even have to close its server in a year or so.
My verdict: Wait for a few months or a year, and see if this game is still alive and have a good community, then, if you still like it, buy it.
Also please note that, if you pay up for this game, you won't have a refund even if you dislike it or the full game didn't lived for your expectations.

So like yeaaah, Mutant Mudds... odd little title but defintely a great one for someone craving a dose of ultra precision platforming. At first the game feels really cumbersome and clunky because let's face it, it's not supposed to play like New Super Mario Bros... You won't be running at top speed and almost sliding off in to a chasm only to do a triple backflip in to a ground pound... nope, none of that here. You walk, you hover, you jump, you shoot... bout it.
This game is very... let's say, square.... or rather pixel perfect... everything works in blocks, rows and lines... so if you keep that in mind when you're traversing the trecherous one hit kill spike traps, you'll be better off. The game is intended as a grueling challenge for older children, around the age of like 10-12... and for someone of that age, I can see this being incredibly frustrating and they will surely deem this game unbeatable... but it's really not.
Don't expect "Impossible Game" or "Super Meat Boy" quality challenge here is basically what I'm saying. If you can tolerate playing most web based flash games for longer than 15 minutes, this game will proove only an above average challenge for you. You shouldn't at any point want to throw your controller at a wall... if you do, then you have no patience because that's all this game really requires.
Sure there's a time limit for speed running levels but that's more of a tacked on thing if you're craving more Mutant Mudds after you've collected over 4000 objects... and if you are, please seek some help. After the inital batch of normal stages and ghost stages I cringed at having to do 20 more stages with good ol' grannie but I actually found those stages the least frustrating after I had finished a few.
All in all the game is good, you can finish everything in roughly 5 to 6 hours which is decent for the price. Other less experienced platformers might take a bit longer but I can't see this game taking you more than 10 hours.
Side Note: There's an exploit where you can stand on the very edge of spikes if they're on a platform, so use that knowledge to your advantage if you're having trouble finishing some of the harder areas.

[Spoiler-Free Review]
Avoiding the "It's a mobile port" diatribe, a review that doesn't mention Mutant Mudds Deluxe's efforts in bringing 3D depth to the 2D plane is missing the point. Multi-layered stages allow for a degree of creativity in level design not easily matched by old platforming standards. What happens when an enemy swings at you from the background for instance? Here, you get thrown toward the player who is now potentially uncertain of the footing available to them. It's analogous to when Mario punched the rotating section of cage for the first time in Super Mario World, and it's why Mutant Mudds works. You have to consider what's happening on different planes simultaneously to ensure the best chance of surviving challenges - backgrounds (and foregrounds) aren't just pretty pictures.
Admittedly, I wasn't a fan of the floatiness of the main character, Max. In Level 1-1 the effect gives the impression the whole stage is moving rather than just the character - less Mario, more And Yet It Moves. Sticking with it though, the controls aren't quite as obtuse as first impressions would lead you to believe. Thanks in large part to a backpack that allows you to hover in mid-air for a few seconds at a time, you're still able to perform precision platforming sections with relative ease. In fact, most stages didn't feel challenging enough (until I reached the expert bonus stages).
The music bleeps and bloops as you'd expect in a retro themed platformer. Most are memorable with at least two or three standout tracks in the bunch (the g-land music is my personal top pick, followed by the ghost music, and the one from the expert stages screaming "fly like an eagle" which is painfully catchy). The graphics are a bit of a letdown however, if you were hoping to run the game at 1080p for a full HD experience, understand that the pixels will still be blocky, just bigger.
I was able to complete the main storyline in one sitting which would usually lead to concerns about game length, but the majority of the game is found "after the break" as it were, thanks to secret stages, sub world stage variations, and expert stages only unlockable by certain characters in the game and/or once you've purchased upgrades. Recommendation - Life is too short to play dull games
If you still love playing stuffy old-school games like Cosmo's Cosmic Adventure or the original Commander Keen without the nostalgia factor, this is the game for you!
Remember how fantastic old DOS game music was? Well, I must admit this one's is too.
Remember how intensely slow and plodding old DOS game movement was? Yup, this one too.
Remember how ridiculously basic old DOS game combat was? Sensing the pattern yet?
Everything about this game reminded me of old DOS games. That might not sound like such a bad thing, but when is the last time you actually played an old DOS game? They're BURSTING with nostalgic goodness and they put a rose-tinted smile on my face, but objectively? They're stuffy, stilted, restrictive, confining, and almost all of that was due to required programming restrictions. Games were that way because they pretty much had to be.
So why would I want to play a brand new game that feels every bit as stuffy as a 20-year-old one, without any of the needed nostalgia that still makes them fun? You know, I can actually play the old games if I want to, rather than a bland similarity of one that only hints at vague shadows of nostalgia.
The art style is pixellated, but uncreative. The enemies are different sizes of round or gumdrop shaped brown blobs. The levels are entirely linear (except for not-so-cleverly-hidden "secret" doors on every single level), and they only last a few minutes at a time. There is nothing overly clever or creative, nothing mind-blowing, nothing exciting, and nothing fun.
If you were desperate for something new to play on your phone in the bathroom at work, this might be able to hold your interest for a while, but on a PC or console (or Vita, where I played it), it is boring, dull, slow, colorless, and any 5 other synonyms for lame. Don't get me wrong, I could see people playing through this game easily. I could not, however, see anyone playing this with a smile on their face or with excitement in their heart.
I've been rather hard on middling games lately, but you know what? I have less and less free time every single year that passes by, and my game backlog is actually getting bigger and bigger. I have games waiting that I am desperately excited to play, so there is simply not enough time to waste playing something that doesn't excite me. The music is pretty great, though (and it's in the game folder in OGG format).

Halo: Spartan Assault is a top-down, twin stick shooter set in the Halo universe, between the events of the third and fourth games. My main bone to pick with this title is the very nature of the game; "the Halo 4 "prequel" isn't a first person shooter."
But, for the sake of this review, I'll look past that and judge the game on its own merits.
Gameplay:
You control your character with the typical WASD movement scheme, and "aim" with the mouse. I say "aim" because for me, it can be rather choppy at times, but it gets the job done. There are quite a few weapons, such as the Focus Rifle, (which I found rather unexpected) and there are plenty of vehicles. The vehicles handle well, as one would expect from a Halo game. Any vehicle centered missions were fun and enjoyable. Speaking of the missions, the entire game's campaign is divided into six chapters, with five missions in each chapter, making for a thirty mission total. Not bad. The missions themselves seem varied, and were quite fun to play through. They're bite-sized, and you could play through five or more in one sitting before you know it. My main complaint with the missions is the pre-game loadout screen. You can select a different weapon, armor ability, or power-up to play the mission through with, but the currency you use to buy these weapons and such pays for a temporary, one-time unlock of said item for the specific mission on which you're about to play. The system seems worthless, considering A) the price of these items and B) the short mission length, meaning you shelled out 750 XP on a Spartan Laser for nothing. Although the opportunity for micro-transactions in-game was made available, Microsoft thankfully did not take that opportunity. Overall, the gameplay is solid, but it could benefit from balancing in the loadout department, and perhaps a level editor. It's worth noting that the console version of this game has a survival mode in which you fight off hordes of the Flood, which would make a great addition to the Steam release of Halo: SA.
Story:
The story, unfortunately, is told through small text blurbs displayed just before the mission start. I expected a larger emphasis on storytelling, but this was not the case. Sad, but it doesn't take away from the aforementioned gameplay. The story itself follows Spartans Sarah Palmer and Edward Davis as they defend planet Draetheus V from a Covenant attack and kill the commander of the particular Covenant splinter faction assaulting Draethus V: Merg Vol. The story is not a direct prequel to Halo 4, which also disappointed me.
Graphics:
It looks alright for a top-down shooter. Obviously, with the nature of the game, they didn't need to render anything too advanced. The models themselves are somewhat low-poly, especially the world models of the weapons. The weapon world models actually could have used some touching up. I looked at an Assault Rifle laying on the ground, and it took me a few seconds to realize that the object I was staring at was, in fact, an Assault Rifle and NOT an abandoned Lego recreation of a deformed spaceship.
Overall:
It's a fair game, especially for the appropriate $4.99 pricetag. I'd give it a 7/10. It's worth picking up if you're a Halo fan. If you're not a Halo fan but you're looking for something inexpensive to play, I suppose this wouldn't do too bad a job of holding you over.
TL;DR:
Good game, and at $4.99, it's worth buying.

Overall, the game is a clear step up from Clear Sky but doesn't reach the heights of Shadow of Chernobyl for me. Unlike previous games, the world consists of 3 large open maps (Zaton, Yanov and Pripyat) as opposed to the dozen or so smaller areas. Mechanically, it's basically a tightened up Clear Sky: weapons, armour and AI all function the same but the guns aren't as ridiculously inaccurate and unreliable and enemies don't spam perfectly accurate grenades. A notable omission is the faction wars system, which I consider an improvement.
The central narrative is alright but suffers from the Oblivion/Skyrim problem of chaining together one urgent mission after another while the game expects you to bum around with side missions and exploration. Also, the ending is rather abrupt (with a Fallout style consequences slide show that really hammers home that tension). And, without spoiling, the mystery is pretty lame this time around. You don't feel like you're discovering the secrets of The Zone... just dropping in, completing a task and buggering off again. Still, it's certainly not a BAD game. The post-apocalyptic atmosphere, loot gathering and emergent gunplay are all here. It just doesn't do enough to move out of the Shadow of Chernobyl.

Full disclosure, I have almost 650 hours in this game and some level of Stockholm Syndrome may be coloring my view of it (which is especially fitting given the location of Paradox Interactive).
If you have ever wanted a game that could transport you back to an incredibly accurate broadstrokes scale recreation of the middle ages, this is the game for you. If you ever wanted to then proceed to completely screw around with history, then this is definitely the game for you. If you wanted to go multiple steps further and become a devil-possessed lunatic master of seduction who also happens to be the Holy Roman Emperor, then stop reading now and buy this game.
The stories you will write in the course of playing this game are no small part of the fun of it. The interface itself is functional, the graphics are excellent for the type of game it is, the music is catchy and then annoying and then catchy again (650 hours is a long time to listen to any soundtrack), but the often bizarre events that will unfold surrounding your many reigns and the story that creates for you is absolutely fantastic. Spend a lifetime creating a mighty Kingdom and loving your children equally, only to play a few hours into the game and as one of your earlier character's sons end up having to behead your brother because he will NOT leave his claim for the throne alone ("I know it was you, Fredo. You broke my heart. You broke my heart!") Or decide to attempt to alter history completely and rule a mighty Basque controlled Europe, or dominate the world as Norse Pagans, or take Britain back for the Welsh. The options are countless, and each will provide you with hours of entertainment.
But, ultimately, it's that freedom of decision that should decide whether this game is for you. Crusader Kings II doesn't hold your hand. There is no one way to play this game, and any real goals in the game are entirely of your own making beyond the "Acquire score points through Prestige and Piety" or "World Domination" type goals. If you enjoy writing your own story and assigning your own personal victory conditions, then this is a fantastic game.
One last thought on the long list of DLC- Paradox Interactive is still updating this game and many of the updates come for free to anyone who owns the base game. Some paid DLC is cosmetic-only, and some adds larger new features. You can pick from these as you wish, and for multiplayer games whatever DLC the host has access to is available to everyone. It can be a bit pricey to buy all the DLC (although it is often on sale), so if you're the sort of person who wants to have everything that's available for a game, that's something to keep in mind before diving in. On the other hand, it helps fund the continued development of one of the most fun games I've ever played, so you'll have my gratitude if no one else's if you do decide to plunge in.

For a free-to-play game, Gotham City Impostors is quite a gem.
Though the idea of a team-based FPS based on a loner superhero without guns may seem wonky, GCI delivers with well-made maps, interesting weapons and gadgets, and an overall-cartoonish style for those who enjoy life's goofy side.
The only big drawback is that, as well as the maps and gamemodes are, they're limited; there are only about seven maps and four gamemodes to choose from, and the only DLC out yet is meant for customizing your character. [Huzzah for microtransactions!]
Despite this, Gotham City Impostors is still wholly replayable, with its tight gameplay and fun weapons; throw in some interesting maps and almost infinite ways to cuztomize yourself, and you've got yourself quite a good game.
For me, Gotham City Impostors earns an 8.5/10, and is a must-play if you're in the market for free-to-play games... or if you can't afford most Steam games.

My playtime in this game is probably enough to tell you tell that I've really enjoyed it. Awesomenauts is a MOBA played in 2D . I picked the game up a few years ago and I still find the game fun to play.
At the start of a match you pick a character. You have the usual classes you find in MOBA:s, such as rogue, tank, support and so on. Every character has their own set of skills and items you get to pick from at the start of the match. Characters and items are unlocked as you level up your account, which is fairly easy to do and comes naturally as you play. The characters in the game all look great I think and they really fit the flippant feel of the game.
As always there are some balancing issues for a time after a new character is released, but for the most part the characters are pretty well balanced and only your skills determine how tough a fight is going to be, not bad balancing. You will learn how to play most of the characters pretty quickly although there are some characters that require more practice to master them, as is common in most games like Awesomenauts. It wouldn't be much fun otherwise.
The ease of learning the basics of the game means that you can get into it pretty quickly and with so many characters with very different playstyles you will want to try them out and in this game you're able to do that in very little time.
Matches usually last about 20-30 minutes and if a player disconnects from the match then another player can immediately jump into the game, which is something that I really like about the matchmaking system in Awesomenauts. The possibility to join ongoing games means that a team where a player disconnects isn't necessarily crippled, as is often the case in other MOBA:s.

To win a match your team needs to destroy the enemy team's base. To do that you have to push through one or two lanes where turrets need to be destroyed in order to process further. Nothing out of the ordinary here. Mobility plays a big role in Awesomenauts. Not all characters are fast and not all characters have skills that help them escape. This means that when you play as the slower characters, typically the tanks, you will need some knowledge of the layout of a map in order to be able to escape. The importance of mobility is something I really like about the game.
I think that the larger part of the community is pretty friendly, but that could just be because most players tend to not say anything in matches. Ragequitting is very common (or at least it was back when I still played) but other than that you'll probably not have any problems with other players.
TL;DR: I would definitely recommend Awesomenauts to people who like this kind of games. Just watch a few videos of it and you should be able to tell if you would enjoy it.

After an extensive amount of time logged in this game, and conversations with peers, I can say that the game does work.
The art, at first looks really nice, but you quickly realize how much deatail is lost with how far out the PoV is. This angle helps with being able to see the action as it happens, but their is very little veriation in the zoom.
I can also say that the frame rate is poor to average, droping sharply in many plot-critical locations.
Speaking of the plot, for much of the game it takes a back seat (if not stuffing itself into the trunk). While the charecter sets out with the noble goal of saving the world and socity as the world knows it, there is so little support by the in-game cast that one can forget the names of most characters, or that they even exist untill one has a quest to go talk to them. There are also so few quests that one can exsaust the side quests in an hour, and I will say that out of a 70+ hour play through, less than 6 hours were actual questing, of any kind at all. as such, one quickly devolves from an archeologist reaserching forbiden parts of the past and re-discovering world alering technolagy into an air pirate, plundering other ships to get the money for training, ammo, and other supplies, as well as ship components.
Another complaint, their is no good dry-dock avalable. In-town, there's just not a lot of space to work with, and out of town, one has to deal with wildlife and other ships while trying to build.
That said, I do enjoy game play. Being able to design, construct, and fly my own armed airship. I enjoy flying around, hunting down pieces of the past, trying to save the world. I love the effort that was put into this game. I love that onw has the freedom to go wherever and do whatever in this game. I even started a second play through to try and get the good toys earlier.
I just still feel... I want to say disapointed, when I play this game. It feels like it could have become so much more, and for one reason or another, fell flat. It hurts even more when you can see how hard Snowed In tried on this. Its clear how much they wanted to do, and were unable to.
But what is here is a joy to play. It is an example of how a game can explore a world with a compleatly different makeup than our own, and even a wonder of its genre. I would strongly recomend it, even with all its flaws.
My Final Verdict: 5/10

Windforge is a very cool game, yet it really needs some balancing and a good patch or two.
I do hope the developers can fix a few things. The way levels are divided into different sections really breaks the combat with the whales, which can easily be lost when they tumble out of the sky after a difficult battle.
The inventory feels is clunky and suffers from tedium. Learning recipes for crafting, for example, means you need to click and drag books one-by-one into your area for active items and using them one-by-one.
Also, mining and building could use some work. The game has a pseudo-isometric design, and it can be unclear sometimes where the cursor is highlighting. It will often make you misplace blocks or mine the wrong areas.
Yet, on the positive notes, combat in Windforge is epic. While even the smallest enemy can easily kill you, the sheer range of options you have in how to approach each battle makes combat very fun. You can jump off your airship, grapple onto an enemy ship, battle its crew, steal the ship and harvest its parts. You can grind up flying monsters with your propellers, blast them with your turrets, or go outside to take them down by hand. You can grapple onto flying beasts, or surf on top of them while blasting them with your pistol.
Every battle will put your skills to the test, and every victory will leave you feeling awesome.
Aside from the overall difficulty, the game is particularly difficult early on. Enemies get harder to defeat the further you get from town. The key to playing is to not rush to quest objectives, and to instead take things slowly and build up your character and your ship.
Building ships is also very, very fun. It may sound like Terraria or Minecraft, but it’s not. The building you do in Windforge is all functional, and gives you very practical tools you can use to customize your playstyle.
Despite its flaws, I highly recommend Windforge to players who don’t mind a challenge, and can tolerate the lack of polish. While it needs some minor fixes, it is a rewarding game that plays with some unique and very fun concepts.

I think there's lots of potential here, but the fundamentals are not in place. Too much of the basic mechanics is awkward. For example, the player moves quite fast, but this makes precise positioning difficult. But to move downward through a hatch you must be EXACTLY in the right spot. If you don't stop precisely in the center, you just run right over it. There are too many hatches in this game to sit there fighting the controls trying to get through each one.
Another very fundamental mechanic with problems is block placement and destruction. They've opted for a 2.5D isometric presentation here, which looks good in screenshots, but causes difficulty during play. Every block is something like 1x1x4, which means they overlap one another and it's hard to pick out exactly the one you want to break, or to place one in exactly the right spot. It's just very confusing compared to the true 2D of Terraria.
At this point I have to recommend NOT to buy this game. Once these fundamentals are addressed, that will hopefully change. There's a lot of potential here.

Make sure to note which version of the game people are playing when they leave their reviews, because if you're not looking to spend any money or are fine with the $30 base game reviews from the other won't be an accurate representation.
As a free game, Atlas Reactor feels more like a demo than a full game. With a rotational hero roster and no way to unlock the other characters, the game definitly feels lackluster. However the full game offers you far more flexibility in that regard, and that is a huge chunk of what makes this game good: finding a character you're good with and expanding on them.
The game overall does a good job with making satisfying puesdo turn-based strategy, and with a good team or friends some moments just feel perfect. Even clutch plays at the end feel incredibly satisfying, and you rarely feel cheated out of a victory if you lose.
However, there are some flaw. The game is visually lacking on mid-range PCs and cluttered on smaller screens, which isn't a big deal but can hamper the experience sometimes. The chracters have neat backstories but there's nothing built into the game to expand upon them, the maps and skins really tell you nothing mor eabout the world or the characters, which is a shame because they have some great potential.
But all of the above problems are just part of the experience. The game plays quite well most of the time, but my two biggest gripe is the lack of communication. Voice communication is limited through Discord, which isnt a big deal except there is no text communication to make up for it mid game. You can see your teammates' moves before they happen, but with only 20 seconds it can be difficult to adjust accordingly, especially if someone is trying an unexpected strategy.
Overall, I do reccomend this game (the paid version), but if you're sceptical wait to buy it. The lack of refunds means you won't really have a trial period, and because the free version really isn't a great representation, you should do a fair bit of research to make sure you want to play this. But like the bigger reviers have said, if you like DOTA and you like XCOM, this game will satisfy you.

Pretty fun game. Controls and platforming are well done.
However, I still have a few gripes with the game. One, it can get repetitive as you will need to play every level multiple times in order to fully complete the game. Two, the level design is a bit repetitive as well. In a Mario or Donkey Kong game, you will get a variety of new platforming elements thrown at you in each individual level you play. The problem with Mutant Mudds is that is has 20 individual levels in 5 total worlds, only each world has variety, not the individual levels themselves. Three, the game was originally designed for the 3DS so the level design will feel slightly awkward with no stereoscopic 3D, but this is more of a nitpick than an actual problem.
The Deluxe version includes 20 extra levels, which are dark world levels. These levels  are the same as the levels you already played except for the fact that you can't kill any of the enemies unless you have a temporary weapon found in-level.
After you complete the game you can also complete the grandma levels which are the hardest in the game but on the flipside you can equip all 3 powerups at the same time.
As a gamer who loves platformers, fully completing the game and collecting all steam achievements took a little less than 8 hours. Overall, If you're a gamer who loves platformers then it's hard to not recommend MM: Deluxe for 9.99. Even with the gripes i'd say the game deserves an 8/10, but this is coming from a person who loves this genre of gaming.

EARLY ACCESS REVIEW.
Fantastic. I very rarely write reviews, I could not normaly be bothered, but this game deserves recognition; these people deserve money.
This game has everything: Mechs, evil Skeleton aliens, strategy, skill requirement, occational panic-inducing Bullet-Storms. It pours on the nostalgia while adding refinements made over the last two decades. The gameplay is smooth, 10 hours in and glitch free, everything works and feels like it should. Even as early access, this game plays like a finished product, that is to say, better than most released games these days.
Pros:
-well balanced procedural map generation: the ships are wierd and confusing, matching the general "horrible"ness of the alien looks.
-all the tools you need to beat the game are there, you never feel like the game screwed you, if you loose, you know it was your fault. Rare for a roguelike in my experiance.
-extremely polished gameplay: the visuals/sound and controls all feel perfectly aligned.
-wonderful weapon selection: every weapon has its place and the game can be beaten with the starting weapons if you have the skill.
Cons:
-the music is uninspired, but it is there i guess :/
-early access balancing. IE: the flak cannon wins everything, they need to make it more expensive.
-the difficulty is all opt-in during the game, no difficulty settings, just personal willingness to punish yourself.
-the game is too short.
Overall I say that this game is very much worth the ~15$ it costs, I will be returning to this game frequently and even if I don't I feel like I have gotten my money's worth at 10 hours. The largest impression I get while playing this game isnt that its too short or that the difficulty isnt right or anything, but that this game has massive potential. I hope they use it.

One thing to really note about this: It's a very bare and straight-forward platformer. No special techniques, no super-insane gimmicks, just you and some pixel perfect platforming. Which, playing through this while playing Strider, was much welcome and deserved.
Mutant Mudds forgoes a lot of detailed mechanics for having the player be precise in his approach to platforming, taking their time through the levels and even being overly defensive much of the time. There were plenty areas where I probably could have just ran through and taken a hit, but the feeling of having to redo half of a level if one more hit is taken can aggrivate some (I know it did for me plenty) but once you've beaten it, there's a great feeling of success I felt that I really haven't felt in a long time. And I haven't even bothered with the Grannie levels.
If you're interested in a platformer that's going to test your patience in both player deaths and level procedure, this is a good fit. The lack of mechanics makes it perfect for the decisive play it encourages. Otherwise, you might want to try something with much more "updated" feeling controls.

Before I start this review, I'm just gonna say I'm going to completely ignore the DRM apparently being in this game situation and just focus on Sonic Mania, the game and what it has to offer. I'd say if you don't want this DRM thing potentially being on your computer then I'd suggest listening to the people who say buy it on a home console if you have either a Playstation 4, Xbox One or a Nintendo Switch. I'm also gonna say there will be SPOILERS in this review so stop reading now if you don't want any spoilers :)
Sonic Mania, this is one of the best sonic games I've played in a long time, I grew up with the Megadrive/Genesis games with the Sonic Mega Collection Plus for Playstation 2 so that's how this game gives me so much nostalgia, if you grew up with the 4/5 classic Megadrive/Genesis games, them being Sonic 1, Sonic 2, Sonic 3 & Knuckles and Sonic CD, then you're going to adore this game.
This game has references everywhere but adding a few new things here and there that work so well with the classic Sonic style. What surprised me was the fact that they even made references to Sonic the Fighters, Dr. Robotnik's Mean Bean Machine, Knuckles' Chaotix and Sonic Triple Trouble which was great to see as I'm personally a fan of Sonic Triple Trouble. Playable characters consist of Sonic, Tails, Sonic & Tails or Knuckles which is really cool and I'm glad that they delivered on the fan favourite playable characters. All of the characters have their trates from the original games. Sonic being the fastest, Tails being able to fly and Knuckles being able to Glide, Climb and Punch. All the characters can spin dash which is always nice to see in Sonic games. Sonic also has a new move called the drop dash which is a neat new move which can be helpful and fun to use at times. Sonic Mania has zones from the original sonic games but also adds new zones to the sonic series that fit so perfectly in a classic sonic game. The level design is fantastic in all of the levels, very nicely detailed and has great platforming and speed sections. I'll go ahead and say that this game isn't really too difficult in my opinion, if you grew up with the classic sonic games and were good at them then you'll have no problem with this one. The elemental shields are finally back and they are just like they were in the original games. There's also a cool power called the hyper ring which can make rings easier to pick up rings if you take damage. The music in all of the levels is nice and easy on the ears, the old levels have been remixed and sound absolutely amazing, the new levels sound amazing too. The specials stages are really good in this game. The special stages for Sonic Mania consist of the Sonic 3 & Knuckles special stages for collecting tokens to unlock extras and a Sonic CD style stages for collecting the chaos emeralds where you have to race and catch a chaos emerald from a U.F.O. I was so happy to see these two types of special stages back as they're some of my favourites. You have to get all the chaos emeralds to unlock Super Sonic and get the true ending.
Other than the main mode called Mania Mode for the single player campaign, there is also Time Attack which is nice for the people who love speedrunning the game, which I can see being very fun in Sonic Mania, and there is Competition mode which is the 2 player mode which plays like Sonic 2's multiplayer mode. One last thing about the game is that it uses the save feature from Sonic 3 & Knuckles.
All in all this game is amazing, not gonna lie, I couldn't stop smiling and going on a huge nostalgia trip with this game and it was brilliant, I'll be honest this game made me cry. Playing this made me feel 10 years old again. Sonic Mania is a love letter to classic sonic fans. It's a game made by fans for the fans. Christian Whitehead, Headcannon and PagodaWest games have created an amazing Sonic game here. If you're thinking of getting this game, I highly recommend it, it's well worth the money. If you're a classic sonic fan, you will love this game. Even if you don't know much about classic sonic and the original Megadrive/Genesis games, give this game a try, I feel this will convince you to go and play the classic games if you enjoy this one and then you can see what inspired this game. I'd rate this game 10/10 it's that good :)

Overall, the game is a clear step up from Clear Sky but doesn't reach the heights of Shadow of Chernobyl for me. Unlike previous games, the world consists of 3 large open maps (Zaton, Yanov and Pripyat) as opposed to the dozen or so smaller areas. Mechanically, it's basically a tightened up Clear Sky: weapons, armour and AI all function the same but the guns aren't as ridiculously inaccurate and unreliable and enemies don't spam perfectly accurate grenades. A notable omission is the faction wars system, which I consider an improvement.
The central narrative is alright but suffers from the Oblivion/Skyrim problem of chaining together one urgent mission after another while the game expects you to bum around with side missions and exploration. Also, the ending is rather abrupt (with a Fallout style consequences slide show that really hammers home that tension). And, without spoiling, the mystery is pretty lame this time around. You don't feel like you're discovering the secrets of The Zone... just dropping in, completing a task and buggering off again. Still, it's certainly not a BAD game. The post-apocalyptic atmosphere, loot gathering and emergent gunplay are all here. It just doesn't do enough to move out of the Shadow of Chernobyl.

It's hard for me to recommend or not this game as this is a very bare bones racing game. Then again maybe that's what you'd expect for the price you pay (which I didn't by the way, game was provided to me by the Developers). The game can be fun, but there are a lot of shortcomings which make it hard to want to keep playing it.
The core Gameplay is not bad, the driving/handling is arcady and fun, there's an option enable Smooth Turning that makes the cars turn a bit more realistically, since with the default setting they tend to be very twitchy and not obey the laws of physics at all. All cars have Nitros that deplete and charge back up with time, there's no bonus that make it charge faster like drifting or drafting, you just wait for them to charge back up which again goes back to how bare bones this game is.
My main complain is how the races just aren't balanced. Even though races are separated by Group Classes, you are forced to upgrade your car if you want to even have a chance to win, and once you upgrade it enough, races become very easy. They are never balanced, you either can't win, or you'll be lapping the other cars with ease. You can change the difficulty but that just seems like cheating, and the game forcing you to do the hard work to the sweet spot, something you'll need to do for every race/upgrade combo.
The career mode consists in selection of randomized races that depend on the car class you have, once you finish a race, that selection disappears and new one appears. There's no real sense of progression here, it's just pick a race (usually the one that gives you the most money), race, repeat until you have enough money to buy a new car, then do it all over again.
There's an online mode as well but I wasn't able to test it as no one is playing this game.
Graphics are... well... serviceable. The colors are a bit on the ugly side and I hated how the game never looks very sharp, i was forced to turn off Anti-Aliasing and Downsample from 4k using the Graphics Card drivers to make it look decent.
Sound is also decent, cars have different sound engines and the game comes with a short collection of electronic music that does a good enough job keeping you pumped during the short races, but soon enough you'll get tired of hearing the same 10 songs over and over.
My humble opinion: If you have 5 bucks to spare, and you need something to entertain you for a few hours (emphases on the few), I guess there are worst things you can spend 5 bucks on, although personally, I can thing of better things to spend it on. I'm gonna give it a Thumbs Up but only because I'm forced to choose Yes or No, and this game isn't exactly terrible.

This game is a lot of fun but it has a lot of problems. The build system gets pretty frustrating sometimes such as when you are trying to put a vertical propeller on and it doesn't snap. The movement is not the greatest, especially when dealing with hatches. The game is also Very difficult. I will kill an enemy and wait for the next to come then I will loot their ships. Then another enemy comes and blows up my main ship while I am looting and I have to go spiderman on them, I sometimes just end up falling off the ship though which is not fun because you go through each load wall until you hit something and die.
There are some performance issues I have noticed such as occassional temporary freezes and whenever you go to the temples or cities, that might just be my computer though.
One of the big highlights of the game is the hunting of these floating whales. In order to harvest the whales they must be above a land mass when you kill them. This can be problematic because some areas don't spawn them. In the upper atmosphere are "Space Whales", these guys are really bad. They have more blubber but are almost impossible to harvest because they go in to anti gravity mode and just float away when they die. The whale carcasses also seem to attract a crapload of enemies making it even more difficult to harvest.
This is an original game and it is pretty awesome. I really hope that all the problems get fixed before its official release. Expect a lot of bugs, performance issues, and frustration. I recommend this game because it is better than most early access games that come out these days. It is a lot of fun and it is still in its alpha stage.
Edit: I have now gotten about 45 hours under my belt. I am adding this part to my review because I feel it is needed. I have gotten to around the end of the game and have encountered many bugs and glitches. Almost 9 of my saves have corrupted, therefore I have kept about 3 saves updated. Every time the quest tells me to meet with someone I go and meet with them and it doesn't complete the quest. This makes it so I can't beat the final boss. All in all, I don't think that this game is ready. It has loads of playability but you will be cringing through it due to frequent short term freezes due to enemies spawning in the area, and save corruption. This game was a lot of fun but I am going to wait until it gets patched a load more. I'll check it out again in a month.

Can be edited in game), and editing the game files isn't as simple as I'd like it to be (have to do it through Access. None of the free alternatives seem able to open the .dat file successfully. You can edit most of the attributes in game, but not all and it will be only for that league, whereas editing the dat will update all new files). The roster isn't up to date (and very few historical options are available, and require seperate purchases.) Comes with 2014-15, so some players are rated far below (or above) where they are now because it was made at the start of that year. Updates are very few and far between. I wouldn't expect any more past the current 1.3 update just released. The game takes up the entire screen, and doesn't seem to have a windowed (as in, scalable) feature. When you double click the top bar to make it windowed, the game screen does not adjust and results in being zoomed in. Need a decent resolution to play (for example, when I try a 1440x900 resolution, everything worked except for the draft, in which the buttons would be blocked with the draft board, thus not allowing you to continue past the draft.). Perhaps it's just that resolution, but I'd highly recommend downloading the demo from their site to make sure no graphical issues take place).
As for the good points, the simulating seems very realistic and is quite in depth. Each player is thoroughly different And allows for a complete team building experience. The difficulty is reasonable, and you won't usually find yourself building a perennial contender in a few years. Their is a coaching staff system implemented, although rather basic. They tried to remedy this in DDSPB 3, where they had offensive sets, but removed it in this version. The 2d play by play presentation is quite good. Trade logic is sound (and sometimes annoying. Haven't gotten close to the best thing from their side, supposedly. Argg) and the game is sustainable for very long associations. It is, in my opinion, by far, and another comma for good measure, the best basketball simulator available.
So once again, in it's entirety, I fully recommend the game, I have spent many, many hours playing the game outside of Steam, and got it on Steam since it was in a bundle and I didn't have to email the developer to deactivate my key when I had more than 2 licenses installed. Now, as I do recommend the game, I would moreso recommend waiting for the next game in the series, Draft Day Sports Basketball 2016. It was announced December 8th of 2015, although not much information is available. Why I recommend waiting? The game will come with a full historical replay feature all the way back to the post NBA/ABA merger. If you're as much of a fan as historical play as I am, this is a must have feature. If you want one now, then this is the best simulator. If you'd rather have a lesser simulator (although still solid) with full historical replay (even farther back. Not exactly sure how back, but before the days of Wilt Chamberlain definitely), then I would recommend Fast Break Pro Basketball. The Fast Break game also has a nifty historical shuffle feature, but this isn't a review for that game, so I'll leave it at that.
EDIT: Now that it's released, I fully recommend Draft Day Sports Pro Basketball 2016 over this or FBPB 3. It has a host of new additions, from new attributes to a new historical mode (start at 1976, play onward). It also is much more stable, in my experience.

Warframe is a complex beast, to say the least.
A free game that makes a whole lotta dosh must be p2w, or a there's a trap, right?
Rather, players
spend money on "fashionframe" and other cosmetics to extend their e♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
Warframe starts of slow and barrages you with information. Shiny new gear and guns are dangled in front of you in the market, and you have no idea where to get the materials for it. I fortunatley had a few friends that play the game already, and they helped me get started.
The difference between Warframe and many other f2p cash grabs is that everything is available from the start. If you need X material, the first 8 planets have everything. So, objectively speaking, you never have to go past the second void tier for the entire game. Of course, you wouldn't as the higher tier planets hold quests and different enemies. Granted, the game is EXTREMELY grind-ey, hence the nickname farmframe.
Complexity is being killed off. Seemingly, this is so that the game can cater to a wider audience. Warframe, much like EvE online defies this trend. As of this review in November 2017, there are about 900 mods in the game, each having an affect on items, both positively and sometimes negatively. Although the idea of 900 mods can be a turnoff, most of the "necessary" mods are given in the first few quests.
I cannot forget the actual gameplay. Warframe feels like a third person Quake title, if you could wallride and thrust yourself forward with great force (bullet jumping). Obviously the movement is great. The shooting does feel a bit weak, but it is compensated for by the sound design. One of the most unassuming shotguns in the entire classification sounds like a flak cannon. The satisfying thump of the shots going off is garnished by the ping of the reload. Needless to say, it's fun to use.
Opinion time: Warframe is not for the faint of heart. It requires time, effort and dedication to get past the mastery levels and form a playstyle. A clan can help, sure, but ultimatley to see what the game has to offer time is required. Personally, I love this game just for the sci-fi atmopshere and the DOTA style cop-out backstories, but the amazing game behind it helps too.

My new favorite game. I rarely write reviews but feel like I needed to quell the F2P complaints. First off, this game is NOT pay to win by any definition. You have a free character rotation that allows you to try characters of each type, support, tank, or firepower. You CANNOT make characters any stronger by paying more. Mods unlock with character levels, but even then, the stock mods are just fine. People saying this game is pay to win have no idea what that means, clearly. The loot boxes can only be opened every 36 hours, but to my understanding, if you decide to purchase the full version of the game you can open them all at once.
My experience was: downloaded the game, played for a few hours, said "yep, this game is awesome, I want to buy it".
I think this payment model will be positive for Trion in the form of revenue, but there will be a few ignorant/misguided reviews that result from it.
Think of it as the Overwatch model with a free to try option. It's NOT a demo. What demo allows you to play endless PVP with a type of character from every class?
Yes, ranked is not available yet. Overwatch did not have ranked for several weeks as well. It doesn't make sense to have ranked available in the first couple weeks as people are becoming familiar with the game and the devs are maintaining the full release traffic.
There is a mandatory tutorial now, which I think is needed. Pay attention and don't just skip through or you'll be here writing a negative review because you don't understand the basics. Of course you won't like it. I saw one review that said "this is a children's game" then went on to say "I don't understand how x y and z works". Huh? You can't grasp what you call a children's game? That being said, there are some deeper mechanics that are not clear, and really aren't necessary for those just starting out (vision is 6 squares away, you can see enemies in the same camo squares if you are close enough, etc), but it would be helpful if there was an advanced mechanics tutorial or something. This info may be available and I may just be missing it, but Trion should make it clearer somehow (load screen tips?).
Cheers and enjoy this amazing game.

One of the most polished Early Access games I've run across.  The core gameplay is solid, the music and sound effects are good, the visuals are a little cluttered but usable.
That said, it's main flaw -- and the main reason that I'm giving it a thumbs down -- is that you're entirely at the mercy of the random map design.  Sometimes you'll end up with something that's navigable and a good balance of open space and hallways, and sometimes you'll end up with something critical hidden in an unnavigable crawlspace.  It's annoying when you end up having to bail on a mission because the map is literally unwinnable, and that seems to happen with some regularity.
There's other balance issues that don't help.
* The timer is too short; if you have more than one "must kill" system then you're not likely to be able to get in under it, and then you're penalized a chunk of change you probably can't afford.
* The rewards are too small, the refund value on your suit too low: it's possible to clear a mission in a single go while completing all the objectives and still lose a prohibitively large chunk of money.
* The gamepad controls are not great; mouse and keyboard ends up being (I think) the best way to actually hit what you aim at, despite the fact that it looks like it was designed with a two-stick gamepad in mind.  Some sort of mild aim assist for gamepad seems like it should be in there, especially given that most of the 'minibosses' require some degree of precision aiming to hit their rather small weak spots.
* The mapping system seems to want you to make a tactical plan but then the waypoint system doesn't really support it.
* The way some systems interact can make certain combinations ridiculously difficult, which I don't think is well reflected in the difficulty estimate when you select a system.  Two spawners and a repair system, for instance.
* Given how tight money is, some of the bonus objective combinations are also prohibitively difficult (6 max hull points while not destroying the alarm, for instance).
So it's definitely a well done game with no real technical issues outside of the map generation; it's just that with the random map issues, the way it requires precision shooting but doesn't have the controls that support it, and the high, extremely random, and unadjustable difficulty level, I just don't happen to find it fun.  To the extent that those issues sound like they'd bother you, you might want to avoid it.

As of v0.25 (although I'm sure the core thoughts will remain same, since game is pretty much finished mechanics-wise):
Cryptark is essentially a bullet hell game with some roguelite elements.
Your task is to explore alien derelict constructs, gather whatever technology you might find there and destroy the core (brain) of the construct to win the mission.
Before setting out, you'll have to configure loadout of your ship. Depending on your picks, you'll have to pay some money.
You can go all-in guns blazing and destroy all enemies, but rewards might not quite cut it for you. So, balancing your loadout price and rewards is very important, since when you're out of money - you lose.
You can get additional money for doing bonus objectives (which can be quite damn challenging). Or by speed running the level.
Take longer than given time and you'll start losing reward money. So, you have to chose between money and that sweet-sweet ancient technology that'll unlock new weapons for you.
Current downsides are:
- Campaign is just 6 missions long, although random generation offers literally infinite replayability here.
- Difficulty is all over the place. I get it - it's randomly generated, so it's quite hard to control it, but sometime it's just too hard (well, for someone as bad as me).
And that's about it. Everything else is just amazing.
So, if you do like some bullet hell games and you think you'd enjoy one with roguelite elements - this game is definitely for you.
