I grew up on classic Sonic, I played my first one when I was still in diapers. Of course the cogniscience and hand-eye co-ordination didn't kick in until a few years later so I never really beat any of them in my younger years.
Then came the PS1 and I eventually decided to go back and retry the series when I grew tired of it. I beat them all and grew to simply adore the Sonic & Knuckles cart and how it worked with Sonic 3 and 2. Then when I eventually got an Xbox one Christmas I got Mega Collection Plus and beat them all over again, only this time I was able to do all 3 with every chaos emerald.
Then the bombshell of Doomsday Zone in 3 & Knuckles dropped in front of me and I was just completely awe-struck by how awesome it was. I was a young teenager at this point and had played through most of the 3D games as well, but after that magical experience I convince myself to do the same in any of the 3D games that had them.
Over the years I started to appreciate the games more on a design viewpoint and started to distance myself from the 3D games. The nail in that coffin came when I got a PS3 with 06 and Unleashed. I LOVED the day Stages on Unleashed but the night ones just curbed that enthusiasm. Then I delved into 06...
Boy of boys was 06 a fun journey. It was a buggy, broken unfinished mess of a game and succeeded in killing any hope of me seeing another good Sonic game. Then came Sonic 4 Episode 1. The way the momentum just stopped whenever I would jump and land made me turn it off before the fourth zone. I was actually a little depressed to think that even the classic line of games had finally been tainted.
Fast forward to 2016 and I happen upon the hilariously bad "that's the sound of 25 years of Sonic" stream. Then out of the blue comes a trailer for, well for something that just screamed "FRESH". Of course I'm talking about Mania's reveal. It blew my mind to see Sega contract their treasured franchise to fans that made several well known projects that had garnered a lot of praise from the community.
I waited and waited, Mania and Bloodstained Ritual of the Night being the only two games I was seriously looking forward to for over a year. Finally, it dropped... On consoles that I do not currently own. Another two weeks of waiting and a copy of Sonic 1 that managed to eat up one of those 14 days and I finally get to install and launch the game.
I sit there for over four straight hours, blast processing my way through zones old, new and remixed. Fighting bosses that challenged everything I knew about the classic games' bosses and then some. Checkpoint special zones that took me to again, old and new levels of my favourite special stage format in the franchise.
I was blown away. I was playing the game in tandem with my friend who I bought a copy for and we were just loving the time the game was eating. I still get goosebumps from some of the new mechanics and a lot of returning enemies that were used in clever and inventive ways to provide a fresh yet familiar experience.
I knew a year ago and I know now, Sonic Mania was a passion project through and through. You can make as many games as you want in a franchise, but there is no substitute for passion. That first playthrough felt nothing short of magical, it was an experience that felt long overdue and I enjoyed and am still enjoying every minute of it.
Sure the always online startup issue was bad, sure there are a few minor bugs, sure the game won't be everyone's cup of tea. But it's enough for me to just know that I honestly and truly got a fulfilling experience from the game.
And I still don't have all the emeralds on any of my files, so I know I still haven't seen everything yet and that very fact is why I'm so incentivised to replay the game many times over. Heck I'll be doing so for years to come most likely. Very few games can make me want to come back time and again years after they're released, but I already know Mania is one for the list.
Christian Whitehead and his team did a phenomenal job and surpassed all my expectations, I honestly will always recommend their works to my friends and anyone who asks for my opinion of them.
TL:DR
I really like this game and recommend at least trying it. Though it might be better for newcomers to play through Sonic 1, 2, 3 & Knuckles and CD to get the same sort of experience I had. Not mandatory of course, a good game is a good game to me.

A puzzle-game where you control a line of light and have to guide other lines of light or evade them. On your way to the end of each level you meet lots of friends and foes, have a happy time together and a sad farewell. Yes, I'm still talking about the same game.
Linelight slowly introduces the player to every new mechanic you need to solve the puzzles and reuses some of them now and then, but not to a point where it would get repetetive. Some of them are simple switches you have to activate, others are quite complicated and include magnets and good timing. It is quite challenging at times, especially when you have to get the timing just right, but not too hard to make someone ragequit; the awesome and calming soundtrack will keep everyone in a good mood anyway.
As mentioned above, at the end of each world you will meet other lines of light that will accompany you on your journey and help you to solve some of the puzzles. And that's where it gets kind of emotional. Yes, emotions in a puzzle game without an actual story or any written text! And that's what I think is kind of fascinating about this.
Conclusion: This is a very cute, challenging puzzle game. It took me about 8 hours to get 100% completion, which is a good amount of playtime. If you're into puzzle-games that at some occasions not only need a bit of thinking, but also quite some skill and right timing, you will like Linelight. And if you're able to feel empathy for some pixels, you're going to love it.

Just to make it clear: I do NOT think this is a bad game, I just don't recommend it.
At first this game might look like the average run-of-the-mill isometric indie crap racing game and yeah yeah rain snow funny visuals blah blah blah BUT! There's actually more to it.
I'll keep the upsides short because you can't make too much wrong for your average top-down/isometric arcade racing game.
Honestly I was surprised that rain and snow aren't merely visually there but really do have an impact on your cars behaviour. Controls overall surprisingly good. This also means you need to master the mechanics in order to have a chance against AI on default difficulty. There are several modes, more than enough track choices and cars (seperated into 5 classes E-A) to choose from. What I found especially fun were the different camera angles/modes, you should try them!
The bad sides though are why I don't recommend it: no "traditional rubberbanding"...I never got why people hate rubberbanding. After a game like this you'll love rubberbanding. Cars have different attributes and there are objective superior cars. When they're in front of you, you're basically screwed. Especially normal/higher difficulties, but even lower levels are not sure wins all the time (of course you'll easily win most, but there some infuratingly frustrating losses too). Difficulty only applies to AI acceleration. When you're starting to become good, become better, then you can try on harder modes.
Getting all the achievements is a chore. There's a good reason minimum %Achievement is the full garage. Cash prizes are dim, car prices are HIGH. Other than that there was no long-term motivation for me.
Unless you plan on getting the game to play it with/against friends this is a rather bland experience, but even if that's your idea keep in mind that you'll have to unlock cars the normal way, multiplayer doesn't have extra stuff unlocked.
If, on the other hand, you intend to enjoy it alone, prepare to experience a quite basic but moderately challenging smooth arcade racer to take your mind off things.
side note: might just have been my controller, but this game does NOT have "full" controller support, better check back in discussions to make sure yours will work

This is the first ever negative review I have made, so I'm sorry if there are a few things misssing from it.
The reason I dislike this game is because nothing is balanced and levels are misleading. I joined my first game (selected one with the average rank of 2.2 because I thought that would be a good starting point) and was annihalated by people who had a higer rank or who had paid to unlock everything. In a good game everyone should be getting an even number of kills and deaths, but in this game I was dying at least three times before I killed anyone. Another thing that I dislike is that when you think you are finally going to get a kill, some sniper or some person with six hundred rocket launchers equipped steals the kill and then kills you.
One time, I was sure I was going to get a kill. He was at a really low heath and I was zoomed right on him with my sniper, so I shoot him... AND HE DOESN'T DIE! This tank was the tankiest (no pun intended) thing ever. I think that a sniper should do more damage because 75 damage can't actually kill anything!
Again, I'm sorry that I have to give this game a negative review, because it runs perfectly, it looks really pretty and I am rarely faced with wierd glitches (only one and for a newish game that's pretty good). But the fact that the new players get mixed with the veterans and the game itself is pay to win, I have to give a negative review.
Points to improve this game are as follows.
-Don't let overpowered players join lobbies with noobs
-Make snipers actually do damage
-More coins should be rewarded per round (1 coin because your team iosn't good enough isn't nice considering its a 10 minute game)
-Everything should be cheaper so noobs actually stand a chance
-Don't mix the pay-to-win people with the people who want to have fun
Thank you.

Pushcat is what you get when you cross Bejeweled with Boulder Dash. Interestingly, the game specifically draws inspiration from the NES version of Boulder Dash, which I have something of an irrational love for after I spent most of my childhood playing it.
The mechanics are very simple: you need to collect a quota of silver coins from each level, but first you need to create the coins by pushing and dropping colored gems into rows of three. Later, there are some other ways that coins are created, as well as some other mechanics like blobs that eat rocks and bombs that destroy walls under certain circumstances. If you collect the coin quota and exit, you can progress to other levels, but you can also aim for a “star” quota on most levels by collecting even more coins. There are about fifty levels in all.
The game has many random elements. Some levels are completely random, others are generated based on a fixed template, but the specific contents of the level will change every time it's reloaded. Naturally, the random elements will occasionally screw you over, but for the most part it works as an interesting challenge feature.
But here’s the problem: about halfway through the game, there's a fearsome difficulty spike, and it basically becomes a masochism game. Ghosts will chase you, bombs will blow you up, puzzles will become super strict, and gem quotas will be so steep that you'll need to really stretch your brain about how you tackle a level and where you push things. Levels can get really long and it may take up to ten minutes just to set up a level correctly to produce the gems you need, especially for star quotas. There is no rewinding, and so dropping one gem in the wrong place could mean you need to start the whole level over again. You might also get caught by a ghost, blown up by a bomb, or trapped between rocks and need to restart. The final boss level can only be described as torture. On a positive note, there are no time limits to be seen, except when the level design creates them.
There’s also no leaderboards, extra levels, level editor, or anything else to encourage replay once you’ve collected all of the stars. At the end of the journey, game certainly feels like it's missing something.
Although I personally enjoyed this game, I can't recommend it to the majority of puzzle gamers. It's not an easy 100% for achievement hunters, and it's probably going to be a bit too far on the frustrating side for most people. If you really love Boulder Dash-type games and you’re okay with a challenge, you might like it as much as I did. Otherwise, there isn’t a lot to appeal to the average player or ease them into the genre, and you might wind up finding a bit too much to hate about it instead.

5min of this game
this is a puzzle match 3 game.
you need X coins to beat a level and/or get a star (stars unlock new areas).
you get coins by matching 3 like blocks of the same color, exploding some blocks, or sometimes they are just laying around a board but there are other blocks around that obstruct you.
most are puzzle like boards (figure out how to match all the blocks), but there are some where you just push blocks around or collect coins that are relatively easy to break up gameplay, also there are boss levels where a ghost will chase you around while you try and complete a level.

Arcade block pusher + match 3 with charming pixel/chip style.
(In the trailer, the camera pans around segments of several boards from the game, but in actual gameplay each whole level is fully visible when you play it)
Pushcat matches up colored gems to turn them into coins, collects coins to unlock the exit. Action & movement are similar to classics like Dig-Dug, Mr. Do, and Boulder Dash. Pushcat can move freely in 4 directions, but blocks & coins will fall down until they either land on a surface or fall off the board. In addition to pushable gems and junk blocks, there are stationary wall blocks and diggable tiles.
Each level has a coin quota you must reach in order to unlock the exit (as well as an optional higher quota to earn a "star" rating for the level), and most levels offer a limited supply of gems with which to create those coins. The trick lies in planning your moves so that you can make enough matches without getting stuck. There's no hard time limit, but some levels feature a ghost which will move slowly toward Pushcat, ignoring walls.
Some of the block matching reminds me of Tetris Attack (or Puzzle League/Panel de Pon, whichever). Sometimes you're moving back and forth to drop blocks down a chasm, other times you're pushing a foundation of blocks in order to transport a few on top.
I really like this game, but there are two intentional features that I don't fully appreciate:
-In many levels, the music is sort of incomplete - some instruments won't kick in until you reach your coin minimum. I actually like when games play around with the instrument tracks like this, I just wish it didn't take until the exit opened for the effect to take place. You really only hear these songs fully when you stick around to try to earn a bonus star.
-You have to push and hold against a block for a bit before it actually moves. There are very good reasons for this delay: You pretty much can't accidentally push a block (important, as there's no "undo", only "restart"). On top of that, allowing you to push blocks with no delay would likely allow you to intercept falling blocks. This would have puzzle-breaking potential. There are times when I let go too early because I misjudge the delay, and I have to go back and push again. Yes, this is my own error, but I feel like making the delay a bit shorter would help this somewhat.
Still, those two minor gripes considered, this is a fun arcadey puzzle game. Give it a try.

Going in, I had a certain understanding of what C:MW seeks to be: an essentially mindless hack-and-slash melee brawler with very little in the way of "deep" gameplay. I held off on playing it until the free weekend, since the genre didn't seem like my cup of tea, and boy, now that I've played it, I'm glad I did. I've played it for 2 1/2 hours and am now gladly uninstalling, with no desire to revisit this game ever again.
First, the combat. For a game that seems to want to be a fast-paced adrenaline-driven brawler, the combat, movement, and controls are clunky and feel unbearably slow. Even the fastest classes have a sprint speed that more closely resembles a leisurely crawl, and it takes painfully long for your character to do something as simple as an archer pulling out his dagger/secondary weapon. Furthermore, the core combat system revolves entirely around a rock-paper-scissors system of attacking, blocking, and feinting which, honestly, would probably suffice for such a simple game if it were actually executed well, which it is not. Some of the objective game modes do have redeeming qualities, but the majority are a horrendous cluster♥♥♥♥ in which far too many players are crammed into far too small a map, leading to frustrating situations such as being spawned directly in front of someone in the process of attacking an entirely different enemy, causing you to be instantly decapitated within half a second of spawning.
Furthermore, I've noticed that the game features $2-3 microtransactions for ALL cosmetics, which as far as I can tell are not unlockable through gameplay. Compare this to a game like Overwatch where all cosmetics can be obtained through sufficient gameplay and a little luck; in C:MW, you could play 20,000 hours and still need to shell out multiple times the game's sticker price to obtain all of the game's cosmetic items. I could perhaps (partially) ignore this ridiculous fact if the game were actually enjoyable, but, as I've said... it's not.
Overall, C:MW fails to deliver anything even resembling an enjoyable gameplay experience, and the presence of pay-to-unlock microtransactions in a $25 game is quite frankly insulting. If you can get it for free, you might give it a try and see whether you like it. If not, I would definitely not recommend spending any money on this game. 2.5/10

*If youre playing with a gamepad, dont let the way the cars handle on the street put you off (if youre trying to stay bettween the road lines, driving racing lines they are ok), the way the driving and physics are as of Update 8, the controls will initially feel darty or sluggish depending on your settings. -	The vehicle building and repairing portion of the game is the best out of any other game I have ever played. Adding and removing parts to and from cars is quick and easy, one mouse click per part.
-	You can buy cars and trucks ranging from brand new to totaled off wrecks and everything in between. At the beginning you won’t have much money so the cars you will be able to buy will need allot of work. Once you have bought your first vehicle you can either buy parts you need or buy and part out wrecks until you have what you need to build something that runs.
-	Most of the parts can be swapped between vehicles. You can make cars into off road racers or trucks into drag cars. There is an extraordinarily wide variety of options for doing what you want to the vehicles.

A good game for all motoring enthusiasts. Has its quirks and is full of glitches, but on a good path.
In Revhead you control an amateur racing driver trying to make his way up the local ladder. The game is divided into three distinctive parts: garage, racing tracks and the town, each with set of activities.
Without further ado:
The Likes.
- genuine feel of backwater, dilapidated garage that sees old jalopys and bangers more often than flashy supercars.
- every car comprises dozens of parts which are removable, configurable and swappable. Need wider tyres? No problem, buy or scavenge a set of rims and off you go. Engine too small? Get a used V8 from an old 4x4 and stick it in. Change the drivetrain to awd while you're at it aswell. Yup. That's how far this game goes in ride customization.
- parts and cars market is accessed through ads section in a newspaper. That's right. No PC or iPad for you. To find what you want you need to scour the ads and hope for the best. I love this, it adds a lot to the flavour.
- driving and racing. At first I shared the view of many reviewers here on steam, that the car driving is unplayable. And then I realised that I'm trying to drive a 20 year old car with 300k on the clock and worn out tyres at 60mph and expect it to corner like a beemer. Ain't gonna happen mate. Change suspension. Install stiffer sway bars. Change tyres. Fix steering. Bam. Car handles like a dream. Even on a keyboard. Stop whining and git gud.
- impromptu drag races in the town add to the range of activities. They're a good source of money and are done onthe main town map. Nice touch.
The dislikes
- genuine feel of an indie game made on a shoestring budget. Requires tons of polish to shine.
- the graphics looks a bit dated for 2017. Cars look unrealistic - we need more dirt! - and are not tremendously detailed.
- the Aussie setting is a bit cheesy and over the top. The game tries to be more Australian than Australians.
- the town feels dead and needs more day-to-day traffic and pedestrians.
- last but not least: Revhead desperately needs more content. More cars, more tracks, more engines, more parts.
Overall, I'd give the game 6.5/10 at the current stage of development. Solid game but requires a lot of tlc to shine.

What a truly relaxing thing of beauty Linelight is...an enjoyable (if repetative) soundtrack but the game is great...drop in..play a few levels and come back whenever...thought-provoking in places but ultimately a relaxing puzzle game if ever there was!!!

I like the idea of calling Linelight an atmospheric puzzle game.
Reason being, Linelight does an amazing job of building a soothing mood. Yes there are puzzles and some of them can be a bit of a brain tickler, but ultimately I didn’t feel like they were the focus. If you look at games like Divide By Sheep and Girls Like Robots, these games are heavily focused on that puzzle element. Linelight feels more relaxed, more focused on its rhythm and fluidity of movement than mind shattering puzzles. To the point that it almost feels like a dance. Now I know that may sound odd for predominantly a puzzle game but give me a chance to explain.
The first time you load into the game you’re immediately greeted by a wonderful piano melody. This beautiful soundtrack continues and completely enhances the game stage by stage. This is one of those games where I HIGHLY recommend purchasing the Game+OST bundle. Obviously graphically, Linelight is on the simple side, but it does make use of bright colors and a colorful cloudy background. Each stage or world usually has a theme that blends into puzzles from that point forward. Whether that be red lines that move independently and can impede your progress, orange lines that move only when you do or ways to make your white line longer. These elements are all given their own world/set of stages for you to master.
Like I said before, I never really got stuck with any particular puzzle. I may have taken a couple more minutes on some, but I never felt like I didn’t know what to do. This isn’t really game you are going to need a walkthrough or a guide, as the game is pretty self explanatory. It’s not a super difficult game but more focused on a pleasant experience. Get a hot cup o’ tea, wrap up in a warm blanket and play this game. I am rather surprised that Linelight isn’t currently on any mobile device, as this would be wonderful to play on a comfy sofa. I really hope that this game is ported to the mobile market, I think it definitely would excel there.
When you’re just about to complete a world the game does a bit of a pivot.
It takes all that you have learned from the former puzzles and does what I can only describe as a dance of lines. These are quick puzzles that usually involve more than one line that you may or may not control. These moments are rather beautiful. Even with the simple graphics. You fly forward as fast as you can, twirling and crossing. It’s something you definitely have to experience to understand.
Linelight is a nice but simple experience. There isn’t really going to be much replay value. There are some hidden puzzles in there but nothing that I felt like I absolutely wanted to find. It’s there if you want it. If you do replay this game, its because you want to chill and relax. Enjoying the aesthetics more than anything else. You can probably complete this game within three to four hours at the most. Linelight currently features Steam achievements but no Steam cards.
I had a good time with Linelight, it’s a great stress reliever and it definitely does things in a unique way. The puzzles were fun, inventive, innovative and the soundtrack absolutely sold me on this game. Any gamer/family can enjoy this game as long as they know what they are buying. Coming in at £7.99/$9.99 it’s not that hard on the pocket either. Just keep in mind, that this is a bit of a short experience.

I bought Little Racers Street ages ago. It's a great casual little game that is fun to play for half an hour or so at a go. I find myself coming back to it every six months or so when I feel like some quick and simple arcade fun.
The premise is simple, you can buy cars, upgrade them, and race them in short races against a varying number of opponents. The races have different weather conditions that affect the handling of your car. The better you do in a race, the more money you win for buying new cars and/or upgrade your current cars. There's also different classes of cars, and upgrading a car can put it into a higher tier. That's pretty much it.
The tracks are generally pretty similar, and take place on a number of shared maps with different routes for the different races. As the name says, you are racing on streets (i.e. not a for-purpose race track) and the courses tend to combine several straights and several sharp turns, with some tracks more winding than others.
Car handling is decent and arcadey, as befits the genre, and you have a nitro that slowly recharges over time and is best used on the long straights. Your car also has a damage metre that rises as you crash into the environment or when you drop from a height, a feature on a few of the courses. The more damage you do to your car during the race, the more money is deducted from your earnings to repair your car.
There's also online multiplayer, but I have never tried it, so I can't comment on that.
I see a lot of references to old-school arcade racers, and Little Racers STREET is very much in the same vein. Personally it reminds me a lot of Supercars (sans weapons and with a different camera view) and Skidmarks (especially the semi-isometric perspective and car handling). At any rate, if you enjoy casual arcade racers, I say give this one a whirl. Just don't expect anything deep and revolutionary.

Having now played 1000+ hours of this game (and really, that might very well be the only recommendation I'd need to give it), having all the DLC, and all that, I cannot recommend this game highly enough for strategy fans.
For those not familiar with Paradox Grand Strategy games, the game is a pausable-real time strategy game.  You let the game run until you need to make a decision or move an army or whatever, and then you can pause it and take as long as you need to give your orders, or even decide what orders to give.  Then you let the game go again, speeding up or slowing down as needed, and pausing whenver you want.
Crusader Kings II is also very heavily RPG influenced.  You will be guiding your dynasty, not just a country.  In fact, you can even choose to be nothing more than a minor count in a major historical empire.  From there, you build an alternative history for your family, setting your own goals.  Do you want to be the most prestigious dynasty in history?  Do you want to build a massively wealthy merchant dynasty?  Do you want to conquer the Midieval world?  It's pretty much up to you.
Paradox also has continued to improve the game both with DLC and free content patches.  This is pretty much par for the course for all their grand strategy games, and it's why I consider Paradox to be my current favorite game publisher by far.
Again, I cannot recommend this game highly enough for strategy fans.

There are two types of levels in the game. Some are hand-made and thus have a set style of solution (with mild flexibility). These are perfectly okay. The other, though, are entirely procedurally generated beyond "there is a gem/rock/dirt in this square", and thus it will change details every time you reset.
Those levels? Not so good. Unless you reset every time you begin, you won't see them coming, and they can go from "Well, this is doable" and you'll never notice, to "having made 3 'wrong' moves the stage is now mathematically impossible, and you won't know until the very end". It's hard to explain without having played it, but basically, this can turn a stage from "you need to consider every move" to "I pushed a gem and half of the level cleared itself before I did anything" ALL WITH THE SPAWN OF THE STAGE. These are the biggest flaw on Pushcat, and the best part about it is that unless you want to clear every level with a star, you can skip them or fake it with just a stage clear.
But if you enjoy the game, like me, you're probably going to go for those stars, and god have mercy on your soul when you hit a procedurally generated stage.
(Other notes: the music is incredibly fun, being a very early cartoon/calliope style, with different layers of the song appearing as you clear the stage to various degrees. Also, some of the premade stages are incredibly clever and I wish the Steam release added new levels or something.)

What a game.  Ignore my steam hours, I recently rebought after losing my original disks.  I've put over a thousand hours into this game easily following it's original release.
Oblivion isn't so much a game as it is a second life.  Cyrodil is like that perfect holiday destination that makes you wish you could retire and just go and live out the rest of your life taking in it's rolling beauty.  Bethesda will always tell you that the world is the star of their games and that sentiment shows through more so in Oblivion than any other game they have ever made imo.  Every city is unique with it's own distinctive architectural style that lends a tremendous air of believability to the environment.  The variety of the landscapes, from the chilly snow covered mountains of Bruma to the dense, marshy forests of Blackwood, this really is a thing of beauty.  A place where you can lose yourself, where time seems to stand still as you're completely absorbed in it's world.
Yes, the AI is clunky, the conversations between them are often comical and have a tendency to repeat.  The combat is ok, but not brilliant.  Spell casting is less refined than in Skyrim.  The NPC's are ugly, sometimes disturbingly so.  Beggars will plead for assistance in the wavering tones of a 90 year old then discuss the Fighters Guild recruitment drive in the tones of an aristocratic socialite.  But these flaws become completely irrelevant and in most cases wonderfully charming once the sheer majesty of the game takes hold of you.
For my money, Oblivion stands out as the jewel in Bethesda's crown, completely outshining everything else they have done.  Aside from the combat, every single aspect of this game eclipses it's younger sibling Skyrim completely.  The main quest is far more interesting, the side quests are far more interesting and often amusing, something which was sadly missing from Skyrim.  The faction quests, Fighters Guild, Thieves Guild, Mages Guild and especially the Dark Brotherhood are just superb and are main quest lines in their own right.  You're pretty much getting five main story lines for the price of one.
If you have never played Oblivion but you enjoy the Bethesda style of the FPRPG then you simply must buy it, right now, seriously.  Do not allow yourself to miss out on what will probably go down in history as the best game Bethesda ever made.  I cannot recommend this game enough and I'm very picky about which games I invest my precious free time into.
TL;DR.  Masterpiece, simple as that.

I was having alot of fun in Chivalry, thinking it for a second to be the best competetive multiplayer game I've tried. Then I discovered free-for-all. It was the worst idea you could have thought of for this game. A more accurate name for free-for-all would be 'get ganged up on' as that is all that happens in free-for-all. Literally the worst parts of the game, made into a game mode.
Once I discovered the first thing I really disliked in Chivalry, I started noticing the rest. No one who plays an archer is actually good at the game, thus why they play said class in a melee-focused game. Close in on those pusillanimous ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s (word hint; it's also a sword) and they drop like flies, even if you actually allow them to draw their melee weapon, and you're one hit from death. The game fails at being either realistic, as most blades are more effective against a knight's steel and mail armour than most blunt weapons, and also fails at being well-balanced, as the biggest sticks pretty much always win, and when they don't, you got ganged up on. In addition, the block time with weapons is far too short, as an attack takes longer, thus you get struck after the block, unless you block at the last second, and the shield literally only works when raised, serving no purpose when lowered or on your back, and even when raised sometimes attacks seem to go straight through it.
Objective game modes are also woefully imbalanced, typically in favour of the defender, as the attacker is the only one who has to kill AND do the timed objective, because the defenders' objective is just 'kill the attackers before they complete their objective, on a timer'. Admittedly, obectives where you have to push siege engines aren't as bad as objectives where you have to destroy buildings or carry flags. Siege engines only have to be pushed over to the enemy, whereas destruction and flag objectives require the team to fight their way PAST the enemy spawn point, and then ignore the enemy fighters for the objective, leading to many backstabs.
These are only some of the mechanical issues with the game, and that's not even mentioning some of the incompetent players who can't figure out to thrust instead of swing when there are teammates to either side of them. There's also a particular habit among many players of ignoring the objective, typically half the team doing so. And why do all the worst archers insist on playing archer every single game, despite killing eight friendlies and one enemy last game?
And my final point... crossbows.

There are a couple bad apples here and there, but by and large, the community in 100% Orange Juice is very friendly, likes to joke around, have fun, and commiserate when we roll a 1 at the worst possible time or teleport away from home right when we thought we were going to win the game.
Basically, the goal is to accumulate as many stars or wins as you can during the game.  Each time you step on a home with enough stars or wins, you will gain another "norma," which lets you use more powerful cards.  There is definitely some strategy involved depending on the character you choose.  Try to pick cards that suit your character's strengths and avoid cards that don't.  A little basic knowledge of probability helps but isn't required.  Also,  pray to the Orange Juice gods and goddesses.  Luck is a huge element of this game, so you will want divine intervention on your side!
Campaign mode can be a little frustrating if you don't know what you're doing, which is why I recommend getting some tips from other players first, but it's also required to unlock most of the non-DLC characters.  This is one of my only real complaints about the game.  It can be kind of unclear how to unlock the characters you want.  When I was starting out, it felt like it took forever to get my favorite characters that I saw my friends using in multiplayer.  If you stick with it through campaign mode, they'll all eventually become available in the store though.
That said, the nice thing about campaign mode is that the story is *incredibly adorable.*  The dialogue in all of the campaigns puts a smile on my face every time, and the characters have very expressive animations.  Personally, I recommend Marc and QP's campaigns for maximum cuteness, but all 4 have nice stories.  Red Barrel all the way!
Most importantly, don't sweat the small stuff.  For every bad roll you get, eventually you'll get an amazing roll to put the smile back on your face.  Meet new people, relax, and have fun.

So many negative reviews.... it makes me sad. This game is actually great. It models things many games do not model...little details like faster times on some shifts, because you hit it just right... the worrying sound of a drive belt squealing popping up in the middle of a race.... parts degrade over time, and you must constantly put love and attention into your car. Oh, speaking of your car.... So, here's how it starts.
One day, while performing jobs for your boss, you look in the paper for some parts.... and you see IT.
IT is the perfect car... a ruined wreck, or perhaps a high mileage family grocery getter.... or perhaps, an old, used up drag racer that has been wrecked. Maybe that old four door gas saver over there in the corner? Let's call this.... The Turd.
So, you buy your Turd. You realize just how much stuff is wrong with your Turd, and how much money you will have to spend to fix your Turd. So, you start spending. Maybe these control arms will be better.... maybe this carb will net me more horsepower... maybe this TOWER SUPERCHARGER will get me where I wanna be... seriously, yes. You can buy a tower supercharger in this game, and then hang on for dear life as your otherwise underbuilt Turd refuses to turn, refuses to brake, refuses to do ANYTHING but GO, shredding your crappy worn out street tires to the tune of a glorious supercharged v8 at full yell, laughing like a complete pyscho. Back to the drawing board....
...... many, many hours later, you have finally built it. The perfect machine.... the unbeatable MONSTER. You proceed to destroying everything within 1000 miles of you. One day, you take her out to the track to show her off to your lesser financed opponents.... you leave the line in a tower of tire smoke. Suddenly, your drive belt starts squealing. You slide more than usual in that turn, because your tires are getting old and worn. You don't accelerate as fast, because from many hard races and some impacts, your tuning has changed for the worse. You realize the brakes feel stiff, responseless. It's time for a rebuild. The sinking depression comes back...
As a professional racer of over fifteen years, I can tell you this game does a better job than any other of simulating those minor and major inconveniences. Oil must be changed. Installed a new radiator? Don't forget to fill it with coolant! Before the race, make sure your tires are inflated correctly...This game will teach you more and give your more of the amateur racing experience than any other game out there. You must pay attention and let the car speak to you.
For the places the game lacks, the developer has great plans. He is very down to earth, does his best to respond to all feedback, and actually LISTENS to his playerbase. Updates come on a regular basis. Yeah, the game isn't perfect, and it's not for people who don't want to have to think. This game will challenge you, make you go HMM, HUMMMM.... make you rage about how "my car didn't do this last time", because it changes every... single... race. That is, until you figure out that you have something broken. Well, crap. Let's look in the paper.......

I've not played this for all that long, but I can tell that even at this early stage this is going to be a fun game. There are a load of characters to level up with lots of different upgrade paths and power unlocks, skins, taunts and other stuff to keep me entertained for a long time. Nit picky things:
1; I would like the countdown timer to last a little longer but I guess in this ADD world we can't wait and make tactical descions over time and plan things out in a chess like manner. Ah well.
2; I also don't like that I have to log into a seperate client as well, that annoys me about a number of games, not just this one.
3; Map rotation sucks so far. I've only ever seen two maps, which is crap to say the least. (Edit: two new maps so I've seen four maps now.)
4; The unlockables as far as I can tell is a bit silly. You use ISO (in game currency) to unlock the skins and they're supposed to be given out on each battle. I've played quite a few matches and only got 75ISO...
Good things:
1; The characters are well designed, fun and quirky enough with enough diversity for pretty much anyone to enjoy playing. No doubt I'll find my favourites after a few weeks.
2; The balance in game is really good and all the characters I've played so far have good strengths and weaknesses.
3; There's a lot to do, from levelling the characters to unlocking goodies.
4; The taunts are fun but I can see them getting tiring if they're overused. (Maybe an option to switch them off?)
5; The specs needed to run the game are nice and low so a lot of people will be able to play this. I think a lot of the time devs forget that not everyone can throw money at pc's everytime a new game comes out, so its refreshing to have a game that doesn't need bleeding edge specs to play.

I'm writing this review from a long time Dota player's perspective. The similarities are few, but the differences are so welcome. I would hesistate to call it a sped up condensed version of Dota, purely because it's 2d. This takes away so many things that the whole experience is different.
Games are handled much more casually, with players being able to drop in and out of matches. There is a level system external to the gameplay which unlocks the first 20 characters each level, and from then onwards unlocks a new skill option, one per level. You will gain one level per match, at least, and if you win probably 2/3 levels. Overall I found I had earned more things from levels than I was able to keep up with, which is a good thing.
The characters are fast to learn and there is not a lot of clutter on screen. The simplicity of some moves can sometimes be annoying, especially when you get dunked several times over by the same combo, but you eventually learn the pattern and solve the problem, much like bloodseeker's rupture. I will say now that the artstyle is great, and the game intro is super ♥♥♥♥ing cool. Also each character has a theme song that plays during your skill selection, pretty nifty.
The levelling system for your character within the match rewards good play and there is almost no (noticable) rubberbanding. Teamplay and foresight are key, being outnumbered is usually lethal. The respawn time is about the same as Dota's, but for the last 10 seconds you get to play a mini game to collect gold before you spawn, although it's not really necessary.
My main criticism is probably that out of the 20ish characters there are 3 that, at the moment, are only available if you pay. And those characters are hard to learn, because you can't use their skills thus can't get a feel for them. I haven't dabbled in any of the cosmetics, but it's worth mentioning there's no pay to play aspects other than purchasing the extra characters.
Overall, as a dota afficionado, I would recommend this game. It captures the frenzy and a small amount of the strategy of dota, without being anywhere near as time consuming or mentally demanding. No real criticisms, it's very well executed and cuts to the chase.

At this moment, 89% of Steam players are recommending this game..
I'm sorry, but I cannot agree with them..
The game as itself is great; a very fun game, nice character, nice implementation with the other Assassin's Creed games, good story.. If you liked Black Flag, you'll like this too, it's very similar.. They made some improvements in the gameplay that are really good.. Then, why do I not recommend this game?
I was really looking forward to this game, to try what it would mean to be a Templar.. Unfortunately, you can't, because after, what, 7-8 games where the Assassins were ''the good guys'' and the Templar ''the bad ones'', Ubisoft decided to change that.. If you don't watch the cutscenes, you'll feel like an Assassin fighting against Templars, where it should be the opposite..
Let me say why I feel this way..
For 8 games, the Templars have always had the advantage, right? Even in the present, they have the advantage.. Well, in this game, Ubisoft decided that Assassins should have the advantage.. They've gangs set up in every city, with headquarters, leaders and power, while the Templars, that ALWAYS had the advantage, even from the crusades, now are nothing more than a bunch of 3-4 guys that fight against the control of the Assassins.. In 8 games, it has always been the opposite..
Anyway, if this reason's not enough for you, there's another one..
Templars are the bad guys, right? They want to control the world, they want to put everyone at their feet, right?
No. Wrong! In this game, the Templars are the one who want to see the colonies become a place of prosperity and freedom.. I'm non exaggerating, those are the exact words of one of the Templars' General.. And the Assassins? The Assassins are the evil gang that, in a mission, create poisonous gases to use against innocent citizens.. INNOCENT CITIZENS.. And you, a Templar, stop them and save the city.. Oh, and don't we forget about the part where the Assassins nearly destroy the world for error, and who's there to stop them again? Oh, right.. You, a TEMPLAR!
C'mon Ubisoft, are you freaking kidding me??

In its current early access state, I can't recommend the game, simply because it's no better, and probably worse than its predecessor, which, due to it being abandonware is totally free. This sounds like a very harsh thing to say, but unfortunately with steam early access, you never really know if the game will ever come out of it.
Everything about the game is worse really. The physics on the robots are inconsistent, despite the newer engine. It makes fighting the robots feel a bit off. You might hit a guy with a spinning disc and have him not move, then he might drive into a wall and that'll be a much larger 'impact.' I didn't use a wedge, but I'm told the chassis of the robot actually makes no difference, ie, if you make a wedge you can't get under people. I can't confirm that.
The building has been 'simplified' to the point where it trades ease of use for clunkiness. For instance, if you try to add a 'peg board' to the edge of a disc, there's about 15 attach points on one side, and 3 on the other. You have to click change attach point about 15 times, as opposed to just clicking the attach point you want, then on the motor. It's just not streamlined at all, and I can put everything inside eachother.
Next, huge lack of parts. The variety dropped pretty hard in general. There isn't enough weapon motors and the best one isn't strong enough. Moving on, lack of part clarity, none of the motors say how much electricity they draw, as far as I can tell. The armor doesn't necessarilly say how effective it is. Is fibreglass going to give me more or less health than carbon fibre? Something about fire resistance?
On a side note, the music is annoying, the sound effects are low quality and just sound weird, and some are ripped from the old game. The graphics, while not that important, are pretty awful. Somehow even though the textures are higher quality, they are just worse looking than the old game. It's hard to explain. They just look like typical stock unity textures, it looks odd and cartoony. I'm sure you'll get the same feeling when you look at the screenshots. I think it's to do with the lighting.
For me, a robot building/fighting game where the building isn't great and the fighting is plagued by weird physics isn't worth the buy. Wait until full release, then look at the reviews again.

At the time I'm writing this, it had been released for a couple of hours and I have played it for just under two hours.  And as much as I love the idea of the reboot, it feels dated.  And sluggish.  I just wish there'd be faster motors, real life robots such as England's own Warhead or America's Bite Force, and a way to make your own drive train, so you can legitimately make either a push bot, or a faster spinner for your robot, or a drum weapon.  On top of that, the motors only seem to point forward when you first put them in, making it a real hassle to make the robot move forward properly.  A majority of the robots in the game as well just feel haphazardly put together as well, with blade spam all over them.
Pros:
+ It's a nostalgic return to the Robot Arena series.
+ Arcade like, and super quick loading times
+ Axe like weapons feel like they can deliver a punch.
Cons: (Oh boy this is going to be long)
- Customisation feels rather limited.
- No faster motors or powerul motors.
- Spinners feel like and look like a wet noodle.
- No real life robots in the game right now.
- Preset chassis are small and unvaried.
- One graphic on a robot replaces all graphics on all robots.  Not sure if a glitch or really poor design.
- Making low profile robots makes awful clanking noises.
- Graphics on some styles of robot stretches and makes it look ugly as sin.
What I would like to see in the future of this game:
*FASTER MOTORS: I want to be able to create a hard hitting spinner bot or a robot that uses a drum weapon and still keep its ability to ram into opponents quickly.
*REAL ROBOTS: I wish to see robots old and new in the game.  Whether or not this'll happen is something completely different.
*ACTUAL STATS ON ROBOT PARTS: One thing I have noticed is there's a lack of info on parts.  If this gets updated I'd be fairly okay with it.
*A DRIVE TRAIN SYSTEM: Having a steering column is nice and all but I would love to make a robot that can steer on a six pence without having to fiddle with motor positioning.  On top of that, I'd love to see a choice between either belt or chain drive, for those who wish to make a robot on a tank drive steering system.
*DIFFERENT FORMS OF LOCOMOTION: Wheels are cool, but tank tracks, Walking legs, or even a Half track system would be excellent.
*WEIGHT CATEGORIES: Right now, all the robot seem to be in the same kind of weight category, which is quite misleading.
*MORE ARENAS!!!: Can't stress that enough right now.  Being in a real arena would be fantastic, such as the old Robot Wars arena or the new Battlebots Battle box.
Overall, this feels really outdated and in need of some more work, if I'm brutally honest Octopus Tree.  It doesn't feel polished, and it feels a little rushed on top of that.  Unless this game gets a really big update and pretty much changes the game into a much more customisable game that actually feels like I'm making a robot, then I'd say avoid this for now.

Free to play, though I would recommend at least picking up the cheap 'Basic' pack if on sale to bypass the annoying 'limited storage for tank parts' feature of the F2P version (I can't remember if Basic also allows you to save up to 3 tank combinations, I think it might be the case). There is no P2W inherent in the game, only Pay2UnlockFast.
This isn't a game that I take seriously enough to play for consistently long stretches of time, but one I keep coming back to occassionally. It's light fun, and its style makes it easy to just hop into matches and start blasting things with buzzsaws and coconuts. And thankfully even after a year post-release I don't have problems finding active matches with dozens of players.
The customization is relatively shallow when compared to somewhat similar games like Robo-somethingsomething or whatever that was called. I think this will appeal to those who like tinkering around a little but really just want to blast things with harpoons and fireworks. If you're a more creative type who spends hours making their combat machines JUST RIGHT in an editor, and then testing it for 5 minutes to find out it actually sucks, so you back to the editor for another hour to make it JUST RIGHT AGAIN - well, the customization in this game will not appeal to you.
You mix and match parts, but no tweaking with the parts. You mix propulsion+body+turret+weapon(s)/supports. There are enough different combinations to accommodate quite a few different playstyles: play a lurking cloak unit with high burst damage by equipping 'stealth' mods and waiting for your prey; grab spider-leg tracks and high-damage sniper rifles and pick off enemies from across the map while hanging upside down from a tower or the side of a wall; go very fast and punch hard if you're willing to sacrifice survivability for speed and firepower; be a healer; float over the water with long-range guns, making it hard for landlubbers to retaliate; put some jumpets and wings on and be a goofy hang-gliding tank with exploding coconuts if that's your thing (that's actually a very fun one, I've tried it).
Game modes are fairly standard-fare DM/TDM/point-control. Surprised there's no CTF, though I think the devs wanted to just have gamemodes that worked interchangeably on the maps they have, and said maps are overall a bit too small for CTF anyhow.
I've not come across any highly organized teams in the game and AFAIK there aren't any - the gameplay doesn't really suit it, even in the team modes. Especially in TDM, you can basically spawn anywhere you want, which makes things very disorganized and hectic. The Control mode allows you to spawn at base or at any captured points, but is still hectic. And the maps are really small.
Only thing that irritates me is the lack of maps in the game ... there are about 5 IIRC, split across the 3 modes. I think this contributes to why I don't play for extended stretches of time, because it does get a bit repetitive on just 5 maps.

It seems I've never written a review for D:OS2, and with the Steam Awards wanting us to update a review, I might as well!
Let me start by stating that Divinity: Original Sin 2 is my all time favorite game. I adored the first one. I'm worshippping the second.
This isn't a game that'll hold your hand, this isn't a game that's easy and laid back. This is the game that throws you in the middle of a world and tells you to figure it out.
It has multiple difficulty settings, so if tactical turnbased combat isn't your strongest suit there ARE easier modes for you! But the harsh combat isn't the only thing that makes this game hard. It's the quests, the world, there is NO handholding. You got to figure out what to do, you got to figure out which quest to solve and focus on. And boy are there many quests to focus on!
Some seem absolutely random, some seem like just a typical sidequest kind of job that ends up being the key ingredient in solving the big mystery! I love that, I love that the first act has you stuck on an island, a jail, and your job is to break out. And how would one do this? There isn't just one way, or two, or three. There are more than that. Way more. And it's up to you to figure out the way.
There are five races, human, dwarf, elf, lizard, and undead. Each brings with their own talents and experience in the game. You might have trouble with certain quests because they hate your race, you might need to find another way into a town because they don't like dwarves. It's extremely immersive, and playing it as a coop makes it even so.
I'm not sure I have words to describe to you how amazing this game is. I like difficult games, I played this on Tactical, which is hard, and on some boss fights me and my coop partner would sit here for two hours. Reloading. Repositioning. Changing skills. Reloading. over and over untill we finally managed to beat said boss. It was one of the most amazing experiences I've had in gaming all year. Just that little bit of having to figure out how something works.
There are Character Tags and Talents that you can choose that really makes this into an immersive rpg. Pet Pal allows you to talk to animals. That sad dog over there, cheer him up and he'll help you. That nasty fire elemental? Guess what! She needs your help!
You can have a talent that makes you stink, and people dislike you because of it.
Larian Studios is a dev team to follow. I cannot wait to see what comes next.
(Voice acting wasn't in the original budget. There was partial voice acting, but somehow they managed to make the entire game voice acted, without starting another kickstarter and without pushing the game back a few months. It was a surprise untill launch and I give them major props for doing this)

100% Orange Juice is a great game to just kick back and have some fun with friends.  The game can be a bit confusing at first, and while there are guides you can read, I highly recommend just jumping into a game and talking to people.  The community is awesome, so don't be afraid to ask questions!  When I first started playing, I had no idea what was going on, but then I met some amazing people that really helped me out big time, explaining some strategies and how different cards work.  There are a couple bad apples here and there, but by and large, the community in 100% Orange Juice is very friendly, likes to joke around, have fun, and commiserate when we roll a 1 at the worst possible time or teleport away from home right when we thought we were going to win the game.
Basically, the goal is to accumulate as many stars or wins as you can during the game.  Each time you step on a home with enough stars or wins, you will gain another "norma," which lets you use more powerful cards.  There is definitely some strategy involved depending on the character you choose.  Try to pick cards that suit your character's strengths and avoid cards that don't.  A little basic knowledge of probability helps but isn't required.  Also,  pray to the Orange Juice gods and goddesses.  Luck is a huge element of this game, so you will want divine intervention on your side!
Campaign mode can be a little frustrating if you don't know what you're doing, which is why I recommend getting some tips from other players first, but it's also required to unlock most of the non-DLC characters.  This is one of my only real complaints about the game.  It can be kind of unclear how to unlock the characters you want.  When I was starting out, it felt like it took forever to get my favorite characters that I saw my friends using in multiplayer.  If you stick with it through campaign mode, they'll all eventually become available in the store though.
That said, the nice thing about campaign mode is that the story is *incredibly adorable.*  The dialogue in all of the campaigns puts a smile on my face every time, and the characters have very expressive animations.  Personally, I recommend Marc and QP's campaigns for maximum cuteness, but all 4 have nice stories.  Red Barrel all the way!
Most importantly, don't sweat the small stuff.  For every bad roll you get, eventually you'll get an amazing roll to put the smile back on your face.  Meet new people, relax, and have fun.

First and foremost, do I recommend this? Yes, for $20? Ehhhh that's kinda debatable, if you have the money to do so, have at it, but if you're waffling back and forth because you don't want to "lose" the 20, maybe wait until it gets updated a bit.
Ok, so from start to finish for my first 3 hour session after buying the game + about 30 minutes of post update testing. (The other hour and a half was from just idly buying used cars and fixing them and nothing else XD)
Main Menu: Lacking, I'd personally prefer it if there was a way to change audio and video settings from the main menu rather than in the game as the music when you first load up the game, doesn't use the same settings as when you're ingame so it's rather loud at startup.
Ingame Menu System: Quite easy to learn, I don't mind it at all... but the newspaper system... ohhh boy. It's cumbersome and painful to use at the best of times, not from a "Darn, they don't have my part" standpoint but from the "Where is the driveshaft supposed to be?" standpoint. The system for switching from garage to driving, or garage to track is very slick and quick with little to no faffing about.
Mechanic System/Aspect: Where the game shines, do a bumper to bumper inspection of each car you get and replace as necessary. The part selection system could visually work a bit better for me personally, I have tough times noticing what is currently being selected, but that's probably just me not paying close enough attention.
Driving Characteristics/Physics: Well, it's better... it was HORRID to start with, very floaty (not saying a 70's muscle car isn't floaty, just not like it's not attatched to the wheels kinda floaty) and I often had issues with random bouncing around, which keep in mind, this was a brand new car I bought and it's like the suspension didn't even exist. Now, the bouncing is not as bad, and I can turn better, the traction is MUCH better, much much better, it's very nice to drive with compared to the start where you could drift a drag car.
Parts Deterioration System: Yes, just yes, it's great and works well, when you buy a car and think "This is perfect!" and see that the exhaust is beat to hell and you HAVE to fix it, it gives you the same "FOR F*CKS SAKE!" feeling as it would in real life (But with less anger :P).
Buying and Selling of Parts: It works.... I already mentioned my gripes with the newspaper system, but once you get past that is just works, it's a good way to make some quick cash so you can buy that supercharger you wanted to get but realized you're $14 off.
Racing System: Just like part selling, it just works, the AI can be tempermental sometimes (I made one literally flip out and get stuck by touching it lightly), but they work about as well as you could hope for a game where it's not the 100% main focus (Moreso 40% from what i've seen so far, maybe just from how i've played the game lol)
Post update bug notes: I own the Narnoo offroad truck (The brand new red one) and it suddenly had almost full body damage after loading the game back in, it cost quite a bit to repair it, which was kinda annoying but at least no parts were missing. Same truck also stopped being able to handle jumps well, it likes to land nose first and pivot on the front wheels almost stopping on the front bumper, before it would just uncontrollably bounce about.
And one mild annoyance... as a car guy.... WHY IS THERE ONLY ONE EXHAUST MANIFOLD ON A V8?!?!?!.... ok heh.... that's done haha.
I know I didn't mention a couple things, but the things I hadn't mentioned, I either hadn't dealt with yet, or didn't see them needing to be mentioned.
Overall yes I do recommend the game, but I feel as though the price point is a bit steep, use discretion when purchasing and remember, it may not say "Early Access" but they're working very hard on it.
Thanks for reading!

Linelight is a game where you play as a small white line moving on certain circuit like paths with the challenge of getting yellow diamonds and reaching the exit screen to proceed to the next stage. That is the gist of the game.
The game does introduce new challenges as you progress further with new obstacles. Further down the line new lines appear on the map which can make you restart the whole puzzle section with just a touch.  And that is where the gameplay pretty much ends.
Linelight takes a minimalist approach to solving puzzles, there is always a soothing feeling while you’re playing this game as it does not punish you too hard on a mistake, is not as much taxing on your brain as many of the games of its genre out there and that might pose a problem with the people who are looking for hardcore puzzle games.
Linelight won’t give you puzzles which are going to take you hours to figure out and such. The whole gameplay is based around giving you a relaxing and calming experience and Linelight excels here.
The game itself is very neat and there is no unnecessary UI or any sort of tutorial and the game fares much better without one. It drops subtle hints towards the future puzzles with its gameplay and expects you to catch onto them.
It is easy to browse through and there are a standard amount of options present to tweak the game’s performance making it run well even on somewhat older machines. I also didn’t find a single bug or crash that would ruin my experience and that is why I consider Linelight to be one of the best minimalist puzzle games to come out in the recent times.
Linelight takes a minimalist approach to its visuals with its representation of lines and puzzles as something that resembles a circuit. The visuals are pleasing to look at and even the hardest of puzzles look like they can be solved just because of their visual flair. Overall, Linelight has excellent visuals that go along perfectly with its gameplay.
A calm and soothing soundtrack makes Linelight a joy to hear to. The random sounds produced by the game are also nicely done and overall the sound design of Linelight just makes the environment of solving puzzles all the more soothing.
Linelight is one of the best minimalist puzzle games to come out in recent time. While it may turn off some people looking for hardcore styled puzzles, it is one of the most relaxing and calming experience you can hope in a puzzle game. Point on visual flair and an excellent sound design makes it completely worth its asking price. If you are looking for a puzzle game which is not too difficult, then Linelight is the game for you.

Linelight is a triumph in terms of discovery through gameplay. There's no tutorial to speak of in this game. Instead, Linelight relies on simple controls and a superb gradient of difficulty that metes out patterns and puzzles gradually. Though the puzzles can become rather complex, the elements are all introduced fairly gradually. This ensures that you learn all you need to before taking on harder challenges. This not only allows for maximum satisfaction when you successfully plot and think your way through an area, but also resulted in a number of fluid, almost unconscious solutions as I sailed through sections feeling very pleased with myself indeed.
Occasionally, when it comes to gaming's more overwrought puzzle experiences, you can sometimes almost hear the designer saying 'look how clever I am'. But the finest puzzle games find a way to allow the player to share in that feeling. Portal, for example, is a game with a brilliantly simple but gloriously clever premise at its heart. It makes us feel intelligent and buoyant when we solve the challenges. It gives us the illusion of agency in discovery, yet still wows us with its design. The same can be said of Linelight, in its own way. Here is a game that delivers moments of pure pleasure. It does so as an aesthetic experience, in the captivating construction of its worlds, and as an arty puzzler yielding precious eureka moments of fulfilment.
I suppose the saddest thing is that it has to end, and you really won't want it to. If I may offer a little advice to those of you who do get it...don't speed through it all at once. Linelight, like all puzzle games really, loses some of its magic in repeat playthroughs, even if there are extra collectibles and hidden puzzles to help prolong the game's life. The first run through will only take you a handful of hours, so savour everything that you can. There are few finer games this year so far.

Oh gods, the feels.
Linelight is a story about introverts and friendship, cunningly disguised as a puzzle game with brilliantly intuitive mechanics. This slice of life starring a set of firework sparks learning to cooperate and help each other realize their dreams, really tugs at the heartstrings. 100% guaranteed to get the waterworks flowing. Definitely this year's most likely to win the "walking in Thomas Was Alone's footsteps" award.
The actual game is pretty great too; very Braid like in the "don't repeat yourself, keep surprising the player with new mechanics" sense. It sits in that magical space of, "was that easy, or just super intuitive and I happen to be a genius?" puzzle space where you're challenged, but the rewards keep flowing. I got actually stuck a grand total of once, very late in the main story game where I'd just plain failed to see the obvious answer. Eventually getting that green star really did make me grin though :)
Finally, Brett the game's creator? Genuinely sweet guy; met him at one of the gaming festivals. This game is already worth it on its own merits, but if you decide to jump in, know that you're also helping to keep alive something genuinely precious in the videogames scene. Hopefully we'll get plenty more where this came from.

Call of Pripyat is perhaps one of the most polished S.T.A.L.K.E.R. games.
But, like all the other installments, is an acquired taste.
What turns off most newcomers is the misleading starting gear in all of the games, which leads players to believe that the combat in this game is strictly and exclusively RNG and poor ballistics. And difficulty decreases all gun damage across the board, so the♥♥♥♥♥♥poor bottle opener of a gun - Makarov PM combined with it's godawful properties becomes an infuriating experience. Luckily there is an abundance of mods to help mitigate this.
If you're a big fan of the series, there is a mod for this particular entry to the series - Call of Chernobyl, which melds together all of the maps and content of the three games, and has tons of replay value.
The graphics, while severely underwhelming, can be atmospheric and immersive at certain points in the game. AtmosFear mod, in my opinion showcases the sophisticated lighting engine very well and turns the already eventful Emissions into a sight to behold.
If you're looking for a atmospheric, moody game, I believe the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series will not dissapoint.

I've got about 13 hours in this game, and I just decided to buy the freelancer version through humble bundle.
Most of the negative reviews I've seen come down to 3 things: people who were expecting a f2p moba and didn't get it, people who couldn't figure out how the game worked, and people who don't find this game thier cup of tea. Aside from the last reason, I wouldn't take the other negative reviews that seriously.
The way I see it, the game is a free-to-try where you can pay to unlock all the content besides what you're limited to. Perfectly reasonable. Also as far as I can tell diffrent people can get different rotations, which is a cool touch that other MOBAs should think about adding. I'm fine with ranked being behind a paywall if the game can survive without microtransactions.
As for people who don't understand the game mechanics, well all I can say is too bad for you. Compared to XCOM and actual turn-based strategy games this game is much easier to pick up and play, and the mechanics are much more forgiving. If you can't read or don't have the patience to think about what you're doing, you really shouldn't be playing these kinds of turn-based games.
28 bucks is a tad much for the game, but with the correct third-party deals it becomes much more reasonable. Overall I'd its already proved to be worth my money more than a lot of the games in my library.
Oh, and whoever says the menu music sucks is lying. Its extremley groovy (and polarizing too aprantly, just like this game as a hole).

When taking off the rose-tinted glasses of how much this game was a success was from the shadow of Unity (basically, this game actually worked whereas Unity didn't), what we're left with is a game that, though it plays decent, fails in the sense of story. It added many new weapons from its predecessor (Black Flag), though the only one which was actually really *new* was the grenades, and added an admittedly interesting gas mechanic to the game. It also was much more filled and felt significantly less grindy than Black Flag; these were all great improvements to the series from the previous title, but unfortunately, these are the only positive things I can say about this game. What this game made up for in being playable, it lost in a dissapointing lack of charm.
**The remainder of this review contains massive spoilers, referrencing the end of the game**
Either due to false marketing on the community's behalf or on Ubisoft, we're lead to believe that the main character, Shay, is the victim of a massive betrayal and seeks revenge against the brotherhood. This story sounded interesting, and for many of us, it was the first time we'd see the story from a Templar's point of view. Or at least, that's what I expected, but not what I recieved. Shay was never the victim of a betrayal, but rather the victim of a mistake in which no one was guilty. Rather than confront his Mentor about what he witnessed, which would be the logical thing to do, Shay gets unrealistically emotional about the situation and blames everything on his Mentor. He then consciously decides to betray his brotherhood, and is retaliated against accordingly.
What follows isn't a story of revenge against the backstabbing brotherhood, but rather a convoluted scheme to stop a man who ends up listening to his own conscience in the end anyways, rendering Shay's entire mission completely pointless. He decides, for no other reason than one of the British officers was nice to him while he was injured, to help his hated rivals, the Templars, and eventually join their Order and assist the British in winning the Seven Years War.
My biggest complain about this game is that under no point of this game do you ever see the positives in joining the Templar Order. The Templars were never painted as the good guys, rather the game regularly reminds you that they are the bad guys, and the reasons for Shay's complete dedication toward the Order seems to entirely ignore his high moral stance which directed him to betray the Assassins. There never seems to be a point, other than the rosey tone of a single man who dies before Shay even makes the decision to join the Templars, where I (the player) feel like I should actually want to be a Templar.
As if the feeling of "why on Earth am I killing the good guys?" wasn't enough to make the game feel horrible, the ending seals this game as completely unnecessary and makes no sense. I'm not referring to the mission in Versailles (though the mission itself feels like an unnecessary and shoe-horned-in shameless advertisement for Unity), but rather the Naval Missions. I was quite confused while trying to complete the Naval Missions (which must be completed if you are to unlock much of the best stuff in the game) in that they no longer let you complete them until you "progress further into the story." This was right before the last mission of the game.
In case that wasn't clear, let me restate this: The final 5 Naval Missions, which are required for completion and for unlocking some of the best gear in the game, doesn't get unlocked until you've COMPLETED the game. Why? Were the developers afriad that I'd be cheating with Altïar's Swords on a mission which doesn't even let you use anything other than your Hidden Blades? Why was this required? So that people would be forced to play hours more of the game after they already completed the story? Who thought this was a good idea??
Overall, I think the game is fine. I never felt like I was doing the right thing, but so what? Plenty of games let you play as the bad guy (though they usually leave out the high sense of morality that constantly reminds you that what you did was morally sketchy and highlights that you're actually the bad guy in this game). The Naval Missions is a cheap and pathetic move on the fault of the developers, but hey, **at least the game plays on PC, Montreal!!**. But would I recommend it, though? No. It doesn't add much from Black Flag, and unlike this game, Black Flag had characters I actually could **care** about. I couldn't have cared less if the characters died; the fact that two of them were Haythem Kenway and Achilles Davenport defeated the possibility of that happening anyways. Comparing that to Black Flag, or more accurately Black Beard, it was geniunely disastrous watching Edward Thatch die. We had actually come to care about him and his death was genuinely devastating. In AC: Rogue, however, none of the characters invoke that amount of compassion. None of the characters seemed to have any real life. When they died, it was difficult to really think anything of it.
This game is fine, but you'd be better off playing Black Flag.
