Devil's Dare is a pseudo 2D beat em up in which the world has been taken over by a zombie outbreak. It's not dark and gritty though, it is in fact full of references and a bit of silliness. Not really funny though, they are just there to be there. Devil's Dare is made for coop (no online) but is perfectly playable solo and you will initially have four characters to choose from while two more are unlockable. They are all nerds transformed into warriors by Navi from Legend of Zelda and all play pretty differently from one another. Kingstone has a golden axe and is slow and strong, he is capable of summoning lighting, as well as shoulder charging enemies. Queenie fights in a giant mech and is able to freeze enemies and use bombs. Jackson is very fast but barely causes any damage and is able to judo throw enemies across the screen and use a flying kick.  Last but not least is Axel who is a jack of all trades, wields the Master Sword and is able to throw a spear chain to drag enemies to him.
Those special attacks can not be used indefinably as using it will cost you one or two bars from your four bar SP meter. It recharges slowly or can be filled bar by bar through defeating enemies. That is something you actually don't want to do if you don't finish them off with a special. Defeating an enemy with a special move causes a “fatality” which causes them to drop money and money is very important in this game. Killing three or more enemies will cause them to drop a health item which makes it a rather easy game. So controlling the crowd is even more important in this game than others of the genre. Annoyingly enough rolling out of the way causes you to lose an SP bar for some reason. Even if the enemy is already knocked down and is no threat at the moment rolling will take off a SP bar. There is no other way to avoid attacks. There is no jumping, parrying or blocking, and insanely enough the run button is the same as the dodge which means  to run you will first dodge out of the way using up an SP bar and only then you can run for a while. You can rebind keys but you can not separate those two from using the same key. It may sound like a petty complaint but is actually quite annoying given the importance of being able to pull of a special attack but having to wait for it to refill.
Getting hit is very brutal in this game. One hit and you will be stunned while enemies combo you into oblivion. You can escape by sacrificing all four bars of your SP bar to pull of a special attack to escape from their grasp. Most enemies take plenty of time telegraphing their attack so you will have a lot of time to roll away from harm before anything happens. Enemy variety is quite decent ranging from your typical zombie to a pregnant women that flings undead babies at you. There is one slime like enemy that if it manages to hit you will reverse your controls. I absolutely hate that in video games. Stun me or whatever but do not mess with the controls. Especially if your games controls are already subpar to begin with. It is hard to explain just what is wrong with them but it feels like there is a very big delay in the time that you press a button and the time it takes for it to register. It's not gamebreaking but in all my time playing I have not stopped noticing  it. Another problem is that the pick up key is the same as the basic attack so if you are attacking an enemy and move near money you will break your combo, bend over to pick up a few dollars and get a shiny new bite mark on your♥♥♥♥♥ He will also pick up money over food oddly enough.
There are 4 boss fights in this game all from popular 80's films and are pretty fun to fight. Not much of a challenge by itself though. There will always be a unlimited horde of zombies attacking you during boss fights so I found it best to just ignore them unless I need health and focus on the boss. If you need extra challenge there are 3 difficultly modes to chose from, the first “Casual” will disable achievements, “Classic” is best suited to start with, and  “Expert” features some special different colored enemies that can not be stun locked. Expert gives you the choice before levels to make monsters and bosses harder for extra reward but that just means you can't stun lock them and didn't really add much. Boss fights are were most of the challenge comes from and are all pretty entertaining to fight though there was one instance where I glitched out of the level on the last boss fight which was infuriating though did not happen again. They also give you a limited amount of time to fight the boss and if you surpass that time you will automatically die so hopefully you have money left to respawn. It usually doesn't take that long to take down a boss if you ignore the grunts and head right for him but with lower damage based characters like Jackson it can feel like an unnecessary nuisance. Like every other enemy you should try to finish the boss with a fatality for a big cash reward at the end.
One of the most unique features of this game is that you can choose any of the four stages to play right from the get go. The longer you put off a level the more nights (sections) it will have. The first stage you pick will only have one night, the second will have two nights, third will have three and so on. That is a really cool feature that adds plenty of replay value if you want to see all the stages. It also means you will have more encounters with that stages boss. If you were disappointed that everyone's favorite alien was a push over, just save his stage for last and you will have much better encounters with it. None of the stages look interesting visually though and are all quite cliché. Stages are “Sewers”, “Train”, “Hallway” and “The Road which are every bit as boring as they sound. Something that they pull off constantly is throw waves and waves of enemies at you before you get to move from that  screen space, to mask how short the levels are and it makes it feel tedious. The brown filter that they added over the game makes everything look dull and lifeless, it really contradicts the goofy nature of this game as well as makes it look terrible for no reason. After a night is over you get to  purchase a upgrade like more health, longer combos, a soul token that lets you continue from the last night if you lose. One cool feature is that each character have some of there own unique upgrades special to him/her like upgrading a Molotov special attack into using a flamethrower. The two unlock-able characters use guns instead of melee and after a certain amount of shots they need  reloading. Can be slightly annoying opening crates and trying to pick up items only to lose a round by accident.
Be warned, if you want to face the last fifth boss and get the good ending you will need $6666 to face him. There is also a survival mode which pits you against waves of enemies that get stronger with each wave, it is a nice little addition if you just want to have a quick game. Devil Dare's soundtrack ranges from decent to amazing and I enjoyed it very much. Voice acting on the other hand was painful to listen to but I guess it fits in with the cheesiness of the game. There is no long winded dialogue thankfully. Just small extremely cheesy quips during battle. Overall I did enjoy this game but it always felt like I was fighting the game itself more so than anything. From the need to finish enemies off with a special attack but sometimes not having any SP due to the only form of avoiding enemy attacks using 25% of the SP bar after each use to the wonkiness of the controls and the inability to cancel out an animation to dodge or attack another enemy approaching from the back.  It had potential but is ultimately held back from some rather odd design decisions. A few patches may easily negate most of my critiques but at it's current state at the time of this review the issues stack up just enough for me to not recommend.

100% OJ is a fun game if primarily RNG party games are your thing. They're my thing, mainly because I get drunk all the time and when I get drunk anything else is jus too frustrating to play.
Basically, it's a board game. you roll a die, move X number of spaces, do a thing based on where you land(fight an enemy, fight a player, drop stars, gain stars, gain a card). Battles are very simplistic, you choose to defend(guarantee of losing at least one health) or evade(either take the full hit or take no damage), and then(or before that) you roll for attack. It works pretty well especially for what the game is going for.
Cards are pretty much the only area strategy really comes into play. You gain them randomly and they provide a wide range of effects. Some take stars, some give stars, some are traps you can set, some hurt other players, etc. Besides stars you have "norma" which is how you win the game. You can either choose star normas or fighting normas. Norma basically means "goal" at least in this game. Either choose star norma and spend the game struggling to hold onto your stars, or choose fighting normas and spend the game looking for players to kill. It all makes for a good party game.
The graphics and sound are unimpressive. The game has a cute aesthetic, which is fun, and the sounds all sound very stock. The VA is in japanese with no subtitles, but that doesn't make it any harder to understand what's going on in the slightest, so it's not a point against it at all. It's especially not a point against it when you consider that most VAs for english localizations of eastern games sound like total♥♥♥♥♥

Are you starting to see the problem here?
There is NO other way to unlock these characters, and it's not just a few characters locked behind campaigns, it's
. If you want these characters, you are obligated to toil endlessly against hours and hours and
of RNG hell in a party game without the party. Thank Jesus Christ for Cheat Engine. I almost want to click "No" down below just because of this, but I'm not that petty.
BUT WAIT THERE'S MORE! I just spent a few matches getting repeatedly and mercilessly disconnected over and over again. Capsized is a fun action platformer that largely involves the usage of its physics engine to set it apart from more contemporary games of the genre. The game starts and ends with very few worlds. You are a nameless astronaut-soldier-person, who gets the ship that he's on attack by an unknown energy source. It's up to you to save your surviving comrades and battle through hordes of savage aliens.
Yeah, it does feel a little cowboys vs natives, but you won't really be thinking about the story since the game usually involes the following:
Shooting things with, I'll admit, a varied weapon set complete with alt-fire. Assault Rifles become shotguns, Flamethrowers become shields, and even a black hole launcher. 9 weapons plus power ups. The enemies are brutal on hard so you need it.
As for physics antics... the best way to describe the physics was if Newton thought the world played like Asteroids. You have a variety of movement options like this energy hook to pull yourself or objects around, an awesome push mode where you can rocket jump with them and send little critters and objects hurling at your enemies. This also means you'll get some awkward levers and buttons, with the way you can send objects while hooked, it becomes a tad frustrating. Especially when you deal with things that repel bullets so you'd have to launch an object at it, sometimes you accidentally push your ammo over a cliff. But, I digress. Some levels do it well, especially when it's more open, but when they cram you into trap pits and the like you might want to break your keyboard.
The main negative is definitely the games best selling feature, oddly. Sometimes you propel yourself too fast into enemy fire, or you gain speed walljumping straight into an almost insta-kill poison trap (which has no indication of being there, besides smoke). Or worse, you have to carry objects to a certain area and the object gets stuck. Frustrating.
So, really, great in an afternoon but it's not perfect. If this sounds good for you, I'd suggest getting it on sale since the most you'll get after the 13 levels is a pretty barebones arcade mode and some modifiers/achievement hunting for the story. These guys really like their physics, and I can't wait to try their other stuff out.

If someone had told me that I would feel true empathy for little bouncing specks of light on a screen after a couple hours playing a game - that I'd feel like I was running around on a playground with them, or choreographing a dance, or training them as one would a pet... I would have called them crazy. But Linelight is magical like that. It's the Journey of minimalistic puzzle games, and that is an amazing thing.
A huge part of it is how the (beautiful) music provides a counterpoint to the game mechanics: you have these "enemy" particles that you'd normally feel like you were trying to avoid or run away from, but the music reminds you that you can harness their behavior to help you out. And each "world" in the game culminates with a series of puzzles, where you use the behavior you've learned to run alongside a "partner" particle, helping it to move forward, helping it to help you to move forward... and then when you inevitably need to part ways, the music is there to underscore the bittersweet end to the partnership. And throughout it all, sound effects blend with the music seamlessly and in a harmonically pleasing way. It's a masterfully calming and thought-provoking experience, and I don't think I've seen anything like it.
Other commenters have described how the puzzles aren't the most challenging in the world, and there's not a ton of replayability. But in the context of the experience, that's okay. You're not supposed to pull your hair out, you're supposed to savor the experience. That said, I'm sure there will be speedruns if this game takes off, and eventually community level editing will increase the longevity here.
One minor gripe is that on Mac OS X, at least with my configuration, there were some screen tearing glitches, and some of the lighting effects could use some dithering to reduce visible "rings" where the color gradient changes. But these are minor, and they don't really break immersion.
All in all, this is a game you're not going to want to miss.

It says "Elder Scrolls", so it can't be bad. And it indeed isn't. Sure, not as gloriously great as Morrowind, but in my humble opinion roughly comparable to Skyrim - with a set of flaws very different from those of the latter game, of course!
Oblivion is kind of the middle ground between Morrowind and Skyrim in terms of game complexity. While not quite as dumbed down in terms of control and game mechanics as Skyrim (so as to please the consolehead simpletons), Oblivion already forgoes most of its predecessor's more RPG-y elements (most notably the statistics-based abilites) in favour of more action-oriented gameplay and simplified controls.
The game's graphics are still quite pretty to look at, especially when employing some texture mods, of which there are some formidable ones out there. In general, there's a plethora of great mods for Oblivion which can offer very interesting changes to the game and increase the fun in re-playing it today.

Devil Daggers is an absolutely fantastic simplistic looking shooter that is anything but simplistic. Armed with basic WASD movemen controls and your left mouse button, you're set to fail time and time again; however, failure is satisfying in Devil Daggers. You will always take something from your last run. I found myself learning audio cues, enemy placements, and optimal aiming and timing skills with each momentous death.
It's tough as nails, but it's worth every second of your time (and I mean every second, as you'll be watching your counter in the top left from the corner of your eye to "NEW HIGHSCORE" your friends or climb the leaderboards yourself.) The UI is clean and minimalistic, only giving you what you need with toggle-able aspects such as the in-game timer. The graphics are gritty and nostalgic but smooth and fresh enough to separate itself from quake shooters of yore.
I heavily recommend picking up Devil Daggers for such an affordable price. It's a must have to play in quick bursts, or to sink in hours on. It may be a challenge, but each second you overcome your last run will be liberating. Remember to take breakes and breathe, you'll be here for awhile. Embrace your hellish arena and survive. You've got this.

I don't hate MouseCraft. I had a good time with what I played, but on my third crash I had to call it quits. Of what I experienced, it's a decent puzzler that does a lot right, but fails on a fundamental level of player engagement. I know it may seem silly that I'm reviewing it after such a poor experience but my interest was already faultering when the third crash wiped a good bit of progress.
Even with bitter feelings, I could see it's ambition and admired the execution, but feel that the style of puzzles just didn't click with my pallete. The production values are phenomenal, and while the soundtrack wasn't anything to write home about, the general atmosphere of testing and stylized assets definitely brought home the package. Puzzles are adequately challenging, and the constant stream of new twists definitely kept the boat rolling (the reputed tetris blocks being the most enjoyable to use), but even with all the right parts of the equation, MouseCraft just didn't do enough to keep my attention.
This is one I feel I may revisit one day if I feel my experience would fare better, but as of now I will give it a hesitant recommendation. I'm highly curious to see, if anything, what the studio has gone on to make next.

This game is, in my honest opinion, one of the most beautiful fantasy worlds ever created. They departed from the alienish landscape present in Morrowind for a more classic western fantasy setting, and while some may complain about that, I loved it. Cyrodiil felt like a paradise on the brink of invasion, which is kind of the premise of the story: in what is arguably the golden age of the Third Empire of Tamriel, the entire empire (but particularly Cyrodiil) is threatened when the Emperor and all of his known heirs are assassinated and the world is thrown to the brink of chaos as hordes of chaotic daedra invade. The player is tasked with finding an unknown and semi-illegitimate heir to the Emperor and restoring him to the throne over the course of various events.
This game has, with the exception of the Fighter's Guild, the best faction quests in any TES game, hands-down. The Companions storyline of Skyrim, as well as the Fighter's Guild questline of Morrowind stomp all over this game's Fighter's Guild quests. :P The Mage's Guild and Thieves' Guild quests are so memorable, but without a doubt, the Dark Brotherhood story in this game is definitely the best in any of the TES games, if not the best in any game containing assassin orders. It could have been an entire game in itself, honestly.
Graphically, despite the game coming out in 2006, this game holds up pretty well even by today's standards. One of the first games to utilize lighting the way it did, the lighting was undoubtedly the thing that made this game shine (pun semi-intended). If you don't have a problem modding your game, I recommend downloading Bomret's Detailed Normal Maps for Vanilla Version 1_1 (I personally prefer this one because it maintains a great graphical standard but doesn't make the game feel too advanced for its time) or Really Textured Normal Maps for Vanilla, along with Parallax Cities Giga-Pack and Skyrimised Water to get a really nice texture look that makes the graphics feel a little more up-to-date. Note: don't hold me accountable if you fail to look into how to install mods properly, as the Normal Map/Parallax Map mods need to be installed a specific way to work right.
Gameplay-wise, this game takes what made Morrowind great, refines those mechanics (they added fast travel which is much nicer than forcing a player to trudge all the way across the world for every quest), and the combat is FAR better than Morrowind's where every time you hit the target, you actually do some damage, and the spells aren't separate so you can cast spells without lowering your weapon. My only issue with the gameplay is the level scaling. While I like the idea in theory, it was really whacky in this game.
Maybe not as beautiful or refined as Skyrim, and definitely not as deep as Morrowind and before, but this game has captured me more than any of the other TES games has. I'll never forget the memories I made of this game. It also happens to have the best expansion I've ever played (Shivering Isles; the land is beautiful, the story is a Lovecraft-inspired madhouse.. quite literally, too. The endgame rewards really appeal to a monarchist such as myself too). Additionally, the GOTY edition comes with KOTN which is a really fun questline that could be considered a full expansion. It takes you across Cyrodiil and makes you into the reborn immortal paladin, the Divine Crusader. Very fun.
10/10. I really don't have any complaints about this game aside from the crazy level scaling. Quite literally the only major  complaint I have about this game.

Ok, so i have played through all of the game and almost gotten every achievement in it, so its time for a review. To start, this is a very fun enjoyable game. Its a basic twin stick top down view shooter but Halo style. This is great for any fans of the series who are looking for a little halo while they wait for the console titles to come out. Also, the game is only $4.99 and is well worth every penny. The combat is very straight forward, walk around and just point and click the mouse wherever you want to shoot and all the guns will just continuously fire like in any twin stick shooter. Along with that, a fun and enjoyable addition is vehicles. The vehicles include Grizzles, Scorpions, Ghosts, Wraiths, and the AA Wraith all of which are very fun to use. There is a wide range of weapons that are iconic to the Halo series. The game has 5 main operations which each have 5 levels, so there is a lot to offer from a $5 game. Along with that, there are in game medals, mission stars, challenges, achievements, and leaderboards for high scores. They game is very relaxing and a lot of fun and a great time waster or game to play when on a time crunch. There really isn't anything to it, the game does offer some challenging sections at times but in general its relatively moderate all the way through. There are skulls to boost difficulty which offers a bonus in xp. XP is used to start the mission off with buffs such as damage or score boost, a different ability, and differnet guns. And thats basically it with the generic operation of the game. My pluses for the game are one its cheep and offers a substantial amount for the price, its simple and easy to get into, its a great time waster or game to play when you aren't in the mood for competive gaming and just want to relax and have fun, and its Halo, can't go wrong there. Remember this isn't a high budget AAA Halo title so don't expect the world out of a 5 dollar game.
Anyways, there are a few gripes I have with it. To start, the damage boost buff is very, very, very over powering. It can turn the plasma pistol into a 3 shot kill weapon again elites and makes the game a breeze to walk through. Another thing I dislike is that I feel like the covenant weapons just plain suck, like it doesn't feel like you are doing any damage when using them and the enimies are just eating damage. I dislike the way that some levels start you off with a terrible weapon combo for the level scenario and in order to do well you need to buy another starting weapon. My last issue is that for me, driving the scorpion or grizzly tank was very clunky and hard to control and was just frustrating at times, while the wraith and ghost were very easy to control.
So thats it,  a few minor gripes and an overall fun enjoyable game thats well worth the $5 price tag. If you play through once, not speed run you are looking at about 4-5.5 hours of game play which is like a $1 per hour which isn't bad. If you try to all achievement or get all gold stars you have well over 7-8 hours. Its fun enjoyable and I give it an 8/10 and recommend to anyone intrested.

A common phrase we use to describe a piece of media is that it is "more than the sum of its parts". One game that immediately comes to mind is
. This Square-Enix title manages to weave an absurdly dark storyline, chaotic music, and awful game-design into something incredible. Unfortunately, Devil's Dare is not a game that fits this description. While it does have numerous issues, it doesn't create the unique and fulfilling experience necessary for them to be overlooked.
Humanity is doomed again. This time around it's a zombie-apocalypse and-wait! Where are you going? Don't you want to know how a plucky group of convention-goers save the world?  Yes, this is a story that we've heard a thousand times. However, since this game is a beatemup I see no reason to be concerned. This is a genre that flourished in the arcades, where stories consisted of a few screens and maybe a line of text. Anyway, there are six playable characters, each with their own weapons and abilities.
This game is divided into 10 stages among four selectable areas. Each area will have one more stage than the last, with the fourth area consisting of four stages and a unique final boss. It's a neat system that promotes replay value. The stages themselves are standard for the beatemup genre: move from left to right (sometimes vice-versa), beat up zombies, avoid obstacles, and fight the boss.
In beatemups that have multiple characters to choose from, there is usually one or two that stand out. In the case of Devil's Dare, Jonathon is just overpowered. He is an unlockable character and his weapon of choice is the shotgun. Aside from being great at crowd-control, he can drop bombs and roll-away. When the bombs are upgraded to land-mines, they become truly threatening. Basically, his strategy for beating bosses will involve hitting them with the shotgun, then setting a land-mine directly on top of them. I'm not sure how, but this causes the mine to do extreme amounts of damage, usually enough to kill. The bosses in Devil's Dare have a lot of HP, but this technique can wipe them out nearly instantly.
As for everyone else:
Queenie has healing and a fairly effective infinite with her ice-beam.
Axel is all-around good.
Kingston can do some decent damage, but his grab-special just doesn't work for this game.
Jack is fast, but most of his moves are really ineffective.
Anthony is the other secret character. He has range, but his machine-gun isn't good at handling crowds.
The key to surviving Devil's Dare is in "herding" your adversaries. When dealing with three or more enemies, you want them to group together. This involves manipulating their attack patterns. It's really easy to figure out, since enemies have certain moves depending on your character's proximity. Also, you have access to a dodge-roll, which makes herding even easier. Once everyone is close to one another, then you unleash combos and special-attacks to wipe them all out. With a bit of practice (and the right character) you can dominate every encounter.
This is the reason why I think the difficulty of this game is overstated. There are limited continues, and yes they have to be purchased with in-game money. However, you're given more than enough tools for not just beating the game, but also cheesing it. Defeating three or more enemies with special attacks causes food to drop. Certain characters (like Jonathon) can wipe out groups with ease and keep their health topped off. Certain bosses can be rough, due to the constant presence of minor zombies. However, it's all a matter of finding the exploit that works. Also, if you don't mind straight-up cheating, you can simply hit ALT-F4 when you die. The game saves the completion of each stage. So if you want, you can merely restart the stage instead of restarting the game.
After beating a stage, you're given a choice between various purchasable upgrades. A number of them - like the aforementioned land-mines - are definitely worth it. The others are broken. From my experience, the defense seed (boosts DEF) doesn't make a difference. The Piracy (free upgrades at the cost of HP) and Free cash ($250) upgrades don't work at all. In some cases the combo-extending upgrade...doesn't extend combos. One upgrade even allows the player to randomly kill an enemy instantly. This is far less useful than it sounds, and is even detrimental. Insta-kills don't get the bonus that comes from performing special-attack kills. Also it makes certain boss-fights absolutely painful, like the TMNT: Turtles in Time-inspired boss. For this fight you have to defeat Terminators, so that they fly into the screen and damage the boss. The problem is insta-kills cause the Terminators to simply explode, which doesn't affect the boss.
A number of other glitches can happen as well. There are female zombies that attack with what looks like a golf club. Their swing actually hits you a split-second before it's supposed to connect. Also, only certain attacks or specials can hurt them. Picking up cash instead of hitting the enemy was already mentioned in a review, but it goes further than that. If food and cash pick-ups overlap, you will ALWAYS pick up the cash first. This is immensely frustrating, since beatemups usually give you a half-second of invulnerability while you're picking something up. I've also gotten stuck in walls and hit by laser beams despite being far away.
Still, it's most important that we look at the bigger picture. Is Devil's Dare fun? Yes and no. This beatemup delivers on the basic thrill of clobbering enemies, but it doesn't get any deeper. All the expert mode really does is raise the costs of revival and spawn stun-immune monsters. The only real advantage the zombies have is numbers, but even that can be used against them, due to the food rewards for massive kills. Most of the playable characters are simply too strong, and not in a way that makes it entertaining. The combos are bland and rely on infinite spams or overpowered special moves.
There's also something to be said about all of the references. As you saw in the trailer, Devil's Dare loves their call-backs. Everything from Ghostbusters to Streets of Rage to Binding of Isaac gets some representation. How much is too much? When your game suffers from a complete lack of identity. I see a ton of stuff that reminds me of other games and movies. Listing them all would be too much for a 50-page review, let alone this one. Altogether these references make the game rather unremarkable. There's no subtlety, no real wit or creativity. It's just "Hey! listen! Doesn't this remind you of something awesome?" Sure it does, but I'd rather be shown something original, something that I might remember years from now.
Even if you can look past the flaws, you'll find that Devil's Dare doesn't do enough to stand-out. Rather, it allows itself to be buried by its influences. It's not a terribly-designed game, but it rarely does anything better than the titles it apes.
, for all its faults, is also distinct and memorable. This game goes too far in showing its love for the classics, even when it comes at the expense of an identity.

Devil's Dare is a rogue-like, 4 player, local co-op, side scroller brawler themed around 80's-90's movies and video games. I highly recommend it.
Pros
+4 initial playable characters with 2 more that are unlockable. All the characters handle very different and each character has their own set of 3 special attacks.
+Risk/Reward upgrade/revive system. You collect money by finishing enemies with special moves. This money can be used for upgrading your character or for reviving yourself. If you die and you don't have enough money, you'll have to start the whole game over. If you pay to revive, the cost of reviving next time goes up.
+If you manage to finish off 3 or more enemies with a single special move, you'll be rewarded with a health drop. This addition makes the combat much more strategic than most brawlers.
+Depending on what order you choose the stages, you'll have to go play more levels of that stage to finish it. (EX: 1st pick is 1 level, 2nd pick is 2 levels, 3rd pick is 3 levels, 4th pick is 4 levels) The levels also have tougher enemies if you choose a stage later.
+Solid replay value between the 6 playable characters, build strategies, stage order, achievements, and the expert difficulty's betting system.
Cons
-No online co-op
-The sprites are gorgeous but the color palette is exceptionally brown. I'm usually not picky about this but EVERYTHING is brown.
-Your character will say something every time they use specials or pick up items. I got used to it but it's still a bit annoying hearing your character say "EASY MONEY" 5 times in 2 seconds when you're collecting money. Although the game has a voice volume slider, it controls both the players and the enemies. The game just doesn't sound right with both turned off.

I will try almost any game with Steam Cloud and Steam Achievements. Full Controller Support is basically mandatory for racing games in my book Trading Cards are a nice bonus if you like those. I really like games that integrate themselves to Steam and this one does.
On top of that, I love racing games and arcade style racing games are my favorite of those.
This isn't the best one ever made, but it ticks enough boxes that I'll recommend it.
The Good:
Races only take a couple of minutes, but are longer at the higher levels. There must be hundreds of different levels, all similar, but with very different routes, which makes for a lot of replayability.
This game, unlike many of these top down racers, actually has multiple camera options, one of which is a behind the car 3rd person view which makes the game much more intense. I play this angle most of all, as it is quite like the normal view in many traditional racing games.
The game is extremely fast paced at the higher levels and quite difficult. You will need lightning fast reflexes to make it through the 90 degree turns that come one after another after another after another in some instances.
The Bad:
The controls are very twitchy and not exactly smooth. You turn in slight increments, which is strange considering this game seems to have a full 3d physics engine behind it. I don't know if this is because I'm playing with a controller or not, but I doubt it.
There is very little artistic variety. There is very little variety, frankly, of any kind, except for with the route of the tracks and the visual style of the cars. This is a game of repition on a theme and gameplay that you had better enjoy to want to play very much of.

Fantastic game that like others have said, is XCOM meets team brawler. The art style is enjoyable and definately like Overwatch in design. This game is a nice idea with a lot of charm, and I'd been looking forward to trying it for a while, but Devil's Dare has too many problems for me to recommend it.
First off, money is extremely important in the game but the only reliable way to get a lot of it is killing monsters with special moves, meaning combat is all about spamming them constantly. Feels restrictive, not to mention that some of them just aren't worth using, or can even miss, since two of them are used by holding a direction and pressing the button. If you die in a stage you can only come back if you spend money, and the cost goes up every time. Don't have enough or an item to save you, and your whole run is gone.
Compounding this is that everything about the game seems designed to punish you if you make any mistake. Get hit by an enemy, and you're stunlocked for a bunch of damage unless you use a move that drains your special bar, keeps you from using them until it completely recharges, and is pretty unresponsive. Die in a stage and you probably won't get a proper upgrade for it. Even helpful things can screw you over, as a lot of the time I got hit because my character decided to pick up money instead of attacking. It feels like they wanted to take everything from the old arcade beat-em-ups, even the frustrating parts that were products of the time.
It does have an easy mode, but even then the game doesn't really feel fun or satisfying to play. This review is done from the perspective of single player, granted, but it's probably not all that likely you'd play it with others, since there's no online co-op. If they added some, maybe it would be more fun, but as it is there are beat-em-ups on Steam already that do grant that option, like Castle Crashers or Double Dragon Neon. I'd try one of them before this game.
Do you have friends? Play this with your friends, I'm sure you'll be alone in no time.

I suppose I'm telling you this because I have a bit of a predisposition towards pretty 2-D games that feature people in spacesuits alone on alien worlds, which is what Metroid and Capsized share in common. It can be easy to assume that they'd share more, like a focus on exploration, creepy atmosphere, and progressive unlockables, but that's not the case despite what you might have assumed from the screenshots. And the Steam Store description. Instead, Capsized is, according to the (partially accurate) store page description, 'fast paced' and 'intense,' neither of which really gelled with me since the controls (and the physics) feel pretty loose.
The graphics are nice, and the physics are fun to wrestle with once you get a feel for them, but at the end of the day, I simply didn't find the game very interesting. Also, this game is somehow rather taxing on my quad-core, 8gb RAM equipped laptop. I had resigned myself to 720p for games like Bioshock Infinite and Borderlands 2, but
Meh.
In the end, my review is an opinion. That's what reviews are. And my opinion is that I didn't really like this game. Brought forth a sense of apathy from me. Sorry, I guess. The developers were gracious enough to put up a demo on their store page, so in the end that's going to be the best determinant for you, really.
There is, however, one thing that really did honestly bother me about Capsized. In the game, you are on an alien planet. There's alien creatures, sure, but also a lot of alien humanoids that look an
lot like a western stereotype of 'jungle natives.' I mean, they shoot darts. Throw spears. Wear tall wooden masks. Sacrifice your little astronaut friends on stone tables. Tiki torches. Magical shamen. Idols. Speak a gutteral language that could be transcribed as “Ooga-booga.”
Your missions generally revolve around killing all of them. And destroying their idols. Yes, there's an achievement for finishing 5 levels without firing a shot, but it's
It's supposed to be hard. Normal play looks a lot like you, a pale man in a spacesuit, committing xenocide (another achievement, natch) with your laser pistol, laser RPG, laser shotgun, laser flamethrower and wiping out all traces of these “primitive's” religion. Hell, I honestly wouldn't care if these alien natives looked
but with how much of the art draws from imagination, and then you're faced with a pretty familiar depiction of
just rubs me the wrong way, especially since the game really doesn't seem to be concerned about it at all.
Maybe I'm just on edge a bit after playing through Uncharted 2 again and (SPOILERS DON'T READ IF YOU HAVEN'T PLAYED IT OR GO AHEAD I'M NOT YOUR MOM) being reminded that the hero single-handedly wipes out an ancient city populated by magical natives (that you are expected to mow down with a variety of advanced military-grade weaponry)
Literally, the hero shrugs after bringing the whole city down. Happy ending. No one cares.
It may seem like a little, arbitrary thing and...maybe it is, but the first thing that comes to my mind after Capsized isn't the gameplay, nor the story, nor even the art, it's the dissonance between the foreignness of an alien world that the developers want me to be absorbed in, and the very familiar feeling of the aliens depicted in the game. That's what sticks with me, and helps me decide to not recommend this game, Steam. I appreciate you listening.

Don't make the mistake I did and think that Capsized is some kind of exploration-heavy metroidvania thing. The mentions of exploring and using tools to navigate might suggest that, but it's a very different beast. What you're getting is a floaty sci-fi platformer with a lot of shooting, a lot of physics puzzles, and a lot of frustration. And it might just be short enough to finish before you get fed up with it.
Capsized sees you stranded on an alien world that wastes no time trying to waste you. The natives are restless and the fauna is deadly, and most levels are going to be spent depopulating the area so you can accomplish your goal. Instead of big, sprawling areas, Capsized takes place in fairly compact levels. Each of these starts you from scratch and tasking you to search high and low for weapons, jetpack fuel, extra lives, and other power-ups. I must emphasize, nothing is carried over between campaign missions, leaving each of the 12 levels feeling a bit thin.
There's not a lot to do besides kill things, collect power-ups if you're having trouble killing things, and finish the level. Sometimes you need to reach a certain point, sometimes you need to collect doodads, and sometimes you really do just have to kill a bunch of stuff. Navigating the levels to do that might prove difficult, as your spaceman is very floaty and easy to send careening around. He can wall jump almost effortlessly, grapple things with a grappling beam, and jetpack at will, all with mounting momentum that can easily get unmanageable.
You'll be shoving and grappling plenty of blocks, too, because Capsized loves physics puzzles. It feels odd calling them physics puzzles, though, because it's usually just a tunnel blocked with junk or a pressure plate that needs to be held down. Finishing said "puzzles" is another source of frustration, since the stones and boxes use the same physics as you and can easily drift away or rocket off the screen. The worst is when you're expected to use a block as a shield against the game's incredibly lethal traps, watching your spaceman get perforated as the block he's holding wobbles around lazily.
Dying is very much the low part of the game, and it comes more and more frequently the further in you get. Enemies and especially traps can do tons of damage, and as they become more dense in the later levels it gets that much harder to avoid big chunks of hurt. When you die you either respawn at the last 1-up you collected OR the start of the level, which is infuriating in the more maze-like levels. Several of your best guns also do splash damage to you, and there are plenty of little critters that love to run up and attach to your face to catch mortars for you.
The art is fantastically detailed, but becomes a bit too busy for a game like this. Sound design is nice and somber but the effects in battle, both audio and visual, are sorely lacking. There's so little impact to weapons you'll never really know how much damage is being done until your enemy (or you) is dead. A few co-op and arcade modes round out the game but the fact is that you're getting a 12-mission campaign that can be beaten in two hours, provided it doesn't make you rage. And whether it be the giant boulder that just will not get out of your way, or the jetpack sniper that runs you out of lives, something will most likely make you jump ship early.

CAPSIZED
-You and your crew crash onto an unknown planet with hostile aliens. You are forced to shoot through them all to accomplish a variety of objectives, such as saving crew members, getting ship parts, and slaying certain types of alien tribal people.
-Most of the missions boil down to either search and destroy or dragging something to a desired location. It doesn't get much more complicated than that.
-Capsized doesn't really do anything differently than any other game. There are a few cool guns, some interesting environments, and various upgrades, but it doesn't really get any deeper.
-The foreground is distracting. Later on the amount of enemies on screen gets fairly insane, and the backgrounds become an eyesore. Though it seems like a lot of work was put into these environments, they are almost TOO complex. I only played for about an hour and had to quit due to a headache.
-Even on easy mode this game is fairly hard. You will die a lot, and sometimes you will have to restart due to an error. A couple of times I had a physics based error that made it impossible to progress. I didn't particularly enjoy any level enough to replay it again, so this quickly became a pain.
-I like the music, but it starts to drone on repetitively after a time.
-It's a cheap game, might be worth the ten bucks, but I can't see this appealing to everyone.
-It certainly didn't appeal to me.
-I may give it a try another day, but Capsized seemed far more frustrating than it was worth. Wonky physics, annoying amounts of enemies, and the lack of anything really that captivating prevented me from enjoying my run.
FINAL VERDICT
-Not really worth the time. This may appeal to people who enjoy sidescrolling shooters, but the controls weren't tight enough for me to enjoy the experience. I like the idea of a minimalistic story told through pictures rather than words, but in the end I never felt like what they were portraying really translated into the gameplay. I can see this being a good distraction for a few hours, but nothing more than that. Despite the almost soothing music and charming art style, Capsized it's a very frantic game that offers a very familiar story that might not be worth the time to relive.

I beta-tested this game a few months ago. My name's in the credits. You may wish to take this review with a grain of salt.
Regardless, Linelight is an exercise in minimalism. Everything takes place on lines. There are no controls besides moving, and two others (to be revealed elsewhere in the game). How many puzzles, then, could someone possibly squeeze out of it?
About 300.
Oh right, you want to know more about the mechanics. As you can see in the screenshots and trailer, there are switches that move lines, switches that open doors, keys that open doors, enemies (some only move when you do, some move to the beat of the music, and some repeat your previous movements), spools that allow your line to become longer (so that it can press down multiple switches, among other things), and... well, not too much else actually.
Yet throughout all this, there is definitely a whole ton of ideas that Brett Taylor has incorporated; he's really covered all the bases with these puzzles. Most puzzles illustrate a neat consequence of the rules (some are "reprises", if you will), so there's not very much wasted space. And for most of these puzzles, there is really nothing quite like them in other games. Using a switch to release an enemy, then getting the enemy to toggle the switch so that you can get to the end is something I don't think I've seen in any other game, yet it's one of the first few puzzles in this game. (It's also Brett's favourite puzzle in the game, if I recall correctly).
Note also the amount of polish evident in the game. There is a very abstract nonverbal narrative involving helping other lines through problems (as opposed to the game being just a bunch of line puzzles, which is what some people who haven't played The Witness think of it). The soundtrack is spectacular and catchy (it's still floating around my head after all this time), and enhanced by the subtle percussion that the enemies add. The graphical effects upon entering a level, collecting a star, and so on, just add that tiny bit of prettiness that says "Yes, the developer put actual effort into this game. Unlike Flow Match or Rolling Shapes.". (And yes, I will be slagging off both of those games in every single review I post on Steam later. Because those two deserve it.) For a one-and-a-half-year one-person project, this is stunningly top-quality. (Unlike Flow Match, which was also a one-and-a-half-year one-person project, and was a complete piece of garbage that I managed to outdo in a single month.)
Some puzzles are a little finicky, but other than that, I honestly can't see any fault with this game. This is a strong Puzzle Game Of The Year 2017 contender. Or at least, it would be if I gave out game awards.
If any puzzle game in January deserves money, it's probably this one; especially if you're at all interested in puzzles. (Though that having been said, I feel like the game's still a little too expensive. Then again, I'm harsh with price.)
(Later parts of the game may not be accessible for people with colour-blindness. You may wish to take this into consideration if you're planning on buying the game during its first two weeks or so. This paragraph will be removed when this problem has been fixed.)

Mousecraft is a fun little puzzle game. Ignore the sales pitch about Tetris and Lemmings though, the actual gameplay doesn't really have much in common with either of them.
The puzzles themselves are fairly traditional fare. For each level you are given a set of blocks that you need to place on the map to guide your mice to cheese and collect as many crystals along the way as possible. Overall the levels are pretty simple, even if the addition of different special blocks in later levels does complicate things a little bit.
The action does happen in realtime, but as you can pause and undo freely, things never get too hectic. Overall the difficulty level was pretty low, there's pretty much always an obvious solution that gets you at least some of the mice and crystals and usually even the perfect solution is not that hard to figure out.
Despite some minor flaws Mousecraft is a pretty enjoyable experience and I'd recommend it to any fans of simple puzzle games.
The good:
- Clear colorful art
- Decent amount of levels
- Good variety of different blocks
The bad:
- Too easy
- No way to check exactly how many mice/crystals you have collected in each level
The ugly:
- Occasional UI issues, restarting the game generally resolved these problems

Good game, but not without it's flaws, especially when compared to more modern games. There are several negative aspects that are to be expected from Bethesda games, but can't be ignored.
- The interface is awful. There are UI mods that I recommend, but even then the UI has some downsides that simply annoy after almost 200 hours of play time.
- Character models is generic. Everyone looks the same. There are no real characters that stand out. Most of time it is only the clothing that stands out.
- Dungeon design is boring after a while. There is a handful of different dungeon type, but these are repeated at many locations with little variation. Very rarely a location is significantly different from the rest.
- Since the game is levelling with you, there is little feeling of power and might in higher levels. You have more options, but are almost never significantly more powerful than generated enemies.
- Enemy variety is limited. They do have different levels, but since they level with you, all you notice is an altered name and maybe a slightly different model. Very few unique monsters.
- Stability is bad, at least on my system, which is very stable otherwise. The game crashes practically every hour with certainty. I do have to say, that I use a couple of mods. but I tried to limit it to some light eyecandy. Performance degrades during play also. For an older game, it should run better. Noticeable was that game registers clicks different, when the frame rate drops. Short, single clicks were then interpreted as long clicks.
- Several known bugs, but most of them can be fixed.
Well, overall I would recommend a playthrough with the vanilla game with very few essential mods, i.e. the unoffical patches, an UI mod and nothing else. I had a couple of landscape mods but never had the feeling that they benefit the game greatly. Most mods promise more than they deliver. And in my case, most of the few mod quests were broken. The mod quests are also very unbalanced regarding loot.
Once you experienced the original game, you might want to test mods. Well, if you want to play an already repetitive game after 200 hours again.

Devil's Dare is definitely a fun game. Full of references, little easter eggs, and a bunch of fan service-y type things. That said... it's not exactly a smooth game. The game controls very much like the original Double Dragon. As in, every action feels very deliberate, and somewhat clunky at times. Button mashing will get you killed. Not paying attention will get you killed. Poor placement / timing / usage of abilities will get you killed.
Devil's Dare is hard, but not unfair. If you like, consider it the Dark Souls of beat 'em up games. Continues are hard won, and levels are usually beaten with a fraction of health left. You have to be smart about the perks you choose at the end of each level, particularly towards the end.
I think one of my favorite things about Devil's Dare isn't that it's meta, but that it's meta about being meta, almost like it's mocking itself for referencing what it is. If you get the bad ending (and I did, at first), the game legitimately shames you for being so selfish / bad. It actually made me want to try again and again.
I'm not sure what the solo experience is like, and quite frankly, I'm glad that it doesn't have online multiplayer. Timing / client issues that would happen aside, this is a couch / party type game, and I can't imagine it would have the same feeling / intensity online as it does when you're sitting next to friends, either high-fiving, or going "Ooooooh nooooooo~" with each other.
Lastly... This isn't really a pick up and play type game. If you play this casually, you will probably not have a lot of fun. This is something you sit down with a group of friends and say to yourselves, "Ok, this is what we're going to do. We're going to kick this game's♥♥♥♥♥ or die trying. Repeatedly." It takes practice, patience, and a bit of dedication to learn how to beat enemies and bosses.
Anywho... It's a good game if you're up for a challenge and are one of those weird people who has friends that can play next to you. Good luck!

Let's get the technical stuff out of the way first. This game is excellently optimized. I'm running it in 1920x1080 on a Core2Quad Q9400 @ 2.66 GHZ, 8 GB RAM and a GeForce GTX 650 1GB, and except for some of the post processing options (e.g. volumetric fog) turned off, everything is on high or normal and the game looks fantastic. Steady frame rates throughout, whether on land or at sea. A little frame drop happens after some bigger ship battles when a lot of smoke and fire have to be rendered during boarding operations, but it's still perfectly playable at that point. A slight sluggishness feeling is the best way to describe it. You could try and tweak overall performance by lowering the resolution a little and then potentially add more effects to see how far you can push it, but that's personal preference. The game looks great regardless.
Ubisoft! I was actually very pleasantly surprised.
The controls are all fully re-mappable as well; both on foot and for ship controls, so you can choose whatever you like at your heart's content. Considering this isn't an option at all in "Assassin's Creed Chronicles: China" at all, to me, that's a great plus.
Storywise I can't really say too much just yet, I've only scratched the surface (will update this review when I know more), but so far it's fun and the scenery is actually really, really beautiful. I suppose you could just blast through the storyline, but I actually enjoy just roaming around a little, procuring some resources for crafting and generally checking out the area.
Bottom line: Whether you're an AC veteran like myself and enjoyed the entire franchise so far, or whether you're new to the Assassin's Creed games, this is one of the best installments of series, and if you want to give any game of the franchise a go without being too picky to play them in order (important plot elements from past games are explained well enough for you not to miss out all too much), I would either go with this, or with Assassin's Creed II.
Having played this now for some time, I can definitely say this is as much fun as Black Flag. It's a bit more of a "civilized" and "tactical" warfare than the random privateering you get in Black Flag, but it's definitely worth it. I'd probably call Black Flag "GTA IV" where Rogue would be "Watch_Dogs". Don't let that comparison frighten you though (if you don't like either or one of the comparisons). It's a great game, you can manage a fleet, resources, follow the much more on-track mission, or just free-roam for as long as you like. You definitely want to grab another hide for that pouch you always wanted. Despite the role change, Shay does grow on you, and the added possible attacks by your former brethren at any turn, definitely are a nice touch.

At the time of my writing this Stalker: CoP is seven years old. And it shows. The graphics are rather dated, there is a ton of much better looking shooters available today. The UI isn't the most userfriendly and for beginners it's sometimes unclear how to get certain things to work (no tutorial). Optimisation isn't great (at least for my 2yo windows10 rigg), I'm having lots of lag-spikes in particular when sprinting.
BUT! HOWEVER! STILL! Even after thinking really hard (within my personal limitations, of course) that's all I can come up with in terms of flaws in the game. Everyting else is just fantastic!
The game is an action-FPS with a wee bit of RPG-elements in a pseudo-open world. You're a Stalker, a kind of scout/prospector exploring the land surrounding the melted down nuclear plant of Chernobyl and investigating the strange phenomena that occur here. There is no hand-holding in the game. There's no creating or choosing a character either. There's no character developement, no classes to choose from, no skills to improve. You'll continue to upgrade your equipment though so your character will still grow stronger over time. You'll get hungry or radioactive or simply wounded and bleeding and you will have to take care of that. You will also get to make some simple but interesting choices relevant to the storylines.
The game's map is relatively small but you'll hardly notice. It covers plenty of different locations. It provides a ton of atmosphere. Unlike in Fallout or Metro for instance the land in Stalker:CoP is not all wasteland. The starting area actually looks for a large part like a nature conservation park with some long abandoned remnants of human industrial activity. Still, it's very dangerous to go on a stroll unprepaired here. Scary mutants of many different types will jump on you regularly and frequently and you'll die often. Some areas are poisonous, others are radioactive. And there is the continuous menace of the Blowout, a sudden "change in the weather" that forces you to drop everyting and sprint for cover or die. If the only cover you can find is a cave filled with scary monsters you'll die anyway. Luckily in spite of all this the game offers many incentives to go out and explore, search for treasure and earn some cash to gear up, investigate the many factions and NPCs and how they relate, maybe choose sides, do some quests, missions or manhunts.
I'm nearly twenty hours in and, as I'm a slow-paced player, I can't really judge the story-telling yet, though at first glance it seems well done. At least it grabbed me in a way that right now I just want to quickly finish this review and continue playing so that's what I'll do.
Oh, hold on, I still have to mention that there are quite a few mods available for this game! Suddenly the question "Do you recommend this game?" sounds rather silly indeed.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Call of Pripyat is a phenomal game, feeling like the love-child of the Fallout series (Pre-New Vegas) and Metro franchise. Thrown into the area surrounding Chernobyl years after its meltdown, you are sent in to figure out what happened to the USS's military operatives.
The atmosphere the game exudes is nothing short of amazing - even with dated graphics the game manages to hold your attention through it's amazing world-building and feeling of freedom. There's always a sense of wanderlust; never being sure of what's to come, a feeling of anxiousness spurred on by your excitement to press forward and figure out what's just over the horizon - it truly is an exhilarating experience! The Zone - a hostile environment that will tear those unprepared apart - offers a unique chance at fortune and glory for those willing to take on increasingly dangerous and unique missions. From helping people with their small, individual problems, to assisting those with intentions to make life in the Zone better for all - there's always a way to make some cash on your adventure.
If you've ever thought about picking up the game or enjoyed the Fallout and/or Metro series, I can whole-heartedly recommend 'S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Call of Pripyat'. While the graphics may be dated, the experience is anything but; and at the end of the day - as you're uninstalling the game - a melancholy wave will wash over you as you realize that your time in the Zone has come to an end, leaving naught but the kindling of the inspirational flame.
...So I have but one question for you: When the time comes for you to pass on that inspirational flame, will you heed its call? Or will you let the ashes drift away into your memories, letting them settle until they ultimately erode into nothingness? The choice is yours, Stalker.

This game is simple racing fun. There's plenty to unlock, a good variety of tracks, difficulty levels (represented by vehicle/course grades) to challenge yourself, lots of achievements to work through if those are your thing, a fun soundtrack, and it's just a nice way to kill a few minutes here and there. The races are fairly short: usually three minutes or so, making it a perfect game to play in bite-sized portions.
Graphics are shiny and serviceable. The vehicle handling varies enough from car to car that adjusting to the characteristics of a new car takes a little time, adding a bit of challenge. Cars don't deform in any way, which is probably good since everyone is slamming into each other (and the walls) constantly. They do take damage, though, and repairs are deducted from your winnings. Curiously, repair costs seem to be deliberately limited such that they never consume your winnings from a particular race, so you'll never end up in a situation where you have a broken car and no money to fix it.
This is a great game for people who like the occasional bit of racing, rather than hardcore digital motorheads (which I am not.)

It's a pretty awesome dota-style game, and one of the few 2-D games of this type. Normally you will have 3 turrets to defend, and one base to defend from enemy attacks. The respawn time is pretty fast, and feeding doesn't seem to be as much of a big deal as it is in other games of this type, making this game fairly new-player friendly. The other team may be way better at player kills, but the winning team seems to usually be the one that isn't afraid to die now and then to target enemy turrets. The game itself is fun to play, but it can get complicated with a plethora of upgrade options, three of which for each category you will need to pick before the match starts in a limited amount of time. To get good at this game, you will want to be familiar with the characters and upgrades that you want to use long before the match starts, adding a layer of depth to the game that may be a bit daunting to new players. Overall, I'd recommend playing this game with friends. Splitscreen mode actually allows you to play on the same computer if you want to, which is rare in the world of PC gaming. The game is mostly balanced after many hours of hardwork from the developers. I do think that some characters are better than others, but the game is constantly being improved. I have yet to see a win-lose record in the game, and the game focuses more on your overall rank than anything else, which somehow makes you feel less pressure if you don't really care about being the top rank. This game is fun, and definitely worth playing with friends.

Bottom Line Up Front: Stable Orbit is a fun game for a few hours, but some improvements can be(and should be) made. Pick it up on a sale.
The Good: This game is very pretty, and the background music is very relaxing. Once you figure out the inital stabilzation and priority of work (basically just follow the "tutorial"), you can build and build and build until you have a monsterous space station that looks like it was designed on the whims on a drunk man sitting in his living room.
The Bad: There are no panels that tell you if you have too many of this or not enough of that. The guagues at the bottom of the screen, to me, were vague at best. For a space station, I would imagine efficency is key, I would expect readouts telling me if I am utilizing all of my storage tanks to capacity or if I've got a bunch that are not needed and wasting space.
The notification panel provides useless information, once I have 75+ people on board and 25+ research projects going on, I don't care when one is completed, it doesn't matter to me anymore. I only care if I lose power or if a module decides to jettison itself back to earth. When a module does blow away on its own accord, the notification panel is useless on telling me where it came from so I can replace it. And that leads me to the biggest problem of this game, once the station is so large, it is difficult to get around it. The camera focuses on the last module you clicked on, so getting from the front to the back is like climbing a ladder, The controls are so simplistic there is no reason I cant control the camera with WASD and free float it around, and if I can do that, it was not clear in the 5+ hours of how to do that.

text:
Counterspell is hard to describe because it has elements of so many different genres in it.
Its got skills and random drops, like an ARPG.
Its got fallout3-esque stealth mechanics
It plays a little bit like a classic shooter, but not quite to the extremes.
It plays a little like an MMO, with a basic quest-guided Kill Five Rats And A Boss structure.
Just listing these ideas out, they probably seem like they wouldn’t work well or would clash, but to be honest that isn’t the case at all. They all flow pretty well with each other and it results in a finished product that’s enjoyable and charming.
The art style, while basic, fits the game and is charming. The screenshots in the store page feature a lot of dark areas, but know that most of the game consists of brighter colored scenes.
The music is enjoyable, if generic. The sound effects are a little cheesy and sound like stuff you would hear in an early build of Minecraft, but they work fine for what they are. I’ve grown to think of them, again, as charming.
The game is extremely easy to jump in and jump out of as you wish. This is a good game to pop into and play for thirty minutes or an hour. I probably would not recommend it for long extended gaming sessions unless you have a lot of friends doing it alongside you.
It’s fun to explore. There’s a bunch of nice little distractions and hidden areas around the map. It’s enough to make it fun to stop what you’re doing and go look at that lighthouse, or to explore the sewer to see if it goes anywhere.
You can pick up your dead allies and carry them around. Aside from being hilarious with friends, this is a great mechanic that gives you control over where you want to spend time reviving them without having to leave them to die because they fell down in a crowded street
The Dev-team is the most active I’ve ever seen. Upon first installing the game I encountered two bugs. Within hours a dev had commented on my page. Within the day a patch rolled out to fix one of the issues, and the other, as it was probably much harder to track down, was fixed two days later.
I have had few issues with the game, and every patch that has happened since I bought the game has worked towards removing the biggest issues. I’ll go ahead and talk about some anyway though.
The difficulty curve isn’t so much a curve as it is a shifting vertical line. This is a small problem with all rpg stat system games, but its hyper-prevalent here. There are many areas that you simply can not do single-player until you are “overleveled” for them due to the concentration of enemies shoved into a single room or corridor. (This has been worked on in patches since I bought it and has seen great improvements with the new loot drop system meaning players are better geared and have a smoother progression, so it is actively becoming less and less of an issue.)
The class balance is awkward. Some abilities are unfinished or are extremely lackluster. A few of the classes feel kind of similar. (I have read that entirely new skill system is being worked on at the moment. If done well, this would eliminate this issue)
The spell graphics get in the way at times. Sometimes the screen gets absolutely covered in a visual effect such as fire or frost, and it makes it hard to know what’s going on.
Over all Counter-Spell is a fun game for when you have a little bit of spare time or want to mess around with your friends. It’s far from a AAA title, but it’s not trying to be one either. You get what you pay for, and it’s pretty enjoyable. It seems to be actively improving as time goes on, and you get a sense that the devs care about the game and the direction it goes beyond just making it sell well.
EDIT: 11/20/2017 I have not played the game recently due to lack of time, but I know that some of the features I mentioned in this review have been added in beta format. As of right now the game still is getting updated frequently and, should I get the time for it, I will check out the new systems and update the review accordingly.

Overview:
Stable Orbit is a simulation and management sim set on a space station orbiting Earth that is largely inspired by the International Space Station.  Gameplay consists of making a space station that can sustain it's sole occupant at the start, then expanding to hold a laboratory, which makes it possible to perform research, which is your meal ticket and means of survival.  From there, you increase the size of the station through building trusses to hold new additions to your station, add solar panels and batteries to make the station capable of supporting more units, storage for food, water, and oxygen, then build radiators to dissipate heat.  From there you can build more nodes to increased the habitable parts of the station, habitat moduels to sustain larger numbers of crewmembers, laboratories to take on more contracts.  After all this expansion, you'll have to eventually build another thruster on the bottom of the station so your amazing creation doesn't fall into the Earth's atmosphere, and totally disintegrate.
Graphics and Sound:
Graphics in Stable Orbit are absolutely nothing short of breathtaking.  If you love space and sci-fi games, you're going to be aroused, and I do mean in the sexual sense!
The view Stable Orbit is in full 3D, so if you get tired of looking away from the Earth, you can always look down at it to see the current location of the station in regards to the Earth.
What if you don't know geography well enough to be able to tell where the station is in relation to the Earth?  Not to worry, there's a map you can access that shows the station's present location, along with the track of everywhere the station goes around the world.
The music in Stable Orbit works very well with the game.  In fact, the music is good enough to where I forget that I should be playing my own sort of music while I play the game.  I wanted to say that the sounds of the game are realistic, except for one problem:  This game is in space, and being in a vaccum, it's impossible for sound to travel anywhere, so if you were actually viewing the station from the angles you can view it, you wouldn't actually hear anything as it happened.
Positives:
Anyone who loves games that involves building stuff will have a great time with Stable Orbit.  Being the management sim lover I am, Stable Orbit fills the bill for a subgenre of games where there's almost nothing in the way of competition.  I've played enough games in Stable Orbit's genre to know that I love building cities, building armies, building sports teams, and even building buildings, so I can honestly say I've enjoyed building a space station in Stable Orbit.
Contracts that are required to make money are all fascinating.  Although it's really just the money that matters, the game does add harmony to the game's experience by telling you just exactly what sort of research you're assigning to any astronauts, and exactly who it is you're doing research for.  (Or at least simply who's paying you to do the research.)
Negatives:
When you're looking down at the planet Earth, there's no clouds to speak of.  Although I personally would like to see the occasional hurricane (or regional varient thereof), but all you're treated to, is a CAVU (Ceiling And Visibility Unlimited) view of the Earth.  Does Earth weather add to the gameplay value?  I'd have to say not really, as nice as it would be to see some variety that makes the player want to point the camera downward as much as the player would like to point it upward to see spectacular views of outer space.
The biggest negative of Stable Orbit would have to be the lack of achievements in the game.  As a result, this motivates the player to almost exclusively take on Earth & Space research contracts, which are the most lucrative sorts of contracts.  (Although the game does provide some balance by making less-lucrative contracts shorter to complete, but it seems pointless given the way that either way, you're going to be waiting in the early stages of the game before you can build additions to your station.)
Conclusion:
Although Stable Orbit represents a niche game which non-fans of management sims would likely find uninteresting, those who do enjoy repetitive games from the genre will find Stable Orbit fascinating.  I was lucky to have been awarded a free key for Stable Orbit, because I found myself unable to play the game I was most hooked upon at the time of the awarding.  The two main questions any game would have, is replayability factor and value for money.  For Stable Orbit, the answers are "yes" and "yes."  If you got the guts (and patience) to take on contracts other than Earth and Space research, you can do that.  If you want to simply try and build the coolest, craziest, happiest, saddest, or perhaps even ugliest space station you can, you can always challenge yourself to do that!  Value for the moeny?  I've played far less interesting games that costs even more money than Stable Orbit (and promptly refunded them), so go ahead and buy this game, and especially if you can buy Stable Orbit while it's on sale, because there's no way you can count on winning a free key!

Before I started playing Linelight I had a strong feeling that I would like the game since I really like these type of puzzle games. Despite high expectations, Linelight still surprised me.
Linelight decides to ditch most gameplay mechanics found in today's games and focus on designing great puzzles. Basically you play as a line segment that moves along other line segments. You need to use the basic mechanics that the game gives you to get past barriers and move your line segment to other lines in order to proceed.
I will admit that the puzzles are a little on the easy side but they are so well designed that I didn't mind. I would classify the early levels as easy and the later levels as easy to moderately difficult. While I wish the levels were a little more challenging I have to say that the game does such a great job using the few mechanics that the game has to create new and interesting puzzles. The game has 300 puzzles (60 being hidden/bonus levels) and every puzzle feels unique.
Even though you can finish most of the puzzles in around a minute or two, Linelight is actually quite long for this type of game. The game has 300 puzzles spread amongst nine worlds. If you don't skip any of the puzzles you encounter I would say that the game will take most people around 6-8 hours to complete. If you want to finish all of the bonus puzzles it would probably take around 8-9 hours mostly due to it being kind of hard to find a lot of the bonus puzzles.
If you don't really like these type of puzzle games, Linelight is probably not going to be for you. If you like these type of games though I think you will really enjoy Linelight since it is one of the best indie games that I have played in a while.

I have had this game in my library for almost a year and finally started playing it to avoid another re-run of Dragon Age. Wish I had played this sooner. Really enjoy the game-play, story and combat. Even the sidequests are fun and sometimes have me laughing - that is when I am not cursing because some Rat Queen is killing me over and over agaiin for hours. It pays to learn the rules to this game and to be innovative in approaches to difficult combat. It is also a beautiful game graphics-wise even if it is dated.

There's some really great design here in teaching the player the mechanics by showing. Optional objectives (diamonds you can collect) also give insentive to make it harder yourself, which I love. Secret levels are much more challenging, plus they're harder to find. The mechanics (up to world 5, so far) feel natural, and increase challenge gradually. You're always given room to figure out the mechanic's caveats before it mixes it with a previous one. The puzzles can get pretty complex, due to how each mechanic meshes, but they're still simple to figure out, and the solutions are rarely tedious.
Gameplay is equal parts logic and timing, but never too hard on either. Difficulty always feels reasonable, never out of your control.
A couple times, the game has gone past the boundaries of my 5:4 monitor, but I know that's an uncommon aspect ratio nowadays. Hasn't made it unplayable, though.
This is definitely a "one solution" puzzle game (if you couldn't figure that out already), so I don't think there's too much in terms of replayability, outside of completing secret levels and collecting all diamonds. I'm hoping for an expansion pack, or a level editor further down the line (no pun intended)
