I really loved this game. BUT: I'm german, this game was written in german, and it implements the german Dark Eye RPG system. So while the basic idea is still that of a CRPG, the game can have a lot of peculiar aspects if you are coming  from the AD&D culture. The game system never developed the kind of depth that can be found in the AD&D system, especially at high levels. And obviously, this game's storyline can't even be compared to the depths and complexity we've seen in the true gems like Mask of the Betrayer or Planescape Torment. Nonetheless, the writers were pretty well-versed within the Dark Eye universe, and the whole thing is a full and convincing implementation of the game's pen&paper base. But if you can't play it in german, most of the writing's qualities are probably lost in translation. The game really lives by athmosphere, by capturing the "feel" of the Dark Eye universe, which is largely conveyed by the language.
Other than that, the Dark Eye game system is also ridiculously complex when compared to AD&D. Where AD&D is optimized for playability and high-level scaling, the Dark Eye is optimized for realism and plausibility. So you end up with a combat system that is complex and difficult to master, yet feels very basic. However that's just what the Dark Eye world is like. Think of it as an "earlier", simpler world than AD&D. It's not as mythical, magic doesn't have as much power, people and their stories are simpler. I used to play some Dark Eye pen & paper, so I knew roughly what to expect, and that's why I loved it.
So, bottom line: If you know & love the Dark Eye, and if you're fluent in german, this is definitely an awesome game. If not, you might still get the hang of the world, its lore and the way it works, but maybe you don't.

This game is dull.  From the incessant fights against uninteresing enemies (wolves, rats, and bandits, mostly) to the boring and unimpressive spells, and the underwhelming combat moves, the game is dull.
The game's storytelling is also dull.  The characters are fairly boring themselves.  If you decide to play it, whatever you do, don't decide to ask a character's backstory.  What you'll get is a tedious dialogue that reveals nothing about the game world and nothing interesting about the character.
If you're like me, and you're looking for a CRPG to pass the time, then I suppose this game will do.  But the pace is slow and nothing about it has yet to enrapture me.
I'd reinstall Neverwinter Nights 2, but that would take me forever and NWN2 has its own issues (bugs, mostly).  But at least NWN2 has some interesting abilities for your character.  Not so here.  I've looked online out of sheer frustration, and it seems the most interesting spell the game can give you is some kind of fireball.
Woo.  A fireball.  The game has nothing with more pizazz than that, I'm afraid.
Otherwise, the game will keep you busy.  There's plenty of uninteresting sidequests, and the main quest seems pretty long.  Unfortunately, busy doesn't mean entertained.
I really wish somebody would make some more CRPGs of the caliber of the first Neverwinter Nights (not the multiplayer one) and Dragon Age: Origins.  But I guess making fun videogames is hard, so it's unlikely we'll see much of that.
Anyways, back to Drakensang:
The combat is turnbased and rather clunky.  Casting spells seems to take several rounds, which is quite frustating considering that the duration of debuffs is about as long.  So by the time you've cast your weeny cold ray on an enemy (assuming you haven't been interrupted, since the cold ray spell has an exceedingly short range in addition to a long casting time), the distracting shock spell you've cast upon your opponent will have run out.  Your party members then have fifteen secodns to take advantage of your enemy's momentary weakness.
Expect lots of waiting around for your character to get his turn to strike.
There doesn't appear to be any significant player choice in the game, beyond turning down quests.  So if you weren't allowed to wander aimlessly, this would effectively be a linear game.
So: don't buy.  It's a waste of time and money.  Unless you're like me and you're unemployed and you need something to kill the time that can run on your dated computer, fun be damned.

Mousecraft is a entertaining puzzle-game, which is basically a mix of Lemmings and Tetris.
You have to guide three mice (which behave like lemmings) through a level full of dangeres to a piece of cheese. To help the mice there are Tetris-like blocks to build a path. New items are introduced step by step in the game which enrich the puzzle experience and bring diversion to the game.
Guiding all three mice to the cheese is more or less easy, but there are also collectible crystals and it can be very tricky to get all of them. Better said: to leed the mice to all cristals.
Despite beeing an indie game programmed by a small game studio  Mousecraft offers good graphics and performance and seems quite professional. And the most important thing: it's quite fun to play!

Overall, Assassin's Creed Rogue shines bright out of the post-Desmond AC games. A combination of excellent story, the return of well proven game mechanics as well as Black Flag's incredibly successful naval combat, and a brilliant soundtrack produce a brilliant secondary title that ties together the events of ACIII-AC Unity.
Story: The story focuses around Assassin turned Templar Shay Cormac. The length of the story is not nearly that of other AC titles, but is far more rewarding. Admittably, I wish they'd spent more time building an attachment to every major Assassin, but the manner in which the story shows Shay's motivation for turning allows the moments when you do have to kill an Assassin to be enjoyable. There are parts where it seemed to run on a bit, I was not nearly as engaged in naval gameplay in this as I was in Black Flag thus those sections seemed far more irritating for me. The out-of-Animus story once again takes place in Abstergo Entertainment where you will intermittently be interrupted by Templar Agents to fix a server. Not the best, but it's better than Unity's.
Gameplay: Black Flag+Revelations+ACII. The game included the return of the zip line (sadly no hook blade), a new "lift", and the return of managing the city's economy. Of course there was Black Flag's naval combat and the movement felt identical to Black Flag. The gameplay of the ground missions reminded me most of ACII, though, possibly from the soundtrack.
Graphics: Do not expect a massive improvement on Black Flag. There are areas where the game looks very nice, but other areas, such as the city you visit in the last memory, do not shine as much. Overall it is pleasant to look at, I ran it on my machine (i7, GT760, 8 gb RAM) very smoothly on max settings.
Overall: I have to be fair because I was extremely disappointed in Far Cry 4 because it was just too similar to Far Cry 3. Rogue is very similar to Black Flag, but I do not share that disappointment with Rogue. While New York definitely gives off a more tropical vibe than ACIII, the game stands strong on its own. It is a fairly big world to explore that definitely looks dated when compared to titles that were not hindered by the Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3, but still looks remarkable in certain areas. The story, if nothing else, is what you absolutely need to experience. It is a refreshing look at both orders that might turn your opinion slightly, but more importantly, it sews together the last several AC titles.

Ive got a small story, this is from Call of Chernobyl(a massive mod, check it out).
I started out with Freedom, got just a USP45 with about 4 mags and an AK74 with no ammo in it. My Comrade tasked me to go stop a group of enemies before they arrive to my base. I asked 3 other men to come with me, as I know I would not be able to take them alone.
In the dead of night during a lightning storm, we moved through the Army Warehouses to an ambush point next to where we would be intercepting, little did we know how close they actually were, and as we tried crossing the road one of my buddies got cut down, so I had to try to drag him to cover to grab his ammo and his rifle, but then I saw the other two men get cut down by something heavy, I couldnt go out of cover to grab his HK416, as I was unsure if I could survive the second I would be out of cover.
I finally braced myself to take them on, gripped my USP tightly, and poked out of cover while turning off my flashlight as to now give away my position, and I saw about 4 silouttes, accentuated by the muzzle flashes of their weapons. I took my first few shots off, taking the first man out, but as I did that I noticed 3 more silouttes coming along my flank, so instead of popping out of cover to try to take them out when I just have a USP compared to whatever fullautos they have, I waited for them to approach my flank and I took them out as they turned.
So that was 4 out of the 7 I knew about gone, and I popped out of cover to take out the last three I knew of, using two bandages and a first aid kit in the process, leaving me just one first aid kit and one bandage. I was finally granted a moment of ease and was able to grab my fallen comrades HK416 finally, unloading the nearly dry magazine and filling it back up. I approched down the road to take cautiously, noting I was fighting Mercenaries and not the Monolith or Duty as I was used to on previous characters. Just as I was looting a dead merc, one of the surviving members who was straggling in the back was approacing and lit me up with something heavy, so I ran to the nearest tree and finally got to put the red dot and the new fancy AR I picked up to good use, and I poked back out and fired three shots, dropping him behind the cover he was hiding behind, he was still alive as I could hear him moaning so I approached to execute him, for one more to come over a hill and I turned to put two in the chest, and one in the head. I noticed that among the dead, two of them had M249 SAWs.
And that was my first encounter in the Call of Chernobyl mod.
And all the STALKER games can create a story like this one, but the point Im trying to get across is that STALKER is probably one of the leading games to make use of Emergent Storytelling(when a player creates their own story instead of the developer), as the atmosphere and setting are incredibly wellcrafted to the point where someone could make a mod that is quite literally just an open sandbox with fetch quests and the such and it still creates these stories, as you know how it goes, its not about the objective, its about the journey to it.
So if you are going to play this game, I highly recommend Call of Chernobyl.

text:
TL;DR Like fallout 3, but improves on it in every way. Instead of having to choose between to black and white factions (enclave and brotherhood of steel).
THE FACTIONS
Fallout: New Vegas provides 4 unique and diverse main factions you can join. The New California Republic, Ceasers Legion, Mr, House, and a secret option (i'll just say it's a wild card). They all have hidden agendas that could or could not be helpful to the people of the mojave wasteland. The NCR, for example, is a faction that is trying to rebuild a democratic nation much like 1800s America. But, if you ask around NCR soldiers and workers, you discover that they are extremely corrupt and are at risk of being beaten by Ceasers Legion, a group of slavers that know how to create a very stable society. FO:NV, aside from the 4 main factions, features a number of other smaller factions. They include the Followers of the Apocolypse, The Brotherhood of Steel, The Great Khans, The Boomers, and another faction that is hidden.
PLAYER FREEDOM
FO:NV may not give you the freedom to do as many things as in Skyrim or Fallout 4, but the player can have a huge influence on the mojave wasteland. By far the way to play the game and get the most freedom, is by leveling up your speech skill. You can convince people and factions to do a huge number of things with a high speech. Don't want the Great Khans fighting for The Legion? A high speech skill can dictate how effective your attempt at convincing them is. Obsidian has done a great job at providing diplomatic options for the player to take.
THE ISSUES
FO:NV, as great as it is, has some big issues. The gunplay is not a very good mechanic. The bandits in this game, although they are divided into seperate extremely small factions, you can't interact with them. You do not have the option to be the bad guy on some quests. Some DLC *cough* Old World Blues *cough* can be boring to do and extremely limited in the ammount of content. Luckily, the game does not have many bugs though.

I am writing this review because I think this game has potential but it needs a little more work. The few major complaints I have about this game is that it cost quite a bit to purchase the essential items like a shuttle airlock (to load supplies and people) and living quarters for the crew. There is no way to generate money on the side to get more items. If the crew complains they need something and do not get it (because you are short on funds) they just leave the station on the next supply shuttle and with not crew you do not generate any funds. The supply shuttle in the simulation portion seemed to not deliver any supplies or empty the waste (another reason the crew would flee the station). Larian have upped the ante with the sequel to Divinity: oringal sin. I don't think there is any part of this game that is not an improvement in some way. The monster designs are excellent with some added imagination yet still fitting within the toine of the world. There's now voice acting for every piece of dialogue with the narrator being a particularly cool inclusion. All of the changes done to combat too are an improvement, forcing more tactical decisions to be made rather than easy chain stunning that was the bread and butter of the previous installment. The writing, quests and worldbuilding are also on point with many memorable locations, callbacks to the previous game and little nooks and secrets that reward explortaion.
Divintiy: Original Sin 2 doesn't just surpass the original in terms of quality on almost every level but it cements itself as one of the best RPGs ever made.

An absolutely exhilarating game. I suppose you can say this is a bit like if Quake and Heretic were put together into a game about surviving an arena with an endless amount of enemies. This isn't an FPS where you can mindlessly run around and shoot enemies, you need to think quickly and react even quicker while you attempt to bunnyhop away from the hordes of skulls that never let up.
A lot of people complain that they can't survive for long, and I know this may seem very unhelpful, but 'get gud' is literally all there is to it. When you first play, you will die over and over and over again. But over time you will learn patterns, how to prioritise your targets in any situation, and generally improve your aim.
But even then, there are many guides that will give you a lot of information on the game and its enemies, such as their health and behaviour (as well as tips for fighting them):
The game's soundtrack is pretty much composed of the sound effects. Everything from the general ambience to the sounds of the enemies gives the game a very uneasy feeling. The game has a (particularly frightening) menu theme, but doesn't really have any music playing during a run (probably since listening for your enemies' audio cues is so important), but I suppose you could just play Quake 1's soundtrack in the background.
The artstyle is also lovely too. Not only does it take direct inspiration from Quake 1's unique gothic looks but it pretty much nails the 'ye olde' FPS look entirely. The devs made sure the 90s look actually looks 90s without lazily making the game look like minecraft just for the sake of 'wow so retro!'
The game on the whole is bloody brilliant, and it's only 4 quid! The game might not have a large amount of content, but you'll want to keep playing due to your desire to get better and beat your times.
The only thing I hope for now from the devs is a sequel that expands the game with a single player campaign. Even if it's not a direct sequel to Devil Daggers, it would still be amazing if it still has the same kind of artstyle and gameplay with handcrafted levels. It would essentially be the Quake 1 sequel we never got (though I suppose DUSK will scratch this itch for the meantime).
Recommended!

This game is a god damn masterpiece.  Most (most) of the negative reviews are from people who played less than an hour.  One of the more common complaints is that it's too hard, and that there isn't enough content.
These people are wrong.
There is SO MUCH MORE to this game than at first glance.  The better you get at the game, the more you see of what lies beyond the first couple minutes.  Not only that, but it's surprisingly strategic.  You will eventually develop a routine for the first minute, and for the minutes after that.  The first two minutes that you struggled with so badly become child's play.
Aside from the gameplay, the leaderboard is one of the best features in the game.  You can watch replays from other players, and go into a top-down view to see the whole playing field.  The best players' replays are the key to getting better.  Watch them, and learn from them.
Honestly I can't recommend this game enough.  It's one of the best shooters I've played in a while, and while it is repetitive, the drive to improve your time by just a few seconds is very strong.  If you buy this game, you need to devote some time to it so you can see what it has to offer.  Don't make a judgement from the first hour.

All the old codes work, nothing's been taken out, and the new additions don't change or get in the way of the gameplay that made this one a classic. Great visuals and soundtrack, rock-solid gameplay. The original game is still pretty cheap and easy to find, but this version will be the main one I play from here on.

(Linux Review - Ubuntu 16.04 LTS)
is a space station management game with detailed, realistic graphics.  The game runs very well on Linux, and I've not encountered any of the issues reported by users of other operating systems.
The game centers largely around managing resources to support the station's crew.  Crew members earn money by completing science experiments.  Earning potential scales with crew size, and larger crews require a larger station.  Building onto the station increases heat absorption, and heat must be radiated into space to prevent station damage.  The passage of time is controlled by the player, allowing for a stress-free gaming experience.
Stable Orbit is an early access game that, in its current incarnation, lacks depth and difficulty.  The only challenges occur early on, as one struggles to understand how resources and systems interact.  Once figured out, designing a stable and profitable station is trivial.
All in all, Stable Orbit is a good game.  It is well-suited for people with limited amounts of time on hand, as well as those who do not wish to devote a lot of time to a game.  At the same time, Stable Orbit is ideal for anyone who wants to spend hours building the largest station possible.

If you've never heard of N2O, you are missing out. One of the hidden gems of the PSX era, it applied modern aesthetics to retro shooter gameplay years before it became a popular trend (which is likely why it flew under the radar when it was released).
N2O is a tunnel shooter in the vein of the arcade classic Tempest. The core shooting gameplay is solid with a nice variety of enemies, bosses, and special weapons. Players can play the game with a traditional fixed camera (probably the best option for a high score run) or let the camera follow the player (the more intense and fun option). It features some satisfying mechanics such as the decision at the end of each round to spend coins collected from enemies for special weapons, extra lives, or a combination of the two, and a bonus round that rewards both reflexes and the ability to navigate a warped landscape. The visuals are bright and trippy while the soundtrack featuring mid-90's Crystal Method tracks matches perfectly with the action to create an exhilarating experience.
While I strongly recommend this game, I have some not-so-kind words for this port. It is essentially the game running in an emulator instead of an actual native port. That means the in-game text refers to PSX controllers and memory cards while all configuration options must be set in a launcher that starts before the game. This also means no online multiplayer or high score tracking. The only new feature is the addition of achievements. This game deserved way better than this lazy port.
Port quality withstanding, this is still a phenomenal game worth the asking price whether you are enjoying it for the first time or having nostalgia about blasting all those bugs.

N2O: Nitrous Oxide was one of my favorite games on the PlayStation system. With graphics that are highly saturated, and trippy, with its high velocity game play, and an experience that is enhanced by the electronica band The Crystal Method cut into the mix, it's a concoction that might not fare well with those prone to epilepsy or motion-sickness, but for those of us who can stomach it, it is an absolute thrill ride.
The game mechanics are simple enough. You pilot a perpetually moving ship through a tunnel and shoot at everything in 360 degree movement. Shoot bugs to explode them and collect coins. If you shoot at the coins their color changes as their value goes up. You run them over to collect them. You can grab power-ups such as extra temporary cool weapons or shields. Shoot the mushrooms enough times to gain admission to bonus levels. The more insects you shoot the faster you travel through the tunnel.
The levels amp up difficulty in a way that isn't jarring or shocking to your system, however, if you're anything like me, this doesn't deter from frequent long strings of obscenities due to stress reactions. If I could describe this game in one word I'd have to say this game is smooth. Smooth, as a jet rocket in a wind tunnel, smooth.
This might sound basic but it is a game that is just simple, straight-forward stuff (excuse the alliteration) with some twists. Nowadays, games are so overly weighed down it's nice to go back to basic. Having said that, it would be interesting to see what this game would look like on today's game engines...
(I would recommend playing this game on a controller as it's kinda painful to play on keyboard. Don't forget to fiddle around with the Settings and Controls before starting a game, like I did, because initial setup is wonky.)

Swing from the ceiling, yank stuff around, repulse matter directly away from you, and even use enemies as projectiles (or meatshields) against their friends. You and your crew have crash landed on a mysterious hostile alien planet and you must fight your way through an onslaught of vicious alien creatures to rescue your crewmates so you can escape. This has been a staple plot line for Science Fiction for almost as long as science fiction itself has existed, there is nothing new with the idea of this setting, or premise; however Capsized manages to take this setting and apply it to an absolutely gorgeous, intense, atmospheric environment paired with equally spine-tingling soundtrack.
The game is a 2D platformer that combines both fast paced action combat and exploration elements. You control your marooned space cadet across various extraterrestrial environments battling your way through herds of fairly challenging Alien creatures with your main objectives varying from “Rescue X amount of Crew mates” or “Destroy X amount this alien artifact”. The controls of the game feel very refreshing and intuitive and you are packed to the brim with weapons and gadgets to choose from. Two gadgets in particular are what really make the gameplay feel fresh and interesting, the grappling hook and gravity ram; grappling hooks can be used to pull yourself to far away areas or can double as gravity guns similar to that from Half-Life, and Gravity Rams can expel massive bursts of energy to send objects or enemies flying.
The entire art style for the game is very beautiful, consisting of complex hand-drawn artwork. The game only offers 12 levels, however the art style for each one feels fitting and sets the mood, whether that be a bright colorful level full of alien life, camps, and monuments or whether they be glum and damp and underground with darkness and danger lurking around any corner. The electronic musical soundtrack perfectly accompanies this atmospheric environment, further helping set the mood for each gorgeously illustrated level. Not only is the level design brilliant, but the enemies are also very well done. You won’t get sick and tired of being forced to fight any one enemy over and over, the game does an excellent job of spacing out various enemies of different species, sizes, and difficulty levels.
Capsized manages to provide a very enjoyable action platforming experience with a stunningly beautiful atmospheric environment. The combat feels good and there a large enough variety of both weapons and enemies to keep the game feeling fun and energetic. The only negatives of the game are that there are times when levels tend to feel a bit tedious and become a burden when slight mistakes cause you to have to retry missions multiple times; however this is merely a minor complaint. I would definitely recommend this game especially for such a low budget price of $9.99. The game plays at its best when played with a friend in local co-op.

I recently wrote a very long review on The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind Game of the Year Edition so this time is the turn of the next chapter in the Elder Scrolls series, Oblivion.
I must be honest I had never played Oblivion before I purchased it here. I had played Morrowind for years and ended up jumping straight to Skyrim (both on the Xbox/PS3 depending on which one you are referring too)
I don't think this was as much a case of oversight as a little research showed me that Oblivion, despite it being a good game, was just released at a time where RPG games where becoming the norm and the market was flooded with a million sub-par attempts. The same could be said for the precursor to Skyrim, Dragonborn, which suffered a similar fate. Not that it really damaged its' reputation at all as Oblivion is still one of the most highly praised games of the entire Elder Scrolls series.
I really settled into this game well. It didn't take long to get going with the first quests of the main storyline which I decided to complete first. It was well laid out and the actual storyline itself was gripping. From semi breaking out of prison to finding the hidden Septim son Martin all the way to the crux of the main storyline where you get one of the most amazing pieces of CGI in a cut scene. I won't go to far into it for those that have not played it yet or have not gotten that far but all I will say is Golden Dragon... (A wimpy girly moment led me to go "ooooh" LOL). Now would be a good time to mention the graphics and scenery which are stunning.
After all of that though, which takes a fair amount of time but is no-where near as long as the mainline in Morrowind, you can then go on to do the two extra DLC's which come complete with the Game of the Year Edition. The first one was The Shivering Isles which is by far my favourite part of the entire game. I just loved everything about it. From the insane world created by Lord Sheogorath to the way the guy speaks. I literally had moments during this part of the game where I was in fits of laughter at some of the things he would say randomly whilst trying to help you prevent the Graymarch.
The icing on the cake of this one is that you get to become Lord Sheogorath, but don't worry you aren't insane and you can come and go into Cyrodill and the Shivering Isles as you please.
The last add on is The Knight of the Nine. This is by far the biggest let down of the whole game. All you do is pretty much run around getting blessings from 9 different shrines and then finding old relics of the Divine Crusader all of which together will allow you to kill Umaril the Unfeathered of which at the end leaves you with a rather large and heavy set of armour and that is pretty much the end of the DLC. This, to me, was just not worth the time put in to find everything (it took a while as this one has little prompt) and was just anti-climatic at the end.
Of course after all of the mainline and add ons were completed I set about clearing up sidequests and doing things for the Fighters and Mages guilds. I also went to the Imperial City Arena and became Grand Champion because why not. But I felt that all of the side quests and the Fighters/Mages guild stuff was just all very mundane and boring and really lacked the kind of thought that had gone into the mainlines in such a way where it almost felt like the creators had, had enough at this point and just wanted it finished. All of this is good fun though, even if walking around everywhere being called Champion, lord, hero, knight, sister ect does get a little tiresome, but of course once the mainline and the DLCs are done there really isn't all that much left to do and really in my eyes at least I felt that the game had ended for me.
My only major complaint though is that it seems that this game suffers from some pretty irking bugs in the quests. I got stuck numerous times where the game just wouldn't progress despite me doing what it asked only to look it up and find that countless others had the same problem. Of course most of the bugs had patches made to fix them but I didn't have time for that so opted for the slight cheat route of using the Console to force the quest along to the next point which works but of course can end up cutting out a huge portion of a quest or leaving you a little confused as to what to do next, in some cases it almost led me to do a quest backwards getting other journal entries about something I had done previously.
I must add that there are hundreds of tutorials and tips and cheats online for the game which do help to make a bit of an interesting character or to get you through a rather tough patch but ultimately it is far more fun to run around and try and do as much as you can for yourself.
One last thing.... Keep and eye out for the UNICORN. It's the only one in the entire game
PS. Why make riding the horses so complicated. You have to control it with the keys alone unlike the character which you can control with both the mouse and keys... This would have been a little more helpful as I spent a lot of time getting stuck on rocks and with the horse looking the wrong way despite what I was telling it to do. Also I'm pretty sure being on a horse was slower than running.
On the plus side I did end up with a series of horses and people following me around all of which would fight/protect/get in the way if I was attacked which made for some interesting moments.

MouseCraft is a puzzle game that should appeal to casual gamers and hardcore puzzle enthusiasts alike. Finding one solution to pass a level is usually trivial, but if you aim to collect every anima shard and get all three mice to the cheese, you might be in for a challenge.
The first stage is relatively simple and does a good job of introducing you to the gameplay mechanics. By the end of stage two though, I found myself genuinely stumped at some of the puzzles. I probably spent a good ten minutes or more figuring out some of those last challenges.
The game also has a cutesy story in between stages that I found charming in a quirky way. If you've played these kinds of puzzle games before, you probably know what to expect in terms of exposition. It's never going to win a video game award for best story, but it serves its purpose in providing some small reward for progression.
Overall, the 80 levels should take 6-10 hours to complete, depending on your skills with puzzle solving, and there's enough variation to keep you entertained throughout the game. There is also a very good and intuitive level editor that should provide additional content through Steam Workshop when support for it is added. In the meantime, it's possible to share and download player created levels via a Dropbox account the developer has set up.
It's a game I don't hesitate to recommend and it is among my absolute favourites in the puzzle genre.

An RPG in a FPS engine?!  Where has this game been all my life?!
Counter Spell lays the foundation for an excellent FPS-shooter engine with classic RPG elements leaving room for virtually unlimited possibilities!
PROS
+ Solid, robust FPS game engine encompassing many RPG elements (gold, experience, quests, etc)
+ RPG elements allow you to level-up and equip character with many skills and items
+ Six character classes with very different skills, spells, and play styles
+ World map is brilliantly designed with interconnecting tunnels and secret rooms and passages
+ Multitude of Co-op and PvP multiplayer modes including Capture the Flag, Deathmatch, etc.
+ Fun quest mode familiarizes you with map, character abilities, and game concepts
+ Level editor included (although I haven't used this yet)
+ Reasonable price!
CONS
- Graphics and sound, while sufficient, aren't spectacular
- First few games can be confusing (not much in terms of tutorials)
- No true AI bots in Multiplayer (random, hostile mobs are optional)
- Quest mode may have limited replayability once you learn location of hidden quest items, etc.
- The term "RPG" may be misleading as Quest Mode certainly is no FF7

An absolutely exhilarating game. I suppose you can say this is a bit like if Quake and Heretic were put together into a game about surviving an arena with an endless amount of enemies. This isn't an FPS where you can mindlessly run around and shoot enemies, you need to think quickly and react even quicker while you attempt to bunnyhop away from the hordes of skulls that never let up.
A lot of people complain that they can't survive for long, and I know this may seem very unhelpful, but 'get gud' is literally all there is to it. When you first play, you will die over and over and over again. But over time you will learn patterns, how to prioritise your targets in any situation, and generally improve your aim.
But even then, there are many guides that will give you a lot of information on the game and its enemies, such as their health and behaviour (as well as tips for fighting them):
The game's soundtrack is pretty much composed of the sound effects. Everything from the general ambience to the sounds of the enemies gives the game a very uneasy feeling. The game has a (particularly frightening) menu theme, but doesn't really have any music playing during a run (probably since listening for your enemies' audio cues is so important), but I suppose you could just play Quake 1's soundtrack in the background.
The artstyle is also lovely too. Not only does it take direct inspiration from Quake 1's unique gothic looks but it pretty much nails the 'ye olde' FPS look entirely. The devs made sure the 90s look actually looks 90s without lazily making the game look like minecraft just for the sake of 'wow so retro!'
The game on the whole is bloody brilliant, and it's only 4 quid! The game might not have a large amount of content, but you'll want to keep playing due to your desire to get better and beat your times.
The only thing I hope for now from the devs is a sequel that expands the game with a single player campaign. Even if it's not a direct sequel to Devil Daggers, it would still be amazing if it still has the same kind of artstyle and gameplay with handcrafted levels. It would essentially be the Quake 1 sequel we never got (though I suppose DUSK will scratch this itch for the meantime).
Recommended!

This game is a god damn masterpiece.  Most (most) of the negative reviews are from people who played less than an hour.  One of the more common complaints is that it's too hard, and that there isn't enough content.
These people are wrong.
There is SO MUCH MORE to this game than at first glance.  The better you get at the game, the more you see of what lies beyond the first couple minutes.  Not only that, but it's surprisingly strategic.  You will eventually develop a routine for the first minute, and for the minutes after that.  The first two minutes that you struggled with so badly become child's play.
Aside from the gameplay, the leaderboard is one of the best features in the game.  You can watch replays from other players, and go into a top-down view to see the whole playing field.  The best players' replays are the key to getting better.  Watch them, and learn from them.
Honestly I can't recommend this game enough.  It's one of the best shooters I've played in a while, and while it is repetitive, the drive to improve your time by just a few seconds is very strong.  If you buy this game, you need to devote some time to it so you can see what it has to offer.  Don't make a judgement from the first hour.

With Death Rally (the original developed by Remedy I mean, not the remake you can get on Steam) being free and working on any modern Windows version, you would think that making a game like this would be as easy as downloading it, and then playing it a whole lot until you get what is that made this genre great.
What you get instead is games like Little Racers Street, where I can't help but feel like the dev team said, OK we're going to make the game we want eventually, but in the meanwhile we need some cash: so they watched youtube videos of classics while thinking about what they're going to have for dinner that day, and after some time lo and behold they've cobbled together a Cargo science version of the classics.
Superficially, they LOOK more or less the part, but play like crap. Little Racers STREET has a sloppy presentation, it almost looks like it could be a freeware game from a few years ago and to say the music is place-holder is to be generous. But the handling? the handling, I hear you ask? It's vacuous at best, and the career progression is grindy. The only good thing I can say about it is that the AI is not as murderous as Mini Motor Racing EVO (that would be, throw your controller at the screen degree of vicious). And that's about it.
Save yourself a few cents and play Death Rally (the free one by Remedy if you don't mind my repeating). Or Slicks'n'slide. Or ATARI's Super Sprint or Ironman Super Offroad: I can guarantee those are good games and if you don't like them, well it means the genre isn't for you. This? This is just going for the nostalgia angle.
Fun as hell! Worth checking out for sure.

Reversion Chapter 2: The Meeting is the second in the Reversion series by 3f Interactive, and this time around there's a physical price tag on it to continue the journey. So you have just escaped the hospital and are now on your way to meet up with someone who might know about the mysterious man that is in a picture that happens to be on your person. Now of course you can't get a straight answer without a little bit of help in return. So this episode is basically all about finding out about the gentleman in the picture.
Graphically is the same game, so I can't say that there's any difference. Now that's not a bad thing, it means that they didn't go off the reservation and try to re-invent the wheel. Yet again you are going to be introduced to an assortment of characters which all look unique and really fit the parts that they will be playing in this game.
Sadly the voice acting does not get any better, its still almost robotic, there's no real emotion in the the characters. It almost feels like they are all so full on mood inhibitors that the only thing they can do is just tell you what is going on, but deadpan.
The controls are the same as well, and that of course, once again is a good thing.
Alright so in this chapter, in which you have to put money down to play, you will be running around doing puzzles, and solving a couple of mysteries. You will get to see a college, a subway, a grave yard, a broken down building, a ransacked house, and you will get the chance to revisit the hospital. Once again there will be a good balance of combining objects and puzzle solving involved to complete this chapter.
Now I know there are a lot of you out there who want me to cut to the chase and tell you is it worth the money to play the next chapter. Well here's the deal, even though the developers are charging you for this chapter the game length does not increase, well I think it increased by a whole 4 or 5 minutes. Honestly I was really disappointed in seeing this. I now understand that the chapters are indicators of when the episode will end. In the first one you escape, end of chapter. In the second one you are building up to a meeting, and of course as soon as that happens, end of chapter. This game looks too good, and feels like there is so much more there to be SO short when it comes to game play, but sadly that's what it appears that the developers are doing. Here's hoping that the next chapter has a couple of big moments that will allow a player to really get emerged into the world before closing the chapter. With that being said I have to give this chapter an even lower score and put it at a 5.6 out of 10. I hate to do it, but when you put a price tag on a game, people expect more, especially if you gave the first chapter away for free.

This game is a perfect example of less being more and simple being better. All of us which are perhaps a bit older were waiting for a retro-ish top down racing game which would bring some degree of nostalgia back to life. Games like Skidmarks or Super Cars are the closest resembles, or a bit newer Gene Rally. Everyone who enjoyed those games will enjoy LRS.
It has a great playability, where career mode is not even the main fun here (probably cause the main goal isn't really that challenging). Playing with friends, or against time brings the best from this game.
But there are a few aspects to this game, which could be better. The main thing which bothers me is a map/city layout, where you drive basically on just two huge maps, where every track has different paths. Problem here is you hardly memorize all those directions and the barrier closing road directions aren't always that visible, especially when you're concentrating your eyes on your car when you're fighting against sharp corners on the road and overlook the barrier cause the road would run smoothly through it, but instead the track goes to some other direction on the junctions.
With all those crossroads it is sometimes very confusing where to drive, especially cause on higher level cars the speed is brutal and the crashes are many.
I know for the developers that kind of layout was a bit easier way to deal with choice of numerical tracks, but cause of this, the game lacks of diversity. This is why I also miss track editor and a choice to make a classic tracks without redundant closed streets confusing the player.
That being said, game IS great, as I said at the beginning. The choice with cameras is absolutely fantastic, lots of different perspectives to choose from and all of them bring additional dynamic and ways to play the game. Some views are perhaps harder to master cause you don't see as much in front of you, but have their own charm nevertheless.
Cars are realistic as it gets. Lots to choose from, lots of micro-managing and tuning of the cars with different drive behaviours.
So yeah, I recommend it, a lot!

[Taken straight from my Desura review]
Nice little indie point-and-click game. TL/DR? Skip to my conclusion at the end.
First, I have to say I like experiencing foreign language/culture in games and movies, so for me I was interested to see how this played out in this and the 1st Chapter (which I played back to back). After finishing the two games, the setting of Buenos Aires did play a small part, with all the Spanish signs and stuff.
The graphics are clean and interaction wasn't too bad. Load times are good, and there is no major waiting between screens. One thing I didn't like however was that the movement is too slow - i.e. when crossing a room - you can double click on the other side of the room to speed things up, but if you don't click in the right place, you either don't get the guy to cross any quicker, or you inadvertently move to the next room or screen.
The background music was well done and nice, while not imposing on the dialogue. The English voice acting was acceptable, although Victoria's tone seemed a little weird, like the actor who voiced her didn't speak English as their first language. All the other voice acting seemed fine though.
I guess my biggest gripe about this game is it's length. There is quite a bit of clicking through dialogue, but it still only took me about 3 1/2 hours to play the whole game (BOTH chapters). The second biggest gripe is it's left on a bit of a cliffhanger - will there be another chapter? If not, I'm pretty disappointed with the ending; yes there are a few questions answered, but there are far too many left unanswered. Chapter 2 has been out for over a year now, I really hope we have another chapter to really finish things properly.
In conclusion, a pretty good game for what appears to be a small devteam, I just would have wanted to see more. Good value? Hmm, well I did like it, I am just disappointed there wasn't more game time - I usually estimate $1 per hour of gameplay, and this didn't deliver that (based on the full price). Maybe Chapter 3 will change my mind on that...

After playing Drakesang for 57 hours i can pretty much say that it reminded me of old-school RPG legends such a Baldur's Gate.
You play the game with a party of four characters and the Real Time with Pause system is the one used during battles. This system allows for more strategic battles and lets you organize your team and the skills to use.
The storyline is quite interesting but i felt that it could be presented in a better way. But what the main story may fail to deliver all the other things of the Drakesang universe you can find out make up for. The world has a history and it's really interesting to discover bits and pieces of it all over. Also there's really not any character progression regarding their personalities. At the end of your adventure you and your companions will be exactly the same persons as you were at the beginning.
The game is hard but that makes the battles really interesting and fun. You have to use diferrent skills, spells and items if you want to make it. What i really liked is the leveling system because it allows you to use your experience points in order to improve your skills whenever you want to. So if you feel like it you can wait until later to use them when you will be more certain about what type of characters you want to build.
Keeping in mind that the game was released in 2009 the graphics are pretty good. As for the soundtrack i can't say i really noticed it.
I strongly recommend Drakesang to all the old-school party based RPG lovers. I'm sure you will have a good time playing it.

Capsized is a sci-fi, indie platformer from Alientrap Games Inc. that puts the player smack in the middle of a (predominantly) hostile alien planet. Your goal: find your crew mates and get off the planet alive. It's an old theme, but that doesn't mean it can't still give us a few kicks.
II - UI [8/10]
The user interface was simple and got the job done. I never felt confused as to what needed doing or where I was headed. Weapon and item pick-ups could have used better labeling (in my opinion), but it wasn't anything to cry over. All in all, the UI was well put together and was user-friendly.
III - Gameplay [7/10]
I am a big fan of platformer games, but the control over character movement in Capsized has a special place in my heart forevermore. The physics were simply marvelous and the player's earned mastery over them (compliments of jet pack and Gravity Hook) make exploring their alien surroundings utterly enjoyable. Not only did this allow for great vantage points from which to dispatch enemies, but it also allowed for new dodging options when faced with enemy attacks.
The enemies, however, tend to be fairly frustrating at times. I found myself often faced with enemies who were not necessarily "difficult" in any sense of the word, but became increasingly obnoxious over time. That being said, it only detracts a little from the atmosphere of Capsized as a whole.
My only other real complaint was that my remaining ammunition in various weapons (and fuel for my jet pack) did not carry over with me to the next level.
IV - Content [8/10]
Being an indie game I didn't go into Capsized expecting it to have a terribly large amount of content and it didn't (per say). The content it does have though is very unique and serves to make the game feel that much bigger. There were plenty of different enemies to slay with a modestly wide variety of weapons. That, in and of itself, is more than most games have going for them in the first place.
V - Visual [10/10]
The graphics in Capsized are all hand-drawn and they are spectacular. Every visual aspect of the game seems very unique and makes it a pleasure to trek through such a hostile planet. From the exotic landscapes to the ferocious, indigenous population, this is an unforgettable journey in terms of aesthetics.
VI - Audio [8/10]
The music and sounds of Capsized are great and they add a lot to the game. Even at lower settings though, I sometimes felt that the music drowned out the sound effects of the game and interfered with the ambiance of it all.
VII - Overall [7.7/10]
Capszied is a genuinely fun platformer and, though at times it can be frustrating in terms of combat, it all works out and is a solid piece of work.

If you came here for a review you've come to the wrong place. But if you've come for a banana bread recipe then you've come to the right place.
No need for a mixer for this recipe!
Clean-up is easy too, if you want, you can mix everything in one mixing bowl.
The best bananas to use for banana bread are those that are over-ripe. The yellow peels should be at least half browned, and the bananas inside squishy and browning.
Ingredients
2 to 3 very ripe bananas, peeled
1/3 cup melted butter
1 teaspoon baking soda
Pinch of salt
3/4 cup sugar (1/2 cup if you would like it less sweet, 1 cup if more sweet)
1 large egg, beaten
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
1 1/2 cups of all-purpose flour
Method
1 Preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C), and butter a 4x8-inch loaf pan.
2 In a mixing bowl, mash the ripe bananas with a fork until completely smooth. Stir the melted butter into the mashed bananas.
3 Mix in the baking soda and salt. Stir in the sugar, beaten egg, and vanilla extract. Mix in the flour.
4 Pour the batter into your prepared loaf pan. Bake for 50 minutes to 1 hour at 350°F (175°C), or until a tester inserted into the center comes out clean.
5 Remove from oven and cool completely on a rack. Remove the banana bread from the pan. Slice and serve. (A bread knife helps to make slices that aren't crumbly.)

Phew! I've just completed the game and may I say it's beautiful. Also, the game is VERY hard. You can't choose a difficulty level, so you'll have to play at the game's "default" and only difficulty level. Common enemies are usually only hard when they're in packs, but bosses... Let's say bosses are TOUGH. There are a few boss opponents that will require you to think of some unusual tactics, because there's simply no chance you'll handle them going head-on. And yeah, bring A LOT of healing potions to final battle. I've just finished it without a single potion, and it's been a REAL STRUGGLE. Two hours or so...
Game's core RPG mechanics is so much like Neverwinter Nights that sometimes you almost feel like you're playing NWN. I liked the mechanics. It's a pity you only get to buy good spells after the middle of the game, I'd like to see more spells and get them faster. By the way, you can increase character's skills (spend your experience points) at any time. This makes levelling up pretty much useless. And having to buy all the spells and active skills makes levelling up even more useless... I didn't like that. In Neverwinter Nights, you receive spells and skills as you gain your level. Here, in Drakensang, you receive experience points and increase your skills, and levelling up is just... Levelling up. That's pretty much it. "Player has reached level x", and that's all, nothing more happens.
I enjoyed the main storyline. There's plenty of side quests, and they are ok, and the main quest is great, and soooo long! Completing the game took me 45 damn hours... But it was worth it. Some of the plot twists were somewhat unexpected. However, the main storyline is solid, but it's not a masterpiece.
I liked the world, graphics are awesome (considering the game is 4-5 years old). Characters are great, I liked my companions and it was somewhat sad to finish the game, because I realized my adventure with these characters is over.
By the way, there's no fast travel system in this game, so you'll have to walk through the huge Drakensang maps on foot. Well, it didn't bother me.
And the dialogues. I've read a bunch of reviews before buying the game, and almost every single one of them said the game has awfully written dialogues. Well, I have to admit that sometimes you hear or read something funny, and dwarves speak with significant accent. However, those facts create unique atmosphere. Nothing feels uncomfortable, nothing feels out of place. So if you're afraid of possible flaws in dialogues, don't be, they're OK.
Overall, if you like old-school RPGs (pretty much like Baldur's Gate, Neverwinter Nights or Dragon Age), I think you'll really enjoy this game. Buy the game on sale, and it will be totally worth every cent spent on it.

So, Capsized.  Here we are.  I finally made myself finish the game.  Here's the thing with Capsized -
The aesthetic is AMAZING.  Few 2D games look this freaking amazing.
The music is spot on, and Solar Fields not only capture the atmosphere, but add to it tremendously with one of the most chillaxed and haunting videogame OST's ever.
The movement is appropriately floating, given the alien landscape, and this is both a good and a bad thing.  It's bad, because it feels so unnatural and unintuitive, in a way, and this usually is a blemish on any other game, but because of the setting of Capsized, I find it acceptable, and actually necessary to sell the fact that I'm on this strange and scary world.
Combat is okay ... feels very much like a twin-stick-shooter, despite being 2D, side-scrolling, open-level platformer.  I think there were too many weapon options.  Honestly, I think about 4 of the weapons were nessesary, and the rest were filler that the devs probably thought were cool.  Maybe they were, but I stuck with what worked, and didn't spend a lot of time with many of the weapons.
The story is okay ... a little bland, but I'm not here for the narrative, so I don't really care ... I like bland stories in games.
Overall I recommend Capsized to anyone who likes playing twin-stick shooters with their keyboard and mouse, who are willing to spend some times on an alien planet, fighting lurking wildlife and natives.
Oh, and I guess there are "secrets" in this game, but I certainly didn't care one whit about finding any of them.  You might like that more than me.  Give it a try!

EDIT #2 Post release:
So I picked the game up after playing a bunch of old games in my library that were in EA. This game has gotten alot better than it was before. You can customize your playstyle pretty well depending on what you like to use. I made a priest to go through the story again and used daggers rather than a staff. Lots of new abilities on some of the more lacking classes of old. New areas that are optional, new game modes that are even fun against bots alone.
There are a lot of game modes that I havent tried out yet. I tried most of the classes in the campaign for a few quests/levels then went to go try out survival and played that 3 times. There's a lot of replayability in this game from what I can tell. Due to the different game modes that provide pvp/solo/co-op. There's a good handful of maps that all connect together from the campaign that you can play all of the game modes on, as well as what seems to be 2 separate maps that don't connect to the rest of the game, but I haven't tried them yet, so that's just speculation. The random dungeon generator is probably whats going to keep me playing this game for a while though. I'd love to see some more classes, or the current classes to be expanded more (There have been new spells/abilities added from patches so far).
The only real problems with the game that I've seen so far are:
Stealth - There are a lot of lights around the maps that make it hard to really go full stealth through everything. You CAN stealth though, I've assassinated a good bit of things. If there were a way to temporarily knock lights out or just less lights in some areas, stealth would be an option a lot more often.
AI - Pretty basic, just needs some patching up. They mostly just run at you or strafe around trying to shoot you. Spiders are probably my favorite AI because they actually lunge at you and if you dodge it, they'll go flying past you, which is better than just "out run the enemy". I cant complain about it too much though, its EA so it's kind of to be expected.

Oblivion is easily my favorite game of all time. I put in over 500 hours on the PS3 version, then another 200-300 hours on the non-steam PC version.
If you can get past its quirks, Oblivion has a lot to offer. There are so many unique quests and characters, I can't even begin to explain them here. If you're coming from Skyrim, it will definitely take some getting used to the more complex gameplay mechanics, but it's well worth it.
If you've never played before (or have never played the PC version), a few warnings:
-The default UI sucks for KB&M, and there is no controller support. Do yourself a favor and install DarNified UI from the Nexus.
-Oblivion's level-scaling system is extremely aggressive, much more so that Fallout 3 or Skyrim. By level 20, you will see common bandits sporting full daedric armor. There are many mods out there that fix this--my favorite is Oscuro's Oblivion Overhaul, which makes the world completely static, à la Morrowind. It also adds a ton of new content.
-The leveling system punishes you if you don't build your character right. Your health increases every level based on your endurance stat, and it doesn't work retroactively. This means that if you don't prioritize endurance, your character will be extremely gimped in terms of health mid to late game. Look up efficient leveling, and learn how to do it, or download a mod that overhauls the leveling system. Oblivion XP is a good one.
-The character models have not aged well. Seriously, everyone looks like Mr. Potato Head. Oblivion Character Overhaul v2 does a very good job of making them look better, but it's still nowhere near today's standards. The lighting and environments still look passable, but the distant LOD looks like pea soup. Also, expect a lot of pop-in.
-The Nexus Mod Manager does not play well with all Oblivion mods, especially those that came out before NMM was released (which is most of them). I would recommend using Oblivion Mod Manager of Wrye Bash to manage your mod list.
-The game engine Oblivion runs on is 10 years old. It was not optimized for modern systems. Don't be surprised if your framerate tanks on your Titan X after installing a few graphics mods, even if they don't seem like they should be too demanding.

Assassin’s Creed Rogue was one hell of an adventure and honestly, despite it not being as long or as filled as the other games, it is possibly one of the best Assassin’s Creed yet and far better in story and gameplay than Assassin’s Creed IV: Black Flag or Assassin’s Creed: Freedom Cry, it is a must play (PS, it respects the lore of the Assassin’s Creed franchise and kinda feels like a fan service to the Assassin’s Creed community ;P ).
The story of Shay Patrick Cormac, he is Irish by the way if you cannot tell by his super Irish name (maybe another reason why I love this character so much, is the relatable ethnic group) is one of the mots well developed, emotional, immersive and sympathetic storyline in the Assassin’s Creed franchise standing next to Assassin’s Creed: Brotherhood in my personal opinion.
He actually questions what he is doing and why he must do it. He feels guilt for killing people unnecessarily. He actually says no to those in charge because of morality. He feels like a human being. He gets sad. He gets angry. He feels guilt. He feels sympathy. He feels like a real person and the story, despite it being only about 6 hours, expands on that and throws you into this emotional twist of a game game that is his struggle to find truth and to seek his personal redemption. It is different from the other Assassin’s Creed story while, yes, it has the typically Assassin’s Creed revenge aspect, it is not focused around it like the other Assassin’s Creed games are. It is one of the best stories in the Assassin’s Creed franchise.
Add that ontop of the beautiful open world where this time, the world actually encourages you to explore it. You feel the need as the world, whether it be the Arctic or River Valley (or the recycled New York city which is done better here than Assassin’s Creed III, don’t get me wrong, I just expect Assassin’s Creed games not to recycle main locations), it feels fresh and immersive. I spent a good 10 to 15 hours just exploring the River Valley and the Arctic and loved every moment of it!
And to visit the city of Halifax was one of my favourite things! I have been there in real life but to see Ubisoft’s historical version of it was beautiful and immersive and I loved it!.
Overall, you have to give this game a try. I spent almost a good 30 hours on it and most of it was exploring the beautiful open world. The only downside, the story is short, 6 hours for me and I took my time. Shorter if you rush it.

Funny, entertaining, sometimes infuriating and packed with far more content than you might have imagined; 100% Orange Juice is a mixture of boardgame, card game and dice game that pits four characters in heated battle to gather resources and become the best cameo from games you never played. With boards not unlike those of Mario Party yet sans minigames, 100% OJ is based not so much on the stages themselves but rather in the interaction between the character you pick, out of an available 15 plus 7 DLC characters (more on that later) and a very simple deck of event cards that you can build before each match.
While it's a bit complicated to explain, here's the basics: Characters are essentially defined by simple stats (health, attack, defense, evasion and how easy they are to revive) and an unique "hyper power" that all help define their playstyle. Cards on the other hand, and by extension the decks that you build, are gathered into a communal pool that ALL players in a game can draw from and in doing so define the rhythm of the game; hopefully somewhat in your favor if your deck construction was good and you are lucky enough to draw cards that benefit you. In this way you get characters and decks that, for example, are more suited to travel all along the board and gather stars while others are more suitable for walking around and beating up both enemy players and the NPCs that are scattered throughout the board- with both "stars" and combat "wins" being the resources that you need to level up your character and in the process win the game.
There's more to it than that, too; like the fact that cards can cost stars to activate as well as require your character to be a certain level before use and that for you to level up, you actually need to land in specific "goal" tiles that act both as base and healing spot for the characters while they make their way around the board. It's easier to understand once you play the game, and do note that there's a demo available, but it all comes down to fast (15 minutes, tops) and more often than not pretty entertaining matches- even if they DO have more than a fair share of RNG involved (mostly RNG, some would say.)
So, while the gameplay can be a bit nebulous to explain, what does the game actually include outside of that? Well much to my surprise the game is legitimately full of content and features that are pretty impressive for something that's obviously a shoestring budget game. With four single player campaigns (as feather-light as the one plot for them all might be,) extra scenarios, custom games, online multiplayer, achievements, VAC protection, trading cards and a progression system that unlocks characters, maps, cards and even character customization options as you progress through the campaigns and play multiplayer matches; there will always be something to play for if you do decide to go deep into things.
Now, it is important that I bring special attention to the unlock system as it is something that will both draw in some people and turn off others: You see, you start the game by picking ONE character out of four available choices and to unlock the rest you need to play and beat the different scenarios in the single player campaigns. Usually each new scenario is another character that you can unlock and then purchase ingame (with ingame currency, something that you obtain after every single game you play whether you win or lose) so while the game DOES have a lot of playable characters, the choice to keep them locked at the start is a bit of an odd decision that is sure to annoy some. The same limit applies to cards as well, with "booster packs" purchasable in the ingame store and that randomly unlock all the available cards for you to play with. Last but not least, the store also includes certain maps and color packs that are basically palette swaps for character's clothes.
It doesn't stop there either. Separate from the campaign and exclusive to the online mode, multiplayer games in turn give you experience points that can then be used to unlock discounts on the ingame store, even more palette swaps and a special set of characters that all have very marked gimmicks and are separate from the "main" cast of the game. Each multiplayer match played also has a chance to reward you with special customization options that take the form of different hair colors for the different characters and ones that can't be obtained any other way. This means that even if multiplayer does have a genuine sense of progression without actually affecting gameplay that much, completionists will probably suffer with the random nature of drops. Fortunately the multiplayer mode is pretty alive, albeit at the time of writing probably especially so because of a recent sale, so getting a game shouldn't be hard.
Finally and especially after the mention of so many unlockable gameplay features comes the topic of DLC characters and game balance. The question that most of you still reading this huge review probably have is whether or not
the different characters and cards are actually balanced and thankfully to that I can say: yes. While the DLC characters are unlocked as soon as you purchase them, none of them are actually stronger than the regular ones but rather they have different gimmicks. The same applies to the cards from the DLC pack, doubly so thanks to the fact that all players can draw and use them as long as one player with the DLC includes them in his deck. It IS true that some characters are easier to use than others and that some need to get very specific cards to truly succeed but the balance is good DLC or not and on top of that game is so random that matches are pretty much unpredictable one way or the other. Do note there's actually 7 DLC characters at the time of writing; 6 available in DLC packs and 1 available only to players that purchase QP Shooting - Dangerous!!, another game from the company that brought us 100% OJ.
In conclusion: 100% Orange Juice is one of the cheapest, most unique and most enjoyable multiplayer games that you'll find on Steam as long as you are into the kind of gameplay that it offers. Good online boardgames in general are kind of rare to find, doubly so as proper full-fledged games; so whether you have a hankering for something like it, a pack of friends that dig ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥tting around or even just a few extra dollars in your pocket, this game is a must-have.

I played this game enough to complete absolutely everything, so I can't claim I didn't get my money's worth, but honestly it's not a very good game.  It starts off well enough: the early classes are fairly fun, the game moves at a decent clip while remaining decently controllable and the races are short and varied.  However, once you advance through the classes the game's issues start to become apparent.  First of all, there isn't a lot of variety to the game's tracks, and by your hundredth race or so, you quickly start to feel like you've seen it all, a problem which is compounded by the fact that the later classes have unreasonably many laps per race.  There's simply nothing interesting about racing around a course for more than 3 laps, which is particularly compounded by the fact that every race is decided in lap 1.
You see, by far this game's worst problem is its idiotic car damage system.  Every time you touch a wall or another car, even if it's just the lightest of taps, you take damage, which reduces your top speed.  There is no way to repair damage during the race, and if you take enough damage you simply cannot win because you won't be able to pass your rivals.  This is particularly vital in the higher speed classes as these cars are hard to control and are very fragile, extremely careful and meticulous driving is the only way to go with these flimsy rides.  This turns this game into a frontrunner's dream, the first place racer can drive carefully and safely navigate the course while taking little damage, while the racers behind have to be more aggressive to try to regain ground, but in so doing they damage their cars to the point where they cannot possibly catch up to the relatively unscathed first place driver.  Almost every race on A class either ends up in humilating defeat or with you lapping the other cars several times over, close races are virtually nonexistant thanks to this mechanic.  As if this wasn't bad enough, your prize money after each race is garnished to repair your damage, and in the A class cars, even if you have almost no damage it will always take 80% (the maximum amount) since these cars are so expensive, meaning that A class is terrible for making money and thus the pricey final cars take FOREVER to earn.
There are further problems, too, like bad car balance (Grip and Power are the only stats that matter, never increase the others), and some challenges taking way too long to unlock (though this is really one of the only good points of the game), but this is really just more water under the bridge at this point.
Overall, this is a game that had some potential but was hampered by poor design decisions.  It can be a bit of fun in short bursts but the problems quickly become apparent the longer you play.  The developer also seems to have abandonned this game as it has not recieved any updates in a long time, so I wouldn't expect any new content or anything like that.  If you want a top down racer there are many better ones available.

Really quite fun, and well polished.  I've been looking for a tactical team-based game where I don't have to break my hands micro-managing a million abilities or constantly clicking creeps.  This game manages to be satisfyingly crunchy without requiring high speed rapid input.
Each game plays out very differently; there's the MOBA-like variety of champions and their moves -- each of which can be "modded" in different ways pre-combat to give slightly different bonuses -- and there's also the importance of long-term planning in positioning for an attack next turn, or the reward of guessing your opponent's next action, both of which can swing games dramatically.
That said, there is definitely a learning curve to the simultaneous turn-based element.  This game does timing in a unique, multi-layered fashion, and the tutorial is quite short.  Basically, everyone has 20 seconds per turn to decide on 1 action, and then all the actions play out over 4 steps, with the sequencing depending on the type of action each player selected.  Some kinds of actions go off early -- prep or dash -- while others go off later -- like attacking or walking/sprinting.  This opens the door up to cool moments where your prep or dash action screws up your opponent's attack or move action, for example, either by disrupting it or changing your position before it can go off.  There are some good videos online explaining the mechanic -- I recommend taking a look before the tutorial just so you have some context.
Graphics and audio are both great.  I like the Blizzard-esque cartoony style.  Some characters have more personality than others, but they're all well presented, and the voice-acting is overall very good.
I'm definitely curious to see how they will develop the game with new modes, maps, freelancers, etc.  But for now, I'm pretty satisfied just playing matches and slowly improving.  And my hands are thanking me.

(Note: I show 0 hours with Altas Reactor because I've been playing it with the Glyph launcher directly, but I've actually been playing the game since it was in alpha.)
Atlas Reactor is an arena team deathmatch game that pairs MOBA-esque characters with simultaneous turn-based resolution ala games such as Laser Squad Nemesis or Frozen Synapse.  (or if you're really old-school like me, like RoboSport)
In each game you bring a character into an arena as one of two four-man teams, and fight it out.  Each turn, you can take an action and then move.  (subject to some special cases like free actions or abilities that use up both moves)  All eight players resolve their actions simultaneously in four phases: prep, dash, blast, move, and then a new turn begins.  This repeats until a team reaches five kills or 20 turns have passed.
In short, my opinion is that Atlas Reactor is good fun.  The gameplay is solid.  The UI provides a lot of useful feedback, showing you where your teammates are planning on moving, where friendly attacks will land, and where enemies were last sighted.  The controls are fine, albeit occasionally a little awkward.  Presentation- graphics and sound- aren't great but are serviceable to the task.
The biggest flaw with Atlas Reactor, IMHO, is that it's a bit slight.  Small-ish arenas, short games, no MOBA-style character development, and simple objectives (get 5 kills) limit how much strategy can develop over the course of a round.  On the other hand, it's a reasonable time investment, good fun for what it is, and there's a reasonably-sized roster to let you mix things up and try new characters.  I don't expect I'll be reinstalling and re-visiting it over the years like I do League of Legends, but I enjoyed it in alpha and I've come back now that it's out and am enjoying it even more now that it has a bit of extra polish and a few more characters.
Assuming you've bought the game and have access to the roster- I'm unfamiliar with the free demo mode of the game- the monetization is pretty negligable.  There's three main components to it:
First, there's a bunch of Overwatch-style skins, taunts, badge paraphenalia, etc, which I'm entirely not tempted by.  The characters in the game are not as good looking nor as personable as Blizzard's roster- they're very low-poly- and they're generally seen very far from the camera and leave me feeling little attachment to them.  It's cool when I unlock a nice skin via the normal progression, but I don't feel the slightest urge to spend more money on it.
Secondly, there's mod tokens, which are the heart of the matter because they're the purchase with in-game mechanical effects.  Each character can modify each of their abilities to make it better in one of several ways, subject to a cap on the total cost of all of your mods.  Characters start with a full loadout of mods, and mod tokens can be spent to get variants.  So far, this hasn't bothered me that much.  The starting loadouts are so good that I've mostly found myself just keeping the default loadout, and you get six mod tokens after a handful of games with a character which is more than enough to completely revamp that loadout to something you'd prefer.  If you want to experiment early and a lot these would be the thing you're scarce on, but I haven't been yet.
Thirdly, there's "GG boosts", which are one-use XP boosters that accelerate your access to mod tokens and skins by letting you level up to earn them quicker.  As I don't really want much more of the first two, I don't really care about getting more of these, either.
Overall, as a paying customer I haven't found the monetization aspects of this game particularly onerous- as it shouldn't be with a $30 price tag for a relatively slight package.
On the whole, I'd recommend Atlas Reactor if you're interested and not particularly strapped for cash.  It's not necessarily the best value out there on Steam and I'm not sure what sort of legs it will have, but it's been a great way to sit down and duke it for a few quick rounds in the evening before bed.
