So what is Atlas Reactor? Probably one of the most difficult to describe as an actual genre, but its like if XCOM and Frozen Synapse were combined with team-based multiplayer. Atlas Reactor is a turn-based simultaneous arena game, get together in 4v4 matches on a continuing variety of maps to prep, dash and blast your way to victory.
As you can tell I have well over 500 hrs put into this game, probably closer to 1000 before it was added to Steam. I've played through alpha, beta and now going into open and I have to say I absolutely love every bit of this game. The strategy, the abilities, the characters and the world. But by far, the community is one of the best I've ever had the pleasure of playing with. Nearly everyone who plays is pretty friendly and helpful, especially those that use the Atlas Reactor official Discord.
The game itself is Buy to Play to unlock everything permanently, the only thing actually buyable in-game currently are loot boxes, which give you nothing more than cosmetic stuff, which can just as easily be bought using the in-game currency for specific cosmetics. Nothing in this game is pay to win. And if you dont know how you feel about the game yet, there is a Free Mode, which is essentially a demo that allows you to play PvP with other people freely, but are limited to a rotating roster of characters. Play around on it for awhile and I'm sure it'll have you hooked if you enjoy tactical strategy games.
The learning curve on the game itself is easy to get into-hard to master type approach, with each character having their own separate learning curves as well. Also, every skill in the game can have variations to them in the form of Mods, which you adjust prior to playing and can change your strategy quite a bit. As far as character (known as Freelancers) types, you have the basic three, Firepower(DPS), Frontliner(Tanks) and Supports. However quite a few of them have hybrid roles at times. Objective is first to 5 kills or most kills at 20 turns, but will occassionally continue a bit passed that, but the matches themselves are fairly quick at about 20 minutes, approx 1 min per turn. You have 20 seconds to make your choices, then the actions play out on both sides, so you have to think quickly and work with your teammates.
I ask everyone to at least give it a shot if you're into multiplayer games and enjoy strategy, this game should be just right for you, especially if you're a fan of tabletop board games like Warhammer/Warmachine/HeroClix

Funny, entertaining, sometimes infuriating and packed with far more content than you might have imagined; 100% Orange Juice is a mixture of boardgame, card game and dice game that pits four characters in heated battle to gather resources and become the best cameo from games you never played. With boards not unlike those of Mario Party yet sans minigames, 100% OJ is based not so much on the stages themselves but rather in the interaction between the character you pick, out of an available 15 plus 7 DLC characters (more on that later) and a very simple deck of event cards that you can build before each match.
While it's a bit complicated to explain, here's the basics: Characters are essentially defined by simple stats (health, attack, defense, evasion and how easy they are to revive) and an unique "hyper power" that all help define their playstyle. Cards on the other hand, and by extension the decks that you build, are gathered into a communal pool that ALL players in a game can draw from and in doing so define the rhythm of the game; hopefully somewhat in your favor if your deck construction was good and you are lucky enough to draw cards that benefit you. In this way you get characters and decks that, for example, are more suited to travel all along the board and gather stars while others are more suitable for walking around and beating up both enemy players and the NPCs that are scattered throughout the board- with both "stars" and combat "wins" being the resources that you need to level up your character and in the process win the game.
There's more to it than that, too; like the fact that cards can cost stars to activate as well as require your character to be a certain level before use and that for you to level up, you actually need to land in specific "goal" tiles that act both as base and healing spot for the characters while they make their way around the board. It's easier to understand once you play the game, and do note that there's a demo available, but it all comes down to fast (15 minutes, tops) and more often than not pretty entertaining matches- even if they DO have more than a fair share of RNG involved (mostly RNG, some would say.)
So, while the gameplay can be a bit nebulous to explain, what does the game actually include outside of that? Well much to my surprise the game is legitimately full of content and features that are pretty impressive for something that's obviously a shoestring budget game. With four single player campaigns (as feather-light as the one plot for them all might be,) extra scenarios, custom games, online multiplayer, achievements, VAC protection, trading cards and a progression system that unlocks characters, maps, cards and even character customization options as you progress through the campaigns and play multiplayer matches; there will always be something to play for if you do decide to go deep into things.
Now, it is important that I bring special attention to the unlock system as it is something that will both draw in some people and turn off others: You see, you start the game by picking ONE character out of four available choices and to unlock the rest you need to play and beat the different scenarios in the single player campaigns. Usually each new scenario is another character that you can unlock and then purchase ingame (with ingame currency, something that you obtain after every single game you play whether you win or lose) so while the game DOES have a lot of playable characters, the choice to keep them locked at the start is a bit of an odd decision that is sure to annoy some. The same limit applies to cards as well, with "booster packs" purchasable in the ingame store and that randomly unlock all the available cards for you to play with. Last but not least, the store also includes certain maps and color packs that are basically palette swaps for character's clothes.
It doesn't stop there either. Separate from the campaign and exclusive to the online mode, multiplayer games in turn give you experience points that can then be used to unlock discounts on the ingame store, even more palette swaps and a special set of characters that all have very marked gimmicks and are separate from the "main" cast of the game. Each multiplayer match played also has a chance to reward you with special customization options that take the form of different hair colors for the different characters and ones that can't be obtained any other way. This means that even if multiplayer does have a genuine sense of progression without actually affecting gameplay that much, completionists will probably suffer with the random nature of drops. Fortunately the multiplayer mode is pretty alive, albeit at the time of writing probably especially so because of a recent sale, so getting a game shouldn't be hard.
Finally and especially after the mention of so many unlockable gameplay features comes the topic of DLC characters and game balance. The question that most of you still reading this huge review probably have is whether or not
the different characters and cards are actually balanced and thankfully to that I can say: yes. While the DLC characters are unlocked as soon as you purchase them, none of them are actually stronger than the regular ones but rather they have different gimmicks. The same applies to the cards from the DLC pack, doubly so thanks to the fact that all players can draw and use them as long as one player with the DLC includes them in his deck. It IS true that some characters are easier to use than others and that some need to get very specific cards to truly succeed but the balance is good DLC or not and on top of that game is so random that matches are pretty much unpredictable one way or the other. Do note there's actually 7 DLC characters at the time of writing; 6 available in DLC packs and 1 available only to players that purchase QP Shooting - Dangerous!!, another game from the company that brought us 100% OJ.
In conclusion: 100% Orange Juice is one of the cheapest, most unique and most enjoyable multiplayer games that you'll find on Steam as long as you are into the kind of gameplay that it offers. Good online boardgames in general are kind of rare to find, doubly so as proper full-fledged games; so whether you have a hankering for something like it, a pack of friends that dig ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥tting around or even just a few extra dollars in your pocket, this game is a must-have.

A good little racing game that could have been great and even become a cult classic as
once did. If the visual execution and the gameplay feeling of an arcade racer are skillfuly done, there are too many flaws that cannot be simply overlooked. Some are detrimental to the game, some just minor details. From bad to worse:
- The algorithm that randomize each race does not seem to adjust the number of racers to the size of the race, transforming some of them into stock car racing where you spend a lot of your time shouting "Get out of the *@%*$ way" at your screen, which was not my idea of the game. Unless it was endorsed by NASCAR, which it is not.
- The AI racers become more skilled after each lap (so do you, which is a good kind of balancing), but over 10 laps (the random factor allows 15+ laps races), the other racers attain near-perfection driving, forcing your loss in a way. Capsized is somewhat a flawed gem.  At its core it has interesting game mechanics with the gravity hook and gravity ram.  With the hook you can swing around across platforms like Tarzan while firing at enemies, solve small puzzles by bringing weights to deactivate traps, and even grab enemies if you dare.  The ram at first appears to be only useful for blasting objects away, but you'll quickly realize that it's actually an effective way of launching yourself into the air as well as skipping rapidly across terrains.  The combination of these two creates an interesting fast paced way to move yourself through the levels.  The gunplay is also fairly satisfying and has the standard automatic weapons and explosive weapons as well as some more interesting ones such as a Quasar Array that creates a miniature blackhole.
The level design is where it suffers a bit.  The more obvious complaint about the design is that it is possible to get into a situation where completing the level is impossible.  For example, at one point when taking an elevator down to a lower part of the stage, a certain amount of weight needs to be on the elevator before it will move down, much like the force needed to compress a spring.  So weights in the form of huge boulders have to be added onto it and combined with the character's weight, the elevator will move down, but if you're unfortunate enough such that one of the rocks roll off the elevator once it hits the bottom, the elevator will begin to move back up.  Then you're stuck because you have no more weights and can't get back down, or other weights are far enough from your position that going back to retrieve them will most likely get your player killed because you'll have to go through traps.  If you're collecting the secrets this becomes doubly painful.  Although this is the most serious case of the problem, similar issues crop up at different stages of the game that involves weights deactivating traps.
Another issue that I found annoying was the range of the enemies.  Once the character has been detected by enemies, not only are they able to keep track of you through solid walls and floor, they can shoot at you from off the screen and there isn't a peeking feature that allows you to see farther from your regular view.  It's hard to accurately return fire yet they have a decent chance at hitting you.  These aren't game breaking but can be fairly frustrating at times.
The last minor one is that powerups are frequenly found to be unuseful because to get to them involves wiping out enemies in the nearby vicinity, and since they're activated once picked up they aren't nearly used to their full effect.  No need for an energy shield if the nearest enemy is far enough that the time it'll take to get there is longer than the duration of the powerup.
Even with these problems, this is a worthwhile game to check out.  There are twelve levels and the difficulty rapidly ramps up after a certain point so it'll probably appeal more to those who enjoy difficult platformer shooters or if interested in a co-op experience.  I feel like if the developers took another look at the game and made some adjustments for a sequel, a very solid game can come out of it.

I can't speak highly enough of this game. As someone that grew up playing all the 8-bit and 16-bit Sonic games, and who stopped after S3&K due to thinking the franchise became weird and cringey after they added voice acting, terrible and unnecessarily complex stories, a billion side characters and restrictive on-rails 3D gameplay, Sonic Mania is a perfect return to form. It perfectly captures the look, sound, physics and general feel of the Mega Drive-era Sonics.
But when you look a bit closer you realise this is no Mega Drive game. No, this is the mainline Sonic game for the Sega Saturn that we never got. The backdrops are more detailed and with many more layers of parallax. The sprites have many more frames per section of animation, and the whole things runs at a silky smooth 60 fps. The music has that Mega Drive sound but with more channels, better percussion and frankly just sounds awesome, like any good Sonic OST should.
The game is of a good length - twelve zones, putting it on par with S3&K. The zones are a mix of old and new, and wonderfully borrow elements from all the classic Sonic games (I even saw a couple of references in there to the Master System titles!) The level design is fantastic and nails the complex, many-pathed nature of the classic games, packed with hidden secrets. If you hadn't played the originals, I think you'd be hard-pressed to say which were new zones and which were remixes. The variety and inventiveness of the gimmicks and set pieces in each stage, and the overall flow of gameplay, makes it clear this was a game created by fans who love and understand what made original games great.
The new special stages are great ... they are original, though contain elements of Sonic 2 and Sonic CD special stages. Sonic 3's blue spheres make a return too (completing them can unlock extra game modes and bonuses, but they aren't relevant to the main storyline). They seem a bit more challenging than the ones in Sonic 3, and there are more of them. In fact this is one of my only (minor) criticisms: you only need 20 rings when hitting a checkpoint to trigger one of the blue sphere stages, and because this is relatively easy, you can spend a LOT of time in these stages instead of progressing the main zones/special stages. Yes, they are optional, but if you see those stars spinning there, you're going to jump into them more often than not. I feel that they should have kept the threshold to trigger these stages at 50 rings like the checkpoints worked in the original games.
The only other downside is the DRM that was ninja'ed onto us without warning. I haven't personally had a problem with it, but it's an anti-consumer move that is a huge headache for anyone without a solid internet connection or who wants to play this game on the go while travelling. It speaks to the general disdain that Sega seems to have for the PC as a platform in general. I mean, it's a sub-$20 USD game ... why encumber it with this rubbish? I'm not going to give Sonic Mania a negative review for this reason alone though, as the DRM has nothing to do with the game itself, and by all accounts the actual devs (Whitehead et al.) did not make the decision to include it.
Overall, just an amazingly good game. It almost feels like sacrilege to say it but ... possibly the best Sonic game ever made. If not, it's at least as good as S3&K.

Since leveling in modern RPGs has become mostly just a matter of dumping points into strength if you are melee, dexterity if you are ranged, and intelligence if you are a magic user, it's refreshing to see a modern RPG that actually requires you to do math and plan ahead if you don't want to mess up your game. In Drakensang, almost every action is determined by a formula that factors in 3 seperate attributes as well as skill points. If you invest in one attribute it will always affect several different things, which means that you are rarely boxed into one role. So, for example, if you want you can play as a rogue/mage hybrid who specializes in long bows and still be effective. There aren't many CRPGs left where you can do stuff like that. The writing isn't great, although it's kind of charming in the way that it avoids the "grim dark" fantasy tropes of modern RPGs and instead harkens back to lighter fair of the 1980s and 1980s.  But spotty writing aside, the combat and character customization are the real reasons to play.
You haven't played Oblivion yet? What's wrong with you? Play it. Just. Play it.

-There are DPS, tank, and support classes.
-Each character has a primary attack, 3 abilities on cooldowns, and an ultimate.
-Using your abilities gives you energy, which is used for ultimates.
-The attacks, abilities, and ultimates all allow you to customize them with 1 bonus (extra movement, damage, etc)
-Each of the bonuses costs between 1 and 3 points, and you can spend up to 10 between your abilities.
-Each turn has an action, and then movement.
-The actions are broken into three phases done in order: Prep (typically heals/shields/etc abilities), Dash (typically combat movement abilities), and Blast (mostly attacks)
-All abilities are triggered simultaneously for each phase. The game determines the order of certain things (for example, if characters are knocked away before or after an area attack)
-Movement happens after these phases. If you did not use an ability during the turn you can move farther.
-When each turn starts, you have 20 seconds to select what ability/abilities you will use and how, and where you want to move after. There are 2 times you can take an extra 5 seconds.
-You also receive 3 "Catalysts" (just extra once per game abilities), one for each phase. You choose between different options to customize your character how you like.
-You can see every character's health and energy while in game.
-You can practice characters and builds against bots to get the hang of them before jumping into PvP.
I'm really enjoying this game. It really rewards you for knowing what all the characters can do, paying attention to what abilities of theirs are ready or on cooldown, predicting movement, etc. It's obviously not going to be everybody's thing, but if you like turn-based strategy this one is definitely worth a look. What I posted above should probably give you a good idea of whether you'll like it or not.

Of all the small racer games i have played this one is one of my favorites for long time playing. In the beginning when you play the game the graphics and modelling of cars is a bit meh as one may be accustomed to more cartoony racer games like Bang Bang or Mini Motor or even 'realistic' looking like Real World Racing. This game reminds me of the later Slicks'n'Slide games on the looks. Few liked those either.
As you play the game starts to open up a bit and you start to like this more and more. Also filling up the garage with different cars and using them in various situations opens up entirely new scenarios that extends the experience.
Career mode is grinding - lots of it as prices of cars and tuning parts are very high -  but still interesting as you buy and customize cars and do challenges using certain types of cars. There is always something to aim towards to.
Best part is probably multiplayer design. You can just put it on and either pop into someones game or host it yourself and keep on playing and if someone joins then they just join and there is no change to ever flowing races that keep on rolling with 5 sec lobby wait intervalls. No need to separate Career, achievement hunting or multiplayer. This is a brilliant idea from the devs as they probably knew multiplayer is going to be dead anyways so why not make it as open as possible to encourage social playing. No other racing game in my library has this. Others - that i have tested atleast - force you to wait in a lobby hoping that someone might pop in. Dead wrong! That does not work. MP is dead - universally - everyone is playing whatever is the genre leader. iRacing, Dota, whatever... dont even know if this particular sub-genre has a game that 'everyone plays' ?
Daily challenges keep one entertained too. Very tough times to beat there. but not impossible to reach a relatively high position either. i seem to score world spots 3-5 all the time so it can't be that bad.
Controls are spotless and car turns precisely like you want it. And getting good lap times is purely about skill.
9/10 - This one takes a well deserved spot in my library along with Mini Moto Racing Evo which is another game that i regard very high. Points could be perhaps a bit higher if the awesome MP section would be even more open and certain menu items and in game indicators would be more clearer.

I don't know what to think of this game. It is nice to look at. The music is relaxing (until you get you hear the vocal track). The idea of building my own space station is interesting. It was interesting enough to make me buy it while it is still Early Access. Something I swore that I would never do again.
I've only a hour play time before this review, and there probably won't be much more. Not in its current state. There doen't seem to be a point to the game.
Build enough core items (water tank, oxygen generator/tanks, power source, etc) to keep a person alive. Build a science module to give said person something to do, and to earn money. Use said money to build the same, and additional living quarters, for more people to arrive at your station. Repeat. Repeat.
There is some forethought needed in planning your station. Although I'm not sure how much. Does the science module in front of the solar array actually effect the amount of power generated?
Give me a challenge. Some random events. Something that makes my crew come down with Space Madness. Make the powers on Earth demand that a indepth study of Pigs in Space, and all the resulting puns, is required to ensure the funding continues. And let me be able to delete messages.
I understand what Early Access is. I understand the game is intented to evolve and grow. I understand that this may never become the game I want.
Can I recommend the game as it stands now?
I am hesitant to do so. If you want any kind of challenge it isn't for you. Not yet.
Would I recommend the game, if the developer actually completes everything on the development roadmap?
Yes. Without hesitation.
I guess it comes down to the fundemental flaw with early access. Do you trust a developer enough to pass over your money? You already know my answer to that question.

When I first saw this I was excited, I've been wanting an escape game featuring a girl, and this was it.
But oh boy, this was nothing that I wanted.
Gameplay: It's a 3D platforming puzzle game.  You push around blocks and break blocks to get through to the door.  There are swinging axes and shooting discs which will hurt.  That's everything.  For the most part it's easy, but the puzzles get a little unclear for some levels.  A great thing is there appears to be more than one way to solve a good number of these levels.  The R18 version has miscellaneous torture obstacles around which are easy to avoid if you know they're there, and easy to escape, but it does drain your health gradually.
Over all, nothing is too challenging platforming wise, except for a few sections where axes swing with the path your traveling.
Story: It's a nice story that really made me think.  There's two different endings, and the true ending makes a statement, if you're into that.  It's like old games where there's not that much story, but it's a really small game so I felt it fit.
The downsides.  It's not cute.  This is a game for sadists.  It's got bondage, abuse, and molestation throughout.  More so in the R18 version.
It's an easy achievement game though, so there's that.

I can't speak highly enough of this game. As someone that grew up playing all the 8-bit and 16-bit Sonic games, and who stopped after S3&K due to thinking the franchise became weird and cringey after they added voice acting, terrible and unnecessarily complex stories, a billion side characters and restrictive on-rails 3D gameplay, Sonic Mania is a perfect return to form. It perfectly captures the look, sound, physics and general feel of the Mega Drive-era Sonics.
But when you look a bit closer you realise this is no Mega Drive game. No, this is the mainline Sonic game for the Sega Saturn that we never got. The backdrops are more detailed and with many more layers of parallax. The sprites have many more frames per section of animation, and the whole things runs at a silky smooth 60 fps. The music has that Mega Drive sound but with more channels, better percussion and frankly just sounds awesome, like any good Sonic OST should.
The game is of a good length - twelve zones, putting it on par with S3&K. The zones are a mix of old and new, and wonderfully borrow elements from all the classic Sonic games (I even saw a couple of references in there to the Master System titles!) The level design is fantastic and nails the complex, many-pathed nature of the classic games, packed with hidden secrets. If you hadn't played the originals, I think you'd be hard-pressed to say which were new zones and which were remixes. The variety and inventiveness of the gimmicks and set pieces in each stage, and the overall flow of gameplay, makes it clear this was a game created by fans who love and understand what made original games great.
The new special stages are great ... they are original, though contain elements of Sonic 2 and Sonic CD special stages. Sonic 3's blue spheres make a return too (completing them can unlock extra game modes and bonuses, but they aren't relevant to the main storyline). They seem a bit more challenging than the ones in Sonic 3, and there are more of them. In fact this is one of my only (minor) criticisms: you only need 20 rings when hitting a checkpoint to trigger one of the blue sphere stages, and because this is relatively easy, you can spend a LOT of time in these stages instead of progressing the main zones/special stages. Yes, they are optional, but if you see those stars spinning there, you're going to jump into them more often than not. I feel that they should have kept the threshold to trigger these stages at 50 rings like the checkpoints worked in the original games.
The only other downside is the DRM that was ninja'ed onto us without warning. I haven't personally had a problem with it, but it's an anti-consumer move that is a huge headache for anyone without a solid internet connection or who wants to play this game on the go while travelling. It speaks to the general disdain that Sega seems to have for the PC as a platform in general. I mean, it's a sub-$20 USD game ... why encumber it with this rubbish? I'm not going to give Sonic Mania a negative review for this reason alone though, as the DRM has nothing to do with the game itself, and by all accounts the actual devs (Whitehead et al.) did not make the decision to include it.
Overall, just an amazingly good game. It almost feels like sacrilege to say it but ... possibly the best Sonic game ever made. If not, it's at least as good as S3&K.

Gear up is an amazing game where you battle, level up, upgrade, repeat (Unless you didn't get the free version. In that case, you have a lot or everything unlocked). You can hover, fly, crawl, or just stick with ordinary wheels and tank tracks. There are many weapons such as flamethrowers, shotguns, machine guns and much more. You can even change the color of your vehicle.  There are 4 modes:  Conquest, DeathMatch, Team DeathMatch, and Tag. In Conquest, your team's goal is to capture all 6 towers by standing in a specific area near the towers. In Deathmatch, it's everyone against everyone for 10 minutes. Team DeathMatch is the same thing, except you're on a team against another team. Lastly, I'm not sure what Tag is because there simply weren't any servers for the gamemode.

This is one of the best damn Sonic games on the planet. I may have been born in '93, but I was not part of a SEGA household growing up. We had Nintendo and Playstation, that was about it. My first Sonic game ever played was Sonic Adventure 2 Battle; and I didn't get a taste of the classic Genesis titles until Mega Collection on the GameCube. That being said, Classic Sonic still feels new to me, and not like something I grew up with, therefore, it feels fresh.
And Mania is the best damn thing since Sonic Sliced Bread and truly a love letter to Classic Sonic fans and even just Sonic fans in general. This game is so full of love for its fanbase. =Story===
เนื่องจากภาคนี้ไม่มีโหมด Multi เกมจึงจะเลือกที่จะเน้นไปที่เนื้อเรื่องซะเป็นส่วนใหญ่ โดยเกมจะเลือกเล่าเรื่องในมุมของเทมพลาร์ที่คุณไม่เคยรู้มาก่อน และ ด้านมืดของแอสซาซิน ถึงกับต้องบอกเลยว่าเนื้อเรื่องของภาค Rogue นั้นเข้มข้นแล้วสนุกมากจริงๆ โดยมันจะซ่อนมุมต่างๆ ที่จะเชื่อมโยงต่อๆกับภาคๆอื่น หรือเล่าในสิ่งที่ภาคที่แล้วขาดไปได้อย่างสมบูรณ์แบบ คุณจะได้รับบทเป็นแอสซาซิน Shay Patrick Cormac โดยเนื้อเรื่องในเกมนั้นจะถูกเล่าหลังจากภาค 4 หรือ Black Flag และเป็นช่วงก่อน ภาค 3 เล็กน้อย
=Gameplay===
ถ้าให้พูดถึงระบบของเกมนี้หลายๆคนก็คงรู้ว่าเกมนี้มีระบบที่คล้ายกับภาค 4 แต่จะพูดแบบนั้นก็ไม่ถูกตัวเกมนั้นได้ถูกอัพเกรดและเปลี่ยนแปลงบางส่วนซึ่งทำให้เหมาะกับการเล่นในภาคนี้มาก ในระบบขับเรือเราจะไม่จำเป็นต้องเน้นในการอัพเกรดเรือแบบภาค 4 อีกแล้ว เพราะภาคนี้นั้นตัวเกมได้เน้นระบบเดินเท้าในเนื้อเรื่องมากกว่า โดยไม่จำเป็นต้องคอยมาอัพเกรดเรือของตัวเองเรื่อยๆ เพื่อให้เล่นมิชชั่นไหว มาในภาคนี้เกมได้เพิ่มระบบที่เหมาะกับสภาวะของหิมะโดยมันจะมี ภูเขาน้ำแข็ง และ พายุหิมะ ช่วยให้การขับเรือไปมาดูมีอะไรมากขึ้น ส่วนระบบอัพเกรดเรือนั้นก็ไม่ต่างจากภาคก่อน คุณสามารถปล้นของจากเรือของศัตรูแล้วนำมาอัพเกรดเรือของคุณได้ แต่ในการอัพเกรดขั้นสุดนั้น ตัวเกมจะให้คุณนำแปลนมาเพื่ออัพเกรด แต่จะแตกต่างจากภาคที่แล้วมาก เพราะแปลนนี้มันไม่ได้มาจากการที่คุณไปดำใต้ทะเล เพราะเกมได้ตัดระบบนี้ออกไปแล้ว คุณก็จำเป็นที่ต้องหาจากแผนที่สมบัติและการทำมิชชั่นเสริมของเกมไป พูดถึงระบบเรือมาเยอะแล้วมาดูระบบเดินเท้ากันบ้าง เกมได้อัพเกรดระบบที่ผู้เล่นหลบซ่อนอยู่และผิวปากตัวเกมก็ได้เพิ่มระยะในการผิวปากให้ผู้เล่นสังเกตได้ง่ายขึ้น ในระบบการต่อสู้นั้นแท็บไม่มีอะไรแตกต่างจากภาค 4 เลย แต่เกมได้เพิ่มอาวุธที่มีชื่อว่า Air Rifle ซึ่งตัวนี้จะคล้ายกับ Pipe ของภาค 4 ที่เราจะเลือกยิงกระสุนยาสลบ กระสุนที่ทำให้ศัตรูเป็นบ้า และเกมยังเพิ่มมาอีก คือกระสุนพลุที่จะใช้ดึงดูดความสนใจของศัตรูได้ พร้อมกับปืนยิงระบบที่ติดกับ Air Rifle อีกแล้ว ในเรื่องมิชชั่่นของเกมนี้นั้นมันได้เปลี่ยนไปโดยสิ้นเชิง โดยคุณต้องมาต่อกรกับฝั่งแอสซาซิน ทำให้คุณต้องสังเกตแล้วคอยระวังพวกนี้ และ ยังมีระบบที่เราขัดขวางการฆ่าของแอสซาซินอีกด้วย ซึ่งระบบนี้จะใช้เหมือนกับระบบ Multi ของภาคที่แล้วที่เราจะใช้หาแอสซาซินแล้วโจมตีพวกเขาก่อนที่จะเข้าถึงเรา นับว่าเป็นมิติของเกมแอสซาซินเลยก็ว่าได้
=Graphic===
ถึงภาคนี้จะไม่ได้สวยเหมือกับภาค Unity แต่ภาคนี้ก็บอกได้ว่ามันเป์นมิตรกับ PC สเปคกลางๆ ซึ่งภาพของมันยังสวยได้เหมือนภาค 4 แต่ที่น่าตกใจคือมันกับกินสเปคน้อยกว่าภาค 4 และไม่มีปัญหาเฟรมเรทตกเลยแม้แต่น้อย และตัวเกมก็ยังไม่มีปัญหาบัคทางกราฟฟิคที่เคยเกิดขึ้นกับภาค 4 เลยอีกด้วย หากคอมคุณสามารถเล่นภาค 3 ได้สบายๆ ภาคนี้ก็คงไม่ใช่ปัญหาที่ต้องนำไปคิดเลย
=Verdict===
ระบบแนวการเล่นใหม่ของเกมนักฆ่า พร้อมกับมิชชั่นเสริมมากมายที่จะทำให้คุณเล่นโดยอดหลับอดนอนไปเลยก็ว่าได้ ถ้าหากคุณเป็นแฟนคลับและชอบเกม Assassin's Creed อยู่แล้วก็ไม่ต้องลังเลเลยว่าจำเป็นต้องซื้อภาคนี้ไหม เพราะว่า Assassin’s Creed Rogue นั้นไม่ใช่ภาคเสริมอะไรทั้งสิ้น มันคืออีกภาคของ Assassin’s Creed ที่นับว่าสำคัญ และ สมบูรณ์แบบมาก

Having played other hidden object (HO) games from Artifex Mundi (AM), one can tell "Time Mysteries 2: The Ancient Spectres" is truly one of the first modern games of their hand. Respecting chronological order, prior to this one, i completed TIme Mysteries: Remastered. It clearly shows they've put a lot more effort, probably due to their former experience(s), in Time Mysteries 2. Design, art, interface, ... basically everything is better developed, which gives a much better overall experience to the player.
The story itself takes place in an large mansion, with an eerie, atmospheric feel to it. The player can shift through different eras, effectively showing the settings in their former and newer glories. This means there are a lot of locations and a lot of hidden object scenes. To a point they might have overdone it and the game becomes tedious. The HO scenes have objects in them that are harder to locate than in other AF HO games. There's an achievement which requires you to solve an HO scene in less than 1 minute. Took me through 75% of the game before i managed, whilst in other games i mostly get this achievement after 2-3 puzzles. The non-HO puzzles are fun and excellent on difficulty rating.
Overall a game i enjoyed a bit less than other AF HO games.
Recommended for:
-HO gamers in general, HO gamers with experience in other AM games
-achievement hunters looking for another perfect game
Less recommended for:
-those new to the genre, since the game is rather long and tedious, and the hidden object scenes can be considered hard in comparison to other AM - HO games

Assassin’s Creed: Rogue (AC:R) has turned into one of my favorite Assassin’s Creed (AC) games of the series.  Set between the opening acts of ACIII and Unity (AC:U), the curtain opens to find Assassin Shay Cormic struggling between obedience to his betters and following his conscience.  This story ties into the events of ACIII, Black Flag (AC:BF), Freedom Cry (AC:FC), and AC:U in a way that no other game has yet done, and it does it with remarkable success.  While a step back from the fancy shmancy graphics, details, and crowds in AC:U, Rogue suffers from none of the many bugs that its sister game did, and its seemless gameplay combined with Shay’s compelling story certainly make this game very much worth picking up.
POSITIVES:
-	More of the duel naval/land action and side quests that made AC:BF such an interesting game.
-	Compelling new characters, and a few more chapters with some old favorites.
-	Largely bug free, relying and improving upon the mechanics developed in AC:BF
NEUTRAL:
-	It felt sometimes like a huge AC:BF DLC due to the similarities in game play.
CONS:
-	There are only 7 sequences as opposed to the amount that we have come to expect from AC games.  That said, this did not necessarily feel like a short game – there is plenty to do – but I do wish it had been longer.

It's ironic how Unity was promoted as the big next-gen game while Rogue was underplayed as AC 4.5 for current-gen. As we've seen in the past few months, Unity has flopped horrendously while Rogue has stood out as a worthy successor to the AC franchise. Sadly, much of this is mostly because Rogue is simply NOT Unity.
The fact of the matter is that Rogue WORKS. The game is pretty much an extension of Black Flag. It doesn't change much, if anything, but that isn't a bad thing. Black Flag was exciting. Great soundtrack, fast-paced combat, huge world and naval exploration. Rogue has a somewhat smaller scale, but has more areas in New York, the North Atlantic and North America. But it has the same charm and the same feel. Perhaps it could've used its setting more effectively - lots of locations aren't used and New York is mostly a backdrop to several story missions, while Black Flag took you everywhere. But it's still better than Unity.
The story works well too. Ubisoft seems to be trying very hard to make memorable characters like Ezio but in the span of only one game compared to the AC2 trilogy. Shay Cormac is a relatable character - not as epic as Ezio, but within the constraints of only one game, Shay's story comes across very nicely. Sure, it's a token rogue story, but Shay pulls it off really well, going through the moral conflict, becoming jaded with the Assassins and becoming an integral part of the Templars.
Perhaps the most underrated part of Rogue is how it connects the AC universe together. It brings back Black Flag and Freedom Cry through its heritage of older characters. It serves as the prequel to ACIII, with references to George Washington, Haytham Kenway and the fall of Achilles. And, as an extra bonus, it links into the events of Unity. If anything, Rogue stands out by making the other AC games better. The supporting ensemble complement Shay nicely, making the cinematic experience more enjoyable than Arno's attempts in Unity.
The modern-day story is also very well developed. You are once again an Abstergo Entertainment employee, but this time under the control of the Templars directly. It introduces new supporting characters and a whole new aspect of the modern story while retaining the familiar setting from Black Flag, It really does play out as a sequel to Black Flag, and is executed far more fluidly than Unity's excuse for a modern story. In fact, it seems that Unity was made by Abstergo rather than Ubisoft as a ploy to make Assassin-based games utter crap while making Templars games really good.
And that would make a good plot twist.
Ultimately, Rogue stays true to a working formula. There are elements that don't make a lot of sense, but we've come to expect that from open-world games and the series. The story is satisfying, the gameplay is sweet and the soundtrack is epic. Surely, there can be no greater nostalgia trip than when you open the menu and hear Ezio's and Connor's themes mashed together. Rogue respects the series and in turn forms a deep bond with everything that came before it. Perhaps it is a greater unifier than Unity.

Cinderella Escape! R12 is a clever, kinky and interesting twist on the Cinderella storybook. Her Prince Charming is not as charming as you might think!  Cinderella must climb, kick, push, pull and intelligently make use of her limited resources to complete each puzzling conundrum within the prince's dungeon.
Once upon a time, there was a girl named Cinderella. She was very beautiful and she was kind to all.
However, her stepmother didn't like her one little bit and treated her as a slave.
One day a letter with an invitation arrived. The letter explained that a ball was to be held at the palace and the Prince would choose a girl to become his wife.
She made every effort to get rid of all troubles to go to the ball.
She was on her way to the ball, when she witnessed the Prince killing his father, the King, in order to usurp the throne.
The Prince quickly claimed that Cinderella had killed the King andCinderella was arrested and locked in the deepest, darkest part of the dungeon...
Can she escape from the dungeon?
Will Cinderella have a happy ending?
Only by solving and navigating the dungeons deadly traps with help from her fairy god mother, will she ever see the light of day again...
Cinderella Escape! is a 3D Action Puzzle Game.
Each puzzle requires use of the 3 main actions to solve the Puzzle and reach the exit.
Cinderella Escape makes good use of RPG elements such as the level up system to allow for the player to increase the amount of jumps and kicks required to complete the dungeon floor.
Gold can be earned in different stages of the game and used to purchase kinky costumes and extra content in a similar way to Blade Kitten.
The puzzles vary from easy to mindbendingly hard while still being fair and completable in your first run through the stage. The game made me think twice before solving it, as one wrong move could send poor Cinderella into a pit of spikes...
The R18+ Patch, which is not available on steam only adds some removed kinky content, but it is not required at all to enjoy the game.  In fact, I'd recommend not installing the R18 patch, as it doesnt add anything beyond asthetic changes.
The art is in an anime-esque style that is well done and is reasonably suited to a game like this.
The main character is beautifully colored, animated, textured and has a hand drawn look.
The cutscenes are well animated with very few major problems across the board.
The only complaint I've got with the game is that the translation is not as gorgeous as the art that accompanies it.
The script is full of translation errors and some characters feel like their speech isnt as fluid as other anime based games.
Cinderella Escape! R12 is an entertaining game full of kinky looking fairytale figures, a twist on the original story and unique puzzle concepts.
Despite being nowhere near the end, I'd imagine this fairytale does not have a happy ending...
But thats what appeals about these fairytale games, sometimes, things are not what they seem.
I'd highly recommend this version to anyone who does not mind a little bit of kinky imagery and a few translation issues.
All up this is a interesting game that is made better by its most recent controller patch.

This game is a puzzle-based game with a tinge of eroge, well more on the bondage and torture part. However, due to Steam regulations, the one here is the R12 version, not the R18. There's not much difference between the two, except the R18 have the secret chamber, where you can torture Cinderella for your viewing pleasure (and I DO mean pleasure), and additional costumes.
Gameplay wise, its a basic puzzle solving game. Move blocks here and there to create a pathway to reach your goal. At certain points (end of sub-level), you will get a bonus objective of rescuing your step-relatives from being tortured, but the catch is that you will be tortured in their place. Don't worry, you can escape from it. You can change the camera angle and view perspective to see where is the goal of the map. This is really much needed, as sometimes it may be obscured by obstacle.
As for the difficulty, its pretty inconsistent. Some maps are pretty straight forward, while some require some retries to solve it. However, I cannot help but being shocked about a certain map, where all you need to do to reach a goal is a curve jump. Yes, you heard me correctly, a curve jump. No block moving, no obstacle dodging, no block demolishing, nothing else. Just a curve jump. It's a fast way for grinding money though. There was that one map though, where you actually need to get hit by the obstacle to reach the secondary objective. That was pretty interesting to me.
Everytime you solve a map, you will get money and experience. The higher level you are, the more chances you are provided with jumping and kicking. They are not limited, they are finite, and once you run out of them, poor Cinderella can't even jump at all, or even kick. Kind of a hinderance, but at the same time its a challenge to use them wisely. You can spend money on just costumes. So poor Cinderella can be dressed as a gothic dominatrix, bunny girl, Santa girl etc. Nothing much here but fanservice .
Since it's an eroge game, there are a lot of boob juggling physics and pantsu shots, since camera angle can be changed, as they are required to solve a map. Upskirts will be pretty common, heck sometimes I do that for fun. The biggest perk of this game is that, it's really cheap. It cost as much as a cheap lunch. It's not a very pricey game.
Overall, a short and cheap puzzle game which can be solved in a matter of hours. If you want some fun doing puzzles (and enjoy the T & A at the same time), go ahead, give this game a shot, since it's really cheap, there's nothing much to lose. Mind you this is the censored version. For the uncensored one, please check the Steam community forums for this game.

Stable Orbit is a really unique and interesting experience. The short time I played this game, I was amazed by the setting and often caught myself glazing at the Earth beneath the Space Station instead of actually playing the game.
However, this game is still deep in Early Access and after about one hour of play time it's extremely obvious why. Once the station is in a stable condition with enough resource containers, solar panels and radiators, there is nothing else to do than build more of the stuff that is already there.
But that currently the only negative thing I have to say about Stable Orbit, since the Developer Roadmap looks pretty ambitious and I am sure that the additional features (like thrusters to maintain the orbit or additional modules) will help the game become better and more long time motivating.
An additional feature I would like to see are Building Missions that provide a target to build a certain amount of a certain module (e.g. "The European Space Travel Agency demands the presence of at least to middle sized laboratories on the station"). Reaching this goal within a certain amount of time could be rewarded with additional funds.
Conclusion: A very promising game. Still lacking of content but on a very good way to become an insider.

Cinderella Escape is a block puzzle game with 3D graphics.
You control Cinderella who tries to escape from the dungeon she'd been thrown to because she saw the King was murdered by the Prince (a little twist of the story).

The main goal is to find the exit door of each room during forty stages.
You can push blocks, jump over them or even destroy them with your kick in a 3d enviroment avoiding some dangers (saws, pikes, blades...).
Some stages have multiple ways to get to the goal and you must plan every move using zoom out key because you have limited kicks and jumps per level and this fact is the main difficulty of the game.
You can earn experience points when you complete levels and increse the number of them.
You can also unblock costumes and change her look during the game.
You can move her using WASD keys, kick and jump using mouse buttons and move the position of the camera using the mouse.
Graphics are correct (Cinderella is detailed modeled), but the rest of objects are simply and their textures very repetitive. Ok, you are in a dungeon but more variety of them will be nice.
Sound and music are correct too.
It has achivements but it's not trading cards, I encourage to developers to add them in next releases.
Nice puzzle game to play a couple of hours.

Well, I wasn't expecting to want to write the review so early. I like to write the review as soon as possible to after completion of the main story. Maybe I update if important information happens in post-game. Regardless, after only 3-4 hours of gametime I've finished Sonic Mania's main story and it was honestly pretty good. I think if you're a fan you've already bought this game, so what's left for Mania is the harder part of the fandom to sell to and the new fan.
I'll preface this with a simple recommendation that you play older Sonic sidescrollers before Mania. You can buy them on Steam or just emulate (legally lol). Sonic 1, 2, 3&K, and CD are all classic video games and will be the BEST way for you to see if sidescrolling Sonic is for you as a new fan or somebody who has only played 3D Sonic! Mania is no different than these four, and I will explain that, although it may be a little harder than the four of those. After trying those games out, if you liked what you played then buy Mania, that's all you really need to really appreciate this game.
Some might have their suspicions or believe this game is bad, that it is not proper 2D Sonic. That's wrong, Sonic is as barebones and classic as in the Genesis games. The levels are an improvement, you have new gimmicks, interesting setpieces, and brand-new level design only possible on this games' engine that fits with Sonic's physics (which are very well done much like CD and the mobile ports).
All in all, a very worthwhile game and i'll be looking forward to what people have to say about Sonic now. The only problems I had with the game were: the floor is lava sometimes. I mean that figuratively and literally. As for the DRM, I hope the team makes the right choice and you can help by deciding not to purchase the game until the DRM is removed.
EDIT: Low rating? I stand by what I said, and I don't see anything wrong with it. Good game good review.

Pros:
* The real-life nuclear bunker setting.
Cons:
* Very highly priced for what you actually get in terms of gameplay. No engaging puzzles or challenging events: you just click your way through highlighted stuff. The only side-activities are based around story related messages, and the collection of wooden figures. It seems more like a commercially failed movie that was later converted to a game, instead of a game that includes elements of FMV.
* The story (in chronological order) is bland and typical B-movie material. It's just some people ratting each other out in a nuclear bunker, all because they have a high sense of egotistical survival instinct. I could not relate to, or care for, any of them. The only thing that keeps things interesting, is the trick of putting everything in non-chronological order.
* Acting varies between decent (Sarah Greene has her moments) and toe-curling bad (John’s broken arm scene).
* No satisfying feeling of influencing the outcome of the story.
* Very little replay value.
Side notes:
* Luckily I bought this during the sales period, otherwise I would feel scammed.
* The ambient music serves its purpose for the setting, but has no quality tracks that are memorable/notable. However, this is usually the case for this type of music. Sadly a lot of musicians focus too much on the ambience aspects, and leave out the melodic aspects. Due to this, one can almost never point to a certain track and say that it's from game/movie X or Y. Even high-budget movies like Blade Runner 2049 are falling into this trap.
* The interactive movie genre is actually quite difficult to execute in a professional way. It's a real challenge to create something that is entertaining as both a movie and a game. Even the more experienced studios like Quantic Dream still have difficulties with the balance of all the elements. I do hope that the genre will soon get some more attention, and will eventually mature into a series of highly respected titles that set the benchmark for all things to come.

Kind of a thumbs-middle review, but definitely more positive than not; it was a good game overall.
As you probably know, The Bunker is a FMV-based game, mostly point-and-click, with a couple of what could be considered quick-time events (QTEs) a certain points.  The first paragraph of the store page summary does a good job in telling you what the game plot is about.
For a game like this to be satisfying, IMO, it needs 1) a good story, 2) good acting, and 3) sufficient gameplay to give the player some amount of agency so they're not just pressing Play to watch the next movie snippet.  Based on those criteria, I'll give it a 4/5 for story, 4/5 for acting, and 3/5 for gameplay.
Pros:
(+) Good premise and story.  The trailers make it seem like an action/thriller.  It's not.  To me it wasn't really suspenseful or thrilling, but it was still enjoyable to experience.  The story unfolds in an interesting way, IMO.
(+) Good acting, especially in the flashbacks.  All of the parts were well-acted, IMO, with the exception of some over-acting during
.
(+) Meaningful collectibles.  Purely optional, but provide additional backdrop to the story.  Tied to achievements.
Neither:
(+/-)  Not really a pro or a con, but just a thought.  You play as a person who's physically and emotionally weakened.  Afraid, neurotic, physically limited...a "Mama's boy."  For some this could be...upsetting?  As they don't want to picture themselves this way, or would otherwise prefer to play a character who is anything but.
Cons:
(-) Some moments are really dragged out.  This is most noticeable in things you need to do (places you need to go) multiple times, or where the protagonist is physically or emotionally impeded.  I'm a patient guy, but after the third time, I just wanted him to go down the stairs already and not hesitate like a nervous wreck.
(-) The aforementioned over-acting in a particular extended sequence.  It also contributed to moments being dragged out.
(-) When it comes down to it, there really isn't that much for the player to do.  There are no puzzles and limited interaction with the environment.  That's sort of the nature of the game, I guess, but it was still a bit too limited.
(-) On the other hand, there are a couple of QTEs late in the game that I think could actually impede some users from finishing the game.  You either have to left-click rapid-fire, or repeatedly mash the 'A' button on the controller.  I'll admit I failed a couple of times; this could be upsetting to users who didn't anticipate lacking the manual dexterity to finish a game like this.
(-) Kind of minor, but the collection achievements require they all be obtained in a single playthrough.  So if you miss one early, you have to replay the entire game and re-collect them all up through the last collectible.  I prefer to be able to play a game without worrying about achievements, then going back (say, via chapter select) and getting collectibles I missed.
Hint for achievement-hunters:  if you think you might have just missed a collectible, you can return to the main menu then Continue the game and you will start at the beginning of the chapter.

Finally, the first Halo game has arrived on Steam. Unfortunately, it's a port of the mobile game which happens to be more of an top-view action game instead of a first person shooter. Does that make Spartan Assault any less good ? Yes and no.
The universe is there, and the atmosphere oozes Halo, it's just a bit less detailed. Same goes for the enemies.
The controls also could've been implemented better but once you get the hang of them they'll do just fine. Controlling vehicles is awkward, though and it takes much more than a little bit of practice. By the end of the game I still wasn't able to drive a vehicle without crashing into something.
You can tell the game was designed for mobile phones because the missions are ridiculously short. And yet some of them are pretty hard. There are 6 campaigns, and each campaign consists of 5 levels, making a total of 30 levels. A level will take you 5-10 minutes to finish. So there's just a couple of hours of gameplay here. Objectives range from defending an area to killing every alien or blowing stuff up. The mission variety is what keeps the game fun because if I had to shoot my way through every level I probably would've stopped halfway through.
Anyway, Halo Spartan Assault is really a game for the action genre and Halo lovers. It's definitely fun in short bursts, but it's not the Halo game we originally wanted or hoped for. Here's hoping Microsoft will someday release the 'true' Halo games. I think this one will sell pretty well nevertheless, if only because of the word 'Halo'.

Interstellar Transport Company is a great simulation game for those who like depth and choice. The game definitely still has rough edges (it's in early access after all) but the core mechanics are quite solid.
Pros:
* Many ships & cargo types to choose from mean you can try a lot of different ways to make money
* Having a lot of different routes and types of cargo moving around feels really rewarding after scrimping and saving to maximize profits
* I've already lost hours to this game by getting sucked into the fun of min/maxing profits on each of my routes and checking out new ship types. Getting into the flow of the game is very enjoyable, especially once you start seeing profits roll in!
Cons:
* Some of the UI elements aren't very clear, e.g., what does cargo maintenance 90% mean exactly?
* Ships don't haul specific amounts of cargo, e.g., 10 units of food, they just have bulk storage that could be food, consumer goods, rare resources &c. This can make it difficult to know if you're properly meeting demand for a colony or just bringing more resources they're already swimming in.
* Game isn't totally finished, so don't expect a ton of content & new ships after 25 years of in-game time

This is a great little racing game with a lot to keep you coming back.  Career mode, time trials and free roam.  Not to mention multiplayer.  There are many achievements, trials to beat the developers times on certain tracks, tons of challenges.  There is car customization and paint and decals too.
The game reminds me of an older game from the PS1 or PS2 days.
Graphics:  The tracks are nicely done but the cars are a bit dated looking but are still very serviceable.  The ability to decorate your car adds a nice touch.  You have the choice of many camera angles from isometric which I like because it is like playing some of the older games I remember so fondly but it also lets you pick chase cams and several in between which actually makes it feel like two different games.  My one complaint is that when in isometric view the buildings can occasionally get in your way and you can't see where you're going for brief periods.
Sound: Standard fare for a PS2 game which isn't bad.  Kind of brings back memories.
Control:  The controls aren't bad but aren't great.  You do get used to them and they don't take away from the game much after that.  I would say that a controller is recommended if not mandatory for most people.
Overall Experience:  I already mentioned the great replayability and this is just one of those games that's just plain fun.  I personally don't need triple A graphics for a game to be great fun.
Summary:
Graphics:  7/10
Sound: 8/10
Control 6/10
Overall Experience: 8/10

is a block puzzle game with 3D graphics. Don't let the name fool you: You wouldn't want to gift this game to your 7 year old cousin.
You control Cinderella who tries to escape a dungeon she'd been thrown to. Along the way you can save your two mean sisters and a stepmother, or you can leave them to rot and possibly die of starvation.
Most stages have multiple ways to get to the goal.
You can push blocks, jump over them or even destroy them with your Falcon Kick, though you have limited jumps and kicks per level.You can expand you limit by earning experience (that you earn by completing levels) and leveling up.
Simple and neat. Not much to say about them since you're pushing the same blocks in the same dungeon over and over again, but I found them nice to look at, for what they are.
Again, I don't have much to say. The only sounds you will hear are the same music that plays in all stages, moanings of Cinderella when she loses health or kicks blocks, and her footsteps. Music sounds kind of sinister and is very fitting to a dungeon. Even though it plays on loop, my fluffy ears are still in one piece. Cinderella's grunts of pain are your typical japanese
grunts, and her footsteps sound like... well, normal footsteps.
I'm kinda dragging the subject here, let's move on...
You use WASD to control Cinderella, Space to jump, LMB to kick, RMB to pan the camera, Mouse Wheel to zoom in/out. It works. You can zoom out to plan your moves, and zoom in to pass the platforming moments.
If you're a big fan of puzzle games and you're looking for a challenge, don't buy this game. If you're looking for a way to stress out after a long day, then give it a shot. I finished the whole game in 2.3 hrs so don't expect a 100 hours long epic adventure though.

If you're a fan of tycoon games, this one is probably for you.  This title offers you the opportunity to start out with a small fleet of ships schlepping food and water to the Moon and transform it into a titan of interstellar commerce.  Will you assist humanity in spreading out to colonize the solar system and beyond?  Or will you operate solely to satisfy your own avaricious desire for cash?  Will you pay to found a colony on Titan that can produce fuel to aid the conquest of the stars?  Or will you ship thousands of forlorn colonists out to the barren moons of Neptune empty-handed, then make a mint selling them the food and water they need to survive but are incapable of producing themselves?
The choice is yours, and Interstellar Transport Company leaves the player free to operate in whatever fashion they desire while the AI opponents engage in similar schemes in an effort to undercut, outpace, or overwhelm you.  The overall mechanics of the game are relatively simple, and yet still manage to produce a surprising variety of emergent game play.  No two runs of Interstellar Transport Company feel the same, and yet are similar enough that the basic skills you learn in your first few runs will soon have you wheeling and dealing like Warren Buffet crashing his Ferrari through the main doors of the Bellagio in Vegas.
It is worthwhile to note, however, that the game is still in Early Access.  There are a few bugs that occasionally crop up with some AI behaviors (like not building maintenance sheds to fix damaged ships) and the user interface is a bit counter-intuitive and difficult to use.  But despite those flaws, there's still certainly enough going on in Interstellar Transport Company to provide you with a sizable amount of entertainment for the price.

If you, like so many, were put off the Time Mysteries series by a poor TM1 (Time Mysteries: Inheritance) experience, know that it's safe to go back in the water. TM2 is a solid P&C/HOG with a decent story, 'okay' graphics, and acceptable VO (btw - I'm referring to the voice acting and not lip sync, which is often off). Mini games were the standard fare. I enjoyed the art and the upper-moderate difficulty level of the hidden object scenes. Also, know there's no storyline continuity lost by passing on TM1 and starting with TM2 (i.e., you won't be lost in the story by starting with TM2). The game played well on Linux Mint 18.
The main issue I had with the game was regarding the high degree of backtracking required (which I don't
consider a bad thing) in context of the configurability of the difficulty settings (two choices: Regular Mode or Expert Mode).
I prefer to play these types of games without the active areas being given away by sparkle (or otherwise indicated by anything other than cursor change on mouseover). To achieve this in TM2, you set the difficulty level to 'Expert Mode'. So far, so good.
The issue for me came later in the game when I wanted to see the map locations of the scenes with available actions (which requires you to be in Regular Mode - which turns the sparkle back on). As many reviews note, there's a lot of backtracking required in this game. And although you often know which items are required next, much of the time those items' location is not deducible, nearby, and/or apparent. Once you have all the levels and scenes opened up, there becomes a somewhat overwhelming number of possible locations (and many times there's only one action available at a time in the whole game). So your choice is to systematically backtrack the entire game (scene by scene - area by area) to find the required item in that one - just now made active by your most recent action - hidden object puzzle or switch from Expert Mode to Regular Mode to see the next available action (and then switch back to Expert Mode to turn the sparkle back off). This became tedious for me and I found myself wishing the devs had made the difficulty level more configurable.
I get that this issue stems from a personal preference and may not bother anyone else. But I thought I'd mention it as it was the main negative I experienced. Besides that, I have no problem giving this game a recommend.
PS I almost exclusively play offline. I typically only play online long enough for Steam to allow me to write a review. So Steam only shows that I played 0.2 hrs as of the time of this review, although I've played at least 8 hrs and have completed both games.

It makes me outrageously happy to play a game where there's nothing random to it, no silly perks or loadouts to contend with, none of that. You just sit and you learn. The more you learn the more the number, your high score, goes up. That's it.
A refreshingly small-scope game that utterly holds to that scope. The graphics and sounds work beautifully, the longer you last the more horrors you eventually see, the game delivers a truly hellish vibe with relatively simple means. The weapon is well balanced, satisfying and rich to use.
The only flaw I find with this game is that the sound for the laughing skulls is a little inconsistent. Sometimes it's quite loud and the skull is far behind you, other times you're caught by surprise because it sounded further away than it was. Just another thing to learn, but it is certainly a flaw.
To bring up any other complaint with the game is usually to say "I wish they made something entirely different." Which is fine, this game is probably only truly for a very small subset of people, but it does what it does and it does it nearly perfectly. An utterly admirable game, even if for only that reason.

After playing a more complicated first-person shooter like Team Fortress 2, sometimes a fun, dumb FPS is a breath of fresh air. One such shooter would be Gotham City Impostors.
Don't let the name fool you: this game is Batman only in title, character looks, and location names. Look beneath DC's branding, and you see a quirky shooter with a lot of personality. The dialogue is funny and varied, seeing as you can change each class's voice pack individually, and the gadget system makes this shooter stand out from the rest.
This game, of course, is Free to Play, but everything in the game except only some cosmetics and loadout slots can be unlocked without paying any money. As you level up you get unlock keys that can be used to pick and choose what you want unlock, so you don't end up with a weapon you don't want (unless you choose poorly of course.)
And let's not forget the customization. You select two weapons, an attachment for each, a support item that can range from a grenade to a health pack, a gadget (most of which are for movement), two perks, a psych profile that gives you bonus points for certain actions while removing bonuses for others, a body type that determines health and speed, a face for your character, and the character's voice. Without paying, you only have two loadouts, but you can earn three through purchases - I have all five, but I still only ever use two. And don't even get me started on costume customization.
Sadly, there aren't that many people who play, so you'll have to face the same guys over and over. Also, the game modes are pretty much limited to Team Deathmatch, Domination, and Capture the Flag, and there aren't very many maps. And the many voice packs I mentioned earlier? Once you've heard them all, they become a bit stale.
Overall, I'd give this game an 8/10. With some wicked fun and fast paced gameplay, this game can be a real joy. Although there is not much variety in maps, modes, and quotes, this game's class customization will keep you coming back for more.

We could easily classify this game as "The evolution of platform/shooters games in flash from the web". A beautiful artistic audio-visual section and solid gameplay make this title a sure recommendation.
- Spotless artistic direction (the style of the characters, enemies, weapons and unique backgrounds give the game its own personality).
- Excellent soundtrack (As a lover of electronic music, i could be listening for hours to the various tracks that create a correct atmosphere for an action/exploration game like this).
- Balanced and varied Gameplay (There is no other term for this, each weapon has its unique feature which makes it useful in a given situation or effective against a particular enemy type, as for the missions, each one has one unique objetive to comply).
- The exploration element is present (many smartly-hidden secrets to discover containing bonus points, weapons, ammunition, equipment, boosters, etc).
- Use of physics for combat and get rid of obstacles (You can create cover from objects that are in the area, pull or push objects that hinder your path or even for use as long-range weapons against enemies).
- Has local co-op campaign mode.
- The extra modes outside the campaign give the game extra replay value (includes a duel mode against bots or against a friend locally, an infinite survival mode and others).
- Hard (Even on the normal difficulty, the game is very challenging. For those achivements hunters like me, this will compensate the short lenght of the game).
- No configurable keys or buttons on the joystick.
- The only joystick recognized by the game is the one from the Xbox 360.
- Some glitches that prevent to close the game normally (in the linux version, i played the demo on Windows XP at the time without problems).
- Some achivements are broken (a logical problem in those achivements that ask a requirement for complete in all the levels of the game).
- Short (can be compensated if you dedicate yourself time to explore the levels for secrets)
- The use of physics in certain situations can be a headache if not used wisely.
- Sometimes a mini-map to avoid getting lost would be useful.
- The developer abandoned this project long ago (no hope for some fixes).
If you like fast action 2D games, mixed with elements of exploration that are accompanied by beautiful graphics and a good soundtrack, this game is a safe buy.
Note: Played it on GNU / Linux (Ubuntu 14.04 LTS - 32 bits)

This is the first review I'm writing, so please go easy on me! Right now, I have a little over 300 hours logged in to Atlas Reactor (or AR for short) and I am enjoying every moment. For this review, I'm not really going to go into the gameplay as I think there are plenty of reviews and information already out there. I just want to correct some misinformation I believe people have about the game and help anyone who has an interest in trying out AR.
First, Atlas Reactor is a buy to play game. The free mode is only a limited version of the game, where you have a number of restrictions. These restrictions are: a limited player unique rotation of Freelancers, a limit to the number of Loot boxes a player can open in a certain time period (I believe it is 1 every 32 hours? may be wrong), and the inability to play ranked or custom matches. Buying the game removes these restrictions and also gives you access to any future content released without restriction. While it does seem at first like the game is tricking you into playing the free to play version first, that is only with regards to the steam formatting system. Since there is a free to play edition, the game has to be listed as free to play even though it really isn't. More details on what is and what is available in free to play mode can be found on the Atlas Reactor website, the forums, the reddit page, the discord, and I'm sure in places I don't know of.
Secondly, I would like to approach the problems that everyone seems to have with Trion. Everyone seems to label them as a bad company and I have done a bit of research into why that is. So it seems that people have issues with the payment system in Rift and the many problems in Archeage (which weren't fixed), both of which I can understand. To start, I want to point out that the team that works on Atlas Reactor is different from the two other games, as far as I understand from a community perspective. In regards to the community, Trion has been great, constantly in direct contact with people through reddit and discord, and I have even talked to and played against The Blue Muzzy, the AR Trion community head myself and he is a cool guy and very willing to listen to ideas that people have. For the payment system, as far as I understand the big problem with RIFT was that it was originally free to play and went pay to win in time, which is fun for no one. However I believe (and hope) that Trion has recognized their mistake and made AR a pay to play game from the start so that no such issues can occur again (like I said, hopefully). In case people didn't know, the developers for Archeage were XL Games, not Trion (Trion was just the commercial front of Archeage). So all of the game issues should be attributed to XL Games. For AR, Trion has been great about getting information on bugs for the community and constantly updating the game through the Beta to work out the problems. I enjoy the game a lot and would be extremely sad if I had to pay more money than I already have to do well in the game.
So, please keep this in mind when you download AR for the first time. Try to let go of any prejudices of Trion and MOBA's in general and just enjoy the game! Oh and feel free to contact me in game (or in steam) if you want to play together or have any questions! Name in game is EarthRat#7792

Short answer: Overpriced DLC IMO but very fun, if you liked AC 3 and especially 4, than buy this .
The story is SHORT. .I guess UbiSoft had some guilt so they marked down the cost by $10.. I have to give them credit though because there wasn`t much that the developers had to do to make this game. The re-use of GFX and characters from both 3 and 4 with some new additions and the exact same mechanics and game flow as 4 with a new story line pretty much sums up the making of this game.
The first thing that stood out to me was that this game to date was the smoothest running right after being released; I was able to max out everything and got a solid 60 FPS 95 percent of the time. The scenery was another thing that really stood out; the colors and dynamics are really beautiful in this game and I often had to stop just to look around, this is a nice change in pace from other darker themed games. You`ll see where a lot of buildings/characters and scenery were re-used, but at least this time when your sailing around you`re not looking at the exact same landscape like you did in B.F. and running around in the snow made a comeback which was really fun in 3.
So we finally get an Irish Assassin and he turns... well.. rogue =\ Even in video game land we can`t catch a break! It is interesting that the writers went down the templar route to keep things fresh. The story brings back some characters, but if you didn`t play Unity, 4 or 3 you`ll be in the dark. The big problem? The campaign/story was short, in fact the shortest in the series which is why I call it a DLC, you spend most of your time exploring and gathering treasure and if you just play the campaign you can be done in under a few hours. Also, the short story also didn`t leave time for you to find the cool treasures like the different armor and Altair's sword set let alone be able to use them during gameplay like in brotherhood and the wolf armor.
NY was laid out like Boston was in 3 and there`s no horse so you had to run around or fast travel which sucked and the stalkers really became a huge pain. You can`t run while in eagle vision so you don`t know where they are and have to rely on the annoying whispers to know when they`re close, but it didn`t really matter unless you were exploring and finding treasures because you didn`t spend much time in NY during the story.
Hunting, crafting, ship upgrades, naval campaign and legendary battles all made a return in this game (legendary battles are much easier which was a bummer). The developers really took the best parts of AC 3 and 4 and made this game which made it really enjoyable to play, it`s too bad it was too short and we didn`t have the stealth movements of Unity because this could have been the best AC game to date, especially after Unity`s failed attempt at upgradable weapons/armor/character and multiplayer campaign; I mean if I want to play an in depth RPG I`ll play games like Baldur`s Gate and if I want to play with people I`ll play games like WOW, but not the place for the AC franchise, stick with what works, stay unique.
As of March 24th 2015 there are still some movement bugs and climbing issues that really make you want to throw your mouse, I even got stuck off the playable map a few times and had to reset/fast travel to reset.
So if you loved 3 and especially 4 than this is worth the money, if you`re a fan of the series but didn`t like 3 or 4 wait for the sale.

Capsized turned out to be far more fantastic than I initially gave it credit for.
There are plenty of physics-based games with transparent mechanics and floaty controls where the player is given the opportunity to mess around with objects and you can be as silly as possible, but in Capsized the physics take a back seat. Nevermind the fact that you can jetpack around lasso-ing objects and enemies alike to navigate- the world itself is the star. The environment is beautiful, full of detailed organic life and creatures and I don't even know what, and an equally awesome soundtrack echoes throughout giving this game an A+ for atmosphere in my book.
I played the game on Hard and it was a fun difficult challenge, when I encountered a few specific types of enemies. If you're looking for a surreal space adventure with some narrative and a bunch of weapons, this is a small-package game done right.
