Because of this, it's hard to compare it to something like a Telltale game, where the illusion of choice still exists. However, you can still say that this is a game because it has a failure state if you don't perform some actions that the game requires.
With this little debate out of the way, I think this is a pretty nice product. It has an interesting story with some intriguing twists throughout the two hours or so that this experience might give you. It also has a nice way of describing characters with flashbacks, without making the main story too tedious. The characters themselves are pretty well acted, but in my opinion they might be a little flat or simple. No that this is a bad thing, but it might throw some people off. The setting is quite convincing and enhances all that psychological horror vibe going around the bunker. Some spooky stuff. All in all, this is a very polished experience with a compelling story which flows easily, without any unnecessary slowdowns.
In conclusion, I'd recommend this product to anyone that has an evening to spare and some cash lying around. I don't really think if this is worth a full $20, but at sale price (more than 50% off) it's a pretty nice game for what it would cost.
no es realmente un videojuego. Es algo más cercano a una película con elementos interactivos en relación a ciertas acciones contextuales, como pueden ser abrir puertas o inspeccionar habitaciones. No escoges opciones de diálogo o resuelves puzzles. Debido a esto, es difícil establecer una comparación directa con otros juegos como los de Telltale, donde estas cosas sí que existen y existe la ilusión de elección que caracterizaría a este tipo de videojuegos. Sin embargo, se puede seguir argumentando que es un videojuego si tienes en cuenta el estado fallido que puedes alcanzar cuando no realizas las acciones que requiere el juego.
Pero con este debate a un lado, pienso que es un videojuego bastante bueno. Tiene una historia interesante con varios giros intrigantes en las dos horas que puede durar, dependiendo de tus ganas de conseguir todos los logros. También tiene una manera bastante amena de describir los flashbacks sin convertir a la historia principal en un pastiche tedioso. Los personajes, interpretados de forma bastante convincente, pueden ser un poco planos o simples. No es que sea nada malo en sí mismo, pero puede molestar a algunas personas. El entorno del juego es bastante verosímil y potencia el horror psicológico que persigue el juego. Logra asustar algo. En general, es una experiencia bastante pulida con una historia atractiva que fluye bastante bien, sin ningún parón innecesario dentro del ritmo del juego.
En conclusión, recomendaría este producto a cualquiera que tenga una tarde libre y algo de pasta rondando cerca. No considero que valga 20€ enteros, pero a precio de descuento (más del 50% rebajado) es un juego bastante bueno para lo que costaría

I have no problem admitting that I am a Halo "fanboy". I played Halo when it was first released, and every subsequent Halo ever produced. With that being said, I'm no slouch and I won't sugar coat this games' flaws just because I love the franchise. Read on for a legitimate review from a player who was there from the very beginning.
This game is short; incredibly short in fact. It was designed around mobile devices that utilize the mobile version of the Windows 8 operating system, specifically tablets. People are going to tell you, "Incorrect, it was developed to serve as an interim game during the time between Halo 4's release, and Halo 5's release on the Xbox One". The sad fact is that this statement is just flat out untrue. This game was designed for the sole purpose of Microsoft attempting to secure their portion of the mobile app/game marketplace. They figured that if they released a "Halo" game for the mobile device world, the name alone would convert a giant percentage of gamers who would be new to Microsoft products, while at the same time getting existing Microsoft/Halo consumers to purchase and subsequently convert to the Windows 8 operating system. This is evident of the fact that Halo: Spartan Assault was initially released EXCLUSIVELY for Windows 8 and its mobile device distribution.
A few months later, once Microsoft realized their fiscal mistake in limiting the game only to Windows 8/Mobile users, they released the game for Xbox One and then the Xbox 360. Notice anything coincidental in the timeline of those releases?
And so all this background information converges nicely into the rest of my review:
Feel and Control:
Cons:
- The aim controls for a mouse and keyboard are weird at best. The crosshair feels like it's on this fixed dimensional grid and you can see that when you try to aim at enemies, it just snaps into the general vicinity of where you want to actually aim, and not directly on what you're aiming at. At least not without a couple attempts. If anyone reading this review is familiar with the aiming system in Alien Swarm, I'm certain you will agree that Halo's aim system falls incredibly short in comparison. Halos aim system transitioning feels incredibly forced when using a mouse and keyboard, and although it's not the absolute worst I've had to deal with, it just doesn't feel right.
- The crosshair and aiming should have been tied directly in to player movement instead of being what is essentially "free". You can have the Spartan looking in one direction and have the crosshair all the way in the opposite direction direction, while being unable to shoot at the target until you move the Spartan with WASD. This system destroys the flow of the game.
Pros:
- The gameplay in terms of graphical smoothness is perfectly fine. Because of its top down nature, there isn't much strain on the processor or graphics card, and so aside from the aiming system, the gameplay is smooth.
- There are only eight or nine(I forget how many exactly) keybinds, three of which can not be modified, which in turn means that the controls are simple and easy to get used to.
- The game offers both controller and mouse/keyboard support. Mouse/keyboard feels forced, but the fact that it supports these two input devices and not controllers exclusively, trumps any flaws that the aim system may have... in my opinion anyways.
- The loadout system definitely offers some variability and is sure to give you some new ways to complete the missions, subsequently raising the level of the games replayability. Not by enough though.
Maps/Graphics/Environments/Storyline:
Cons:
- One thing I noticed that really confused me was that the maps had elevated surfaces in certain spots. This game in particular lacks in the ability to portray depth of any kind, and because of the fact that the gameplay is TOP-DOWN, I can't for the life of me understand why the developers would create maps with any variation in elevation. In a top down video game, the maps should be completely flat otherwise the inevitable happens; because the game can't portray depth well, you find yourself in a situation where it appears as though you're shooting at an enemy but for whatever reason your bullets just stop short. In reality, because the map in that particular area is not flat like it should be, you're positioned at the bottom of the elevation and the target is positioned at the top. You unwittingly shoot at the floor while the bot shoots you dead. -- This situation in particular has happened to me quite often, and occured mostly in the first two missions.
- The game is painfully short, and apparently most of the other reviewers seem to either be in denial, or just hardcore, blind-faith, "drink the coolaide" type fanboys. There is virtually no replayability in this game unless you strive to waste a large portion of your life maintaining a spot on the global leaderboards. THERE IS NO CO-OP ON THIS VERSION. Co-op is offered exclusively for the Microsoft gaming consoles, which means you can't even play it with your friends. Thumbs down.
- The story isn't anything special.
- The game has some issues with multiple monitors. If you have multiple monitors you will see that other than the monitor you're playing the game on, the rest will be blacked out. And it's inconsistent as well; sometimes it does this, and other times the game won't black out your other monitors.
Pros:
- The graphics are smooth, and the environments/maps are also done pretty well with only a couple exceptions.
- The cut scenes are awesome, evident of the typical work from the Halo franchise.
So in the end, is it worth $4.99? Yeah, I would say go for it if you're a Halo fan like I am. One reason I bought it is because it's the only Halo game offered on Steam and I've been waiting for a Halo game to be released on Steam for a long time.
But here's the main reason I bought it: I'm hoping that if enough people buy the game and show interest in the idea of having Halo games released on and supported by Steam/Valve, then Microsoft will, eventually, go through with the decision to port the older games to the Steam platform.
A bit of a pipe-dream you say? Probably. Especially now that Microsoft has formed their own version of an app-store/gaming platform for PC users. I can hope though... I can hope.

Disappointing, to say the least. As someone who has played every AC game (minus the portable/tablet games), I would actually rank this one the lowest.
To me it feels like a glorified expansion for AC4. It recycles all the mechanics from AC4, with a few minor tweaks, and calls it a new game. As someone who has played a lot of AC3 and 4, there was really nothing new here, and I found it rather boring. Even the story, which is mainly what I was interesting in checking out, was a waste. The characters are all two-dimensional, and the protagonist's motivations are paper-thin. Sure, this has become standard for AC at this point, but still sad to see the wasted potential here. All the interesting stuff is actually hidden away in Templar letters that you must seek out as side objectives. And to top it off, [Spoiler Alert!] I was not happy to have to kill Adewale. Wasn't worth it! [End Spoiler]
This should have been a $20-30 stand-alone expansion to AC4. As such, I recommend to anyone still debating buying it to just wait for a good sale on it. Rogue is a game that was clearly made on a shorter timeline with a smaller budget, and to do that they simply recycled assets and ideas from previous Assassin's Creeds, cut the story short, and generally put out a subpar experience.
And I think I'm in the minority in saying this, but I had much more fun with Unity and I would recommend spending your money there instead.

Devil Daggers is one of those games where you can physically feel your progress. No artificial level up systems. No arbitrary acheivements. It's just pure progress in your own personall skill and knowledge.
Your first run will last around 15-30 seconds, usually from an unexpected skull behind you. You eventually learn what to listen for so you can anticipate the enemies. Then you start mastering the shooting mechanics of the game. Then you start memorizing the spawning patterns. Then you start strategizing what enemies to shoot first. Next thing you know, you're already lasting over 2 minutes on each run.
This game is ridiculously frustrating, but it's such a rewarding test of dexterity and on-the-dot strategy. I wholly recommend this game, especially at its low price (it's even 50% off at the time of this writing!).

The Game has pretty much been summed up in other reviews, but I just want to give a quick insight.  When I first saw this game on steam I thought that it would be a game in a similar vein to Illusion Software's titles, based around the neat-ish concept of Cindrella. I thought it was kind of cool something like this could actually show up on steam (on the front page), as it gives it a greater feel of legitimacy, and I couldn't resist the low price. I saw the R12 rating and done some research, obviously finding about the so called "R18" version of the game, I installed the unoffical patch immediately before playing. See Paragraph 4 for differences.
I jumped into the game kind of expecting a different sort of experience to the one I got. I was expecting something light weight, and relaxing that didn't require a huge brain or time commitment and was perhaps mildy sexually stimulating. After Playing The First set of Dungeon's (basically the tutorial), It was clear it wasn't that, I expected some crazy over exaggerated japanese story to kick off (around the actually decent gameplay), with some explicit content in it.
The Game reminded me of Atlus' (excellent) Catherine for a bit, with the block puzzles and general themes. Sadly the similarities stop there. This game basically has no story content outside of the openining cutscene. After finishing the first set of Dungeons, I moved onto the second, only to be dissapointed. I only really went as far as I did due to nostalgia for how good that game was. The sad thing is the puzzles in this game are actually half competent. Someone has clearly put a bunch of work into making them, but the game needs some substance to hold it together, and it has none.
The Whole "R18", "Adult Game" thing is simply ridiculous, and truthfully a scam, as well as a marketing ploy. There is one file difference between the two verisons (file can be found via many steam community guides). And the fact they they are charging 3 times the price for that version is ludicrous. Even in the R18 verison the adult content is extremely light. I switched back to the R12 verison for tetsing purposes. The only additions in the R18 version are more sexy costumes to buy, the ability to remove her skirt (seriously no where near nude), Also a breast size slider (You can scale a polygon), and lastly the inclusion of Torture Traps. The last one is the most meaningful addition as it adds various traps you can interact with around the levels, which cause cindrella pain, They are generally very simple animations, definitely nothing to get *excited* over. I am not a fan of censorship, but this is hardly even that. The traps feel like they were part of the original game, the rest feels stupid and tacked on. There is no real reason why the R18 verison of the game couldn't have be put on steam, other than the fact it was being marketed as a game for adults, and probably so the developers could trick you into paying for their version.

So I have tried playing many crpgs before including classics like bl1, bl2 and even divinity original sin 1 but I think this is the first crpg that I will actually finish. Most times when I have played a crpg game before this, they have never grabed me like this game has or if they have they have done it only for a short amount of time before my patience with the game ran out and I give up on the game. This is the first crpg where I was genuinely hooked right from the start and it kept me hooked even after being 50 hours into the story.
To me dos2 felt like a very streamlined game compared to most crpgs and dos1. The improvements to ui and the inventory system + plus the crafting system are amazing and such a big improvement over dos1. Some people might think its a bad thing but its not really. Its a question of prioritizing what is more important to the player. If you are the kind of person that wants a clunky nostalgic game that deliberately apes even the bad parts of old crpgs than this may not the game for you!!
Also, dont get me wrong I did like dos1 overall but this being a big improvement overall over dos1 is why I loved dos2 so much and only just liked dos1. They made it fully voiced lines right out of the box (dos1 was fully voiced in the enhanced edition) with more interesting characters and companions to chose from and a better character creation and stat system compared to before. The tone of the game has become noticebly darker (it still has whacky humor but not as in your face as in dos1) and the stakes more personel for our heroes and their companions.
The main story campagn is also done nicely and there are some memorable sidequests to waste  time on and get some valuable xp and loot for your characters. (no random fights or locations to go grind in this game, there is a limited number of enemies that you can fight) I played the main campaign in coop mode first and in it you and other members of your party are not neccessarily cooperating more like competing because its the goal of each character to surpass others and actually ascend to
I also played it by myself after that with another character and to me both modes were fun but for slightly different reasons.
Btw gotta really appreciate how replayable the game is. Many quests have several ways you can resolve them (especially quests in act 1 and 2) plus a cast of 6 origin charcters to chose from as your pc and as companions and it all makes the game very replayable.
The combat in this game is turn based just like dos1 and it feels even more special than in other turn based games like Xcom/Xcom2 in which the entire game revolves around just the combat at least to me. Positioning and smart usage of skill combos can ensure you win or lose a fight and your stats directly affect those skills and even how much of an advantage good positioning will give you. Combining various elements with spells and arrows also adds a layer of complexity and makes the whole thing feel very unique and most fights feel engaging.
Many feel that its a drag to have to first have to bring down enemy physical or magical armor before you can actually start having fun with them and having to do this for every enemy you meet but the system is there so unlike in dos1, you cant simply keep enemies cc'd each almost for the entirety of the fight. Another complaint is that many battles ending up with everybody being consumed in flames or poison (which also leads to flames) but its more of an annoyance compared to dos1 because just clicking on your sleeping bag heals the entire party immediately after the fight and if you want to compare it to other crpgs like pillars then its still much less confusing, its mostly easy to see which characters are what they are doing at all times.
My complaints are (more like gripes) are that a) Larian hasn't put enough effort in polishing the game visually and stylistically in some places even when compared to the original Divinity Original Sin enhanced edition. The game could have used better cut scenes and more animations.
Pretty cutscenes and animations aren't what make a game fun but they can make you more immersed and their ability to wow us is why they became such a big part of games.
b) The camera cant be zoomed out enough in the game and often times will clip through objects and just be horrible overall. If I could zoom out more it would have been great. (There's a couple of mods on the workshop for this but they have downsides like disabling achievements and more too unfortunately)
While it does have a few issues like being a tad bit buggy (no more than your average 18gb game in 2017 which is why I didnt dwell on it) I think it’s a very very solid game from larian with a very good story campaign. It has good coop and a unique game master mode plus an arena mode thrown in for free too plus you can also play it split screen with someone if you have two controllers handy making it possible for 4 people to play this with two copies. And considering all of the above its a very good buy!!

This is a YES IF, NO BUT recommendation - This game is currently in VERY EARLY development.
Those are the three words that sum up the 70's for me, but there's a lot more to the polyester decade than Boney M. and the Bee Gees.
Whilst the western world was listening to John Lennons "Imagine" and losing interest in the American Moon landings, the Soviets took their own giant leap for mankind with the launch of the first space station Salyut 1, this was the first step towards a permanent manned presence in space and a proof of concept for the following Salyut missions.
Back in the west there was a very different but just as significant "first" taking place in the form of the commercial release of something called "Pong".
Pong was of course the table tennis inspired arcade machine which managed to introduce "gaming" to the masses and make a buck or two for Atari in the process.
Pongs popularity was such that it led Atari to release "Home Pong" (not something you get when you break wind in your living room but rather a home games console which allowed fans to enjoy virtual ping-pong without leaving the house.)
This was the start of a revolution in home entertainment.
The humble paddle and ball game (well, stick and square game) paved the way to the mainstream world of gaming we all find ourselves living in today, a world where anything can be simulated, from table tennis to truck driving, space invaders to space stations, everything is fair game.
Which is great for us, we're living in a golden age of virtual entertainment, since Pongs release in the 70's the games industry has gone from strength to strength, but can we say the same about our extraterrestrial endeavours?
Remember that space station we spoke about? Salyut 1?
That was launched in the same year as Pongs release, but it wasn't quite so long lived, orbiting the Earth for just 6 months before it fell like a led zeppelin in to the upper atmosphere.
The death of Salyut 1 was followed by several other short lived stations before the construction of the more enduring Skylab and Mir platforms in the 70's and 80's (both of which have subsequently died a fiery death).
Of course we now have the International Space Station, with 4 giant solar arrays providing power to over a dozen pressurised modules, powerful batteries and sophisticated telemetry.
The ISS is a modern wonder and one of mankinds greatest contemporary achievements.
So we have the disco decade to thank not only for a permanent manned presence in space but also for the greatest hobby in the world, gaming.
That's a significant legacy and one which has culminated in the development of a game called Stable Orbit, a space station simulation title by Codalyn which gives you the chance to indulge in your gaming hobby and celebrate our space based ingenuity at the same time.
The first thing you should know is that at the time of writing Stable Orbit is in Early Access (and paradoxically not that stable) so you can expect a lot of missing features, a few bugs and the occasional crash, you can also expect some nausea but I'll get on to that later.
So Stable orbit gives you the opportunity to construct your very own space station.
As it stands at the moment, you start the game with a core module already orbiting the earth.
This provides a limited amount of power, cooling and communication capabilities.
There's also just enough life support to accommodate one brave astronaut.
From these humble beginnings you're tasked with constructing a station to surpass the ISS itself.
You're going to need a source of income to fund your construction ambitions, building a lab module is a good place to start as at the moment this is the only way to generate money (although this will likely change as development progresses).
You're going to need some extra power to keep things ticking over so putting up a solar array might be a good idea, maybe you could build  living quarters too, it'd be good for your solo astronaut to have a friend up there.
Of course you'll also need to construct a shuttle dock so your intrepid new astronaut can board the station, the dock is also important as it allows your station to receive vital supplies from Earth.
Your astronauts have developed an addiction to luxuries like food and water so it's a good idea to fit a "space door" to accept the online grocery orders, after all a dead astronaut isn't great for productivity.
The next problem you've got is that whilst the solar panels are providing electricity to keep the lights on, they only work in sunlight, which isn't much use when you're on the dark side of the Earth and actually need to "turn the lights on" so it might be wise to attach some batteries to help keep things powered when you're orbiting through the shadows.
So now you've got a lab making you money and a living quarters for well... living in, everything is powered and your astronauts are fed, watered and oxygenated but it's still far from an orbital paradise.
Your technological tin can will get pretty hot with all that machinery running and unfiltered sunlight blazing on to its surface, you're going to need to build a radiator or two to regulate the temperature before you cook your cosmonauts.
A few button clicks and a short while later you'll have a Station happily circling the Earth without the need for further input from yourself.
You can click on a module and order some repairs if anything has gotten damaged, you could expand further, build another lab, a larger solar array, a bigger living quarters etc.
Bigger is always better and you can definitely build an impressively large station by repeating basic module construction over and over but therein lies the problem of playing through an early access title like this.
The current lack of content means that things are going to get stale pretty quickly and once you've built a station or two there isn't much left to do apart from admire your handy work in all its glinting metallic glory.
Watching your station orbit around the earth is fun for a while and a game of "find your house from orbit" will entertain for a few minutes more but you'll soon get sick of that and as I mentioned early, you might also get sick in the physical sense too. 
Whilst this "space sickness" might add a little something to the immersion it's an additional level or realism I could definitely do without.
The nausea is caused by the rapidly rotating Earth constantly spinning like a crazed merry-go-round beneath your shiny new space station.
The game currently has 3 speed settings, Too Fast, Way Too Fast and Vomit Now.
From a design point of view there's no denying that you need the ability to fast forward time speeding up the construction of modules etc, but you should also be able to slow things down and catch your breath.
Taking a few minutes to enjoy looking at your creation is part of the fun with this sort of game but with your station hurtling around the world at what feels like light speed, taking in the view can be an eye watering experience.
Stable Orbit desperately needs a "real time" setting so we can enjoy the view without the need for a sick bag.
There's a game I haven't referred to so far and I'm certain that if you have an interest in this type of simulation it will have already crossed your mind.

Through the years I have played many magical games. Games that really can draw person into the world, as if the player were actually there. However, this game is different for everyone. Some will say that they LOVE the TES series; some will say that they LOVE the fallout series; some will say that they LOOOOOVE their girlfriend/boyfriend and to each his own. Although for me there is quirky little game that really spoke to me on a very intimate level.
I started my journey of love a couple years back with Shadow of Chernobyl (you wanna know bout that?! go look at my reveiw there!). It was gritty, it was good, it was clunky as hell but it had more character than any other game that I had played by then. I went on to play the second game and finished the seriees by playing Call of Pripyat a little here and there. It was pretty ok. I mean, it isnt no Ride to Hell: Retribution. NO! this game has the best immersion and best atmosphere of any other game!
STORY TIME! You decide to go out for a little stroll, wanting to explore a little bit like you did back in Skyrim. When all of a sudden! BAM! bullets be flying! you dont know from where, you just know that you need to get your pretty little booty outta there. In the distance you hear "Cheeki Breeki!" not being able to speak the slavic language you shrug it off, as you should. you decide you peak your head out only to get it blown off by your assailants. GAME OVER! you have to go back to your last save which was 4 hours ago. RIP you. So you quit and go back to playing Fallout. You pick up the game after a few months, forgetting everying that transpired last time you played. You decide to go out for a little stroll, wanting to explore a little bit  like you did back in Fallout, when all of a sudden! BAM! bullets be flying! You remember whats going on. Fashbacks of the last time you played dominate your mind, you can feel it all coming back to you. You dive behind cover and save, like the good S.T.A.L.K.E.R. player that you are. You pull out your weapon and peak your head out. Bullets graze your face as you retract back under cover. While your head was out you spotted one of those [insert enemy faction of your choice] dirt bags. You line up your sights on one of them and pop 'em in the face. He drops. You spot his buddy and pump bullets into him as well. The third guy was sucked into an anomaly and exploded so you dont get the pleasure of taking his life. The bulets stop, the smoke clears, you are triumphant. you stroll over and grab their loot. But a bloodsucker comes up behind you and mauls you to death. No one is ever safe in the zone.
But in all seriousness this game is very unique. I think the best way to describe it is rather than a FPS that revolves around a RPG like Fallout or Borderlands it's a RPG that revolves around a FPS. However, it goes above and beyond by also adding in elements of horror and suspense but everything that this game is, is blended perfectly into a great game. As I have said so many times it has the most character an the best atmosphere of any other game that I've played and I believe that is the biggest selling point of this game. NPC's in this game actually do something in their lives. Getting into a fire fight is an actual big deal. You have to tread lightly and be wary of your surroundings. It is a fun and unique experience that I have yet to find in any other game.
TL;DR - atmosphere and unique ideas up the wazoo. Hard and unforgiving but rewarding experience.

I want to recommend this game, and oh MAN does it do some amazing stuff. It's so much fun up to a point. Maybe it's just this one level, I don't know, but I want to put a fair warning out to people. There's a lot of hype for this game, oh boy there's a lot.
And a lot of it is deserved, to a point. That final boss of Chemical Plant zone? WOW, so much fun, and so nostalgic.
But... Sky Battery Zone. SEGA, what happened? This level is... horrible. I just turns up the unfair hits, the buggy spinning propellers, just... wow. It's all so good, why was this overlooked. So many things in that stage aren't telegraphed well at all. I died trying to go back up into the ship just before the first boss so many times because at no point does it telegraph that you need to press
in order to get back.
And then the first boss. No. Just no. It's offensively bad. It takes everything they did to make Sonic "new" and "fresh" and puts it against you. The drop dash becomes a liability you can't avoid. Holding down the jump button just a little too long and you're getting a face full of spikes. I time overed so many times. Those propellers that have a 50/50 chance of flinging you to a safe place or... spikes, that you can't let go of without risk of life and limb. And then... the dreaded...
Game Over
SEGA, get rid of lives. It's 2017. Just because you have to honor Sonic's glory years doesn't mean you can't include some new ideas. Lives are dumb, they extend the game out longer than it needs to be. Having to go through the frustration of Flying Battery Zone over and over was the most frustrating thing I've experienced in a long time. I can pass the old sonics; they're a product of their time, but this is unacceptable.
In essence, if you're okay with a few really bad design decisions, and don't mind slamming your head against the wall for a few hours, go ahead and pick up this game. You're the perfect audience. The story is about a man named John who's born in a nuclear bunker and who's a bit… er, 'special'. I think 'autistic' is both the correct term and the politically correct term but I'm not sure. Anyway, at the start of the game, there are only two survivors left in the bunker: John and his mother. But John's mother is sick and she dies after telling him to keep performing the daily routine to assure his continued safety in the bunker. Soon after, an alarm goes off and John needs to break his routine to venture into parts of the bunker he'd rather leave alone, because the past haunts those areas…
Graphically,

That's an impressive gathering of resumes, although a quick Google search of those names seems to indicate these were all small supporting roles.
Overall, the music is fine but I would have liked to see an option to reduce the music volume as it sometimes drowns out the voices of the people talking. At one time, the music was a resounding, reverberating noise that caused me to reduce the volume of my speakers until that part of the story was over.

Crusaders Kings 2 is for people that look at the more common rts titles and think "this isnt complex enough". It is to date the best sandbox grand rts I have ever played. The only real weakness of it is a rather bad tutorial and the overwhelming scope of the game making it hard to approach if you are new to Paradox Interactive developed titles. If you have never played a paradox grand strategy game before I would recomend playing "Hearts of Iron 4" because of the excellent tutorial of that game but if you have played that for awhile and is ready for a new grand strategy game, this is the game for you.
As in all grand rts titles the graphics really exists to accomodate the UI and little else which as of now it does very well, though it wont win any awards for graphical fidelity or aesthetics. Trying to talk about the mechanics of a game like this is like trying to describe the ocean bucket for bucket, on the whole however as of the date of this review the mechanics are fair and understandable... after understanding how they work. But even getting to understand how the game works is a part of what makes it great, it is one of my favorite parts of paradox grand strategy titles is the exploration of the game mechanics. In that department CK2 really delivers even now I occasionally find out about a feature or a rule that I didnt notise or understand before even after 800+hours of the game.
But if I was going to mention some failings of the game outside of the tutorial then, the norse pagans are somewhat OP but less so than they used to be and this could be due to me playing at too low a difficulty. I have also experienced some very occasional crashes to desktop since the last patch (reapers due), though the yearly autosave makes it rather unproblematic. Mid to late game can become somewhat slow if you have built an empire that becomes "too big to fail", though again might be me playing at too low a difficulty. As an interactive movie, this game is great.  As an adventure game, it's pretty lacking.
The movie itself is well done and features sincere acting, cool use of music and sound editing, and clever flashback sequences as the true past is revealed.  There is a little sloppy thinking to the relatively brief plot, but overall it works, and if you are a fan of FMV, you'll dig it.
However, there is nothing at all to do but click to advance, with a few opportunities to overlook items or scenes that don't matter to the outcome.  The game does NOT let you skip anything you've seen, it resorts to quick time events as gameplay, and it's not clear when it has saved.  Missing a click can result in death in a few places, and you will have to watch some amount of video again without the ability to skip.  I'm not sure all the achievements are working properly, but maybe it's actually possible to fail to find a few hot spots among the grand total of about 50-100 clicks that will get you through the game.  I can't stress it enough: there are no puzzles.  You either click to advance or turn the game off.
I'm glad I bought the game (on sale) and played through twice to see the scenes a second time, but that's all there is to do with it, so I'm done.  The story is maybe an hour and a half long if you play straight through.  But if your tolerance for adventure game mechanics is high and you just want an interactive movie, it's a really good one.

Well, I can not in good conscience recommend the game.
First of all, there are no improvement over black flag, if anything, it is a lot worse.
The map designs are as bad as they are in most  AC games, unfortunately. Free running, but only on paths the level designer allow. So, you end up in many spots, where the ground is just above your knees, and you can neither climb, or jump. You can however take the long way around, which the level designer decided was the only option.
At least, it does not have all those stupid dancers/fighters for hire :).
It does however, suffer from AC1 syndrome, which is grind... Blackflag was grindy, but the amount remained reasonable, coupled with the ship/pirating which was kinda new(with the boarding mixed with all other naval stuff going on). Rogue does not benefit from this "new feeling", on top of this, the map is a LOT bigger than AC4 it seems... sound good right? Well, not so much. When you have only about 5 things you can do, but you need to do them, a LOT. That is grind, it's not enjoyable. AC1 had the same issue imo...
The game also suffers, like most AC games, from consoleportization, an unfortunately common disease these days... As such, every climbable points, will look exactly the same, as usual in AC games I guess. Once you've seen the 3 or 4 possible climbable textures, well, you know how it goes in other AC games... I wish they'd reworkd the maps and textures, pc's are not console, they can handle a little variety... please, enough with level designs made entirely of copy/paste from like 20 items :(.
So the levels feels a lot like AC3/4 materials, slightly altered, and off you go. It does not feel like they bothered to design new models or textures. If they have, the addition is invisible.
The voice acting from the non cinematics is atrocious. If you do not speak french, you'll probably be sorta ok. If you speak french, prepare to be annoyed very quickly... The npc's keeps repeating the same 2 sentences, over and over and over and over and over... It is utterly ridiculous, and there is no immersion at all. AC4 felt a lot better on this point imo. This is particularly bad after helping out soldiers in those mini battlefield side activities. At the end of the fight, they just keep saying there'll be double ration, the captain is an idiot, and we won, non stop, forewer it seems :S. I am hoping it is just a bug, and will be fixed, as it is truly annoying. NPC's in towns/villages also seem to do it, with their not so random chatter, it is breaking the poor amount of immersion there is.
In short, they ♥♥♥♥ed it up :)
I'm nowhere near done with the story, because the game bores me so much, it is actually hard to finish it, due to boredom.
A new "activity' was added, which consist of helping soldier in small battles. You'll get a couple of different objectives, which includes destroy something (one or more), kill the captain, and cut the flag. So, same as a boarding, except it happens in a forest... and this is where it screws things up... to cut the flag, you need to be anoymous, while the flag is usually surrounded with enemies... PRoblem is, if the allies all die, you loose and have to wait to a reset... which means, because they are usually utterly worthless, you'll have to run to the flag, and hope no enemies tags you, otherwise, you'll usually be screwed due to the AI being utterly stupid.
Couple of new weapons have been added, which are the same as before, but with a small AOE effect on them, so hardly "new" per say.
Another addition is "stalkers". Assassin's trying to kill you. While I understand the concept of it, they are simply annoying. While you're trying to hide from guards, or simply exiting a mission area, being surprised by a stalker is fairly annoying. I don't really like those, sure they fit the lore, but do they REALLY need to be that many virtually everywhere? I mean, 7 stalkers, in a non mission area, in a forest, with only 2 collectibles, no village nothing? They certainly want me dead if they're stalking virtually dead spots on the map just waiting for me... Once again, immersion breaking. It makes no sense that they can be present virtually anywhere, including in places only there to make the world seems larger, and are not included in the actual story :).
All in all, get it if it's on sale, as in a really good sale, like 75% or more, otherwise, don't waste your money :)

Ladies and gentlemen. 'Lo and behold! Before you is the ultimate middle age simulator game called CK2! A game with many good sides and few flaws!
What is so good about this game? You play as a landed ruler that has to essentially keep his dynasty in power, during which your ruler constantly switches due to assassination plots, depression, diseases and old age. Sometimes you assassinate people that you should not but you end up doing so for the sake of de jure claims and lands, sometimes your homosexual son who is going to inherit your lands will assassinate you, even if you raised him to be a great ruler. The roleplay-like and immersion-like events are amazing and hilarious when you think about it longer. For example, first you become a viking, then you die due to your heart not handling the action of your lustful wife. And modding is wonderful in this game. There are limitless possibilities to what can be done here with the power of modding!
What is the flaw of this game? It is simple. The dlcs. Without them it is still a full game, but with them it gets even more replay value to the point of almost infinite replays. So you when you end up bored at vanilla you end up buying the next dlc and so on. How is this a flaw? Simple. When I bought this game and as many of the dlcs as possible, I did not realize that I had spent 120 euros in total. I was slightly dissapointed as I had in mind of buying a couple more games, but could not due to this event in ck2.
So is this game worth buying? Absolutely yes. Especially if you like mods, because you can find numerous wonderful mods on Paradox Forums that give you more replay value with the dlcs. With each new dlc and overhaul mod you get more replay value. All in all it is a great game and remember, kids....

If only Ubisoft had further refined this tried and tested formula for their next gen game rather than released Unity 3/4 done, who knows what would of happened.  Anyways, Rogue is a further refined version of Black Flag, with a fun, gorgeous, and expanded naval section and the same Creed land based stealth we've grown to love (or hate). For me, as one who loves the classic AC experience and adored what AC3 and BF did with the Naval parts, this game is the true next-gen sequel in place of Unity. While Rogue visuals aren't quite as detailed on land as Unity, the sea and ships are stunning.  And while Rogue doesn't let you crank up the visuals like Black Flag did to show off its lush jungles, in exchange, you get a vastly smoother experience. Black Flag was very difficult to keep running at 30-45fps without the aid of 3rd party drivers and while I can't speak for Unity's PC counterpart, I doubt it eclipsed 30fps on console or PC in its first few months. Rogue, on the other hand has not dropped below 59fps in my 20+ hours so far (i5 4690k, gtx970) and the few visual options it does offer do make look very pretty indeed.
In short, if you're a fan of Black Flag and are looking for it's true successor, then look no further..

A tough but fun adventure. Ian Livingstone's eerie fantasy world is evoked with sparse, straightforward prose, and Tin Man Games have brought it to life quite well, with new artwork and some subtle but effective music. As tricky as this gamebook is, a "Free Read" mode lets you explore the story backward and forward, trying out every path without worrying about a game over. And even the "Hardcore Hero" difficulty gives you unlimited "bookmarks" (save points), so it's a challenge, but not an insurmountable one. The Steam achievements give an added dimension to the game, encouraging you to visit every location (and you can get them in Free Read mode—well, except the ones for finishing the game on higher difficulties!). So, if you're a Fighting Fantasy fan, or you want to see what old school gamebook fans grew up on, give it a try. ;)

I'm updating my review cause I want a Steam Badge. (and my views have changed a little)
A return to form for CK2. The team that made this dlc understands the core design philosophy of the game and I really appreciate the work they've put in over the past few months. The features they've added might need a bit of tweaking at the moment but I can see them fitting in perfectly as soon as they've been polished a little.
Epidemics are tense and truly deadly to the unprepared. Precautions are costly but a badly timed epidemic can totally ravage your court without protection. A bunch of new traits have been thrown into the mix that add character to your ruler. Interesting events involving your court physician and quarantine spice up peacetime and give you a few more reasons not to paint the entire map as quickly as possible. Everything you'd expect from a disease-focused expansion is here, a lot of new flavour has been added to the game and you're getting good value for your money. New event chains are interesting, especially those that get triggered by secluding yourself at court.
On the negative side, non-epidemic diseases like cancer are FAR too frequent in the game at the moment. It's not unusual to have like 10 rulers die of cancer in a row, potentially crippling you for the entire game in a way you can't prevent. Having a trait like stressed is also a death sentence now, as combined with other new negative health factors you will regularly see characters die of stress in their 20s. It's possible to overcome this as feudal characters while still having an enjoyable experience, but tribals (ESPECIALLY unreformed pagan tribals who will be stuck with elective gavelkind for a long time) are currently not fun to play at all since having tons of sons (meaning constantly losing tons of land due to elective gavelkind) is almost mandatory to make sure your dynasty continues. You can't even build hospitals as tribals, so this is unfortunately the only reliable way. An extra problem is that currently, christian kingdoms and empires will almost all adopt elective gavelkind succession straight away- which is very jarring for the setting and means you'll barely ever see familiar dynasties remaining in power any more.
But here's what I really came here to say. If you're coming back to CK2 after quitting during the Conclave patches like me, you'll find Paradox has done a great deal to fix the game. The devs have offered a ton of useful options to modify your experience when you start a new save file. Notable options (i.e the ones that made me really happy) are:
*Shattered retreat can be turned on or off (works with ironman and doesn't even disable achievements!)
*Defensive pacts can be turned on or off (like the above, works on ironman!)
*Interfaith marriages (I've been wanting these back since forever)
*Turn off AI seduction focus. For the first time since way of life released, you can expect to have a child that's actually yours.
*Changing world event timings. Prefer to start in the 9th century but never manage to play until the mongol invasions? Now you can make them arrive earlier. Want to see the new black plague in action but don't want to play the late start dates? Got you covered.
I'm so happy that I can finally enjoy the latest version of CK2 again, despite the problems I mentioned above. Even if you liked Conclave and the accompanying changes then you can keep playing with all of it turned on. (not judging, whatever you let the game do to you in the privacy of your own dungeon is none of my business) Best of both worlds. This new expansion and its patches allow you to remove a lot of the restrictions that made the game lose its charm for a lot of people. I couldn't be happier with the direction Paradox has taken.

This is probably one of the best PC Assassin's Creed games.  The optimization is damn near perfect, the seamless control switching from controller to mouse+keyboard is amazingly easy.  The touchscreen menu functions are great for people playing on a touch laptop.  Gameplay wise, it's pretty much the same as Black Flag, except now there are more incapacitation options.  The locations are beautiful, the story rival's Ezio's in quality.
Overall, the game is fantastic.  Though no game is perfect, and Rogue is certainly no exception to that.  Like every Assassin's Creed game, the parkour system is imperative to the game's success.  The free-running in Rogue is amazing, the terrain was well built and designed for fast paced running and killing, though the place where the parkour falls a bit short, are in settlements and New York, where there are many buildings with angled roofs.  Now there is a slight problem with climbing up an angled roof from the side.  This problem makes it so you occasionally freeze in place and can't climb up or down until you shuffle to either side before you can move again, even though you should really have no problem with climbing up.  I'm sure this will get patched soon, as it is an easy fix.  The ocean combat is pretty good too.  I haven't played much of Black Flag, and I hated the ship combat from AC III, but I hear it's great in Black Flag, and it's not that big of a deal to keep something that works very well in another game that involves the same kind of setting.  Since this is an Ubisoft game, the enemy spawning is awful, and none more so, than in the ocean.  There WILL be times when you board a ship after incapacitating it, and after you are through collecting your stuff, there would be another ship bearing down on you.  Believe me, when you get good at handling the Morigan, you will be able to dispatch these fools easily, and you will even be able to take on a Man-o-war without much trouble.  But then again, if you are coming to this from Black Flag, you would already have plenty of experience with ocean maneuvering.    Combat wise, it's pretty great.  A major step up from the AC III engine.  Now, there are no longer whole platoons of soldiers that track you down to kill you for bumping into someone.  Hiding is pretty easy, because there are bushes pretty much everywhere, and you can always use them to sneak around and take out a couple of guards, or you can play it non-lethally and just sneak.
All in all, Rogue is an amazing game compared to previous installments in the AC series.  I would highly suggest Rogue over Unity (if you are looking for story quality)  Unity was a bland, dry Ctrl C+ Ctrl V of Ezio's story, Rogue has the main character (as well as you) thinking about your allegiance to the Assassins, and how your ideals may differ greatly from them.

The Caverns of the Snow Witch is a direct revision (which includes an option to play using the original artwork and font type) from the Fighting Fantasy series of books written by Ian Livingstone. (This is the 9th book of the series, circa 1984.) This D&D (Dungeons and Dragons) genre choose-your-own-adventure style book plays exactly as the original book form minus the physical dice. (Paper and pencil are optional.) Here the dice are built in.  Roll for stamina (health), skill (fighting ability) and that all so precarious luck.  Once the character stats are established time for some adventure which includes choosing directions (usually at the infamous 'T' junctions), making decisions (fight that creature or sneak past) and death, if one is defeated, in combat, by a poor decision, or when one's luck runs out, literally, and it always does eventually.
The D&D style books, the precursors to RPGs and their ilk, are as challenging as any AAA game in modern day and as unforgiving as any bullet-hell.
Storyline: Start as a hired sword to protect a caravan going to a snowy hamlet deep in Ice Finger Mountains.  The hamlet is attacked and the caravan owner offers 50 gold to track down and eliminate who or whatever slaughtered the inhabitants.  Off to find the monster (man or beast) with 50 gold gleaming in the eye but with no weight in the pocket, the adventure begins.
Gameplay: This book is divided into four separate sections: 1) Tracking down the beast 2) The Caverns of the Snow Witch  3) Beyond the icy caverns and 4) Breaking the curse (of course there is a curse, a death curse to be precise.  No villian lets the "hero" live if they can help it, even if the villian dies first.  An auxium of Villiantry.)
As I stated before this game is unforgiving, and the "hero" often dies.  However, just with a book, the player has the option to go back a page or two and try a different route or option.  There are also unlimited bookmarks (the equivalent of fingers between the pages) if the player needs or wants to try an entirely different direction or make different choices. (I suggest bookmarking often, at any place with choice and especially before battle).  Plus there is the all-important, and often can save your xxx, DICE SHAKE.  The dice shake is when the player seeing they just rolled an extremely low number like boxcars (1 and 1) on their white dice and who or what they are fighting just rolled a higher number on their red dice.  This higher number will damage the "hero", if not outright kill them.  So the player has the option to quickly (like in maybe in a second) click on the dice again before they settle to get a reroll.  One reroll per dice throw, and the player has to be fast.
There are three modes to this game. 1) Reader's mode (or cheater's mode) which allows the player unlimited health regeneration and the option to avoid all battles and poor decisions by using 'free choice' (which opens all options available to the player even ones they are not 'entitled' to have).  2) Adventure mode or normal mode, play with the stats rolled in the beginning of the game. (Remember the DICE SHAKE works here too.)  3) Hard mode play with a handicap in both stamina and skill (half for both) making battles much harder to win.  (Not recommended unless the player knows exactly where all the stamina, skill and luck power ups are.)
An excellent example of the D&D genre, the storyline is tight and moves along fast, challenging and unforgiving, where battle damage affects the player and poor decisions can have lethal consequences.  A fun read and extras include a brief history of Fighting Fantasy and the "find" art gallery depicting both the original and updated illustrations.
Highly recommended to those who like old school and to anyone looking for a different type of RPG adventure.  (WARNING: READING is NOT optional and spamming will get the player killed, very quickly.)

Excellent:
Theme. The game brings this out very well. It really feels like you are running the company that is responsible for the interstellar expansion of humanity. The visuals work well. The planets look cool. The ships have fun names. The line of ships you get going from home, out a colony, and back looks good. It is satisfying to see the progress as a colony develops. It feels like you are working to established permanent homes other worlds.
Strategy. You have a lot of choices. You are always deciding what ships to buy, what they should carry, and what route they should take. You usually have options that are either "cheaper and better now" or "more expensive and better later." You always have "things to work on." You can choose where new colonies will go. You can tinker with current trade routes to make them more profitable.
Good to Mixed:
Balance. The overall balance seems good for what has been released. There are subtle changes that could improve things, and I think the devs have their eye on that. (They have made a few balance changes since the game was released and all the changes were steps in the right direction.) Later game stuff does need more work, and this is on the dev roadmap forward.
Replayablilty: Generally one game versus another does progress in a similar way. You have information about what is needed and you take care of that. If Mars needs more water you buy a new water ship and send it to Mars. You can get a long way just by playing this way. That said, after a few games you understand more of the subtlties and can min/max your trade routes. I find that I enjoy trying to minimize extra costs and squeeze out maximum profit.
The UI. The UI has improved greatly with the latest patch. It seems that this is where the devs are currently focusing. It does take some getting used to, but with the new changes I feel like I have the tools I need.
The AI. I have played a number of games both with AI opponents and as the only company. Honestly, I've never felt like the AI opponents add much to the game. In games with AI opponents, they sometimes help get colonies going a bit faster, but usually I just notice them doing thing that I wouldn't do because it's inefficient. Generally they serve as a minor hinderance. By late game the AI doesn't have much of a presence. For me, the game is less about beating my opponents, and more about establishing a huge interstellar trade network. Whether the AI is present or not only affects that a little. Also, I have found games without AI opponents to be more fun. Without the AI you have more control in things like in fine-tuning demand without causing famine and deciding what colonies should get limited resourses. If playing against a competitive AI is important to you, this game might not be the right choice. If you aren't worried about the AI and your priority it to build up your trade empire, the weak AI won't hinder that. Also try playing without any AI opponents.
Reasons to wait a bit:
Lack of detailed information. Much of the financial numbers are "under the hood" at this point. There are ways to estimate the cost of a given trade route if you work it out. The calulations that go into how much a route earns is a mystery. The Devs have said that this is on their radar.
There are a few bugs (It's still in alpha). The devs have been doing a good job of dealing with these, but some can be annoying. That said, in my last game, there weren't any bugs that prevented me from making progress.
Overall:
I'm having a lot of fun. The theme is great. Bringing 500 million people to an interstellar Earth-like planet is satisfying. I find that I want to try out new strategies and maximize my income. The devs are working to make the game better, and it is improving. I certainly think it is worth the price in its current state.

I like it! You get to be a princess and solve puzzels and stuff (just puzzels. Not much stuff). But the game is simple, and simple is good. You're a princes being held captive by an evil king, and rather than playing the character of a knight who goes to rescue her, you play as the princess trying to escape.
Yes. The puzzels are fun, but I think the brilliance behind this game isn't so much in the gameplay, but in the concept and story. In this game, Cinderella is a sweet princess who is horribly treated, and on top of that, has the worst luck when she gets thrown in a dungeon for seeing something she shouldn't have. They make you feel very sorry for her. And I think what's great about the fact that you control her character, rather than playing as a hero trying to save her, is that you really feel like you are helping her escape. Like she has literally no friends in the world, no heros, no allies, but you. It doesn't feel like your playing as her, and that you as a player are the important one, but it feels like you are helping this character escape her horrible life. You, as a player, are the one force in the world who can bring justice to this cruel world the princess inhabits
Sure, there could possibly be some far better puzzel games out there where you play as a dot trying to get passed cubes. But I don't care to see a dot succeed. I must help the princess escape! I'm her only hope!
Most likely none of this crosses your mind when you play the game, but I believe everyone feels it in the back of their minds. I know this was very in depth for a simple puzzel game, but I believe it's all true, and just want to give credit where credit is due. So please buy this game. It's very fun and deserves your support!

A satisfying gameplay loop.
Devil Daggers is a pure survival FPS where you're tasked with surviving as long as possible against a demonic horde, with large devils spawning swarms of skulls and bugs to beset you. You have two "guns", a rapid-fire stream of daggers and a quick shotgun like burst you activate with a double-click. You don't run out of ammo. You just try to control the crowd swarming you and eliminate the larger devils before they make it worse. Then you die, respawn, and try again. There is no progress, no advancement, no real change despite the increasing variety and deadliness of the devils.
That all said, it's a very solid little loop of gameplay, owing to the excellent sound design (giving you an aural cue as to the devils around you and their proximity) and the quick nature of the game play. Right now I have the top of my awfully wide Steam friends list at ninety-nine seconds of survival. There's an achievement at five hundred, but I never expect to see it.
If you're up for a punishing, simple, FPS experience loop of gameplay excellently done, this is worth your time. It is exactly as advertised and nothing more, but is priced to match that.

Fantastically quirky short puzzle game. I haven't completed it yet, but I've been longing to play the game since played the demo a few days before the release date.
The game is simplistic, I will not deny that. I also won't deny there are some rather janky mechanics due to the Unity engine allowing you to have a 'cheap' and unintended solution to a level. There is also some jank in the hitboxes of the swinging axes which can be pretty frustrating if you're not thinking and just going by appearance. The levels are rather open ended, so you can solve them multiple different ways.
As many have said before, the game and its story are pretty short, but is novel and unexpected compared to the look of the game. The levels for the most part look the same and you'll probably end up well accustomed to the textures of walls and blocks, and the model of Cinderella herself (which looks alright in my opinion)
There are a couple of customisation options in this version, not as many as the R-18 version you can purchase, but honestly, for such a game I wouldn't really worry too much about not having a skirt disable feature or jiggle physics slider- if this is something that you can't live without then I guess you should get the R-18 one, but this is basically the same game.
So the game is what it is. For a £3-4 game, you can't really say you're not getting what you're paying for. The game works, and works well enough to be an enjoyable experience for anyone who isn't frustrated at puzzle games yet and wishes to sit there pondering the  next course of action!

I'm thoroughly impressed with how this game plays. As a long-time fan of the 16-bit era games who fell out of love with the Sonic franchise shortly after Sonic Adventure, this is a fantastic balance of classic and new. The team of programmers and artists have hit just the right notes of bringing back what I loved about the old games, but dusting them off and freshening them up at the same time.
And damn, if that "you're about to drown" music doesn't still give me minor panic attacks!
I had some trouble with my controller at first (using a Logitech F310 Gamepad), but when I switched it over to PS4 controller settings in the options menu, it worked flawlessly, and in the Get Blue Spheres special stages, I could tell a lot of attention has been paid to the timing of the controls by the way my muscle memory of when to press buttons during these stages instantly kicked in and took over.
The difficulty level seems good to me so far, though admittedly I'm currently only three zones in.
I also like that they're not leaning too hard on story. Big cutscenes in a classic style Sonic game just wouldn't work. I'm not here for story, I'm here to play a good, fast-paced platformer. The decision to include a bit more of the story/context in the user manual (which has been designed with such care and well worth a look in its own right) was a good choice.
And the music! Christ it feels right. Even sitting through the staff credits (available through the options menu) induced a very specific and refined strain of nostalgia. Even new tunes are laced with some kind of throwback drug, I swear.
I've played a lot of games specifically designed to be of a certain era of gaming, and this one is currently right near the top of my list of the most effective and affecting. And I can tell with the vs modes, I'm only scratching the surface of the hours of fun I'm going to get out of this game. VERY happy, and I hope the reaction to the game is solid enough to send a message to Sega that people, despite surface gripes regarding DRM issues, want more installments in this series. Because I sure do.

This is an introspective story on a well-explored topic: the Lone Survivor in a dystopic world.  It's done pretty well too, and has a good soundtrack for the presentation, but it's
a game as the gamer community would define.  The Bunker is an interactive story, where choices matter and actions have consequences.
First, a few notes about the interactive aspects.
1.) Most of the choices you make will be in regards to finding cookies, as opposed to survival.  It's easy to miss the few minor collectables in the game if you're not looking for them, and it's not always intuitive to look where they may appear.  Darkened corners, minor minutia of background details, and simple but unannounced puzzles are all a factor in various scenes.
2.) You generally cannot fail to advance the storyline in a permanent way.  If you don't do the right things, you'll stay where you are, or have to go back to an area (small map, there aren't many) in order to have the correct storyline interaction.
3.) There are four places (that I found) where you have a chance to do something (minor) that will have a small storyline impact, and all four of these are timed - only a couple of seconds to click or not click.  I succeeded twice and wasn't paying attention twice, and there seemed to be no effect on my game, and I still got 100% achis in a single playthrough (read note below about 100% achis).
That said, the story was good, and told in a manner similar to flashback-flashforward.  This is because the protagonist, John (who is alone after chapter 1 - no spoiler, you'll learn this right away), is essentially a blank slate with almost no interactions with people for most of his life, but memories enough to haunt him in the cavernous halls of where he's lived by-the-book.  And I mean literally an 'eat, press all the buttons, toilet, take meds, wait for next day' kind of by-the-book.  He's alone in an underground bunker after the bomb, and was born there, stayed all his life, and outlived everyone else there.
Music/ambiance is acceptable to the setting, genre, and events in the storyline, but there is no music volume control, only a game volume setting - and I think that lacking audio would take away some of the game.
As a rule, during interactive parts there is ample opportunity to roll mouse over the screen in order to locate interactable items/areas, so it's not hard to find everything.
Despite my 5 hours in the game, about 2.5 of that was spent idle for cards, and I'd estimate that the presentation can be completed in about 90 minutes, but that those interested in achis or completionism will probably go about 2.5 hours.
Regarding the 100% achis, there are two endings, both of which can be gained from a single playthrough - but it will require you to reload via the CONTINUE button at game menu after choosing one ending; then you just go back and choose the other from save.  This will cost you about 7 minutes or so because you essentially have to repeat the last chapter, up to the choice at the end.
I think this was worth the sale price, and I don't want either my money or my time back, but there's no way I'd ever recommend spending $20 here.  For $5, go for it and settle in for an evening entertainment, in a "game" where you can eat popcorn and lounge with your pet while you're still paying attention enough to get the needed interactions.
For it's genre (interactive story) I think this is a good effort: 7.5/10.  Good job, Green Man, Splendy, and Wales!

A decently acted FMV thriller, which despite its short playtime and meager gameplay convinces through good direction and an atmospheric dystopian story.
You'll be put in the shoes of John, who was born in a fallout shelter, while nuclear war devastated the UK and which he hasn't left once, until a daily routine he meticulously clings to gets torn to pieces through events unfolding, subsequently leaving him questioning his whole past, throughout which his mother was the almost only human interaction he ever had in his whole life. Well, and that's pretty much all one can tell about the game's story without spoiling everything, since it has a rather short playtime (~2 hrs) and any replayability is quite limited due to the fairly linear experience The Bunker offers, in the end being more of an interactive movie than a game and relying more on QTE's than obscure puzzles classic FMV's were rather known for. There are literally no choices for you to make until the very end, making you more of a spectator than a player, and even though there are interesting collectibles conveniently placed throughout the game, one has to be warned that you'll have to start anew once you miss out on any single one of them since you can't go back or select a particular chapter from the main menu.
Granting its flaws in the gameplay department, The Bunker manages to immerse one in the struggle John faces though and never slips into any cheesiness that would certainly destroy the atmosphere this game thrives off: It has very solid acting, good direction and an intriguing script - all which many FMV's unfortunately lack. It probably wouldn't win an Emmy, but it still creates a nice experience and is equivalent to better TV show episodes or short movies. Reel loops are hard to detect, cuts are nicely done, all the actors provide a good performance and the soundtrack helps to keep the suspense throughout, although it tends to overshadow some dialogue on one or two occasions.
If you're mainly undecided because of its rather hefty price tag, just wait for a good sale, lean back and enjoy a nicely told story, which albeit its shortcomings gameplay-wise got me hooked through its production values and good script.

Reading the reviews for this game, it seems nobody read its description before buying it.
It IS a mobile game ported to PC.  You WILL be disappointed if you expect an Xbox or PC quality type of game.
Halo: Spartan Assault also has nothing to do with Halo 4.  Did people really expect an AAA quality game for $5 ?
What do I think of it ?
It's a pretty damn well polished game for a mobile game.
It feels like a Halo game.  Driving the Scorpion feels like driving the Scorpion from the console series.
The port to PC is almost flawless.  It's not a cheap♥♥♥♥♥port like Microsoft did for Halo 2, they actually took the time to make it playable with a mouse and keyboard.  My only issue is that after an hour playing it, even my desktop struggle to make the game run smoothly.  Memory leak ?
I'd say Halo: Spartan Assault is pretty successful.  Of course the graphics are not that great, of course it's not the FPS we expected.  But it actually has a story that fits within the Halo universe, it's playable, it's entertaining, it feels like Halo and it is Halo.
The cons ?
After a while playing it, the game tends to get a bit laggy.  It IS a mobile game, it is short and does not have high quality graphics. A couple of missions are a bit repetitive (survive for x minutes while we toss infinite waves at your face), it's fun at the beginning but does not really make you want to play it again and again.
The pros ?
The price.  It's Halo.  It's one of the very rare mobile game with an actual story to it.  Even for a mobile game, the graphics are pretty damn good.  Hopefully this is a test from Microsoft to see if they should release an actual Halo game, and hopefully it works.
I think this game is pretty successful and people who are into the Halo series should at least give it a try.  It's only $5.
Kudos to the devs, they did a great job.  9/10.
