I'm not going to tell you that Assassin's Creed: Rogue is a good game. Since AC:3 it's my firm belief that Ubisoft has gotten out of touch with what makes Assassin's Creed such a great francise. Gone are the days of mystery and intrigue, of skillful assassinations and deep character development. In my opinion AC:1 was an absolute masterpiece, with AC: Revelations finishing off Ezio's story perfectly. Since then Assassin's Creed's quality as a series has diminished. Technologically the Assassin's Creed series has flourished, with the world and people becoming much more beautiful. However the story has fallen flat, the idea of 'genetic memories' and Abstergo is being stretched thin beyond its limits. We all thought after Ezio we would finally see the modern day AC game, but that does not seem to be within Ubisofts sights. They wish to continue milking the series with progressively worse off games. Unity was a turning point for Ubisoft. If they mess up the next game, thats it for the series in my eyes.
All of this aside, AC: Rogue does make me happy. It may not be technologically the best AC game, with last gen graphics and none of the improvements that AC: Unity recieved (Although this is more of a blessing considering how shoddy Unity's engine was) However AC: Rogue story once again makes me giddy to play the game, to push forward with the new character, Shay Cormac, my new favorite protaganist. He is the first Assassin to become more self aware since Altaiir, and see that the world is not so black and white, Templars and Assassins. After seeing the darkness and ignorance of Assassin's he goes off on his own, to seek his own path. This leads him to become Templar, and therefore fufill his wish to help the world and atone for his sins.
Cormac is easily one of the best protaganist since Ezio, with an amazing voice actor and real emotions and a true goal. Not only that, but he is also the most well-equipped of the protaganists. Not since Ezio has an assassin had so much gear to choose from. This makes playing as Cormac exciting to play both as a stealth character and a fighter.
The game also loses out on having Assassin minions but it gains the fresh mechanic of constantly being hunted by Assassins, which you must dispatch.
Is Assassin's Creed Rogue a good game? That you will have to decide for yourself. As a whole it is one of my favorite in the series, with the best leading character, the biggest arsenal, fully realized naval warefare, new mechanics, and the chance to be a Templar. The story is short but intense, it took me 15 hours to complete with slight deviation, and I have barely scratched the surface with extra content, as usual AC games are satisfying to complete 100%.
I have changed sides. The Templars are humanities salvation. See the world through Shay Patrick Cormac's eyes and decide for yourself. May the Father of Understanding guide you.

This game is a perfect blend of an FPS and the open-world genre. It's the kind of game that you would play on a Friday night or on a weekend night. Coming back after school/work, getting into the 'TGIF' mood, eating dinner, and then playing S.T.A.L.K.E.R. That was how I spent most of my Friday nights when I was 15.
The game thrusts you into a post-apocalyptic environment teeming with mutants and bandits, with you alone against them.There are 3 large maps that the player can travel among, which are set against the backdrop of the Chernobyl nuclear power plant disaster that occurred in 1986. You play as Major Degtyarev, who is sent into Pripyat to investigate the cause of the crash of 5 Mi-24 'Hind' helicopters. Along the way, you'll meet new people, factions, and encounter powerful mutants.
One of the most famous mods for Call Of Pripyat is Misery. It changes the whole atmosphere completely, massively improves the graphics, and makes the game feel more realistic. Bullet damages resemble real life, with 1 or 2 shots to your body being absolutely fatal when unarmoured. I highly recommend this mod to all Stalkers out there.
Pros:
+ Engaging, deep storyline (some with surprising plot twists!)
+ Extremely well-designed and immersive environment
+ Many interesting enemies and mutants to fight against, with each requiring different tactics
+ Suspenseful atmosphere (you'll never know when a bloodsucker might sneak up behind you)
Cons:
- Dated graphics in original game (by today's standards)
- Bugs (some of them game-breaking, causing your game to crash)
- Lousy AI (blocked doorways is not uncommon, sometimes killing you)
- Installing the Misery Mod may require more powerful hardware to handle the performance
My recommendation is that you get this game on a sale, play through it without mods first, and then play it again with the Misery mod. You will see the huge difference, and you will be hooked for a long time, especially if you're a fan of FPS games.
Overall: 7/10

WARNING!, to understand this Review, you must have played/seen Assassin's Creed IV and to an extent Assassin's Creed 3. Do not issue a bad rating on the merits of you entering in the franchise. Sorry, friend, this review is not for you.
This game can also be described as Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag 1.5. When I finished, I almost wondered why the Installation didn't come with patch notes instead of a features description. Don't get me wrong, it's good, bloody damn good, but read this for a minute to understand why.
The Good "Patch Changes"
- The new Air Rifle is amazing, and doesn't look as, and I hesitate to use the word here, racist or shoe-horned as a bow and a blowpipe. It provides a lore-friendly way of dispatching your foes as well as later receiving a Grenade launcher, which allows you to stun, berserk or just explode a large group of enemies. It opens tactical opportunities to spark a large group of enemies to berserk instead of just one.
- The Outfit selection takes a big dump on the "15 colours of robes & hoods" thing and presents you for once with varied outfits that don't require dlc. I completed the game in the uniform of a Royal Navy Captain.
- The Environment is much more varied. The River Valley is - as the name would suggest - a large map of rivers where you can encounter medium-sized ships and set up clever ambushes. The Ocean map is much wider and you can capture Man'o'War ships there.
- You are a templar now, which means the United Kingdom won't bother you anymore, unless you want to, atleast in the cities. backstab, shoot and murder to your hearts content!
- You can now murder civilians in a lore-friendly way. Instead of arbitrarily getting de-synched at the third mishap like a kindergarten boy being sent home because he threw gobs of sand around, you will now have tough-as-♥♥♥♥e bounty hunters sent after you. they will kill you unless you are smart and shoot them first. But it's lore-friendly and more immersive that way.
- Say goodbye to the always-on, required-to-progress Kenway's Fleet! That's right, the Fleet now is entirely offline, and gives you not only junk househlod decorations but also some very nifty Items and beautiful cosmetics. Also, it's optional, so if you are not interested in the Naval Campaign, good riddance for you, but it will generally give you money, as it works on the ingame currency now, the pound, instead of the arbitrary-a*s "Gems" that were ripe for mobile mini-transactions from the word go.
- New York makes its return from AC3. I find it to be the more ugly of the two cities, boston was always more to my liking, but they managed to spice the city up by restoring the burned-down districts and adding a less depressive day-night cycle. Since I played AC3 the colour orange gives me spontaneous cataract!
- Getting boarded is fun. It eventually ends like the other boardings, you can only be boarded by assassin brigs and pirate-hunters and you might lose up to 7 crewmen, but it's fun.
- The Elite Upgrades for your ship are not buried in some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ places that you will only visit once for the entire game
- You now have frequent ammunition chests in the cities to refill your special ammunition for free. It gives a shoddy amount of bullets, but I'll get to that eventually.
- The sailors of the Morrigan look like Royal Navy sailors. BRITANNIA RULES THE WAVES!
The bad changes... and yes, there are some.
- When you capture an enemy fortress, your boarding crew does not follow you on land, which is sad. I liked the atmospheric fortress battles even though the teleporting ship crew in ACIVBF incited philosophical discourse with other players/co-workers at the water dispenser.
- The highest-Level set of pistols and the only pair of the main game that kills grenadiers/captains/assassins in one shot is locked behind a challenge. Alternatively, you can buy the DLC and aquire the Russian Flintlock pistols. It's just a scheme to funnel more games into buying the DLC.
- Shay, the Protagonist, is a dunce at looting conventional bullets from corpses. While Edward could restock himself twice over by just stabbing some guards in the middle of the street, Mr. Cormac needs his reading glasses whiped for him because he only loots one or two cartridges off a rifleman. This is a big deal, because in the marine sessions, assassins hunts and time-based objectives as well as the main missions, you will be heavily relying on your pistols. Unless, of course, you are sneaky. Which I ain't.
- Ammunition does not refill when you get onto your ships. They really don't have a crew chest where I could "borrow" some of these precious blackpowder lifesavers? REALLY? Edward Kenways crew was cool about that. meh.
- The story is a bit short for my taste, but that is only because they had to develop this game alongside the *spontaneous irony* colossus of cultural value and perfection *irony end, cough cough* that was Assassin's Creed: Unity.
-IN SHORT-
If you couldn't already guess, I am going to recommend this game, because my complaints are all tiny things.
So, that's about all I got so far. I might add more grins or gripes in the future. Keep the discussion in the comments civilized. And have fun if you decide to buy! I guarantee you almost certainly will.

This game is definitely a must play for any Assassin's Creed fan who enjoys both it's rich narrative and insanely addicting gameplay. I think it's best to compare to AC Liberation. Liberation introduced a character tied to Connor Kenway in AC3, much like this game introduces a character connecting to Haytham Kenway, Adewale, and Achillies Davenport. I feel that, in terms of lore, this game holds a lot more weight than Liberation and is overall a more polished and envigorating experience. It returns to the excellent naval gameplay of AC4 whilst bringing back some favorite characters from AC3. In addition, Shay Cormac allows us to experience the Templar Order in a new light. When we got to play as Haytham Kenway in AC3 we got a glimpse at what the Order was really about and how their goals aren't so different from the assassins. Shay offers this same opportunity - as players used to fighting for the assassin cause, Shay enables us to question their true motives, making for a really interesting story.

I hope that this game gets more attention because people deserve to know that this game carries great weight in the AC universe and it's concepts could and should be given the opportunity to return later on in other games to continue to delve into the understanding of the ideological war between Assassin and Templar.

TL:DR: The bottom line is, Sonic Mania is so refreshing to play. Its combination of old and new make it a great game for both fans of the game and newcomers alike.
Gameplay? Fantastic. Many people think Mania is like a remastered sonic, but that's not the case. It's and entirely new game, but just recycles some assests from older levels as homage to the previous games. The older levels are remixed in different ways with new paths and obstacles, typically in Act 1, then do something new with completly new mechanics in Act 2. (Chemical Plant Zone Act 2 is a good example). Unfortunately they brought back the stupid "Get the Blue Spheres" minigame, however they built an actually good minigame for getting chaos emeralds that you'll want to play. Overall the gameplay is the shining gem of sonic mania, and makes it one of the best 2d platformers on the market.
Controls? Fantastic. You will need a controller to enjoy the game the most, so once that's taken care of you'll have tight controls reminiscent of the genesis era. The twist? Everything runs smoothly and they have added some intuitive new tweaks that make the game play like a dream. Granted, I did have a few control hiccups, but I think that has more to do with my skill than the game itself.
Performance? Fantastic. Everything runs at a smooth 60FPS with no lag or the genesis audio glitching (where  the system would miss parts of the MIDI because its too busy computing the graphics).  I haven't run it on my ultrabook or anything so I don't know how optimised it is for non-gaming systems (I used a 1070 lol), but the consistent framerate vastly improves the experience.
Sound? Fantastic. If you grew up with Sonic, there are plenty of old tracks and SFX thrown in that get your nostalgia off. If you didn't, Sonic music is already pretty good FYI, but mania also takes the music, like the levels, and remixes them to give a nice blend of old and new.
Visuals? Again, Fantastic. The 60FPS really allows for some amazing animations to find their way into the game that makes the game so much better. It's hard to describe, I suppose the modern tech driving retro visuals simulate what it was actually like to experience what was once cutting edge graphics back in the day. Like for example, there are some 3D objects, backdrops and some sprites that that match the early-90's 16bit 3d, but would be unable to be run on an actual genesis. I dunno how to describe this "new retro" feel, I'm not an art critic. The game just looks good and feels both old and new.
Overall, this is a fantasic game. I would have easily more for it, and I'm really glad SEGA decided to hire fangame makers rather than giving them DCMAs. I think Sonic Team finally realized how to make Sonic good, and I'm hopefully optimistic for where the franchise is going in the future. The bottom line is, Sonic Mania is so refreshing to play. Its combination of old and new make it a great game for both fans of the game and newcomers alike.

Again, I'm no Poirot but I'd figured out what was happening/happened pretty quickly.
But it does do something new - FMV is no longer grainy clips in a small box, its full screen HD in your face and I'm sure with a bigger budget and more time this team can develop someting good.  A few pedant points though - who cuts the protagonists hair in the bunker and an S10 respirator needs a filter to work!!  I'd give this a solid 7/10 and you should probably play it through once and then maybe go back and get all the achievements (if you have OCD).

This game is a true example that FMV games aren't just a cesspool of joke games with terrible acting and scripts.
This is a great interactive film,
, with tremendous acting and portrayal of characters.
The camera work is spot on, the scenery and prop use is brilliant and truly makes the game atmospheric.
You play as a man that was born in a bunker that was built to protect its inhabitants from nuclear war, in other words you've never seen the real world, you've been isolated from the outside your entire 30 years of life and you end up being the last person alive in the bunker, the 2nd last person was your mother which you loved deeply, she did a lot of things to keep both of you alive, to prolong your lifespan.
It becomes apparent quite quickly that John,
, are struggling with some sort of mental illness, an inner demon, from being isolated, from being alone for so long.
John, after his mother dies, tries to keep his same, dull and dreary routine alive, day in, day out.. but eventually systems within the bunker start to fail and John needs to repair them.
There are some moments in the game where the acting is not top-notch, or you notice something that's just a bit off, something that didn't flow as naturally as everything else, but in my opinion the good outweighs the small amount of bad by a long shot.
I wish for nothing more than a sequel, or another FMV game made by the same developers.
I recommend this to everyone who may be interested, new comers or FMVeterans.

Oblivion was great for its time. Released in 2006, that was the year before I graduated high school and attempted college. I played it to death and back on the Xbox, probably netting a few hundred hours. I remember getting the manual and reading it in class, like it was any other textbook.
Now I've recently returned to it, several years later with an improved computer and modding capabilities and it does breathe some life into the game. While I can agree that Oblivion, by itself, has not aged well... It helps to mod it up to increase resolution, textures, and getting a mod to make everyone's faces look a lot more... normal. Doing all of that, it's like coming back to an old (but prettier) friend.
Shivering Isles also continues to be a fairly fun expansion to play through. With two whole armor sets to work towards, dungeons with great loot, and a main quest that is extremely rewarding in terms of magical powers and loot, it's great to play through once more. (Incidentally, SI is also the most stable part of the game. Not a single Crash-to-Desktop or bug to be found while I was running around the Isles. Perhaps I was lucky, but perhaps the expansion just runs that well).
I can understand how newer aged gamers may not care for the game too much... But Oblivion is worth exploring for some retroactive nostalgia if you started this franchise with Skyrim. Play this, and I'd also recommend Morrowind while you're at it.
Happy gaming!

I've played guitar for over a decade, but wanted to get into playing bass. I self taught the guitar through tab and listening to songs over, and over, and OVER until I mastered them. I figured I'd look into Rocksmith as a new alternative to learning to play.
So far I've found it quite enjoyable. I'm breezing through learning the bass guitar, much faster than I did with guitar. I still don't understand any theory, but I can hear and make sense of the notes and rythms.
Playing the "career" is fun because you get to learn new songs, but if you really want to get good at learning your new instrument, you NEED to spend 10x more time in the "techniques" section than in the actual career. Practice each technique and earn GOLD in all of them. But don't just go for the gold, play it until you can perfect it and you'll learn how to play 100x faster than just playing "good enough" to pass the required scores to perform &/or get the gold. If you're not perfecting each song or technique, you're not learning anything.
They say practice makes perfect; WRONG.
Perfect practice makes perfect. If you mess up, play through it until you recover. Then replay it again.
Though the methods of learning may change, one thing will ALWAYS stay the same. Repetition, repetition, repetition. Don't think that you can just skate by on the minimum require score to complete the "career" and call yourself a guitarist/bassist, because you'll really only be a medeocre wannabe. Just put your heart into it, and you'll master the instrument.

Capsized is the first commercial title from Canadian indie developer Alientrap. At first glance it looks like a familiar side-scrolling, run-n-gun platformer, but is set apart by its detailed visual-style and variety of gameplay mechanics.
The campaign's story is very bare-bones and basic, as is the comic book style by which it is conveyed. A series of beautifully drawn images, sans any dialogue, are shown panel-by-panel telling how a spaceship of Human astronauts is hit by an unidentified object, so they are forced to suit-up and evacuate via the ships escape pods.
Brief, 1 to 3-panel story strips also serve as introductions to each of the stages and your objective in them. The introductory strip for the first stage shows one of the pods crash-landing (upside down, I suppose where the name “Capsized” came from) onto the jungle-like surface of an unknown alien planet. You play as the spaceman that steps out of it and you proceed to follow your first vague objective: explore the alien planet.
Capsized's gameplay is mix of exploration, puzzle-solving and shooting action, using WASD to move and the mouse to aim your targeting reticle. Objectives are usually simple; reach the end of the area, destroy certain targets, collect items etc., though completing them often requires more thought as puzzles are introduced and the enemies get progressively heftier,  more wily and numerous.
The stranded astronaut can use a nice variety of futuristic weapons to blast away alien scum who are selfishly trying to protect their home world. Though you start each stage with just the puny blast carbine, there are plenty more to choose from should you discover them within the stages. From basic pulsar rifles and flamethrowers to advanced homing nano-bot launchers and the devastating “Quasar Array”, there's a suitable weapon for every situation.
Aside from the weapons, you can also jump and stomp “plumber style” on weaker enemies with your hefty space-boots, or use the handy grappling beam to grab rocks (or, indeed, small creatures) to launch at your foes. The grappling beam also serves as alternative means of traversing the environments; you can use it to pull yourself towards surfaces or swing throughout the planet like Tarzan in an spacesuit.
You also have a handy jetpack, activated with the spacebar, useful for boosting around the more open areas, provided you discover fuel for it. Jetpack fuel, as well as ammunition, extra lives and various powerups, are hidden throughout the stages. To reach them you need to find secret passages through the walls, basically by bumping against the edges of the map until you fall through it. It is usually worth scouring the terrain for these goodies to gain the edge, particularly in the latter half of the game where I found the difficulty seemed to spike considerably.
Physics play a big part in the game's mechanics; using the grapple beam is essential to pull levers, or lift rocks to drop them onto pressure pads and to open doors and access new sections of the maps, or to simply knock away debris that is blocking your path. There are situations where you will need to haul items across the stage to dump it onto a pressure pad on the other side (made somewhat easier by the low gravity), either dodging enemies or clearing them from the path in advance, the latter being my preferred method as some will actively hunt you when the see you.
Moving objects around can be problematic and was a major cause of frustration, particularly in enclosed spaces as they will get stuck in the terrain occasionally. Also in areas where you must carry rocks to pressure pads, I often found myself reaching them only to accidentally launch the rock off a cliff edge and groaning as it tumbled back down to the surface.
The music of Capsized consists of some nice atmospheric synth-tunes, though overall it lacks variety. The tracks are also usually rather slow-paced and, well, relaxing which I thought doesn't really fit an action game. Each stage has a different theme, but you will often hear the same tracks repeated in the background. This doesn't really detract from the experience too much, but I felt a lot more could have been done with the music, even if it is nice to listen to.
As for sound effects, there are plenty of background noises such as sounds of unseen wildlife tweeting or making insect-like clicking sounds, giving a nice feel of a living world. You've also got the basic laser weapon “zaps”, alien creatures' screeches and grunts and explosions and whatnot, all of which mesh together nicely.
One stand-out aspect of Capsized is the gorgeous, hand-drawn art style through which the vibrant alien world is visualised. While the environments are limited to the similar-looking overworld regions or caves beneath the surface, the amount of detail is impressive. Vines sway, docile indigenous creatures can be seen wandering about in the background, also weather effects such as sunshafts cascade over open areas in daytime stages, while mist and rain add to the visual ambience of night stages.
I managed the main campaign in around 6 hours, a decent length for an Indie such as this considering there's a good amount of content included to keep up the longevity.
There is a local co-op mode; you can team up with someone via two Xbox 360 pads to take on the campaign together, although I lacked the equipment to try it out. In arcade mode, there are other game types to play such as survival which pits you against waves of enemies, time trial where you must traverse stages in search for oxygen capsules to stay alive. You can also duel against another player, though only locally using two game pads as there's no online option sadly.
Overall, Capsized is a good game and although it is frustrating in parts and not particularly deep, it has enough variety and challenge to keep it fun and interesting during the 5-6 hour campaign.

Warframe is "bold, brilliant, but flawed."
PROS
Gameplay
There's many good things to say about this game and its developpers. For instance, the gameplay can be very engaging, especially because it feels like you're a constant power-fantasy in a way with how much destruction and havoc you can create. You can somehow perform a slide into a super long jump called "bullet-jump", only to follow it with a flip in the air and a mid-air roll, just to gain a ridiculous amount of momentum and distance. Digital Extremes, or DE in short, have a very bold and strange way in approaching their game designs, and it shows already in their movement mechanics.
Art
Their art's also a part where it shines brightly, if not the most, for many people. There's a reason why people often half-jokingly say that "Fashionframe is the true endgame of Warframe." While DE does take into consideration aesthetic, you can see in their designs that their vision don't always cater to the popular, more "slick" looks of other games such as Destiny, Halo and the likes. You want a gigantic robotic bow that shoots energy arrows which explodes into a sphere of ice? Sure, pick the Lenz. You have a thing for a writhing mass of tentacles that shoot viral darts out of its mouth and feeds on your arm to gain ammo? Take the Hema as your rifle. While I focused a lot on the visual arts, its music's also not to be ignored. You simply have to listen to "This Is What You Are (full version)" from the OST, and you'll get a good idea.
Community
There's lots to be said about its community too. It is, in my opinion, one of the most friendly and helpful online gaming community I've come across. While that comment may not hold much weight since I mostly play single-player games, I compare my experience with my friends who play such other games. It's surprising how our community can be quite caring to each other at times. And of course, Fashionframe unites a lot of us, as we post pictures on many platforms of our gears, or even color schemes to share ideas. We also can't forget about the developers and the community managers, who are probably one of the most interactive and, to some degree, transparent devs in the gaming industries. This is especially true if you compare to the recent fiascos with not only EA-DICE regarding Battlefront II, but also Activision-Bungie with the whole XP gain lies.
CONS
Now, Warframe's not all sunshine and rainbows. As much as I can praise the game, I can also criticize it very thoroughly without restrain.
Gameplay
Warframe, sadly, can be quite buggy. While there's the occasional visual artifact or inconsistency, the most jarring aspect has to do with how DE can take a whole lot of time before addressing certain bugs, even small ones that technically could be fixed easily. This happens even with some huge, progress-breaking bugs, such as the Jordas Verdict "Raid" that can bug out during one of its important phases. The boss has been buggy since its release and for years now have never been fixed properly.
And while earlier I said DE are bold, they're inconsistently bold as they may take a huge amount of time before even thinking of addressing community concerns on some gameplay elements, lasting for more than a year before starting the discussion again. This can happen even after a big major update that overhauls a gameplay, the overhaul itself still being flawed but not being updated properly, in favor of adding "new content."
I understand that a Free-to-Play game needs to constantly have new toys to keep players interested, but in the end, without a solid foundation to hold on to all the weight, it will eventually crumble into dust. DE, while bold on certain aspect, often (not always) find themselves shy away from good community constructive criticism if it targets some core gameplay elements. At least that's my impression.
Community
While I did say the community's one of the best I came across, one thing I often find is how entitled and vocal some people can be about the game. The passion can be seen, but often instead of giving constructive criticism, they rant on how the game should be without giving proper and better suggestions than what we already have. Adding to that, ironically enough, a lot of such topics in the forums that are short and "passionate", though sometimes borderline disrespectful, can get DE's attention to fix small issues. On the other hand, topics that detail the bugs or give feedback with images to illustrate their points don't even seem to get a glance at, or at least if they did, don't get taken into consideration compared to the one above.
There's a disparity in attention, which I can understand in a sense since DE's quite a small company, but the disparity is, sadly, quite consistent. A month-old Forums topic on a bug's being bumped up, linked to in each updates, with no attention received, but then one person comes and starts ranting loudly about the same bug a month later and DE immediately fixes it. I will be the first to admit that I'm feeling bitter about this because I relate to this subject.
New Players Experience
DE's been trying to make the NPE better throughout the years, but ultimately it falls very short. I personally believe it relates to the very first topic I talked about, how they favor "new content" instead of reworking old ones. New players come into the game bombarded with too many things to do and very little direction to go. Yes, the tutorial section made it better, but the lack of ingame description on many things and the reliance on the Wiki can be an annoyance to newcomers trying to immerse themselves. While I'm not asking for them to spoonfeed us everything, there's still a lack of helping hand for the massive content newplayers come across very early.
This, unfortunately, was made worse by Plains of Eidolon.
I will paraphrase Youtuber and Warframe Partner "Skill Up" on this. DE performed a masterstroke of a design by implementing the quest called "The Second Dream" behind a lot of hours of gameplay, especially because of its significance and how it recontextualize many things that happened before it. If you're a loremonger like me, the reveal during The Second Dream was probably a huge treat. I felt rewarded from my 3000+ hours of gameplay, felt rewarded from learning this "truth" after waiting for more story content for so long. I felt proud that DE didn't cater to "hype" by putting this reveal at the beginning of the game. They took a huge risk with The Second Dream, and in my opinion, it paid off.
However, the same thing cannot be said about Plains of Eidolon because, unlike The Second Dream, DE wanted to give as much early access to that location as possible. Instead fo creating more hype, to me it only hurts the already-fragile new player experience, by throwing them into a place where it's completely separated from the rest of the game, both gameplay and style-wise. Frankly speaking, new players should NOT be in the Plains already as they're still learning the game, and PoE introduces too many new stuff that will just confuse players.
For instance, there's no high mastery lock for the higher level bounties. New players may find themselves fighting enemies that are way above their level, and if they do succeed in the mission, they may get items that they don't even know what use they're for (Breath of Eidolon, Focus Lens, etc). Most of the content in PoE is locked behind The War Within quest, a quest that comes after The Second Dream, and so new players will be left confused as to why they can't have access to these content yet.
CONCLUSION
I still recommend this game, but I also recommend to thread carefully. Try not to rush through the content. Try to learn a lot yourself without spoilers, and don't feel bad for leaving the game aside for a while. You may come back to surprising updates at times, though I can't say Plains of Eidolon was the one.

An amazing game that combines grand strategy over an exhaustively long time period with RPG-ish elements brought in  through actually playing each successive ruler through history.  The many things to keep track of (quality of your heirs, who is currently plotting to depose you from your throne, how big is France getting, etc.) keep it challenging throughout.  The details are all interesting and compelling (to me, anyway), so the micromanagement doesn't seem to be tedious.
I particularly enjoy the challenges to playing a particularly moral character- what do you do when you're just trying to be a good Catholic king, not murder anybody, and then, out of nowhere, suddenly one of your children is possibly the spawn of Satan? (ridiculous storylines like this don't happen often, but they are wonderful)  Kill this possibly innocent child, or let the legions of hell come and help you to wreak havoc over Europe?  In Crusader Kings II, the choice is yours!

First and foremost: rocksmith 2014 (remastered) is this game, but better in almost every part. Get that game over this one, no matter your skill level.
You can also import the tracks from this game over there (at a one-time cost), which means the 'should you get this game?' question becomes more of a 'should you get this game for any other reason than importing the tracks to RS2014?' question. That's a more tricky one...luckily, you're reading this review so you can at least get MY answer to that.
That I thumbs this up is mostly a "how would one rate this game if RS2014 wouldn't exist?". The short answer: it would be a great game. I'm not even sure if I would mention most of the things I'll mention here.
This game is, simply put, guitar hero with an actual guitar (far more than RS2014). You have a bunch of rock tracks that'll steadily unlock, venues to go to (that feature a 2D gif of an exstatic crowd for some reason), minigames and lessons to unlock and scores to achieve to progress throughout the game. It has guitar lessons and some guitar minigames, but the gist of the game is, obviously, play songs. It's almost like an executive at ubisoft said "wow, let's not get TOO innovative here...we'll make it for real guitars, but for everything else we're copy-pasting things!". Without 100% hindsight, I would probably even agree with him.
The thing is: learning guitar is far, far harder than anything on plastic instruments. Breaking up the song in sections that increase or lower difficulty depending on how you do was a good thing, but not enough. Practicing one of those parts on a loop, on a different difficulty setting or speed is, alas, missing in this game. And I feel like the difficulty comes at some spikes (it's not because I can play a simple chord that I can churn out chords that require a proverbial seventeen fingers). On the plus point, I feel like the songs are overall less hard than in the sequel. And it might be personal taste, but it feels more like they belong on the same radio station (RS2014 has a mix of all sorts of genres, and thus misses this a bit. In other words: they both have their merit).
Where was I? Oh, yes...difficulty. I'm in no way a decent guitarist, but revisiting the same lessons after RS2014 feels like a step back as well. I honestly can't tell how to judge the mellow, smooth lessons from someone who doesn't sound like he ever even held a guitar before. I don't like how it is now (why can't I just see which notes I've missed in the practice track?), but I may have been spoiled.
Pleasant surprise: the minigames. Since I've got to unlock them it'll take some while to get to them, but the few I played I liked actually MORE than rocksmith 2014. Reason: multiple lives. Both have a duck hunt game (this one even two), but on 2014, missing out means restarting the game. Here your game is less a minigame and more an activity.
Worst part of the game is easily the menu UI. It's like someone looked at the xbox360 and windows 8 interface and said "amateurs...we can make it MORE counterintuitive!". Since you'll be holding a guitar, easy back/forth navigation should be easy with one hand. Alas...it's a creative maze with left, right, space bar, enter and escape to get anywhere. Having to retune everytime you want to play something gets irritating as well (it was E standard for the last four songs...it's not changing that fast!).
...but I digress. I thumbed this up. Not so much because you should get it (again: get RS2014 if you want to guitar things up), but mostly because feedback of this game allowed their sequel to be what it should be: a tool to learn guitar. It shouldn't be "a game"...if the main mechanic is fun enough (cue an army of guitarists franctically agreeing with this), you don't need a points system or unlocks of venues or virtual guitars. If you need a reward for playing, you shouldn't be playing. Playing should be the reward.
And don't get me wrong: despite all I've said, playing guitar is awesome in this game. It's not because an other game does it better that that experience is in any way bad. Playing songs is just awesome. Hence: thumbs up.
EDIT: after playing for 5-6 hours and importing all the tracks in RS2014, I feel myself less and less drawn to the original. This isn't so much because of the progression system ("no, you can NOT play slither until you've scored this many points on other tracks"), but because the note highway is a lot more convoluted in this game. It may look similar on screenshots, but when you only have a glance and are busy putting fingers correctly and strumming, those things become important ones. It's pretty hard to make out how a bend should be played, and the lack of numbers underneath the notes make it tougher to see where you should place your fingers. In other words: it's a whole lot easier to play the same (imported) song in RS2014. Still...the track list is pretty decent. If you pick up this game in a sale and get the disc import tool (which IIRC is always 10 bucks), you have PLENTY of extra songs to play.

Deadbeat Heroes. Another fine title made possible by a dev team’s collaboration with Square Enix through its Collective program. I must say, unlike the utter failure that is the Steam Direct initiative, Square has proper QA in place and really won’t allow any “floodgates” to be opened for digital drivel. It’s refreshing to see a company that cares more about its public image than sheer profit. That being said, this Steam debut for Deadbeat Productions has its small but noticeable flaws that prevent the game from truly reaching its potential.
An aging vigilante can’t shirk his duties and London in the ‘70s is still in dire need of a hero. Or several, in this case. The arrest and incarceration of the Kray twins left a power vacuum in London’s organized crime, but one which threatens to fill up just as swiftly. Captain Justice steps in and despite his back pains, shall still coordinate an unlikely team of would-be crime fighters. Judging by Captain’s motto, “No Super, All Hero!” it’s safe to say that Felix, Felicity, Betty and Max are average folks which benefit from the use of a Power Glove which grants them the enhanced speed and strength required to perform the stunts and takedowns which entail each level. So they’re more likely regarded as secret agents relying on gadgets than superheroes.
The Justice Team may not possess much in the form of an initial arsenal or even means of transportation. Felix, the first unlockable protagonist seems like a Kingsman type with his quips, tailored suit and eyeglasses, yet he’s forced to travel across London in a “Justice Scooter”, before the car becomes available. A rental I presume, since Captain’s pension most likely can’t support even a second hand purchase. It would have been even more ironic to have Felix deliver pizzas between preventing bank heists and park attacks, but Deadbeat Heroes doesn’t want to ridicule its characters to such an extent.
Even the villains, in spite of their caricature-like appearance and mannerisms, have a certain Evil Genius appeal to them. Linear or not, the story holds its own and being structured into chapters, it ensures that a sense of progression is well simulated. Even if you’ll only play in singleplayer mode, unlocking new moves, powers and team mates, prove the perfect motivation to look past the less diversified enemies (looking more like clones of each other) or the obviously few environment types. You can expect plenty of sarcasm and violence in Deadbeat Heroes, but sadly no adult humor. Archer or Austin Powers: the video games will have to wait some more, I reckon.
Not enough information to confirm it’s a Unity Engine project, but I suspect that’s the case, judging by how it named its preset settings (“Fantastic” as maximum setting for graphical quality). In anycase, Deadbeat Heroes looks the part. Cel shading goes hand in hand with the comic book style this game wishes to evoke. Its “console legacy” however, is less pleasing since we’re discussing the PC version here. There is no mouse support, everything’s done through the keyboard (or controller, if you own one) and while the environments themselves are fairly destructible along with the graphic depiction of dead foes, those vanquished goons and various gang members are vanishing from the map in a matter of seconds. Surely a PC could sustain those digital corpses in a persistent mode, right?
Remember, Deadbeat Productions that a PC port is more than just the console version of the game, which you offer to a larger player base. The gameplay must remain the same, I agree. But you can make some concessions or improve the stability and graphics on a PC version, because most systems will accommodate the changes, unlike the Xbox version of the game. And by the looks of it, Deadbeat Heroes has few flaws apart from the stage scenery which consists of mostly indoor sections that aren’t distinct from one another. Whether we are talking about banks, office buildings or parks and subway levels, the variety mostly comes from the day/night cycle, not the object  repositioning. Boss fights at the end of each chapter, seem to focus on a single warehouse environment as if both factions set up a meeting in that place every time.
Nothing to complain about the sounds though. The voice acting is top notch, with the majority of characters sporting a proper British accent while the soundtrack didn’t disappoint either. The various stop motion screens featuring the written equivalent to comic book-style sounds made by kicks and punches, really confirm the particular type of atmosphere which Deadbeat Heroes wishes to convey to its players. It’s not a spoof, of that much I’m certain.
As an almost light-hearted version of a superhero video game, Deadbeat Heroes never depicts its violence and gore in a manner that might be considered disturbing. It’s more visible than in the Freedom Force series, but still manageable even for a teenage audience. At its core, the game might be regarded as an enhanced brawler since the Justice Team relies more often than not, on the hit-and-run tactics. Up close and personal, melee combat that has to be compensated by swift stunts such as wall runs and mid-air dashes, since some of the foes are packing heat. Shooting at you with all sorts of firearms and explosive devices. The title’s difficulty stems from clearing rooms in a timely manner while avoiding most incoming projectiles. Defeating certain enemies, you will access more power-ups which allow for one-hit knockout moves. So in a sense, you’re “borrowing” super powers for a limited time, rather than have constant access to them and be overpowered.
Our heroes’ health pool is limited to absorbing three consecutive hits before you’ll be forced to restart the level. Some enemies drop health bonuses but from what I’ve noticed, those aid kits and consumables are a far too rare sight on later levels. Be on the move at all times and don’t be afraid to experiment with combos and evasive maneuvers. All that counts, is that you dispatch the goons efficiently and without getting hit. Each stage has an annoying final rating and the more you advance through the storyline, each chapter will feature more pretentious prerequisites that will have you “failing” the level even if you successfully defeated all the bad guys within it. The chapters themselves are divided into 3 or more sublevels and a boss fight stage which only gets unlocked after you reached a  certain rating. They never get properly explained and the golden rule is to use combos as fast as you can.
A masked time trial is even worse than an honest one but Deadbeat Heroes is ideally played in co-op, so perhaps the challenge and those absurd ratings are lesser issues when two players are combining their efforts.  I knew that the moment I saw its interface, but I still expected Deadbeat Heroes to offer a smooth experience for singleplayer fans. I hope it’s only a matter of future “gameplay optimization”. It remains to be seen. The title can be enjoyed as it is right now, but be aware that if you play solo, it won’t be nearly as easy as in co-op.

Finally a Halo title on Steam... Albeit the crummiest, most god-forsaken half♥♥♥♥♥release of the franchise I cannot bring myself to call it a bad game. It may just be my devotion to the series and being a huge, life-long fan of the universe that is fogging up my glasses of reasoning, or it may be the atmosphere the game immediately creates with the un-mistakable sound track. Either way, I’m pretty damn happy with the $5.00 I spent acquiring this fairly respectable game. Whilst in no way does it do the franchise any justification or could even sit amongst the many flawless titles that have been released over the last 14 years, I’m happy to have it in my steam library and I’m pleased by the trading card support that includes some great art-work which keeps the universe alive and cements its place on the PC platform. I sincerely hope the cement is not the tombstone of it here and that now Microsoft, the owners of the series will publish other great titles onto Steam. Wishful thinking, I know. But there is plenty of reasoning to suggest it could happen.
The game it’s self is obviously one created for a sub-pc platform, phones, tablets etc. It does feel like a lame implementation of something that wasn’t made for Pc however holds a decent arcade element and has some okay level content. The missions are a bit short and lack anything to get your teeth sunk into but again it must be remembered that this game was likely something people would play on the train to work.
At the end of the day, if you enjoy the Halo series you will buy it because it is only $5 and gives you some nostalgia. I just hope it is not for that reason Microsoft have released it to lure PC players back to the console and boost Xbone sales or plug a new Halo game. As much as I want to relive it all and embrace a new title, my console days are over – I’ve made my bed and I will do as my father always told me – lay in it.

I can't stress enough how much fun I've had out of this little gem. For a start, it's nice looking, with improved graphics over the xbox live indie game it started out as.
The real fun though, is in its feel and handling which is a joy. It reminds me of older classics like Skidmarks, Super Off Road Racer, Mashed (without weapons sadly) etc. The car handling is varied but superbly enjoyable and there's a simple pleasure in flinging your motors around the multitude of tracks that are made up of routes within 2 cities. It's kind of like Metropolis Street Racer/Project Gotham Racing mixed with Skidmarks and you actually get a whole lot of game for your money. This includes a comprehensive single player campaign with multiple/customisable car classes and challenges, time trials, daily challenges, online play for up to 12 people and a dev that appears to listen to the feedback from gamers.
It can be a bit buggy at times but the fun I've had far outweighs any frustration from problems I've experienced.
It's just a joy to play and captures something magic that a lot of newer games sometimes struggle to do. To put it simply, it's just good fun and to me that's what games should be about.

Top-down racing games in more recent years have been very hit and miss affair more often than not missing the 'fun factor' that makes this sort of game appealing. Little Racers STREET is an exception, although basic in respects to lacking the powerups & weapons often seen in the genre, the straight racing aspect is very enjoyable. You have good control over your car through the hundreds of combinations of tracks created through two larger city block maps. Having just the two main locations though, does result in some lack of variety on the scenery & terrain front.
The selection of camera views, from more traditional top-down to the more modern chase views let you play how you want - you could even play this more like a third person racer if you wanted!
The career mode is extensive, with lots of challenges to complete & cars to unlock as you work your way up the classes from E to A. Racing really starts to become fun from Class C onwards as this is when you need to start using brake/handbrake and drift around more. Cars can also be upgraded and you can modify the paint & pattern. There is no story or anything exciting to mention in career mode, rather more of a 'grindy' career covering things like .. win xx races, win xx races with xx car - same goes for most of the achievements. You can progress the career mode online which makes it more challenging and also more fun than racing the AI.
Races are quick, generally lasting just a few minutes but this suits the gamestyle - this can be increased in multiplayer mode only if you host. Playing against your friends is where this becomes the best fun but online against others is still a fun challenge. Thankfully the multiplayer doesn't suffer from an nasty bounce corner moves or other dirty play but do expect some fast drivers! Since the LRS has only just been released at time of writing this, it is not too hard to find an online game currently (will have to wait and see if the community hangs around). There is no way to select your track or setup a tournament through multiplayer which is a bit of a let down.
It's an XBox Live port but has been programmed well for a change for the PC with detailed graphics & smooth camera work. It's not perfect but it is pretty good.
There were some things that I didn't like so much, such as the sound effects and music were bland; nothing great. Music selection is limited/repetitive and car sounds and impacts are pretty basic to my ears. Also, all the AI racers feel the same, follow same paths and make the same mistakes - there are a few tracks you will easily win due to AI crashing out on a corner every time getting stuck. Harder AI simply seemed to mean they have faster cars putting you at a clear disadvantage - no better drivers as such which makes the harder difficulty not more challenging just more frustrating!
Some more variety in game modes would have been good too. Given the cityscapes a timed live-route mode (ala Grid 2) would have been great along with other skill challenges such as how fast you could go without hitting anything. More jumps (bigger jumps!), more elevation, more race shortcuts, more drifting & various hazards all would add so much to the experience.
It has the basics in gameplay well refined which is thoroughly enjoyable, but falls short of being a classic due to the limitations I mention above. Still worth checking out if you like these sorts of games, good value and is one of the better ones on Steam!!

This game is a perfect blend of an FPS and the open-world genre. It's the kind of game that you would play on a Friday night or on a weekend night. Coming back after school/work, getting into the 'TGIF' mood, eating dinner, and then playing S.T.A.L.K.E.R. That was how I spent most of my Friday nights when I was 15.
The game thrusts you into a post-apocalyptic environment teeming with mutants and bandits, with you alone against them.There are 3 large maps that the player can travel among, which are set against the backdrop of the Chernobyl nuclear power plant disaster that occurred in 1986. You play as Major Degtyarev, who is sent into Pripyat to investigate the cause of the crash of 5 Mi-24 'Hind' helicopters. Along the way, you'll meet new people, factions, and encounter powerful mutants.
One of the most famous mods for Call Of Pripyat is Misery. It changes the whole atmosphere completely, massively improves the graphics, and makes the game feel more realistic. Bullet damages resemble real life, with 1 or 2 shots to your body being absolutely fatal when unarmoured. I highly recommend this mod to all Stalkers out there.
Pros:
+ Engaging, deep storyline (some with surprising plot twists!)
+ Extremely well-designed and immersive environment
+ Many interesting enemies and mutants to fight against, with each requiring different tactics
+ Suspenseful atmosphere (you'll never know when a bloodsucker might sneak up behind you)
Cons:
- Dated graphics in original game (by today's standards)
- Bugs (some of them game-breaking, causing your game to crash)
- Lousy AI (blocked doorways is not uncommon, sometimes killing you)
- Installing the Misery Mod may require more powerful hardware to handle the performance
My recommendation is that you get this game on a sale, play through it without mods first, and then play it again with the Misery mod. You will see the huge difference, and you will be hooked for a long time, especially if you're a fan of FPS games.
Overall: 7/10

Lots of potential for this game, and only really held back by the need for optimization. There's a sense of expansion at every step, and there's a sense of grandeur as you build your trading empire. However, if you haven't already figured out, there's really only one path currently to succeed at the game.
Hints if you are struggling to keep away from bankruptcy:
Machine and rare material production simply does not ramp up quickly enough, so it's pointless building machinery cargo on your ships. Right now, machinery is a newbie trap. Let the bots transport machinery, since it will quickly run out on Earth. You can get away with transporting only a small amount to make a little bit at the beginning of the game. Otherwise you will be wasting a lot of cargo room.
Once you unlock Jupiter's moons and the Gorman Dart, you can just transport 30-40% passengers and the rest water/food, and demand for food and water will quickly rise on that moon, activating a subsidy. You can easily just make millions off of it. I found this to be a very reliable way of racking up a large sum of money quickly.
Another tip is simply to cash in on Luna, then get to transporting food/water/passengers to Mars quickly. Luna makes a lot of money early, but it becomes pretty competitive once the AI starts transporting stuff. You will usually find yourself losing money after the development reaches 100%.
Currently, development and population doesn't seem to have a large effect on resource production and resource profile. I hope that the devs will update this, so then planets can begin to produce more rare minerals and detritium.

100% Orange Juice is a turn-based board game in which you play a cute anime character. You have to help your character achieve certain goals (such as collecting stars or beat an amount of enemies). The Player who achieves the goal first wins.
In each turn you get to roll the dice once and depending on what square you land on different "events" are going to happen. For example you can encounter enemies, collect stars or lose them but also find cards. There are many different cards and each has it's own effect. Plus, you are able to beat other players too. If you win the fight, you gain a specific amount of their stars. Each character has different stats (health, attack, evasion and defense) so that you can choose one that fits your current way of playing most.
I had a lot of fun with 100%OJ so far but it can make me really mad at the same time. Everything in this game should happen by accident but in the "story mode" (if you can call it that. It's actually just about pudding) you feel like you are more unlucky as usual. That's what makes me angry sometimes. It should be based on luck but here it's clearly not. However, the game would be too easy if this weren't the case. That's why I'm not completely sure wether that's a good thing or not.
You can also play the game online which is the most fun. Luck isn't influenced here, you can play against actual people and also write with them.
All in all, I am having a love-hate-relationship with this game since you can be in first place and in the next turn the last. Sure, that can be annoying but that's also what makes the game exciting. You never know what happens or who is going to win. ;) But I'd say it's definately worth playing.

TLDR: The level design is incredible, catchy soundtrack, obviously well done art. They set out to make a platformer like the old sonic classics and succeeded in all the right ways.
Now, I, like many people, did not enjoy/play the vast majority of modern sonic games. There were a couple that I thought were just “good.” But nothing special.
Nothing truly amazing like Sonic 2, Sonic 3, and Sonic and Knuckles.
What made those games truly amazing? Mostly, it was the level design. Yes, the art and music was also phenomenal. But the level design is what made the game so repayable and those games are still among the best of platformers in my opinion.
Sonic Mania was clearly looking at those games as a role model. And I’d say Sonic Mania is one of the best platformers I’ve played in a very long time.
So, onto some grand generic grading categories even though I give high scores anyway:
10/10
The art and aesthetic is what got so many people excited for the game in the first place. I don’t think I’ve ever been excited for a sonic game. I played all the "classics" when they were all on a Gamecube disc together. Suddenly Sonic Mania showed up and they sure did present it well.
Not much else needs to be said. The game has a perfect retro look and is insanely colorful which is a good thing I’d say. The screen can be a bit cluttered at times, which may or may not bother you.
9/10
Again, no real faults here. I’m awful at critiquing music but the soundtrack sounds retro and modern... does that make sense? Probably not. I found the boss themes pretty underwhelming. To be honest, I was kinda hoping they would just have a remaster of the Sonic 2/3 boss music for some of the bosses.
9/10
The game looked great, but of course sonic has burned many people with expectations in the past, though Sonic Mania looked like it had everything from the trailer... but of course we didn’t know how good the level design was. I’d say it’s on par if not BETTER than the old school sonic games.
If you don’t know what makes the
so great about the old sonic games, and Sonic Mania: it’s basically that the levels have a start and end point, but the way to transverse the levels is very non-linear. There are a multitude of paths to take and this is apparent from the first level. Upper paths, medium paths, lower paths, secret paths, and secret items and rings. Not a game where you’d think you could explore, but you certainly can.
There are a couple levels that are a lot less open ended. The majority of them ARE, there’s just a couple exceptions (Lava Reef being the main one.).
Arguably the best open-ended platformer level design ever, it’s up there at least.
On top of that, the 7 chaos emeralds are a thing again. From what I can tell (you can google it to verify if you want. Although I encourage you don’t look anything up at first) each act has 2 hidden “Big Rings”. If you find one, then you go into this 3D minigame where you have to chase a UFO around a race course while collecting rings that slowly drain, and speed orbs so you can catch up to it easier whilst avoiding obstacles. Some people will probably find the minigame annoying, I didn’t greatly enjoy them myself. But they were fairly enjoyable.
Finally, I’ll try to keep this short since I doubt anyone is even reading this: the bosses. They’re okay. No bosses that really stood out to me, I found the final boss and true final boss to be very underwhelming. I got a hopeful impression that there was going to be a second phase to the true final boss but nope. The game shines mostly in the levels, not the bosses. And, it's worth noting that the game is very easy.
9.5/10
At the end of the day, they set out to make a Sonic game like the old classics, and they did that in spades. If you enjoyed the classic Sonic platformers, I see no reason you won’t enjoy this. And if you’re a fan of platformers in general, I’d also say this should still be a game you should pick up.

Team turn-based strategy gameplay is incredibly fun in Atlas Reactor.  Group coordination by voip is essential to pulling off some amazing strategies, and the best part is that you can actually watch how your teamwork comes together thanks to a system that has players input orders and then showcases the resolution for everyone.
As a person who tends to enjoy playing supporting characters in other games, I quite like how Trion has balanced the characters here.  Killing a support is useful, but not essential, as they do more than simply heal or shield, and often it is far more ideal to kill an exposed melee character, burn down an enemy ranged damaged dealer, or just go for maximum overall damage in order to wear them down.
I've also enjoyed how close the matches have been.  Big turnarounds are entirely possible with some teamwork or where the enemy has made a bad mistake, such as chasing too far, staying in the firefight too long, or not paying attention to who has which movement powers off cooldown.
If you enjoyed games like Final Fantasy Tactics, X-COM, and MOBAs, then this blended game has a lot to offer.

Ok where do I start?
This game is freakin' amazing.
One of the best RPG games I've ever played
If you're looking for a good RPG to play this game is the one for you.
This game is the fourth in it's series (Not including Tamriel Online) So if you like this game check out the others.
Oblivion is a very heavy RPG, you can change between first-person and third-person.
At the beginning of the game you get a little clip of what's going on in the game.
After this you're placed in a jail cell where you start creating your character.
Now this game is heavily based on character creation. YOU CHOOSE WHAT KIND OF PERSON YOU WNAT TO BE!!
You choose what race you are and your race basically tells you what that race is acvanced in. (like a Khajite is good as a stealthy character)
After you pick a class you can change how your character looks in a Sims 3 like manner.
Then you have to go through the Tutorial learning how to play. Near the end of the Tutorial you can pick your Birthsign and Class.
A Birthsign basically is like an Ability ( The Birthsign "Shadow" gives you a magic spell called "Moonshadow" that makes you invisible for 60 seconds)
The class basically picks out your major skills.
Major skills are the skills you need to level up (by using them alot) to actually level up your character.
There are many different classes but a cool thing you can do is make your own class.
You first pick your main type of character you want to be (Strength, Magic, or Stealth) and then you pick your major skills.
After when your released you start off on the storyline. Nowwww you can do the story Orrrrr you can go make your own path and do what you want.
There is so much content in this game you'll never actually "complete" the game (unless you spend way too much time to even count)
I rate this game a solid 10/10.

Among the many impressions I've gotten from Oblivion, "buggy" and "awkward" are probably the most recurrent ones. This game is filled with examples of poor design and flawed execution of ideas, and it crashes and breaks in almost every imaginable way.
It's not a terrible game, though. I don't think it's nearly as good as many of its fans say, but I appreciate the effort that went into it. However, I cannot give Oblivion glowing praise when it constantly reminds me how broken and badly designed it is every time I try to play it.
There are too many individual problems (thousands) to list in a review, so I'll cover the worst flaws of this game, as well as what Bethesda did adequately well.
Before I continue, let me make it clear that I'm focusing on the unmodded base game. Before anyone yells "Boo, mods fix everything!": No they don't, and I wouldn't care if they did. Mods should not be required for a game to be good. That mentality encourages unfinished and broken games, and the rabid complacency many of you have for said games is a blight on the entire industry.
[Interface]
Let's start with GUI: Something that should be made especially carefully. Unfortunately, Oblivion's interface is shamefully bad, and has few redeeming qualities to make up for its atrocious design.
The character menus are all nested tabs, making navigation tedious. There are actually hotkeys for some tabs, but they use the function keys, and can't even be viewed in the controls menu.
An obscene amount of screen real estate is wasted in the character menus (usually over 60%). Everything important is restricted to a window in the bottom left corner, while the rest of the screen is either empty space or an unnecessarily large preview of your character. Most buttons and list entries are bulky, so there's little useful information visible at any given time; for example, you can only see an average of five inventory items at once.
When you drop, sell, or otherwise move more than two of the same item, a little menu will pop up asking you the amount to move. It's a useful feature for moving more than 10-20 items at a time, but its threshold is set to a paltry THREE. Confirming the action takes longer than just clicking the item a few more times.
Even the map is annoying: You can't zoom in/out, and it's in a little box that doesn't even cover 30% of the screen. It's like having a nice big map, then shoving your face onto it and only using a magnifying glass to look around an inch at a time.
The alchemy interface may be the most tedious of all, since it takes at least six clicks just to make a single potion. Experimentation is dull and time-consuming, and generally not worth it unless you want to spend several minutes at a time clicking away in the alchemy screen.
I hate lockpicking in Oblivion. Its interface makes no sense (sideways locks?!), and the controls are incredibly sluggish and clumsy. Rather than focusing on subtle and careful movement, Bethesda made lockpicking a luck-based, illogical annoyance that's more like a quick-time event than anything else. Finding the right height for each pin just involves clicking within a very precise time interval, which is semi-randomized every time you try to move a tumbler. Unless you have a high lockpicking level, the lock's tumblers will reset if your pick breaks, which will happen all the time due to the randomness.
Overall, Oblivion's GUI is monumentally unintuitive. Almost every step through the interface seems designed to hinder the player, and there are such glaring design flaws that I'm almost surprised they survived the game's release.
Despite its horribly flawed function, the interface's leather-and-parchment aesthetic is nice, and adequately reflects the pseudo-Medieval tone of Cyrodiil. The overwhelming yellow and brown hues can get tiring on the eyes after a while, but otherwise it's not a bad appearance.
[Stability]
As is standard with Bugthesda, this game is riddled with literally thousands of technical issues, ranging from harmless to permanently game-breaking. They're so prevalent that problems can begin stacking up from the moment you start a new game.
Here's the worst thing: Game-breaking bugs will inevitably happen. If you seriously try to complete a save, it will be impossible without the game glitching in some way or another. Parts of the world can start crashing the game, quests won't trigger properly, unique items can vanish, the entire save might get randomly corrupted, the list goes on and on. Last but not least, the game will slow to an unplayable crawl after a couple hundred hours, if one of your saves actually manages to survive the bugfest that is this game.
All games should have completely stable save systems, especially ones as long as Oblivion. However, there seems to be no limit to what can be permanently broken in this game's saves. I keep getting the impression that I'm playing a mid-beta game, rather than a fully released title that's been updated multiple times.
[Combat]
Combat in Oblivion is lackluster. Melee attacks go straight through almost everything without resistance, and everything just seems floaty due to little visual feedback.
The staggering mechanic is a good idea with flawed implementation, as is typical with most of the game. When staggered, your character is unresponsive and doesn't move; in the meantime, you can't even change spells or look around. Staggering basically means "remove all control for two seconds and make the character wobble." Given how commonly it can happen, it can waste a lot of time and even stun-lock your character.
Archery is just laughable. I'm not sure if Bethesda didn't know how bows actually behave, or if they had to make arrows pathetically slow so this game wouldn't break itself even more. Arrows have next to no speed when released, and drop to the ground almost immediately. It's probably the worst archery I've ever seen in a game thus far, if you can even call it archery. You could throw arrows in real life better than you shoot them in Oblivion.
[Character limit reached. I've actually written quite a bit more on the rest of the game, but I'll stop here]
SUMMARY
Oblivion shows hints that it had potential for greatness, but nigh-innumerable flaws in its construction have sullied its quality. If not for its mod support (which is also rather flawed and prone to breakage), I would consider it a mediocre game at best. As it is, it can be a mildly okay game with the right mods, but it still doesn't deserve the amount of praise it gets.
Why am I not recommending Oblivion? Because I have quality standards. Because I'm not going to mindlessly praise everything Bethesda makes. Because this horrendously unstable game has broken every single save I've tried to complete, and crashed hundreds of times during normal gameplay.
Here's my final advice: Don't take this game seriously, regardless of the developers' intentions. If you can somehow ignore Oblivion's shoddy technical quality or your standards are low, I actually recommend getting it. Otherwise, it will lead to disappointment, wasted effort, and repeatedly ruined immersion, thanks to its ludicrous instability and awkwardness.
Strengths: Music tracks, story/lore (soiled by the game's awkwardness, but still decent in writing), natural environment design
Weaknesses: Terrible stability, unintuitive interface, consolitis, a lot of bad voice acting, many awkward animations, bad weapon and armor design, quest railroading, copy-pasted interiors

I went into
with a open mind - I knew it would be short and more like a interactive movie, I knew that the interactions would be limited - my expectations were in check. But by the end I still felt... underwhelmed... I had expected more, and I'm sitting here trying to figure out where it went wrong.
So, was it the gameplay? It started out well with a balance of simple choices and interactions which settled me nicely into the world of
the protagonist. I think up until the sixth or seventh chapter I was still on board, but it was beginning to be clear that my perception of simple gameplay was quite different than the reality. Ok, so this was a bit of a letdown, I was expecting a little more depth.
So, what about the story? The story and the acting seems to have been the main focus of the designers - and it wasn't bad, especially from what I've gleamed of other FMV games! The production value was high and the acting was good. Everything was shot with cinematic flare so I never doubted the authenticity of the location and It was well shot. So I think they nailed the production side of things.
The story was cohesive and unfolded neatly into what I'd consider a interesting short film.
So, what was it? For me this was neither a game or a movie, but something else that sat a little uncomfortably in-between. I found the gamey elements would more often disrupt your immersion than add to it and the limitations of using live action footage to convey interaction combined to make a slightly stilted and unsatisfying experience.
It was flawed, but I would still recommend a play through. And if your even slightly interested in this genre of game to buy and support it. The next one might be great!

Implementing some stupid real-life regulations is obviously more important than making a game for the player...
Since the engine limit was introduced with the November '17 update you can no longer drive faster than 80 kmh. driving on the highway-autobahn has become very slow and boring instead of challenging and fun. the fact that this speed limiter can not be turned off is a major letdown.
instead of driving on the left lane trying to outrun the AI cars you are now bound to the right lane at 80kmh max and get overtaken even by AI busses all the time which imo is dumb, boring and even frustrating ...pressing the gas pedal no longer helps.
according to the law regulations troxytronxynix is trying to simulate here, the trucks are completely restrained in their power while AI busses/coaches are allowed to go much faster.
however, I would really like to enjoy the full power the trucks technically have to offer and the challenge to master the physics and test my driving skills - without any artificial limitations. they could easily give the option to turn the limiter off - like it was before the update and like any other game would do it.
So, now the driving experience is indeed very limited. be it realistic or not .. the restrained versions of the machines are nowhere near enjoyable and my playstyle of driving a bit faster than 'allowed' is no longer supported.
Therefore this review can only be: Overwhelmingly Negative.

Let me start by saying that I enjoy playing HO adventures. This game, however, is an exception. The plot is interesting and the time travel aspect is well implemented. Puzzles are the usuall package that can be seen in most Artifex Mundi's HO titles.
However, this games is plagued by couple of things that the developers didn't bother to patch up so far.
- Some mazes are bugged to a point where you can't solve them unless you press the skip button (and miss the achievement). For example the clower puzzle. You can actually press and depress buttons even prior to optaining all the missing pieces. If you do, the puzzle starts with only one button off (should be two) and cannot be solves, so you will have to restart the game.
- HO scenes are pretty baddly designed. The whole scene looks like it has been upscaled from a VGA resolution and the item description list is quite horrible. The developers decided to use same words for multiple object (e.g. bow often means that you are actually looking for a bow tie, but can also refer to a bow). On some scenes there are moving objects (e.g. chest opens) and when you trigger the object it can also cover items that you will be looking for when you revisit that HOS (and yes, you revisit most HOS multiple times).
All in all it's an OK game if you get it in a bundle or on sale, but can't justify the 9.99$ price tag. There are better Artifex Mundi titles that are well worth the price.  For example, Abyss: The Wraiths of Eden.

Let's just put it out there.  Little Street Racers is just awesome and is the pinnacle of a genre that has sorely lacked any incarnation of excellence. First impressions:
Little Racers STREET is a top-down racing game, originally released on Xbox under the name “Little Racers”. The game doesn’t seem to have anything going for it, other than the fact that its the first game like this that I’ve seen on Steam. Other than that, it’s a rather generic game.
The controls are responsive when using a controller. These types of games go best when used with one, don’t even bother using keyboard controls. I probably wouldn’t recommend the game if it only supported use of mouse and keyboard. The game is top-down, so expect some getting used to in terms of turning in the game. I got the hang of it almost instantly, due to my prior experience in games like this, mainly back when I played a ton of games on my old iPad (I remember a game called “Death Rally” that was similar to this, minus the guns).
The game fails to set itself apart from all other similar titles, however. It just felt like your generic top-down racing game. Nothing too special, although this is the first game like this I’ve played in years. If you’re looking for straight-up racing, no gimmicks, then Little Racers STREET is for you. If you’re looking for a unique experience, you may want to turn elsewhere.
