This is one o' them "deceptively simple" contraptions you hear about on the news.
Easiest way to describe this game is "first-person Geometry Wars." High skill ceiling, easy to learn. The game takes place on a relatively small platform that you strafe and circle around while floating skulls trail and chase you. That's not to say the game isn't dynamic, however, as new types of skulls and "daggers" (spawners) are slowly introduced that all require their own unique approach and strategy.
Your score is determined by how many seconds you survive, and honestly if you're not interested in competing for high scores among friends or the world, you may not find much to entertain yourself here. But if you do like games built around high score challenges, this game is almost perfect because of its bite-sized game durations and a natural progression of difficulty that makes it easy to play it over and and over and notice yourself slowly getting better at the game without even being very intentional about it.

The second issue is the voices, they're not really well done and have some errors (wrong voice assigned etc); it's not a big issue but it adds to the unfinished game feeling.
However the biggest issue is the display: if you have a wide screen monitor you will be stuck with a stretched display and there's no work around, making all game's graphics distorted and blurry, turning all the hidden objects scenes into a nightmare. And fiddling with the monitor display and the desktop setting won't help. So unless you have a 4/3 monitor, forget this game.
If you don't have a wide screen monitor, you should still wait for a nice discount, the game isn't worth it at full price.

Devil Daggers is an incredibly challenging and refreshingly old school first person shooter that does not advertise itself as such, therefore you know you can trust it. I actually would classify this game as an "experiemental indie title" similar to games such as Hylics, Hotline Miami and Void & Meddler. It REALLY does have that sort of atomosphere for me.
The graphics style is a mix of Doom, Quake, an old VHS tape, and the inside of Satans brain. The art style is slightly minimalistic and the mosnter designs remind me of Shadow Of The Colossus and maybe even. . . Brutal Legend? It's so hard to even classify, the monsters definitley look absoulutely stunning either way.
Devil Daggers gameplay is placed purely on skill and nothing else. There is no upgrade tree, no item shop, no story, no world building, no multiplayer. There IS however a scoreboard. For some people that is a turn off (However that 4.99 price point definitely was a turn on for me) and those people need to understand that this game is NOT for someone who loves competiveness or perhaps even someone who likes the old FPS games. Its difficulty is staggering (very reminiscent of Dark Souls, or God Hand, you must take time to hone your skills or this game will punish you brutally) and it only has one arena. Everything is smooth, quick and fluid, as is death. It will come very often so prepare yourself.
All in all, play it. It's literally 5 bucks, it's super fun, and hell, why not? 9/10 easily. If you want some gameplay to play in the background on your Youtube channel while you talk about some edgy subjects then this is one of your best bets.

I have not played the game so long yet, but I already made up my mind about this one. There are some things that I realy enjoy, but could be done much better, for example the AI: In the first Halo game you threw a plasma grenade near by an Elite and sometimes it did not react, but this is okay for a halo game which was realeased 2001. That time it was excaptable, but in this time a Halo game should not be like this. Sadly it is...
Besides the AI issues (there are more like in mission A-3 where you have to escort the Wolverines: Focus on the marines which are roadkilled by the Wolverines, but do not die, but act like they were diying for some strange reasons), the game has also techniacl issues in the shooting system. You will not realize this if you are firing an automatic rifle, but if you want to shoot with a semi-automatic weapon, like the Magnum or the shotgun you have to hold the fire-button, and I do not want to hold the fire button when I am shooting a semi-automatic rifle, but otherwise the spartan will not shoot, he will only aim.
One confusing thing about the aim-system is that it will not always cooperate with you, sometimes it just decides to shoot slightly off where you aiming at, or the turret that you can control shoots surprisingly in the ground instead of shooting forward. Another annoying thing is the spawn system, which does not realy exists. If you die in a mission you have to restard the mission which can be frustrating for one or antother.
I think this were the major issues that I discovered in only one hour play time. There is still a thing that is kind of getting on my nerves: If you upgrate your stuff, your upgrade will only remains for this time you play this mission. It will be not be unlocked for another mission or for the seconde play through of the same mission. You have to unlock the "upgrades" over and over again. Technicaly I would not call this an upgrad.
On the other side I enjoyed that you could take over a turret when it is engaged by a Grunt. But this feature is not fully worked out: I tried to take a wraith over like in other Halo titles and I just could not do it, or maybe I am just too unable to do it.
Let us now talk about the graphics and the sounds (including some music). Well it is done pretty good. Except the german voice acting, but this seems to be a problem in nearly every game.
In terms of gameplay I assert some missions are boring, because you just have do defend some waves of Covenants and the mission is done or you have to escort vehicles. Though there are other mission where you can drive a wraith. All in all the gameplay is diversified, but sometimes a little bit dull, nevertheless they got some cool ideas for the gameplay and I definitely see a lot of potential in there.
Although I will play more, because of one thing: I do not really mind this issues, because that were all issues that you can ignore. You still can enjoy the game!! For me the issues are not that seriously as I described them, but I think I should mention them, because others can be bothered by them.
The reason why I ignore this issues and why I still enjoy the game is because firstly it is a Halo title and I am a Halo fan, secondly I saw foreward to play it since it was realsed for the Windows Phone and thirdly Halo is not a Triple-A title where you can get a new game of the series year by year, and I hope this image will stay.
But what I mainly want to say is I cannot play a single Assassins Creed anymore, because there are too many of them (I am stuck with "Black flag" and there are already two more out, "Freedom Cry" and "Liberation"). Since this is the most played game in my Library I think it's high time I give this game a proper review, with as little jargon as possible for potential players to understand.
Pros:
-Unique gameplay
-Good sense of progression
-Playable for high-latency connections (you can play with anyone from around the world with little to no lag due to the turn-based nature of the game)
-Easy to learn, hard to master
-A F2P game in which a new player has the same chance of winning as a paying player, with only experience being the difference between the two.
-While the F2P version has a weekly rotation of the character roster available, it is unique to each player so you will not see the same characters throughout matches (looking at you, Dirty Bomb)
-The pace of the game is relaxed, you can chill while playing.
Cons:
-Matchmaking can be a little bit janky, resulting in a team composition that is less than ideal. (But if you're like me you'll take it as a challenge to improve the way you play given worse circumstances.)
-Little bugs whenever a new major update comes out, though with frequent, consistent feedback from the players they usually get addressed quickly
Suitable demographic: Chess players, fans of turn-based action, people who want to play MOBAs but don't like needing to have high reflexes
Unsuitable demographic: People who hate turn-based games and co-operative gameplay

I originally played this game on Xbox 360, where it quickly became my favourite video game of all time. I can only imagine the PC experience is much richer.
Before discovering The Elder Scrolls, I had very limited experience of playing RPGs - the only ones I can remember playing were Pokémon and FInal Fantasy VIII. Both of which I enjoyed immensely, but I still stuck to action adventure games, strategy games and first person shooters.
Then Oblivion came along and changed my life. I mean it - this game has affected the way I look at sunsets ever since. Some real sunsets I've seen have almost been as pretty as those in this game.
Bethesda's mantra is "be who you want to be" and Oblivion allows you to do just that. The early moment in the game where the protagonist steps out of a linear, grey darkness and into a sumptuous open world of possibilities accurately reflects my own gaming life upon discovering this game.
Unfortunately, as has happened with its predecessor Morrowind, Oblivion has become dated and now seems rather clunky and rough around the edges. It might be difficult for a player used to modern open world RPGs to step back and enjoy Oblivion in quite the same way I did. But damn, I just want everyone to feel the way I did when this game's world eclipsed my own.

I was a little apprehensive in buying this game after AC Unity.  I wanted to skip this title because of the poor state of Unity in general upon release, but I am a fan of the series and so I blindly pre-ordered it taking yet another risk.  I can safely say this game so far is very well done.
The frame rate seems smooth and although I expected the graphics to look no better than Black Flag, being on the same engine, I have to say the games looks better in almost every respect.  It is no AC Unity by any means, but the anniemations, physics, and details are pushed further than Black Flag with improved frame rate.  AC Rogue runs great. It is obvious the extra six months in developement for PC was worth the wait.
The gameplay is smooth and what you would expect from AC.  The game plays just like AC Black Flag. I am not saying this game is without glitches, but I have not experienced any crashes at all.  I have however jumped out of trees and landed under part of the map structure like a rock twice.  Porting out to another area solves the problem, but remains an inconvenience. I also dislike the camera view that oddly puts me out of combat at times and I must center my view to correct it.
The story line is impressive and sets the transition for you to become a templar. I never thought Unbisoft would pull this story off so well after seven years of killing templars (release of Assassin's Creed 2007).  I found the story itself a little lacking in that it seemed rushed at times or like a book that has had several chapters cut out to meet a page limit. But overall, the story does what it is ment to do and it does it well. Spoiler alert, if you have played AC III, you may have some mixed feeling about this story line.
If you have played earlier Assassin's Creed games, specifically Black Flag, you will feel right at home.  If you have only played Unity, it is a step down in just about every respect except the bugs and lack of polish found with Unity's release.  AC Rogue is designed on a dated engine for last gen consoles but it truely offers one of the best AC experiences to date.  I honestly feel Ubisoft should have pushed Unity back another six months to a year and completed the release on Rogue on all platforms rather than holding Rogue back for PC only to push Unity for next gen.  Unity was obviously not ready for release on any platform, especially PC while Rogue clearly is.

The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion is one of my favourite RPGs and a good example of how good writing and immersion can save bad and unfavourable design choices. One of the only things I dislike about its otherwise wonderful successor Skyrim is the lack of character balance. Yes power fantasy can be fun in the right context but for an Elder Scrolls game its a little antagnistic to the role play aspect of a roleplaying game for me. Oblivion, like some of its other siblings, make me feel more down to the reality of things, at least to whatever you consider reality to be in a fantasy RPG, and while Skyrim is my favourite this game is just really good and has aged very well to me. Morrowind's saving grace for me is that while its boil is horribly slow its immersion factor is very powerful and arguably the main thing that keeps me in the game. Still Morrowind's boil is painfully slow even if it gets considerbly stronger later. So I like Oblivion's pacing a bit better. I still cant decide if I prefer its pacing over Skyrim or the other way around, but I like the pacing of both more than Morrowind. My favourite critic said immersion is Oblivion's weak point and I have to strongly disagree. That immersion is one of the things saving the game for me and allows me to focus more on the things I like such as the writing, world, and combat rather than focus on the countless things I don't like voice acting, and models among other things.
This is a good game despite its flaws than really makes me feel invested in what I do and the world around me.

Awesomenauts is a weird game for me. It's a weird game because it's a game that I was sure I would hate until the day I begrudgingly played it after picking it up from a bundle. The character design and overall humor will likely either drive you away or pull you in hard. The goofy concepts, interesting abilities and awesome character specific killing spree anthems make it a pretty fun experience win or lose. The games on average feel a bit shorter than your typical DoTA2 or LoL match which is nice, with some quick games mixed in with longer games when teams are more evenly matched. It's absolutely not without its flaws, a team with bots is almost always at a disadvantage (though they're not terrible enough to be useless, so better than a dropped player) and hosting can get wonky from time to time. That said, it's definitely worth a shot as, if nothing else, it's an interesting experience that's relatively unique to itself.

Surreal, serene and sublime.
---
A lone courier en-route to an elusive highway known as The Zero gets terribly lost and actually stops for directions. As unlikely as that may seem, the advice he receives from a ragged gas station attendant is rather unhelpful, and the hallucinations are starting to become disorienting. Still, he trudges on with the goal to deliver his final package before he must close the books on his small business once and for all.
---
Kentucky Route Zero is a fantastical story about near-aimless travels all alone on the open road. You'll eventually meet up with various misfits along your adventure and learn of their dreams, passions and misfortunes.
As allies are acquired, you end up taking part in all their stories (as breif as some may be) and the decisions you make for them shape others' lives as well in some small way.
The game's varying perspectives allow you to ponder the nature of its reality as no single character possibly could. You are an outside observer while also being an invisible, guiding force, leading these weary souls toward their respective destinations. The story goes from dreary and delirious, turns to full-on science fiction, veers near surreal comedy and then comes full-circle again as you realize the whole thing is a tragedy.
It's a refreshing experience as you tune into the static and droning harmonies of the Zero to navigate its ethereal roadways. Each new location is a sublimely exciting find. Even if you stumble upon a simple text story, it's backed by a haunting soundtrack and imaginitive soundscapes.
If ever you thought yourself a fancier of adventure games, you'd be doing yourself a disservice if you were to never experience Kentucky Route Zero. It's wholesome, yet it tunes you into what makes you feel dead inside. It's cheerful, all the while edging these characters toward dismay.
It's sometimes social commentary, but without any nudges and winks. It's a thinking-man's journey, but there are no puzzles to speak of. It's a meditation on being lost in the dark with only the stars and roadway reflectors as guiding lights. It's an homage to what it means to be human, unsure of your life and the largely aimless journey towards death and acceptance. TL;DR: Crusader Kings II takes a long time to learn, so don't buy it expecting it to be something you can just jump into unless you play a lot of strategy or Paradox titles. If you have a lot of time to kill, are imaginative, and love character oriented games then this will probably be a good fit for you. There is a wide range of mechanics from choosing a spouse to trying to assassinate anyone (in the entire game, no essential characters). The DLC isn't as money-grubbing as it may appear at a glance. Not all the DLC may fit any one person's preferences, so I recommend researching what the expansions are and what they contain. I approve of this game!
Crusader Kings II is the game that I absolutely must review (133 hours and growing playtime). I will do my best to remain impartial throughout this review and to address the game as it is, while offering some opinions on things such as DLC, despite being somewhat biased. The game is rather difficult to learn at first, so if you are not a patient person or do not have the time to learn the game and want something you can just jump into, then Crusader Kings II probably isn't the game for you (it took me 8 hours to learn how to play).  On the other hand, if you like strategy titles, participating in assassination plots, conquering lands and have a lot of time to kill, then this might be a game that you'll enjoy. For the most part, I think Crusader Kings II has something to offer everyone, even the strategically challenged (like me. I'm awful at this game and therefore use console commands, but it doesn't hamper my enjoyment at all).
At it's core, Crusader Kings II is more about the characters than conquering everything. Indeed, the game ends at a certain date (1453) rather than when everything is under one's thumb or certain conditions are met (excluding the date being reached). Characters have their own randomized events (often fun and quirky) that can shape their stats and relationships with each other. Events can range from having an affair to being possessed. Some events have choices, while others do not. In addition to events and the obvious fighting, there are also plots which allow you to do things like try and arrange someone's death through assassination, go on hunts, or hold a feast. I know I'm really starting to beat a dead horse here, but nearly everyone that has played multiple games of Crusader Kings II has that ONE character that sticks in their mind (mine was a guy that adopted a cat, lost an arm in battle, held a massive funeral for said cat when it passed of old age, and then died of an infection shortly after the cat's funeral). The characters of the player's and game engine's creation are something so wonderful.
Some other mechanics include: Marriage (anyone of opposite gender can be married if conditions are met), Lovers (same-sex or otherwise), dungeons with prisoners that can be executed, ransomed, or released, fabricating claims on land to go to war, going to war, hiring mercenaries, converting areas to your religion, and whatever mods may add. The mod community for this game is really awesome, variety-filled and big!
One thing that I rather dislike, but makes sense, is that you have to have a Casus Belli (cause for war) to be able to declare war and go out to fight. This is either achieved by being of a certain culture, having differing religions, or a claim (fabricated or legitimate). On the bright side, this does prevent the AI from ganging up on you.
Something rather off putting to a newcomer of the game, at least it was to me, is the large number of DLC. Most of the DLC is cosmetic in nature, while a few do add some changes to the game (improvements or otherwise, I'm looking at you Conclave). The really neat thing, in my opinion, about   the DLC that adds functions is that some of those functions are patched into the game for free. One such example would be India's landmass was patched into the game for free so that players may fight and conquer India, but to play as an Indian you must own the DLC. In terms of which DLC to buy, I'd say use the search engine of your choice, figure out what the expansions are, and then what they contain (if that strikes your fancy, of course). I will say that while amazing, I don't feel the DLC are necessary and that the base game provides more than enough entertainment, but they certainly are fun!

I really enjoyed playing "The Bunker". What impressed me most was the intense atmosphere. I have played guitar for many years and got this as a way to keep my chops up while not currently playing in a band. The verdict: it works! I recorded the same guitar part before and after about a dozen hours of playing the game's career mode and there was clearly an improvement in both my timing and phrasing--also the number of tries it took me to get a decent take when from like fifteen to one or two. I maybe would have seen the same result practicing along w/ a metronome but this seemed like more fun.
The one major caveat for experienced players--esp. ones like myself who have never played anything like
--is that this is entirely unlike how most people typically learn to play songs. Normally, you learn part A, B, C and D or whatever and then the solos if you want and piece them together. This just throws sort of a fake book simplified version of the entire song at you all at once. As  you get better, it starts to fill in the notes until you are playing the actual guitar part. It's strange and sometimes frustrating but if you keep plugging away you will get through and eventually you learn to read the game's kinda 3D, color-coded tablature quite well and the process becomes quicker.
My other complaints would be it can be a bit too lenient on timing and sometimes it lets you fudge chords. If you let the game's scoring dictate how you play, that can lead to bad habits. You need to show discipline on your own and play the parts correctly even if you can cheat a little and get a better score. Also, even using a relatively high end pro-sumer type soundcard (Focusrite Scarlett), there is a slight delay to the audio which you get used to but is enough to be annoying. It reminds me of playing on a digital guitar amp circa-2000, more of a feel thing but that matters.
Overall though, this is a fun way to practice and I've found myself playing guitar more both with and without the game. I am just letting the game pick what songs to learn and am finding even the songs I don't like are actually fun to play. Also, like most people, practicing on my own, I tend to just practice the things I am good at and letting the game pick songs forces me out of my comfort zone. Definitely check this out if you are looking to improve your existing guitar skills.

This is a really mixed bag, providing some of the best and worst traits of any game of the Artifex Mundi canon. The good points are very very good, and the bad points are very very not-good.
The good: most puzzles and hidden object screens are quite challenging*, and the travel mechanism is pretty cool (although it gets somewhat tedious and repetitive as the game moves forward**). The art is very well executed, as you'd expect from A.M., although not as awesome as some of the other titles.
The bad: *some of the puzzles are terrible (illogical, simple) and there seems to occasionally be terms lost in translation in the hidden object screens. The game also has a really cool backstory, but no story or character interaction or development, and **progress is unceremonious at best.
A lot of potential, and still quite fun to play, but definitely least recommended of the Artifex Mundi games I've played. I would give it an endorsement, with reservations. [ 6 / 10 ]

You are in an arena, you shoot endless waves of skulls with hand magic, you dodge the endless waves of skulls over and over as more things made of skulls appear, you die with one hit, you hit R and the game resets, you try to get a higher score, forever, and ever, and ever, and...
Devil Daggers is one of the most niche FPS games I've played in a long time. It is something you will likely understand in about 10 seconds and then it is purely down to player skill regarding if you survive. The premise is there is a "devil dagger" (I think?) and once you pick that up you can shoot magical bullet things from your hand. You transport into a circular arena with a deadly drop at the edges and then an eternal wave of enemies begins to pour in, from skulls, spires made of skulls, spiders made of skulls, snakes made of skulls, other types of skull related things come in, skulls, skulls, skulls! You shoot the skulls, and that is it. As a result its simplicity will no doubt be off-putting to many: it appears shallow both in its enemy variety and weaponry (magic hand, that is it) and the fact there is no easily defined plot. This simplicity is Devil Daggers strength, it does very few things, but that which it does do is VERY well done. If there is any comparison to make it would be a Serious Sam arena stripped of all the level design fluff leaving only the bare combat, making you scoot about prioritising enemies and considering when to fire and when to not fire, when to use the basic magic machine gun attack or hold off for a second for a single magic shotgun burst, or when to stop firing altogether to make the power-ups  fly to you. Everything is fast, instinctual and reactionary and for that it is possibly one of the most ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t free FPS games I think I've played in many, many years.
The simplicity of Devil Daggers makes me hold back from saying I advise it. I conditionally advise it. It is so basic that you will either love it or hate it.
Do you like FPS? If the answer is no, stop.
Do you like realism? If the answer is yes, stop.
Do you need deep narrative? If the answer is yes, stop.
Do you like twitchy, fast paced games? If the answer is no, stop.
Do you like score attack games with no real greater purpose than just fulfilling your need to have an endorphin rush, something to sink time into now and then rather than a long and meaningful experience that the games industry seems to keep pushing? If the answer is yes, maybe this is the game for you.
Just remember, if you stop moving, you die.
I just can't stop playing this game. I've tried, but I can't.

Hidden object games do something sinister to my obsessive-compulsivity. There's just something about them that's like a drug that won't let you go. After seven hours with this game, I'm almost inclined to go cold turkey.
This is the first hidden object game where I've ended up dreading going into new puzzles. Mouse clicks don't always register on legitimate items, and in a few cases objects are ambiguous-- there may actually be two of an item on screen, but only one will satisfy the game. Almost as frustrating, the game recycles hidden object scenes to an absurd degree, going back to the same well over and over again. That backtracking is really the meat, rather the gristle, of the game. It makes sense within the context of the time travel angle, and the puzzles that emerge from that, but you're visiting the same rooms and performing the same puzzles over and over again, and that wears itself out very quickly.
The rare one-shot puzzles aren't necessarily much better. Most follow a logic that is easy to work out. Others are simply baffling, accompanied by an unhelpful, cryptic comment by the protagonist if you click outside the playfield. The follow-up adventure is particularly bad for this; I'm not sure that one of them even works properly.
I get the feeling that this is one of Artifex Mundi's early efforts, because I've played a couple of their other titles and they seemed much more polished and enjoyable. I'm disappointed, because the gimmick of a family of time travelers is intriguing, and the time traveling mechanism is elegant, but the game felt like it was padded for length.

Just look at my hours in this game and think about it.
Yeah, I am most likely just a person who doesn't know how to discover new games.
But. I can say a few things about this game.
Yes, this is a "slavic brother of Fallout". A lot grimmer, darker, less comic and a bit older (in the first iteration of Shadow of Chernobyl that is), but still - similar story of similar situations. Brilliant post-apocalyptic atmosphere, brilliantly set-up immersive world and storyline that will leave you wanting more information. That is what I got from "vanilla" game experience.
However. I don't have 213 hours in the game because of vanilla, oh no. The only flaw of this game, I would say, is that it can be finished in literally under 10 hours, if you don't read anything and just do quests. No matter if those are side or main quests, there aren't many of them in general. The lack of accessible fast travel and dragged-on battles and quests elongate the experience just a tiny bit, but not enough for it to be really time-consuming (in contrast to Fallout, there are no skills or personal characteristics to upgrade besides your equipment, which means nothing slows you down).
So, back to the huge amount of hours in-game, I would say definitely a thing that Fallout and S.T.A.L.K.E.R. have in common is the modding community. But where I see tons of immersion mods for Fallout, I see tons of battle system rebalances and quest addons for S.T.A.L.K.E.R.
The amount of hours you spend in S.T.A.L.K.E.R. are definitely quality hours, and that is the difference between it and Fallout series. For what little it's got to offer, the setting and story behind it are so rich in detail that there can't be any further immersion past what it already is. Whereas in Fallout, even though rich on the story, it sometimes is redundant and can lack detail in places. Believe me, look at my hours in Fallout 4, I know.
You don't need to experience first two parts of this series - they are all standalone stories, even though "Clear Sky" is technically a prequel to "Shadow of Chernobyl". That means you can guiltlessly get this game, play it, and then other series without any particular order, if you'd like. But, obiously, I would recommend you play all 3, in some way, because you WILL want to know more by the end of this story.
So, I definitely recommend you pick up this game, experience it as is, and then head over to modding community, pick flavors you like and play it again. It is worth it for sure, and the story never gets old. There will always be details you somehow missed. I promise.

The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion is one of my favourite RPGs and a good example of how good writing and immersion can save bad and unfavourable design choices. One of the only things I dislike about its otherwise wonderful successor Skyrim is the lack of character balance. Yes power fantasy can be fun in the right context but for an Elder Scrolls game its a little antagnistic to the role play aspect of a roleplaying game for me. Oblivion, like some of its other siblings, make me feel more down to the reality of things, at least to whatever you consider reality to be in a fantasy RPG, and while Skyrim is my favourite this game is just really good and has aged very well to me. Morrowind's saving grace for me is that while its boil is horribly slow its immersion factor is very powerful and arguably the main thing that keeps me in the game. Still Morrowind's boil is painfully slow even if it gets considerbly stronger later. So I like Oblivion's pacing a bit better. I still cant decide if I prefer its pacing over Skyrim or the other way around, but I like the pacing of both more than Morrowind. My favourite critic said immersion is Oblivion's weak point and I have to strongly disagree. That immersion is one of the things saving the game for me and allows me to focus more on the things I like such as the writing, world, and combat rather than focus on the countless things I don't like voice acting, and models among other things.
This is a good game despite its flaws than really makes me feel invested in what I do and the world around me.
Of course I recommend it!

For only 5 bucks for another dip into the Halo Universe while we wait for Halo 5 isn't that bad of a deal.
It was originally made for the mobile platform before being ported to the X1 and 360 Arcade- and now is on Steam.
Let me tell you one thing- it's not a game for everyone and is catered to casual players or fans of the lore. It's your top down twin-stick shooter game with nice responsive controls whither you play on Keyboard and Mouse or your 360 Wired Controller.
It also has options for touch screen for those with the capabilities but I'll leave that out of the review since I don't have one.
Graphics- not much. It was made for mobile phones so don't expect to be blown away from them- but with capabilites of 720P and higher resolution with up to 8xAA it won't look that bad.
You can cap your FPS at your full refresh rate or half of it if you want (standard 60Hz, 30Hz) or none at all. It was kind of funny to see 500FPS average with my GTX760. My card actually downclocked itself since it was pretty much running idle. The cutscenes are beautifully animated and well drawn while being short.
Gameplay- Fast pace with a strange Halo echo to it despite being a major departure of the standard FPS shooter. You aim with either your mouse or right thumbstick (aim assist on the controller is prevelent) move with the left stick or ASDW keys and fire with the mouse or trigger buttons. The basic premises of the story is that you are re-enacting events in the past via simulations where you play as various Spartans in the sudden new Covenant War. Animations and sound feel and look like Halo, watching Grunts cower in fear like previous games is just as satisfying as it was back in Combat Evolve. The game is divided into Operations A-F and then x-5 with 30 playable missions in all- however, missions are brief and last no longer than 3-5 minutes.
One problem I've seen is that the 'upgrades' (overshield, sentery turret, and seeker drone) and 'weapons' (the spartan laser, sniper rifle, and rocket launcher) are single use and would have to be bought again with EXP you earn in the game. Haven't never played the mobile or arcade version of the game, this kind of screams micro transaction left over which may seem kind of lazy.
The Iconic Skulls make a return to the game to increase your game score multiplyer, such as Hollow where the Spartan has no health and only shields, or the classic Famine where ammo drops are less than usual. However, the famous IWHBD Skull is absent from the game as enemies make no understandable noises other than screeches and bellows.
Games are replayable, where you can compete in online leaderboards for the highest score. Assault Ops are the are challenges players can choose to pursue. There are weekly and mission specific missions you can undertake- such as Kill 250 Covies in Operation C for Weekly and Kill 50 Grunts in A-1. Completing these earn you EXP that you can buy said weapons and upgrades.
All in all, the game is a nice time passer for only 5 bucks with enough replayability to warrent multiple playthroughs. While not deep gameplay wise it's still a pleasent experinece for those itching for more Halo action.

This game is a masterpiece of stunning sound design, subtle minimalist visuals and a compelling narrative that sucks you in.
But also?
...have you ever seen Lost?  You know how for every answer, there are 40 more questions?  KR0 feels like that.  It's the most masturbatory hipster magnum opus on Steam; the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child of the gimmicky narrative of House of Leaves(this road goes a certain way BUT ONLY IF YOU POINT IN THAT DIRECTION) wrapped in cringeworthy Vogon bureaucracy fetch quests(you literally have to go back and forth looking up files and talking to clerks), pretentious contemporary art forcing you to interact with it(why am I interacting with this bird cage that sounds like a xylophone), all seasoned with smarmy, hipster, tongue-in-cheek humor, random for random's sake(why are there bears.).  You can just FEEL the beanie-bedecked, Weezer glasses wearing, skinny-jeans-and-curled-beard designers giving each other high fives each time they got a boner when their narrative switched from first person to staticky-vinyl-third-person-observer, or when the shadow hillbillies played bluegrass in the foreground as the characters exited a broken down mine the designers would never see in real life. because they're busy hanging out on the lounge chairs in Starbucks, romanticizing a mountain culture full of 'noble savages' they wish they could appropriate while deep-throating their venti mocha chai unicorn dust latte.
Magical realism is my jam - this world they built *is* a compelling and urgent dystopia, and I was begging for a reason to come back to it!  But none of the tidbits are connected.  I don't want backstory about the random hobo on the side of the road, or the janitor at the storage unit place.  I don't need my storylines handed to me on a plate, I enjoy a little reading-between-the-lines and conversatin' about the nature of the narrative... but a couple of hours in all I got was 'hey, this world is kinda weird and that one road works funny.'  And after the hours I put into this, my PC is starting to smell like sandalwood and beard oil, and I kind of hate it.

While I’m not going to give anything but props to Adam Brown’s cringing, panicked performance, the real star of the show is the bunker itself. Draped in darkness and retro-obsoleteness, it sets the stage perfectly for the game’s cold-war-gone-bad aesthetic. The bunker’s basic control system has been manufactured by Commodore, reintroducing those old enough to remember the name to long-forgotten blocky green text on sheer black backgrounds. Nuclear war broke out in the eighties, so those who managed to squirrel away underground are stuck with the technological trappings of their time. In promoting this, the bunker itself is a fantastic resource.
In order to stay alive, John needs to explore his environment thoroughly, glumly discovering more and more reasons to continue his descent to the lower floors. Upon stumbling into locations not visited in years, he triggers regressed memories of the bunker as it existed in his youth. People worked there. People lived there, sharing their concerns on the fate of the outside world and wondering how long their little community could hold out. As is the trend, John find most new information through little snippets of letters that were tidied away in long-forgotten draws, or on the corner of abandoned desks. Or he stumbles across items or locations that force a memory to resurface, whether he’d like it to or not.
It doesn’t take long before John finds The War Room. Here, on transparent charts, are maps of the United Kingdom. Checking some of these out zooms the camera in on a sharp red circle, drawn just to the south of London. Then, in the disinterested tone of someone regurgitating long-accepted fact, a female voice starts recounting the theoretical effects that a nuclear strike on that location would reap. Using just the smallest bomb as an example, she talks about the thousands that would die in the explosion, then the tens of thousands that would perish in the nuclear winds. She notes the major towns that would be wiped out in seconds from this one strike, all while the camera pans back and reveals a map that is absolutely littered with red marks. If that map is accurate, the UK has been obliterated.

Do you enjoy unintentionally (or intentionally...?) marrying your younger siblings to your elderly parents, or conspiring to murder every member of your family, in order to work your way onto the throne? No? Well good, as that probably means you're perfectly sane.
However, if you enjoy hilarious occurrences such as this in video games, (especially when they're entirely unplanned!) as well as plenty of random events to help mix things up, I have no doubt that you'll enjoy Crusader Kings II; as CK2 is essentially a peek into the lives of medieval murderers, sex-fiends, club-footed harelip Dukes, as well as many more different combinations of humorously incapable royals inbreeding their way to glory!
UPDATE: After a whole string of expansions came out since originally writing this review in Feb 2012, I've decided to re-write it and have added in the list below, containing some of the more essential expansions, as not all are necessarily required:
LEGACY OF ROME - This pack adds retinues and factions. As I recall it originally got a bad rap as it didn't unlock additional regions of the map to the player (like Sword of Islam, for example), but these days it really is a staple expansion, and adds a lot to the game.
THE OLD GODS - Vikings! And an early start date. Honestly, I feel that the Norse add enough that this is worth putting on the 'essentials' list, as it does shake things up a bit, from the standard 'European feudal lord' formula. Might want to get this after playing a game or two of CK2 though, as a regular feudal lord, perhaps.
WAY OF LIFE - I might get flak from some people by putting this into the 'essential' list, but it adds a lot more to do, during peace time. Plus Paradox has fixed the Europe-wide orgy caused by the 'seduction' focus being super-powerful, so it's not as crazy as it was right after its initial release. (For better or for worse! :P )
And now for a "good to have, but maybe don't get it until you've played the game a few times" list. (Rolls right off the tongue, eh?)
SONS OF ABRAHAM - Adds more options, events, etc. for the three Abrahamic faiths (Christianity, Judaism and Islam). Solid expansion, but not strictly required. Good for a second playthrough, or if it's on-sale when you first buy/play the game.
CONCLAVE - Kind of goes hand-in-hand with WoL above, I feel. Adds more to do (particularly during peacetime) as you're not the sole power within your realm, as your council will try and gradually curb your power and become a force to be reckoned with - so don't underestimate your councilors! Definitely adds a fair bit more difficulty though, as this expansion can result in a lot more civil wars occurring, if you aren't adept at ingame diplomacy and gaining favours, etc. so you may want to save this for your second playthrough.
SWORD OF ISLAM - Makes Muslim rulers playable, and adds in decadence mechanics for them. Good for a second or third playthrough, after you have your fill of playing as a Christian.
THE REPUBLIC - Same as SoI above, except it makes Republics playable. Adds in trading post mechanics (among others) for more money-making opportunities.
REAPER'S DUE - This pack expands upon the existing disease mechanics, and makes the Black Death a very real threat! It also allows you to hire a court physician, who will then proceed to cut your leg off and/or gouge your eye out, in order to cure your cold. Fun expansion, but not essential.
CHARLEMAGNE - This adds in a start date even earlier than TOG's start. Good if you want extremely long games that wind up taking a heavily alt-history route, but be aware that Europe will most likely be occupied by 4-5 huge blobs by 1066, so it might become a bit of a slog, late-game.
RAJAS OF INDIA - OK if you want to play in India, but be warned that unless you get a huge, sprawling empire going, there won't actually be much (if at all) interaction between India and the rest of the game world. Really, I think they could've just made this into a separate game mode/campaign option.

You play as Esther, a lady trying to learn more about your lost family after you receive a letter from a distant relative that suggests you to investigate an old mansion, which is, of course, full of mysteries.
During your adventure you'll come across multiple hidden object scenes and puzzles of all sorts of difficulty. The hidden object scenes are nicely drawn, but it's often hard to find the objects because they're quite well hidden and undistinguishable from the others. Most scenes come with a color palette containing many shades of gold, orange or brown, and these can be incredibly difficult to complete. Nevertheless, there is a hint button that recharges almost instantly, in case you get stuck.
The novelty that this game brings is the travel device that allows you to travel to important moments in your family’s past, and the actions you do will alter the future scenes. The device also serves as an incredibly helpful map - you have different symbols for the rooms you need to visit (those that have incomplete actions), for the unexplored rooms and for the scenes that change due to actions in the past. It also serves as a fast-travel device, even within the same time.
I found the game very enjoyable and interesting, but I wouldn't recommend it to people that are beginners in this genre because the difficulty of the hidden object scenes will probably set them back.

Artifex Mundi has a bunch of really great hidden object games out, but this one is probably the worst of them.  It's not uncommon to have to click on a object 2-3 times to get the game to recognize that you've found something, which is pretty much a no-no when you're dealing with achievements awarded for minimal clicking.  The design of the story can also be prety frustrating here, and it's not intuitive compared to a lot of their other games.  Also, the achievements are a little lacking compared to A.M.'s other games... there's no tier of achievements tied in to the mini-game that substitutes for the hidden object scenes.  Perhaps most egregious of all though, is the fact that several of the objects in pictures are literally hidden COMPLETELY behind other objects.  No recognizable piece of the object sticking out, literally the ENTIRE object is obscured by something in front of it.  Which means in several of the hidden object scenes, you're going to end up just randomly clickling around hoping to find the object behind other objects.  If you want a great hidden object game, check out Enigmatis 2, Nightmares From the Deep: The Cursed Heart, or Abyss: Wraiths of Eden.  All three of those games are much better in their design.  Even Clockwork Tales, a smaller effort, feels of a piece with those three, and the sequel to Nightmares From the Deep, while not as good as the first, is certainly worth playing.  Time Mysteries 2 feels like it was designed by different people, from the cut scenes, to the structure of the gameplay, to the hidden object scenes themselves.  It's a bit frustrating when played after the standards set by those other games.

Think you're good at FPS games?
Devil Daggers will completely destroy your confidence.
It is as raw an FPS as you're likely to get. There are very few of the tropes that most FPS games carry as baggage. In Devil Daggers...there's no map, no health kits, no lives, no continues, no save points, no plot... and no escape.
You have death constantly rain down on you and swirl around you. You fire back with daggers to hold them off.... and that's IT.
You will be lucky to last a minute before death finds you and ends your game.
...and you will play it again and again and again. Much like the arcade games of old, it's easy to play - and near impossible to master. The difficulty is brutal and unforgiving... which makes it great for a high-score challenge, and great as a casual game that you don't want to invest much time into (not that it will let you anyway!)
After suffering death and reincarnation over and over again.... you will have a religious experience. Your mind will become Zen. You will FEEL where those skulls are behind your back without even seeing them. You will be at one with the force, and then... only then.... you might last an entire **three minutes** before dying!
Devil Daggers has the best impression of hell that I've seen in a video game. Visually, sonically, and stylistically, it is downright evil... and to top it off the gamplay is addictive while being utterly merciless. Most soul crushing of all is being able to witness replays of the uber-humans who have survived past 500 seconds on the leaderboard.
Why am I dying to live, if I'm only living to die?
Just buy it

When I switched to PC gaming I never thought I'd miss Halo as much as I did (and still do). I've played Halo 3 since december 2008 and I played it untill the very last day I played anything on my Xbox 360 back in late 2012. That's four years of playing Halo 3 almost every single day. Needless to say but Halo was definately one of the best gaming experiences I have ever had, period. Fans and gamers alike have been waiting (begging, even) for Halo on Steam. Thus far the PC has only seen Halo 2 for Windows, but never before has a Halo-game been released on Steam. Until now, that is.
makes its entry to Steam as the very first (and hopefully not the last) Halo game ever to be released on it. Coming at a steal of only 5$ you get a complete Halo experience that is not only a fun Halo game, but also a great twin-stick shooter, offering quite a lot of content with endless replayability.
The Good:
· Solid controls allow for intense firefights set on beautiful locations filled with authentic Covenant enemies (like Grunts, Jackals and Elites).
· The Challenge System is back from Halo: Reach and Halo 4, bringing you more challenges several times a week. This adds a huge replay-value. One challenge may have you completing a level with at least one skull enabled, while another one will have you killing 200 Grunts with Assault Rifles in Operation B. Each challanges gives you additional experience to compete against your friens (and foes, if you're the competetive kind) in the leaderboars.
· The story, albeit quite forgetful, is a prequel to Halo 4s Spartan Ops mode without ever attaching too much to it. It's a story of its own that introduces new and old characters to the audience. Beautiful art-styled cinematics and gorgeous environments are a treat to look at and a blast to play though.
The Bad:
· No co-op or multiplayer. While the singleplayer offers a high challenge and huge replayability, the lack of co-op or multiplayer is rather disappointing. Gunning through the missions with a friend could on its own offer even more replayability, and the multiplayer could soak up hours of gameplay of Halo- and twin-stick-fans alike.
· It's not Halo 3, Halo: Reach or Halo 4, but it's still fantastic to have a Halo game on PC.
The Ugly:
· Stunning cinematics with solid gameplay set on gorgeous and varying planets make this game just as much fun to watch as it is to play it. Add authentic Covenant enemies and iconic Halo guns and this game makes for a gorgeous wet dream for any Halo fan on PC.
Final Verdict:
· If you love twin-stick shooters, get it. If you love Halo, get it. If you love games with high replayability, get it. For a 5$ price tag,
brings you a high-quality twin-stick Halo shooter that will have you coming back and replaying every single mission long after you've completed the main story. 9/10.

Blowing up ice bergs in battle is neat as it causes a small wave that damages smaller ships.  The story feels like it is lacking a little bit right now, it's not really explaining much of anything.  Hopefully that picks up.  Combat mechanics are fluid and ship battles are still epic even without the storms (again I don't know if they exist or not).  By the way, you can pick up bodies and toss them in the bushes which is a big plus.
I do feel that it doesn't quite live up to the epicness of Black Flag like I had hoped, but fun nonetheless.  It is pretty much a gigantic expansion pack worth about $35-$40 in my opinion.  I'd wait for a sale, but if you don't mind spending the money go for it.  I'll try to remember to update this review after I complete everything.

But the game kept getting weirder and weirder, without anything ever being explained for God's sake.
The dialogues are EXTREMELY long, boring, and meaningless. The gameplay is not good either. The only gameplay mechanics are walking and choosing between dialogue options, which gets hellishly boring and repetitive too soon. And the story cannot save the day either because it does not make any sense after some point. I have had enough by the end of Act III and skipped most of the dialogues in Act IV, because I simply lost interest in pretty much everything in the game. I hope the developers explain at least some things in the upcoming Act V. But up until then, I do not recommend Kentucky Route Zero; it just isn't worth $25.

What an incredible, beautiful experience this game was—haunting, melancholic, eerie, artistic, and familiar all at once. As others have said, it’s more of an experience than it is an actual game; I’m not sure that any of the choices you make have any bearing on what happens, which, honestly, is fine. Like the characters themselves, you, the player, are more along for the ride than you are in control.
I wondered in playing Kentucky Route Zero how much of the way it affected me was because of its familiarity, since I’m originally from Kentucky and many (not all, of course, at least not in a literal sense) of these places are real. Driving up Dixie Highway or flying over Nolan Lake felt like navigating places I’d known once, only irrevocably estranged, and even when locations aren’t “real” (is anything in this game?) they still felt familiar. It’s difficult to talk about a game being so rooted in a location when it’s just as obviously unreal, but the heart of it draws from Kentucky so much that even the Zero itself feels like a place I’ve travelled. (The first time you get directions—“Head north-east on sixty-five, and turn left as soon as you see that ugly tree that’s always on fire. Look for the barn at the base of the mountain there; can’t miss it.”—I laughed because those are actually the kinds of directions I’d expect from an old gas station attendant in Kentucky)
But while I think that the location of Kentucky Route Zero is integral to the game, what made it such an overwhelming experience for me was the slow burn of the way the characters’ stories unfold. There’s a sense of a sort of inevitable tumbling forward—sure, it’s ethereal and otherworldly, but it also explores very real issues at the heart of the human experience. Conway’s life of alcoholic dissolution, Shannon’s experience with loss and grief and determination, Junebug and Johnny’s navigation of togetherness and individuality, Ezra’s early abandonment—to say nothing of all the side characters who wander in and out of your story with their own contained joys and griefs—feel real and familiar despite their strangeness. The story touches on immigration, healthcare, poverty, love, family, abandonment, the automation of jobs, aging, the government, and the way that our choices lead us onto some paths while forever closing off others. It’s a sad game in some ways but it never forecloses off the possibility of hope. And the concert—! I honestly think that Junebug and Johnny’s performance changed this from “a beautiful game” to “a work of art” for me. I never expected to be so blown away and slack-jawed over a song in a video game, but here we are.
I can’t possibly recommend this game enough. If you want a story that rewards patience and melancholy then this is absolutely the right thing to turn to.

I wanted to like this game. I mean, everyone had been saying it was such a great "journey" with a cool story. Well, after finishing Act 4 of the promised 5, I have to say that I didn't see any of that. What I did see is a game that suffered greatly from any lack of direction in making the story and dialogue. You keep hoping that at some point the devs will tie something, anything to another point in the game, but it never happens. After 7 hours spent to play all 4 available acts, I literally have no idea why this game even exists because it didn't tell a story or serve any real entertainment value.
As for performance and issues, apparently the bugs and crashes have mostly been patched out, but I noticed a fair amount of typos and incorrectly spelled words which after 4 years in development is plain silly. They may have a small team, but things like this are easy and cheap to fix, so do it.
In the end, if you like random "moments" with no real connecting story or interesting characters, then this game may be for you. I however, found no entertainment value from it and can't recommend it whatsoever. Do yourself a favor and put that $25 towards a real road trip that you'll enjoy much much more.

At first glance, 100% Orange Juice seems to be the perfect solution for those of us who would love to play a relaxing multiplayer game with friends. Animations are cute, the board is colourful and the gameplay seems fun. A playable 4-person multiplayer? Sure! please sign me up.
Oh boy, how wrong was I ! This is why no one should ever judge the book by its cover.
The gameplay is the bare definition of dull. It offers nothing short of dice rolling miniaturized-monopolyesqued version of a boardgame where luck is the only thing that matters. The deck building (which is done prior to a match) has little to no strategy at all and drawing them (or not) depends largely on luck as well. Anyone with an aversion for luck-based games should definitely look elsewhere. For those who enjoy luck-based game, there is not much diversity in the game to warrant long-lasting gameplay as each different stages only offer a different board that has the same basic concepts and winning conditions. In fact, you do so little that you basically spend most of your time staring at the screen.
Kudos for fruitbat factory though, for coming up with such an attractive game name undeserving of its gameplay quality.

I purchased this game on a holiday whim not really expecting too much from it.  Fortunately, I was quite suprised by the attention to detail and the enjoyment I experienced exploring this game.  The developers really should be commended for the incredible detail they have embedded in to this game.  I'm not just refering to the truck driving simulation, but all the other unexpected details.  Things like construction sites, hidden police officers, accident scenes, skateparks, and pulled over speeders with overhead helicopter.  It also goes beyond the visuals and includes the subtle sounds too.  Passing a construction site and hearing road construction noises is awesome.  The audible rumble of roadside warning bumps.  These touches really add to the simulation experience and they are incredibly fun to experience in game.  While I'm enjoying this game very much, it's not without annoyances.  First, the police are just annoying.  Yes, realistic addition, great sounds, but they come out of no where at times.  Sometimes, it feels like I just get a ticket and I don't even see the police car.  Also, the red light tickets needs to be tweaked.  Approaching a light too fast but still stopping can sometimes get you a ticket (even if you don't run the light).  Also, right turns on red swung too wide can get you a red light ticket.  I'd like to see these aspects of the game play improved.  Otherwise, worth your time and money.  I highly recommend.

I've played MOBAs including the two main ones, DotA and League of Legends both with their pros and cons. As well as various other MOBAs that have dotted up.
But I have to say, Atlas Reactor takes the cake and eats it too. It's a fun blend of MOBA and RTS with a turn based system. The characters are unique and whilst may not have a large amount of lore behind them, I don't feel that puts you off loving any of them any less.
Best fun in a MOBA I've had in a long time, the community isn't too bad though I've so far encountered little team talk which is a shame as this is a strongly team-based game. An in-game VoIP would do wonders to this or perhaps including a 'chat phase' before each turn, someway of better communicating what you plan to do instead of just relying on chat would be great. Though despite this, it doesn't take too much away from the game and if you're really into the whole team tactics then you shouldn't have an issue finding a group or friends to play with and using Skype or Discord.
With each turn consisting of phases that breaks it down it really makes you think about what to do in your turn. Do you attack? Do you focus on moving to get a better spot? Do you dash to avoid an incoming attack or increase the distance? All these choices are up to you and dependent on your situation but it's what makes this MOBA so fun, you really need to think about what you're going to do a lot more than say DotA or League.

Atlas Reactor is a superb turned based multiplayer game. If you mix the colorful and diverse characters from Overwatch and Dota 2 and put in the strategical depth of Xcom you get, Atlas Reactor.
You don't wait for your turn , in fact everybodies turn happens simealutaneously. How does this work? Each action is divided into phases.
Prep Phase > Dash Phase > Blast Phase > Movement Phase.
Prep Prep phase is the phase where buffs, debuffs and traps are placed. Its the phase where you get ready for the incoming damage or predict where the enemy will dash too and throw a trap.
Dash Phase is the escape phase. Many characters have a dash move, when you're certain you're going to take lethal damage in the blast phase, you can dash out of the way and avoid the damage. But you have to be careful you dash into a trap an enemy prepared in the prep phase.
Blast phase is where the most damage happens. It's where bullets fly, electric blackholes suck you in, swords stab, dogs munch on you. It's crazy and fun to see how things play out.
After that it's the movement phase where you reposition yourself, another very important part of this game is positioning. As a tank you want to be in the thick of things but as a healer you don't.
Trion has made a very special and unique game. It's very satisfying predicting what your enemies will do and pulling off a kill they wouldn't have expected. It's fast paced for a turn based game and each turn will leave you tense as you try to survive. There's a free mode that acts like a demo where you can try the game with limited freelancers (hero's) But I can assure you the game is worth $20 just for the sheer fact there's no other game like it out there. This isn't just another MOBA or another class based shooter.
I think it's silly to write this game off just cause the devs did some errors in their past games, lets not pretend other devs are angels and have only done the right things in all of their games.
In the end, Atlas Reactor is a great game with a nearly toxic free community ( Face it every multiplayer game will have a few toxic people) and it's cheap. Yes there could be more content and there will be but hey it's $20 not $40 or $60 like many other games sold with just as little content kekeke.

is a very nice adventure game cleverly using what the RPGMaker programming softwares have to offer.
It's a sequel to the 4 chapters of the
serie, though it's enjoyable even without knowing those previous episodes.
is truly faithful to
spirit, as far as the storyline, humor and, to some extent, philosophical questioning are concerned.
For those who yet don't know the background: the saga is futuristic. It depicts a sight of what's left of humankind in the XXIIth century (if I recall, maybe later), in far away galaxies. There's much about politics, some sorts of foreign affairs between factions, war and terrorism. From a certain point of view it's very relevant and up-to-date with the world we're living in (differently thinking people trying to share the same place.. some more peaceful than others, but all willing to gain power and rule over the others, hence leading to conflicts).
The storyline of this chapter continues to be deeply interesting and the game ends, leaving suspens behind and leaving us wanting more and impatiently waiting for the next episode !
As in the 4 previous episodes there are 2 levels of storyline.
-The background story : what's happening on a wide scale / the political situation. Where are what's left of humankind and this new world going?
-The plot itself, on a lower level : what's happening to the characters / their personnal life. Why and how are they involved in these political events?
Some characters from the previous serie are back, notably the main characters Gail and Sabina.
In this new chapter you'll mainly play as Maggie, a teen girl rescued by Gail during a mission. You'll also play some parts of the game as Gail. And you'll recognize Sabina's delightful sarcasm ;D
At first when I realized I was going to play as a teen I thought "Yikes.. it's going to be boring". I was wrong, deeply. The girl and her school friends are quite funny and bluffing.
The relationship between Sabina and Gail is still at the heart of the plot too (I believe this was an important trait of the 1st Space Pilgrim saga, from an emotional angle).
As for many other (adventure) games I do think it tends to get easier and for that I am a bit disappointed. When I play an adventure game, the least i'm looking for is a bit of challenge, seing various options that make me wonder and hesitate, trying some that make me fail, trying again until I find the right "path".. not only clicking on obvious objects, making the only possible combination of items, using the one clickable tool of the scene. Sadly I didn't encounter any difficulty till the end of the game.
Therefore my playthrough was not very challenging. Getting the non story-related achievements was quite easy too.
However I recall getting stuck and scratching my head in the previous episodes, and also having trouble unlocking some achievements, being compelled to realize absurd and mind-twisted tries. That's where the funniest lies and I missed that..
I nevertheless recommend
because I definitely think a great and rare effort is put in the script, the whole story and the overall spirit. I totally love them and I am ready to support these precious elements even though the gameplay seemed a bit less challenging.
Besides the game lifetime is quite fair, especially considering the (low) price.
A tip to achievement hunters : Remember to save before entering any class room of the academy (when playing as Maggie) since in each class there is an achievement to get (a non-story related one, that is, you can walk by it). For these you'll need to give the right answers (all of them) or correctly complete the tasks the teacher will give you. You might make mistakes on your first attempt, so bare in mind to save at least before each course That way you won't have to restart from a far away save to unlock some achievements if you fail on your first try. You'll easily recognize where to get which class-related achievement (those achievements descriptions are quite explicit).
There's a tiny thing I didn't like too. Gail's and Sabina's faces thumbnails (their avatars during dialogues) changed.. but not for the best. Sabina now resembles a man, though she used to be a beautiful woman. The worst change might still be Gail who now looks dumb! Her eyes make her look like she squints.. I'm truly sorry for those who suffer from that sight disease and who I don't mean to offense, I just think it's a weird choice and the change is for the least amazing for those who played Space Pilgrim I, II, II IV and who were committed to the characters former apparences!
But since amongst the game main topics one can rapidly notice that high values like brotherhood or equality are far more important than superficial aspects such as physical appearence and since that's a lot in regards to those perspectives that I do love the Pilgrim saga spirit (trying and showing what's deeply important in life or in relationships, including the fact that true kindness or inner beauty are far more important than your haircut or the color of your skin), those physical changes for both main characters are only a tiny little (and superficial!) disappointment ;)
I strongly recommend
, as well as the 4 previous
.

Really solid Sonic game.  It's what Sonic 4 should have been.  The game feels fun, the levels are well designed, the sound is good, the package has tons of extras and unlockables.  Overall, a really fun game.
If you've played the classic Sonic games before, this is another one in the same style.  If you haven't, the game is a 2D platformer with a heavy emphasis on speed.  Sonic (and the other playable characters, Tails and Knuckles) move around the level very fast, doing loop-de-loops and flying off ramps and bouncing all over the place.  It's a very approachable game for players: the controls are simple (you can run and jump and if you hit jump in the air sometimes something will happen depending on your character but otherwise, it's just controlled with the d-pad and one button) the damage model is forgiving (getting hit makes you drop your rings, you don't die unless you get hit with no rings, so as long as you pick them back up you can keep going) and the stages have a lot of emphasis on fun, fast paced gameplay.  For more skilled players, there are challenges like special stages and bonus unlocks and time attacks to sink a lot of time in to.
The graphics are pretty amazing, looking a lot like the original Sonic from the 16-bit days but with much more animation and a deeper color palette.  The game incorporates some basic 3D elements for some of the visuals (the special stages are reminiscent of the Sega CD special stages, except with a polygonal Sonic) but keeps the feel of a mid ninties console game really well.  The music is pretty solid, and the sound effects sound like they're mostly lifted right from the old games, so the presentation here is pretty much spotless.
The game itself isn't exactly without flaws, some of the bosses are a bit of a chore and I have some issues with the autosave system (which automatically saves after act 2 of each zone but not after act 1 and there's no way to manually save) but outside of a few nitpicks, overall it's a great game.  If you don't like Sonic games, this one probably won't change your mind, because a lot of it is like a "greatest hits" collection of levels and gameplay ideas from the old Sonics, but if you ARE a Sonic fan, you should definitely check it out.

After a little back and forth, I decided to recommend this game, but although I loved the original Space Pilgrim series, this game stumbled a bit...although I have faith that the developers will hit their stride with the already-promised sequel to this, and it genuinely has a lot of good going for it, so I encourage people to give it a try.
I would usually do a pros and cons list, but I don't think that would adequately express both what I liked in this game and what I didn't both of which were plot/character related, so instead I will be focusing on those elements.
What I liked:
The new characters were charming and wonderful.  I genuinely liked all of the children, and while Maggie perhaps should have shown a little more indication of trauma after the game's opening, that wouldn't necessarily lend itself to a good game, so I'll let it pass.  Maggie is cheerful, sweet, and sarcastic...the perfect video game protagonist imo.
Although the pacing was a little weird, I did like the back-and-forth between playing as Gail and as Maggie, investigating what was going on through the eyes of a child, and of a war hero.  It made the game seem less silly than it would have had it been another 'child saves the day' epic, but firmly differentiated itself from the previous Space Pilgrim games by not focusing on Gail.
The characters from the previous series have genuinely grown and changed and are leading their own lives.  I really liked that the devs weren't afraid to go somewhere new.
Zubar's return.  'Nuff said.
What I disliked:
The 'in class' sessions felt too drawn out.  They were interesting (and I'm ocd enough to have gone back to make sure I got the achievements for completing them perfectly), but took away time that would have been better spent developing the characters or plot.  Further, they seriously threw off the pacing of the game, moving from fairly fast-paced moments to 'oh, now I'm playing a memory game' to creepy horror moments that just didn't work or build the story well.  It was an interesting idea, but I wish they had cut back on the number of in-class sessions.
Original series easter eggs -- yes, a lot of characters from the original series turn up, but I was really disappointed that Ashanti, Gail's father, and Jojo didn't...they were three of my favourites!  I understand that due to
it would have made incorporating them more difficult, but it was disappointing.  Further, Gail's character lost a certain sparkle of what I loved about her...
It took the positive element that is a character I'd grown attached to, and spoiled it a little.
The worst element is, I think, that the game generally felt like it just needed another good edit.  The writing is good, as always, and dialogue is engaging, but there were certain elements that felt weirdly tacked on.  For example, at one point (and even though I'm putting this in 'spoiler' blackout, you could probably read it because it really had no impact on the plot
in a throw-away line.  Now I get that it probably has something to do with the game's ending, but it just felt out-of-place and like it should have been mentioned elsewhere.
Finally, I wish there had been more time developing the antagonists.  I DO like that they are left as a bit of a mysterious evil, but some hints as to societal problems that might be driving them, even if those reasons aren't outright stated, would have made the universe feel a little more flushed-out.
Oh, and as an afterthought...the character portraits were really missed.
That all being said, I am definitely looking forward to the sequel's release.

You know that feeling when you take a wrong turn at night, and just keep driving? You never feel anxious or lost, but not quite good either? Kentucky Route Zero manages to capture that feeling.
This game has some strong characters. They all have deep, interweaving, backstories. I can't figure out a good way to say this, but I felt like I knew these characters for a long time. I found myself saying “Well yeah, isn't that obvious?” and then realizing that, no, isn’t obvious. I don't know. I can't quite put that feeling into words properly. Just play it and find out.
Kentucky Route Zero is cut into 5 episodes, 4 of which have been released. Those episodes are chopped into scenes. The game occasionally would do gimmicky once-scene narrative changes, like having time flow from left to right, or having the scene shot exclusively through security cameras with commentary from security guards. I love that sort of♥♥♥♥♥♥ It keeps you engaged with the story.
So about that episodic release schedule. It’s slow, apparently. Very slow. I wouldn't know, I bought this game a while ago. It can take up to a year of an episode. Many people have called it a scam, or accused the devs of abandoning the game. I think that’s bs. Each chapter is longer and higher quality than the last. Each chapter is also riskier than the last. Chapter one was pretty much a side scroller, while chapter three is mostly 3D and has cinematic angles. I would rather have a good game with long development than rushed garbage. But hey, that’s just my opinion.
Speaking of cinematics, this game looks pretty damn good. It nails the minimalist low-poly aesthetic. The game’s use of color is pretty great too.  Most of the game is dark and cold, but the bits of psychological horror are warm. It’s a nice change.
Overall, this game is amazing. I look forward to re-reviewing this when episode five eventually comes out.

Disclaimer, I know the solo developer for this game, so I was extra patient when starting out. It's incredible to me that he made this all by himself, art, music, design, programming. Tons of time and effort put into this project, not as another mobile ripoff to make money, but as something actually creative, innovative, new, and fun. Knowing all that made it worth my time to stick with it long enough to develop the skills needed to enjoy playing.
So I've managed to get 4 out of the 9 orbs so far, and I'm finally starting to believe I can beat this game eventually.
As others have said, the game is very challenging, but it's mostly about learning new skills. We've all played a million platformers. When we start a new one we don't have to learn how to play. This game is different.
Watch someone play a normal platformer who has never played one before. They will almost certainly get frustrated at first. That's how this game is, but for everyone.
Now, stick with the game for a couple hours and you'll start to learn new ways to hold the controller, new ways to approach puzzles and enemies, etc.
Best of all, once you manage to get past that awful unfair impossible puzzle...you'll find you could do it again pretty easily. Which means it's fair after all, just not the way your brain was thinking before :D
Side note: somebody should use this game in a study of how bad humans are at multitasking :P
TL;DR; Game is awesome and challenging but you have to be willing to learn new skills instead of just playing the same way you've been playing every platformer you've played the last 20+ years.

Great concept with pretty thorough execution. Good pixel graphics and cool enough soundtrack. Even if you find that you’re not very good at Lost Bros I believe that you will find the concept interesting enough to give it a playthrough. Whether that means you wait for it to be bundled is up to you but at just $4.99 the value is there.

Gear Up is an insanely fun and beautiful little free to play game. I had a lot of fun playing it.
