For instance, if someone with a heavy build can aim really well they can pretty much dominate the playing field. Meanwhile if someone with a light speed build knows what they're doing they too can top the leaderboard. It is in no way a P2W game. I can certainly say that it has more content than COD that's a given. So the game is very balanced and very fun. For a while...So what's the catch...?
My biggest problem with the game is how repetative the game gets as fast as it does. There are about 5-6 (give or take) maps total in the game. Two of which are only used for a single game mode, conquest. Which hardly no one really plays, or atleast any full servers of which when I played. I have yet to be in a full conquest server. Although that may just be me and my crap luck :(  Who knows? So you have about 4 maps, not counting the night versions (which are absolutly stunning to see the lights and colors of the mechs.) Eventually I just got bored of the whole game since I only used like 2 mech combos. Another thing is the lack of players. I have found an almost full server everytime I played the game, but only 1, sometimes 2. And they're are almost always TDM or DM. Overall a fun game but lacking in variety. Except for the mechs, you could tinker with them for longer than my total play time. Seriously go crazy. Anyway, i'm not going to say to avoid the game by any means, it's still F2P and I understand that, just don't get your expectations up too high. The style alone is enough to atleast give it a try. You won't regret anything if you do download the game though.

The Bunker is an FMV Video Game done very much in a similar vein to it’s 90’s predecessors. Featuring Adam Wood, the game takes you through a tense story arc where the character John battles against the decades old failing equipment while slowly dredging up memories of the past that allude to a horrible tragedy.
The story in the game is amazing and the acting is exceptionally well done, providing a wonderful atmosphere for the tense and tragic story arc. It is an experience that I feel is well worth the asking price and definitely something I am well able to recommend to my viewers.
However, bear in mind that the game is not without flaws. I did encounter one bug involving the child-John on the stairwell that forced me to exit and reload as I missed the quicktime event and the game would not let me continue. Also the gameplay being considered “barely present” Would be an accurate estimation and I feel the game could have benefited from a more robust system to back up the incredible story.
It is also short. Clocking in at under 2 hours, the game is short and that is mostly due to the lack of any in-depth gameplay mechanic. And as was the curse of the original FMV’s, the replayability is, while not nonexistent, extremely low.
All told, I ranked this a solid 8/10. The Devs did an amazing job for what they were intending to accomplish and all those involved should give themselves a pat on the back.

The incredibly fast paced nature of the gaming industry means that once you play a game like Breath of the Wild, all other open world games suddenly seem less special. Once you play Half-Life 2, it's harder to go back to the simpler FPSes of old. This happened to me with Kentucky Route Zero. I played this amazing little game called Oxenfree a week before trying this one, and boy was the difference staggering.
I know it sucks to put older games on the same standard as new ones, so consider this a retroactive review. If you ask me if I can recommend Kentucky Route Zero today, the anwser would be no.
The first problem is that I do not play games to read. If I wanted to read I will read a book. It's easier on my eyes and portable. Games as a medium has the advantage of voice over. You may say that books don't allow you to choose dialogue options. That's a great point, one that I'll address with my second problem with the game.
It's a classic problem that I wouldn't even see as an issue if it weren't for Oxenfree. Almost all story driven games have it: that artifical back and forth dialogue between npc and player. You wait for the other character to say their peice, and then you must choose a set of 3 dialogue options to continue. Comparing that to Oxenfree where the player can interrupt other characters with their diaolgue, or even choose not to say anything at all and simply wait for the conversation to naturally end, Kentucky Route Zero feels stiff. A lot of the time it doesn't even matter what you pick, so it would be better if you didn't have to choose between 3 meaningless dialogue options and just give me the most interresting choice, one that reveals the most about a character, like how they do it in a book.
Still. If you don't mind or even prefer a traditional text based adventure. I'm sure Kentucky Route Zero is good. I just don't have the resolve to sit through it when I could play Oxenfree again and see what dialogues I've missed.

Amazing game, I shed actual physical tears three times.  If you're looking for a good story and excellent character development with a detailed strategic combat system, this is one of the best I've played.  It's highly linear, as expected for this genre, you don't get to decide how the characters react at all, you just watch the cutscenes.
Definitely play First Chapter (FC) first, though this game does pick up faster.  FC was a bit slower to get into.  You could start with this one technically, and I bet you'd understand the plot eventually, but you wouldn't get as attached to the characters.  I played on Hard mode, which I'd recommend for more challenging battles.  If you do try Hard, the prologue is quite difficult, and not indicative of the rest of the game.  Use up any one-shot consumables in the Prologue, you'll need them, and can get more later.  The rest of the game up until the  battle just before the end,  is not as hard.  Most of the fights you can beat on Hard with the proper strategy, only a few (Prologue end, and the one just before the end boss) you'll also need some luck.  It's easy to restart if you get unlucky on those few fights, loading is fast.
There is a sequal to this  (Third Chapter (TC)) that completes this trilogy.  FC ends in a sort of cliff-hanger, while this game doesn't really. There are issues to be resolved, but you could take a break before TC (Third Chapter).

I'm a big fan of FMV games, but this was pretty much 100% linear where you just click the screen from time to time (along with pretty much no risk involved). Hardly any interaction at all or real choices. I pretty much just sat back and leaned forward to press a button every few minutes. Perhaps I'm spoiled, but I'm used to stuff like Fox Hunt or Silent Steel, or better, Phantasmagoria or The Beast Within in terms of FMV interaction video games (or heck, even Bladerunner could have been made an FMV).
In general, you're watching a movie and clicking the screen from time to time. No real choices, mind you, it's literally just a movie where you click on move spots...though the game is so linear that there's no real point. Every so often, you'll get a big circle that shows up and you click that too. That's literally the entirety of the gameplay outside of one puzzle (yes...one puzzle to solve in the entire game).
There's also no player freedom. There's a single linear path in the game. If you try to go off of that path, such as going through an unlocked door that the game deems as not the "proper" path, the guy just says something like, "I don't think I should go that way."
I recommend to NOT buy this. Just watch it on youtube.  It's practically the same as playing the game.

Well, what a wonderful game.
Honestly, got is a part of indie humble bundle. Thought I'd try it out because was quite bored. And it turned out to be my favourite game of the year as of now.
AS a 2D platformer it is quite demanding on your system - however nothing an average system can't manage (integrated graphics cards tend to have little support and in that regard run the game quite sluggishly. if you've got a separate gpu then it's gonna run smoothly). Nonetheless personally I think it's a beautiful game, even stunning. Mechanics are great - very enjoyable fighting, nice variety of weapons available and they all feel different too (a bit too "soft" and "smooth" for heavy guns like a rocket louncher or so, but it's futuristic plasma rounds that you're firing so I think it reflects on that well). Many different kinds of opponents that you will have to figure out how to kill, so it's not too much of a straight 'shoot em up' platformer.
Where this game really excels is its soundtrack.
The atmosphere it creates is simply... breathtaking. As a part of bundle I received it separately as mp3, and am listening to in on a regular basis - it's that good.
You will quickly notice that this game is not lengthy. Still it leaves plenty of room for prolongued gameplay, especially if you like picking up achievements and accomplishing everything to perfection.
To round up, as mentioned I was so blown away by this game - gameplay, soundtrack and (forgot to mention) story wise. Definetely pick it up if you're a platformer fan (imho it doesn't redefine the genre in any way - however it does show that it's still got that kick), and, well, even if you're not. I guarantee you will not be let down.

American Truck Simulator takes the already proven formula of Euro Truck Sim and improves upon it in several aspects.
The richly detailed landscapes coupled with dynamic roadside events like police stops and traffic accidents bring a fresh sense of realism to the world. Having grown up in California I've driven the routes featured in this game many a time and can attest to the nostalgia-inducing attention to detail that the developers have put into the environment.
More importantly, however, I was able to fulfill a lifelong dream of mine and finally drive up one of those runaway truck ramps.
There is still room for improvement, the AI is essentially the same as ETS2. It'd be nice to see car accidents or police stops happen in real time at random. Also, there are only two truck brands to choose from. I'd love to see more classic brands like Mack or Freightliner. However, for the price I definitely think ATS is worth it.
If you're a fan of Euro Truck Sim, you'll love the improvements that this game has to offer. If you're a fan and you're from the U.S. then this is a must have.

So far the best part about the game is that its Halo. If it wasn't Halo, this type of game probably wouldn't draw as much interest from me to be honest. Its pretty basic. It looks like there are 4-5 operations with 5 or so levels each. Each level so far has been pretty short, it maybe only takes 5 minutes to complete. Similar to mobile games, each level has a possible 3 stars (bronze, silver and gold) based on how many points you earn during the level. At the start of a level you are able to select a load out of two weapons and some type of armor upgrade. The default load out is "free" and to change the default load out you must spend XP gained during previous levels. You can also select from 6 handicaps (up to 2) that will multiply your XP gained during that level. It looks like in order to get a gold star at the end of the level you probably need to use a handicap. Examples are: one handicap makes your armor deplete as you are firing a weapon, another gives weapons you pick up less default ammo. You get points or XP from killing enemies and from kill bonuses like double and triple kills, etc.
Its what you would expect from a Halo game in terms of the types of aliens you are fighting and the weapons that are available. Like other Halo games you usually run out of ammo from your default load out and have to pick up enemy weapons along the way. You also get grenades, which are fun, and some levels have cannons that you can get inside and blow up aliens.
Each level has some type of objective you have to complete, like destroying 3 objects or escorting vehicles.
The game has steam cloud support, achievements and cards, which make it very Steam friendly. Even if you don't like the game you can get cards to sell or a badge to craft or if you are lucky a booster pack. The game also has full controller support, which I haven't tried yet. I wish the game had some type of local/online co-op.
The game is fun, but not mind blowing. Definitely a casual unless you go for 3 stars on every level, but even then so far the levels have all been so short its probably not a huge pain to grind out the 3 stars. All in all I am glad I bought it, but unless you are a Halo fanatic there probably isn't a huge rush to go out and buy it. Its currently on sale on the Windows 8 Storefront and xBox Live store, so I would expect this to be on sale at some point.

This game is simply amazing. It's a classic that I keep coming back to and feel bad if I haven't touched it in a few months.
First things first, though. The negatives:
1) The graphics are seriously dated. NPC models are almost comically bad. That said, the art style makes up for the rest.
2) The base game (without any mods) only has 3 maps, and if you're an experienced player like myself, you can breeze through it in around 10 hours or less. New players will take longer, though.
3) There is a steep learning curve. New players should not attempt higher difficulties if this is their first STALKER game. If you've played any of the earlier games, you know what I'm talking about.
Ok, onto the good stuff:
1) The game's difficulty really becomes its own charm. This is the only game in my mind that is a Shooter, Open-World but story-driven, RPG, FPS, Horror, Survival, Zombie, Action, and Drama game all in one. It manages to be all of these and not suck. You feel the progression like an RPG, but fights are still clearly FPS-based, and even the biggest badass can go down with proper aim and a decent gun. There are some really tense moments against some of the mutants (poltergeists and bloodsuckers can kiss my♥♥♥♥♥.
2) The mutant AI is really damn good. I still jump at some of the scares from the monsters. The weaker mutants choose to hide behind corners and jump out or run at you in swarms. Even something as weak as the mice can be a threat if not addressed appropriately.
3) The enemy human AI is a little less than perfect (they often ignore very long range sniper fire, or sometimes have ungodly aim at long distances). They also do some of the annoying shooting while strafing issues that plague these sorts of games. That said, they feel appropriately tough but not bullet sponges (assuming you're playing on normal difficulty)
4) The game is very atmospheric, and very Soviet. You will definitely feel like you're in the Ukrainian version of Fallout, but without the ease of the Bethesda Fallouts.
5) The game is moddable! There's a huge community that popped up around the game. If you want to try a mod, I highly recommend the "Call of Chernobyl" mod. It adds all the maps from previous STALKER games and lets you play as any faction you like.

WOW! there is absolutely no other words to describe this game it is fantastic!. The story is set in the mid-18th century during the Seven Years' War, and follows the story of Shay Patrick Cormac, an Assassin turned Templar. Gameplay in Rogue is very similar to AC Black Flag with mixtures of ship-based naval exploration and third-person land-based exploration with loads of new features added. Naval aspects from the previous games will return with you controlling Shay's ship, Morrígan.
A New feature include new ship-based weapons including releasing an oil slick which can then be ignited, Puckle guns, and the ability for enemies to board Morrígan during ship to ship combat. The arctic environment also features into naval gameplay and exploration, as certain icebergs can be rammed with an icebreaker. In combat, the game introduces a air rifle, which now allows Shay to silently take out enemies at a distance. The air rifle can be outfitted with a variety off different projectiles, such as firecrackers.
Also you can use a grenade launcher, which fires shrapnel grenades and berserks. Hand-to-hand combat has been slightly altered, now the enemy attacks also can be countered with timing, similar to the Batman: Arkham game franchise. Enemy Assassins feature archetypes similar to previous games, using the skills you used throughout the series; they can hide in the bushes, blend in with crowds, and perform air attacks against you. The poison gas can now be used as an environmental weapon, and now Shay also has a gas mask that can mitigate its effects.

Reflecting on Shay's role as a Templar, the game now introduces a new side mission: Assassin Interception.They mirror the Assassination side missions in previous games. After you intercepted a messenger pigeon that is carrying a assassination contract. He must prevent Templar agents from being assassinated by finding and killing Assassins hidden nearby.
I would give Assassin's Creed Rogue an overall rating of 10/10 stars. The PC port is very well done with no FPS or any kind of other issues. This is definitely a MUST buy for fans because I'm just absolutely without a doubt 100% sure that Assassin's Creed Rogue will not disappoint at all!.

is a retro trial-and-error game developed and published by Wheat Muffin Games. This is easily

You play as three bros who go back in time to save a member of their band who got sucked into a time vortex. There are 9 levels, each with a different setting, including the Stone Age, Ancient Egypt, Feudal Japan, Ancient Greece, the Far West and the Future. I liked the variety of settings, but the actual story (which parodies the simplistic nature of time-travel movies and games) isn't a selling point, nor does it want to be.
Powered by Unity, the pixelated and almost hand-drawn levels are full of details in the background, including a different Game Over screen based on which level you are playing. However, it will start looking a tad repetitive, especially in the Far West and Piracy levels.
In each level you guide the bros to the end while avoiding traps and fighting enemies. One bro can use a sword and walk while crouched, another can jump and shoot rockets, and the last one can punch and use a shield. This is pretty similar to the SNES classic
, but instead of switching between characters, you control them at the same time. The controls aren't intuitive, and playing with a controller is a must, since using the keyboard is extremely awkward.
Forget
and
. Lost Bros is the hardest and most frustrating game I've ever played. In over two hours I beated the tutorial, died over 250 times and managed to fail every single attempt at finishing a level. The difference between the aformentioned games and this one is that this game is not enjoyable. The levels feature a lack of a learning curve and an astonishing amount of obstacles (as well as friendly fire) that will make you more and more depressed, until you start asking yourself why you are still playing, if you just keep dying in miserable ways.
While a couple of sound effects get a bit annoying, the soundtrack fits every time period perfectly. But prepare yourself to listen to the same 20 seconds of music every time you respawn.
For you masochists out there, there are multiple levels of difficulties that make the experience even more unbearable. There are also 26 achievements to unlock, so prepare yourself for many hours of swearing and violently smashing your controller to the walls.
Overall, Lost Bros is a competently made game that, unfortunately, lacks any kind of reward and enjoyment. I can't, for the love of God, recommend this game to anyone except fans of hardcore frustrating games.

In some games you make choices based on whether you want to be a pure goody two shoes or a demonic jerkoff with no real consequences, making numbers go up and down, or figuring out some convoluted mess of a puzzle (to be fair I do like many games that do any of these). In this game I made choices that made me reflect on how afraid I am to get hurt enough to go to the hospital and get a medical bill I can't pay, because of this country's intentionally broken healthcare system. I made choices that showed how ashamed I am of my father's slide into alcoholism, and how ashamed I am of myself for feeling that way.
Not a book nor a film, and it wouldn't really be the same if it was either of those, Kentucky Route Zero is a game that puts you in characters' shoes and asks you "how would you feel in this situation?" It's a point and click with no puzzles, and I don't miss them at all because they would've been meaningless distractions in a game that is so
with meaning. Believe me when I say despite the game's reputation as being very weird, the story at the heart of it all is based in a crushing reality; the characters here are in debt and losing their honest jobs to the machine of capitalism, among other situations I could easily understand to make choices for them when I was literally put into their shoes. The surreal aspects are there as metaphors to highlight the desperate emotions of what's really happening, and sometimes to make it all absurdly funny. The writing is slow but understated and subtle, patient with you to dig deep into it.  Not to speak lightly of the gorgeous atmosphere created by the visuals and audio, warmly inviting you to dive into all its dreamy mystery.
Kentucky Route Zero is one of my favorite video games ever. I've wanted to see a game like this for a long time. Please try it because I guarantee you haven't played ANYTHING like this.  I understand wanting to wait til episodic games are finished, but honestly I would've kicked myself for staying away from KR0 for so long if I had done that. The wait is fine with me if this is the quality we can expect for the last act, and even if it never comes out my opinion of this game won't change. And it's best to play this slowly anyways, without blowing through it in one go.
I also recommend these free games made by Cardboard Computer that expand on KR0's universe. They're not demos so much as experimental little things that are really interesting and unique, and they'll give you an idea of how committed the devs are to their art:

Another excellent Space Pilgrim adventure.
As the blurb says, this game takes place after the end of  Space Pilgrim episode IV. Eight years have passed since the events of that game and things have moved on. Gail Pilgrim is now an ambassador with responsibilities, the life of a roaming space captain behind her. In the opening she rescues a young girl, Maggie, from a mysterious attack on a seemingly mundane industrial research facility. Placing Maggie into school at a local academy, Gail sets out to find out what really went on at that research base.
Gameplay is divided between both Maggie and Gail, as Maggie deals with school work and gets to know her fellow students while Gail does some hands on investigation. As with the Space Pilgrim Saga, the games story is well written and engaging. The central story will keep you interested and it also has some good humour too. As this is an episodic game there is enough left open at the end that when the credits roll you will be eager for the next release.
Just to be clear to anyone who hasn't played the other Space Pilgrim games, these games are not RPG's, they are adventure games. Expect lots of conversation and some puzzle solving, but there are no stats, levels or combat. So long as you go in knowing what sort of experience you are in for you should have a good time. Speaking of the other Space Pilgrim games, you don't need to have played them to enjoy Academy, but you will get a lot more out of it if you have and the other games are excellent and very well priced so I recommend you go through them first.

Scope, scale, depth, everything you could possibly want in a grand strategy game...with caveats. That's CK2 in a nutshell.
On the whole, I definitely very much recommend this game, particularly for fans of the grand strategy genre. It has a level of detail and sandboxy goodness almost impossible to find outside of Paradox's repertoire of games. It's a great game on the whole, but particularly post-5000 DLCs, comes with some important drawbacks that must be stated as well.
Passable. They're not exactly grand scale graphics on the level of Total War: Attila, or extremely detailed on the scale of most modern shooters, but they get the job done. If you're playing a grand strategy game for the graphics, you're playing the wrong genre.
Here is where Crusader Kings 2 really comes into its own. While it's certainly not for everyone (there may be a few too much technical stuff for many, as you'd expect from a grand strategy game, and the abundance of menus necessary to contain all of the available detail can seem a bit daunting), the gameplay itself passes smoothly and without many major niggles. For the kind of game it is, you're both rarely wanting for something to do, nor likely to have much trouble doing it.
In addition, there is a lot to be said for the amount of addicting detail this game possesses, and the sheer variety of different situations your character can be placed into or you to deal with. Every major religion has a different playstyle, different cultures can have different bonuses, different government types play completely differently, and historical characters have even more going for them. Events are generally varied and interesting, and it can often be fun just to sit back and let the game run to see how the world evolves on its own.
All of that said, we come here to our first and most import caveat, and the one that leaves this at only an 8 rather than a 9: DLC. A good 2/3rds of this game is locked behind the various dozen or so major DLCs for the game. Want to play a Muslim nation? Nope, DLC. Want to play as the nomads? Nope, DLC. Want some extra variety for the Christians? Nope, DLC. Want greater interaction with your subjects? Nope, DLC. This game is heavily bloated with DLC, and it shows, especially if you're only going to buy the vanilla game, and not all of the major DLCs are at all worth the purchase. My suggestion is to be wary and read the DLC reviews. You're going to like some a lot less than others, which is important considering how much each DLC changes the game.
AI has been a bit of a rollercoaster ride over the course of CK2's evolution from day one. At times it'll seem humanly intelligent, plot several moves ahead of you and sabotaging you at every turn. Other times, it'll seem like you're playing against the village idiot, purposefully sabotaging himself so that you'll be able to take over and he won't have to do any more work. Be prepared for a wild variation in AI quality over the course of different situations, as its quality is wildly unpredictable. As of late, it also seems to have an exceptional ability for blobbing (forming gigantic nations that just won't collapse no matter what happens, and just keep eating more and more land).
Oh, also, be prepared for more raiders each in-game year than in the entirety of Fallout 4, and that's saying something.
As mentioned above, the main issue with the UI is the abundance of menus; HOWEVER, in a game with this much detail, menus are a necessity, so it doesn't phase me much. Otherwise, everything is smooth and easy to use, and it even looks pretty good.
Music is varied and interesting, though with the amount of time you'll be playing the game, it may eventually start to grate on you. My suggestion is to install a mod that allows DLC music to play regardless of what culture/religion you're playing in the game, to allow yourself more variety. But of course, as mentioned above: DLC. Most of the time I play now, I just turn the music off and run Youtube in the background.
Customization is DLC locked as well. However, if you do get the DLC, you're granted the ability to custom design rulers with one DLC, to custom design titles with another DLC, and more. There's plenty of opportunity to create a dynasty based on yourself or a character you like, as long as you pay for the DLCs.
The sandboxyness is the absolute reason I recommend this game. The amount of different insane situations you can get into, and all the variety of goings-on you can see unfolding around you, this is what makes the game worth it in my eyes. A ruler stealthily assassinating another so that his heir will inherit that ruler's land? Check. A queen poisoning her husband king so she can marry another man? Check. Child possessed by the devil? Check. Sandbox at its best.
All in all, I do highly recommend this game, if you're willing to shell out the money for the DLCs. While it's no longer quite my favourite game and I don't recommend it quite as much as I used to, due to some of the more recent changes that have taken place, it's definitely high up there even so. With mods, it can be even better, and by Gord, are there ever a lot of mods. This game is modder heaven, so even if the game isn't quite like what you want, it CAN be.
So give it a try. You won't be disappointed.

On first hearing about The Bunker, I thought it looked just to be another average horror game skinned on a gimmicky mechanic [that being the use of FMV] but after watching a short play through of the first five minutes, I knew I was wrong.
Aside from the brilliant camera work and acting which i'm sure you can read all about in these reviews and on websites, The Bunker has a brilliant story beneath all the horror and occasional jumpscares. Sure it takes aspects from other stories with that apocalyptic setting and feel, and I garuntee this isn't the first you'll find with the idea of a small isolated group running out of supplies, or the 'you're not alone down here' thing which many games do, but the sharp writing takes full advantage of what most people would expect and turns it upside down.
Many talk about the length of this game, and i'm happy to say that like those people I felt satisfied with the two hour [minimum] length. The cinematic feel allows you to stay interested in what's happening, and a need to want to know how it will all end shows that this game has great, engaging writing.
There is more depth to this game which I cannot go into without spoiling it but if you really take a hard think about this game after the credits begin to roll, you will begin to understand just how smart it is.
As for flaws, I can only say that I had a few audio issues with the voices being in sync, and also one situation later on where a quicktime event plays out at a very fast rate, and if not completed fast enough you will have to replay about a three minute segment. I didn't find it much of a bother but some might grow impatient with little things like that.

The following is my review in pseudo FAQ format. Enjoy! :)
I bought this as a way to learn to play an electric guitar - something that I (and I suspect many others) have wanted to do since childhood but never really had the right tuition or couldn't quite follow along with a book/video. Mainly because you can't necessarily trust an instructor to be able to tell if you're hitting the right notes/chords and a book/video may assume a skill level or familiarity that you, as the learner, just do not possess.
Also, as per usual, it was in a sale and it's taken me at least a year to get around to buying a Real Tone cable once the price had come down in price to £20 on Amazon.
Yes. Yes you do.  You start with simple single note arrangements of songs, leading to complex single note arrangements and then on to a combination of single notes and chords before going to full chords.  The speed at which you do this depends on what Rocksmith thinks is best for you in terms of your actual ability, with arrangements being made simpler or harder (or truer to the actual song being played if you prefer).  You can also practice specific chords of a chosen song, any part of a song, different arrangements, or change songs in your "setlist" to ones you're more familiar with and/or genres you prefer.
Starting with single notes, you are also memorising your guitar's fretboard and how far to move your fingers without even counting the frets as you go.  As you progress further, Rocksmith will introduce new elements such as sliding from one fret to another - both as part of the song you're playing
to further cement fret positions in your mind.  Even after a few days to the end of your first week of playing, you'll find yourself being able to play songs with far fewer mistakes (perhaps even perfectly, as of course everyone learns at different speeds).  Certainly, you would have started developing those all important calluses!
As a game, Rocksmith is far more entertaining than say Guitar Hero/Rock Band in that you're genuinely playing along with a real guitar (that needn't cost the same as a Guitar Hero/Rock Band accessory), and is always just challenging enough in difficulty and the side games provide a welcome relief to learning songs and using a real guitar as an alternative controller whilst
being educational.  The Rocksmith Points that you get for completing songs and side games all add up to your resulting score and is a good objective metric of your progress/ability.
Speaking of side games, these are unlocked as you progress so that you're never in a position where you are in way over your head.  For example, the first game unlocked is the Duck Shoot where you play single notes on the 6th string in particular fret positions to shoot the ducks, simple enough. But from there as you progress, you'll unlock the scales mini game and so on, providing an incentive to carry on and is yet another way of letting you know how far you've come from starting out.
Additionally, there is a multiplayer mode and it's up to you and those you're playing with if you want to be competitive or use it to encourage as a group to all learn a skill.
Like a higher priced budget collection in that all the songs are well known and like all budget collections, you'll be a fan of some more than others (perhaps by a great margin).  For example: if you want popular 50s rock artists like Chuck Berry and Bill Haley? You're out of luck. There aren't any TV/Film themes either (which are almost traditional to learn) or rock instrumentals such as FBI by The Shadows.
If you like Nirvana, Snow Patrol, The Red Hot Chilli Peppers and the like (generally popular rock from the late 80s onwards) then you'll be escstatic and perhaps disappointed your favourite song wasn't included, which is small beer when compared to those of us who prefer 1950s-1970s rock given that we get 8 songs (three of these being by The Rolling Stones - with none of them being Paint It Black! Have to upgrade to Rocksmith 2014 to get that one) out of a total 57 that come with the base game (6 are unlocked as you play, all of which are from 2011).  For the sake of completion, two of the songs from 1988 onwards are Run Back To Your Side by Eric Clapton (2010) and Jarvis Cocker (formerly of Pulp fame) represented with one of his solo efforts "Angela" (2009).  For Clapton and Pulp fans (of which I'm neither), this is something of a raw deal given the  respective back catalogues.
Yes and no. If you live in the US? You'll be fine, all the DLC is available to you. In the EU, not so much. I'd like to be able to buy "Roadhouse Blues" by The Doors along with packs only available in the US region (the orchestral/classical selections should be royalty free by now the world over, so why only a US release Ubisoft?).
Rocksmith is a good learning tool to practice to your preferred songs (where available) and if you prefer mid-80s onwards, you're very much catered for.  I'd also recommend Rocksmith as a solid stepping stone to give you a head start when it comes to training DVDs and books, given that you'll have at least a working knowledge of playing a guitar.
I'd also advise going in with the mentality of treating songs by artists you're not fond of (or even heard of depending on your tastes) as a level to be mastered.  It works, but songs you actually enjoy may help you better - each to their own in that regard!
Have fun though, learn, and impress yourself if no one else that you've learned a new skill!

Do you like deck building? Do you like RNG and seemingly-rigged AI? Do you like destroying friendships? Do you like anime girls? Then you might sorta kinda like 100% Orange Juice.
In a way, OJ is kind of like Monopoly: you make your way around the board, trying to collect money (or in OJ's case, Stars), avoiding bankruptcy (or death), all while trying to hinder your opponents with your own Mario Party-esque arsenal.
The game works well, especially since the majority of the cast is tailored for a specific playstyle; very few characters can efficiently aim for KO and Star Victory Conditions. In response, you'll have to use different card combinations, which at the very start of the game can admittedly be a bit boring. But with each game getting you in-game currency, you'll soon be expanding your card repertoire.
My main issue actually lies in this expansion. If you enter the store, you'll find that the majority of the content is locked behind conditionals: a price, and a level. Normally this would be fine, since one would assume that every game grants experience - NOPE. Only multiplayer games give you experience, so you'll first have to run through AI matches to get Stars to improve your deck to a decent level, then play against people who know what they're doing to unlock all the content in the game.
I like multiplayer. I also like single player. I kinda wish that I wasn't forced to play with randoms (none of my friends own OJ), but it was a necessary sacrifice to unlock things. It's better than the microtransaction option however, so I'll give it that - no pay to win is always a good thing.
So for the most part, I recommend 100% Orange Juice. Unless you have no friends. Then it might not be as fun for you.

Atlas Reactor, a fun game about playing a Freelancer in a fast paced turn based strategy game that is oh so slightly reminicent of Xcom. The game takes place on a 20 second turn timer were you set up your move and see what your team mates are doing. Then those moves you set up happen in phases. The phases are as follows. The Prep phase is where healing, support, and trap like actions occur, This makes it so you can keep up yourself or your team before the figurative (sometimes literal) bombs drop. Next up comes the dash phase, were you get to do a quick, most of the time short move. Almost every freelancer has a dash abillity they can use, They can do damage, stealth you after a short teleport, stop the enemy from moving later, and save you from a bad situation such as an entire team surrounding you. The next runner up is the Blast phase. This stage, unsurprisingly, has a lot of blasting. Almost all abillities in this phase go in a sort of order that you more or less learn by playing. It's made so that the abilities that deal straight up damage go before the abilities that move people around go. While this keeps a lot of cockblocking from happening, poor team coordination still ♥♥♥♥s things up. Finally there is the move phase, where you move normaly if you're still alive after all of that.
You keep doing this until one team gets 5 kills, or has more kills than the other at 20 turns. There are 3 or 4 maps that have enough variety in how you play on them for you to notice. That's about it on the gameplay side, time to get to the big issue.
I haven't read much into why Atlas is like this, but its a free to play, but as Trion is involved with it, there's something off. The one thing that could ruin this wonderful, hero based game, is by restricting heroes. You see, Im not sure why this is, and it might just be a slow adjustment out of EARLY early access, but you have to pay to be able to have access to all Freelancers at all times. It tries to make up for this with a free rotation change that happens every two weeks, and is unique for each play, but it doesn't work to well when you want to play who your comfortable with after a bad losing streak. It also tries to make up for it by giving you access to lootcrates in the free version, and you get to open one every two days or so. This lets you have a wide variety of cosmetics that you would have to pay several bucks for in any other game. Once again, you can't own freelancers, so it's like getting nothing but that loot you didn't want when you pay for those keys or chests in other games like TF2 and Smite. So, if they get rid of this and make it a proper F2P with a sort of Ultimate Character Pack like the other good games, then I would totally be 100 percent reccomending this game.
So, in short, the Gameplay is wonderful, most fun I've had with friends since I started playing smite about 3 years ago. But, at the moment, gameplay is all it's got going for it. If it wants to be popular in any way, shape, or form, then it's gonna have to fix how it's doing it's free to play.

So far I love the game. The characters are so fresh and interesting and Shay is portrayed really well so far. I have now played 4.2 hours an definetely feel that sam addicting vibe I had from ACIV:
The mechanics are familiar to anyone who played Assassin's Creed IV Black Flag. The best way to describe it it going in methodical, but also quick so as to get 100% on missions. So far only playing as an assassin is identical to Edward Kenway in Black Flag as you start off with dual weapons, a sword and knife, but new animations are nice and its cool to see Shay fight with the smaller weapon. The parkour/movement is next to perfect as you'll occassionally wonder if you can climb some rocks or materials or simply take a few tries to climb trees or builidings. The naval battles come back again and are as fun as ever with the 4 direction shooting system being directly taken from Black Flag, which I thought did much better than Assassin's Creed III. Long story short: If you loved Assassin's Creed Black Flag gameplay combt and movement wise, you'll love this game as well
The air rifle is pretty hany and I feel really cool to have. I just started getting into the Assassin hunting mechanics which are actually really fun. If you played the Assassin's Creed Multiplayer portion, you will feel at home as you have a compass whenever you are going up against assassins in which the compass will start to fill up whenevr you are close to an Assassin. You also however can be stalked by the assassins and actually do have to pay attention more than usual.
So if you read in the community hub, you can see that a lot of people are reporting on great optimization. That may or may not be true however. This game looks nice but is hardly current gen graphics. The graphics are definitely not as high quality as Black Flag and may be in between or on par with Assassin's Creed III. The hair and textures do not look very realistic at all and detract if you look long enough at them, although you really only notice this during cutscenes. Another major complaint is the lack of antialiasing options as Ubisoft only gave FXAA, despite having MSAA and TXAA in both Assassin's Creed Unity and in Black Flag. While the game does run nicely, I would appreciate it if I could make lines less jaggy with better AA tools. Character Animations are smooth and cool to watch as you get to watch and appreciate how Assassins move and kill in this game more than before. Another big selling point about this game is again how little hardware it takes to run as I can max it out on my laptop which as an intel i7-4710hq @ 2.5ghz (3.5 turboboost) and an GTX 860m 2gb graphics card.
A great addition to the game is the music, as I loved Black Flag and Assassin's Creed II's soundtracks. The only bad thing I've heard music wise is just recycled sea shanties from Black Flag. I found it so great that they made a new updated version of the Assassin's Creed II song "Ezio's Family" (btw one of my fav songs from that game) for the title sreens and it sounds great. I also just like listening to the background music while playing, osmething I did not really remember or enjoy from both Assassin's Creed Unity and Assassin's Creed III.
Overall I would recommend getting this game for now as it definitely is polished for PC and I have had no bugs yet. The voice acting is great and the characters aren't simply cutouts or meaningless cameos. The gameplay is as tight and fluid as ACIV but for sure not as pretty looking as ACIV. You also should not have any trouble running this game as it works well and is easily maxed.

So it's not Halo 3, who cares? As much as i love H3 (being my favorite Halo of all time) this game is a totally different experience from most any Halo game you have played before and coming from a Halo fan, It's really not a bad thing. The Halo Universe has allways been a rich canvas for creative minds to come up with something truly interesting, just because it isn't an FPs that doesn't mean it's not worthy of being a Halo game.
Anyway, I've speant an hour with it and i'm planning to spend many more with it too, It's a solid game as far as gameplay is concerned the mini-story is also pretty interesting but you honestly won't stay for the story, it will become background noise to the sheer fun of point based gameplay.
First off, don't expect this game to be deep, You do earn experience but you don't level up, your experience can be used to buy one time upgrades to help you in your missions such as more powerfull weapons (Ammo is limited and can't be refreshed which adds a decent challenge even if you do go for the powerfull stuff) It doesn't just stop at weapons though, you can buy armor abilities too or stick with the standard ones that they give.
EXP you earn through missions is very limited but to help you along the game has general and mission specific challenges, completing one can earn you big experience, another thing that adds a lot of replay value.
You can also buy boosters with your EXP, A boost to your shields, damage or a booster to increase your score, and the best thing about all this is they didn't go the cash store route, it's all paid for using experience earned in game. Once you get into the missions the game is instantly playable, there is no steep learning curve and what you need to do and where you need to go is made extremely clear throughout each mission.
The game is point based and there are point milestones, you're earning stars so the first milestone is a bronze, second is silver and the highest tier naturally being gold. this adds replayability, to make getting those high scores easier you cna buy the score booster and you can turn on skulls (Yeah that's right, this game has those damn skulls) The skulls increase your multiplier, six in total but you can only use two at a time.
The game has no difficulty setting so the skulls you use pretty much help bump up the difficulty while rewarding you for it. I've only played for an hour but the gameplay is smooth and polished, i'll probably find some bugs down the line but so far i's awesome.
It's £3.99, and for that you get 30 missions worth of content, while some can be short it's still a great ride. The game supports Steam Trading cards, has FULL Controller support and steam achievements. It's a cheap, fun and most probably short game in terms of A to B but i have a feeling i'll be playing this long after i've finished the game to se how i stack up against others in the leaderboards.

Initial feelings:
While I have only just started playing it, I can safely say that this is the best optimization that I have seen on a Ubisoft game. I am playing this on a laptop with a GeForce 860M and I am maintaining a very steady 60fps on High/meduim graphics with 1080 resolution. As of now the story is pretty great, especially if you played the other AC games. There are cameos of a bunch of old characters like Adewale and Achilles. So far, the game is shaping up to be pretty awesome. So, if you like AC games (especially AC 4- Black Flag), then you shoud definately keep your eye on this game. (It shows promise for better obtimization from Ubisoft in the future. . . hopefully lol)
Edit:
Upon playing more of Rogue I have come across a few issues that I think I should address. All of these have only happened once, so don't panic. I got stuck in a loading screen when transitioning between to areas (it just did not finish loading - it sounded like it did but I had to restart the game to fix it). I also loaded in once and could not move. This one might just be a problem with my laptop, but if not I thought I should mention it.
Nevertheless, the story is even more intriguing as it progresses and the gameplay, though mostly the same as Black Flag's, has its own elements that make it stand out as its own game (i.e. avoiding assassins trying to assassinate you, etc...)
Edit:
I just wanted to mention that I did bring my graphics up a bit and I still maintain about 60 fps (once in a while it drops to 50, but that is during really intense battles). But there was one time during the story when I was taking down a man-o-war that my fps dropped to like 35ish, not unplayable but definately noticeable. Besides this, the story is coming along nicely, and I am curious to see how it will end.
Story Completion:
I have to say that this is an overall good game. I did experience a few bugs, all of which are mentioned above, but only a few. The story did feel a little on the short side compared to Black Flag, but it was still a decent length (about 9ish hours I'd say). Shay is a cool character and this game really ties all of the other ones together (even Liberation). It is fun and a great addition to the AC series.

Probably one of my most played game (right up there with Monster Hunter and TF2), this game has made quite the impression. It's a MOBA, ultimately, but easily the least MOBA-esc of the genre. It plays a lot like a 2D brawler, does not have real levels (all upgrades work through in-game currency called "solar"), and has only two abilities per 'naut. Each of the arenas are significantly different than the last, each with their own gimmicks and typical time-span. It's considerably more easy to get into than it's MOBA counterparts. The game is notably stylish, it has a great cartoon art-style and energetic music to help the blood pump. Now that we've gone over the basics, let's get into the specifics:
Let's start with the good. Awesomenaut has the most unique and different characters of any MOBA game, easily. There are no copy characters, period. They all have standalone abilities that distinguish them from one another. The addition of styles of movement and jumping (even flying and hovering) adds a lot of personality to each charater, and the platforming element is very prevelant. Awesomenauts completely defies the style of the genre, which is dominated by look-a-likes like HoN, LoL, and DOTA 2. Awesomenauts plays, on one layer, totally differently, and it's really fresh.
Awesomenauts is also a much simpler game. This might be a deterrent to some, but I consider the deletion of the redundent and cluttered item system is a very welcome aspect. It's all simplified into a customized shop system. You earn "solar" by killing creeps, turrets, other 'nauts, and naturally over time as well. You then spend it on particular upgrades specific to your 'naut throughout the game. The game is much more streamlined then previous DOTA style games. The balance is middling. It's impressive for how different this MOBA is compared to its peers, but there are very clearly "better" 'nauts, as one can clearly tell from the leaderboards. Team composition is also much more important in Awesomenauts, maybe even more important than in a lot of its more competitive members of the genre. It's very important to get 'nauts that synergize.
And that brings us to some of Awesomenauts' problems. The game's matchmaking and server system is, simply put, abnormally and surprisingly bad. Not all the more casual aspects have cleanly transfered into the DOTA realm, and the "drop-in-drop-out" mechanic is the prime example of this misfortune. Dropping into a game that is already lost is infuriating, as it's basically a free leaderboard ranking drop. Similarly, with only three legs to stand on instead of the typical five, one incompetent team member is usually fatal. And the server system, oh the server system. It runs on a host system, and if you have any experience like mine, the host will disconnect messily and the match will crash about once every play session (sessions being about an hour and a half to two hours). Let me note that a match ending due to a disconnect counts as a loss in the rankings. With all this mixed together, you have an absolutely atrocious ranking system. It can amazingly terrible. This is unfortunately somewhat indicative of the genre, but in Awesomenauts it seems especially bad due to the embarrassing connection issues and idiotic matchmaking. For a vast majority of players, the game is near impossible to play solo competitively. You almost require a team to stay in League 1, I've only been able to stay in for a week or so before falling out to obviously much more coordinated teams which specialized compositions. There is no voice communication, and no way to coordinate before the match. At points like these, Awesomenaut's trying to eat its cake and have it too, at times it can decide whether to be competitive or casual, and at these times it fails to be either.
Yet, for what it is, Awesomenauts is extremely impressive. It's been able to more successfully transform its genre than any other game in the genre before it, and it didn't fail. Far from it, in fact. It has some kinks, and some mistakes that seem surprisingly stupid, but for what it is, Awesomenauts is quite the feat. I fully recommend getting into Awesomenauts, it's been one of the best games (even with some of the stupidest mistakes) I've played in quite a while.

Can be a very challenging game. Earning even one of the few achievements will be demanding on your arcade skills. Mage battling mage, variety of spell casters with strengths and weaknesses, special abilities unique to each caster -- all good. Spells organized into four categories; choose your poison. Learn what the stats mean as you level up and choose what to raise and which new spell to learn. Develop a winning battle plan that may not work on every opponent. With all the spellcaster types, special abilities, stats and spells, you can easily sink hours into making different combinations that may or may not work. Game is fast-paced and experimentation is essential. Graphics are simple, but the explosions are colorful and in every battle you are treated to a light show. Main problem is that there is no standard save system, which means that if you fail a tough battle, you cannot repeat it. The game simply moves on to the next opponent, which sucks if you want a second or third chance at defeating the final opponent, DEATH INCARNATE, and earning a tough achievement. Might be worth it to some at $9.99. A steal if on sale. If you always wanted to be a spellcaster and battle other spellcasters, you should get this game.

Divinity is the first game to really suck me in in a while.
The world and story that Larian has crafted are both very detailed and immersive. The tactical combat is superb and very involved(in a good way!). There is rich lore to be found through quests, dialouge, and books found all over the game world. Many interesting characters and sidestories to come across as well!
Choices in this game do matter I feel which is great and leads to multiple endings for some quests and also some potentially very big consequences if you choose to do certain things. Little actions as well are very open ended. One of my favorites tiny things being: can't lockpick that chest? steal it and break it open later!
also, the game really lets you play how you want and is open for experimentation. (Honestly, some might not like this, but I personally loved it) The game, later on, gives you the ability to basically respec all your skills and abilities. Want to go from a frontline tanky damage dealer to an archer who rains death from above? go ahead! want to become the greatest thief in all the lands? dump all your points into sneaking and thievery! It is limited though by your money. You'll have to buy all the gear and skills for another class if you decide to switch which I think is a good limiting factor.
A side note: Game relationships/party romance: Some people want it, others couldn't care less; either way is completely fine and up to individual taste. For me, it's something I love in games. You do have the ability to become close and form relationships with your party members in divinity, however I kinda felt it lacking. I may have missed some things, but I believe you can get one or two scenes plus a bit of extra dialouge, but that's it. It's okay though, I still love this game and this doesn't detract from that fact much at all!
Some things I didn't like/thought felt a bit lacking: Overall, I love this game and feel the devs put a huge amount of work and love into it as well. However some things feel like they're missing polish. Some quests don't seem to resolve or are possibly bugged? Also, the locations in which the game takes place are great, barring the final area. I'll avoid spoilers and just say that I felt that the last area could have been so much more. More characters, quests, and things to do in general could have been there. You never know though, maybe the devs ran out of time or something else. I still enjoyed my time there, but I also found myself wishing for a bit more.
Overall:9/10 If you like RPGs and tactical combat, definitely pick this up and at least give it a shot! In my opinion, the game had some shortcomings, but only very minor in comparison to what the game does right which is a lot!
Side note:I never played the first divinity and I don't think I missed out on any references or anything else in Divinity 2. ie: Don't have to play the first to enjoy this one.
Thanks Larian for this amazing game!

I often ask myself whether I like this game or not.  On the one hand it's a beautifully crafted rpg world, it has ridiculous amounts of options to deal with any challenge the game throws at you, it surprises and delights (just ensure Fane is in your party and he *likes you*).  On the other hand i find myself having wasted many hours bored while i deal with bag space and when i reach a new area i struggle for hours with the battles.  Most of this is my fault (not lowering the difficulty, picking up what's actually trash and not worth my time) but this game encourages you to play how you're inclined, even when that goes past being fun and detracts from the story.
My recommendation then... buy this game if you either know this type of game (certainly if you like tabletop games, rpg stories, games that allow you to come up with novel solutions to problems or xcom style strategy games) or want to try perhaps the best example in many of these genres, providing you don't hate the others.  Once you buy it, try to ignore completionist/hoarding tendencies and concentrate on enjoying the game (unless you seriously enjoy bag management).
Even then it will still consume far too much of your time but it will be memorable and fun.
If you don't like any of the types in the above paragraph... probably best you avoid it as it has those elements in spades.

My main reason for this prematue review is to let OS X user's know this games works great on my MacBook Pro.  I will update this once I play more.
PROS:
+10 different magic user's to level up and build to your liking.
+Nice character customization with skill trees for each one.
+Each character is different and has their own special skills.
+Many different spells to use and stack to make them stronger.
+Different types of spells including damage based, protection, summoning, etc.
+The whole UI fits on one page during battles.  No needs to change screens during battle.
+Great descriptions of everything!  You can right-click on anything to get a detailed description of what it is and what it does.
+Indepth tutorial!  A little confusing at times, but it corrects you too! Oh boy does it correct you! lol
+The ability to queue up spells for strategic attacks and defense.  You can also remove spells from your queue to change strategy on the fly.
+Simple but very strategic gameplay.
CONS:
-You cannot name your character.
-The tutorial was a bit confusing, but that was probably my fault.  I'm getting old.
-The game had one bug so far.  After completing the first tutorial battle, I went to the main menu and viewed my Grimoire, which is basically your progress screen.  My "Wins" score was incorrect.
-There is an age limit (I think 50 years) where you must fight the final boss.  I guess the game ends then.  Not sure. Each battle is a year.  So 50 battles it's bad I guess.  There are 10 characters to build up, so it has replayability.
-Not much of a story, but this games doesn't really require one!  Just battle it out! :-)

It's "TUG-OF-WAR" with fireballs and techno-liches.
Other games come to mind, like
"Aeon Command" (space battles)
"Samurai vs Zombies Defense" (goofy samurai warfare)
and
"Puzzle Chronicles" (the illegitimate child of Tetris and Mortal Kombat)
These game elements are constant:
- try to hold the line
- manage your defences
- beef-up your attacks
- spam your enemies to death
In Magi, you start by opening magical "channels." These channels enable your spells and strengthen them. Then, it's a real-time battle as you queue-up spells for casting. It's like the building queue in Starcraft or Civ... only it's your shield spell, or a magic missile, or summoning an imp. As your mage is casting one spell, you have time to set up the next. And the next. You can plan a bit... or panic. Apparently, I'm still fond of panicking.
These are the fundamentals. Crank up your juice, then blast away. It's incredibly linear, but because these are Magi it gets complicated/interesting...
- - I'm actually trying to write a decent review, here, because this game deserves one.
This game is strategic at heart. It's simple, but executed with nuances and depth. This fits the theme. Your own cleverness and guile might even help with the immersion... it's a bunch of brainiac wizards, afterall.
After each battle, your character gains experience and can be developed as you choose. You can increase one of your five attributes, and pick a new spell from an evolving list.
There are different characters to choose from, with different strengths and unique "special abilities." You can tweak their attributes before playing, also.
The graphics are sorta minimal and retro, but quite classy. There's occult-looking crap here and there... I'm not sure how the ratings system handles that. This isn't walla-walla-bing-bang; it really is Doctor Faustus.
Everything can be played with the mouse. Icons and commands are accessible, and the UI is good. Right-clicking gives explanations for EVERYTHING.
Okay. I confess to liking 1) tower defense games, 2) RPGs, and 3) strategy games with a good user interface.
1) This is a grindy power-struggle in each battle, and each win is dearly earned. Each victory is worth AT LEAST one cookie or a couple nachos.
2) There's a rich variety in characters, with an old school feel. Compare character graphics with "Risk Of Rain" and maybe "The Immortal" from the [classic] NES system... the character models are proportionally accurate. This is not cartoonish.
3) It's such a simple idea, but expands to pretty involved gameplay.
Old-school RPG, solid time-critical combat, and much replay value in a dark thematic setting.
I played D&D back in the early 1990s. This game is like distilled moonshine of whatever wizards could be. It's mage duels, done well.

The sound is great and the choices of music gives it a good atmosphere. This is probably the only game I've played where I stopped progressing just to listen to the music.
As I wait for Chapter V to come out and wrap up the story, part of me hopes that we get some explainations to the madness that's been going on around the characters... And a bigger part of me hopes that it remains unresolved and keeps that air of strange mystery to it.
All in all, it's a really unique narative game that gives you tidbits of flavor the more you explore. If you're looking for some grand purpose to it all, you  may want something else... Rather obviously, you play as a tank. A single tank with a cannon. Enemy is an undefined alien adversary with an army of tanks, usually better equipped than you.
Your mission?
Drive them back to where they came from.
As a tank, you can shoot in the four cardinal directions. As a protagonist of the story you have two advantages against the adversaries:
There are 150 missions, 25 for each "planet" (essentially a tile set). The few mission types range from destroying enemies to stealing energy crystals to escaping through the portal. Mission types can be mixed together, creating some much-needed variety.
Generally, the levels are reasonably varied, though the confines do keep them slightly to the boring side.
Missions usually contain a few "Titanium" cubes that can be used to buy permanent upgrades to the tank, rendering it stronger, more resilient and generally more tanky. This makes the later levels easier, since health becomes essentially a resource.
Power-ups and bonus weapons don't transfer between levels, so beating each level becomes a self-contained action puzzle, with certain weapons or shields sometimes becoming essential to beating the level. And sometimes they are there just for the blasting fun.
AI is pretty stupid. But it is logical stupid, which allows the puzzle-nature of some levels.
Basically, the enemy tanks will just move randomly or chase and shoot at the player if seen, sometimes obliterating the destructible walls in the way. They don't communicate with each other
They know to avoid being shot at though, so if they can't see the player, they will attempt to dodge any bullets still heading their way. You may even use cover fire to deny them from entering an area.
There are also stationary turrets. An important bit is that while the enemies won't generally shoot at each other, they will shoot at the player if no allies are in front of them. Hence, going between two tanks or turrets will make them shoot each other, gloriously disposing of two opponents at once.
Music is surprisingly fitting and sometimes almost relaxed. Graphically, it's a simple pixel-art game with an old TV style (though you may turn the effect off as well).
I have one qualm to mention: The tank always moves at the same, snailish pace. Admittedly, enemies have the same pace (important when being chased in a narrow tunnel), but once everything has been destroyed, you still have to lumber towards the objective.
For me, the 150 levels (and the accompanied story achievements) lasted about 5 and ½ hours. Considering it's a 2$ game and currently on sale for less than 1$ (personally I got it from a bundle), I think it's worth its small price.

So, as you can see I'm leaving a positive review for this game...however if you've ever listened to my podcast I'm going to pull one of my patented "*" out of the bag.
I recommend this game *IF you know what you're getting into AND you're okay with that.  So with that being said, what is this game?
Well it is basically not a game at all and more of an interactive movie.  You watch scenes, you click on icons to advance the story, you occassionally participate in bare bones QTEs, and once...yes only once...solve a pretty simple puzzle.  Oh and it's over in about 2 hours...
Reading that, you might think I'm sounding negative about the game...so why am I recommending it?
Well that's where that * comes in.  I knew what this was before I hit purchase, so when it turned out to be exactly what I thought it was, I was fine with it.  After watching the Giantbomb quicklook the story had me hooked, and in the end I wasn't disappointed.  By the end I was intrigued by the direction the story had taken and I didn't see the final reveals coming.  Of course I will preface that by saying that stories that involve alternate history, and what mankind does when everything falls apart tickle the happy parts of my brain so I was definitely the target audience for this story and that factors into my enjoyment of the game.
So if the story interests you, and you're okay with bare minimum gameplay elements I recommend you pick it up.  If not, then give it a pass.  And if you're on the fence, watch the GB quicklook and maybe wait for a sale...

Having spent hundreds of ours in Euro Truck Simulator 2, I was curious about American Truck Simulator but a little hesitant due to the fact that it just looks much the same.
Well one thing is for sure, ATS is much the same as ETS2. The same game engine, the same UI and so on. It's basically the same game but in the USA, so in that sense you could even call it a game expansion. You also only get a handfull of trucks (this apparently has to do with licensing issues but regardless of the reasons it's still the case) and nowhere near as many options to customise those trucks as in ETS2. The landscape is also much less variable than in Europe but that would be down to the states they have released so far.
The good news is that they seem to have taken everything they have learnt developing scenery in ETS 2 and put it into ATS. One of the things that bugges me the most about ETS 2 is that after driving through the beautiful Scandinavia or France DLC you go through Germany. Germany has amazing scenery but in ETS 2 it is part of the vanilla game is is comparitivley boring to drive through. There is nothing of the sort in ATS, even the original states are leaps and bounds ahead of the original ETS 2. Whats more, America feels like America. This is something I think they got right in both games and I really like the feeling of going for a road trip.
So far I have really enjoyed ATS and I'm glad I got it but I'm sure not every owner of ETS 2 will see it the same way.

This is, hands down, the best free-to-play third-person shooter on the market, if not ever.
Warframe goes all in with the "Space Ninjas" theme with futuristic environments reminiscient of Star Wars, and elements of the kinds of ninjas we've known from the likes of history and fantasy alike. Its free-to-play model is microtransactions done right, between discounts ranging between 20%-75% for the Cash Credits known as "Platinum" given to the player often, and allowing the currency to be traded in-game for items such as modifications and blueprints for weapons or warframes.
The desire to have a certain warframe, weapon, modifications, and others often are what drive the player's objectives. Much of the equipment available can be obtained through creating them with blueprints using resources or items given as mission rewards, with a select few available straight from the marketplace for in game currency. Some blueprints need to be obtained through other means, such as research from a clan "Dojo", or in the case of "Prime" equipment, completing "Void Fissure" missions to open "Relics", a possible mission reward. This does tend to require players to play a single mission several times over to get the mission reward they want, especially in the case of Primes.
Equipment ranges from conventional, proceeds through medeival, and lands squarely in the place you find utterly  rediculous but decide "Eh, why not." Rifles, machine guns, shotguns, bows, pistols, knives, stars, daggers, swords, hammers, scythes, polearms, chakrams, boomerangs, lasers, grenade launchers, rocket launchers, and more await to be employed by you. By themselves, they can be powerful weapons. Through modifications, they become far more effective. Want a rifle to fire bullets that set a target on fire? Add a Heat damage mod. How about a bow that can shoot through walls? Put on a Punch Through mod. How about throwing stars that explode? A flamethrower that spews radioactive clouds? Laser beams that infect enemies? A tesla coil that is so corrosive it melts the armor off your enemies? The player is free to try all these combinations and more, find what works, and custom-tailor their loadout to fit their next mission.
Warframes vary in equal diversity, comprising of ninjas, fairies, a dragon, lumbering hulks, a magician, a clown, a priest, Davy Jones, the Monkey King, a DJ, an experiment, an enemy type, a mummy, the Grim Reaper, a bird-person, and more, each with their own unique set of powers, movement speeds, and idle animations. They are highly customizable between color palattes, skins, alternate helmets, idle animations, and various attachments, on top of their own subset of mods, even some that modify how one of their powers work.
Much of Warframe takes place in stations or ships. Your goals for a particular mission vary between rescuing prisoners, sabatoging equipment, infiltrating high security vaults, painting the walls red until the enemy is broken, and more. Early missions are fairly easy for the new player, while harder missions may find the player needing a particular set of mods, weapons, and/or warframes, possibly friends as well, to be successful. All missions grant the player credits, resources, and even more mods, sometimes blueprints as well. They also grant affinity, used to level up the player's equipment, and allow them to have more powerful and/or additional mods, as well as unlocking powers in the case of warframes.
Gunplay can depend on how effective you are against your enemy, as it is with any game with varying enemy levels. You can be cutting down swathes of enemies with a sword or machine gun in one mission like it's a Warriors game, and be playing defensively and need to place shots carefully the next. The sound and modeling departments had their work piled mountains high, with no two kinds of weapons sounding completely alike, and the gore from splitting an enemy in two and not stopping there. All weapons however operate and sound in ways that make sense: a machine gun with a fast and loud rattle spreads its fire in a cone, a beam weapon whines and whirrs as it emits the beam in a straight line, or spins up and down while charging and discharging the weapon. This carries over to melee weapons as well, the sounds conveying the weight of the weapon used, though it can seem silly if an attack speed mod was used and the player looks like they're playing in fast-forward.
While this makes for a very interesting Player Vs. Environment system, it is too much for a Player Vs. Player system. As a result, only certain weapons, warframes, and mods can be used in the Conclave's free-for-all, team deathmatch, and capture the flag modes. The introduction of Lunaro, a more sports-like ball game mode, also keeps the chaos down. PvP used to be more integrated into the game as clans battled for control over "Dark Sectors," missions that grant increased credits, resources, and affinity to be taxed by the controlling clan. That is currently inactive until a better system can be developed.
Microtransactions appear to have a heavy hand, showing up first whenever you open the marketplace or look at a particular peice of equipment. However, much of the equipment available has a blueprint to create the item without asking the player to open up a wallet, and more blueprints become available if the player is in a clan. The items exclusive to Platinum are skins, color palattes, and equipment slots. Equipment slots are very limited to a free player, but with the current trading system in place, a free player only needs to sell a few parts for a Prime to other players to get enough for another expansion. Some would argue that this is a "Pay-to-Win" model, and they would be technically correct. But, by making equipment available to be created using materials earned through normal play, and allowing existing equipment to be modified far beyond original capabilities, while providing means to trade for and with Platinum, that gap is easily reached and crossed.
All in all, Warframe has built its game around replayability, and has done so very well. It doesn't strain the new player too much, while also providing challenges and objectives for the experienced player, and even carried this forward into the Plains of Eidolon expansion, made for free to the playerbase and accessible after making your first Mastery rank. Microtransations are definitely present and their impact is definitely limited. If you wanted some cross between Destiny and Monster Hunter, this is it, and it has aged well.

The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion is straight up a good game.
It is worth buying, and worth paying the full steam price for. Don't let my "hours played" fool you... I've played hundreds or maybe even thousands of hours on a disc copy, and I can tell you these things from experience. It is immersive, fun and rewarding. Good quests, decent story, great things to be found. The Shivering Isles expansion that is included is one of the, if not *the* best expansion in a single-player game that I have ever played (the Bloodmoon expansion from TES III: Morrowind would be a close second).
Overall, 9.5/10, an instant classic. (But do yourself a favor and get Oblivion Character Overhaul from the nexus for free to drastically improve the quality of the npc and pc faces. Other than that I would recommend only a few lore-friendly mods during your first playthrough to get a clear and mostly unbiased opinion of the base game).
But this is probably the best advice I could give: If you like older games, get The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind and play it first. It will only add to your appreciation of Oblivion, and the TES series' lore and setting in general. It's a good game, and cut from a very different cloth than the later games in the series... if/when you have played it for a while, you will understand fully what I mean, and probably want to thank me for the advice. It can take some getting used to an older game of that speed, but give it a chance and you'll love it. Trust me on this.
But anyways, Oblivion - good game and worth the buy.
