Fresh off the boat from Vvardenfell, I was hard on Oblivion early on. It's appropriate to compare the two games, but not as closely as I did. And while I still got far more hours and enjoyment out of Morrowind, there was a depth of charm to its successor that I had long overlooked.
On a technical level, I find little opposition that Oblivion broke new ground in making such a big world function as well as it did. The employment of Bethesda's new "Radiant AI" served as a welcome relief to the NPCs of Morrowind, whose highlight of day-to-day activity was walking twenty steps to the left. While there were aspects of this innovation that Skyrim would later improve upon, it was awesome to see the people around me wake up, go to work, go to the tavern, go hunting, eat, sleep, pray. Population centers felt alive and I started to feel the community instead of trusting that it was there.
Voice acting was another... "improvement." You didn't have to read large blocks of text anymore because God forbid. Bethesda boasted that dialogue took up half of the game's data with over two full days of voice recording.
When I first learned this, I felt reluctant. I feared that no matter how much voice acting one is willing to pack onto a DVD, there isn't enough time or money to capture the alluring exposition of Morrowind, the details of the relationships and backstories; no voice actor Bethesda got their hands on could hope to capture what I imagined when I spoke to a Telvanni lord.
Well, I was right. Long, detailed information was butchered, mainstreamed. There were hardly any topics to discuss, and I didn't feel like I could have a true conversation with anyone the game didn't deem important enough. Talking to a random bystander about their trade not only developed a character, but the world. I didn't have that anymore. Every gender of each race (for the most part) had not only the same voice, but the same speech. It was almost silly. With the big step forward in immersion with Radiant AI and voice acting, it was a shame to take such a step back in what was perhaps my favorite aspect of Oblivion's predecessor.
I also had mixed feelings about the induction of fast travel. I let it go; if I wanted the immersion, I could always refuse it (even though I knew any such commitments wouldn't last). Looking on the bright side, I could enjoy completing quests and keeping the story going. Returning instantly to the doorstep of my favorite places would help me savor and rediscover them, when before I might have put it off for dread of the trek until I was too powerful to care. So, while I will always appreciate the punishing journeys of Morowind, I suppose I can mark fast travel as a net positive.
And they finally added horses to make travelling faster!
Um... okay. Maybe they would provide some other combat or burden benefit?
No. Not really. So, uh... moving on.
The graphics are beautiful. Stunning. I was impulsively critical of the "normality" of the setting compared to Vvardenfell. Yes, Cyrodiil is more familiar, but in hindsight I don't see why I should have trouble accepting that this particular part of a much larger and dynamic fantasy world is simply inspired by Medieval Europe like many other works of fantasy whose familiarity I forgave, even welcomed.
Maybe it's because I expect more from a game, maybe it's because the story left me wanting (which it did, but it's not that simple--- more on that shortly). The vistas of Cyrodiil ran unrivalled in gaming at the time, and few with today's technology can match its brilliance, especially when considering how interactive and detailed every yard of it is. Now, Dagon's plane of Oblivion, for which the game is named, that's where I stop defending the lack of inovation: classic Dante. And Daedric architecture was, altogether now, far more intriguing in Morrowind.
Just as Oblivions's landscapes hold up today, the general facial designs of NPCs were subpar even then (aside from the beast folk, but then I resented that they were streamlined to equip footwear).
But where did Oblivion shine? Where did Oblivion not only stand up to Morrowind but arguably surpass it?
The faction questlines.
The main questline was not very interesting (still blows away Skyrim), though it managed to turn out a few likeable characters (Baurus, Martin, uh... Jauffre was okay, I guess). But the faction quests were truly the greatest strength of a solid game. Morrowind's were less linear, giving players the choice of advancing through work in different parts of the map (the superior concept, in my opinion); Oblivion allowed a single path, but not only provided a heavier narrative, they gave the feeling that you were part of something. Both systems have their strengths and weaknesses, but Oblivion's Mages Guild combined the two...
You had to impress the leader of each installment of the Mage's Guild, each with their own personality, style, and agenda, much like Morrowind. Once they are in agreement, you're rewarded with access to the previously locked mechanic of magic-making and enchanting in a place that felt like a functioning school. There, you work your way from grunt to archmage in a series of quests that begin benign but gradually rise in importance to the finale. Was it perfect? No. But the structure and pacing brought the experience to life for me. I enjoyed every quest.
In terms of story, the best of Oblivion (and the series as of Skyrim) was the Dark Brotherhood. The characters, the atmosphere, the plot and the individual quests were beautiful. Sometimes it felt like a different game entirely. I'll never forget when it was all coming to a head, I stepped out of a lighthouse and the brutal, depressing scene it housed, and spent a quiet moment watching the sun break the horizon over the sea, uncertain of the future. It was magnificent.
The Thieves' Guild came close to the mages guild in terms of structure, and close to the Dark Brotherhood in terms of story: a well-balanced and enjoyable adventure.
Oblivion's factions set the bar, and I couldn't wait to see what Skyrim... well, we'll get to that another time.
Finally, on to combat. Yes, it's more fun to swing a sword when the sword is going to hit its target, and the employment of modern physics made it satisfying to knock your enemy over a table with a deathblow to the face. What's more, Oblivion did what I would have sworn was impossible: it made magic even more useless than it was in Morrowind (at least then you could cast offensive spells through items--- laughably overpowered, but I loved it).
When Bethesda made Oblivion, they set out to build a whole new game from the ground up. As to be expected, there were changes that I liked, changes that I didn't. Did Oblivion stand up to Morrowind? I think not, but given the style of its development, it didn't have to. I can't help but respect Bethesda's willingness to drop all their assets and start anew. While Oblivion belongs to a series, it belongs to its own part of the series, just as Cyrodiil itself lies as its own little world in widely-varied Tamriel, and in ways neither can nor should be compared to the others.
In the end, we need to be realistic: how many games lie outside Bethesda's world so big, where no matter which road you choose, whether you take a road at all, you know you're going to find something worth seeing? That is the marvel of Bethesda, the greatest RPG developer there is.

Now let us see why Awesomenauts should be in the Library of everyone who owns a steam account:
1) ADDICTIVE 3v3 COMBAT. That's right you and two friends can kick butt together! You don't even have to all buy the game; that's right this game has local co-op as well as online multiplayer!
2) A GREAT CAST OF CHARACTERS. Now in every MOBA the characters are important right? Don't worry Awesomenauts has got you covered. It offers a variety of characters that will fit anybody's playstyle. You can play as a huge robot with some serious anger issues and tank it like a man! or play as Leon; the deadly chamelon assasin. The character roster spans from space kraken all the way to monkeys with jetpacks. Yes. Jetpacks.
3) PRACTICE AND HONE YOUR SKILLS. Awesomenauts has a great learning curve. With 5 levels of bots to choose from you can practice and find out what character your best with and then go online to wreck havoc!
4) NO, AND I DO MEAN NO 'PAY-TO-WIN FEATURES'
Yep. Awesomenauts requires skill and time to get good at. Ronimo doesn't offer you an easy way out by paying with real money.
SUMMARY:
I've spent countless hours playing Awesomenauts with friends and even my family, and I plan on spending countless more. If you're looking for a MOBA that offers fun, exciting action and you have $10.00 laying around than I highly suggest you pick this game up.
PROS:
Great simple gameplay
Amazing and varied character roster.
Easy to get in to, and easy on your wallet.
CONS:
Not a single one! So what are you waiting for?

As stated elsewhere, one of the best supporting arguments for games being "serious" art and really explores the video games as a narrative medium.
With that out of the way, KRZ so far (up through Act IV) has been one of my most favorite video game experiences of all time. The following acts haven't elicted quite that response from me (perhaps as I've gotten used to how KRZ operates) but I love how KRZ always dares to experiment with the norms of the point-and-click adventure experience, how narrative and both character- and visual-perspective can be manipulated, etc. and I find myself thinking about various bits from the game when I'm away from it (lately, this particular haunting musical moment in Act IV has been stuck in my head).
It's not a game for everyone and doesn't offer a traditional gaming experience, but it's an endlessly innovative, narrative-driven interactive experience that's surreal and dreamlike but at the same time grounded and emotional.

Atlas Reactor is a great new game with a player friendly transaction model.
Take a fast paced, turn based game - which usually isn't the case. Mix it up with an interesting and customizable cast of characters, and you get Atlas Reactor.
The game exists somewhere between a MOBA/Final Fantasy Tactics/XCom style gameplay.
It's all done on a grid in a 4v4 arena with powerups scattered around. Each team takes their turns at once, 20 seconds for the entire team, and then the actions resolve. Abilities are considered Prep, Dash, or Blast and then "Move" in that order of resolution.
For example,
You start your turn, buff your damage in the Prep phase to lay a huge blast on the enemy. He chooses to use a dash ability which moves him out of the way before the Blast phase when you actually fire.
The game has a ton of interplay and a high ceiling for teamplay.
As for the economic model - the game is free to play with a changing cast of free to play characters each week. You can play for free forever and never be at a disadvantage - you cannot buy power at all. Only cosmetics.
At first I assumed you would receive a currency per match which was used to buy characters. This is not the case. The free to play version is simply a limited version that allows you to play, but on their terms.
Before release, the basic version of the game is $20 - it'll go up to $30 after release. A special package exists with more skins, but doesn't offer anything that will change the gameplay - just skins.
So that's it - a nice little package of a game that is incredibly fast paced, requires tactics and teamwork, and isn't full of artificial P2W / F2P garbage.
The downsides at the moment are minimal - mainly optimization which isn't too bad as the game is turn based, and then queue times can be a bit rough at first as the community and game is just starting out. That said, I'm still able to get games at 2am PST here in the USA, so it isn't too bad. Servers are likely global as well due to the turn based nature of the game.
I hope to see more out of Atlas Reactor - it's a brilliant re-imagining of what would typically be a tabletop game into the PC game genre. A brilliant little offering from Trion who I haven't had much experience with previously.

First let me say that this game is pretty good as a learning tool. It's a nice way to work up a song that in the library of Rocksmith. But there are some problems I've encountered with the game.
First the timing is a little off. If I wait to pluck the indicated string on my guitar when the note bar hits the string shown on the screen then the timing will be late. I had to pluck the string a little before the bar reaches the string just so the note will be in time with the song.
I think that there is a problem with Rocksmith hearing that a note has been played. When I play "Scale Racer" in the arcade section Rocksmith, for some reason, doesn't recognize that a note has been played.  I will pluck the string in plenty of time, & the finger is on the correct string at the correct fret, but the car still crashes.
There have been several times in Riff Repeater where I play the section with 0 misses, but there have been no increases in the difficulty. It will start the passage around 75% speed, & with each success the speed will increase but the difficulty stays the same. I'll go through this 5 times, & then get bored playing the same very simple passage over & over with no changes in the difficulty. It would be nice if it would increase the difficulty, closing in on how the song is actually played. Also there have been times Riff Repeater has given me only 1 note to play, there is no lead in or clicks for timing so as I mentioned earlier with the poor timing of the bar hitting the string shown on the screen & playing the note makes this difficult.
There also have been times when I don't play everything correctly, & Riff Repeater will slow the passage down. Unfortunately many times the voice over will talk right into the start of the passage making it difficult to start playing when the passage starts.
Many of the lessons don't sound like there are for Rock, but designed for a Country & Western app.
The tuner isn't that accurate. It will lock in tune even before the pitch of the string is exactly where it should be. Then when I check this Rocksmith tuning to my Snark, &  Belcat tuners I find that my guitar is tuned flat. If I tune my guitar to one of the tuners, then the other one agrees that it is in tune. But when I check the Rocksmith tuner, it tells me the strings are sharp.
When I go to "Learn a Song" unfortunately it always loads at the same song, & I really don't like that song so it's annoying to have to hear this each time I start this feature to learn a song. It's too bad that I can't change the song that "Learn a Song" loads with. It's too bad that Rocksmith doesn't have a tab sheet for the song in "Learn a Song" that could be used for practice. Speaking of reading tabs, the layout of the strings in Rocksmith is opposite of how the strings are shown in written Tabs.
I've demo'ed playing Rocksmith 2012, & found it to be very confusing. The 2014 version is a noticeable improvement from 2012. So all in all, even with all of the problems, it's not a bad game. And as I mentioned earlier it is a helpful learning tool. If someone asks me about Rocksmith, & if I would recommend it I would have to first let them know about the problems Rocksmith has before I recommend it.

The Bunker is an atmospheric full motion video (FMV) adventure with an interesting story that plays like an interactive movie.
You play as John, and you are the last man alive in the nuclear bunker. You adhere to the daily routine, until one day, things start to go wrong. The game is story rich, and as you move through areas of the bunker, you have flashbacks of your once repressed childhood memories. These memories fill in the backstory, and reveal the hidden truths that lie within the bunker.
As far as the gameplay goes, your interaction is done using the mouse, kind of like a live action point and click adventure. You click to move and interact with objects. Expect a lot of cinematics, but as the story progresses, there are times where you can choose to react, and then other times where you must react and click things quickly.
It’s been about 15 years since I’ve played a FMV style game, and they did a really good job with The Bunker. It feels like an interactive movie, where you’re more heavily invested in the story and its characters because you are directly controlling it. This style of game isn’t for everyone, but those who enjoy interactive, story rich adventures will most likely enjoy this game as well. I’m pleased with the overall experience, and my only real complaint about it is that I wish it had been cheaper since it is a short game.

The Bunker continues the trend of the British doing a quality job bringing back FMV games. The game is about John, a man that’s lived his entire life in a bunker in the English countryside after the Cold War went hot in 1986. For more than twenty years he’s lived alone with his mother in the bunker after a mysterious disaster killed the other survivors until his mother passes away. John tries his best to continue living his dreary and monotonous existence but as the bunker systems start to fail he’s forced to venture into parts of the facility he hasn’t in been in in decades.
Gameplaywise The Bunker is a tad bit lighter on the gameplay front than Contradiction or Her Story (Investigation and FMV really go together well) but it’s still engaging enough. It’s mainly simple puzzles and exploration. The atmosphere is where the game truly shines though. The cinematography is head and shoulders above its FMV forbears, really doing a great job immersing you in the actually real bunker that they filmed the game in. The sound design is also nicely subdued.  It’s not scary, but it definitely maintains this bleak sense of loneliness throughout. The acting is really nice, namely Adam Brown, who really sells how broken and pathetic John but as well as his perseverance as he ventures through the bunker.  The writing is good and kept me interested, though the characters aside from John aren’t as well fleshed out. The game’s pacing is pretty good, it’s not a long game, but it doesn’t feel like it drags or it ends abruptly.
Overall The Bunker is another quality entry in the reemerging FMV adventure genre. While it lacks the gameplay and story integration of Contradiction and Her Story, its atmosphere makes it well worth playing.

Awesomenauts is a fun MOBA that plays 2D platformer style.
One of the reasons that Awesomenauts is so great is that it suits all players, regardless of how little or how much experience they have with MOBAs. The game is easy to learn, but hard to master. New players can easily grasp the concepts of the game and how their abilities work, and the character builds are simple to put together. There isn't a whole lot of explanation required. However, even as a long term player I am constantly learning and observing new tricks and tactics, and am genuinely challenged by the other players in my league.
The community as a whole is really great. You won't be ridiculed or cussed out for being new or inexperienced, and no matter how much their team is sucking, players will always bite their tounge and give a gg, wp (good game, well played). I would be lying if I said there were never any ragequitters, but one of the great things about this game is that people can join mid-game, and replace the member you've lost.
All in all, I have had a great time playing Awesomenauts, and I'd reccommend it to anyone.

"I haven't beat the game yet, but I saw no reviews and thought I might help some people who are on the fence out. What seems like a crappy cash-in on a big title to create an arcade game was actually a pleasant surprise. I purchased this game on a whim for a few reasons: It was only $4.99, I'm a fan of the Halo series, and the screenshots reminded me of one of my favorite (though definitely less popular) Halo Games, "Halo Wars".
Instead of your typical "point a to point b" halo missions, you now have various objectives per level and some can be quite challenging. Defending bases, gathering resources, keeping all your men alive, and all out surviving hordes of enemies are just a few of the multiple tasks at hand. As you can see from the screenshots and game description, this game is not a first person shooter. It's a top-down shooter. You use WASD control scheme to move your character and use your mouse to aim and shoot as well as a few other keys for shields / upgrades and switching weapons. I believe that anyone who likes a challenge and strategy games would be particularly fond of this concept. The game features a nice layout and the animations and graphics are about as good as you would expect for a $5 arcade game in 2014. The AI in the game was fine. They'd always shoot with good accuracy, some would hide behind shields while others would charge you with energy weapons, etc. You choose your weapons at the beginning of levels as well as upgrades and you don't have a seemingly endless supply of ammo like the other Halo games, thus adding to the challenge. So strategize how you will use your ammo. Perhaps let your allies take care of the low-threatining grunts or use a secondary weapon, and use the big guns when the time arises. The game features multiplayer, but not for the campaign mode. There are a nice variety of levels and you will be encountering the covenant as well as my favorite, the flood. I don't think the typical fan of the Halo FPS games would enjoy this.
I would recommend this game to a few types of people:
1. Those who enjoy strategic top-down shooters.
2. Those who enjoy casual games (though some missions are pretty tough at times, it is definitely fair all around).
3.Those who are big fans of the Halo universe and don't mind stepping away from your typical first-person shooters.
The game is $4.99. An incredible price in my opinion as it's $10 on consoles. I already know that most Halo fanboys and FPS fanboys won't like this game very much. The game is exactly what you see in the screenshots and videos, so if you don't like what you see, then don't buy it. In the end, it's a $5 so don't expect anything revolutionary... If you don't mind dropping a few bucks to enjoy a pretty good all around game that is different in the series, then I say go for it. I'll play this game and beat it, and then I'll come back every now and then to replay some of my favorite missions. The game has a nice touch of adding scores, upgrades, and weapons so it has pretty good replay value. It is worth mentioning though, that the game features microtransactions. You can purchases weapons and upgrades early (that are all completely unlockable for free as you play the game). While I won't be purchasing any, and honestly see no reason to put this in the game, the option is there for those who wish. I give Halo: Spartan Assault a 7/10."

In Knot, you have to disassemble tangled three-dimensional solids into their separate parts.  As you progress, the constructions become more complex and require more planning and time to disassemble.  There is no time limit, so you can take as long as you need.
These are very good puzzles, they still look fine at high resolution, and the physics of the interlocking parts behave just as they would with actual solids.  Still, the game itself has some rough edges - the rotation mechanics are cumbersome, and sometimes you have to restart a puzzle when you have maneuvered yourself into a situation you cannot undo; a rotation reset button would be welcome here.
There is only one option, and that is to mute all sound.  Though the menu has an 'Extras' entry, clicking on it shows there are actually no extras.  The 'Tutorial' is just a list of keyboard and controller behaviors.
Though the puzzle manipulation is a bit rough around the edges, I still recommend this to those who enjoy finding the right way to disassemble things.  Thankfully, you do not have to put them back together.

There are a lot of games I love. Games I play over and over again, or love to talk about. Ones that inspire me and move me and entertain me.
Few haunt me though, few follow me around and show themselves in quiet corners and just off the interstate and in sunsets and shadows and DMV lines and beach parties like Kentucky Route Zero.
To get the obvious out of the way, no, there are no tests of reflexes, no stats to track, no enemies to speak of, no puzzles to solve. I love all of those things, but they are not here and they are not missed.
Instead you have a gorgeous twilight world, people and places just on the other side of fantastic, cyborgs and thunderbirds and skeletons and bureaucrats and truck drivers and thereminists. The world of KZO is both utterly original and also a saturated and shadowy reflection of our own, utterly familiar and utterly alien.
My best recommendation is just to trust your instincts; if you're intrigued by what I and others have said here and the pictures above, and you aren't turned off by the absence of more traditional "game" elements, you are in for a gorgeous, meditative, and unique experience.

This is a well crafted FMV interactive movie.  It is a game in the sense that you must, at times, click the prompts.  But that is not the essence of this little gem.  The well balanced story telling is where this game shines best.  Yes, at $20, one could argue that it's overpriced for a movie, however that is what one would spend on a Blueray or digital download of a new release title.  I personally have no problem spending such money to support a studio that is creating a unique experience.  Others may feel differently and that is just fine.  If you want to wait for a price drop, good on you.  But the price should not reflect the review.
The Bunker is a story about love and what it can make a person do.  It is a story about survival in the worst possible conditions.  It is a story about the ghosts that haunt the choices we make.  As the protagonist you must push forward through difficult odds and in so doing expose the story of The Bunker.  It is a well thought story that reveals itself to you as you move to your ultimate goal.
As far as FMV games go, this is one of the best acted I have ever seen.  The lead actor, Adam Brown, was given a difficult role in a difficult medium, and at times can seem over dramatic or forced, but that is a limit of the "game" format more than a reflection of his acting.  The cut away scenes are well directed and believable.  I would have liked a bit more written background in these scenes as it would have made the story richer, but it's likely the creators had to balance the flow of the game with the story itself.  In the end all is revealed and it is a satisfying and some would say disturbing tale.
People who enjoy FMV and games such as "Her Story" as well as a story with a twist will enjoy The Bunker.  It is not ham-fisted or corny like "Contradiction" which I also loved, but it has it's place as a serious FMV story game.  I completed it in under two hours, so it can be done in a single playthrough.  There are acheivements, it is not possible to complete them all on a single playthrough.  I did not get all the acheivements because I did not feel that was a purpose behind the product, but more of a steam addon.
I would recommend this game to others, and if the price is too steep go ahead and wishlist this and wait for the holiday sale.  Enjoy.
EDIT: Nominated for "I thought this game was cool before it won and award".  Because I think it really deserves one.

is a tense, thrilling and, in places, scary (albeit largely in a jump-scare sort of way) FMV story set in a bunker in post-nuclear-apocalypse Britain.  I was interested to pick it up as soon as I saw it played on Jim Sterling's YouTube, as I love post-nuclear scenarios, and the 1980s UK setting was particularly appealing to me as a 30-something Brit who grew up with the threat of The Bomb still hanging over the world.
It's important to understand that it's short - around 2 hours - and basically an interactive movie.  Interaction is largely limited to clicking on the next step in a linear path, with the occasional QTE.  There's only one puzzle in the game, which you'll probably solve quickly and which will be irritating if you don't.  There's very little optional content, just a few flavour items in each area that you can choose to read/listen to or not.  I'd recommend you do, as they help flesh out the background.
That said, the interaction does generally help to involve the player in the story, although there are times when it can also hinder.  If you fail a QTE - as I did once to see what would happen and a second time accidentally - it simply repeats the last few minutes of (unskippable) video.  There's no branching story, no way to change the linear path the character is on.  If you do the wrong step, the character will tell you so: "no, I need to do X first" and the like.
As a FMV game it lives and dies on the script and the acting, and these are pretty good.  Both are realistic and believable.  The protagonist does veer slightly towards chewing the scenery at times, but much can be forgiven for a character who has spent their entire lives in a bunker surrounded by the constant threat of death. The FMV itself is of good HD quality, and well shot and directed.
The plot becomes a little predictable as you near the end, and would seem extremely shallow and inconsequential if it had to survive alone as a TV episode or a movie.  It's really just about what happened and how, with no depth of character to anyone.  But it's unusual in a game setting, and padded out by the interactions and with tension raised by an excellent score and suitably atmospheric sound effects, there's just enough to work in this setting.
Things fall down a little right at the end, where the final scenes feel the need to force home what happened, when any player is likely to have worked out most if not all of the details already.  After this there is a choice for the character's final ending, which is notable as the only real choice you ever have in the game.  I appreciated the fact that it gave the player one chance to decide what the character might do - or to decide for him what they think he
do.  Beyond that though the choice has little meaning, as the two alternate endings are each only about 20 seconds long and show little.   You do get the chance to go back and do the other ending without repeating the whole game, though you will have to replay the final five minutes.
After you complete the story you shouldn't expect much, if any replay value.  There are some collectibles in the game, and I failed to get them all, but feel no interest whatsoever in finding the rest given they appear to add nothing further to the story or even to the background flavour.  The only scenario in which I can see there being replayability is if you avoid all optional flavour items the first time around and then go back in later to access those.
I played on Mac and had one worrying glitch within minutes of opening the game, where it crashed on one of the first interactions.  But after reloading it was fine the rest of the time.  As the game is basically just a fancy video player, technical problems should not be expected on even low-end systems.   Given this, there are a few more loading screens than I would have expected, though none lasted more than 15 seconds (playing the game on SSD.)  Perhaps there are/will be console ports which necessitated this.  It would have been nice if they hadn't have been there, but I didn't feel that they impacted the mood.
Overall I'd definitely recommend the game to anyone who thinks that they will both enjoy the setting and themes and who is OK with spending the money for a two-hour experience.   A little more ambition and depth would have been nice, but if you know what you're getting it's worth your time.
I definitely hope this developer and others continue to make new new FMV games because I think The Bunker - and Her Story before it - proves they can work if done carefully.  The stench that the 90s smeared on the concept is long behind us :)

What a game.
With nostalgic PS1-style graphics and sounds, and basic but exciting and enjoyable gameplay, this is as good an ode to old-style gaming as you will find.
The concept is simple: fire endless streams of daggers at endless hordes of various demons until one kills you. As time goes on, more demons will begin to spawn around you. That's it. This sounds monotonous but the sheer difficulty and unforgiving nature of this game means that you die over and over and over again but you don't get frustrated and you don't get bored. I say unforgiving, the arena is relatively small and there are often more than fifty of these demons to contend with. Take into account the fact that one touch from any enemy will end your run, and it is clear to see how this game would be a tough one.
Regardless, it's dirt cheap, the controls are as simple as they come, (requiring the use of just WASD, Space, and the mouse) and the atmosphere the game creates, especially when played in the dark with headphones on, is incredible- one of the best I've ever experienced in any video game. Each demon has its own individual 'cry,' meaning the player knows, if they listen carefully, which demons are in the arena at the given time, and more importantly, where they are.
This is without doubt my single favourite release of 2016, definitely my vote for game of the year. I wouldn't hesitate to recommend this to anybody.

This is a great game, however it does have some flaws. I will be focusing on the flaws in this review but don't let that deter from buying the game. It is excellent, buy it and play it.
My main complaint with this game has to do with the combat. Even on master difficulty I found the game to be pretty easy as most firefights against targets with firearms just devolved into the classic shooter "Wall hide" tactic. The AI seemed dumb and was almost always a pushover. I finished the game having completed every quest I came across and looking back I haven't felt like i've been in one firefight that felt worthy of this game's incrediable atmosphere. Don't get me wrong, the combat is great but it just doesn't mesh well with the terrifying atmosphere of this game. There's something off about being on edge for 2 minutes sweeping an abandoned laboritory thinking there's going to be a bloodsucker or shotgunner around every corner just to find a group of zombies that fight like mentally challenged kindergardeners. I guess my main point is that the AI just isn't challenging enough.
I also don't like how the more dangerous mutants like the Turors, Chimeras and Psuedogiants are boring bullet sponges to fight. I remember one time I was sweeping through an underground complex when I came across a large mutant resting with it's back turned to me. I unloaded my G36 into it's back expecting it to turn around and come rushing at me trying to tear my face off and instead it just slowly got up and loped after me. The fight devolved into me training it around for 5 minutes pumping bullets into it. I ended up running out of ammo for my rifle 500 rounds later and had to resort to my shotgun to kill it. Luckily it only took 40 or 50 more rounds from that. The entire fight was boring as the mutant moved at snails pace and simply ate bullets without even reacting.
Also the ending seemed anticlimatic and a bit easy.
But nonetheless STALKER Call of Pripyat was one of the best shooter experiences I've had. The amazing atmosphere and sound design of this game blew me away. Definitely pick this game up.

Halo Spartan Assault is average at best. The game looks very much like the mobile game in which it is ported from, and it feels like one too. The game lacks full rebindable keys, and the game feels all in all very clunky to play, especially when driving human vehicles such as the Scorpion MBT using the keyboard.
Missions can last anywhere between 2-6 minutes in length, and they offer very little in terms of replayability or variety, generally consisting of "Get to objective X", "Kill X amount of targets", or "Defend X for Y amount of time". Each mission begins with a loadout screen where you can select your loadout which consists of a primary weapon, secondary weapon, armour ability and power up (not active by default), however you may only change your loadout by spending your in-game currency (XP), but there is no need to do so as the game is very easy without such purchases, as there are many other weapons, vehicles and stationary cannons scattered around each level that keep you stocked up long enough to complete the mission with very few issues.
The story is very basic, and your average Halo fare: A human planet is under attack by covenant forces, lo and behold: the forerunners seems to have had a foothold on the planet before they died out, and then the UNSC and the Covenant duke it out to try and reclaim whatever technology they left behind, and to stop the Covenant from destroying humanity etc etc. It is not going to be the most memorable story, or even memorable at all, but what makes it worse is that missions are explained with a small block of text, and cutscenes are reserved for the completion of each “Operation” (every 5 missions), these cutscenes, whilst nice to look at with their graphic novel style presentation, only last a few seconds, and do little to break up the monotony of the combat.
Graphically the game is very impressive for a mobile port. DX effects are squeezed in to make explosions look fairly impressive, as well as cramming in a large amount of particle effects such as embers and snowflakes which all make the game look alive. The lighting and background effects (post Operation C) are also very nice to look at as it obtains every bit of colour that Halo is known for, a refreshing break from the flurry of grey/ brown games that we are so very accustomed to seeing now. One huge downside however is the lack of graphics options past AA, resolution and refresh rate. Where are the texture options? V-Sync? Or even a colourblind mode?
The sound design is very good though, the weapons sounds are taken directly from the Halo console games and thus are of a high quality (although they do sound a little muffled), and whilst the original music composed by Tom Salta (Halo: CEA) is very good, the music feels like it is implemented incorrectly, as the music that often accompanies combat is very calm and whimsical, not the epic music that I would expect from such a scenario (see Halo: CEA OST's "Strung"). The game feels very Halo-y in how it sounds, but it is a shame that this feeling does not carry over to the rest of the game.
(As of the launch day) As expected, I did encounter a few bugs and issues during my time playing this game. I experienced a couple of crashes (which are inexcusable), as well as one irritating bug that causes the game to go into windowed mode when tabbed out, which makes this extra annoying because the options menu cannot be accessed whilst you are in the middle of a mission, and because there are no checkpoints, you will either have to finish the mission in windowed mode, or quit and start again. (There is no "Fullscreen" option in the menu, requiring the player to change the resolution of the game and then reverting it to your preferred resolution, or quitting the game).
Halo: Spartan Assault is the first Halo game to reach the PC platform since Halo 2 back in 2007, but it is a shame that this is the Halo game that we got. If you are a avid Halo fan like myself, you probably already have it, but if you are on the fence about it, it might be worth the try just because of it's low price, or maybe just to convince 343i and Microsoft that the PC is a viable place to put Halo games both new and old, but otherwise, I find it hard to recommend.
UPDATE: Completed in 4-5 hours, that is including mission failures as well as being AFK.
NOTE: Unlike the mobile and console versions of the game, the PC version does not feature microtransactions at all, however it is painfully obvious as to where and how they were implemented. Also, the emblem, weapon and armour skin rewards for Halo 4 do not appear in the PC version of Halo: Spartan Assault.

Driftland is a mix of Majesty and Northgard that has a lot of room to improve.
The good:
+ Neat and pleasant graphics and art design.
+ Decent gameplay reminiscent of Majesty (you recruit heroes that you can't control) and Northgard (you expand by absorbing nearby provinces and you spend much time juggling resources).
The bad:
- Tiny units - can't see what's going on. Majesty had large, cool-looking units.
- The units in Majesty had distinct personalities. One reason for that is that those units had more to do. There is little to do in Driftland and the units are bland.
- The races are mirror images of each other. Think Warcraft not Starcraft.
- The AI posed zero challenge on normal.
The EA:
- Right now you can only play skirmish.
- Only two of the four races are available. Once you win a map on hard with either race, there isn't much else to do.
- Some new feature involves accumulating "knowledge" to do global research; but right now the bonuses are too weak and the rate of knowledge accumulation too slow.
The game could develop into a new Majesty or Northgard, but it's not quite there yet. At it's current stage it's decent fun for 5-10 hrs.

Gear Up is a interesting little tank walker racing death simulator with far too much lack of pay to win. Free to play puns aside, everything is relatively easy to get (minus decorations) and each item feels unique, which is hard to say with any given game.
Build your own thingamajig-
Wheels, tracks, legs, hovers... Chromehounds definately inspired the selection of mobility in this game. The weapons are all usable to various degrees, each maintaining a good balance of nice and easy to use overall contrasted by oh god not that guy running the weapon that counters me. You can also swap parts mid game to get sweet sweet revenge.
Learning Curve-
You start with a Scout- A fragile speedy all terrain MONSTER. (The scout is nimble, and armed with a powerful, accurate, rapid fire cannon) Within two matches, I was able to dominate most other players with sheer speed and a little bit of accuracy. After that, I went to build on to my mobile monster, giving it a bit more HP to survive Snipers. As long as you jump in with the mentality that you will likely die, you'll do just fine. Just take whoever killed you with you. Do be mindful that ammo exists.
Sounds and Such-
The sounds are... ok. You hear what you need to hear, but the game doesnt go above and beyond.
Maps-
Most maps are fun, with variable height and defendable locations, marked with good vantage points and sniper dens. The main issure here is the lack of multiple maps.
Community in game-
Honestly, quiet, or funny. Havnt met a saltlord rager yet, then again, this is after 4 hours of playing. You do get plenty of good sportsmanship though at the end of matches.
Snipers/Camping in general-
Snipers have 6-8 shots. They gotta get ammo sometime, and then, its just a matter of waiting them out of their favorite spot. Or, swap to sniper, and pick them off.
Progression-
You progress via match completions more than not. It seems you get 1 "gold" per ten kills, 1 for participation, 2 for winning, and in DM, 4 for 1st, 3 for 2nd, so on and so forth. As most items in the game cost 4-12 Gold to buy, (average being like 5-6 not counting decorations) 2 decent matches means a new part. Matches vary from the killaholic 30 minute or more, to a 10 minute skirmish.
(Edit Addition) Spawns-
In DM, your spawns are randomized, but usually out of sight and danger. In TDM, you spawn where you damn well please (mostly), making killing spawn campers more fun. Swapping to heavy hitting arms and armor just to smush a Spawn killer, is refreshing. In Conquest, you spawn at your main base, or any captured point.
Overall-
A quick in and out game thats fun to play, and experiment with to find your favorite combonation of parts to make the next dude you see regret crossing your path. And or die trying to do said above mentioned stuff.
TL;DR, 8/10, Solid quick tank fudgery with solid progression and a fairly balanced stand on all parts.

This is one of those games where I have to give it a recommendation but I wish there was another button for "recommendation with reservations." This game will not be for everyone (of course no game is) but there is a certain pretentiousness to this game that I think will be hard for some people to get around. Having played through all four acts, I think the game peaked for me in episode three, because for a while the game actually started to feel a bit more like a video game... I started to have a sense of the rules in the "zero world" and was enjoying following the cryptic instructions to get around.

The story is abstract and surreal through the whole thing, but honestly Episode 4 really started to push it to the point that I was starting to really wonder about the point. Through the first three episodes we're primarily tied to Conway and his silly quest to deliver some antique packages. Man does he need google maps! But in Episode 4 we shift primarily to Shannon's POV. This is fine, but Shannon for some reason seems like she is going to follow Conway's quest, which just... doesn't make a lot of sense? I mean even in the strange abstract logic of this world. Conway's character also changes severely in episode 4... perhaps with good reason, but it was still very jarring since he had been the POV character through so much.

Still, despite my frustrations with Episode 4 and the overall weirdness of this series, I do recommend it because it is just so different. It really wants to be different, and it is selling itself on its different-ness, which is a bit pretentious, but it still more or less works. If you get it as part of a bundle deal or through some promotion like Twitch, I do think you should take the time to install and try it out. I think you'll decide pretty quickly whether you want to bother with all four episodes or not. I got it through Twitch Prime myself, and I think not paying full list price made me more okay with the Time investment of 6 hours I put into the first four episodes.

As I play through Kentucky Route Zero, cheeky one-line reviews pop into my head, in a feeble attempt to describe what I'm feeling. Some of which include:
These perhaps don't do the full experience justice, but we're talking about a "game" that is not really a game in the strict sense of the word, nor is it a full, finished experience. To be perfectly clear: I don't
KRZ. But I can not in good conscience recommend it to anybody. I'm glad I was able to pick it up in a Humble Bundle, because I may have regretted paying full price for this experience.
What I absolutely praise this game for is the art direction, and the dialogue writing. It's beautiful in every way, and the characters, despite being in inexplicable situations, feel as real as a friend or family member while you're engaged in conversation. Folks who enjoy dialogue systems with multiple (yet often superfluous) choices will find a lot of mileage here. Review: 9/10 -This game is absolute hell... And I love it.
Graphics: Very good. Love the art-style and rendering they chose to go with. seems like Devil May Cry in a 199X shooter.
Gameplay: Instant classic. Reminiscent of the old days with Doom, Quake, Hexen and Heretic.
Soundtrack: Meh. Only realized there's a song in the main menu, needs a Devil May Cry/Metal soundtrack!
Basics: Old-School shooter WASD movement and mouse shooting.
Mechanics: Hold left mouse button for full-auto fire and press left mouse button for shotgun blasts.
Aiming down and shotgun blasting causes "Rocket-jump" boosts.
Shoot the weak-spots of everything and collect red gems, after 10 red gems, your Devil Daggers upgrade.
After a few more gems they upgrade again. Be careful of different enemy types and take them out in tactical order of which is most threatening. Survive for over 500 Seconds to beat the game!
Story is weak, but could be as follows:
Imagine you're a young sorceror/sorceress who has been experimenting with black magic and portals and one day, you wake up someplace you definitely did not go to sleep the night before. You look around the room and find yourself on a big, floating platform. Your agility is great as ever but you feel a strong, dark energy from the center of the room...
The Devil Dagger you have read all about in your books, said to cause great power and torment, is right in front of you... You know that once you pick it up, you will be hunted, but also have the power to fight back.
Your Book of Shadows tells you that once you touch the dagger, you will have to survive for at least 8 minutes or you will be right back where you started, this will forever loop until you defeat the clock and then, then you will be free.

Take my hours for granted- I played during the Alpha/Beta and I loved the hell out of this game. But then it went pay to play, and I just can't afford games these days.
This game feels like a Free to Play game. It has all the workings of something like Smite or League of Legends with the skins, the loot, etc. I won't get too deep into it because my initial experiences were only the Alpha and Beta, and the Free to play mode.
First off, the game is fun. I'll give it that. But I cannot recommend it to people who are going to play it for free. Buy it or don't play it.
Reasons you shouldn't play unless you buy it? Easy. They list the differences on their site when you go there to read up on their free-play mode. If you didn't buy the game, then you can't; Unlock and own a character, Buy the special type of loot crates, Open more than one loot crate every 36 hours, or enter competitive ranked matches. I played one round on the free play mode and I have to say; I felt cheated. The game, itself, was fun but there was minimal pay-off, no real felt reward or progression beyond the 'profile' and individual 'character' exp/leveling. That was all I managed to get. Give this game a try if you're considering paying for it. And even if you do, they want you to buy their loot crates.
Great game,♥♥♥♥♥♥motto in my opinion. After all, I've played LoL, Dota, Overwatch, and a few other F2P games. What I'm saying is that this -feels- too much like a F2P game rather than a 'premium' buy-to-play.
Now, if you do plan on buying it, then this game is a solid recommend, and you should do what they want you to do. Spend your money to buy a game. It's no Overwatch, but I guess it can be a somewhat stand-in until you can buy that, too. After all, both games let you buy loot crates even though they're already buy-to-play games.- That's a shot at the 'buy-to-play with micro transactions motto, if you couldn't tell.
Still, fantastic gameplay, I found, and finding matches for PVP wasn't difficult. I think it popped me into a match after roughly 30 seconds? So there are a lot of people playing this. It also seems that there are a few players on F2P mode playing the game. So you can easily trounce them. Many people complain about the matchmaking, low-levels getting paired up with higher levels. I haven't seen much of this. My first match was up against to a maximum of lvl 15. First match, too, and the game went into overtime. So lvl 15 doesn't seem like a far grind.
[Edit]
In the comments, a Developer actually took the time to reply and place a ton of information below. So if you are interested in Free mode, there is a ton of information right down there. As a person who does play a lot of F2P games, personally, I expected more from this game. To me, it just feels uncomfortable. And yes, I am judging a F2P mode as a standard F2P game, here. So don't mind if I seem a little harsh.
TL;DR
Pros
- 6, not 5, but 6 free heroes on rotation every week -with- the possibility of having your favorite stick around in said rotation. Your rotations are different than everyone else's.
- You get 'seasonal'  levels
- You can level/rank up the characters you do use/Learn to play
- For a Beta, the game is still fun and enjoyable. has a more casual and relaxing feel to it/not too stressful like LoL or Dota 2
- Ability to unlock earned loot crates for free once every 36 hours. (You can earn loot crates, but only unlock them once every 36 hours)
- Progress carries over from Free-play to buy-to-play as one would think.
Cons
- Player segregation with the inability to play in Ranked/Competitive if Free-play
- Inability to earn your favorite characters
- Open a loot every 36 hours, unable to actually buy the loot crates(They're earned as game rewards, so you don't need to actually buy them- but you can't if you wanted to without buying the game.)
- Glyph. BEWARE. If you buy the game, it comes with Glyph. Glyph counts as 'game time' to steam and if it breaks- and it does for a lot of people- and you spend x-hours trying to get it to work, Steam won't refund you due to their policy. So download Glyph to see if it does run before you buy.

You are probably saying to yourself "why would I buy this game when clearly there are better MOBA's like LOL or Dota 2? Why would I go through the trouble of paying for this game when I could play them?" Well if you have found yourself asking that I have plenty of reasons why Awesomenauts is far greater than any MOBA I have played before.
To begin with I find the community absolutely great. There is the occasional ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who will scream "Lol you suck" in chat but apart from that I find that Awesomenauts attracts a great deal of funny and good sportsmanship players. I don't really have too many MOBA's I have played to compare communities with but I played one game of Dota and it had me being called a ♥♥♥♥ing noob and... yeah so I never played again. I'm not too sure if I just got unlucky but it didn't seem like a great community of people to be playing with. Everyone (well most) in Awesomenauts just want to have fun!
Then there is the way the game looks detail wise. This may just be me but I find myself looking in wonder at all the detail the developers put into the game, no cartoon games should look this good. All the little things that I just can't help but really apreciate. How the background is animated, how in one of the maps you can see sunlight flaring through the trees. The way the water captures your characters reflection seems so awesome compared to other games I have played with water. Also something I really like about the character selection screen is how the characters animate and shine.
Ronimo has done an amazing job creating so many characters all with completely different attack skills and ways to help out your team. I often find that people will always complain in chat about how overpowered a character is and yet I have seen every character be played so well. It really matters on how you use a certain character however some have a huge variation to how you can use them. This gives it a ginormous strategy aspect to the game (as most MOBA's do).
So to sum it all up if you want to get that warm fuzzy feeling you get after killing someone in a video game try this game because every time I kill someone I feel like I have just gotten a cookie. And if you have given up on playing MOBA's because of how people treat you over the internet give this game a go, it will surprise you.

My conclusion after 180h playtime:
If you liked the prequal you´ll get basically a polished version of that with even a much larger playtime. In this sequal alot of background story about your companions will be told in a very long-winded game. Also, typical for a trilogy, this is the main part which will answer most of you question in a big climax. Sadly though, you´d have to play for a very long time to get to this point. This game´s athmosphere is exactly the same as in it´s prequal, due to same graphics, same (sometimes realy overdone) dramatic situation and same polished combat system. Also, you´ll walk on the exact same map as in the prequal and will have to read tons of dozens of text. At this point I can tell, without spoiling, that the story feels finished after you completed the game although there´s a third part.
To sum in up in a pro/con comparision:
PRO:
- 150h of pure playtime with main- and sitequests
- fans get exactly what they wanted
- overall a polished "Trails in the sky first chapter"
- great soundtrack with old and new tracks
- a credibly told story with authentic characters
Bonus: The story´s main plot is surprisingly close to our modern worlds problem
with digitalization and KI invading our life.
CON:
- you´ll face a wall of text, young padawan
- some characters act realy flat, like your main character (Estelle)
- a dramatically told story about "staying together and we can reach everything" which is not for everyone
- very long-winded story, which need some serious time to evolve
- combat system that needs some time to understand (putting quarz in the right orders)
NOTE: If you havent played "Trails in the sky first chapter" you are missing some serious
background knowledge to understand what´s even going on. So I highly recommend
playing the first game!

okay, first of all- this is probably the hardest game I've ever played, and that's coming from someone who's beaten Supermeatboy and HotlineMiami 1&2. That said, it's also one of the best games I've ever played. I would describe it as a hardcore arcade game for people who enjoy first-person shooters. Because that's essentially what this game is- an arcade game- since the only object of the game is to beat your previous highscore. Theres no levels, you're always on the same huge platform floating in the middle of a black void. There's also nothing in the way of a storyline, but I think that was intentional, to emphasize how gameplay-driven this game really is. You can tell that a lot of effort was put into perfecting the physics- running, strafing, jumping, and rocket jumping feel seamless. The game makes you feel like a worthless weakling every time an enemy kills you in one hit, yet God-like when you've upgraded your weapon a bit, and you rocket jump around the map like a gleeful idiot, just absolutely shredding through enemies. The level of difficulty in this game is relentless, and if you're up for a challenge (which you should be) it'll drive you to get better. And once you're good at this game, you enjoy it all the more. I've put about 10 hours in to this game so far, and I can anticipate puttin in many many more in the future.

This game isn't a combat sim. It's arcade all the way with totally unrealistic combat mechanics, abused by veteran players to destroy the lower skilled opposition. The small playerbase it still has is mostly very toxic and/or arrogant.
-
I've played the game up to level 46 and got all achievements for it. So I've seen a fair share of it.
When the game was released it was very good. Fun and challenging to play, while still somewhat fair and with very few if any toxic players.
Then one day came the infamous patch or simply known as 'The Patch'. It made the game less challenging, more friendly to newbies and introduced some awkward game mechanics that changed a lot about how the game was played. The patch also killed the competitive clan scene over night and led to the demise of the average player base. With it dwindling, the remaining playerbase became more toxic, more trolling and more abusive. Cheating was also a big problem since the game has no anti cheat whatsoever.
Over time a small group of veteran players figured out ways to cheese the combat and movement system of the game to a degree that makes them almost untouchable while still allowing them to hit their opponent within milliseconds with killing blows of the largest and theoretically slowest weapons. The are other mechanics as well that allow them to stab over and around shields or make their attacks unblockable. The dodging mechanic of the 'Man at arms' class is another stupid thing. Also the perceived reach of weapons doesn't match their actual reach. Often you'll get hit by strikes you thought are to far away, with the weapon not reaching you at all. That might be due to bad netcoding or simply due to bad design.

Updated: 5.9 hours of gameplay:
TL:WR - Recommended, it's already got a very solid base game in place and has an interesting background and some very fun mechanics. A few clunky aspects, but overall worth it from what I've seen. And o/c, still in Early Access, so bound to improve in quality (and cost) by the time of final release.
Gameplay: 7/10
AI: 6/10
UI: 5/10
Units: 6/10
Buildings: 8/10
Graphics: 9/10
Tutorial: 7/10
Campaign: N/A as of this review.
Mulitplayer: N/A as of this review.
Overall: 6.9/10
The game is, obviously, incomplete as of this review - it is still in Early Access. Gameplay is slow-paced, but lacks any form of tactical pause beyond the menu which prevents interaction with the game. AI for barbarians and wildlife, collectively referred to as "hostiles" is well done so far, they will retreat when losing and will attack on their own as well as defend their own home-base. AI for player units is also pretty good, though it would be nice if we had more ways to control them (a "hold here" or "retreat" option would be nice). AI for NPC empires is incomplete, they don't attack the player even if the player starts it. They will, however, defend themselves fairly well. It feels like the NPC empires don't have proper use of the game controls, honestly. Hurts playability, but not to a dangerous degree.
Finite resources per island is a bit of an issue, but one I enjoy because it makes you ration supplies to a degree. Can't just build endlessly or you'll run out of building supplies. This is slightly negated by the ability to create and destroy islands - if you manage to get late enough in-game to run out of natural resources, you can just destroy empty islands and create new ones with limited resources on them. The buildings needed for these resources are all well-designed and overall both functional and attractive to look at. Some of the details could use work, and it would be nice to have more upgrades and larger towers, but overall it makes sense. Could use walls & gates.
Units are fairly diverse and well designed, with different abilities, upgrades, and a leveling system. There are also artifacts that they will, I assume, be able to collect later on, but those have not been fully implemented yet (or it's a bug, idk which). Units are divided into 3 classes: Melee, Ranged, and Magic. All units can be mounted on one of the 3 types of flying animal (ravens, eagles, and dragons) which can be gained by conquering their respect nest types and recruiting them. Mounting will happen automatically and cannot be directly decided or controlled by the player.
Both Multiplayer and the Campaign are still in the works, but I will update this review again once they have been released and I play them through. Only 2 of the 4 races are active as yet (Humans & Dark Elves) so I can't wait to see what the other races can do.
Overall, this game is fun and has a unique premise with the moveable floating islands. Needs just a few more features (would be nice to steal islands from people, for example) and an AI upgrade for the NPC empires, but can't really say I regret buying it at this time. Go for it folks!

This...thing, is brilliant. It's not a game in the classical sense, it's really more of a graphic novel with narrative choices frequently left up to the reader. It's less like you're controlling what the characters do and more like you're controlling who these characters are. They're going to do what they're going to do largely regardless of your choices, but the choices you make flesh out the characters' pasts, thoughts, and feelings.
Now I've played a number of artistic "games" or interactive stories or whatever you want to call them, and I've usually been like "Okay, that was interesting, cool" but they often either feel vaguely forced or pretentious, or they just feel more like a museum gallery of interesting things. This game however, manages to do something I've never experienced with other artistic games. It manages to give me the feeling of a really good, challenging book, while at the same time creating a visual world that is both beautiful and complementary to the story. The story-telling skills, both visual and literary, of the developers is impressive. The experience flows from mundane to bizarre and back again so smoothly that it all feels somehow natural.
I'm sure this game will still feel pretentious to some people; most really artistic things do. But to me it feels sincere and thoughtful, like the creators really care about their characters and world and the atmosphere they've created is just beautiful in about all the ways a thing can be beautiful.
It isn't an exprience that everyone will appreciate, especially if you're looking for a game, but it is an incredible experience, and if you've thought any of this sounds like something you'd enjoy then you'll probably love it.

Kentucky Route Zero is among the best case arguments I've ever seen for games being art. It is entirely unique, and I don't want to say too much at the risk of spoiling it. It's sort of like classic "adventure" games of yore, but with very modern sensibilities and captivating graphics and sound design. Rather than choosing the direction of the narrative as it unfolds, it's more like you're writing your own story as you go along, often filling in background details about characters with your choices that don't really affect gameplay, but inform your mental portrait of what this story is and who these characters are.
The writing is VERY smart, and these faceless, flat-looking, low-polygon characters seem more like real people than most games I've ever played. They stick with you the way characters from your favorite books or movies do. As of this writing, the game is only partially released, with the fifth and final chapter still in development. There are, therefore, still loose ends to be tied up. But will they be? Truthfully, I don't even care. This game could end without answering any questions and I would still be happy to have taken part in the surreal journey.
I put off getting this game for ages because $25 seemed like a lofty price to pay for something I'd never played before and was only partially complete (I think only two chapters were out when I bought it). But a friend bought it for me for Christmas and I've since passed that favor along by buying it for other people because I am so enthusiastic about it. I think people need to experience this game, particularly if they are interested in the debate over whether or not games can be art. This game is as high of art as a game can be, and it deserves your attention.

Kentucky Route Zero has to be one of the most contemplative experiences of my life; the atmosphere is perfect to be enjoyed late at night in a dim room. The feeling of the game is difficult to describe and is something I highly recommend everyone try out and experience for yourself. Yes, $25 may seem like a lot of money for an adventure game, but how often do we pay upwards of that for dinner? This game is food for your soul and will pay itself off if you listen to its tale.
(P.S.), many people seem to think that this isn't a "game." And that may be because it doesn't follow conventional gaming structures. The emphasis isn't on how your play effects the game world, but rather what your play style reveals about yourself. There are hosts of dialogue options that build the history of each individual character. Plus, if you read the synopsis about the game right above the reviews, it reveals "a focus on characterization, atmosphere and storytelling rather than clever puzzles or challenges of skill." If you can read, you have to know what you're getting yourself into.

Atlas Reactor is a simultaneous turn-based multiplayer game. In a match, players will first select the freelancer (heroes which you might be more familiar with in MOBAs) they wish to play as along with their loadout. Everyone has 20 seconds to set their actions for that turn and then watch as everyone's action unfold simultaneously in the same turn.
The game used to be buy-to-play, which meant that you had to purchase the game first before you could play it. Recently, they released a free mode update wherein players can now try the game beforehand to see if they would be interested in such a game. Free mode acts as some form of demo mode wherein you'll be given a unique set of freelancers you can play as that rotates every week. Free mode also allows you to open loot matrices every 36 hours which contains cosmetic items. Purchasing the game will give you access to every current and future freelancer and remove the 36 hour limit on opening loot matrices, allowing you to open any loot matrix you obtain any time.
With around 250 hours logged into the game at the time of this writing (more if you count pre-steam release), I would highly recommend buying it if the game interests you after trying it out. Free mode was a nice idea as it gives people the chance to try the game out beforehand, since the unique gameplay might not be up to everyone's tastes. If you have some free time and wish to try something a bit different, I recommend giving Atlas Reactor a shot.

I used to play Guitar Hero with friends, got pretty decent at it, until I realised it was stupid spending that much time learning to play a piece of plastic. Soon after i got bored of it and stopped playing while thinking "it's sad you can't do the same but with an actual guitar so you'll learn to play it".
So when I found out about Rocksmith, it sounded pretty much like what I had always hoped for a rythm game and I had to give it a shot, bought a boxed game version with the original cable (30€ on Ebay) and a (very crappy) 50€ second hand guitar from a brand even google never even heard of. Thing is, I'm freaking poor and couldn't afford spending 200€ on a decent guitar just to "give a shot" at Rocksmith and risk wasting it all if disapointed.
So what do i think after a few weeks of trying? Well in short: HELL YEAH! If you're hesitating just go for it, you won't be disapointed. After years of unsuccessfull attempts to learn bass guitar, i can tell for sure i made a LOT more progress in only one week of Rocksmith than in 5 years of solo learning, and that's in both Bass and guitar (since a friend brought his bass to my place to play with me).
I would'nt say for sure that Rocksmith will make you a guitarist/bassist, I think you'd still have to get a teacher at some point if that's really what you want, but if you want to learn the basics, improve your skills and check out how guitar work for you, Rocksmith will give you full satisfaction. You just skip the annoying, long, repetitive hard work part to go straight to "now I enjoy practicing" part. I only wish I had something better than that crappy guitar as it's becoming an obtacle to my progress, I'm currently trying to save up for that.
My only advice: If you're buying a guitar for this game, don't go too cheap, you'll have nothing decent under about 200€ and it'll ruin a lot of the experience.
Pros:
-Excellent concept
-Very entertaining
-Very well done overall
-Absolutely suitable to learn
-Handle either guitar/ emulated bass (on guitar) / actual bass guitar
-Allow 2 players to play together
-Impressive real time adaptation to your skills and progress
-Tyranics Mini-games to force you progress faster on a specific technique
Cons:
-Menu is a little hard to navigate at first
-The cable have some misses, I have to unplug/replug it every now and then, not dramatic but could be improved.
-I miss a function to alternate players quickly, instead of changing profile after every songs.
-We can't skip the noobish tutorial when creating a new profil, why would you do that? Just... why? Some player know how to press a string, they don't need an unskippable 15min lesson on it.
-The songs database is a little short and not very diversed (pretty much only classic rock), and the songs to buy in the shop are quite f***ing expensive, 3€ each, not allowing poor players like me to enjoy many songs they really like.
Conclusion:
Very good game, such learning, much buy, wow.

Probably the most player-friendly MOBA I've ever played, being extremely easy to learn and having a decent enough community, combined with a bright and exciting bunch of playable awesomenaughts to play as, each one having something different.
The artstyle is lovely and unique, with nothing looking quite the same, everything is different.
While it has relatively few characters compared to larger MOBA's, such as LoL or DotA 2, each character can be differently built in ways that directly affect your abilities, giving endless possibilities to what you can do.
With the nice community, teamwork is possible as long as everyone cooperates, and will largely profit your team.
Sadly, the game has a tendency to be onesided. There are certain HP related items, one such example increasing your health by 20 points for every purchase. If you aren't aware, 20 health is quite a lot of HP in Awesomenaughts, with some of the harder hitting attacks hitting for 40 or 50. For killing two heroes, which happens a lot since the "lanes" basically push themselves, an entire team can usually buy this health item, making even the squishiest support 'naught a tank, removing any hope of strategy or winning.
And this usually leads to intense snowballing for one team, making comebacks impossible as you valiantly try to defend your base. And by doing this, communication isn't very worth it because there's nothing tactical or planned left to do, making the game much less enjoyable until it ends.
Overall I give it a 9/10, mostly for how fun the overall game is, but missing that one point for how hard the game can be for even the slightest of mistakes. Still, I highly recommend this game.

text: It's like For Honor with Honor. 11/10.

Disclaimer: As ETS2 is more popular I am comparing it to ATS. Besides that, I think that most people considering buying this game will have played ETS2 first.
After having this game on my wishlist for a few months, I decided it would be time to buy it on the Steam Winter Sale 2017. Having played almost 200 hours of Euro Truck Simulator 2, a new map and different trucks sounded really appealing to me. I spent 5 euro's on this game and to be honest, I didn't expect it to be as good as ETS2. After I played through the tutorial and started delivering my first cargo, I immediately noticed that the map is far more detailed and connecting than the ETS2 map. The different roads you can drive really give you a feeling of more freedom than I experienced in ETS2.
Having played about 20 hours in the first 4 days, I realised that I really like it, maybe even more than ETS2. So I bought all the DLC, including the New Mexico map expansion. On my way towards the new state I came across different, very detailed places, junctions and landscapes. You can really tell this map isn't just copying and pasting cities and junctions as in ETS2 (especially in Germany), the roads do not get boring at all. For a quick overview, I'll sum up my pros and cons below.
+ Different routes give you more a sense of freedom
+ Very detailed roads and surroundings
+ Something different around every corner
- Not all trucks are as fast as in ETS2
- Only two different truck brands you can buy
- Not that much customisation of your truck and no DLC for it (yet)
- Sometimes a bit low fps (but I have a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ laptop, so no worries)
Now, is it better than ETS2? In my opinion it is, but the game definitely needs some more work. A few more states (Utah and Colorado for example) will result in you not driving past the same cities every time, but I do understand that this will take a lot of time to develop. New trucks however wouldn't be such a big change in my opinion, but it will be a big improvement. If SCS continues to develop ATS as good as they've done until now, it will definetely overshadow ETS2 by far.

The card effects are interesting and they bring some variety to the otherwise boring mechanics, but don't get to attached to your cards, because all players share one big deck and your opponents cannot only get the cards you picked before the game, but can also steal the cards in your hand with some effects. This game is very unforgiving to newer gamers. Beginning your first few games may take some time as your team will kick lower level players. Just after joining after half an hour of jumping servers, you will find that everyone else in this game seems to know exactly how you'll act, where you'll be, and are just five times harder to kill than you are. So you'll jump into training, learning the ropes, trying the other stages up, seeing their layouts and gain a few levels in the process.
Now is when the game gets fun. You can join a game much faster and you can actually pick off more of the higher leveled enemies.
The item system is similar to COD, with a flair of TF2 thrown in. Weapons, identities, voices, and psyches are unlockable through keys earned by leveling up. You can also purchase clothing for your character with coins earned from each battle.
The game is quite inventive in areas, while in some it feels a bit rehashed. My only issue with the game was differentiating teammates from enemies. Unless the jocker class is wearing bright pink, they appear batlike and you'll receive a cakle from the offender if you decide to ignore them, and vice versa.
Sadly, last I was on, the servers were sparse, and only people over level 50 frequented more of the team oriented games.
I recommend this for those who want a quirky FPS team orient game for free. Or you can run off to TF2 which will definatley have a full server no matter where you turn.

TL;DR: A unique take on rts games that still manages to hit all the core features rts veterans love and expect.
One key element that I have noticed is the players' "mana" and abilities grants a high potential for having different balanced focuses and tactics that essentially run off a risk/reward system.
Do you invest lots of a small amounts of mana to scout and then play pinball off floating islands in search of treasure and the enemy? Do you use a little more mana to chain together as mana islands as possible, risking fights with neutrals but snowballing your economy? Or do you use your mana sparingly, saving it for defense or when you need it most?
Since the maps are proceduraly generated you will have to be adaptable to utilize what you are given as efficiently as possible and use it to steer your overarching strategy.
There are only two negatives. The first is the worker system is a little more dense than it needs to be-- which means as a casual player it is hard to forsee the shape your economy will take-- ending with you rushing to place buildings down as rapidly as possible with little thought beyond the next move ahead. With experience you will know exactly which resources you need for what but the lack of resource theme makes it less easy to catch on than the casual gamer might prefer.
The second negative is that the game is so good you won't want to wait for the next wave of features you know will be great! (Early access probs).
