I quite like the game and I can see in my minds eye where it is going to go. The only thing I could really fault in this game are two things.
First - The Economy. The game is all about gathering resources gold, wood, food etc. etc. but there are only two ways to generate gold. You either have idle citizens or work a gold mine. Working the gold mine isn't really the greatest option though, as the idle citizens earn almost the same amount of gold if they weren't working. Everything in this game is reliant on gold, and the further away you build your islands, the more upkeep and everything in general costs. You can sell things at the market but generally, you don't get much.
Second - Hero units. The Hero units you get in game are not really heros. They are simply soldiers, mages and archers. There are scout's as well, but I don't really count them as a hero. Now you will find yourself in combat fairly early on, nothing difficult but bothersome depending on where your barracks are located as the units just simply have a nice stroll to fight the enemy. If you don't put a gold price on them though, your Heros only attack one at a time. The combat simply could use some work.
Now apart from those two things above the game is great, but please don't take this the wrong way. The economy and heros are a different system but completely workable. The game play is solid, graphics are very pretty, music is good. Moving islands around and that sort of thing are great as well.
Whilst I know this is early access, I do recommend this. At this stage, I would rate this a solid 8/10. With further updates, I look forward to see what else comes along.

What do you think the game did well?
I am enjoying the story a lot more than I thought I would as it draws me into it with its mysteriousness. Some new spells and actions require the player to have points in multiple skills which offers a more varied combination of abilities. There are a lot of laugh out loud moments when encountering NPCs or interacting with your companions. The game doesn't limit or punish you for thinking outside the box in order to win. The difficulty is well balanced and challenging which encourages players to tinker with their character builds. The crafting is a lot easier and doesn't require points in a crafting skill to get started. I like how the NPCs react to your characters race and gender which offers replay value so you can experience all the possible interactions. The inventory system is a lot better to navigate with a more intuitive GUI. Once you read a skill book for a spell or action it will stay with you. Action points have been simplified and add new obstacles to combat. Runes are a nice addition rather than using crafting to modify weapons. The character models are a lot more unique looking and adding the undead as an option offers up some great challenges. The option to view line of sight helps with sneaking around and stealing.
What do you think the game could do better?
The pain of managing backpacks is still in the game and I wish I was able to rename the backpacks at least. Fort Joy level feels a bit too drawn out for me and having to repeat it for a character reroll pains me. A lot of the recipes from the first game are not in this game, which is good as some were redundant, but crafting weapons or armor isn't very lucrative now. Certain situations can cause your companions to get stuck like something in front of the ladder stops them from climbing up or a bowl keeps them from moving forward. The log book is still a working progress as I see patches to it all the time to bring clarity to confusing quests.
Do you recommend this game?
Most definitely, YES! The developers have done a fantastic job at listening to the community and ensuring their fans enjoy their experience. I haven't tried multiplayer or GM content yet but I have heard great things about it. Lots of potential for modders.

In case you missed that title card, this is Trails in the Sky SC. This game is a direct sequel to the first Trails game, and as such if you jump in without playing that game, then you'll probably be very confused. Gameplay has been expanded upon from Sky 1 due to increased stat pool and magic availability. Heck we even get a party menu this time. As a standalone game SC is still good, but it is a poor starting point as the first 2 sky games were originally designed as one game. If you enjoyed the characters, story, and gameplay of the previous installment. Then this game shouldn't disappoint. But as I said before, this is as direct a sequel you can get. In order to get the full experience, you have to play the previous installment first for sake of awareness & continuity.

This game provides a pretty interesting diversion--matches are dynamic and surprising, rarely playing out in the same way twice. Match length is typically about 10 to 15 minutes, and rewards come frequently enough to make you say, "Okay, just one more," until next thing you realize, it's three hours later.
I don't do much in the way of competitive gaming, except as a side activity in some MMORPGs that I've played, and to be sure, what little I've played of MOBAs had me scratching my head, as I didn't find them fun at all and they seemed to have a high barrier to entry.
Atlas Reactor piqued my interest, however, when the advertising invoked the name XCOM, since I love the turn-based strategy in that series. To be sure, actions play out pretty differently in this game to the way they play out in XCOM, largely because of the necessary reversal of movement and action on each turn, but it's still a reasonable comparison even if it only gives you a vague idea of what to expect.
Anyway, I've had a lot of fun Beta testing this game, and as of right now, I haven't actually encountered any venomous manchildren. Occasionally somebody will get a little irked by poor play, but what I've found is that experienced players are usually willing to offer more guidance than incrimination. I suppose that's bound to change at some point, though, but maybe because the game is such a niche experience, a lot of the bad sorts won't notice we're having good clean fun over here.
Fingers crossed.

Here's how the game mostly works.  The game requires a special cable that allows you to plug your guitar into your computer.  So just downloading the game won't allow you to play it unless you have that special interface cable.  Once you plug in and tweak your options, the basic campaign will give you the simple "Rocksmith" experience.  When you first start, all of the songs are not yet "leveled up," so you only need to play just a few notes of the melody, and probably no chords at all.  But as you play each song again and again, the game figures out which sections of the song you're getting good at, and increases the difficulty, add more of the melody's original notes.  This goes on continually, for every song you play, making the game increasingly more challenging the more you play it.  After you have played each song and "leveled them up" to maximum, you'll basically be playing the song as it was recorded.
As a "guitar instruction" method, I really think this has potential.  The early part of the game is simple enough that really ANYONE could play it, and the more you play, the more the game challenges you as a guitar player.  Each song as a few different arrangements, some focusing on lead, some on rhythm and chords.  The game is a harsh judge, so make sure you hit EVERY note, not just the ones that are easy to play!
As some who already plays guitar, I found the game was most rewarding when I was selecting individual songs to play from the game's catalogue, without bothering with the campaign at all.  I sort of knew how to play Outshined already, but learning how to REALLY play it without cheating was a treat.  I pick a song I like, and practice all the parts of it individually until I can play them all, then I try to put them all together by playing the complete song on the maximum level.  Sometimes I can pull it off, depends on the song.
So if you're already a guitar player, or you are really interested in learning to play, this game is definitely for you!  Tons of new songs to play as downloadable content.  But if you're a "gamer" who's not really much of a musician, even if you really liked Guitar Hero, I'd say this game is probably not your cup of tea.  It's more of a "musician's thing" than a game.
The game also features support for basses, and an entire campaign just for bass players.  FINALLY, some respect!

I think this might be the best written game out there. The illustration, animation, and sound are also all beautiful, rich, and specific: just watching the character Conway walk lets me feel like I know how he feels; some of my favorite moments here just involved choosing to wait in a particularly beautiful environment while a song plays out.  Every setting carries a rich sense of place, that is simultaneously surreal and rooted in specific American landscapes. What this game put forwards is the idea that a player can choose how the characters experience and react to events, rather than affecting the outcome - and oddly that this can lead me to feel even more stake in the characters stories than I do in games where I make many plot-significant decisions. Though note, it's closer to interractive fiction / animation than game, and the plot itself is mostly linear. Whatever you want to call it, it's one of my favorite adventure games, works of magic realism, or just examples of storytelling in any medium

This is aside of the Borderlands-series the only open world-game I really enjoyed and that didn't start to be boring after a certain amount of time. It manages to capture this postapocalyptic feeling in a much more realistic way than for example the Fallout series and the constant feel of danger. As, how the game puts it: Not the factions or the mutants are your true enemy here. The Zone itself is what truly wants to kill you, spit on your corpse and kick you out again. And this hostile environment is in no other game better captured than in the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series. Especially the beginning until you have your first "real" gear the zone will toy with you like your a dandelion seed in a hurricane.
PROS:
+ So far the perfect example of "hostile environment"
+ Manages to convey the dullness and loneliness
+ Gun play is good
+ Incredible amounts of mods - recommend you to go to modDB since they should have most mods up there
+ Due to being quite old it also runs on potatoes
+ Graphics can be pushed with mods to look decent even nowadays, especially ATMOSF.E.A.R. - a weather mod does a tremendous job
CONS:
- Especially on higher difficulties (and with difficulty-increasing mods) very unforgiving
- You will die a lot in the beginning as the game has the same concept of a "tutorial" as the Souls-series (none)
- Nothing for those with problems with jump scares - not as much as the game does it on purpose, but you WILL sometimes just hear a mutant a split second before it is on top of you

This game is total butt juice,
Once you understand how it works( by yourself, because even thought the basics are really simple the developers didn't have the time to implement a 1 minute fahking tutorial) you'll realize that this game is based on luck and luck alone.
You would literally have more fun just watching the bots fight among themselves because there are no choiches in this game. Every time you are prompted to do one of a few things you can just figure out which is the optimal strategy instantly. The few times when you can actually gamble are rather insignifacnt and will rarely change the outcome of the match.
The concept of the card game proper is okay, but it becomes incredibly dull and predictable after about 1 hour.
The CPU players feel like they're cheating a lot of the time, especially at the end of the Kai scenario or when they choose to use a point stealing card on you even though there are CPU players with way more stars.
100% Orange Jucie is pleasing to look at. It has a nice interface, simple but cute animations and nicely illustrated cards.
The characters however, while being as good as one dimensional characters come, are very forgetable.
The studio behind this game should have realized that their other games aren't big enough to warrant a game with an all-star roster comprised of their characters, since no one knows them.
The music is okay, but if you intend to play this game for more than a few hours you will have to turn off the audio because there are very few tracks and the announcer voice becomes exhausting after you realise that they recorded only 1 single fahking clip for everything. No action has any alternative voice clips. None. How did they expect anyone to listen to that ccunnt for as long as it takes to finish the entire campaign ?!?
The card effects are interesting and they bring some variety to the otherwise boring mechanics, but don't get to attached to your cards, because all players share one big deck and your opponents cannot only get the cards you picked before the game, but can also steal the cards in your hand with some effects. I have no complaints here.
The lack of local multiplayer is not only disappointing, but stands to show how bad of a choice the devs can make. The only argument against this features functionality is that your hand of up to 3 cards won't be secret. SERIOUSLY? Did anyone EVER think that would make the game less fun? It would just be a different way of playing. That would've added SO MUCH to this horrible mistake of a release. Do you really expect me to get 3 other people that I know to buy "this", just so we can play a fun board game once and then forget it forever? They really think to highly of their game, these devs. It's fun, but it's not THAT good.
The DLC is okay, and I like the idea of being able to buy chunks of the game at a different time, just so you don't pay all the money up front and regret it later(I might've♥♥♥♥♥♥on the devs before but I really like this decission, great job), but I do feel like the price of the game + all DLC is steep. I want to be able to recommend this, there is A LOT of good in this game, but man there is SOME baaaaaaaad. This game gets really dildoes at times and it makes me feel like I have NO AGENCY when I play.
If you find this on sale and feel like trying a weird board game, go for it, you should find stuff to enjoy, but don't expect too much.

“Undefeated” is a decent, if somewhat bland, JRPG that nevertheless plays well. You get a limited selection of characters to use, so you’re pretty much stuck with a fixed party for most of the time, but to compensate this you get a large variety of special moves and spells, which you’ll need to use judiciously to win the fights with various enemies (especially at higher difficulty levels). The story is the usual “save the world” stuff, with side quests to enrich it, and the total gameplay is something around 8 hours. Graphics is mostly a standard JRPG set, and the music is nothing extra either but it’s good enough to listen during the game. Overall, “Undefeated” probably won’t stand against such JRPG gems as Millennium or Moonchild, but if you like this genre, and have already finished the titles mentioned above, then this game is worth a try.

Gotham City Impostors (рус. Самозванцы из Готэм Сити) - многопользовательский шутер от первого лица, основанный на комиксах про Бэтмена. Бэтмен и Джокер покинули город, но война продолжается! Теперь между обычными гражданами города. Местное население, накинув плащ Бэтмена или разрисовавшись в цвета Джокера, пополняют ряды соответствующей армии и ведут войну за Готэм Сити! Игровой процесс очень напоминает более известный шутер Team Fortress 2, однако у Gotham City Impostors существует ряд отличий, которые делают игру уникальной. Gotham City Impostors доступна для игры на ПК, Xbox360 и PS3. Практически сразу после релиза, игра стала распростроняться на основе Free to Play в Steam. Игра создана на движке Lithtech Jupiter EX. Игра отличается очень хорошей графикой для онлайн-шутеров. Городские уровни на максимальных настройках качества графики можно сравнивать с игрой Crysis 2. По этому системные требования написаны не для галочки. После запуска игры сразуже брасается в глаза рисованый Бэтмен в левом нижнем углу экрана. Он даёт различные подсказки и показывает tutorial при покупке новго оружия (сразу вспоминается Vault Boy из Fallout). Настроив игру должным образом в разделе Help & Options, перейдем к самой игре, нажав в главном меню Play Now! Игра рекомендует пройти Initiation - некий быстрый tutorial, дающий ознакомиться с игровыми примочками. На данный момент имеется пять игровых режимов (не включая Initiation): Team Deathmatch - классический командный десматч, Fimigation - захват и удержание контрольной точки, Psych Warfare - необходимо найти батарейку и вставить его в проигрыватель своей команды (похоже на захват флага), Bounty Hunter - необходимо убить противника и подобрать жетон для увеличения счета вашей команды, и Challenges - одиночная игра, где нужно на время выполнить определенное задание. После начала игры нам предложат выбрать набор снаряжения (Loadout). Это может быть один из готовых стандартных наборов, либо свой собственный набор. Собственный набор можно укомплектовать по своему усмотрению, однако по умолчанию все оружия и примочки закрыты. Разблокировать одно из оружий или гаджетов можно за ключи разблокировки, которые можно получить в конце матча, либо купив в игровом магазине. Перейдя в главном меню в раздел Secret Identity, мы попадем в раздел настроек персонажа. В игре существует система уровней персонажа (максимальный уровень - 1000) и местная валюта в виде золотых монет, за которые можно купить одежду для нашего героя. В заключении хочется сказать пару минусов об игре. Во-первых, хочется чтобы оружия в игре было немножко больше. Во-вторых, нет возможности выбора сервера. Игра сама закидывает в лобби, которое считает нужным: может оказаться, что игра забросит вас на сервер с огромным пингом, где играть вообще невозможно, да ещё и поиск сервера иногда может затянуться до нескольких минут. Но игра развивается, выходят новые патчи и нововведения. Пожелаем разработчикам дальнейших успехов в обновлении игры. Поклонникам Team Fortress 2 и Call of Duty играть обязательно! :) Смотрите полную версию обзора на сайте:

Undefeated is a well-rounded adventure RPG with a solid story, combat system, and inventory arrangement. The game is customizable from the start, with options for difficulty level, and whether you want visible or invisible enemies. The main quest takes about 12 hours to complete.
Things gets started quickly, as you are thrown into the action early in the game. The premise of the story is that you and your party are military recruits who get mixed up in a more advanced situation, and must find out what is causing mutant creatures to leave the wilderness and invade the local towns. The story has a very good plot, which leads you through the main sequence of quests; the characters are well developed, but do not factor into the story much. Towards the end of the game, however, the focus of the story is lost as it becomes secondary to a series of progressively more difficult battles, and a lot of loose ends were left untied.
Your initial party includes three recruits, and a few others come and go along the way.
There are a large number of side quests, but most of them are very similar, and involve delivering a message or item of some sort to one of the hundreds of NPCs that populate the map in each town. Completing them is a matter of talking to every person in every town multiple times, which can grow tedious. Furthermore, the world map doesn't always allow you to travel where you want, and tends to force you along the way to complete your main quest. Many side quests will be left behind. There are also areas of the world map that you are never able to travel to (as far as I could tell).
Gold is acquired by searching hollow logs and crevices on the area map. There are 25 secret rooms in the game, which can also be found this way.
Combat is well done, with normal difficulty presenting a nice challenge. All characters have unique skill sets, which develop as you progress through the levels. Strategy is an important part of battles.
There are no hitches to this game, although some battles are difficult enough that you might have to repeat them multiple times. There is, however, the possibility of running out of supplies, and if this happens while you are in a place called "the wilderness" (roughly the last third of the game), you will have to warp back to buy new supplies. Before entering the wilderness again, you must obtain rings which ward off sickness, and you are only allowed to do this once, apparently, so be cautious. The game tells you all this anyway.
Overall, the game feels like an epic through most of its progress, but the ending is rather sudden, as if we are expected to continue the adventure in a sequel.

I have to admit I am a little dissapointed.  The story never really took off for me and before I knew it, it was over before I ever really felt like it got out of what would be "Chapter 1" in a novel.  However, other parts of the game where enough to push my verdict to "Recomended" in light of it all and I hope the developers can look on this with a bit of advice for suture titles.
This was one of the larger areas of dissapointment for me.  It started off very unique and well.  The music in the barracks and intro scenes fit the mood very well and the way the proffessional soldiers talked to you as a cadet was good.  It really set the tone of life in the military as best as you can do in a RPG Maker game.
But as the story progressed, everything centered around the wasteland spreading and turning monsters into tougher opponents.  Even when you make it to the village completely destroyed, it still did not feel like it was a very menacing backstory to be afraid of.  In addition, the lack of villians in the game meant that your characters pretty much just stumble on new items instead of actually having any sort of real mission.  You are mainly just being sent to investigate over and over again.  There was no one to fight or scheming to stop you it feels like.
The ending was the worst.  I don't want to divulge too much for sake of spoilers, but that ending was borderline M. Night Shyamalan style like the Mist where it just vanishes or the Happening where it too
The "big" revelation at the end really had as about much impact as it instead being a early game boss instead of the "grand" finale.
Lastly....there is way too much dialougue and interaction in the game.  Kudos for not being lazy...but it was just way too much and it makes the player immune to when something is being said instead of engaged in a cutscene because half of the game some form of text is popping up every 20 seconds.  Streamline and gut it to only concentrate on the main story and then every once in a while...very rare times...add in parts that help build character identity more.
This was a solid B+.  Almost everyhting is custom, but I would harp on the quality.  In total honesty I think default RPG Maker parts would had been better in many spots like many of the battle backgrounds and sprite work in dungeons.
But heart and soul was poured into this area I can tell and that can always be appreciated.
Music and ambience matched very well.  Will give this a solid B+ as well.  There where no tracks that took my breath away, but everything fit well together.  Only area I saw that could be easily improved without having to find new commission work would be the battle background music.  Mix it up from time to time.  It gets old hearing the same thing from beggining to end of game minus boss fights.
However, there must had been 30 tracks and again...although they did not blow me away, they still all fit very well together.  Great attention to detail.
Undefeated uses a very different style that is for sure.  I would recomend narrowing those dungeons by A LOT.  Eons of running around vast open areas with enemy encounters happening every few seconds is not very enjoyable.  Perhaps it was a method used to not have to make but 7-ish main dungeons in the entire game?  I dont know. This game is kind of a 3D Death Rally (the original one, not the remake). You start with a crappy car and climb your way up the ladder, upgrading your ride as you get cash from races. You have cars mounted with weapons, and mario-kart style powerups (with a serious tone, no throwing turtle shells here) that litter the road... along with a lot of destructible obstacles. You can either outrace your opponents or destroy them.
The racing and the shooting feels rather good, but I would've appreciated a slightly more realistic physics model: as it is driving on sand, grass and asphalt feel almost the same. Track design is good so far with a lot of shortcuts, jumps and choices between the fastest lane or picking up a powerup.
Graphics are nice overall with special mention to explosions and particle effects: the road littered with burning wrecks is quite a sight as well as being a challenge to navigate.
So, recommended for the single-player, and I think it must be very fun in multi. Not sure about the longevity of the game due to the rather low skill ceiling though: getting those curves right was more of a challenge in the old top-down Death Rally from what I remember.

I picked this up for 5 bucks and have been playing for a while now.  It could be so much better than it is.  The "challenge" seems to come from worse and worse car control as the game progresses.  Seriously, it's less about your opponents than it is just trying to keep your car from bouncing all over like a pinball.  It totally detracts from the game and makes progress a real chore.  The upgrades to your car are pretty much pointless because you'll spend your time wondering why you keep randomly veering off the road and going the opposite direction that you're pressing on the controller.  The harder you try to fight to go back onto the track, the more you get pinballed around and bounced further away by logs, rocks, snow, and just bad car physics.
The battle races are also pretty much pointless.  It sounds fun on paper, but in practice it's just sorta "meh".  See, the object is still to come in first place, not take out the other racers.  So while it would be fun to be able to just devote your time to attacking your opponents, you can't.  The guns aren't that strong and there are gobs of repair powerups scattered all over the place.  So if you devote your time to combat, you find that you fall further back in the pack as your weak guns don't really do much damage and they'll just run over a repair powerup anyway.  Ironically the best races are the ones with no guns involved, simply called "classic races".
For $5 it's worth the price, but I wouldn't pay anything more for it.  If I could some up this game in two words it would be: Unrealized potential.

As a person who's first video game ever was Halo:CE on the original Xbox 12 years ago in 2001, I've spent the majority of my hours in my gaming lifetime playing inside the Halo series. I've clocked about 7K hours total in all the Halo games combined, and I'm extremely critical of anything Halo. Unlike most I won't say no just because this game is not an FPS, but I will look at it as a game in general. Halo Spartan Assualt is a simple top-down shooter that was literally made to pass the time when you are bored. This game does not have much depth to it, the story is based around past battles in the Universe and all the missions are "simulations" as all the virtual walls surrounding your play area identify.
Graphics - For a $5 game that is also a mobile game, this game is beautiful. The ground textures look crisp, the animations are stellar, and it does a pretty good job of keeping your eyes glued to the game. The character models are fairly good, however the Grunts and Elites don't exactly look like their FPS counterparts in terms of color. Most of the Grunts are Yellow, and most of the Elites are Purple(Based on how far I've gotten in the game so far, will update once 100% done). This ticks me off because in the FPS versions, Grunts are Orange and Elites are Blue. On the lowest rankings that is. As of now there are no Red/Black/Camo Elites, but there are Gold Elites and White Grunts though, so that's a change.
Story - So far, there is little. The Story is based around the Covenant breaking the Treaty it has with the UNSC by invading Draetheus-V and it's moons. This game is set after the events of Halo 3, but prior to Halo 4. This is the answer as to why the UNSC and Covenant where fighting when Halo 4 began. I'll leave the small details to you. But on terms of levels, the levels are layed out as Operations, there are 5 Operations total, each having 6 Missions in them labeled as (Letter) - (Number) to keep this simple. In the beginning of each of those 5 Operations is a well done cut scene expalining the next bit of the story. They're rather short, but get the job done. There hasn't been any voice overs mid fight, or much explanation other than the caption in each Mission before you start playing(they are interesting to read if you know the Halo Universe through previous games/books). Those captions add new Characters we have not seen before, such as Spartan Davis. I'm disappointed in the story, but for a game like this that was not intended to be very story driven it is understandable.
Gameplay - Ah, the important question. I'm not gonna lie, the gameplay is damn fun for this genre. This game has a solid feeling of when you hit something and when you do not, enemies respond accordingly to hits, and won't just immediately walk into your wall of fire from the UNSC/Covenant Turrets. Gameplay is fast and responsive, and it makes getting Killionaires and other high multi-kill medals fairly easy. One gripe is that there are missions where you actually do specific tasks like destroying AA-Wraiths or Escorting Wolverines, but there are others that have you survive for a certain period of time and wait until your ride comes to pick you up. In the mean time of that they throw countless enemies at you just to try to give you some entertainment. It felt like the Deadpool game in those moments(even though it was for only 3-4 minutes).
Audio - I had to give this it's own segment, the audio in this game is amazeballs. It's really clear and great quality. But, they didn't keep all the original sounds from previous Halo games. The Shotgun sounds like something I've never heard before, and all the others sounds faintly similar to their FPS brothers. Obviously this is a different game, but it just didn't feel like Halo there.
Final Thoughts - For $5 this game really is pretty damn good. It's not the usual Halo experience(neither was Halo Wars but I enjoyed that game too) however it gave a great experience with a good bit of fun to be had. For this price, it's an easy buy for any Halo fan that wants another taste of the series.

First things first: I perfectly well know that this is early access, so I really do hope there will be significant improvements considering unit intelligence, first and foremost. After playing a few hours, it is up to you if you want it right now, or in a few weeks after a patch. The review could also be thumbs up - but I chose thumbs down for now. See unit behavior
The economy is slightly (only) odd - achieving even a balanced economy is rather difficult, despite the small tech tree, as well as the quickly to grasp resource system ingame. You need to read/do the tutorial, to avoid applying mechanics of other games that do not work here. So READ or do the tutorial first, or discover your mistakes with low gold income ingame later, as I did.
Generating research points is, early acces test or not, rather insanely time and resource consuming, considering the use of research. 100 points for the first economic benefit, -2 building upkeep, needs more than an hour with one sages building. 60+ minutes for the first tech-tree update.... REABALANCE needed.
The tutorial is good, but slightly lacking at the explanation that range to castle increases upkeep costs. Furthermore, space limiting farms to often only one per shard, but requiring a manyfold in food per accomodation unit, makes expansion and extension/updates of upkeep intense farms a neccessity.  Getting some stone and wood then either takes a lot of time, since you can barely spare coin to use it on workers, or you need to wager your goods or mana in the market for needed goods. Let alone high level resources such as gemstones.
(Destroyed a lot of buildings, and rearranged the islands as best as possible. Also learned that updates are a must for a balanced economy, same tier multiple buildings do achieve less considering the upkeep and input.  Also, after almost two hours, islands with resources on had no, and I mean, no access point to place the corresponding building. I discovered this when the first extractors had done their job and removed the deposits.) To sum up, bigger is better, the more high tier buildings and shards the more stable becomes your economy.
(Game against AI on random/generated map with 2 of 4 mages/races available is the only game option I had - there will be plenty more)
Units are nice, a standard variety, massive spells and updates, all nice, BUT:
sometimes, without any attack commands, one knight after the other goes rampage, on suicide missions to attack alone, while the remaining keep wandering around, then join the fight after all warriors are dead. Enemy levels up. Investing all resources I had, equipped a good party, full updates, tier III , and hey, the same number of enemies, though tier I-II level lower than my soldiers, pop up, and my soldiers and marksmen all die. Then the mage dies, not casting any healing spell at all despite having full mana and the spell... . After that happened for the third time, after one game of almost three hours, I rage-quitted. Units wandered into enemy AI killing zones on their own, dying and dying and dying, wasting all resources I had accumulated, and literally feeding the enemy. Trying to keep the units near my base was useless, and after the first try, I stopped giving them mount updates. Simply too suicidal. REWORK unit AI and rebalance please - greed is good, so they do the highest bounty missions first, but if there is no real quest, they shall not go on suicide runs. Also, considering the mount costs, the utility they provide is by far not worth the effort, and the vastly improved movement options increase suicidal tendencies.
What I noticed was that enemy units worked better than my own, having a far better targeting priority for example. My knights stumbled around, only to attack the tank, while being hit for two minutes by several archers next to them. Bounties didnt change this at all. Finally, attacks on enemy territory are also suicide, because your units fight to death, or glory, and nothing else. Hence the enemy can cast spells on his territory, and you cannot, say goodbye to your max leveled heroes without anything gained.
Magic is essential, useful, but: you have a fixed radius of casting-possibility. So, you need to build towers to extend. Updating the main building is extremely expensive, that is ok and inteded,
Thanks to Hamsterbryans comment, I realised that again I must have had bad luck that it didnt work in my game when I tried it out.
Sadly, these two flaws make this game, as enjoyable as it was, a bit frustrating and not unplayable at the moment. Let us be honest, if all your highly leveled and best equipped heroes go on suicide quests after you pampered them for hours, it is frustrating. I will update this once patches are done. (1 update)
Optics:
On the graphics side, the game looks very good, altough it took a dedicated mid-to high end gaming pc more than two minutes to start, I think loading or compiling the intro was the issue.
I had no glitches or bugs with animations so far, and I am sure the attack animations will be improved as well, but those that are are ok to good. Game ran without any fps drops.
Shard mechanic:
really innovative, well implemented, I think you can say THAT makes the game the most interesting. Animations, interaction, all looking great and well done.
Interfact: Really good, intuitive, most information is well displayed.
Unit rooster overview: nice feature, but you really get frustrated once they all go suicide-hunting
Unit update buildings and updates:
nice features, reasonable, really useful and needed, some improvements are somewhat redundant, but this is early access after all.
The fortress:
good idea, especially the fortify option, but some adjustments are needed because it feels somewhat unimpressive to have a bassive castle
Building updates and general build animations:
like in the intro, very smooth and good looking. Seems really poished.
Fun factor (before massive frustration due to suiciders) was really high.
As with many games, I suppose there will be massive optimisations for hardware requirements during finalisation.

For the first chapter of this game I was thinking 'wow, this is Southern Gothic like I've never seen in a game before.' I loved its aesthetic, the sound design, the little hints of Lynchian weird, but I was blown away by what it becomes. This is a slow-paced game which oozes with atmosphere and you should stroll through it. There are almost no puzzles, just a linear path you can deviate from slightly and often discover little side stories which put a smile on my face. There are dialogue choices throughout pertaining to past and present, and whether or not they have real impact on the game, KRZ really succeeds at making you FEEL like they do. With each chapter it becomes something entirely new, expanding way beyond its initial setting into some seriously bizarre and utterly original locations, and tackles some profound themes with emotional depth.
In later chapters you will take control of other characters, at times choosing one leg of the journey and forfeiting another, and it's a testament to stellar writing and sound design that character models with no real facial features can be so emotionally evocative. The sentimental scenes don't feal overwrought, the political scenes don't feal preachy, and the meta-narrative doesn't get pretentious. The storytelling here is up there with the best of adventure games and I can't wait for the final chapter.
TL;DR
Slow-paced, story-rich with dialogue choices and minimal gameplay mechanics. Well worth your money if you want a slow ride through Gothic Americana with added interdimensional trips, socio-economic critique, stunning music and sound design, and characters you'll fall in love with

Note the date of this review before reading it: March 17, 2014.
A lot of people have complained about problems in this game, which primarily include matchmaking, lag, and balance issues.
Matchmaking - Yes, matchmaking is an enormous problem. You could very easily be queued up against people that have logged 200+ hours your first game. You could also be thrown into a one-sided game where the enemy is already sitting in your base. Why this is, not a lot of people know. You are ranked leagues in this game, and matchmaking tries to find a game that has people in it that average out to be in a league that is the same as yours or adjacent to it. Now this seems ideal, but if you were league 6, and league 1 player could queue up with a league 9 player and you could face them in a match. This does happen sometimes, and the problem certainly needs to be addressed.
Lag - Some hosts are very bad, and it makes competitive play obsolete in some cases. People overexaggerate this issue, however. All it normally does is result in an ability hitting you just barely outside of the range that it normally would.
Balance - Patches, however infrequent, have made the whole balance issue a lot better. Some characters are a lot easier to master and are better on some maps than others, but it all really does come down to skill. I've seen some of the "worst characters" carry teams.
These problems aside, I think the game is really fun. Excellent soundtrack, mostly a good community, and a neat gimmick to thrown into the MOBA genre. There aren't many characters yet, and none have been added in the 5 months I've been playing. If you get bored in MOBAs playing the same character, this game is NOT for you. However, if you want a relaxing little Saturday afternoon brawler MOBA to play with your friends, pick it up. It's addicting and fresh.

First off - it´s not a new game, and there are already plenty of in-depth-reviews out there, I guess.
If asked to briefly sum up my experience, I wouldn´t really know where to begin. Also, I´d have to ask myself if such an approach doesn´t spoil someone´s experience with the attempt to breach that surface, to "elevate" things from their sub-concious dream-like continuum that are so rarely verbalized in this game.
That´s what it feeds on: A lot of it is sub-text and imagination, non-linear and intuition (which is not surprising, given the sources of inspiration of the creators).
Characters are sketchy at first, but as your journey down this road continues, their dialogue options and choices become the bits that fill the empty spaces and before long it will feel like you actually inhabit these characters to some degree.
Everything remains vague while familiarity creeps in. One starts to wonder what lies behind some of the ghost-like appearances and the cursed world they inhabit.
Anyone with a tolerance or maybe even a soft spot for this kind of narrative should pick this up. I waited for a rather long time after I discovered Kentucky Route Zero, because you could read that the developers were taking so much time to complete the game. It would not have been the first game to fall short of hype and expectations...
However, fear not - even at this point it is well worth the money. Time well spent. I´m still playing it and haven´t had the time to take everything in, let alone decypher it with three acts completed. It may even be quite replayable.
Some more superficial remarks:
- The minimalistic visuals are carefully composed and very appealing
- Audio design is spot on - there is not one tableau or scene in this game where something really seems out of place or overbearing

What can I say about this beautiful game? It was a wonderful experience, and I'm almost sorry it had to end. If you want a traditional JRPG with a metric ton of world-building, then this is your game. The battle system is straightforward and simple, but is constructed such that there can be a lot of different ways to approach battles and construct a strategy to win them. The magic system, which consists of an orbment device that you place pieces of 'quartz' into slots in order to mix and match spells, is unique and fun. I got excited every time I was able to upgrade to a few new spells. Especially near the end when Kloe becomes an absolute powerhouse.
Speaking of the characters, you will fall in love with them in this game. It's why I played almost 90 hours (not including the 45 I put into the First Chapter). This has to be one of the longest JRPG's I've ever played, and there is a ton to do in-game. The sidequests almost always build character growth (except for the monster-extermination quests), but you don't have to do them. I recommend it though if you want to be strong enough at the end of the game. Back to the characters: they are charming, varied, and you will love following their journey. Estelle is a delight as the main character, and the way they built her closest relationships was fabulous.
Seriously, if you like old school JRPG's, intricate storylines, lots of world building, and lighthearted fun, you will love Trails SC.

First let me say I have played guitar on and off for over 15 years and never had the urge to learn songs by other bands.  I bought Rocksmith because I was hoping it would make me want to play more... and it did not disappoint.  Whether you are just starting out or have played for years, Rocksmith will keep the fire going.  The first day I played 4-5 hours straight, and I can't remember the last time I did that.
I always approached the guitar like an experiment; finding my own style and chord changes with little help from outside instruction.  But there is valuable knowledge in learning real songs because you learn new chords, different styles, and new ways to play.  The songs are already written, you just have to learn the changes and finger placement.
There is a plethora of training games that will keep the novice guitar/bass player interested, a riff repeater if you are having trouble with certain parts of a song, and 2 or 3 different parts to choose from for most of the songs (except songs like "I Can't Hear You" by the Dead Weather).
It comes with a nice variety of songs to start with, but the downloadable song library is a little thin.  They may have released more for the Rocksmith 2014 version.  In any case, this is an excellent game for anyone interested in learning guitar/bass or simply wanting to keep their skill level up.

Then even deeper in the game, more planes on land and in the air. And for the sake of higher scores, the job will pragmatically involve more non-real-life bug-solving e.g. redirecting 3 planes from landing on the same stupid runway, or stop that Concords from bumping into slow propellers in the front, or order your Corcord to steal that 1 second gap in the intersection and take off, etc. These will keep you busy enough and suddenly your game ended because planes have crashed in somewhere you neglected, or too many planes simply clogged the choking points, regardless of your best efforts. It is sometimes nonsense and mentally punishing, but you always enjoy it like your weekly high-level Sudoku and calls it a day.

It's time for a revised review to do this game justice. WARNING SPOILERS
Graphics: Decent. Some mapping errors which can be bothersome when searching for the secret rooms.
Music: Decent
Gameplay: It basically boils down to casting status ailment protection, buffing and beating the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of the enemies until they stop moving.
Spelling and usage of words: The language feels stilted. The dialog is sometimes cheesy. It's an JRPG, alright.
Characters: Decent. They are easy to distinguish yet I still can't remember their names. The only one I can remember is the villain and he shows up at the very end.
Story: The only strong point this game has besides the characters. Our heroes must save their homeland from a mysterious corruption that is slowly spreading and mutating animals and plants. The main villain needs more buildup to be effective. He just shows up after one of the party members sacrificed themselves to stop the corruption from spreading.
I would have given this game a recommendation if it hadn't been for the laziness that are the different endings.
Background information:
Our heroes must enter the corrupted highlands. Entering it without protection will give them an uncureable disease that lowers their stats and deals damage every turn.
The Highlands can only be entered twice. For the second visit, they need to visit a herbalist and get a second set of protection.
There exists the so-called "bail-out-token" that allows our characters to instantly flee from anywhere.
At the end of the highlands, our heroes find a lake that is the source of the corruption and spreads it.
The magician sacrifices herself and unleashes powerful magic to destroy the lake so the highlands can eventually return to normal and the corruption is stopped.
After this, our heroes meet Naltus, the villain that is shown on the titlescreen. He explains that due to our heroes destroying the lake, his people are finished since they need the corruption to survive.
So, where is the problem?
Good ending = Magician sacrifice -> Naltus Fight -> Good
Bad ending = Flee the highlands twice
There is no in-between and it doesn't matter, what you do.
Let's say I never fled the highlands, my magician has sacrificed herself and I instantly use the bail-out token or use it after I talked with Naltus. I have to visit the herbalist and go back. There is no "Let's go to our commander and tell him that we saved the day but that the villain is still out there."
There is no ending.
Let's say I fled the highlands once and I do it again right after the magician sacrificed herself. I get the bad ending where the magician who just sacrified herself SPEAKS to the captain and the corruption spreads!!
This makes no sense! HOW?!
The bail-out-token just shouldn't function to prevent this but it works so this is just disappointing.
Let us look at the conditions and how this could be used for different endings:
Arrived at the lake? Defeated Naltus? Visited the highlands twice?
Good ending one: Our heroes do everything
Good ending two-a: Our heroes destroy the lake but bail out and tell their boss that Naltus is still out there. The boss just sends professionals to deal with him.
Good ending two-b: Same as two-a, just that they wait out until Naltus dies because the corruption has stopped
Bad ending one: Our heroes just run away twice.
Bad ending two: Our heroes get defeated in the highlands, captured and mutate as the corruption spreads
Bad ending three: Our heroes die in the fight against Naltus
There is so much potential and this potential just wasn't put to use.
This negligence is the reason why I can't give this game a recommendation.

is the sixth release and a worthy ATC (Air Traffic Controller) RTS contender by
within the Airport Madness series of games and beyond.
Released in 2014, almost 3 years after the excellent Airport Madness 4, it raised the bar of the ATC simulation genre to a new high, mainly due to moving from the current fantasy style airports into real world examples, in addition to improving gameplay in almost every aspect. Here's why:
+ A mix of 12 real-world famous airports (5x USA, 5x Europe, 1x Alaska, 1x UAE)
+ Efficiency/performance meter to benchmark progression
+ Optional cloud cover for increased realism and difficulty level
+ The addition of window mode (at long last)
+ Progressive rankings and leaderboards (with increasing difficulty)
+ Steam achievements and trading cards
- Would have liked a broader mix of airports from other continents/countries
- Too many Concords thrown in the mix for my liking
- Not as challenging and with less diverse achievements than its predecessor (AM4)
- No custom scenarios/challenges/disasters to solve
- The window mode is not scalable (looks really small in a 4K VDU)
- No steam workshop integration or any kind of customisation
-----
TL;DR: Even though
is an overall improvement over Airport Madness 4, it's predecessor felt more complete and satisfying overall, perhaps due to all the extras it included. Still, AM:WE is as addictive and as stats show the most popular title of the series to-date, so a definitive thumbs up from me as well.
-----
PS: Perfect game achievement was accomplished in under 20 hrs, so more seasoned ATC players should be able to get it much faster than that.

An anime-based strategy board game that combines combat and card playing in competition to achieve a chosen goal and earn the highest level. And I use the term strategy loosely, you will depend on luck... ALOT. Seriously, I mean, ALOT. You could be right about to win and just constantly keep getting the worst rolls until someone else catches up and wins ahead of you. You could get stunned for turns on end because every 'Random KO' card that keeps getting played lands right on you for no particular reason. It wouldn't be such a big deal if games didn't take forever to complete, around 20-60 minutes a game. I mean, the RNG is a problem in almost any board game but this game appears to be atleast 70-80% luck, 15% strategy, and the rest just relying on the other players not having a vendetta against you.
Even through it's flaws though I still can't stop playing it. The characters are all engaging and you can sort of build your strategy by placing your own cards in the global deck. You can choose to focus on turn-locking players, design your cards for pure combat, or design your cards to gain more stars. All excellent ways to win as you can level up either by having stars or having combat wins.
This game truly shines in it's PvP area, which really seems like the only truly enjoyable part about this game. Playing in PvE is one of the most annoying things as it seems like everything is set up just to make the player lose and the AI win, even on normal. In PvP you'll still see players that seem to win every single roll, I've been beaten by players 15 times in a row even when I've had +5 stats and they had no buffs. Almost any game I've played I'll be right about to win and the entire cosmos will seem to turn against me to make sure there is no hope for me to win.  Just somehow it seems much more enjoyable when you atleast have other players having just as bad luck as you are.
3/5
I'm about to win and the boss comes over and one-shots me. As soon as I revive a random player uses a KO card, then when I revive I get hit by two damage cards and the boss comes back and finishes me off then proceeds to win the game. You either love or hate the random number generator...

There are some UI issues and gameplay frustrations, like the lack of a zooming-to-mouse cursor option, the lack of adversity for the first hour or so, the lack of factions (currently) and a few other things that I’ll be posting about on their forums when I’ve had more time with it, but these are all things that can be addressed in EA. I have faith based on what’s here already.

If you liked the game Majesty, you'll love this game. Stop reading this review and go buy Driftland. Right now.
I remember when Majesty 2 came out. I had such high hopes of a "newer" version of Majesty with deeper gameplay and better graphics. I drove 60 miles round trip to pick it up at my nearest EB. Unfortunately, what I got was a game that was kinda OK, but that had huge (to the point of extreme frustration) difficulty spikes from scenario to scenario (with no way of bypassing them). Even worse, it had no random map generator (which was one of the most replayable aspects of Majesty 1).
Driftland wasn't even on my radar and came out of the blue, but it really feels like the spiritual successor to Majesty 1 to me. The biggest point of comparison to Majesty is that you build structures (such as a Wizards Guild) & hire units, but the units act independently. To get them to do tasks for you (such as attack a certain creature or explore & clean out an area), you place "flags" with bounties to attract them into action at that location. That game mechanic is pretty unique and while it might sound convoluted or overly difficult, it really works very well.  It's nice to have my AI guys taking a little initiative and doing something beneficial for me instead of me needing to control their every movement for a change!  :)  The one downside, is that they will often fight to the death, but this has been discussed by the developer (in the forums) and they're already working on a mechanic to address that issue.
Driftland has a lot of features that Majesty did not. This is a multiple resource economy with gold, food, stone, wood, iron, etc., that requires you to build structures and to assign citizens to "farm" them. The land masses on the map are islands, floating in the air, that you have to use magic to pull closer to you and build a bridge/portal to be able to occupy/exploit the resources (an idea that I thought I'd really hate, but have grown to really like). There are other creatures in the game that you can defeat for their treasure stash or in the case of the giant birds in the game, you can take over their nests (which allows you to "tame" them, build them as units, and your warriors will independently mount them to become aerial units... Pretty darn cool!). The economics are somewhat of a balancing act of growing your population, growing your army, and collecting resources. It all works together very well. I could go on and on describing the game, but it has a relatively simple learning curve that's filled with discoveries and realizations. If you like this kind of game, you should go try it for yourself. I doubt you'll regret it.
At present, I'm only 7 hours in, but I have already gifted this game to a good friend. To me, Driftland is like a cross between Majesty and Civilization-lite. I know its early access and to some gamers (that have been burned before), that's like showing Dracula the Holy Cross. But to me, the game is already fun, the developers have been very responsive to posts, and I'm really looking forward to what this game can eventually become. Best of all, it's already scratching that Majesty itch that I've been waiting for years to scratch. Thanks for that alone, guys!

It is like fresh water in a desert, like a cup of coffe at the work after a 2 hours long boring♥♥♥♥♥meeting, you know it..
There were a lot of rpgs in the past few years, but this one brought back the feeling of a proper crpg like Baldurs Gate 2.

You also have a gravity ram ability, which is essentially a powerful headbutt that knocks back enemies and objects.  Still, guns are your primary defense against the alien life forms and most are fun to play with, each offering two unique attacks.
Capsized clocks in at only a few hours and offers Steam achievements, high resolution and several additional modes of play to mess around with once you finish the story.  There is gamepad support but it's not as accurate or easy to adjust to as the keyboard/mouse controls.

Chivalry offers a partial dream come true to the gamers who always wanted to fight against others with classic medieval swords and shields, plate armor outlook on both indoor and huge outdoor scenarios.
Gameplay - It has a straightforward gameplay mechanic with some tricky technicks which can be mastered only if you are quite aware of the basics and well practiced or examined those with others. Some battles against someone with the knowledge of these rare technicks (for example dodging attacks simply with looking away with the cursor etc.) can be really frustrating if we are not initiated with it.
The game offers countless of weapons for each class as you level up, but these merely change the status of yours in practice. There are classes which are seemingly overpowered against others (for example knight vs. archers), that's why it is needed to understand the mechanic this game has to take over the enemy in anykind of disadvantages you get in, and these are often focus and skill demanding.
The atmosphere of these battles are quite fun, giving both teams specific objectives to break down the opposing forces where of course the outcome is mainly based on the quality of the teammates, however if you are a gamer with good spirit and devotion many miracles can be done on the battlefield and sometimes this effort is righteously rewarded; which means you end up being the winner.
Graphics - The visuals are fantastic with no extra to offer but they are overall sufficient. The animation, movements are well made, the lightnings are realistic within a quite well detailed world.
Longevity: The game is simply designed to be fun and to offer great time for both friends and enemies, and even after a long run it can give you some good experience, but also many frustrating ones too.
Rating - 7/10

I've been addicted to this game and have been playing it nonstop over the past few weeks. With that in mind, I was compelled to write a review for it.
100% Orange Juice is a board game with characters from a number of Orange_Juice's other games like Suguri, QP Shooting, and Flying Red Barrel. It's a luck-based dice-rolling mayhem that's as entertaining as it is frustrating.
+ The art style is cute and makes for nice visuals, and there are some catchy tunes to go with it.
+ The characters have different attributes and hyper cards that make the game fun and unique.
+ The DLC/bonus characters have their own little niche yet do not make the game pay to win.
+ Playing online is quick and easy and doesn't have very many problems. Disconnects happen, but they're rare.
- It's heavily RNG based. Everything runs on dice rolls - from collecting stars to attacking opponents - which means that very little skill is involved. This will be a turnoff for some, but it also makes for very entertaining matches.
- Some rolls are rigged. This only applies to Tomomo's rolls in the last part of the campaign (where she is more likely to get 5's and 6's), but it is still a pain. Getting through the last chapters of the campaign (and Tomomo Hell) takes a long time as it is hard to defend against Tomomo's attacks or stop her from winning.
- The game is hard to pick up. You'll probably want to read the guide first before actually playing as you're thrown into the game without being told what happens. This is a rather big flaw, but, if you're able to look past it, you can enjoy the game.
100% Orange Juice has some flaws, but it's still worth getting if you've been wanting to play a fun board game with friends. If you don't like RNG-based games, then... this game is not for you.

Let me start with this: This game is essentially the Mario Party of the PC world, minus the mini-games. It's a very well balanced and addictive card and board game combination that has a relatively easy learning curve. I highly suggest you purchase the 4 pack and have fun with your friends as you're guaranteed to have a blast, especially if you're very competitive.
The controls for 100% Orange Juice are very simple. It's essentially a point and click dice rolling game. Controller support implementation would have been awesome, though I really don't mind it the way it is.  The music in this game is mostly upbeat and fun, though I would suggest putting on a Katamari playlist as it does tend to get repetitive after a few hours of gameplay. 100% Orange Juice has cutesy Fruitbat Factory Anime-style characters all around. There's some really cool paralax-ish scrolling backgrounds. It seems that the actual game board is floating or flying the entire time.
Campaign mode will have you ripping your hair out at times as Marie Poppo can oftentimes be cold and ruthless and luck definitely reigns over skill. If you can handle being bested by a pink haired, pudding loving lady this game's for you. In closing, the fact that you can unlock and purchase cards, customize your character, and play with anyone in the world on servers is an awesome addition that truly adds to the replay value to this game. Even if you're someone who's not into this type of animation/anime, I'm confident that you're bound to enjoy this game.

This is one where I wish steam had a neutral option.
Its a casual air traffic management game (not complex enough to be called a simulator).
What you get is 12 different airfields (and they do feel and play different from one another).  You manage landing, taxi, takeoffs, as well as speed and choosing which runways to use. The game uses 2D graphics, which frankly doesn't bother me one bit. The graphics do not have a negative impact on the gameplay and I find the retro feel to be cute.
The one big feature that is missing from the game is managing planes in the air circuit (aka traffic pattern for USA people), which was dissapointing.
Still, there's several modes you can play and 3 difficulty settings, which work well. Hard will prove challenging and its for those who really want to improve their multitasking skills. Easy offers a more relaxed and casual experience.
CONCLUSIONS:
I bought the game on sale for 5 euro and its not a bad price for it. I'd certainly reccomend it for this price.
However I feel cannot entirely reccomend getting it for the current full price of 10 euro. Don't get me wrong - the game is fun but doesn't have enough content to justify the normal price.

There are very obvious flaws with an RTS game that doesn't allow you to control units.
1. There are no orders. Instead there are goals. These goals reward money to the units that partake in them. Every unit for a goal costs 10 gold. Got an army of 60 units? Be prepared to spend 600 gold per goal.
2.  After each goal is fulfilled, the units will return home. Be prepared for half of your army to be running in the opposite direction while you are spamming the next goal.
3. You can't do attack goals on areas covered by fog of war. If your army doesn't move up enough, get ready to be annoyed.
4. Your army doesn't amass. In fact, they are going to trickle in while the defender kills them off one at a time. There is no way to stop this from happening right now.
5. Magic has limited range. You attack them? They'll be able to use magic. You won't.
6. What happens when you are on a very, very large map and two players are very far away from each other? Like on opposite corners of the map? Get ready  to get creative to try and get your army to their base. With limited magic range, you won't even be able to cast anti-fog of war magic to order your units to their base. You'll have to send out flyers to explore. After this, how are you going to get ground units to them? Well, you won't be able to get the islands close enough to even connect to their base because they will be out of range. You'll have to really get creative. I know that after around 20 minutes, I finally found a path that I could use to connect to the last player's base and take them out.
What happens if that last player doesn't develop enough? Get ready for a draw because they won't be able to attack you and you won't be able to attack them ;D.
I'm not going to mention quality of life things like the UI as this game is early access and those elements can be improved. These things I have mentioned are pretty core gameplay mechanics, which leads me to believe that this is a fatally flawed game.

Let's get the negatives out of the way first: Definitely needs some work, but that's what early access is for, isn't it?
Two things that stick out to me immediately: There should be the option to scale the UI so that you don't end up with tiny buttons, and there should be an option to not lock the mouse cursor into the window in windowed mode. As someone with rather specific needs out of a game, those particular options are important to have for me, and for accessibility in general.
It could also stand to have a pause button to allow you to place flags and such over a wide area, and to allow the player to think over their next move. It's entirely possible that there is such a button and I was simply unable to find it, though.
Now on to the positive things. This game is very polished for a game from a brand-new studio. The visuals are well-done, the intro sequence is impressive, and the interface is, while not the best I've ever seen, certainly easy to use and I'd have a hard time picking out specific improvements that could be made (though I probably would find my grievances with it after playing for a while longer; but then, any UI is going to have its annoying quirks).
The one annoyance I had is that while you have to right click on an island to place a flag, if you want to place a flag on a unit (e.g. to order an attack), you have to _left_ click on the unit. I do hope these will be separate settings when the control config is implemented (you can't change controls at the moment, though there is a space in the options for it).
All in all, it's a well-polished, if unfinished, fantasy RTS. What's not to like? Fantasy themed games like this are rare.
------
On to a few other thoughts, of possible improvements: The selection of races to play as feels a little limited. Humans, dark elves, elves, and dwarves (with the latter two being locked at present). I'd like to see a little more variety, particularly in the non-humanoid area. It's a fantasy game; cat-people and lizard-people are practically mandatory! More seriously, some other less-humanoid playable species would be nice. Perhaps a civilization of golems left over from the ancient war that shattered the world, or a varied alliance of beastmen races, from kobolds to lizardfolk to gryphons and centaurs, like Master of Magic had.
Some more diversity in the existing races would be nice as well. I've been noticing lately just how many games have all white people, and I think some variety in the existing humanoid races would be good to see. Personally, I think the way to do this might be to implement sub-races (think how TES has Nords, Bretons, and Redguards, all of whom are human), or to simply give a random skin color to each unit (or random fur color, scale color, etc, if you add non-humanoid races to the game).

It's difficult to articulate why I like this game, if you can even call it a game in the traditional sense.  It's more like a graphic novel that allows you to choose the dialogue, or a text adventure with moving pictures.
I've read it described as a ghost story, where there is always a vague sense of forboding and mystery.  Whatever it is, it's very unique and original.  It focuses heavily on cinematography, character development, and a soundtrack that matches the minimilast aestetics of the environment and character profiles.
The story follows a growing variety of characters who find themselves dealing with difficult situations.  As one of the creator's said, its not a game about people who are in power, but people who have been disempowered by circumstances.  You start out as a tired, old truck driver looking for directions to the mysterious highway called the Zero.  However, the game's narrative doesn't take place through the eyes of just one character.  The controls seamlessly switch from one player to another.
The game's characters stay true to the story the creators are telling.  Instead of having absolute control of where your characters go and what they do, you simply choose what they're thinking about while they're doing it.  You begin to surrender to the storytellers, and just accept the bizarre environments and directions they take you in.  Additionally, the conversations feel more natural than compared to other games.  That although you have the option to select the dialogue, it always progresses the conversation forward, as opposed to the hub and spoke dialogue options you typically see in RPG's, where once you've depleted a path of dialogue it returns to the root phrase or sentence.
I skimmed through a review on The Guardian
that describes the game pretty well.  "This game induces a mood that is rare and hard to describe: a feeling of unhurried and joyful uncertainty, of being in the hands of master storytellers and surrendering to whatever they might have to offer."
Unfortunately, the pace of the development matches the pace of the game. Although you receive access to all episodes when they are released for the retail price of $24.99, it's hard to justify that price for what is currently available.  I bought it on sale for $12.49 and I'm totally cool with that.  It took me almost 5 hours to complete I-III, and played together they can still give you the feel of a full game.  If V ever comes out it will just be a nice bonus.

I bought this game a year or two ago on a whim based on its positive reviews. I thought “finally, a game that will have a great visual aspect, amazing soundtrack and an enthralling story.” However, for the most part I was disappointed, but I would still like to give this game a thumbs up, and here’s why.
Act 1 – 3: I played the first three acts all in one go. I didn’t actually realise that this was a five-part game until I had finished act 3, but that’s my error for not reading the description thoroughly. The first three acts were pointless, to say the least. You are presented with the idea that you are a guy who works at an antique store, having to make one finally delivery to a mysterious address. The whole game supposedly revolves around this, however after act one, the story gets lost, and you begin meandering between places full of loosely connected stories that don’t make any sense. This is the aspect that I hated about the game. I thought that there would be some interesting depth to this game, but instead I got a game created by people who were high on weed. But I persevered. I started to accept that this game wasn’t going to give me any answers and that it was absolute madness, but that didn’t mean that I liked it any more.
Act 4: That was until Act 4, however. This Act is probably the least gamey of them all, but is the one I enjoyed the most. I would describe it sort of like the calm before the storm where not much happened, but you felt relaxed and pleased. What this act delivered on (something that had been lacking for the most part) was story. This act saw you mostly travelling down a river on a boat, stopping off at different places along the way. These stops are where the story actually came. Although yes, some of them were ridiculous, I actually enjoyed them. The whole thing reminded me of the podcast “The Lighthouse Painting.” The whole act was just people telling their story, why they live along the river, why the river is so strange etc. and it was something that I liked. Beyond that it actually started to develop the characters. We saw a deeper connection between Junebug and Johnny, and we felt Shannon’s worry over her sister. I honestly felt that this was the best act by far, and I actually can’t wait to play the next one.
If the developers do the next act right, then my attitude towards this game could actually improve for the better. Therefore, I would definitely recommend this game. But be warned. If you want to play an actual game, don’t buy this, perhaps go for Undertale. But, if you want a unique experience, then this is definitely worth your while, just maybe get this on sale though and you’ll probably fell a lot better about your purchase.
So, while I’m waiting for Act 5 to come out (please let it be good), I’m think I might play a little bit of Hotline Miami 2.
