Gameplay:
You play as a land-holding individual (The game only let you play as European feudal lord when it first came out, but now you can play as other characters suchs as nomad, tribal leaders and such), and the goal of the game is the survival of your family name until 1453 AD. Nothing is off-limit when it comes to survival. While you are likely to survive by being content as a minor figure in the world, your chance of survival greatly increases as you wage war, forming alliance through marriage, plotting the demise of your rivals, and use everything to your advantage, even yourself.
The game gives you plenty of tools to achieve your goal, and it also throws countless monkey wrenches to destroy your scheme. While the game could get slow from plotting all the action, it speeds up ones you, or your rivals are ready to make the move, so savor those slow moments.
Music & Sound: Since I mentioned you will be waiting a lot before you make your move, you'll be hearing a lot of those. There are many good tracks even without the DLCs, and the DLC tracks just gives you more flavor as you move out of Europe.
Graphic: Good enough. You can see where you are going, and you can see what your character looks like. It is interesting to see the world changes itself in different seasons, and how your character grow old. It's the little flavors in the game that makes the graphic, not the shiny trinkets.
Replayability: There are thousands of characters to choose from, with different culture, religion, regional interest, potential disaster to face. You will be well into hundreds of hours and still not understand the game fully. Plus, they are still releasing new DLCs to enrich the game experience.
Do I recommend it? Oh yes. A game that mends history and strategy together will always get a yes from me.

First off: I played this game for countless hours on CD before buying it on steam.
The third of title in the S.T.A.L.K.E.R series, the game doesn't offer as much freedom as the Shadow of Chernobyl, but is a much more polished and straight-forward title. The story is not as open, there aren't as many factions, but what's there, works far better without mods than it does with its predecessor.
It's therefore not a bad idea – if you don't mind a few spoilers – to start your journey into the series with this one.
I don't think I need to tell you about the general setting, it's already well explained in the store-page and by other reviews.
What I want to tell you about instead, is my personal experience and the memories I've shared with this game:
There are few games that are this unsettling on an almost primal level. I was never a fan of the Fallout-esque style of post-apocalypse and neither of stuff like Mad Max. I don't know if it's the eastern European Atmosphere, or the way everything seems so dire, but something in the Stalker series (not writing the proper name anymore – ♥♥♥♥ dots!) just tickles me in the right places.
I believe there's really a sense of venture, pioneering into a dark place, that the Stalker series does so well. Coupled with an eastern European attitude towards things (if something works, it works, while the german engineer would get one aneurysm after another) that puts a glimmer of hope across the entire fictious zone. In the deep darkness of it, there's a sense of comfort. Characters may seem opportunistic (most of them are, actually) and you shouldn't trust anyone, but again – somehow I can't help but build a deep feeling of sympathy for each and every one of them.
To sum it up: No rose tinted glasses, you'll see visages of monsters, people and even yourself growing accustomed to this harsh world, but everyone is bonded by the sentiment of terror towards the things even worse – the oines you're not able to see.
So, travel into the zone, but be warned: It might not stay a venture, but becom a second home.

100% OJ is an anime boardgame where you select a character and move around a board attempting to accomplish enough achievements to win the game. You accomplish achievements, which you set at various placed around the board, and then go about accomplishing them by winning fights and collecting stars. Each square on the board has an event tied to it: draw a card, gets stars, fight, random movement, etc, all which are accomplished by dice rolls. Each time it's your turn you can select to play a card, if you have one or if it's applicable, or move (by rolling). When you get into a fight you have four stats (attack, defense, evade, and hit points) that modify your dice rolls (minimum of 1), each fight allows you to hit once and then decide whether to defend or evade you opponents attack. The person who started the fight attacks first. You win the fight if you knock your opponent to 0 HP, which also nets you some of their stars. You can have direct conflict with other players. If you get knocked out by your HP going to zero you then have to spend each subsequent turns rolling the requisite number to be revived, luckily it gets easier every turn.
This is game is completely random in nature, meaning it takes no skill to play it - or another way of saying it: this game plays you. There are multiple campaigns and multiplayer to contend with if this is your style of game. I could barely handle playing a single game, and I like boardgames. It just seemed to drag on and there isn't much variety and no skill involved in playing it.
Things I recommend you do if you decide this is the game for you: Increase how fast your opponents turn plays out. Things devlopers should have done: each opponents unique color associated with their banner should be flashed across the screen while it's their turn, instead of the same color for each character. The problem being that the pictures look close enough alike (except for the single boy) that I spent my time trying to figure out which character was who. Eventually I just stopped caring and waited for the round options to pause.
This might appeal to people who like anime themed boardgames, but to me it was like trying to play a slightly more complicated Shoots & Ladders. Pass on this one. I got this game as part of a Humble Bundle.

I’ll be brief as this is a game that just kept getting better with time. But I’ll only talk about what they have now and not the past.
This is an ARPG (In my opinion) with increasingly more as story and gameplay come more and more with each patch. It is also a free game that allows you to get everything just through sheer grinding and dedication. Allowing you to use both Keyboard and Controller with ease. You are called the Tenno. A mystical race of lost warriors from the Orokin era that use an exo-armor called a Warframe. You are guided by a mysterious person known only as the Lotus (aka Space Mom), flying around space with your custom Orbiter ship and the talkative Ordis (Cehpalon…like an onboard computer). Currently you can choose up to 34 Warframes and counting, along with many more Primary, Secondary, and Melee weapons. You are capable of picking a companion ranging from Sentinels (Hovering robot), Kubrows (Space Dog), Kavats (Space Cats). Of course, but not least you are also able to loadout an all-purpose suit for battles in space known as an Archwings with their own sets of weapons and gear. Of course, these pieces of equipment have levels reaching to a max of 30. Allowing you to insert mods that allow beneficial effects for you and allies, or detrimental for foes. Some of the more powerful weapons can only be unlocked through Mastery Rank, a system based off each unique equipment you fully level up once.
You plan attacks using the star chart that has 16 accessible planets along with the Orokin Derelict and of course, the lovely Clan Dojo (Guild home base). From here nodes in each of the areas that you have selected will depict what type of mission is available, the faction you will be fighting, level of enemy forces, and a little picture of the tile set (map type) you will be fighting in. The missions can be anything from Exterminate (Classic annihilation of enemies), Capture (Find enemy HVT), Mobile Defense (Hacking various computers and protecting them), etc. Currently if I’m not mistaken, there are 19 such missions that you can encounter. The lore and story behind the game is wonderful. Don’t get me wrong, it was somewhat blain in the beginning, but they have added to the game and continually doing more in that aspect. We even got our first open world area instead of the somewhat close room to room maps we are all use to.
The mechanics to the game are not hard to employ for the first time and even at mastering it with new tricks. You can roll, flip, slide, wall climb and run (Miss the old one), vault off people, double jump, zipline, etc. Wonderful things you thought a space ninja could do and a bit more.
All in all, I love this game it is masterfully done. Of course, not everything was right in the beginning and elements were missing but hey, they came through and kept adding more and more. Making an old favorite a mainstay. I didn’t mention anything about the graphics so in short, takes my breath away. Bloom is sometimes a bit much, but you can always adjust lol. Test it out for yourself and you can see a bit of why I recommend this game to the community. Hope this helps some.

I think the first thing I should mention is the enormous Elephant in the room, Denuvo DRM, yes it does include it, and it seriously fudging sucks, Sega are cretins for forcing this upon us, and if this is enough to warrant a boycot in your eyes then please do so.
Having said that though, if you do that, you're missing out on one of the greatest Sonic games since Sonic Generations, and in my honest opinion, this is so much better it's not even funny.
The soundtrack is glorious, including some of my favourite pieces from past games, Chemical Plant? Oh yes please. Green Hill? Absolutely devine. But it doesn't just include classics, it has some new tracks, which, while they don't quite have that punch of the classics, they're still bloody brilliant, the soundtrack alone is worth the price of admission.
But the real meat of a Sonic game is how it plays, and in this regard, it's perfect, the characters all move exactly as they're supposed to, this is no Sonic 4, this is proper 2D Sonic, with razor sharp movement, fast gameplay and the kind of precision that you'd expect from a laser, Christian Whitehead and the rest of his team have done a phenominal job in this regard, it plays like all the best parts of Sonic 2 and S3&K, and I can't think of any praise higher than that.
In regards to bugs, I have had exactly one, I managed to get stuck in a piece of scenery in Act 1 of Titanic Monarch Zone, but other than that, the game has been rock solid, and while YMMV in this, I feel confident in saying that this game is Sega's most stable release in at least a decade, perhaps even 2.
The only criticsms I can lay at the game aside from the Denuvo nonsense is the level design has some weak areas, some of the levels don't flow quite as nicely as they should, for example Green Hill has been reimagined, and includes some new areas that really slow Sonic down , and jar badly with my memories of Green Hill, but I would imagine that once you get used to the level design and find optimal routes, this will cease to be an issue, but it is still something to be aware of, the other criticsm I have is that some of the levels are very busy, too busy in fact, and seeing exactly what is and isn't ground you can run on, and spotting enemies can get frustrating at times.
If you're expecting a long game, deep story and more than just running, jumping and collecting rings and Emeralds, then sorry, you've come to the wrong place, but if you really want classic Sonic and a proper sequel to S3&K, then you'll feel right at home, the is everything I have wanted from a Sonic game since S3&K, and while it does have its issues, it's a glorious comeback for the blue blur.
All I hope is that Sega will patch Denuvo out, because for me, that is the only sticking point, it shouldn't be included, we have Steam for DRM, legitimate buyers shouldn't be punished with more DRM, especially as draconian as Denuvo is.
I think that I'll be spending the next 25 years playing Sonic Mania, just as I did with Sonic 2, and if that doesn't tell you just how much I love this game despite its flaws, then nothing else will, it's a gorgeous, fast paced blast from the past, and takes me back to my childhood, and that was what I wanted from Sonic, and that is what I got today, and I couldn't be happier.
P.S. Tails' animations are absolutely adorable, seriously, he is so cute.
Edit!
Super Tails is available in the game! I am incredibly happy about that, although he doesn't have his flickies with him, which has nerfed his power considerably, although it's been long enough without Super Tails in a Sonic Game that I'm happy that he was even included in the first place.

Disclaimer: I have not used every character, largely sticking with supports (because none of my friends know how to take one for the team) so I feel like this can only be viewed as a "first impression" review. Also, I was not paid for this review.
My take aways are this, for a Early Access title, this seems very polished, but not without a few bits that aren't quite shiny yet. This game is very much so strategic/tactical and you have to make decisions in a fairly short amount of time, so if you are not competent at/do not enjoy "He'll think that I think that he will do this", then this game is very much so a pass. For examle: one of my first games in PvP, my whole team unloaded our ultimates into the area the enemy was, only for every one of them to teleport out of range and then destroy us next turn, largely because we chose to play this as a straight team deathmatch instead of what the game actually is.
The game suffers, currently, from a slightly below average playerbase, or at least it feels like it. I've matched up with the same guys a time or two and wait times are basically on par with Paragon wait times, despite there being 2 fewer people per match in comparison. This is, of course, anecdotal, and also something to be expected of an early access title. Also along the lines of matchmaking, the game is currently not above putting you on a team of one tank and three supports if you are solo-queueing, so be warned on that front. The game is fun so far, I've never really felt cheated, and I always want to play one more round, especially after a loss. Speaking of losses, the game is fairly balanced. I've never been on the giving nor receiving end of a blowout, but as player skill increases a meta is bound to pop up. Going back to "cheated" really quick, though, there has been a time or two when I have queue'd up my "GTFO" ability because I knew a gank was incoming, and ended up not actually using it when it was supposed to...resulting in my untimely death. HOWEVER: This is a bug, not a feature, so I do not blame the game for those instances, but rather the development cycle.
The combat is just, simply, fun. It doesn't feel forced, every character feels like they carry a justifiable amount of weight (I have, as a support, often seen myself as participating in every kill, sometimes landing the killing blow), and you can augment your character's abilities to create a variety of builds. The abilities are also all very much so as colorful as the characters, or at least they fit very well within the character's (aka, Freelancer) design and theme. My current favorite is Dr. Finn as a Naga-esque fish guy who squirts water around and shoots eels at his opponents, which totally feels right.
All in all, this is a beautiful game with a good sense of humor, fairly balanced characters, and a community that wants the game to thrive. With the current sale going on and the fact that being a founder guarantees you every character they will release for the game ever, I think the $15 price tag is more than worth it, and I would feel the same for the standard $20 it normally runs.

So, I finally got around to playing Moribund with another 3 friends and I'll just summarize this review in 3 words; Fun, Exciting, Bloody.
It may feel redundant to say this, but these games reveal the depth and complexity of their gameplay once people familiarize themselves with the controls and start acting smart about that first place. Since this is an early Alpha we had the winner not pay for their order-out dinner which gave all of us the incentive to become competitive. Boy, did we enjoy ourselves.
On the graphics department, the background landscapes are gorgeous and level design is up there with the best of the indie industry. As others have said, model visuals could stand a bit more so as to have more character, but it is no eyesore by any means. The gore is satisfying from the first to the last drop of blood and the ragdoll system is functioning as it should. Nothing could be more awesome than nailing the upper torso of your friend to a wall while he was dropping from a ledge.
On the sound department, the game is accompanied at all times with a few background beats that don't seem to tire (though to be fair, playing with friends always seems to drain everything else but the frantic screams and flurries of "insults"). Pretty good loops overall. The Ambient sounds of the game are truly spot on as well, giving off a sense of dread, so you don't want to try if the door smashing on the ground will pulverise you or not. It will. The sound makes sure you understand that.
The voice acting is functional at its worst and superb at its finest. Some of the lines will have you laughing at your friends face and in some cases mimicking the characters to bring further shame to your friends' skills. There are 1-2 characters that could use a redo, but hey, it's an alpha. And for the standards of an Alpha, this is more than just fine.
I will try and keep it simple in the gameplay department. Depending on the competition and how quick of a learning group your friends are, this can have you playing for days on end. We promised we'd only play for 20 minutes or so and we couldn't get off our chairs. It's addicting because of the number of ways you can outsmart your opponents. One has to play the game to understand what I'm ranting about here, but there truly is so much you can do to achieve victory in a wild "cat vs dog vs cat" hunt, where even retreating can turn into a sudden offensive. It's simple, easy even to pick up and be able to play, but mastering it takes practice and a lot of joyful dismemberment experimentation on your friends' favourite characters.
For the current pricing and the fact that this is an Alpha, this is a definite have for friend gatherings.

For an Early Access game, Moribund is at a complete state regarding its core gameplay mode. The content provided is more than enough to have fun with your friends, especially regarding the available levels. Moreover, I didn't encounter any bugs affecting the experience.
Regarding gameplay, you may need 10 minutes to get a good grasp of the game. Trying to escape by pressing continuously the A button is really rewarding when accomplished, but also infuriating if you are the executioner, which helps build a competitive atmosphere with your friends, and scream eventually in their faces. One of the most well done aspects of the game, is the level design. You can ambush or escape using multiple routes, while the traps are well thought out and add to the gameplay.
It would be nice if the character's visual appearance popped out more. Some of the voice overs may need more work. I would like to see in the future team battles, more levels and traps.

Subject your bridge to the tests required and if it succeeds, you win! Sounds easy right? WRONG. This game poses a formidable challenge for those architecturally ignorant. Even if you know a great deal about architecture, the physics engine will stop you in your tracks. With inconsistent performances you never know if your bridge will really work. That being said, Bridge Project is still a good time and does a good job of being a fun game. The ambient music does not get repetitive easily and there are enough puzzles to keep a person busy for several hours. Pick it up if you enjoy puzzle games that require a building aspect, but only on sale. 7/10

Devil Daggers is an extremely pure gaming experience. The core game design is fairly similar to a classic arcade game - there is no way to progress except by learning the patterns and getting better at dealing with them. When you die, you start over. There's no "level 2" to reach, no checkpoints, no continues. Play until you lose, then try again from the beginning.
The game itself has the appearance of a mid-90s FPS, and all of the mechanics are implemented exceptionally well. Movement and shooting feels great, enemies have interesting swarming behavior, and the sound design is incredible. Each enemy type makes a unique sound, and with the positional audio you can often know exactly what enemies are present and where they are without even needing to see them.
Highly recommended for anyone that enjoys fast-paced FPSes and playing a game solely for the sake of improving at it. And if you can get some friends to play, competing with them on the leaderboards can be a lot of fun (especially since you can watch each other's replays).

Call of Pripyat is the best game in the franchise. I think it is by far the most polished game out of the three, you can tell that developers took what they learned from making the first two and used that experience to make the ultimate Stalker experience. It’s the only game in the franchise where I felt compelled to do the side missions, mainly because of how good the ui is compared to the other two, I was able to navigate through the menus much easier and track each quest I was doing easier too.  The open world feels alive no matter where you are, you could be on the left side of the map but you feel like there is stuff going on the right side of the map without you even being there unlike most other open world games where it feels like the world is waiting for you. They did add repairing and upgrading weapons and armor in Clear Sky but it feels much more refined, thought out and balanced in this game making it a real addition and improvement to the series. The gunplay feels the most refined out of all three games, the difficulty on master feels balanced again which it wasn’t on Clear Sky. The first few hours of the game is great which it wasn’t in the other two, it was usually very frustrating because you were so weak and were not able to hit anything with your weak weapons but in Call of Pripyat you are able to obtain a very reliable inventory of weapons by just doing a few side missions in the starting area. The side missions also offer up a bit of variety to the game and also some small side stories that are cool to experience that have no ties to the main story, they are pretty well executed overall. The story is the most simplistic out of the three, I was never found the story to be a very strong aspect of the franchise so I was ok with the story being very minimal in this game. The only negative I can think of in this game is the travelling between locations can get pretty boring at times especially compared to other games like fallout where you can listen to a radio while travelling to keep you occupied or other open world games where you can use a vehicle or a mount to get around. Looking at the series as a whole now it feels like Shadow of Chornobyl was the main story while Clear Sky and Call of Pripyat were the prologue and epilogue which I think is interesting. I love this franchise overall and like I said in my Shadow of Chornobyl review, mods are definitely not needed.

Conan Exiles is a decent game, but it is no where near ready for launch in May 2018, as it suffers from numerous bugs, is very grindy, lacks a lot of content, has a finicky modding system, has a bad initial start and it lacks a ton of character creation options. I like the game, and overall enjoy it, but I wouldn't recommend it either, for the below reasons:
1. Lack of Character Creation Options = The game uses a specific color picker system, and more often than not, it will not have the color you want to choose; I like to play as golden blonde or ruby red female characters, and there isn't any good colors for these. It would make a lot more sense if the developers implemented a RGB color picker, that allowed the player to finetune what color they wanted, rather than use specific preset colors. Next, the game offers a decent number of options for modifying the players face, and I did find that it was easy to create a decent looking face for my character, so I applaud the developers for that. However, the game has very few options for modifying the rest of your body. There is a bust option for females and groin option for males, there is a muscle physique option and a height option; that is it. The issue I have with the lack of options here is that, the game comes with an impressive b00b, butt, pen1s, and leg jiggle physics system, yet, only allows for a b00b/pen1s slider. The game really does need a hip slider, a butt slider, an arm slider and a leg slider. The physique option only modifies the texture applied to the skin, rather than actually making the arms/legs appear thicker and more muscled; personally I'd rather have this physique slider broken up into multiple sliders, as I like the muscle texture for the belly and legs but not so much for the back or butt or arms. For a game that has good looking characters, pretty good graphics, reliable framerate and body physics, having a more robust character creator is a must!
2. Overall, I like the idea of being left for dead in the middle of nowhere, in a blistering hot desert, butt naked; left to fend for yourself and its up to you whether you want to endure and survive or not. I applaud the developers for having the start of the game in this matter, as I really like it. What I don't like however is that there was a waterskin at the very start, that I missed several times, because its out of the way and when you hover your cursor over it, you don't get a prompt to pick it up... and thus I ignored it. Another reason the start of the game isn't very good is that, the game doesn't tell you anywhere that the "Journey" tab will help to walk the player through the initial parts of the game and help them to avoid frustrating deaths. Problem is, I had to go through many frustrating deaths, before I realized the Journey was there to help me avoid those deaths. Finally, there are no prompts telling you that hitting "E" (for keyboards) will grab rocks, branches, and shrubs off the ground to get your initial crafting resources needed to make the most basic of equipment. The developers need to address these points, to avoid having new players give up before actually getting into the game.
3. The game lacks a lot of content, in terms of clothing, armor, and optional cosmetics. In character creation, you can apply makeup to the eyes (eyeshadow) and makeup to the lips (lipstick?), but, there could be potential for so much more. Things like warpaint, in addition to makeup (rather than you have to choose one or the other), scars, freckles, body piercings, tattoos, etc... As for clothing or armor, I literally ran around in the same basic clothing for the first 3 hours of gameplay, and couldn't craft anything better. Maybe I missed something, somewhere, but after crafting the Armorers Workbench, I didn't get any new recipes, and thus was stuck with what I had.
4. The grind is pretty harsh; I'm used to playing grindy games, and this is up there in terms of grind (somewhere between Diablo 3 grind and World of Warcraft grind). It takes a long time to gain a level, and the rewards at level up aren't super great, particularly as it is often very unclear what each attribute does. Plus, it takes a long time to gather specific resources, particularly hide; there are numerous little turtles about that give between 2-4 each, but larger creatures like a crocodile or the big turtles, don't get significantly more hide to compensate for their difficulty. Thus, it means it will take a while to craft even the simplest upgrades or build workbenches.
5. As for bugs, I have a lot of trouble with the combat system. Hit detection always feels off, and weapons that state they have extra range, don't really have extra range. Enemies don't appear to ever get winded, have unlimited ammo for their bows, and hardly get stunned from rebounding off your shield. Plus, I've never seen an AI with a shield actually block with it. Falling damage seems to be too high and a slight drop can kill you. The climbing system will often be about to pull you up and onto the above surface and then, fail, and you fall back down.
6. Finally the modding system is quite finicky. You have to fully launch the entire game to access the mod menu and then any adding or removing of mods forces you to restart the game completely. As it takes me about a minute to launch the game, this gets really annoying, real fast, when you have to troubleshoot conflicts. It would be so much better to have a mod launcher outside of the game, that could be used to load or unload mods. As for the mods themselves, there doesn't appear to be a way to merge two mods together that modify the same thing. For example, with the aforementioned lack of colors, I found a mod that gives Golden blonde hair and not much else, but then another mod that gives a few new character options, but doesn't have Golden blonde. So, as I want to play a Golden blonde character, I have to choose between the mods, rather than merge them together... like Wrye Bash in Elder Scrolls, or ScriptMerger for Witcher 3; yes those are modder built utilities, but still. To make mods you need to use the UE4 DevKit, which can be quite daunting for mod makers and if you having build issues with the mod, it can be very hard to troubleshoot those problems too.
I think if the developers get their stuff in order, and address the above issues, then the game might be ready for May. But,  as I've seen in general discussions on the forums for the past several months, that several of the above things I mention have been suggested a lot (particularly a booty slider), I doubt that the game will be ready for May. Perhaps I'll be wrong. If they end up fixing the issues I've had and add in a variety of content for cosmetics and character creation as well as improve the start of the game, I could easily see myself giving the game a glowing positive recommendation. Until then, it will remain not recommended.

At the time of this review I got about 33hrs on the clock. I've played other truck sims in the past, starting with Hard Truck and Hard Truck 2 way in the day, soldiered on with whole 18 Wheels of Steel set and both ETS games. This being the latest in the whole set is most disappointing to me to be honest.
The thing is, since the 18WoS:ALH I feel like the series is moving backward. It's true we get larger and more detailed maps, licensed trucks, better graphics and sound, but core gameplay is moving backward with every new game. Let me point out the things that bother me:
So, in 10 years time since 18:WoS: American Long Haul we got a game that is prettier, has a tool for making pictures and regressed in gameplay to the turn of the century. I still kinda enjoy it, but I just can't recommend it. It's a glitter covered shell of what the 18WoS games used to be.
UPDATE: Since many people in the comments are pointing out that "there are mods!" I think I need to address this here. Mostly because I'm bored of repeating this in the comments.
I know there are mods. I know mods can do many things with the base game (more trucks, more accessories, bigger map and whatever). Thing is, when I bought the game there were no mods installed. To be honest, I visited Steam workshop after about an hour or two into the game, because it felt incredibly empty. 4 trucks, few AI traffic cars, few options to customize a truck. I then wasted another hour or two picking through workshop for few decent mods that weren't paint-jobs. Only then the game got some more content. Content that the developers didn't put in there. Now I know that there are many other sites with various mods for ATS, but the first wall I got was "for version x.xx". So, every time a game gets an update and the mod doesn't I'm expecting trouble and if there are trouble I'm expected to dig through the mods to find the one's busted and update or disable it. Definitely NOT the experience I paid for. The second wall was that many trucks don’t look on par with SCS-made trucks. I know there are people who don’t care about it, who are able to spend 5 hours fixing stuff so they can play for another 5 hours, well I’m not one of those and I know I’m not alone.
Another thing to point out it, the game was released in Feb of 2016, so as I’m writing this it’s out for almost 2 years. At no point in that run it was marketed as an “early access” sort of thing. So every argument of “it’s being made” is invalid. It’s done and finished, just still supported. There’s a difference.
Lastly, like I pointed out in my original post, I know all previous 18WoS games had made-up truck makers, but had a lot more of them as a result. And I’d rather have 30 detailed and polished trucks made by devs and a mod to swap the logos for original ones (as I had in ALH and PttM) than 4 trucks with license.

American Truck Simulator is by far one of the best driving simulators on the Steam market, with a low price. The minimum system requirements SCS states are not really what you're gonna need. I ran this game on my ancient laptop that couldn't watch YouTube videos without lagging. All I had to do was turn the graphics settings down to the lowest level. The amount of options to customize in this game is insane. You can drive your semi truck like an F1 car and turn your brake sensitivity all the way up and your speed limiter off, or drive like a sane person with Trailer Stability and Advanced Couplings. The 4 states this game has are incredibly detailed, and take up about 8 GB of my storage (but I have stacks on stacks of mods, so I wouldn't consider my storage space the most accurate). The driving is amazingly realistic and has controller support and wheel support, so you can drive a big rig like my crazy neighbor does. The variety of trailers and jobs you can take are insane. It's so detailed that they include how much you'll get paid per mile. There are around 50 profile pictures to choose from, all very different. It's not like it's one guy at different angles. Graphics are amazing when turned up and if you have graphics mods installed. The engine sounds are pretty realistic for trucks nowadays, but if you want that deep-tone diesel with the high-pitched supercharger, just go grab a sound pack off the steam workshop. You can install trucks to drive if the trucks included in the regular game don't suit you. You can drive anything from a Scot to a Volvo. Someone has ought to have made a tesla semi truck for ATS by now, not sure though. As for multiplayer, there is a online version of the game, found at
(it isn't always updated right after an ATS update occurs, it takes a couple of days to hit). Multiplayer doesn't allow any mods except for ones verified by TMP staff, so nobody can cheat on online. The economy in-game is pretty realistic, there's a bank that allows you to take out loans and there is a cap on how many loans you can have, measured in money. You can customize your truck almost endlessly. Damage isn't all that good,  and there's no visual on damage, but engine malfunctions happen and happen more frequently when you accumulate more damage, which you can fix by going to a service station or getting towed to one and paying like $1,000. $3,000-5,000 in the middle of nowhere.
If you don't own this game and you enjoy driving simulators, I suggest you buy this game.
I've accumulated almost 600 hours on it at the time of writing this comment, and I still have schoolwork & making money to focus on. If that doesn't describe how good of a game this is, I don't know what will.

Okay, let me start this off by saying I highly prefer SoC over CoP. The reason being is quite simple:
In Shadows of Chernobyl, you are a Stalker trying to make their way through the Zone with a simple task: To kill Strelok. If you want to, you can completely ignore the story and just carve out your own path doing Stalker-like things. On top of that, the Zone herself is fairly dangerous and desolate, and in an odd way, fairly beautiful as a result. However, in Call of Pripyat, you're no Stalker. You're military. You know, those guys forcing Loners to pay just to pass through Cordon without getting shot. You're -pretending- to be a Stalker just so you can safely find out what happened to some downed helicopters, and that honestly ruined the experience for me right off the bat.
I really tried to like this game since it's still a S.T.A.L.K.E.R title, but that one little fact really soured the milk. Maybe I'm being petty, but after fighting against the military and seeing my fellow Loners get gunned down, I can't just switch sides. Especially since I prefer to role play while spending a few hours in this setting. And yet, here I am giving this game a positive recommendation, and that's all due to mods.
I've tried Misery, and as much as I loved how it made the game considerably harder, I got the feeling attempting my first playthrough this way was a mistake, so I'm back to vanilla for now. However, not too long ago I learned of Call of Chernobyl, and holy hell did that save this game for me. Add to it the add-ons from DoctorX (Questline, Faction Relations, and Dynamic Faction Relations), and I'm now going through what I had hoped this game would have been. I'm a Stalker again. I'm a Loner. My motives are my own, and I do what I must to survive. That is why CoP still gets a recommendation from me.
...Oh, and speaking of CoC, I'm currently in a playthrough in which Duty and Freedom have declared an alliance.

After playing Sonic Mania on console, I didn't mind repurchasing it on Steam for ease of use on my laptop. This was hindered when I learned that there was an additional DRM (on top of Steam) being added to the game called Denuvo. I think it is quite redundant to apply a second layer of DRM to a game that is already locked behind Steam.
As for the game itself, the new levels really shine through. It is nice playing the classic levels from my childhood, but playing the new levels leave me wishing that there were more included.
Until the DRM issues are cleared up though, I cannot recommend the game and advise anyone to purchase it on console if possible instead.
I tried it, but I didn't care too much for it. Trying it doesn't cost you anything, though.

Gameplay:
You play as a land-holding individual (The game only let you play as European feudal lord when it first came out, but now you can play as other characters suchs as nomad, tribal leaders and such), and the goal of the game is the survival of your family name until 1453 AD. Nothing is off-limit when it comes to survival. While you are likely to survive by being content as a minor figure in the world, your chance of survival greatly increases as you wage war, forming alliance through marriage, plotting the demise of your rivals, and use everything to your advantage, even yourself.
The game gives you plenty of tools to achieve your goal, and it also throws countless monkey wrenches to destroy your scheme. While the game could get slow from plotting all the action, it speeds up ones you, or your rivals are ready to make the move, so savor those slow moments.
Music & Sound: Since I mentioned you will be waiting a lot before you make your move, you'll be hearing a lot of those. There are many good tracks even without the DLCs, and the DLC tracks just gives you more flavor as you move out of Europe.
Graphic: Good enough. You can see where you are going, and you can see what your character looks like. It is interesting to see the world changes itself in different seasons, and how your character grow old. It's the little flavors in the game that makes the graphic, not the shiny trinkets.
Replayability: There are thousands of characters to choose from, with different culture, religion, regional interest, potential disaster to face. You will be well into hundreds of hours and still not understand the game fully. Plus, they are still releasing new DLCs to enrich the game experience.
Do I recommend it? Oh yes. A game that mends history and strategy together will always get a yes from me.

The good:  A very polished game, stunning graphics, voice acting, drop in-out co-op, multiple paths, re-play off the chain.  Game Master is a legitimate contender for Roll20 and like web sites for RPGs. They should try and copy what this game has done, but with more of a D&D rule system.
The bad:  If you like the PC doing the random save versus spells, you will not like the Magic and Physical armor combat.  This is not D&D rules.  Combat will always come down to keeping your armor up while trying to strip the enemies and using a bundle of crowd control to keep them from attacking you. I wish enemies scaled to your level. Example, if you fight hard enemies of superior level early, you will have a great challenge and might have to do multiple re-loads to win…BUT later you go to areas you missed or should have hit earlier and completely walk over the enemies who are of lower level.
The mix:  Once you understand the game mechanics and accept them, you begin to understand how to win battles against superior AI opponents through solid strategy.
The meh: The PC AI is hit or miss.  While there are times the AI does smart counters to your efforts, often it is the AI’s lack of intelligence that allows you to overcome those odds and cheapens the victory.
I can boast that I finished the game and will likely do multiple runs. Second, I have completed a lavish GM campaign that I will post in the workshop, so I have a complete understanding of the game.  Lastly, I’ve been gaming since pong…need I say more?
Final thought:  If you want to experience everything this game has to offer, it would take multiple play throughs…some might see this as good, while others will see it as just too much an investment.  With GM mode I give this game an 9/10, without it an 8.

I think the first thing I should mention is the enormous Elephant in the room, Denuvo DRM, yes it does include it, and it seriously fudging sucks, Sega are cretins for forcing this upon us, and if this is enough to warrant a boycot in your eyes then please do so.
Having said that though, if you do that, you're missing out on one of the greatest Sonic games since Sonic Generations, and in my honest opinion, this is so much better it's not even funny.
The soundtrack is glorious, including some of my favourite pieces from past games, Chemical Plant? Oh yes please. Green Hill? Absolutely devine. But it doesn't just include classics, it has some new tracks, which, while they don't quite have that punch of the classics, they're still bloody brilliant, the soundtrack alone is worth the price of admission.
But the real meat of a Sonic game is how it plays, and in this regard, it's perfect, the characters all move exactly as they're supposed to, this is no Sonic 4, this is proper 2D Sonic, with razor sharp movement, fast gameplay and the kind of precision that you'd expect from a laser, Christian Whitehead and the rest of his team have done a phenominal job in this regard, it plays like all the best parts of Sonic 2 and S3&K, and I can't think of any praise higher than that.
In regards to bugs, I have had exactly one, I managed to get stuck in a piece of scenery in Act 1 of Titanic Monarch Zone, but other than that, the game has been rock solid, and while YMMV in this, I feel confident in saying that this game is Sega's most stable release in at least a decade, perhaps even 2.
The only criticsms I can lay at the game aside from the Denuvo nonsense is the level design has some weak areas, some of the levels don't flow quite as nicely as they should, for example Green Hill has been reimagined, and includes some new areas that really slow Sonic down , and jar badly with my memories of Green Hill, but I would imagine that once you get used to the level design and find optimal routes, this will cease to be an issue, but it is still something to be aware of, the other criticsm I have is that some of the levels are very busy, too busy in fact, and seeing exactly what is and isn't ground you can run on, and spotting enemies can get frustrating at times.
If you're expecting a long game, deep story and more than just running, jumping and collecting rings and Emeralds, then sorry, you've come to the wrong place, but if you really want classic Sonic and a proper sequel to S3&K, then you'll feel right at home, the is everything I have wanted from a Sonic game since S3&K, and while it does have its issues, it's a glorious comeback for the blue blur.
All I hope is that Sega will patch Denuvo out, because for me, that is the only sticking point, it shouldn't be included, we have Steam for DRM, legitimate buyers shouldn't be punished with more DRM, especially as draconian as Denuvo is.
I think that I'll be spending the next 25 years playing Sonic Mania, just as I did with Sonic 2, and if that doesn't tell you just how much I love this game despite its flaws, then nothing else will, it's a gorgeous, fast paced blast from the past, and takes me back to my childhood, and that was what I wanted from Sonic, and that is what I got today, and I couldn't be happier.
P.S. Tails' animations are absolutely adorable, seriously, he is so cute.
Edit!
Super Tails is available in the game! I am incredibly happy about that, although he doesn't have his flickies with him, which has nerfed his power considerably, although it's been long enough without Super Tails in a Sonic Game that I'm happy that he was even included in the first place.

This game is incredible.  Easily one of the best games I have ever played.

The freedom to create different outcomes in this game is unparalleled.  it is truly a DnDers wet dream.  It feels like most NPCs have some sort of quest, with a variety of different outcomes, and your decision will affect the game down the road.  For example I restarted the first act a couple times to experiment with different builds and each playthrough was completely different.  Whether it be companions and their effect on the game (ahem.. Sebille), NPC interactions that change dependent on your race, persuasion skill, and traits like scholar, jester, etc, or battle strategies.  Everything has this deep level of variability that makes the game highly replayable.
The game has a bit of an inverse difficulty curve in that the beginning can be VERY hard (especially on tactician mode) because you are more limited in your spells and abilities.  There is a great workaround, though, in that you are usually free to challenge higher level enemies than yourself, and even enemies 1-2 levels above you can make battles very difficult.  The depth of the combat is extremely rewarding, but the pace can be slow, which I have no problem with.  Many things must be taken into consideration: turn order, enemy resistances, high ground, and a huge variety of environmental effects that you can manipulate to your advantage.  Cast a rain spell to make puddles -> electrify the puddles with electric discharge -> shoot the electric puddle with a steamcloud arrow to create an electrified steamcloud -> move the electrified steamcloud onto a group of enemies with terrain transmutation -> condense the steamcloud with pressure spike for more damage.  There are so many more combinations like this it's incredible.  You really start to feel powerful as you level up and are able to synergise more skills together.

Builds are very important in this game, if your characters don't synergise and you start throwing your skills into unneeded areas the game will become nearly impossible, inversely, it is definitely possible to break the game with insanely overpowered builds and exploits that make battles trivial.

Overall I think this game is better than D:OS1, and there are a couple big differences:
-The story is much better
-Much less control over AP, I disliked this at first, but it really makes combat more difficult and tactical
-No more DnD style saving throws, all characters now have physical and magical armor which block those respective statuses. Makes the game a bit more predictable, as you can't inflict statuses until armor is depleted
-crafting is much less useful, one of my only complaints about the game, it's not worth it to craft weapons or armor anymore, stuff you find will be much, much better

Combined with the previous chapter, this is one of the absolute best games I've ever played. Gorgeous soundtrack, an aesthetic that has resisted aging, and a plotline that stays engaging throughout, along with a basically grind-free gameplay arc and some really interesting mechanics - these things are all well and good, but it's the writing (and localisation!) that take the crown. For a jRPG villain to monologue usually means switching off your brain for five minutes while they babble some incoherent Babby's First Negative Utilitarianism half-baked philosophy, and conversely the heroes' response is typically pretty vacuous as well. Not so here, to say the least. And in every scene, there'll be some character saying something that's just *phrased right*, in some hard to define way, and it makes you smile or laugh or cry along with them.
This game takes the jRPG genre's flaws - edgy protagonists with dark pasts, settings that seem confused about whether to be sci-fi or fantasy, daft plotlines that take forever to get anywhere - and doesn't so much refute them as forgive them, accepting that they're going to do those things and then showing how they can be done right and more than right. Given that this is also in a sense a large part of what happens in-game, I think it's safe to call this one of the great reconstructions.
It's not often you see a game this good. Play this series.

It keeps you playing because it never takes it away in the first place, and the very lush visuals.
Gameplay is paced with a sense of exploration and tactic choices in combat, you can simply run in and try to shoot everything but that is simply the choice of the player. Capsized gives you options in how to approach combat with assortment of weapons or even better yet, clever use of physics to drop or even projectile heavy objects.
With only a crew of two who made this game the attention to details are massive in both visuals and the super responsive controls.

The game is early access. Expect many, many, many, many, many bugs.
Game used to be great but with the addition of these -gamebreaking- bugs - it has become relatively unplayable.
Somethings to expect:
[BOW DEATH]
- Your bow sometimes will no longer fire arrows. When this happens, it will no longer fire arrows until you do one of these two things:
1) Accept this, use another weapon instead until you die. It will then fix itself.
2) Accept this, switch to melee stance by equiping your sword&shield (or just two melee items in either hand) then switch back to bow&arrow - This will allow you to fire a single arrow then you need to repeat the process to fire another and so on.
[COMMS DEATH]
- The game likes to interfere with comms related programs like Discord, Teamspeak, etc. Your mic suddenly stops detecting audio as a combination of being used at the same time as Conan Exiles. This is due to the in-built voice communications program that can never be disabled. I attempted already to remove the key to use the voice program but it makes no difference. Your comms will be fine and then randomly, just stops detecting audio on these programs.
[BEDSPAWN DEATH]
- Bedspawns [Game-Breaking]. You can try and register your location at bedspawns and about 70% of the time, it'll register it. There are three errors related to this;
1) If your bed is moved, or registered by another player - even if you re-register it to yourself, it will not re-register. Instead, when you die - it'll count as if you haven't registered a bed, in which some mad crazy decision by the developers of this game, instead of implementing a /base /home or some other kind of command, you spawn to the south of the map. My base isn't even too far away from the base but the repeated long travel there is enough to make you eventually just uninstall the game.
2) If you die by falling and land on an odd piece of badly programmed terrain (pretty much anytime you die by falling and don't land on directly flat land, which lets face it - most falling deaths are from climbing and running out of your ridiculously fast depleting stamina bar) - your bed for some reason doesn't count and you spawn back at the beginning of the map down the south and have to run back.
3) Sometimes, for no reason other than I guess just bad programming - your bed just doesn't register anyway because, why not? In these instances you again have to run back from the start zone.
[MOB DEATH]
Firstly the mechanics that have been changed make the game 'stupid' in some occasions. For some reason, they've tinkered with the stamina bar, this now depletes rapidly quickly and makes no sense whatsoever as this makes things unnecessarily difficult when it comes to climbing and some combat stunts. In a saving grace, the AI is programmed badly - jump on even the slightest, smallest rock or hide inside the doorway of your base and enemy AI suddenly panics and just stops, or repeatedly attacks the frame of the door rather than entering (Yes, this means you can simply climb a ledge and even take down elephants with arrows while it sits there and stares at you blindly....) And if you find that combatting AI can be rather (what's a word that means easier than fighting a lamppost?) - then you can also have an even easier time fighting enemies when mobs glitch through the world and get 50% of their body stuck in the terrain immobilising them in place - although don't expect loot from these mobs because on death, they simply fall through the world - never to be seen again until they respawn.
[BRAIN DEATH]
The frustration behind these 'newly developed errors' (None of these existed in the earliest form of this game I played) is that they really mask the enjoyment the game begins. The game was actually fun, it did actually have a lot going for it but I hadn't played it in a long-time and came back because I heard they updated it. These updates (which triggered everything mentioned above) - have ruined the game. I wish they would fix these errors and many many more. These are just the ones that come to mind. A tip if you attempt to play this game - Pick Set as a religion. Any other religion will mean insta-death if you fight anything with poison for too long (Too long being anything longer than 3 seconds).

My Grandfather smoked his whole life. I was about 10 years old when my mother said to him, 'If you ever want to see your grandchildren graduate, you have to stop immediately.'. Tears welled up in his eyes when he realized what exactly was at stake. He gave it up immediately. Three years later he died of lung cancer. It was really sad and destroyed me. My mother said to me- 'Don't ever smoke. Please don't put your family through what your Grandfather put us through." I agreed. At 23, I have never touched a cigarette. I must say, I feel a very slight sense of regret for never having done it, because this game gave me cancer anyway.

While I feel the first chapter of this game was slightly better, this is still a very very good game.
There was not much change from the first game; combat, gameplay, and story were similar.  Once again the characters steal the show, as they expand on everyone's characteristics, background, everything really.  The amount of detail put into characters like Agate, Kloe, Tita, Olivier, Schera, Zane, etc is something I wish more games did because it helps get you invested into the game and the story.  They are very easy to relate to since everybody has their strengths and their flaws, like we all do irl.  Of course the game revolves around Estelle and Joshua, both of which really get expanded roles since they are away from each other for an extended time, and helps the player really get to know who they are, almost like you're walking alongside them.  And that reunion, my God, that reunion I had such high hopes for and it did not disappoint at all.  Very powerful moment.  That whole Estelle-Joshua relationship really felt special to me.  With characters like these, it makes the game so rewarding to play, because you want to learn more and you want to experience more, just for the sake of the characters alone.
But the reason I praise the characters so highly, is because the game fell short in a couple of ways.  First the story, while good, felt forced near the end, sometimes lost focus, and was at times not paced very well.  At the end I basically willed my way through the final dungeon without paying much attention.  When I played the first game, I tried to complete as much as possible, and it took me 50 hours, but the story gripped me.  This time, same approach, and the hours jumped to 73 hours, and I felt the game could have kept the story untouched but still shaved 15-20 hours of extra stuff that didnt need to be there.  I didnt change anything  I did from the first game; I didnt really grind, I did as many sidequests as I found.  I also thought that the final boss was a little generic for this game's standards.
Finally, I have to give a tip of the cap for the treasure chests.  Its not only clever, I was rolling on a few of them.  The Monty Python references made me die laughing.  Just watch the sketch that got referenced by the one German speaking chest.  Its a little touch, but it shows me that they take the time to really care about making sure every part of the game was up to par.  And as a gamer, I appreciate that effort.
If you're prepared to put time in, play this game.  The character work alone makes it rewarding.

This is a fun survival builder game.
Usually in games like this one eating, drinking and repairing equipment become more onerous than fun for me. In this game food is easy to get and has about a half hour spoil rate (depending). Even at low levels you can make a water skin with multiple uses, alleviating the tediousness of simply staying alive.
Another thing I usually dislike about games of this genre  is the difficulty in reading enemy movements and visualizing where their attack hitboxes are. I like playing ranged characters (due to the dislike of repairing armor) but games like this usually force you into melee combat because it takes longer to kill enemies than the time it takes them to reach you.
One of the revolutionary aspects of this game is the ability to climb. Being able to climb up cliffs/columns and snipe enemies from long range with a bow helps with survivability and allows me to fight enemies without worrying about repairing armor all the time. Because I usually play games with the bow, the combat is a lot like Skyrim, minus the stealth. To make up for the lack of stealth though I just usually hit enemies from far enough away not to aggro them, or climb up to a vantage point where the melee combatants can't hit me. Yes there are ranged enemies that can still hit you, but the flight of their projectiles are easy to see and can be dodged.  There is a dodge function that can be used to evade enemy attacks. I use it when surprised by a melee combatant or when I'm in locations where close combat is harder to avoid (like in caves). Enemy attacks are easy enough to read that dodging the attack is entirely feasible and makes the combat more enjoyable.
As for repairing gear, you can tame/enslave special npcs and attach them to your crafting stations to reduce the cost/time/effort put into repairing said gear.
Being a ranged fighter there is one annoying glitch that finally convinced me to put on some armor. (For the longest time I was just running around in the default family friendly loincloth). Enemies that hit you stagger you unless your poise is high enough (the poise stat coming from wearing armor), and if an enemy hits you while you're drawing back your bow or if you roll while drawing back your bow, an arrow gets eternally stuck in your hand. Relogging or dying fixes the glitch, but for a perfectionist like me it is super annoying!
Avoiding armor also makes surviving the harsh weather conditions next to impossible. Can't say how many times I died to heatstroke before I found that drinking cools you off. Haven't been to the winter zone yet. I imagine a loincloth there won't be feasible either.
The game has some fun weather. When it rains, everything gets wet and it's sorta peaceful. When a sandstorm blows, it's friggin' awesome. Night time has a short time of pitch black which is all kinds of exiting.
The building in this game is really easy and intuitive as well. A lot of games have issues with placing foundations, walls, stairs and other parts into existing terrain, but this game allows placement of said building parts with relative ease. I did notice that you can't place angled walls into the ground (I was trying to snap one to the underside of a stairway halfway stuck in the ground to close it off), but placing them into terrain walls is no problem. So while there are limitations in the building, it is by far the most terrain friendly system I've worked with in this genre.
The character models are great and there are lots of emotes you can find across the map. The female walking animation (which plays while encumbered or when toggled) is a bit assymetric as one arm swings way more than the other. Besides that the animations are really fun and well done.
For a game in beta it's a really good game. The climbing and ease of building into existing terrain are probably the highlights for me, and the arrow glitch is prolly the low. I don't know if I mentioned the arrow glitch yet. An arrow gets stuck in your hand. And doesn't dissapear! It just stays there forever. And doesn't go away. Unless you relog (which I've done so many times), or unless you die (which I try to avoid).
Great game overall.

I feel like TES games got smaller each time, slowly cutting out elements that were big for long-time fans, but would not appeal to a larger casual market (where Bethesda would make the most money). With that said, Oblivion was probably the last TES game that had a fair amount of depth in its lore, story, character building, dialogue, etc... Compared to Skyrim, it’s a lot cluckier, messier, unbalanced and a complete pain in the butt to deal with at times but it’s all these 'difficulties' that make it worth your while. There is a whole lot more here to offer a person looking to dedicate many hours into a highly detailed RPG. You don’t just pick up great gear and one shot enemies with your bow, you struggle to defeat even the most basic creatures, spam the space bar everywhere you go to level up acrobatics, and in short, you are forced to WORK for your rewards; which in turn make you actually feel like all your efforts meant more than just fiddling with a super basic child's puzzle in a dungeon and then receiving a high damage fire inflicting sword.
Don’t get turned off just because this game is a lot more challenging and requires more work. If you're a filthy casual, turn away, but if you want to set your feet deep into a colourful yet dark world with a meaningful story that'll have you struggling to become a champion yet really feel like one after all the work-  This game, without a doubt, needs to be in your library.

Pretty cool indi game that takes 3-4 hours to finish the campain solo.  Its a bit of a throwback in turns of gameplay since it fits in the 2D metroidvania style.  I found the controls to work pretty well, although they do not allow for precise control, but more of a sliding control.  I did not find this game difficult - 7 of the 12 levels I beat without dying.  Basically this game you wonder around the level doing whatever task you are assigned.  Make it to the exit, collect something, kill something, ect.  The early levels are short and the last few levels take 20+ mins.  I enjoy using the guns since each level has a ton of them and no reason to save them.  Some of the bosses are interesting.  I found myself only able to play this for about an hour at a time, not sure why... I assume its because I was uninterested in the slow controls on what could be fast combat.

This little platform game hit me by surprise when I first got my hands on it. The gameplay is simple in principle, but becomes loads of fun when you start getting the hang of it. You actually work your way to survival by utilizing physics and insane space technology, while battling it out against hordes of nasty alien creatures that want you off their planet - you and your fellow marooned space men. The controls are easy and very precise, while the graphics are gorgeous 2d art. The music is some kind of techno trance that works quite well here. There are several game modes besides the campain too, including bot matches, survival and multiplayer for extra value. And it also comes with steam achievements and a low price...Granted the campaign might be somewhat short and the general idea won't allow tons of gameplay depth, but it is a game that succeeds to offer what it is supposed to : a great platformer and a quick time waster fix.
Verdict : Great actually! 8/10

Capsized is amazingly fun for people with refined reflexes. Between the gravity ram propelling yourself 2 screens over, the grappling hook with great physics (not just for going over pits), the jetpack, and super-simple wall jumping, you get a ton of movement options all the time. Mix in the 8 guns, with different ranges and all of them have an alt-fire, and I found my self committing genocide on every level for fun.
The music is fantastic for the world, and is seamlessly sown together. Made me think back to Mass Effect 1, while I explored for hidden passages and stared whimsically at docile space-bugs.
The main campaign is rather short (2.5~ hours if you rush everything and don't explore at all), but there are several of different modes and coop (which I've yet to try, boo.) Overall, a very fulfilling experience.

This game is amazing.  Its is reminiscent of the 90's era where platforming games like Jazz Jackrabbit and Commander Keen were a solid example of great gameplay.  However, Capsized comes with a new array of features which makes every level a blast to play.
I beat the single player Campaign in 3 hours.  Its fairly short with about 12 levels, but extremely fun and somewhat challenging.  There are hidden secrets in each level as well as 3 difficulties.  If you're going for achievements and whatnot, I'd say the game's length would be about 5 hours.
The levels start small but get huge, with plenty of exploration and a plethora of weapons to use against the planet natives.  Though I won't call them 'puzzles', there is a multitude of challenging scenarios which you will have to use your brain in order to solve.
The developers really put some artistic talent into this game.  Each level is a work of art and the music is awesome.
Definitely worth its price in gold.
